headline: Detroit Red Wings Dylan Larkin, Lucas Raymond headed to 4 Nations Face-Off tournament
fullText:
Two of the Detroit Red Wings' top players will be busy come February.

Dylan Larkin made the cut for the U.S. squad, while Lucas Raymond made the Swedish one ,both of which will take part in the 4 Nations Face-Off tournament that this season replaces the NHL All-Star Game.

Larkin was named to the American team Wednesday evening, several hours after Raymond was named to Team Sweden.

The U.S., Sweden, Canada and Finland will compete in the event to be held Feb. 12-20 in Montreal and Boston. Each team will play three games, with the top two teams playing a winner-take-all finale. Teams are made up entirely of NHL players.

THE NEW KID: Top goalie prospect Sebastian Cossa excited to 'live this lifestyle' on Red Wings

That Raymond would make the Swedish team was a given, but Larkin withstood competition from a tremendously deep forward group vying to represent the U.S. Larkin is having a good season, though, with 12 goals and eight assists in 25 games. And, while this is an NHL event, Larkin has represented his country at the World Championship in 2015, '16, '17, '18 and '19.

The rest of the U.S. team features forwards Matt Boldy, Kyle Connor, Jack Eichel, Jake Guentzel, Jack Hughes, Chris Kreider, Auston Matthews, J.T. Miller, Brock Nelson, Brady Tkachuk, Matthew Tkachuk andVincent Trocheck; defensemen Brock Faber, Adam Fox, Noah Hanifin, Quinn Hughes (Michigan), Charlie McAvoy, Jacob Slavin and Zach Werenski; and goaltenders Connor Hellebuyck (Commerce), Jake Oettinger and Jeremy Swayman.

Goaltender Cam Talbot was having a good season before suffering a lower-body injury last weekend, but Canada went with Jordan Binnington, Adin Hill and Sam Montembault.

headline: Belleville's Bryce Underwood, Elijah Dotson set lofty goals after signing to Michigan
fullText:
The man of the hour at Belleville High School arrived at the school cafeteria dressed for the occasion, ready for the attention.

Five-star Belleville quarterback Bryce Underwood showed up to the school's signing day event for all seven seniors going to the next level rocking a blue Michigan sweatsuit and diamond Cartier glasses. He was met by a packed room anxious to see him sign with Michigan football during the early signing period.

"It's just a blessing," Underwood said. "A blessing I've been working for my whole life."

Underwood and four-star safety Elijah Dotson made it official with the Wolverines on Wednesday afternoon, along with five teammates headed elsewhere. Underwood and Dotson signed the papers just after 5:30 p.m., joining the Wolverines' 2025 recruiting class.

CLASS OF 2025: Meet Michigan football's top-10 recruiting class, highlighted by QB Bryce Underwood

Underwood's commitment marks the first milestone recruiting win for Michigan head coach Sherrone Moore and his staff. Underwood is ranked as the No. 1 overall prospect and quarterback in the 2025 class, per 247 Sports' composite rankings, and flipped his commitment to Michigan in mid-November after spending most 2024 verbally committed to LSU.

He said he decided to commit to Michigan when it came down to what would help his family the most.

"Honestly, when I had to figure out where my perspective was on everything that will help my family out the most," he said of when Michigan came back into the picture. "And also, me knowing that I got to go to school as well."

Underwood said Michigan's standing as an academic school helped sway his decision and declined later to answer a question about the school's NIL push. He also said the attention from Michigan alumni such as Tom Brady was "nice", but he was more focused on the academic aspects.

"Honestly, school," Underwood said when asked why Michigan was the right fit. "School is a big thing as well. My education is everything and also me pushing my hometown school, my hometown big college, to the next level and to a couple of national championships."

IN HIS OWN WORDS: I'm Bobby Kanka. Here's why I signed to Michigan football 2025 recruiting class

He didn't have an interest in tamping down expectations, doubling down on the goals of leading Michigan to the national championship.

"Yessir (that's the goal), definitely," Underwood said. "No question."

Underwood is the second No. 1 overall consensus player to join the Wolverines, following edge Rashan Gary (2016), and is the program’s highest-rated quarterback commit in the modern recruiting era (2002). Underwood is expected to be Michigan's long-term solution at quarterback after the Wolverines struggled in 2024 with Davis Warren, Jack Tuttle and Alex Orji splitting time.

But Underwood is just focused on what he can control when he starts at the next level. He and Dotson both graduate from Belleville on Dec. 19 and are planning to enroll immediately at Michigan for spring practices. Asked about the change at offensive coordinator, Underwood said that was the coach's decision, not his, and also said it is not up to him if Michigan decides to add another quarterback through the transfer portal.

"I'm willing to do whatever it takes to be the best," Underwood said.

At 6 feet 5 and 200 pounds, Underwood is a true dual-threat quarterback who consistently showed an ability to deliver accurate passes at all three levels with Belleville, while shouldering a considerable load in the zone-read running game. He led Belleville to consecutive Division 1 state championships as a freshman and sophomore and finished as the school's record holder for passing yards and touchdowns while compiling a 50-4 record.

"I'm ready to bring my talents, my athleticism that I'm capable of bringing to the next level," Underwood said.

A LATE ADD: Michigan football adds DL Travis Moten to 2025 recruiting class on early signing day

Underwood's mom, Beverly, said the most memorable moments of her son's recruiting process were his ability to stay focused and humble despite all of the outside noise, growing into a man capable of handling the outsized attention. She said her advice to him was to follow his heart and he ultimately made the decision to flip to Michigan himself.

"It would have to be academics, where you can fit in, where you see yourself for the next three to four years, where he can make a big impact," Beverly said of her advice to her son.

After they were done speaking to the media, Underwood and Dotson waited to take pictures and sign autographs for the dozens of supporters. Underwood said he will be bringing his fans to Michigan as he tries to help the Wolverines get back to regularly competing for national titles.

"More than likely, record breaking, honestly," Underwood said of his expectations for college. "Just doing what I'm supposed to do and what I have been doing throughout my whole life."

Elijah Dotson wants to be the next great Michigan DB

Dotson only played one season with Underwood after transferring to Belleville for his senior season. The Detroit native started at U-D Jesuit and showed up to his signing wearing an homage to his new school and home city — an identical sweatsuit to Underwood'sm with gold and navy blue Cartier buffs. It was a signature Detroit look — and also the turnover prop for the Wolverine defense he's joining.

"It's a Detroit thing, you know I had to rock out with the Buffs," Dotson told the Free Press before signing.

Dotson is a four-star safety and rated as the No. 2 recruit in Michigan, behind his quarterback, for the 2025 class. He originally committed to Pittsburgh in May, but flipped his decision to Michigan just days before Underwood followed.

"It started with the new staff coming in at Michigan to build that relationship with the new staff," Dotson said of his process. "But once I got that relationship, I know that's what I wanted to do — stay home. I have a great relationship with the new staff. Great men, great coaches."

Dotson played both defensive back and wide receiver for Belleville. He was a downfield receiving threat and also played both cornerback and safety in the Tigers' secondary. He is locked into playing safety at Michigan and is eager to carry on the Wolverines' tradition of great defensive backs, mentioning following in the footsteps of cornerback Will Johnson — a fellow Detroiter — and safety Makari Paige.

"One of the best DBs to ever come out of Michigan, that's my goal," Dotson said. "I'm going to work to get to that goal and it's going to happen."

Jared Ramsey is a sports reporter for the Detroit Free Press. Follow Jared on X @jared_ramsey22, and email him at jramsey@freepress.com.

headline: Detroit Tigers' Tarik Skubal elected to MLB Players Association executive subcommittee
fullText:
Detroit Tigers left-hander Tarik Skubal has become a key member of the MLB players' union leadership.

Skubal — the winner of the 2024 American League Cy Young Award — was elected Wednesday to a two-year term as one of eight players on the Major League Baseball Players Association executive subcommittee. He is one of six newcomers.

Player representatives from each of the 30 MLB teams voted on the leadership positions. Right-hander Casey Mize is the Tigers' player representative.

BEFORE BASEBALL: Once upon a time, Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal dreamed of playing Division III basketball

There are four types of roles within the MLBPA's eight-player executive subcommittee. Skubal is one of two alternate pension committee representatives, alongside Baltimore Orioles outfielder Cedric Mullins.

The other six members of MLBPA leadership: Texas Rangers second baseman Marcus Semien (association player rep), Toronto Blue Jays right-hander Chris Bassitt (association player rep), San Diego Padres infielder Jake Cronenworth (alternate association player rep), Pittsburgh Pirates right-hander Paul Skenes (association player rep), Cincinnati Reds left-handed reliever Brent Suter (pension committee rep) and Tampa Bay Rays right-hander Pete Fairbanks (pension committee rep).

Semien and Suter are returning members, but the other six players are new to the committee.

There were six players who completed two-year terms: Lance McCullers Jr., Jack Flaherty, Ian Happ, Austin Slater, Francisco Lindor and Lucas Giolito. The departure of those six players created openings for six newcomers, including Skubal.

Skubal, 28, posted a 2.39 ERA with 35 walks and 228 strikeouts across 192 innings in 31 starts in the 2024 season, winning the AL pitching Triple Crown. The former ninth-round draft pick has completed five MLB seasons.

Skubal is set to become a free agent after the 2026 season.

headline: Detroit Pistons blasted early by Boston Celtics, then rally in 130-120 loss
fullText:
For three quarters, the Detroit Pistons went bucket-for-bucket with the defending champs. 

But ultimately, they couldn’t overcome a big deficit. The Pistons fell to the Boston Celtics on the road, 130-120, after their comeback attempt fell short. They trailed 109-89 early in the fourth quarter, but cut it to five with a minute left thanks to strong play from Cade Cunningham and Tobias Harris. 

Cunningham scored eight straight points to lead a 13-4 run that cut the deficit to five, 125-120, with a minute remaining, Harris knocked down the final bucket of the run, a 3-pointer that was the 20th of the night for the Pistons, a season-high. They made more than half of their 39 attempts, shooting 51.3% overall from deep.

The Celtics were also hot from 3, knocking down 21 of 53, and Payton Pritchard’s dagger 3 with 45 seconds left sealed the loss for the Pistons (9-15). Cade Cunningham finished just shy of a triple-double with 27 points, 14 assists and nine rebounds. Harris also scored 27 points, and Malik Beasley added 23. Harris and Beasley each hit six 3-pointers, accounting for more than half of the Pistons’ total. 

NBA CUP: For Detroit Pistons, finale loss to Milwaukee feels like a missed opportunity

Jaylen Brown led the Celtics with 28 points and nine assists, and Kristaps Porzingis added 26 points and nine rebounds. They were without Jayson Tatum and Jrue Holiday, who had right and left knee tendinopathy, respectively. 

The Pistons were without Ausar Thompson due to “medical condition management,” less than two weeks after returning from blood clots. 

Bench, small lineups shift tide for Pistons

The Pistons started the game flat on both ends, and the Celtics pounced, building a 26-7 lead by the midway point of the first quarter. Boston knocked down six 3-pointers in the first six minutes of the game, fueling a 15-3 run that the Pistons ultimately weren’t able to overcome. 

Cunningham picked up two fouls in that stretch, and took a long rest on the bench from the midway points of the first and second quarters. The bench stepped up in his stead. 

Ron Holland was the team’s most alert perimeter defender and had one of his better offensive games of the season. He prevented Brown from taking a wide-open 3, sprinting and arriving in time to block the shot from behind. On the other end, he hit Marcus Sasser with a behind-the-back pass for a 3 from above the arc. 

Beasley got hot early, knocking down back-to-back 3s late in the first period. Sasser was a pest, coming up with seven points and three steals in just seven minutes. The second unit, which also featured Isaiah Stewart and Simone Fontecchio, injected life into a game that appeared to be over early. 

In the fourth quarter, after the Celtics opened a 20-point lead with 10 minutes remaining, the Pistons went ultra small, with their bench joining Cunningham and Harris. Their furious rally followed. The Pistons knocked down five consecutive 3-pointers — three from Beasley and one each from Sasser and Harris — and cut the deficit to six with a 17-3 run. 

The small lineup couldn’t finish the game after Porzingis checked back in, but Bickerstaff might’ve found a spark plug for an offense that, at times, has sagged this season. Sasser finished with 12 points and Holland scored seven with a pair of 3-pointers.

headline: Michigan State basketball clinical in Big Ten opener, crushing Minnesota 90-72 on road
fullText:
MINNEAPOLIS – The defense and rebounding led to running, which in turn led to a big run for Michigan State basketball.

And Coen Carr seemed to be in the middle of it all.

The sophomore delivered a highlight-reel sequence at both ends of the floor with a block, an alley-oop dunk, then a steal and three-point play during a 17-0 run in the first half at Minnesota. That helped the Spartans pull away to open Big Ten play with a resounding 90-72 victory Wednesday night at Williams Arena, avenging a crushing loss here a year ago.

Carr finished with 12 points while seven others scored seven or more points, with Jaxon Kohler putting up an 11-point, 11-rebound double-double. Xavier Booker had eight of his 11 points after halftime, and Jeremy Fears Jr. added 10 points.

The Spartans blew a nine-point lead in the second half and lost to the Gophers, 59-56, in their last visit to The Barn on Feb. 6.

"Every win is a great win" Carr said. "Last (season), we came here, we were up, we got complacent and we lost. But this time, yeah, we had some up-and-down runs during the game. But all in all, we came out and fought and played the whole game.

"So just doing that and knowing that everybody knew to keep the foot on the gas and extend the lead instead of giving it up is great."

MSU (7-2, 1-0 Big Ten) returns home for its second and final league game of 2024 when it hosts Nebraska on Saturday. Tipoff is noon at Breslin Center in East Lansing (BTN).

BIG DAY IN FOOTBALL: Michigan State football flips RB Jace Clarizio back from Alabama in stunning reversal

Dawson Garcia had 18 points and 11 rebounds, while Mike Mitchell Jr. added 17 points and made five 3-pointers for Minnesota (6-4, 0-1).

Returning from Maui feeling good (who wouldn't)?

Minnesota entered as one of the nation’s top defensive teams, allowing just 58.9 points to rank 13th in Division I.

MSU nearly reached that in 20 minutes of basketball.

The Spartans dominated on the boards early, getting 10 of them to the Gophers’ one during their nearly seven-minute, game-swinging run. They went into halftime with 24-8 rebounding edge and 20-10 scoring advantage in the paint.

After opening with a 9-2 lead with its starters, coach Tom Izzo’s reserves struggled initially defensively. The Gophers recovered and took a lead after a Garcia 3-pointer and layup from Parker Fox, making it 14-12 with 12:21 to go in the first half.

That’s when MSU took off.

After a Kohler free throw, Jaden Akins attacked the lane and flipped it to Carr, who had cut baseline, for a dunk in traffic. A pair of Fears free throws followed after a media timeout, leading into maybe Carr’s best sequence as a Spartan.

It started on defense, as Carr spotted Minnesota’s Trey Edmonds out of the corner of his eye delivering a handoff and cutting to the basket. He reacted from his weak-side defending position and retreated into the paint, elevating and leaping with a perfectly-timed swat of the Gophers' dunk attempt.

That got MSU out in transition quickly, and Carr trailed the play in a hurry. Fears weaved up the right wing and sent a lob to the cutting Carr for an alley-oop.

"I was just doing my job," Carr said. "They said the fifth defender was gonna be a big part of the game, so I just tried to come over and help like they told me to. It just happened he was going to dunk it, and I blocked it. And I came down and caught a lob after that. So just bringing energy, playing hard, doing what they need me to do – I'll do anything to help my team win."

Then as play returned over midcourt, Carr plucked the ball away from Mitchell and raced off for a layup, finishing through contact from Mitchell and hitting the ensuing free throw. The fuse was lit for the Spartans' clinching run.

The Spartans poured it on with an Akins 3-pointer off a drive-and-kick from Frankie Fidler, then Tre Holloman hit another after Minnesota’s timeout. The Gophers responded to that one, but MSU would continue to build its lead to 14 after a Szymon Zapala putback and another Carr free throw to take a 42-30 lead into the locker room at half.

"We hadn't been shooting real well, and it was a good game for us to come out of it," Izzo said. "I thought our running game really helped us. We got some open looks, and our running game looked more like old us."

This was pretty basketball

Some of MSU’s biggest problems early in the season got fixed as well.

Outstanding ball movement off dribble-drive penetration led to open looks from 3-point range. Booker benefitted from that with a pair of second-half 3-pointers, and Fidler drained a confidence-building triple with 8:57 to play. Kohler added another late as those three combined for 22 points in the second half. MSU went 7-for-10 from deep after halftime and 11-for-22 from behind the 3-point arc for the game.

The Spartans also dominated on the glass (39-27), particularly early, and ran in transition to a 27-2 advantage, getting 25 assists on their 29 made baskets. Minneapolis native Tre Holloman started his second straight game and had eight points and eight assists, while Fears had five and Jase Richardson four.

"Obviously, the game versus North Carolina, we won and it was a big win. But we still had work to do, we still had stuff we needed to improve on," said Booker, who made three 3-pointers and added two blocks and two rebounds. "So kind of just building day by day, game by game, that's just our mindset with everything. And that's what we did today, we just gotta keep building every game."

Akins and Zapala each finished with nine points, while Fidler had seven. MSU went 21-for-26 at the free-throw line and, after committing seven first-half turnovers, committed just two in the final 22:51 and none in the last 14:15.

Kohler said the way the last visit to Williams Arena ended "was brought up a lot of times in preparation for this game" and played a factor in the push for perfection.

"For all the returners, it really did leave a bad taste in our mouths, and it was a game that we should have won," he said. "Coming back … this was our first game in the Big Ten season. We wanted to come out and make a statement and kind of set the tone for our team. And I feel like we did a good job."

headline: Detroit's Renaissance Center: Historical photos take you back in time
fullText:
Detroit's Renaissance Center, a long-standing piece of the city's skyline, is facing the possibility of demolition under a newly released plan for the struggling set of office towers.

The home of General Motors, the RenCen was first proposed in 1970 by Henry Ford II, who envisioned it as a bold statement of Detroit's resilience and economic potential.

Under the proposed revamp, the tallest tower of the RenCen would stay standing while two others would be demolished, costing an estimated $1.6 billion, including $250 million in public support.

The announcement comes amid reduced demand for downtown office space and as GM prepares to move its headquarters several blocks north, to Dan Gilbert's Hudson’s Detroit development. 

However, days after the newly released plans were made public, the automaker told the Free Press: If General Motors and Gilbert can’t secure the public funding necessary, the automaker is prepared to demolish the five towers it owns and bear the full cost. 

Opinion: As GM prepares to move out, let's be honest: The RenCen is an embarrassment.

headline: Duggan's independent gubernatorial run is rare and untested. Could it work?
fullText:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect the correct number of signatures needed by an independent gubernatorial candidate.

That Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan announced he will seek to become Michigan's governor in 2026 is not surprising. Speculation about a potential run by Duggan was rife even before he said last month he wouldn't seek a fourth term running the state's most-populous city.

But the Wednesday announcement that Duggan — a Democrat who's been a longstanding ally of President Joe Biden — will be running for governor as an independent candidate, did take many political prognosticators in Michigan by surprise. And while it does raise questions about the feasibility of a statewide, independent campaign, given winning political efforts in Michigan have historically been tied to major parties, Duggan's tenure in Detroit and history as a candidate there could make him a formidable challenger for the governor's mansion, even as an independent, analysts say.

Duggan said he was running as an independent because of partisan bickering being an obstacle. "The current system forces people to choose sides — not find solutions," he said in a news release. "It’s time to change that."

There's not a track record of successful statewide campaigns run by independent candidates in Michigan, however.

John Lindstrom, retired publisher of Gongwer Michigan and a longtime member of Michigan's political press corps, noted Duggan's first run for mayor in 2013 was as a write-in candidate, seen at the time as an uphill climb.

"He's obviously surprised us in the past with some unorthodox moves, but independent, that's a whole new game in many respects," said Lindstrom, who is also a contributing columnist for the Detroit Free Press.

Lindstrom said party infrastructure is typically key to building a winning coalition throughout Michigan, given they have existing assets vital to running a campaign. Duggan may have enough cachet to run as an independent in metro Detroit, but areas like Lansing, Grand Rapids, Flint, Saginaw and elsewhere throughout the Great Lakes state are also key to winning statewide.

"Not having a party infrastructure can in fact be a big disadvantage, unless you have the money and individual ability to organize a structure to make up for it," Lindstrom said. He pointed to donor lists, campaign staff and volunteer networks, campaign software and more.

"There's a ton of different things that having access to a party can help," Lindstrom said.

Duggan, 66, is likely better poised to break from having party backing than typical independent candidates. He has a history of being a capable fundraiser, routinely outpacing challengers during his reelection campaigns in Detroit. And Bill Ford Jr., executive chair of Ford Motor Co., announced in a news release Wednesday he was endorsing Duggan's campaign, a sign of support from a major figure in Michigan's automotive industry.

Adrian Hemond, CEO of Lansing-based consulting firm Grassroots Midwest, said Duggan is uniquely positioned to run as an independent. He can point to accomplishments during his mayoral tenure like less violent crime in Detroit and, for the first time in decades, the city seeing population growth, Hemond said.

"For Mike Duggan, it's a smart move," Hemond said. "I wouldn't recommend this to any other candidate, but I think it makes a lot of sense for Duggan."

Hemond also noted that by not entering the Democratic primary, Duggan won't have to appeal to the party's base in Michigan as early as other Democratic candidates, and instead can pitch himself as a moderate. Duggan's presence in the race also could be problematic for Republican candidates, given they'll need to win over swing voters as well.

"I think that a Duggan candidacy is going to make the Democratic and Republican candidates in the November election in 2026 look more extreme, because there's not going to be as much room to tack towards the center if Mike Duggan has been out campaigning and securing those votes for more than a year and a half before they start pivoting towards those voters," he said.

Matt Grossmann, director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University, said Duggan enters the race with considerably more name recognition and political cachet than the typical independent or third-party candidate.

"He has both money and media attention, which are both things independent candidates typically lack," Grossmann said. "Usually you wouldn't have an independent candidate be the early-announce candidate."

Duggan is the first major candidate to enter the 2026 race, although there's been speculation about who else could jump into the fray. Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II, Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson and U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, who lives in Traverse City, among others, have all been raised as potential Democratic candidates. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat who's handily won both her gubernatorial campaigns, will exit due to term limits.

Although there haven't been as many names bandied about on the Republican side, the GOP could have a crowded primary field, as it did in 2022.

Duggan's departure from the Democratic field does remove a major player from the party's primary, Grossmann added, making the field slightly less challenging for others. Polling will shape how candidates, Duggan included, proceed in the race, he said, noting U.S. Sen. Krysten Sinema, of Arizona, ended her reelection bid as an independent after polling found her trailing both the Democratic and Republican candidates.

Benson appeared to react to Duggan's announcement, posting on X "I’m proud to be a Democrat" after news broke of Duggan leaving the party.

To get on the ballot, state law requires gubernatorial candidates to submit at least 12,000 valid signatures. That figure is likely attainable for Duggan, although recent gubernatorial and congressional campaigns have been upended in Michigan due to signature scandals.

There isn't much history of independent gubernatorial candidates succeeding in statewide elections in Michigan — the last candidate to win on a ticket that wasn't Democratic or Republican was William Woodbridge, a Whig who was in office in 1840-41 before leaving to become a U.S. senator. Josiah Williams Begole won election in 1883 as a "fusionist" candidate on the Democratic ticket, as well, but he's the last candidate to become governor of Michigan without running on a strictly Democratic or Republican campaign. In a two-party system, independent candidates haven't routinely fared well throughout the U.S., analysts said.

But the timing of Duggan's decision to run as an independent is notable. Democrats are on the heels of an adverse November election, losing the White House to former President Donald Trump. Throughout the U.S. and in Michigan, pundits and Democratic figures themselves have said the party needed to do better with working-class and blue-collar voters. Duggan can pursue those voters from the jump, Hemond said.

"Mayor Duggan has a story to tell," Hemond said. "He's got a story to tell those voters, and it's exactly on point with the issues voters were telling pollsters and the media were most important to them in this election cycle. It's crime, it's jobs and the economy, housing. He's got a story to tell in Detroit about all of those issues."

Michigan's next gubernatorial election won't be decided until November 2026, but Duggan is the first major player to officially enter the fray.

headline: Focus: HOPE seeks volunteers to deliver food to 1,500 low-income seniors
fullText:
The nonprofit Focus: HOPE is looking for volunteers to deliver food to hundreds of seniors across metro Detroit on one Saturday later this month.

This year, the Detroit-based organization is expanding its annual holiday delivery efforts to include 100 more seniors, up from 1,400 the year before. On Dec. 21, volunteers will deliver holiday-themed food boxes to low-income seniors who are struggling to afford the basics in Oakland, Wayne, Macomb and Washtenaw counties.

"The seniors in our food program are making some extremely difficult decisions with their money every month," said Rachel Sherman, manager of the volunteer department at Focus: HOPE. "They're deciding between purchasing food or purchasing medication. They're deciding between purchasing food or paying a phone bill or their electricity bill."

The senior holiday delivery is expanding to 1,500 recipients this year because Focus: HOPE has additional federal money for its food program, Sherman said. It's timely because the need for food assistance continues among seniors.

The senior holiday delivery is a part of Focus: HOPE's Food for Seniors program, which provides monthly food boxes to more than 42,000 seniors in nine Michigan counties, from Wayne to Huron. Those packages typically include produce, grains, milk and cheese. The upcoming special deliveries are geared toward the holidays, offering cake mix, frosting, cornbread and a frozen turkey, alongside fresh produce and shelf stable items. Recipients were randomly selected for the special deliveries from Focus: HOPE's Food for Seniors program.

"It's really nice to be able to give them this additional holiday box and use this money for that because it's something that they want. It's not something that they're just needing to survive," Sherman said.

More: Detroit kids spot themselves in vibrant new mural celebrating African-forward culture

More: The right athletic program makes a difference for kids with special needs

Focus: HOPE is looking for about 150 more people to join the 500 volunteers needed to get the job done. Volunteers can make food deliveries, load cars or direct traffic on site. Deliveries run from 8 a.m. to 10 a.m. on Dec. 21.

Interested volunteers must sign up by going to www.bit.ly/fHshD24. For questions, call Focus: HOPE at 313-494-4270 or email volunteer@focushope.edu. The deadline to register to volunteer is Dec. 17.

headline: Can Wenceel Pérez become super utility player? Here's what Detroit Tigers think
fullText:
Wenceel Pérez is a switch-hitting outfielder who impressed the Detroit Tigers throughout his rookie season in 2024, but he still needs to establish himself in the big leagues.

The 25-year-old hit .301 with an .819 OPS in his first 29 games, and despite hitting .223 with a .612 OPS in his final 83 games, he provided key hits to help the Tigers complete their run to the postseason after returning from a month-long stint on the injured list with a left oblique strain.

Imagine if Pérez turned into a super utility player.

ANALYSIS: Pros and cons of Tigers trading for All-Star third baseman Nolan Arenado

It would certainly create more playing time for the up-and-comer in a crowded room of outfielders.

"I don't know about the infield yet," said president of baseball operations Scott Harris at the general manager meetings in early November. "We haven't really had that conversation. We're going to probably have it with the infield guys. But the fact that he's a switch-hitter that can play all three outfield positions is a good start."

A SKUBAL STORY: Once upon a time, Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal dreamed of playing Division III basketball

Here's the catch: Pérez is already an infielder. He had been an infielder for his entire life — until the Tigers put him in the outfield for the first time in late May 2023.

Before then, Pérez hadn't played any positions other than shortstop, second base and third base.

Pérez signed with the Tigers out of the Dominican Republic in July 2016. He spent his first three seasons as a shortstop, from 2017-19. In 2021, Tigers shifted Pérez from shortstop to second base and third base. In 2023, the Tigers added center field, left field and right field to Pérez's defensive profile in Double-A Erie and Triple-A Toledo while continuing to use him at second base.

Everything changed in 2024 spring training.

Errors — specifically throwing errors — had been a problem for many years, so the Tigers changed Pérez's status to outfield-only after one game as a second baseman in spring training, completely turning away from his previous role as an infielder.

"He's going to focus primarily in the outfield," Tigers manager A.J. Hinch said in late February 2024. "Some of it is the reps that we have, some of it is his best chance to contribute faster in the big leagues is going to be in the outfield. I'm not saying it's forever, but it is for this camp."

By early April, Pérez made his MLB debut as an outfielder.

Pérez hit .242 with nine home runs, 32 walks (7.5% walk rate) and 92 strikeouts (21.6% strikeout rate in 112 games in the 2024 season, though his first 29 games were significantly better than his final 83 games.

TIME FOR A REUNION? Ben Verlander: 'I think there's a chance' Justin Verlander returns to Tigers

On defense, Pérez was worth plus-1 defensive runs saved across 647 innings in right field, minus-4 defensive runs saved across 179⅓ innings in center field and plus-1 defensive runs saved across 20 innings left field.

Pérez didn't get any reps in the infield.

"He's really good in the outfield," Harris said of Pérez, whose fielding run value ranked in the 48th percentile. "I'm impressed not only by how good he is but the rate at which he got better."

Maybe Pérez could be the next Willi Castro, an All-Star in 2024 for the Minnesota Twins. Remember, the Harris-led Tigers cut Castro — a switch-hitting super utility player — in November 2022, rather than paying him approximately $1.7 million.

MORE ABOUT HIM: Tigers switch-hitter Wenceel Pérez fulfills childhood dream by making MLB debut

Two years later, Castro — who continues to thank Hinch for transforming his career with defensive versatility — became an All-Star with a rival team in the American League Central. In 2024, Castro became the first player in MLB history to play at least 25 games at five different positions: second base, shortstop, third base, left field and center field. (He also had two pitching appearances.)

"I think I'm in a way better spot," Castro said in early July, two weeks before he was named an All-Star for the first time in his six-year MLB career. "In Detroit, it wasn't going so good. They had to get guys that would do the job better than me."

Castro credits playing time for his rise with the Twins.

"Probably the time that I've been playing more every day," Castro said. "Being an everyday player is something that I really needed, probably in Detroit. But they gave me the opportunity here (in Minneapolis) to play every day and play all those positions."

headline: Detroit Lions vs. Green Bay Packers: Dave Birkett's scouting report, prediction
fullText:
Detroit Lions (11-1) vs Green Bay Packers (9-3)

The coaches: Lions — Dan Campbell (40-34-1 overall, 35-27-1 with Lions); Packers — Matt LeFleur (65-30 overall, 65-30 with Packers).

Last game: Lions beat the Chicago Bears, 23-20; Packers beat the Miami Dolphins, 30-17.

Last meeting: Nov. 3, 2024: Lions won, 24-14.

Key matchups

WIN AND THEY'RE IN! Detroit Lions playoff scenarios: 10 ways they can clinch in Week 14

Lions S Kerby Joseph vs. Packers QB Jordan Love

Joseph might as well have an ownership stake in the Packers. In four career games against Green Bay, the Lions’ third-year safety has four interceptions. He picked off Aaron Rodgers’ last pass as a Packer, and he returned a Love interception 27 yards for a touchdown in Week 9.

Love is tied for third in the NFL with 11 interceptions. His pick in the first game against the Lions was a careless throw against a blitz. He’s prone to mistakes, but has played turnover-free football the past two weeks.

The Lions need to get back to their turnover-causing ways on defense, and Joseph is usually the catalyst for that. He has seven interceptions this season, tied for most in the NFL. If he can bait Love into another Thursday, it will go a long way toward helping the Lions win the NFC North.

Packers DT Kenny Clark vs. Lions LG Graham Glasgow

Clark is usually the first player Lions coach Dan Campbell mentions when talking about Green Bay, a physical do-it-all lineman who has the potential to wreck games.

“He has just been super disruptive no matter where he lines up on that defensive line, and that’s been for years,” Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson said. “That’s even before coach Campbell got here. He has been a forced to be reckoned with. I know our interior guys, Frank (Ragnow), Graham, the guys that have played him for a long time, they understand what a problem he can be.”

Glasgow’s play has been up and down this season. He wasn’t at his best against the Bears, but he helped hold Clark without a tackle in the first meeting. The two should match up plenty Thursday.

Scouting report

Lions run offense vs. Packers run defense

Jahmyr Gibbs had only two carries in the second half of last week’s win over the Bears, but should be featured more prominently Thursday. Gibbs is 27 yards short of the first 1,000-yard season of his career and averaged nearly 6 yards per carry in sloppy conditions against the Packers last month.

DO IT ALL: Lions' Jameson Williams wants to return punts — and definitely wants more hurdles

Gibbs and David Montgomery are the NFL’s best running back tandem, with a combined 21 rushing touchdowns. They combined for 138 yards rushing in the first game against the Packers, though Green Bay limited the Lions to their second-lowest per-carry average (3.9 yards) of the season.

The Packers struggled against good backs like Joe Mixon and Saquon Barkley early this season, but have allowed 83 net yards rushing the past two weeks. T.J. Slaton has played well next to Clark at defensive tackle, but the Packers will be without linebacker Edgerrin Cooper because of a hamstring injury. Edge: Lions

Lions pass offense vs. Packers pass defense

Campbell talks often about playing complementary football, and how the Lions can win different ways based on their personnel. With so many injuries on defense, this might be a game where they feel the need to ride their high-powered offense to victory and put a lot on Jared Goff’s plate in throwing the ball.

Goff had a five-interception game against the Houston Texans last month but otherwise hasn’t thrown a pick since Sept. 22. He leads the league at 8.8 yards per attempt and he has two potential 1,000-yard receivers in the reliable Amon-Ra St. Brown (76 catches, 820 yards) and the dynamic Jameson Williams (34 catches, 630 yards).

The Lions will be shorthanded at offensive tackle without Taylor Decker, and his replacement, Dan Skipper, broke two ribs earlier this season and is playing through bruised ribs now. The Packers counter with an attacking defensive front led by Clark and Rashan Gary. They don’t have a player with more than 4½ sacks, but they generate enough pressure they rank fifth in the league with 23 takeaways. Top cornerback Jaire Alexander will be out with a knee injury after missing the first meeting as well. Edge: Lions

Packers run offense vs. Lions run defense

Lions defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn said the Packers offense has evolved in-season to rely more heavily on running back Josh Jacobs, and that has helped curb some of Love’s turnover woes.

“I think what they've done a really good job of is saying, ‘Listen, Jacobs, you’re going to run this team and everything is going to go through you, which, Love, that’s going to make you even more effective,’ ” Glenn said. “Cause now, man, you have to try to stop this run, cause he’s doing a really good job of running the ball and now he’s going to get more of his one-on-one matchups and those throws might be somewhat easier for him.”

Jacobs is third in the NFL with 987 yards rushing and the Packers are averaging nearly 150 yards on the ground per game as a team. The Lions rank fifth against the run (93.5 yards per game) and haven’t allowed more than 98 net yards rushing since the last Green Bay game, but their front seven has been ravaged by injuries. They’ll need a big game from Jack Campbell to stop Jacobs, especially with DJ Reader (shoulder) ruled out. Edge: Packers

Packers pass offense vs. Lions pass defense

Love played his best football last season in the second half of the year, and after some early-season injury problems this fall, he has posted three straight games with a passer rating of 107 or better. Turnovers have been Love’s bugaboo, but the Packers do a good job protecting him up front with a sack rate of 4.32%, second-lowest in the league.

HARD FEELINGS: No love lost between Detroit Lions CB Amik Robertson and Packers: 'They know it's smoke'

The Packers don’t have a true No. 1 receiver, but they have a bunch of capable pass catchers led by Jayden Reed (15.8 yards per catch) and Romeo Doubs, who will miss this game in concussion protocol. Tight end Tucker Kraft has had a breakout second season with six touchdowns. He needled Joseph this week, telling the Green Bay Press-Gazette he doesn’t appreciate some of Joseph’s hits and “if I get a chance to get my hands on him, you know, playing football."

Starting cornerback Carlton Davis III is expected back Thursday after a one-game absence due to a knee injury, and Joseph and Brian Branch might be the best safety tandem in the NFL. But the Lions will have to work to generate pressure with a front that has already lost its top three pass rushers, likely for the season, and will be without Josh Paschal and Levi Onwuzurike. Edge: Packers

Special teams

Jake Bates is human. The rookie missed his first field goal of the season last week but remains an impressive 19-for-20 on the year with five kicks of 50-plus yards. He and punter Jack Fox give the Lions one of the league’s most dangerous kicking games when it comes to controlling field position. The Lions could use St. Brown or Williams on punt returns, and in a game of this magnitude, it’s always wise to keep an eye out for Dan Campbell dialing up a fake punt.

The Packers are a well-rounded special teams group similar to the Lions. They rank eighth in punt return defense (7.7 yards per return allowed) and had a big blocked field goal to escape with a win against the Bears two weeks ago. Brandon McManus is 10-for-11 on field goals since replacing Brayden Narveson as kicker, and Keisean Nixon is one of the most dangerous return men in the league.  Edge: Lions

Prediction

The Lions are riding a league-best 10-game winning streak and have looked like the best team in the NFL for much of that stretch. They have a high-powered offense, a playmaking defense and one of the best kicking games around, but their roster has been decimated by injury and that’s the league’s great equalizer this time of year. The Packers are a good football team and mostly healthy right now, while the Lions need nametags to know who’s lining up next to each other. They’ll have to shut down Jacobs, win the turnover battle and outscore Green Bay to win this game, all things they’re capable of doing. But in a division game with so much on the line for both teams, I think points will be tough to come by and the Lions’ winning streak will come to an end. Pick: Packers 27, Lions 24.

headline: Mike Duggan's independent run for Michigan governor is a risky gamble | Opinion
fullText:
"Like most people, Mike Duggan's best thing and his worst thing are the same thing. For Detroit's mayor, it's that he's the guy who gets stuff done."

I wrote that back in 2019, after the Detroit City Council delivered a short-lived rebuke to Duggan over a bond sale to fund a new round of neighborhood demolitions. (Later that year, he got it done.) That’s always been Duggan’s calling card: He’s the guy who isn't afraid to roll up his sleeves or break a few eggs to make an omelet. And even if you actually wanted scrambled, hey, it's still breakfast.

This week, Duggan, who cut his political teeth as the lieutenant of legendary Democratic party boss Ed McNamara, announced that he's running for governor in 2026 ... as an independent.

If you follow Michigan politics, that first part was old news two years ago, but the last part was a real plot twist.

Explaining his decision to run as an independent, Duggan said that he never fit comfortably into the dogma of either party, which is surprising, because Duggan has been one of the most powerful Democrats in southeast Michigan for almost 40 years. He surely would have entered the Democratic race with significant advantages, instead of the uphill climb he’s now facing as a third-party candidate in a state where that sort of thing has never really caught on.

But Duggan likes improbable odds, and he usually beats them. With this, he hopes to replicate the up-from-behind nature of his 2013 mayoral primary victory, when he mounted a successful write-in campaign after failing to meet the term of residency required to make the ballot.

There are a dozen ways to understand this maneuver — just today, I've oscillated from "good for Duggan, bad for Democrats?" to "weird for Duggan, definitely bad for Democrats" — and just as many questions to ask, some of which even have answers. So, let's get to it.

More from Freep Opinion: It’s time to let go of the past, Detroit. Let the Boblo Boat sink.

Why?

There is really only one answer to this question.

Duggan told me Wednesday that his decision "seemed to me like the obvious thing to do," although he acknowledges that this was not the universal assessment.

Gallup polls show 63% of people don't connect with either major party, the mayor explained, but you don't need a poll to know that. Americans — Michiganders — are at each other's throats. Politicians don't tell us what they stand for, Duggan said, they tell us the other side is evil.

"I've dealt with Lansing for 30 years, and I've never seen it this toxic," he said. "You've got to have people from both sides working together, and I just don't see that happening in this environment."

By eschewing party, Duggan believes he can cut through the fray.

Duggan said he wants to run a people-focused campaign, replicating the Detroit house parties that buoyed him into the mayor's office “from Flint to Alpena.” He wants to understand what Michiganders need, and how to make it happen.

These are the sorts of things a gubernatorial candidate should say, but come on.

Duggan hasn't just been active in Democratic politics for four decades, he's been good at it. He was the guy McNamara sent to broker tough deals, like stadium taxes or a new airport terminal. He's the white guy from Livonia who won Detroiters' votes on a write-in ballot. Whatever you think of him, it is, historically, a bad idea to bet against Mike Duggan.

For Duggan to run as an independent, the answer to “why?” has to be “because he sees it as the best path to victory.”

And that’s the part, despite the last 40 years, that’s puzzling.

Duggan, 66, would have entered a Democratic gubernatorial primary with name recognition and a healthy campaign warchest, but also significant challenges: A white male boomer asking for votes from a primary electorate that has tended to favor women and people of color, against a field of strong opponents. He's the mayor of Detroit, and to a lot of folks outstate, or even in the city's suburbs, that still means crime and dysfunction. He's the status quo, and if there's one way to interpret the last 14 years of Michigan election results, it's that voters are neg on the status quo.

Running as an independent gives Duggan control, former Michigan Gov. Jim Blanchard told me this week.

Duggan won't have to duke it out in a Democratic primary with other potential contenders, like Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II, U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, D-Royal Oak. A tough primary leaves scars, Blanchard said. Duggan will be able to conserve his fundraising dollars for the general election.

“When you get into a primary with a bunch of people, you don’t know what can happen,” Blanchard said. “The dynamic changes.”

He'll be required to collect fewer nominating petitions — 12,000 valid signatures compared to 15,000 for party-affiliated candidates — and can file in July, months after his Democratic and Republican opponents.

And, I imagine, Duggan would like to be free of the baggage Democrats have acquired.

More from Freep Opinion: As GM prepares to move out, let's be honest: The RenCen is an embarrassment.

A middle finger to Democrats?

But that part is a real gamble.

Duggan is not wrong about Americans' distaste for party dysfunction. Democrats have struggled to define the party's objectives, or to explain what it has delivered for its constituents. Consequently, Democrats lost badly in this year's elections, including declining vote share in Detroit and other heavily Democratic areas, as Republicans won the presidency, the U.S. Senate, the state House and expanded their majority in the U.S. House of Representatives.

But this is the sort of moment in which a Mike Duggan might have been exactly what the Democrats need: A proven leader who has defined and executed policy with specificity, who could have made the case for pragmatic, Democratic politics with tangible benefits for working- and middle-class families.

For critics, it’s confirmation that the Democratic brand has become unpalatable. But if that were Duggan’s angle, it doesn't track: Dems may have gotten pasted last month, but American politics are cyclical, and the party that voters couldn’t stand in 2024 will look a lot better by 2026.

“In two years, we’re likely to have a major pushback on Donald Trump,” said Blanchard, a Democrat. “We had that in 2018, where we swept everything, and all these new governors — including Gov. Gretchen Whitmer — got elected. If there’s a pushback on Trump, I believe we’ll gain the House back, and gain some new governors, and that could cut against someone who said, ‘They’re not good enough, I’m better.’”

Now we’re just spitballing

Where does Duggan's defection leave the party? Nowhere good, and some of the Democrats I’ve spoken to this week are pretty angry about it.

Because one really likely outcome in a three-way, Democrat-GOP-independent general election gubernatorial contest is a split Democratic electorate, and a Republican governor. Another likely outcome: a drop-off in straight-ticket Democratic voters, hurting candidates from the U.S. Senate to downballot races like the state Legislature and state Board of Education.

“Everyone is going to aim at Duggan,” said Andrea Bitely, the founder and principal of Lansing-based Bitely Communications, a Lansing-based public affairs firm (and, full disclosure, a Free Press’ conservative contributing columnist). “It gives an opportunity, if it’s, say, Duggan vs. Benson vs. a generic Republican, that Democrats could split the vote, giving a less well-known Republican an opportunity to skooch in there and win.”

(If you're wondering, the Republicans who come up conversations about 2026 include state Sen. Aric Nesbitt, R-Porter Township, U.S. Rep. John James, R-Shelby Township and former gubernatorial candidate and media personality Tudor Dixon, who lost by 10 points to Whitmer in 2022.)

Duggan may woo some GOP voters, but it's hard to imagine the party's MAGA base crossing the aisle to vote for southeast Michigan's foremost Democratic powerbroker, even if now he says he's an independent.

Traditionally conservative Republicans simply don't exist in numbers sufficient to sway elections — or at least haven’t been willing to break ranks with their party to do so. Still, Blanchard notes, Republicans who aren't Trump loyalists populate Michigan's business community, and they like Mike Duggan. Those Republicans also tend be the folks who bankroll political campaigns. Ford Motor Co. Chairman Bill Ford has already endorsed Duggan, and other members of the billionaire class will certainly follow.

Will Democrats back an independent? Your guess is as good as mine, but it largely depends on whom the Democrats nominate. All of the likely candidates have strong resumes and popular appeal, and represent the party's future, not its past.

Will Detroiters back an independent?

As a popular mayor, support from Detroit voters ought to be one advantage Duggan brings to 2026. But Detroit is a straight-party kind of town, where more than 95% of voters routinely cast ballots for Democratic candidates.

Duggan pointed to his conventional-wisdom-bucking 2013 write-in primary and general election victories ("I had all the people who told me that voters wouldn’t vote for me because of my skin color, and they turned out to be dramatically wrong"). But the counterpoint is former Detroit Police Chief James Craig, who briefly ran for governor in 2022, and whose announcement that he had secretly been a long-time Republican did not play well in the city.

But how important is Detroit to a statewide win? In the 2021 municipal election, when turnout is notoriously low, 69,329 Detroit voters, or 75%, cast ballots for Duggan. In 2022, When Benson (who is also a Detroiter) ran for re-election in 2022, she won 161,947 votes, or 94%, of ballots cast in the city.

All of this underscores the risk that Duggan would be a spoiler, sandbagging the eventual Democratic candidate without pulling sufficient votes from the GOP candidate to get across the finish line.

How would an independent governor govern?

Duggan believes this isn’t a big deal.

“You’ve had five states elect independent governors since 1990, and my approach is going to be that I don’t care whether you’re a Democrat or a Republican, I’m going to build a coalition in the middle,” he said. “I know the far left and far right are going to oppose me. They always have. The far left and the far right have always opposed me as mayor.” (“There’s a far right in Detroit?” I asked. “There’s a few,” he replied.)

But Whitmer, who spent years in the state Legislature before winning her seat, approached the office with a similar playbook: She focused on common sense, dinner table issues, like fixing roads and schools, and pledged to work with anyone who’d work with her.

Instead, she got legislative stalemate during her first term, when the GOP controlled the state Legislature, and two years of stop-start after Democrats won the majority in 2022.  

Onward to 2026

Mike Duggan has always been the guy who gets things done. Detroit is a different city than it was when Duggan took office a decade ago, and by nearly all objective metrics, it’s a better city.

That’s his best thing.

But sometimes, results come at a cost. Like too many Detroiters who still feel left out or left behind, or a demolitions program that took down thousands of blighted structures, but sometimes released toxic chemicals into residential neighborhoods, or left vacant lots that may never be rebuilt. Or turning a blind eye to police reform protesters who begged the city to see their pain — and then dedicating significant resources to prosecuting those protesters in court. Or backing a slate of state House candidates who pledged to reform no-fault auto insurance, a policy Duggan later acknowledged hadn't resulted in sufficient savings.

The most direct path forward isn’t always the best path forward. And that’s Duggan’s worst thing.

With one announcement, Duggan has changed the 2026 gubernatorial race. He's dominated the news cycle, and crafted a pitch that sounds no-nonsense and common sense, even if there's little evidence that third-party (or no party) candidacy is a viable path to victory.

Still, Duggan is the guy who gets things done, for best or worst. Which is it this time? We’ll find out.

Nancy Kaffer is the editorial page editor of the Detroit Free Press. Contact: nkaffer@freepress.com. Submit a letter to the editor at freep.com/letters and we may publish it online and in print.

headline: Lions host Packers in key Thursday night showdown: 'We're in playoff football right now'
fullText:
The NFL playoffs are a month away, but in Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell’s eyes, they begin now.

“We’re in playoff football right now,” Campbell said Tuesday. “That’s where we’re at. We’re in December, and our schedule says that, man. We play tough opponent after tough opponent, and we’ve got another one.”

The Lions host the Green Bay Packers on Thursday night at Ford Field with a chance to clinch a playoff berth for the second straight year.

At 11-1, they should make the postseason no matter what happens Thursday. But despite an NFL-best 10-game winning streak and the best record in the NFC, the Lions are locked in a tight battle for playoff seeding and division supremacy that makes Thursday’s game a high-stakes affair.

The Lions lead the Packers (9-3) by two games and the Minnesota Vikings (10-2) by one in the NFC North with five games to play. They need a win over Green Bay to stay ahead of the Philadelphia Eagles (10-2) for the No. 1 seed in the NFC and homefield advantage throughout the playoffs.

If the Lions lose Thursday and both they and the Eagles finish 15-2, the Eagles would win the tiebreaker based on having a better win percentage against common opponents.

More: No love lost between Detroit Lions CB Amik Robertson and Packers: 'They know it's smoke'

The Lions have the third-toughest remaining schedule in the NFL, according to Pro Football Network, with games left against the Packers, Buffalo Bills, Chicago Bears, San Francisco 49ers and Vikings. The Eagles, who play just two teams with a winning record the final five weeks, have the league’s seventh-easiest remaining schedule.

“Especially for how tight it is for us in our division, every game means something so you just got to have the mindset that we’re just going to go in and every game can either make or break your season,” Lions defensive lineman Pat O’Connor said. “So it just heightens the intensity in every shape.”

Campbell said this week he likes the thrill of a tight race, and how it brings out the best in coaches and players.

“It’s exciting and it’s competitive and it’s just – I mean this is why you’re in this business,” he said. “Like I know Minnesota just won (a close game against the Arizona Cardinals). It’s awesome. The race is on and it’s just good. This is top-tier stuff and it’s for the best of the best and this thing’s going to go down to the wire and we just got to worry about winning the one in front of us.”

The Lions beat the Packers in Week 9 at rain-soaked Lambeau Field, 24-14, and hold the tiebreaker over the Packers and Vikings in the division.

But the Lions have hemorrhaged defensive talent in the month since that game and enter Thursday’s showdown with a reconstructed front seven on the league’s second-best scoring defense.

Defensive linemen DJ Reader (shoulder), Levi Onwuzurike (hamstring) and Josh Paschal (knee) will miss Thursday’s game, and linebackers Alex Anzalone (broken forearm) and Malcolm Rodriguez (torn ACL) have suffered significant injuries in the past four weeks. Rodriguez is out for the season, while Anzalone will be back for the playoffs and could return before the end of the regular season if the Lions still have something to play for.

The Lions have filled the holes on their defense – starters Aidan Hutchinson, Marcus Davenport and Derrick Barnes also are out with potential season-ending injuries – with experienced veterans who either know their system or have been a part of playoff pushes before.

They acquired pass rusher Za’Darius Smith from the Cleveland Browns at last month’s trade deadline. They elevated O’Connor, a Super Bowl winner with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2020, and defensive end Al-Quadin Muhammad off the practice squad. And this week, they signed linebackers Kwon Alexander and Jamal Adams, the latter to the practice squad.

Campbell said the new faces have benefitted from having “plenty of guys who understand what we’re trying to get done around them.”

“Plus this coaching staff has done a great job, been burning the midnight oil getting these guys up to date, getting them ready to go,” he said. “And they’re football players, so we’re going to let them cut it loose.”

The Packers have won seven of their past eight games – their only loss since Oct. 1 is to the Lions – and have played some of their best football in wins over the 49ers and Miami Dolphins the past two weeks.

Quarterback Jordan Love is healthy after battling injury early this year, but Green Bay will be without top cornerback Jaire Alexander and No. 2 receiver Romeo Doubs.

“This is the type of stuff that you live for,” Campbell said. “It’s also the type of stuff that gets you ready for the tournament. So, yeah, we’re a resilient bunch and nothing’s going to change that. We’ve just, we’ve got to worry about the one in front of us.”

headline: These 4 Michigan football recruits could see playing time as freshmen
fullText:
Free Press sports writer Tony Garcia highlights four members of Michigan football's 2025 recruiting class who are leading candidates to see playing time as freshmen in Ann Arbor next season.

QB Bryce Underwood

Ranking (per 247 Sports' composite rankings): Five stars (No. 1 overall).

Vitals: 6 feet 3, 205 pounds.

The buzz: There are rumors Michigan could be interested in Miller Moss, USC's former starting quarterback, and someone like that could push Underwood in this room. Short of a proven Power Four starter with immediate NFL upside, it's hard to imagine anyone other than Underwood will be under center on Aug. 30 when New Mexico hits the Big House. Michigan flipped the recruiting world on its head when it came up with reportedly one of the most lucrative NIL deals to keep the local product home. And for good reason. There are few 18-year-olds who are as physically ready as Underwood, and even fewer possess the dual ability to change the game with their arm and their legs. All freshmen (yes, even those as talented as Underwood) go through growing pains, but there's not a team in America that wouldn't want the most talented young quarterback on its roster. Michigan is the one that has him.

ANALYSIS: In firing Kirk Campbell and landing Bryce Underwood, it's a new era for Michigan football

DL Nate Marshall

Ranking (per 247 Sports' composite rankings): Four stars (No. 55 overall).

Vitals: 6-4, 265.

The buzz: The Wolverines are expected to lose a ton along the defensive line, including Mason Graham, Kenneth Grant, Josaiah Stewart, TJ Guy and possibly Derrick Moore and Rayshaun Benny. Position coach Lou Esposito is going to have to turn the room over in a big way and while it's difficult to play on the line as a freshman, Marshall is one of the few who enters with the skill and size to do so. Remember, Graham began to start in base packages by the mid-point of his freshman season, and Marshall — a one-time U-M commit who flipped to Auburn in August but flipped back to the Wolverines this week — is also perceived to have NFL upside. While he remains raw, given the need at the position he feels like a candidate who could break through. "Combo of athleticism and versatility make him a high-end prospect," 247 Sports recruiting analyst Allen Trieu wrote. "Has to continue developing from a technical standpoint with his hands and get stronger, but he looks like he will be a starter for high-major program and has the baseline tools to play beyond college."

WR Andrew Marsh

Ranking (per 247 Sports' composite rankings): Four stars (No. 70 overall).

Vitals: 6-1, 180.

The buzz: There's an argument to be made that the Wolverines had the most lackluster wide receiver room not just in the Power Four, but all of America in 2024, without a single wideout with either 250 yards or more than two touchdowns. Enter Marsh, a rangy pass-catcher capable of lining up out wide or in the slot. He is seen as one of the top 10 recruits at his position in America. A Navy All-American Bowl commit, Marsh finished his senior season with 65 catches for 1,172 yards (18.0 yards per reception) and 11 touchdowns, according to MaxPreps. If there's a player not named Underwood who's a near-lock to make an immediate impact, it's the wideout from Fulshear, Texas, who can run after the catch, corral the ball in tight spaces and make grabs at all three levels of the defense.

THE RECRUITS: Meet Michigan's top-10 2025 recruiting class, highlighted by QB Bryce Underwood

DB Shamari Earls

Ranking (per 247 Sports' composite rankings): Four stars (No. 86 overall).

Vitals: 6-2, 180.

The buzz: Michigan will need to replace perhaps the nation's No. 1 defensive back, Will Johnson, as well as an athlete who emerged in his absence by seasons end, graduate transfer Aamir Hall. Even beyond that, Jyaire Hill was trending the wrong direction at season's end, and with Makari Paige heading to the NFL, there's a good chance Zeke Berry could slide back to nickel, essentially leaving the starting cornerback spots entirely vacant. That's where Earls comes in, a big, physical defensive back and one-time Georgia commit who flipped to the Wolverines in early November. Andy Irvins, 247 Sports' director of scouting, did suggest he may need a year or so of seasoning before making an impact. Still, he also added Earls has all the tools. "Imposing perimeter corner with the ideal blend of size and speed," Irvins wrote. "Has made an impact in all three phases of the game since he was a sophomore in Virginia’s highest classification and has experience working in a variety of different coverages."

This story was updated to remove tight end Andrew Olesh, who on Friday afternoon flipped his commitment from Michigan to Penn State.

headline: Detroit Lions keep winning despite injuries. But are they close to a breaking point?
fullText:
(This story was updated because an earlier version included an inaccuracy.)

Despite all kinds of injuries, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn has kept this team winning, using smoke and mirrors.

Then again, I’m pretty sure smoke tore an ACL and mirror broke into a million pieces; and they both ended up on injured reserve along with everybody else.

Because, well, it’s the 2024 Lions.

Still, the Lions keep winning. They are 11-1 – their best start in franchise history – and that’s a tremendous accomplishment, considering all the obstacles this team has faced.

But as the injuries have mounted and the schedule grows increasingly difficult, I gotta admit I’m having doubts.

There was a time when I was 100 percent certain the Lions were going to make the Super Bowl. I bought a plane ticket to New Orleans, and the return trip to Detroit the day after the Super Bowl was so stupid expensive that I’m fairly certain there are a whole bunch of Lions fans who have done the same.

The Lions were rolling, absolutely crushing teams. This team looked complete and balanced in every way – offense, defense and special teams – and my confidence went to a new level: they aren’t just gonna make the Super Bowl, they are gonna win it, I thought. It seemed like the only thing could derail them was a Jared Goff injury.

MORE SEIDEL: Lions showed creativity and new way of thinking with this draft pick – it's paying off

Goff is still chugging along, having a tremendous season.

But the defense has been decimated by injuries, and my one-time certainty has been replaced with a growing concern.

There has to be a breaking point, right?

You can’t lose more than half your starting defense to injuries and not suffer ramifications.

More: Lions take back Thanksgiving despite tug of war with Bears

If the Lions were to play the Philadelphia Eagles right now in the NFC championship, I’m not sure the Lions would win anymore.

The Eagles are ascending, while the Lions are limping along, just surviving.

Why?

One simple graphic sums it up. ESPN put up a list the other day that told the entire story, showing the Lions roster and the injured players or players no longer with the team had lines drawn through their names.

Defensive tackles (4): Alim McNeill, DJ Reader, Levi Onwuzurike, Makhi Wingo.

Defensive ends (5): Aidan Hutchinson, Marcus Davenport, Josh Paschal, James Houston, John Cominsky.

Linebacker (6): Alex Anzalone, Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, Jalen Reeves-Maybin, Ben Niemann.

When you see it laid out like that on a big screen TV, it puts everything into perspective.

Especially for a team that will play Green Bay Thursday night – its third game in 12 days.

And now, you can add Reader to the list of cross-offs, as the big defensive tackle will miss the Packers game with a shoulder injury.

A team of replacement parts

It’s hard to sustain excellence in the NFL, much less win a single game, when you have a rash of injuries and there are so many replacement guys in the Lions' locker room that they have to walk around the facility with little sticky notes on their chest that read: Hello, my name is…

Kidding, of course.

The Lions haven’t done that. Not yet at least.

JUST KEEP WINNING: Detroit Lions tinker with more replacement parts to spark victory

Besides, Za’Darius Smith, one of those replacements, doesn’t need to. His name is tattooed across his upper back, right where the nameplate would be. It’s like he’s wearing a jersey, even when he takes it off.

Well, thank you – that makes it a heck of a lot easier.

The fact that the Lions have the best record in the NFC, despite all these injuries, is nothing short of remarkable.

They have continued to win because the offense has been relatively healthy, though left tackle Taylor Decker will again be out for the Packers game.

They have continued to win because of the outstanding play of safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph.

They have continued to win because Jack Campbell has been a rock, as Glenn said so precisely.

They have continued to win because they went out and traded for Smith; and Reader has been a force, right up the gut.

And let’s be honest.

They won on Thanksgiving Day, in part, because former Chicago Bears coach Matt Efferflus had a brain cramp and melted down in the final minute.

For that, he was fired.

And the Lions kept winning.

Schedule is getting incredibly hard

I still have complete faith in general manager Brad Holmes, who is scouring the Earth, finding replacement parts and he’s done a masterful job at it.

I still have faith in Dan Campbell, who continues to push the right buttons and set the perfect tone.

AMAZING STORY: After fighting through an illness, Lions rookie thankful for this 'surreal' opportunity

But now, this journey to New Orleans is about to get even harder because the Lions are about to face the Green Bay Packers and Buffalo Bills, with a rematch against the Vikings looming at the end of the season.

That’s three incredibly tough games, even at home.

The Packers are particularly daunting for a decimated defense. Green Bay has a talented group of receivers – four of whom are averaging 40 yards per game, which will put a different kind of stress on the Lions secondary, who like to play man-to-man.

To make it worse, the Lions defensive line is banged up, and that means it’s hard to generate a pass rush. It stands to reason the Lions will blitz the heck out of Jordan Love, who struggles against pressure. But that means even more pressure will be placed on those DBs in man-to-man. They gotta be perfect.

So, how can the Lions beat the Packers and Bills?

I think we saw a hint on Thanksgiving Day. The Lions focused on putting together long, time-consuming drives. What’s the best way to stop an opponent from scoring? Keep them on the sideline.

But there is another way; and it involves tremendous risk.

It seems logical that we are going to see good ole Gamblin’ Dan Campbell once again, like we saw when this team didn’t have much of a defense in years past.

I think Campbell is going to take some calculated risks – like the old days – trying to extend drives.

In essence, trying to steal a possession or two.

Because one possession could win or lose one of these games.

But any risk is worth the reward. Because it’s impossible to overstate how big these games are against the Packers and Bills.

Win them both and you can see a clear path to playing at home in the NFC championship.

Split them and it gets iffy – every game will get magnified even more.

Lose them both and they might just end up being a wild card, especially considering they still have to play the Vikings.

The entire season – and everything that once seemed so certain – is teetering in the balance.

Having said all of that, let me present one final positive to consider.

If the Lions can just hang on and get through this stretch, as they have to this point, some of these injured players could return.

And that’s a significant kernel of hope in this swirl of concern.
