headline: In firing Kirk Campbell and landing Bryce Underwood, it's a new era for Michigan football
fullText:
During the same afternoon Bryce Underwood officially joined Michigan football, a reporter noticed someone peeling Kirk Campbell’s name off the plate marking of his assigned, but now vacant, parking spot outside Schembechler Hall. It was a symbolic moment that signified this is indeed a new day for the Wolverines’ offense.

Within a span of 24 hours, head coach Sherrone Moore dumped Campbell, his embattled coordinator, and welcomed Underwood, the Belleville star who is nation’s top quarterback recruit. The close timing of these two events seemed hardly coincidental.

Before the Wolverines pulled off their monumental upset of Ohio State last Saturday, the story of Moore’s first year in charge was defined by his team’s struggle to score points and pass the ball. The failure to find a suitable option to succeed J.J. McCarthy this past offseason is what caused the reigning national champions to lose five games and fall out of College Football Playoff contention by mid-October.

Moore cycled through three starters before finally settling on Davis Warren, a former walk-on who began the year as Michigan’s QB1. It was a mess. But in retrospect, it may have been a blessing in disguise because it created urgency for Moore and Michigan’s wealthy boosters to seek out a solution that would fix the problem.

It led to the heavy pursuit of Underwood, the local star who had long been committed to LSU. Underwood’s main attraction to the SEC school was Brian Kelly’s high-octane offense that featured the quarterback and was supported by an abundance of outstanding outside skill players. Last year, dual-threat dynamo Jayden Daniels made the most of the system, winning the Heisman Trophy before being drafted with the No. 2 overall pick.

McCarthy, meanwhile, played within the confines of a run-heavy scheme that Moore seemed reluctant to change when he was promoted to replace Jim Harbaugh last January.

“We will smash,” he said at his introductory news conference.

NAMES TO KNOW: Meet Michigan football's top-10 2025 recruiting class, highlighted by QB Bryce Underwood

The Wolverines attempted to do that up until the final minute of their win over Ohio State because they had no other recourse. Warren threw for just 62 yards against the Buckeyes while commanding the second-least productive passing attack in the Power Four. Although Campbell vowed Michigan would be “extremely explosive,” it was anything but that. The Wolverines finished the regular season as the only Football Bowl Subdivision team without a completion of 40 or more yards.

“There might be people that want us to perform at a high level as much as Coach Campbell, but there’s nobody that wants that more than him,” tight ends coach – and now Michigan’s interim play-caller – Steve Casula said in early November. “We very much aren’t a finger-pointing operation. We’re all responsible for how we perform on offense as offensive coaches.”

But Campbell, because of his position, was assigned all the blame. When he kept proving he couldn’t deliver positive results, Moore had no choice but to remove him.

“Had to make a change,” Moore said. “Thought that was the best direction we had to go.”

It was a sensible decision because it creates the possibility of a reset. While Moore maintained he still wants a balanced offense, it’s clear Underwood will influence how it is shaped.

“It is a process no matter what,” Underwood said. “I’m willing to be the best no matter who the coach is.”

Moore described Underwood as an "excellent player” with an “elite skill set” who can throw accurate passes at all levels “from the pocket” and out of it, too.

“He’s talked to me about different things we want to do with him to expand his game,” Moore said.

“He wants to earn everything. He doesn’t want to be given anything.”

But it only seems a matter of time before Underwood is the starter, considering the multi-million-dollar name, image and likeness investment that was made to get him. Moore further lent credence to that expectation when he mentioned that quarterback development will be one of the priorities of Michigan’s next coordinator – a man who will have a lot on his plate.

On top of nurturing Underwood, Campbell's successor will be tasked with rejuvenating a depressed sector of the team that for the second straight year will undergo some significant personnel changes. The most productive pass-catcher, junior tight end Colston Loveland, is projected to leave for the NFL. The team’s leading wideout, Tyler Morris, just announced he is entering the transfer portal. The eligibility of Kalel Mullings and Donovan Edwards, Michigan’s top two ball carriers, will soon expire.

It is also unclear if Michigan has replacement-level players capable of offsetting those losses. While the Wolverines added two blue-chip receivers and a pair of four-star running backs Wednesday, few underclassmen emerged this past season. That was the ripple effect of the underwhelming recruiting classes the Wolverines cobbled together in the previous two cycles. Yet, despite all this, Moore believes Michigan will have no shortage of candidates who will want to take the offensive coordinator job.

The addition of Underwood has a lot to do with that, of course.

“It probably helps,” Moore said. “Being here, it’s the Mecca.”

But in terms of modern offense, it seemed more like Siberia this past year.

That figures to change. Campbell is gone and Underwood is due to arrive later this month to begin his college journey.

And how does Michigan’s prized new quarterback envision his future at Michigan?

“More than likely record-breaking,” Underwood said.

headline: Fast-growing online casino live dealer firm Evolution employs 800 in metro Detroit
fullText:
The secret to a fast-growing segment of Michigan's online gambling market can be found in a Southfield office tower.

Don't look for a bunch of computers generating random numbers and fancy animations.

The secret is the hundreds of real people working there, dealing cards and table games in front of cameras and hosting interactive "game shows" — and all of it streamed live to mobile phones and casino gaming websites across the state.

They are employees of the U.S. division of Evolution AB, a Sweden-headquartered firm that is one of the world's largest developers and producers of content for online gambling apps, particularly "live dealer" games with real humans.

The company got its start in eastern Europe in 2006 and went live in Michigan in 2021, when online gambling and sports betting became legal in the state.

Evolution says it is growing fast in Michigan and employs more than 800 people at Southfield Town Center, and anticipates adding "several hundred" next summer when it opens a studio in Grand Rapids.

The company's executives say they've found that some online casino players are more likely to trust actual people whom they see on camera dealing real cards and spinning real roulette wheels, as compared with a generic mobile phone app that is all graphics and algorithms.

Players also are more likely to feel a connection with a live dealer than an app, as Evolution's platform features a players' chat window that dealers will respond to on camera.

"There’s been random number generated casino games for a long time. But what we’ve found was that players don’t necessarily trust it," Jacob Claesson, the CEO of Evolution's North America division, said in an interview last week. "They want that human factor. They want the real dealer, the real person they can interact with."

Evolution is the largest of three live dealer firms in Michigan. The company's years of experience running live dealer studios in Europe gives it an edge when setting up for new markets like Michigan, Claesson said, as Evolution has studio designs, employee training protocols and a catalogue of live dealer games ready to go.

“Online casinos have existed in Europe for probably 20 years," he said. "So a lot of the things that we have learned we are now bringing here."

Operating like a land-based casino

The company's live content studios operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week — the same as Detroit's land-based casinos — because there are always people eager to play at all hours.

Participation in live dealer games can scale up beyond what is possible at land-based casinos, where only so many players can physically take part.

For live dealer games, “at a single game on a single table, there can be 350 people sitting at home playing that same game at the same time," Claesson said.

Although Evolution employs the dealers who interact with the online players, Evolution is in fact a business-to-business company and its customers are Michigan's licensed gaming operator brands, such as MGM, Draft Kings and Fan Duel.

So the content produced by a single live dealer can be used on multiple gaming websites and casino apps. Evolution earns revenue by getting commissions from the operators.

In Europe, live dealer content is often shared across different national markets. But U.S. gaming regulators generally require content to stay within state boundaries. That means the live dealer games produced at Evolution's Southfield office are strictly for players of Michigan-licensed online casinos.

The geographic restriction wasn't a deal killed for Evolution, as Michigan's 10 million population is bigger than that of many European countries.

Evolution is a publicly traded company on Nasdaq Stockholm, formerly known as the Stockholm Stock Exchange. Companywide, its operating revenues were up 20% to 1.59 billion Euros ($1.68 billion) in the first nine months of this year compared with 2023 and profits for the period were 867 million Euros ($914 million), according to its latest earnings report.

The firm's annual report describes how the online casino industry worldwide had a 21% annual growth rate between 2019 and 2023, with the live dealer and game shows segment the fastest growing segment of that market.

Evolution also makes traditional online casino games with computer graphics and no live people, although they represented just 18% of its global revenues last year. (The bulk came from live dealer and game shows.)

The company last year had 2,662 U.S.-based employees and 17,763 in total.

Evolution's dealer workforce in Michigan isn't currently unionized, unlike their counterparts at the three Detroit casinos. However, the workers recently voted to join the United Auto Workers and are already bargaining for their first contract, according to a UAW representative.

Dozens of dealers at individual tables

On a recent afternoon at Evolution's Southfield office, there were dozens of card and table game dealers gathered in a large red-carpeted room, each seated at an individual table under bright lights and livestreaming cameras.

Because Evolution operates under strict restrictions from the Michigan Gaming Control Board, no outside photography is allowed in its live dealer areas.

The dealers were dressed formally, like those in actual casinos. Some sat before specially designed backgrounds like the BetMGM lion. The games on display included blackjack, roulette, baccarat, craps and three card poker.

Roulette is the company's most popular live dealer game in Michigan and gets about 200 players at any one time during the evening, Claesson said.

It's 'Crazy Time!'

Nearby were several enclosed studios for the company's game shows, each one with an elaborate set design.

“Some of our most popular games have never existed before," Claesson said.

Evolution's crown jewel is "Crazy Time," a game show it debuted in 2020 that features a giant vertical "Wheel of Fortune"-style wheel and a rotating cast of charismatic hosts.

To play, players place bets on numbers — 1, 2, 5, 10 or a bonus game — then watch to see where the wheel stops. There is upbeat music and many sound effects: drum rolls, slot machine jingles, stutters from the spinning wheel.

One daytime host goes by the stage name "Moolah." She is 36, lives in Southfield and has worked at Evolution since 2022, starting as a live dealer and moving to "Crazy Time" last spring after her successful audition for the show.

Like other "Crazy Time" hosts, she works in shorter time increments than the live dealers because putting on the show requires constant high energy, nonstop chatter and regular "shout outs" to the individual players at home. Her theatric work uniform is burgundy and gold with tassel shoulder epaulets.

"Let’s go! Get crazy, get crazy, get crazy!" she told the online player audience recently, stepping on set for a noon shift. She spun the "Crazy Time" wheel several times. It gradually slowed, landing on the number 5.

"I've got five on it!" Moolah exclaimed, an apparent reference to a popular 1990s hip-hop track.

And a moment later, the results of the spin were in: "We got 18 winners out of 37."

The earning potential

Claesson said the earning potential for live dealers varies and depends on tips from players, which are generally pooled for all dealers to share.

The guaranteed minimum for a dealer is $18 an hour, he said. He declined to give figures for the higher earners, saying their pay can fluctuate a lot week to week. But he said game show hosts generally earn more than table game live dealers.

While some dealers previously worked at Detroit casinos, most arrive without previous casino experience, he said.

“There are a lot of young people, and for a lot of them, it’s their first job," Claesson said.

“There is quite a bit of turnover, but the ones who stick around tend to stick around quite long," he added.     “Most of the turnover happens in the first few months, when you realize that maybe this isn’t for you. It’s a tough job; it’s challenging. But we have a lot of people who have been here since the studio first opened.”

The company generally finds applicants for dealer positions through job listings, he said, and a few even arrive from acting programs at local schools.

Evolution also operates in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut, Delaware and West Virginia, with content for their Delaware and West Virginia markets produced in the New Jersey and Pennsylvania studios, respectively.

headline: What will Michigan's lame duck session look like? 'Everything is on the table'
fullText:
LANSING — As Democrats return to Lansing for the final month with their party controlling both chambers of the state Legislature, their agenda remains elusive.

House Speaker Joe Tate, D-Detroit, said his legislative wish list includes increasing Michigan's unemployment benefits, creating a new fund to support public safety and violence prevention measures and water affordability, in an interview with the Detroit Free Press on Wednesday. He described those as personal priorities — not yet ones that are part of some consensus lame duck plan with Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, D-Grand Rapids, and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

"Obviously there's going to be a lot of overlap there," he said. But, he said, there are "three legs of the stool," referring to the governor and Democratic legislative leaders who are about to lose their governing trifecta with Republicans set to take control of the state House next year.

Brinks, for her part, described the lame duck possibilities as somewhat endless. "Everything is on the table at this point," she said in an interview.

But Brinks specifically said she'd like to see the Senate bills that have stalled in the state House cross the finish line before the end of the year. For instance, Senate Democrats passed legislation last year to create a prescription drug affordability board but the House hasn't taken it up. Whitmer previously called on lawmakers to create a board that would be empowered to set an upper payment limit for specific drugs. Tate said it's not clear from looking at other states that a board would lower prescription drug costs. "I think the jury's still out on that one," he said.

Brinks also said she wants to see the House pass legislation subjecting the state Legislature and the governor's office to public records requests. The Senate already approved bills expanding Michigan's Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Brinks said she'd be proud to make increasing government transparency part of the legacy lawmakers leave behind during lame duck. Tate said he's open to supporting the FOIA legislation. But when asked during Wednesday's interview whether he'd back the FOIA bills if they were up for a vote later that day, Tate declined to say whether he'd vote yes.

Whitmer press secretary Stacey LaRouche did not respond to a request for comment on how the governor has worked with Democratic legislative leaders on the lame duck agenda and what's going to be on it. LaRouche said in a previous statement last month that economic development remains a focus of Whitmer's.

Musing on the lame duck uncertainty, Zach Gorchow of Gongwer News Service — a Lansing-based Michigan politics media outlet — recently wrote, "If Whitmer, Tate and ... Brinks assembled a list of what they want to get done, it must be under lock and key and hidden under the catalpa tree on the Capitol lawn because no one seems to have seen it."

A lame-duck legislative session gives retiring and defeated lawmakers one final chance to wield their power. Since their election losses, the 76 Democratic lawmakers still serving — 56 in the state House and 20 in the state Senate — have essentially operated their own mini lame ducks, shepherding their priorities with a flurry of last-minute bill introductions and a frenzy of committee votes to advance legislation to the floor for a vote.

But what will actually muster enough support to make its way across the finish line? No one knows.

"I don't know. I mean we're looking into a black box," state Rep. Ranjeev Puri, D-Canton Township, told reporters Tuesday when asked how many pieces of legislation realistically have the 56 Democratic votes in the state House needed to pass bills over unified GOP opposition. Puri serves as majority caucus whip and was chosen by House Democrats to serve as minority leader next term.

Michigan Legislature: The Democratic lame duck is a rare species in Michigan

Whether Democrats can stick together to vote on bills may not be their main challenge. Instead, it's unclear they'll show up to session to vote at all. In the state House, the support of every Democratic lawmaker is needed to pass legislation that doesn't have a yes vote from any GOP lawmaker. State Rep. Reggie Miller, D-Van Buren Township, has been out this week with a health issue, according to House Democratic caucus spokesperson Jess Travers. And state Rep. Rachel Hood, D-Grand Rapids, who previously threatened to stay home if she doesn't see movement on her priorities, didn't show up to either Tuesday's or Wednesday's House sessions.

"I'm here in Lansing writing and testifying on my bills, rallying with stakeholders, meeting with lobbyists," said Hood in a text message Wednesday. "All around me people are sharing their astonishment at the days wasting away to move vital legislation. My team and I were brought to tears today by parents advocating for their daughter, an auto victim, whose care has been cut. The people I serve here have thanked me for taking a stand. I'm ready to vote on vital bills anytime I'm called. In the meantime, I'm putting my last days here in Lansing to the best and highest use. I'm not needed on the floor if we are passing non-controversial bills. My constituents do need me to write good bills while I can, get them introduced and if possible, heard. I am doing what I can to avert the worst outcomes of the state's extended infrastructure crisis unfolding, to avert the economic disruption and high costs that will be caused if Michigan's immigrants are deported, and to prepare the state for the deadlock split of state government."

Brinks criticized Hood's approach. "I think it's important for people to do the job that they were elected to do, and that they owe it to their constituents to finish strong. This is a unique opportunity to complete some things that need to be done that require only Democratic votes, and it's a team sport so we work with each other to see what we can do to accomplish each other's priorities," Brinks said.

Michigan Democrats haven't had much lame duck experience. The last time Democrats had a trifecta during lame duck was 1934. Since that year, there have been nine lame-duck sessions in Michigan when Republicans had a trifecta. This year's lame-duck agenda is still taking shape and it's not clear how Democrats will ultimately end this chapter. It's also not clear when they can write the next one.

headline: Buy local 🍺
fullText:
Good morning, subscribers.

From 2019 until earlier this year, I occasionally wrote about Michigan craft beer, a billion-dollar industry for the state with hundreds of operating microbreweries from Copper Harbor to Temperance. I'd write about seasonal recommendations, top beers of the year, the latest trends, new brewery openings and, sadly, brewery closings.

While my beer writing has taken a backseat due to my new role as digital director at the Free Press, I still keep in touch with brewers, brewery owners, enthusiasts and fellow writers, and attend as many Michigan Brewers Guild beer festivals as I can to stay close to my passion. Yes, it's about the beer itself - I'd be lying if I said it wasn't - but it's more about the people involved, the hard-working Michiganders who channel their own passion into bringing local communities together.

I wish I were here writing under better circumstances. I certainly could offer a slate of Michigan beers to warm you up this holiday season, from hoppy double IPAs (Hopslam, anyone?) to thick barrel-aged stouts, and there are plenty of both on the market these days if you're looking for one. But I'm here with a different, singular recommendation: Buy local. Any local.

Michigan craft beer needs help. It is still abundant - perhaps more abundant than it's ever been - but the industry is not immune to the intense headwinds facing all of hospitality, from inflation to health-conscious consumers staying home. And we're seeing it play out across the state, with many beloved brewers shuttering. Here are just some of the closures announced this year:

  • Ascension Brewing Co. in Novi.
  • Jamex Brewing Co. in St. Clair Shores.
  • Arctic Circle Brewing Co. in Chesterfield.
  • North Center Brewing Co. in Northville.
  • Brewery Nyx in Grand Rapids, the first fully gluten-free brewery in Michigan.
  • Grand Rapids Brewing Co. in Grand Rapids.

In addition, 8 Degrees Plato, a beloved beer store in Detroit's Cass Corridor, is closing at the end of the year. And just Tuesday, as I'm writing this, Waypost Brewing Co. in Fennville announced it will close Dec. 28.

I'd been to all of these establishments at one point or another, and can point to at least one or two beers from each that were so good, I would gladly buy a four-pack and polish them off over a long weekend. Ascension was notable for its line of Gorilla Juice imperial stouts released every December. Jamex was always dependable for a juicy, fruity IPA or sour. And North Center Brewing Co. had one of the best Belgian tripels in the state in Pain Killer.

It's true that these closings are somewhat balanced out by new openings such as Florian East, Hamtramck's first microbrewery, and Stumblebum Beer Co. in Troy. But it's also true that these new establishments need the same help if they're going to stay afloat. And even if you're not into craft beer, chances are you have that go-to local restaurant that might need your patronage more than ever.

So, I'll repeat: Buy local. Any local. Next time you're in a new Michigan town, stop by the local brewery and have a pint of its flagship beer. Next time you're planning a date night, skip the national chain and try a new local joint. Even if you're currently avoiding eating out and watching calories, buy some gift cards to local establishments so you're paying it forward. You never know when these places could really need it.

Cheers,

—Brian

Watch for our annual list that will post online later today or Friday and will be on the food page in Sunday’s Entertainment section.  Many of these cookie walks provide a variety of holiday cookies, from decorated sugar cookies to classics like snowballs (a.k.a. Russian Tea Cakes or Mexican Wedding cookies) and gingerbread.

headline: Macomb Executive Mark Hackel: Get things done through partnership not partisanship
fullText:
Put aside partisan politics and work together.

That was the overarching theme of Macomb County Executive Mark Hackel's annual address Wednesday night on the progress of Michigan's third most populous county, with a look toward the future.

Now that the election is over, Hackel asked, "can we just set aside the blue versus the red and the Rs and the Ds? And I've said this many a times before, and I think it's starting to catch on in light of what I've been hearing recently, it's time to stop reaching across the aisle. Let's forget about reaching across the aisle. It's time to get in the aisle and get things done on behalf of the people."

Hackel's 12th State of the County address was held before about 1,000 invited guests, including countywide elected officials and judges and leaders from other metro Detroit counties, including Oakland County Executive Dave Coulter, with whom Hackel celebrated the 1 millionth ride on the Detroit People Mover earlier in the day.

Hackel said: "The way we get things done in Macomb County isn't through partisanship, it's through partnership."

Hackel, sporting a suit and tie, graced the stage alone at the Macomb Center for the Performing Arts in Clinton Township, a venue decorated with clusters of red poinsettias and a large video screen for visuals. He breezily walked and talked, reciting his approximately 45-minute speech, complete with punches of humor and upbeat music.

In an unusual move, Hackel left the stage to recognize a woman who will turn 102 on Friday. He asked friends in the crowd to gather around her as a cake with burning candle was presented. He and the crowd sang "Happy Birthday" before she received a standing ovation. She's a member of the county's 100 Club, which celebrates centenarians. Hackel said the county's 100 Club has welcomed 44 members.

More: Mayor Mike Duggan aims to bridge division in gubernatorial run as independent candidate

As in past addresses, Hackel ticked off stats on community metrics: population (more than 880,000 residents, with more than 100,000 who are foreign-born); housing (2,300 homes have been added to the inventory in the past two years); jobs (nearly 460,000 residents are in the workforce); education (61% of residents have some level of college education); income (median household is near $79,000, which is $11,000 higher than the state average), and finances (the county has had a balanced budget for 14 years, a more than $120 million fund balance, and a recent Aa1 bond rating with a positive outlook.)

"All of this tells us that the state of Macomb County is strong," he said.

Hackel cited a half-dozen areas where there have been partnerships with communities, nonprofits, businesses, schools and other entities on projects within the county, which has a $53 billion economy and 19,000 businesses, including manufacturing, and is home to 450 working farms.

More: Lake St. Clair, a destination for fun and source of life, drives $1.6 billion in impact

For example, Hackel said, "with Ford and the village of Romeo, we are examining ways to repurpose the Ford Romeo Engine Plant." He said U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., secured federal funding for a Northern Border Coordination Center at Selfridge Air National Guard Base in Harrison Township — and, Hackel added, "we will continue to fight for those fighters (jets) through the runway expansion project."

And a $15 million grant at Macomb Community College, Hackel said, will launch a training program where students will learn how to build the next generation of nuclear submarines.

More: Write-in candidates in elections 'always have a chance'

Among the many highlights for the county Hackel mentioned:

  • Planned redevelopment of the Lakeside Mall site in Sterling Heights, which is to demolish the 1.5 million-square-foot mall and replace it with a more than $1 billion town-square-style project of apartments, retail, restaurants, offices and public recreation space.
  • Plans for General Sports and Entertainment to build a new headquarters with a restaurant and corporate event space in downtown Utica, home of Jimmy John's Field and the four-team United Shore Professional Baseball League. 
  • Plans for a $5 million reenvisioning of Cherry Street Mall in downtown Mount Clemens.
  • A $1 million grant for a new pedestrian bridge over the Clinton River Spillway in Harrison Township, and preserving 64 acres of land near Selfridge Air National Guard Base to create a nature preserve and monarch butterfly habitat.
  • The Innovate Mound road project in Warren and Sterling Heights, which last week he said was selected as one of the top 10 road projects in the country by a national roads and bridges publication.
  • Formation of the county's Elder Justice Alliance, which has more than 80 groups, to combat elder abuse and exploitation as well as senior scams.
  • New Community Impact Fund in the 2025 budget to allow the county to partner with Advancing Macomb to target grants and philanthropic dollars to invest in nonprofit development, parks, public spaces, small business innovation, senior citizen advocacy and childhood achievement.
  • County's Juvenile Justice Center in Mount Clemens, which serves eight counties in the region as well as helping the state health department through a contractual relationship involving a state-run detention and treatment program.
  • Construction of the county's new Central Intake and Assessment Center at the jail complex in Mount Clemens, which is getting recognition for its unique approach for centralized intake and assessment for medical, mental health and pretrial services at booking as well as front-end diversion when appropriate.

"When I look around, I see everything that's happening here because of our partners that are coming together to try to make this place more special than what it was when we first started off as kids," Hackel said of the county.

"As you can see, a lot of great things are happening here in this county. And the question sometimes is, what's behind it all? I don’t know that there's a single answer to that question, but I think there's a reason that sometimes often gets overlooked. It's our values. Our way of doing things sometimes is just different.

"You see, we believe in doing things together. Not alone. We believe in bringing people in, not shutting them out. We believe in lending a hand, not pointing a finger. We also believe in giving credit where credit is due and not assigning blame. ... We truly believe in the power of a partnership. Quite simply, Macomb County is a place where collaboration turns ideas into realities. And I think you'd be hard-pressed to find that in other communities."

To watch the entire address, go to macombgov.org.

headline: William Roberts, longtime mayor of Walled Lake, remembered for public service, dedication
fullText:
William Roberts, a political animal who loved Walled Lake, his wife and serving the Lord with equal vigor, died Saturday after a long illness.

It may have been a natural extension of his career as a salesman at Hudson's, but Roberts, 78, was a tireless promoter of his hometown and an unabashed champion of its causes.

"Bill was dedicated to the citizens of Walled Lake," said Mayor Linda Ackley, who worked with Roberts during his more than four decades as a councilman and mayor. "He lived and breathed Walled Lake."

Roberts, a Democrat, counted Sen. Phil Hart among his aquaintances. Hart, known as the "Conscience of the Senate," served Michigan in Washington, D.C. for more than 16 years. Former Gov. Jim Blanchard once gave Roberts a ticket behind home plate for a Detroit Tigers World Series game in 1984.

"He knew a lot of people," Ackley said, adding that he liked to mention his connections. "He loved politics and there wasn’t a person he was afraid to go up and talk to."

Ackley said Roberts helped her learn the ropes when local officials went to Washington.

"It didn’t matter where they were or what the situation was," she said, adding that her friend would walk up to bigshots and say, "'I’m here, I’m Bill Roberts, I’m the mayor of Walled Lake.'”

Roberts became one of the youngest elected officials in the country in 1968 when he was elected to the Walled Lake City Council at the age of 22. That was the same year Roberts attended the infamously chaotic Democratic National Convention in Chicago as a member of the Michigan delegation.

"As a young man, he was enthralled by nomination process and dismayed by the violence out on the streets," said his stepson, Bryan Droste. "Both incidents were very memorable for different reasons."

The experience did nothing to diminish Roberts' passion for politics.

"Bill was a walking encyclopedia of Michigan politics,” Droste said.

Roberts was elected mayor in 1973, serving the first of seven terms as Walled Lake's top elected official.

During his tenure, Walled Lake got city water and sewerage, expanded police services, built a fire hall and department of public works building, doubled its population, experienced a housing boom, extended Maple Road and paved all of its streets.

Ackley said Roberts helped Walled Lake evolve “from being a little country bumpkin town to what we are today.”

Roberts always seemed to be serving the public, as an elected official, in various roles with the Episcopal church and as a salesman at Hudson's. After starting at the flagship J.L. Hudson's department store in downtown Detroit in 1967, he quickly transferred to the Pontiac location. There he sold luggage, summer furniture and menswear.

His move to the furniture and carpet department in the 1980s proved fortuitous after he met a customer named Alicia, who became his wife.

“He cared very deeply for Alicia,” Ackley said.

Roberts was active in many government organizations, too, including the Southeast Michigan Council of Governments (SEMCOG), where his 17 years of service included being chairman from 2007 to 2008.

After retiring from Hudson's in 2009, but still serving as mayor, Roberts became an Episcopal deacon in 2010. A year later, he was ordained as a priest.

Roberts retired from elective politics when he decided not to run for re-election in 2013. After St. Anne's in Walled Lake closed in 2016, he ministered to residents in senior and assisted living facilities, which he said he "found gratifying."

Survivors include stepson Scott Droste.

Visitation will be from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. Friday at Lynch & Sons Funeral Home, 340 North Pontiac Trail, in Walled Lake, and from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. on Saturday — which would have been Roberts' 79th birthday — at The Cathedral Church of St. Paul, 4800 Woodward Ave., in Detroit. The funeral service is scheduled for 11 a.m. followed by a reception in Barth Hall at the Cathedral.

Burial will take place privately with the family at Walled Lake Cemetery.

M.L. Elrick is a Pulitzer Prize- and Emmy Award-winning investigative reporter and host of the ML's Soul of Detroit podcast. Contact him at mlelrick@freepress.com or follow him on X at @elrick, Facebook at ML Elrick and Instagram at ml_elrick.

headline: Michigan winter storm radar: Heavy snowfall to hit parts of state
fullText:
Several Michigan regions are currently under winter storm warnings in effect until as late at 1 a.m. Friday.

Portions of nothern Michigan, the Upper Peninsula and West Michigan are expected to see heavy snowfall and high winds.

The winter blasts come after snow accumulations over 2 feet hit parts of the regions last week.

West Michigan winter storm warning

West Michigan is under a winter storm warning until 1 a.m. Friday.

Allegan, Barry, Kalamazoo, Kent, Lake, Mason, Muskegon, Newaygo, Oceana, Ottawa and Van Buren counties are included in the warning.

Travel could be difficult, especially during the Thursday morning and evening commutes.

headline: How many versions of 'The Grinch' are there? Where to stream every version this year
fullText:
When it's time to sit down and watch Christmas movies with the family, the Grinch is likely in the mix someplace.

And that's where the arguments may begin. There are several movie versions, the original cartoon, and even an animated sequel or two. Which one do you watch?

Figures like Santa and Mrs. Claus, or Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer represent the charm of holiday classics.

However, the Grinch is known for his abhorrence of Christmas and everything the season represents. The Grinch, a moody, green character, has become key to Christmas pop culture: He's in a book, Broadway musical and on-screen.

If you're a fan of the Grinch, get ready to enjoy one of the three Grinch films from the comfort of your home with a mug of hot chocolate or a bowl of popcorn this season.

Here's what to know.

Who is the Grinch?

The Grinch is a green, furry character known for his grumpy attitude and hatred of Christmas. The character originates in the 1957 Dr. Seuss children's book "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!," according to Dr. Seuss Enterprises.

The character became a TV fixture after the premiere of the 1966 animated special of the same name.

The Dr. Seuss character went on to become part of Christmas pop culture, with adaptions on screen, as a Broadway musical and as a video game.

More: Christmas TV schedule 2024: Where to watch animated classics like 'Charlie Brown'

How many versions of 'The Grinch' are there?

There are several versions of "The Grinch" in television and film, according to IMDb.

The original version, "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!," came out in 1966, a 26-minute television special. The animated TV show follows the journey of the Grinch as he tries to ruin Christmas for the Whos of Whoville, according to IMDb.

A live-action version of "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," a 1-hour, 44-minute feature-length film, premiered in 2000. The movie featuring actor Jim Carrey brings to life the Grinch's plot to steal the Christmas joy for the Whos, according to IMDb.

The most recent version, "The Grinch," came out in 2018, a 1-hour, 25-minute computer animated film. Returning to its animated roots, this film brings back the struggle between the Grinch and the Whos over Christmas, according to IMDb.

Another live-action movie from 2020, "Dr. Seuss' The Grinch Musical" was made for television.

And, finally, there is the 1977 animated 25-minute TV special "It's Grinch Night," which tells the story of a strange wind that blows into Whoville, making all the inhabitants stay indoors. Residents know the wind means the Grinch will be in a foul mood and out to do harm, but, young Eukariah decides to confront the Grinch, IMDb says.

Where can you stream 'The Grinch' movies?

This Christmas, you can curl up on the couch and enjoy any of the versions of "The Grinch" from your favorite streaming service.

The 1966 television special "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!" is available to stream on Amazon Prime Video, Hulu and Sling TV. It will appear on NBC on Dec. 5.

The 2000 live-action film "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" can be streamed on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+, Fandango, fuboTV, Google Play, Hulu, Sling TV, YouTube TV.

The 2018 animated film "The Grinch" is available to stream on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+, Fandango, Google Play, Hulu, Peacock, Sling TV and YouTube TV.

The 2020 live-action film "Dr. Seuss' The Grinch Musical" premiered on NBC and is not available to stream.

The 1977 animated special "It's Grinch Night" is not available to stream.

headline: Pearl Harbor plunged the US into war. What to know about the surprise attack
fullText:
More than eight decades ago, naval and air forces from Japan plunged the U.S. into World War II when they attacked the naval station at Pearl Harbor and air bases in the Hawaiian island.

Saturday marks the 83rd anniversary of the attack, which then-President Franklin D. Roosevelt called "a date which will live in infamy."

The aftermath of the attack and ensuing worldwide conflict saw millions of people killed and shaped the world for decades afterward.

Here's what to know.

When was the Pearl Harbor attack?

The Pearl Harbor attack occurred on Dec. 7, 1941.

Who conducted the Pearl Harbor attack?

The Empire of Japan launched the Pearl Harbor attack.

What was the Pearl Harbor attack?

The Imperial Japanese Navy's Admiral Isoruku Yamamoto dispatched all six of his “fleet carriers” across 3,000 miles of open ocean in secrecy, with the fleet arriving a few hundred miles north of the Hawaiian islands.

The carriers launched their aircraft early on a Sunday morning, the National World War II Museum said on its website. U.S. forces were completely unprepared, and in less than 90 minutes, Japanese planes destroyed or damaged 19 ships and 300 aircraft, and killed more than 2,400 servicemen.

Almost half of the dead were crewmen from the battleship USS Arizona, which sank within minutes after a bomb struck its forward magazine, igniting more than a million pounds of ammunition.

More: Haunted by military past and leg amputation, Army veteran fights back to run marathons

How many people died in the Pearl Harbor attack?

More than 2,400 Americans were killed, including civilians, in the Pearl Harbor attack and over 1,000 injured, according to History.com.

What motivated the Pearl Harbor attack?

The attack was an attempt by the Japanese to remove the U.S. as an impediment to expansion in the Pacific, according to the World War II museum.

Japan was already engaged in a war in China and was short of crucial materials needed for that effort. With European powers diverting men and supplies to Europe in 1939-41 to battle Nazi Germany, colonies in the Pacific were mostly undefended.

The U.S. had placed economic sanctions and trade embargoes on Japan in response to its 1937 declaration of war on China and resulting atrocities, per History.com.

Roosevelt hoped that embargoes on arms (1937), scrap iron (1938), and eventually oil (1941) would hurt the Japanese economy sufficiently to halt Japan’s war in China, the WWII museum said.

How did the Pearl Harbor attack change the U.S. position in World War II?

The Pearl Harbor attack sparked outrage across the U.S. and led the nation to enter World War II, declaring war on the Empire of Japan on Dec. 8, 1941, per History.com.

More: Let's settle the debate: What's the perfect thermostat temperature for Michigan winters?

How did the Pearl Harbor attack change U.S.-Japan relations?

The Pearl Harbor attack marked the beginning of all-out war between the U.S. and Japan.

With the U.S. Navy temporarily out of the way, a massive Japanese offensive overran the European and colonial empires in Asia: Hong Kong, Malaya, the Dutch East Indies and New Guinea. U.S. possessions, too, came under attack: the Philippines, the major U.S. base in Asia; Guam; and Wake Island, the WWII museum said. At Singapore on the tip of Malaya, 80,000 British, Indian, and Australian troops went into captivity in February 1942.

Eventually, the tide turned and, in 1945, the U.S. dropped two nuclear bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing more than 100,000 people, according to History.com. A few days following the attacks, Japan's Emperor Hirohito announced the nation's unconditional surrender.

What do people who were involved in the attack have to say?

The U.S. Department of Defense maintains videos of attack survivors discussing their experiences.

What is the USS Arizona?

USS Arizona, was a 31,400-ton Pennsylvania class battleship built at the New York Navy Yard, Brooklyn, New York, and commissioned in October 1916.

Arizona was moored in Pearl Harbor's "Battleship Row" on the morning of Dec. 7, 1941, when Japanese carrier aircraft attacked. She was hit by several bombs, one of which penetrated her forecastle and detonated her forward ammunition magazines, the Naval History and Heritage Command said.

The resulting massive explosion totally wrecked the ship's forward hull, collapsing her forward superstructure and causing her to sink, with the loss of over 1,100 of her crewmen.

The battleship's hull remained where she sank, a tomb for many of those lost with her. In 1950, she began to be used as a site for memorial ceremonies, and, in the early 1960s a memorial structure was constructed over her midships hull.

It remains a memorial operated by the National Park Service.

Will there be ceremonies marking the anniversary?

Yes, there are annual commemorations of the attack to honor those lost. The events are livestreamed. Events include both public and private remembrances.

Many local veterans organizations also commemorate the event and may share details on their website or social media.

headline: US auto brands suffer as influential report hammers reliability of new tech, early adopters
fullText:
The reliability of hybrid and electric vehicles is improving, but U.S.-based brands continue to trail their competition, according to Consumer Reports’ influential 2025 Automotive Report Card.

From EV startups like Rivian and Tesla to established brands like Chevrolet, Ford and Jeep, brands that eagerly embraced new technologies routinely suffer quality woes, said Consumer Reports director of automotive testing Jake Fisher.

“It’s all about growing pains,” Fisher said. “Incremental changes equal greater reliability. Newer technologies, like electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, are less reliable.”

That simple rule applies across the board, he said. “Manufacturers who embrace the idea of incremental change do better. All the manufacturers in the top 10 keep systems and perfect them over years.”

That means even initially troublesome systems like BMW’s infamous iDrive can evolve from sore spot to selling point, as it has with the addition of simpler menus and a touch screen. BMW placed No. 8.

CR’s survey findings were announced Thursday at an online news conference hosted by the Detroit-based Automotive Press Association.

More: 54-mile EV range puts a charge in 2025 Mercedes GLC 350e plug-in hybrid

More: 2024 Chevrolet Equinox electric compact SUV sets the standard for price and range

Owners and road tests tell the story

Even the most reliable automakers have troublesome vehicles.

Subaru, the No. 1 brand for the first time ever this year, has one vehicle with below average predicted reliability — the Solterra, its first electric vehicle, which Toyota, the No. 3 overall brand, builds and sells as the bZ4X.

The rankings are based on Consumer Reports' own vehicle tests and reports from owners who subscribe to the publication.

CR defines a reliability problem as anything that requires down time or loss of function. It surveyed readers this spring and summer and crushed data on 300,000 vehicles from the 2000-25 model years and surveyed readers this spring and summer.

“Whenever there’s a new platform or new electronics, we expect problems,” Fisher said.

The variation within brands is so great that Fisher recommends shoppers use individual model ratings rather than the brand rankings for guidance.

Top-rated U.S.-based brands on reliability

  • Buick: 11
  • Ford: 13
  • Chevrolet: 16
  • Tesla: 17
  • Jeep: 19
  • GMC: 20
  • Cadillac: 21
  • Rivian: 22

Not every brand is on every list

Rivian rated last in CR’s overall list, which left out a number of prominent brands because of small sample sizes, including Chrysler, Dodge, Land Rover, Lincoln, Mercedes, Porsche and Ram.

Many of those did make lists broken down into mainstream and luxury cars, making the overall picture a bit complicated.

For instance, Chrysler is the highest-ranked U.S. mainstream brand at No. 8, a spot ahead of Buick. Tesla was 10th, followed by Ford.

Jeep ranked last among mainstream brands, Rivian last among luxury.

“U.S. brands are investing heavily in EVs,” Fisher said. “Some have been problematic for reliability.”

Cadillac dropped seven spots on the overall list — to 21st — solely because of early production problems with its electric Lyriq, for instance.

GM’s EV program hit full stride this year, as vehicles in every segment from compact SUV to full-size pickup and large luxury SUV hit the road.

“Time will tell” if widespread quality flaws remain an issue, Fisher said. "We need another year on the road to know.”

EVs and hybrids improve

The report shows rapid improvement among EVs and hybrids, which trailed the century-plus-old internal combustion engine (ICE) technology badly last year.

Hybrids now have the same average problem rate as ICE. Problems for EVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) both fell about 50% from last year.

EVs now have 42% more problems than ICE, versus 70% last year. PHEVs, which are in some ways the most complicated technology because they combine elements of ICE and EV, came in at 70% more problems — not much of a bragging point, except when compared with last year’s 146%.

“Strap in. We’re going hybrid,” Fisher said. “The consumer has spoken.”

headline: AG's Office says Michigan residents can deter porch pirates. Here's how
fullText:
If you're waiting for a Christmas package and want to ensure it arrives without being pilfered off your porch, state officials have some advice.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel's office is urging consumers to take proactive steps in protecting their packages from theft.

“Whether it's a package or a piece of mail, unattended deliveries are easy targets for porch pirates,” Nessel said in a release. “By planning ahead and taking security measures, you can make sure your well-deserved gifts and packages reach you safely while keeping thieves from stealing your holiday cheer.”

Nessel's office has launched a "Holiday Consumer Protection Campaign" focused on ways Michigan residents can protect their information. The campaign launched on Black Friday.

Why does package theft matter?

Nessel’s office noted that mail and package theft are leading causes of identity theft crimes.

With an increase in online shopping during the holidays, consumers face a heightened risk of "porch pirates," who target delivery packages, the AG office says.

Use secure delivery options to safeguard packages

Ship packages to a secure location, such as Amazon lockers, FedEx offices, or your workplace if permitted, the AG's Office said.

Improve visibility of your doorways to deter thieves

Keep your porch well-lit and consider adding motion-sensing lighting, the release said.

Create an illusion to make thieves believe you are home

Even when you're not home, make it look like someone is present by leaving lights or music on.

Use technology options to prevent theft

Install a porch camera or motion detector that can alert you to activity and allow you to monitor deliveries in real time.

Use the US Postal Service's free delivery tool

Consumers can use the USPS delivery tool that provides digital previews of incoming mail and allows user to track packages, reschedule deliveries and manage delivery instructions.

Are there penalties for theft?

First-time offenders can face fines and up to one year in jail for stealing mail or packages while repeat offenders' risk up to five years in prison under state and federal law.

Officials say if a package is stolen from your residence, you should first confirm that it was actually delivered. Then contact your local police department.

What else can I do to reduce ID theft chances?

Consumers can also reduce their risk by opting out of pre-approved credit offers, which thieves can use to apply for credit in someone else’s name.

To stop offers, opt out by visiting the official Consumer Credit Reporting Industry website or by calling 888-567-8688.

For additional consumer protection resources or to file a complaint, visit the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Team. 

Jalen Williams is a trending reporter at the Detroit Free Press. Contact him at jawilliams1@freepress.com.

headline: Experts predict surge in new car sales before Trump takes office
fullText:
With the presidential election in the rearview mirror, consumers have shifted from a wait-and-see approach to car buying to a better-buy-now attitude, industry watchers say.

That change in mindset is causing a surge in new vehicle sales that are expected to deliver a strong December that will continue into 2025, they said.

Research firm Cox Automotive said that while new-vehicle sales data for November is still trickling in, early results indicate that retail new vehicle sales are gaining momentum to finish the year higher than expected. Cox's final tally and analysis won't be available until early next week, but "all signs point to a surprise, hotter-than-expected result" and the market is poised to end the year on a strong note, wrote Mark Schirmer, director of industry insights and corporate communications in a news release Wednesday. 

The upswing in new car sales momentum is likely due in part to a postelection shift in consumer mindset, Cox chief economist Jonathan Smoke said. It is a move from "it's better to wait" to "better buy now."

His conclusion follows a quarterly dealer survey Cox did earlier this fall, which the Detroit Free Press reported in September, that showed 49% of franchised car dealers surveyed blamed the uncertainty around the political environment at that time for holding back business. Now that consumers know the election outcome, the new uncertainty centers on how the second Trump administration might change the auto landscape.

"If experience is our teacher, the future Trump administration will sound a lot like the prior Trump administration, where ongoing trade skirmishes roil the markets and stress the when-to-buy calculation that in-market shoppers face every day," Schirmer wrote.

GM hints at high November sales

Stellantis, which makes Chrysler, Dodge, Jeep, Ram and Fiat brands, does not release monthly sales data. General Motors also does not share its monthly sales figures, only quarterly. But in a presentation to investors Wednesday, GM CFO Paul Jacobson indicated the automaker moved a lot of metal, both in retail and fleet sales, during November.

“November was a strong month for us and for the industry,” Jacobson said. “We’re continuing to drive more EV momentum. I think we’ll probably end up around a 12% market share for EVs for ourselves, so we’re outpacing the general adoption rate."

Jacobson, who made those comments at the UBS Global Industrials and Transportation Conference in Florida, said GM sold 15,000 EVs during the month. Through the end of the year, he said, GM can further grow EV sales while preserving or increasing its market share of gasoline-powered vehicles. Jacobson said he is comfortable with GM's present level of inventory at dealerships, which is about a 50- to 60-day supply.

"It was also a good month for fleet," Jacobson said, but he did not provide any numbers.

Ford reports record sales

Crosstown, Ford Motor Co. does report its overall monthly sales. For November, Ford reported a sizable gain over the year-ago period and a record month for its EV sales.

In total, Ford sold 166,373 vehicles in November, a 14.3% increase from November 2023 and outpacing the industry sales increase of 11%. Sales of EVs hit a monthly record of 10,821, a 20.8% increase from the year-ago period. Year to date, Ford has sold 84,774 EVs.

A main driver for Ford's sales growth last month was the F-Series pickup, with sales totaling 67,459 for the month, up 27.1%. Ford said it was the F-Series best November sales since pre-COVID in November 2019.

Ford's luxury brand, Lincoln, reported sales up nearly 49% driven by new product. The new Nautilus doubled its sales with 3,292 SUVs sold, its best November sales results in 17 years, making it now the best-selling vehicle in the Lincoln portfolio.

Unknowns ahead, so buy while you can

But once Jan. 20 hits and President-elect Donald Trump reenters the White House, uncertainty will once again rule what goes down on dealership lots.

Trump has expressed disdain for EVs and has talked about repealing parts of the Inflation Reduction Act. Most observers expect him to wipe away the $7,500 federal tax credit provided on many EV purchases.

Trump has also threatened 25% tariffs on goods from Mexico and Canada, which would require the Detroit Three to make adjustments to their manufacturing. GM, Ford and Stellantis have factories in Mexico and Canada that make vehicles sold in the U.S.

If that happens, it could raise costs for the automakers, but on Wednesday GM's Jacobson stopped short of saying whether the automaker would pass those prices onto consumers. He did say GM has several plans in the works to react to any of the possible Trump moves. Stellantis leadership also addressed the topic of tariffs on Wednesday indicating there's a possibility of shifting production if Trump imposes high tariffs.

Analysts at Cox noted the recent rhetoric around what Trump might do is good for short-term car sales.

"Goodbye, national EV tax credits? Possible. Shutting the leasing loopholes? Maybe. Tariffs on vehicles from Mexico and Canada? Could be. Or maybe not," Schirmer wrote. "The future is unknown, but for in-market buyers, none of the known unknowns suggest a wait-and-see attitude is a winning strategy. Best to buy now."

December deals ahead

Cox senior economist Charlie Chesbrough said there may be more pent-up demand than data crunchers initially estimated.

"I think the consumer may surprise us a bit in the coming months," Chesbrough said, "as consumers put the national election behind them and take stock of the better loan rates, improved financing deals and a lot more incentives. After a relatively slow summer, the retail market seems to be coming alive at year's end."

More: Stellantis CFO: Automaker could shift production to US to cope with tariffs

More: If Trump relaxes regulations, GM may offer fewer hybrids, EVs, CFO says

As the Free Press reported last month, the shift to more supply in the second half brought down the average used and new vehicle list prices from the year-ago period, CarGurus, an online new and used vehicle shopping site, said in its U.S. 2024 October Intelligence Report. The average used vehicle list price in October fell to $28,200, 5% lower than a year ago, when the average price was $29,700. The average listing price for a new vehicle in October was $49,700, down from $50,700 a year ago.Cox data showed in October the average incentive spend by automakers was up 60% compared with the year-ago period. Cox said in October that automakers spent an average of $3,708 in incentives per vehicle, compared with $2,305 in October 2023. It was at the highest point since early 2021, Chesbrough said, predicting that November likely saw even more discounting. When the full results are in and analyzed, if the November new vehicle sales turn out to be near a 16.5 million vehicle annual sales pace, it would be the strongest pace in more than three years, he said.

With growing inventories and additional discounts, Cox analysts predict December will deliver too.

headline: Detroit Tigers re-sign Wilmer Flores, Eddys Leonard to minor league contracts
fullText:
Two former prospects are returning to the Detroit Tigers in the 2025 season.

The Tigers re-signed right-handed reliever Wilmer Flores and infielder Eddys Leonard to minor league contracts. Both players received a non-roster invitation to MLB spring training, according to sources with knowledge of the agreements. For now, they have been assigned to Triple-A Toledo.

Flores, 23, will earn $1 million if he makes the majors; Leonard, 24, will earn $760,000 if he makes the majors.

IN THE MAJORS: Can Wenceel Pérez become super utility player? Here's what Tigers think

The two former prospects were removed by the Tigers from the 40-man roster Nov. 19, non-tendered into free agency Nov. 22, then re-signed by the Tigers to minor league deals Nov. 23. The Tigers cut Flores and Leonard from the 40-man roster to create space for new prospects who needed protection from the upcoming Rule 5 draft.

Both players had injury-riddled 2024 seasons.

[ MUST LISTEN: Make "Days of Roar" your go-to Detroit Tigers podcast, available anywhere you listen to podcasts (Apple, Spotify) ]

Flores — the younger brother of San Francisco Giants infielder Wilmer Flores — posted a 7.84 ERA with 25 walks (16.3% walk rate) and 29 strikeouts (19% strikeout rate) across 31 innings in 20 games, including 16 games in Triple-A Toledo.

For the Mud Hens, he registered an 8.53 ERA with 24 walks and 23 strikeouts across 25⅓ innings. Although Flores finished the season healthy, he missed more than three months on the injured list with a right shoulder injury.

MORE ABOUT HIM: Tigers prospect Wilmer Flores throws 99.9 mph, seeks to be 'power pitcher' again

His four-seam fastball averaged 95.8 mph, maxing out at 99.9 mph. His slider generated a 34.6% whiff rate and his curveball generated a 46.7% whiff rate. He showcased an above-average pitch mix, but he struggled to locate his pitches inside the strike zone.

Flores needs to put the finishing touches on his development as a pitcher before he will be able to reach his potential as a high-leverage reliever in the big leagues.

Leonard, whom the Tigers acquired from the Los Angeles Dodgers in August 2023, hit .253 with 11 home runs, 21 walks (6.3% walk rate) and 86 strikeouts (25.7% strikeout rate) in 82 games, including 67 games in Triple-A Toledo. For the Mud Hens, he hit .263 with 10 homers, 17 walks and 74 strikeouts, posting a .781 OPS.

He suffered two injuries that forced him to spend more than two months on the injured list: a left oblique strain from early April to late May and a right hamstring strain from late June to late July.

MORE ABOUT HIM: Tigers' Eddys Leonard does not care where he plays. Just put him in the lineup

He averaged a lower-than-expected 86.8 mph exit velocity, but despite some flashes of hard contact (such as a maximum exit velocity of 114.3 mph), he had a Javier Báez-esque 31.9% whiff rate. (For comparison, Triple-A Toledo teammate Justice Bigbie averaged an 89.7 mph exit velocity with a 24.1% whiff rate.)

Leonard is infield depth in Triple-A Toledo. He has experience at shortstop, second base and third base, along with limited reps in the outfield, but until he cuts down on his swing-and-miss rate, he might be stuck in the minor leagues.

headline: Michigan's State's 'Zeke' gets his own bobblehead. Yes, fur real
fullText:
Michigan State fans can enjoy a bit of wobbly fun by purchasing the first bobblehead of Zeke the WonderDog, celebrating MSU's longstanding unofficial mascot for on the animal's 10th birthday.

The licensed bobblehead produced by the National Bobblehead Hall of Fame and Museum, in conjunction with university and Zeke's handlers, is available for purchase, the museum announced Thursday.

“Zeke promotes Spartan love,” said Jim Foley, Zeke’s trainer.  “From the tailgates to the end zone, his charm and charisma have made him a fan favorite, uniting Spartans everywhere with a love for the game and a dog that truly represents the heart of MSU."

The bobblehead is $30 to purchase. Fans who buy the bobblehead during the presale can expect it to ship in April 2025.

Michigan State has a canine mascot?

Yes, more than one. In 1977, the tradition began after Ezekiel placed second in the World Canine Catch and Fetch Championship in Pasadena, California. He was 3 and had won the national semifinals a day earlier.

Once word surfaced that Ezekiel held his own in competitions, he was invited by Eddie Rutherford, a Michigan State athletic department official, to perform at a football game. 

After that game, the invites kept coming. Ezekiel's reputation soared to the point that he was given the name "Zeke the Wonderdog" by a Lansing State Journal reporter after one of his first shows.  

When the football season kicked off in 2018, Zeke the Wonderdog IV — all 55 pounds of him — extended the tradition. 

What's the National Bobblehead Museum?

The National Bobblehead Hall of Fame and Museum's founders began collecting in 2004 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The bobblehead museum collection opened in 2019 and has about 10,000 of sport teams and figures from around the world.

What other Michigan-based sports figures can I find?

The National Bobblehead Hall of Fame and Museum has a cutout of the Grizz, the official mascot of Oakland University and a bobblehead to celebrate the 2023 Michigan football national championship.

What MSU figures are depicted?

What University of Michigan figures can I find?

There is a Michigan-Minnesota football bobblehead, the national championship bobble and a top 25 tracker.

headline: Detroit Lions picks vs Green Bay Packers: Will the Lions clinch a playoff berth?
fullText:
OK, while we count down the minutes to the Detroit Lions’ “Thursday Night Football” game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field tonight (8:15 p.m., Amazon Prime Video and WJBK-TV in Detroit), let’s go over what’s at stake.

The Lions already made history last week with their first 11-1 start in franchise history. Likewise, a win would give them the first 12-1 start in franchise history.

Then there’s the streak: The Lions’ current 10-win run is tied for the longest in franchise history, set way back in 1934 — their first season in Detroit after moving from Portsmouth, Ohio — when they opened with 10 straight (all shutouts, a franchise streak that likely won’t be matched any time soon) … then lost three straight to finish the season three games back of the undefeated Chicago Bears. So a win would set the franchise mark in consecutive wins, too.

THE GAME: Lions host Packers in key Thursday night showdown: 'We're in playoff football right now'

(And because we know you were wondering: 33 teams in NFL history have won 11 straight in a season with 26 of those coming in the Super Bowl era. And of those 26? 13 made the Super Bowl, and seven won it. And since the NFL went to a 16-game schedule in 1978 — and 17 games in 2021 — there’ve been 22 teams with 11-game streaks, with 10 making the Super Bowl and five winning it.)

And, of course, that brings us to the big prize: A win tonight would lock up a playoff berth for the Lions — with four games still to go. They’re not out of it with a loss, though — there’s a bunch of scenarios, but if the Lions lose, they’ll be rooting against the Falcons (playing the Vikings), the Buccaneers (playing the Raiders) the Cardinals (playing the Seahawks) and the Rams (playing the Bills). Losses by one of the two NFC South teams and both of the NFC West teams would lock up a spot for the Lions, too.

So, will the Lions lock up a playoff berth tonight, or will they have to do some scoreboard/Red Zone Channel watching on Sunday? Four Free Press sports writers have their thoughts.

Dave Birkett

The Lions are riding a league-best 10-game winning streak and have looked like the best team in the NFL for much of that stretch. They have a high-powered offense, a playmaking defense and one of the best kicking games around, but their roster has been decimated by injury and that’s the league’s great equalizer this time of year.

The Packers are a good football team and mostly healthy right now, while the Lions need nametags to know who’s lining up next to each other. They’ll have to shut down Jacobs, win the turnover battle and outscore Green Bay to win this game, all things they’re capable of doing. But in a division game with so much on the line for both teams, I think points will be tough to come by and the Lions’ winning streak will come to an end. The pick: Packers 27, Lions 24.

Carlos Monarrez

Sure, the Lions have won 10 straight games, and they’re the class of the NFC. But they got lucky against the Bears and they haven’t had a resounding win against a good opponent since they beat the Texans a month ago. With injuries piling up on defense, this one will come down to Ben Johnson matching the Packers’ hot offense, and then Jake Bates’ leg in overtime. The pick: Lions 30, Packers 27 (OT) .

Jeff Seidel

At some point, all these injuries are gonna come back to bite the Lions. At some point, it’s not sustainable.

But at this point? This is a monster game for the Lions in their quest to get homefield advantage in the playoffs. Offensive coordinator Ben Johnson will dial up just enough explosive plays, Dan Campbell will make just enough calculated risks, and Jared Goff will flirt with perfection again — back in Ford Field — as the Lions will simply outscore the Packers. The pick: Lions 31, Packers 27.

Shawn Windsor

The Lions are due for a stumble, and the injuries keep mounting. But it’s hard to pick against a team playing with the secrets of the universe. Jared Goff and the offense haven’t played a complete game in a minute, and they will need to against Green Bay. Here’s guessing they do, and hang on in the end. The pick: Lions 29, Packers 26.

headline: Couch: Invigorated, Jonathan Smith offers illuminating look at MSU football's recruiting, NIL and hopes for the future
fullText:
EAST LANSING – Jonathan Smith looked and sounded Wednesday like a coach who’d had a good 24 hours and his first winning fourth quarter in a while. In this case, a strong finish to a recruiting class that will be part of the backbone of whatever he and his staff are able to build at Michigan State.

It was an illuminating half-hour with MSU’s now second-year football coach, four days after the end of a 5-7 first season that wrapped without any positive momentum.

Hours earlier Wednesday, running back Jace Clarizio and defensive back Aydan West — two of the more coveted members of MSU’s 2025 recruiting class — had provided a needed jolt from a sinkhole of negativity that had ensnared a depressed fan base. Their signatures saying they intend to play football at MSU certainly elevated Smith’s state of mind, too. West had rebuffed a late push from Ohio State and Virginia Tech to keep his pledge to the Spartans. Clarizio, the hometown star at East Lansing, who had flipped his commitment from MSU to Alabama recently, flipped back to MSU at the 11th hour.

“You just keep competing,” Smith said of convincing Clarizio to stay home and come to MSU. “All of us felt really, really confident that our place was a great fit for him, and not just because he is a couple of miles away from the campus. The relationships we built, learning him, his personality type, his attributes, his family, that we got the chance to (build that relationship) that over a long period of time, and so you just keep competing, all the way until the end. And really reassuring, re-echoing some messages (about) where we're headed with this program, how he fits, how he's got an opportunity to be a legacy at this place.”

RELATED: East Lansing's Jace Clarizio finds way back to MSU football: 'Something in my head just switched'

Until recently, the December signing day — which used to be three weeks later — was the defining moment of an offseason, entirely telling of the program’s direction. Now it’s just a start, falling days ahead of the opening of the transfer portal (Dec. 9, which will open again in the spring). Plus, high school prospects are no longer bound by letters of intent. They’re free to change their mind until they enroll. Eleven of MSU’s 18 high school signees are planning to enroll in January. So, in four weeks time, MSU will have them for sure for four months. What a world. 

The Spartans’ 18-member class is far from acclaimed — 247 Sports' composite rankings have MSU's class pegged in the 50s nationally. But having West and Clarizio, along with four-star prospects Derrick Simmons, a defensive lineman from Frankenmuth, and linebacker Charles White, from Orchard Lake St. Mary’s, gives this group more juice than it might have had.

RELATED: Meet Michigan State football's 2025 recruiting class, highlighted by LB Charles White

“We believe in us,” Smith said, “and so I think (those top guys choosing us) shows a great direction of where we're headed. I'll say this, though: We are going to make our own evaluation, too … whether they're highly sought after (or) guys that have great senior years and continue to work and fit us. We want to be able to compete at the highest level. And also trust deeply our own evaluation.”

You might have heard the same thing from Mark Dantonio and Co. early in his tenure, when his classes weren’t knocking anyone’s socks off. The best players from Dantonio’s first couple classes were all relatively unheralded, several of them two-star recruits, back when that was a more of a thing. So if Dantonio is the benchmark for MSU football coaches, there is nothing about Smith's early recruiting to suggest he's behind. 

Where Dantonio has Smith beat is post-first-year vibes. The Spartans finished that 2007 season 7-6 and playing pretty well. Moreover, after they lost to Michigan that year, Dantonio delivered a sermon on the mount for the ages that Sunday, including, “It’s not over. It'll never be over here. It's just starting.” Smith did not come close to such a response this season. 

They are different men, different personalities. And those were different times. Dantonio’s first team didn’t require 61 new players. The transfer portal didn’t exist. 

On the other hand, the transfer portal today cannot be seen as a detriment. Only a tool. If you’re looking for promising signs from Smith, perhaps this is one: He sees MSU’s recruiting classes being close to 50-50 between high school prospects and transfers each year. And he doesn't sound at all deterred by that.

“Early on (in the portal era), I still liked the idea of majority high school (recruits) and you supplement through the portal,” Smith said. “But with this landscape and with so much movement and player freedom to move, we're not going to (say we) have to get to 50-50, but I just think that might be a reality.”

Perhaps another positive sign: Smith didn’t try to downplay the importance of NIL for his program or sound like he's short on resources to do the job this offseason. He repeatedly thanked MSU’s primary football collective, Greg Williams-led Spartan Nation NIL, for helping to sign his latest recruiting class, and for allowing MSU to set itself up to retain its roster and, next week, go after transfers.

“It was a vital, vital part (of all of it) as we continue to build this program,” Smith said.

The counter would be this: If NIL isn't at all a limitation for MSU, wouldn't Smith and Co. have been able to land a few more heralded high school recruits?

“I’m not here to say stars don't mean anything at all,” Smith said, talking about his class and the recruiting rankings. “Again, I go back to, we will trust our evaluations.”

It’s also clear that Smith is looking forward to July 1, when schools like MSU begin to pay athletes out of their own budgets, about $22 million annually for all sports — a lot of that will go to football — part of the revenue sharing agreement from the House v. NCAA settlement.

That’ll be a better system, though outside NIL will still play a role, especially at the top of the sport. 

“We're definitely having conversations on the revenue-share side, and that kick-starts July 1, and that being a piece of the pie,” Smith said. “And then I go back to Spartan Nation NIL. Huge. And they need to continue to be through January to the July 1 timeline, and in regards to packages that were discussed when recruiting and retaining a roster.

“I think we want to be in a constant state of improvement across our program — coaches, players, and then outside, Spartan Nation NIL. It makes a big difference, but I’m confident in our approach, as we continue to improve, to be able to compete at the highest level in recruiting over the next six months.”

Also coming before next season: A change in roster sizes, down to 105 total players, though football teams can have up to 105 scholarships, rather than the 85 they have now. It seems unlikely most schools will do that, because it’s an unnecessary number, eats up more of the revenue share, eliminates walk-ons and all but requires that you take those 20 scholarships from other men’s sports. 

Smith said right now MSU is operating under the plan of having 85 scholarships for next season, keeping 20 walk-on spots.

He sounded invigorated Wednesday to a degree he hasn’t in more than month — since MSU beat Iowa in October. It’s as if there was nothing the coaches could do to stop the bleeding at the end of the season and they knew it. Now the season’s over and the bleeding’s done — cauterized by getting Clarizio to reconsider MSU and West to stay solid in his commitment. 

Maybe that’s as much perception as reality, but the same could be argued about the dismal outlook on life after a tough November in Year 1.

“We got to get better,” Smith said. “I am optimistic with some of the young talent that is currently on the roster. I think about Aidan (Chiles), watching his development his first year as a starter and really statistically on the back half of the season, he improved. You can blatantly see it on paper, let alone watching it on the tape. We've got some good young talent around him on the perimeter. We’ve got to take a step at the line of scrimmage. And again, we got a couple players that have a chance to be back and get better. We’ve got some young talent that needs to continue to work and then we’ve got to add to that position. 

“You flip it on the other side. Same thing. We’ve got some young talent that got some meaningful reps, especially in the back end. And those guys taking a step will be important. So I got some confidence. Again, this is a big month to add.”

Smith knows fans aren’t happy right now. He wasn't blind to the empty seats at Spartan Stadium on Saturday. 

“You want people excited about what the product is and where we're headed and all that,” he said. “I understand it was Thanksgiving weekend, it was cold and all of that. So I’m not panicking. There's another piece of motivation. You look around and where the game ended, how many people are in the seats — which I appreciate everybody who stayed to the end. But I'm using that as a motivator of how fulfilling it's going to be when this place is packed again and we're playing for our 11th or 12th win.”

That’s all anyone is asking.
