headline: Why this metro Phoenix town was once the Hay Capital of the World
fullText:
Once known as the hay capital of the world, Gilbert is now the largest town in America with a population approaching 290,000.

Although Gilbert dons the title of a "town," it's far from it. Gilbert is the fourth largest municipality in metro Phoenix with a population larger than Salt Lake City and St. Louis. It ranks in the top 100 largest cities in the nation.

Gilbert is estimated to approach build-out by 2030 with a population of 330,000. It's home to top employers like GoDaddy, Banner Health, Dignity Healthy and Deloitte.

The town had explosive growth in the late 1990s, and it celebrated the centennial anniversary of its incorporation in 2020.

Here’s what to know about the history of Gilbert including how it got its name and when it was founded.

When was Gilbert founded?

Gilbert was founded in 1891 when the first homestead was purchased in the area. The town was incorporated on July 6, 1920.

Here's the history: Where did metro Phoenix streets get their names?

How did Gilbert get its name?

The town got its namesake from William “Bobby” Gilbert who sold a part of his land for the Phoenix and Eastern Railroad in 1902.  

The rail line was laid in 1903 and 1905, and a depot was built on the acquired property. The building was called the Gilbert Depot, which established the town’s name.

Gilbert is buried in an unmarked grave in the Mesa Cemetery.

What is the history of Gilbert?

The construction of the Roosevelt Damn and the Eastern and Consolidated Canals in the early 1900s, two key water projects in Arizona, helped Gilbert prosper as a farming community.

Gilbert residents farmed alfalfa, dairy and cotton in the early days of the town which gave the town its reputation as the hay capital of the world.  During the World War I period, Gilbert farmers supplied the U.S. Army with hay for their horses, according to the Gilbert Historical Museum.

Ten years before Gilbert was incorporated, A. W. Ayers opened the first store in the town. It served as a place for to buy groceries, shoes and dry goods.

As the decades went on, Gilbert remained a tiny town even while other neighboring cities began to grow in size and population. Anticipating growth, the Town Council annexed 53 square miles of unincorporated county land in the 1970s.

That decision helped Gilbert become one the largest municipalities in Maricopa County.

headline: Holiday ice rinks 2024: Here's where to skate outdoors in metro Phoenix
fullText:
Just because you live in the desert doesn't mean you can't partake in one of the most beloved winter traditions: outdoor ice skating.

There are pop-up outdoor holiday skating rinks in Scottsdale, Glendale and Mesa, plus a slew of indoor rinks open year-round if that's your preference.

Skaters of all ages and abilities are welcome — and rental skates and socks are available.

If you're looking to live out your Hallmark Christmas movie dreams this year, here's where you can go holiday ice skating in metro Phoenix for Christmas 2024.

Looking for the best things to do in Arizona? Sign up for our newsletter. 

Fairmont Scottsdale Princess: Christmas at the Princess

What's better than experiencing a winter wonderland of holiday lights surrounded by the Sonoran Desert while skating with family and friends at Christmas at the Princess, the resort's signature winter event?

The Desert Ice Rink encompasses 6,000 square feet of real ice, and the Alpine Skate Trail winds through the heart of the property. A pass for unlimited skating costs $35 in addition to admission to Christmas at the Princess.

Details: 5-10 p.m. Mondays-Thursdays, 4-11 p.m. Fridays-Sundays, through Jan 4. Fairmont Scottsdale Princess, 7575 E. Princess Drive. Admission is $35; parking is an extra $35. scottsdaleprincess.com.

Skate Westgate in Glendale

The real-ice rink at Skate Westgate is back at the Westgate Entertainment District in Glendale. All skill levels are welcome, and tickets can be purchased near the rink in Fountain Park.

Admission with skate rental for adults and children is $25, $19 if you bring your own skates. Toddlers with shoe sizes between 9T and 12T can skate for $19. Military members with ID can skate for $19 with skate rental.

Details: 4-9:45 p.m. Mondays-Fridays, 11 a.m.-10:45 p.m. Saturdays, through Jan. 20. Westgate Entertainment District, 6770 N. Sunrise Blvd., Glendale. westgateaz.com.

Winter Wonderland Ice Rink in Mesa

Boasting 6,000 square feet of real ice, the Winter Wonderland Ice Rink is at City Plaza at Mesa City Center.

Admission includes one hour on the ice and your skate rental; there's no discount if you bring your own skates. You can register at merrymainst.com to pay in advance for a specific 60-minute session. A limited number of walk-up registrations will be accommodated per session.

Details: 5-10 p.m. Mondays-Fridays, noon-10 p.m. Saturdays-Sundays through Jan 12. City Plaza at Mesa City Center, 56 E. Main St. $10 for one hour; includes skate rental. merrymainst.com.

AZ Ice in Arcadia, Gilbert and Peoria

If you prefer to skate indoors, AZ Ice has three indoor ice skating locations that offer public skating year-round.

The Arcadia location has one ice surface, a restaurant, bar and coffee shop.

The Gilbert and Peoria locations each have two ice surfaces, two restaurants and a bar.

Public skate times vary daily. Check the schedules at azicearcadia.com, azicegilbert.com and azicepeoria.com.

Details: AZ Ice Arcadia, 3853 E. Thomas Road, Phoenix. AZ Ice Gilbert, 2305 E. Knox Road. AZ Ice Peoria, 15829 N. 83rd Ave. $11 per session; $9.50 for ages 4-12; $7.50 for ages 55 and up; $5.50 for military; free for age 3 and under; skate rental is $4. azicearcadia.com, azicegilbert.com, and azicepeoria.com.

Ice Den in Chandler and Scottsdale

Both Ice Den locations offer public skating year-round in addition to being home to numerous amateur hockey clubs and junior teams as well as hosting USA Hockey and U.S. Figure Skating Association tournaments.

The Scottsdale location features three NHL regulation ice surfaces while the Chandler location has two. For public skating, reserve your day and time online in advance. Registration opens 48 hours ahead and closes when it hits capacity or one hour prior to the session.

Check the public skating calendar at icedenchandler.com and icedenscottsdale.com.

Details: Ice Den Chandler, 7225 W. Harrison St. Ice Den Scottsdale, 9375 E. Bell Road. $14 for two hours; includes skate rental. icedenchandler.com, icedenscottsdale.com.

headline: Daniel Craig trades James Bond for William S. Burroughs in fantastically ruinous 'Queer'
fullText:
Luca Guadagnino has a thing about stares.

The director held Timothée Chalamet’s face in the frame for an extended period at the end of “Call Me By Your Name” as Sufjan Stevens’ “Mystery of Love” plays. That stare alone helped make Chalamet a star.

Daniel Craig is already a star — a former James Bond, no less. In Guadagnino’s sumptuously strange “Queer,” Craig also stares at length into the camera, though the situations are markedly different. Chalamet’s character just had his heart broken. Craig’s just shot his arm full of heroin.

This isn’t the end of the film, however. It’s somewhere in the middle and a part of William Lee’s life. Craig plays the character, based on William S. Burroughs, on whose short novel the film is in turn based, with a workaday sense of emotional letdown, the edges of his disappointments worn down until he wears them like he wears his rumpled, dirty white suits in the heat of Mexico — with a kind of wounded aplomb.

Is 'Queer' based on a true story?

Burroughs had a wild life. (The repeated William Tell-like instances of people putting glasses on top of their heads as targets in the film have particular real-life significance.) Lee, the movie version of the writer, is in Mexico in the early 1950s, on the run from weapons and drug charges. He smokes and drinks all day, is a heroin addict and obsessively wonders who among the other people in the village where he lives are gay. “Are you queer?” is, to him, the most pressing question he can ask someone.

Or want to ask. It’s the one he’s dying to ask Euguene Allerton (Drew Starkey), with whom he first locks eyes at a cockfight. Lee has encounters with plenty of other men — there is a fairly thriving gay community in town — but he’s taken with Allerton. Allerton also seems taken with Lee, except when he isn’t. He’ll flirt with Lee and then ignore him, playing chess with a woman in the same crummy little bar every night.

Well, not every night. After a couple of weeks of hanging out intermittently, Lee and Allerton consummate their relationship (the film does not shy away from explicit sex scenes). But if Lee had hoped for a more consistent relationship with Allerton, he doesn’t get one. If anything, Allerton seems intermittently disgusted with Lee and himself, then attracted to Lee again. Nothing about Lee, including his relationships, is healthy.

Then, the movie changes. Lee invites (begs) Allerton to take a trip farther south. He is in search of yage, which Lee believes promotes telepathic powers; he read about it in a magazine and thinks the Russians are using it for mind control. (Again, the real-life Burroughs was wild.) The tonal shift goes from melancholy dissipation to ruinously adventurous.

And the filmmaking goes bonkers, mostly in a good way. Lee and Allerton show up at the viper-protected hut of Dr. Cotter (Lesley Manville, having a grand old time), fully deranged and paranoid and living with a younger man (Lisandro Alonso) in the middle of the jungle. She knows all about yage. There’s a bit where Lee, not exactly an experienced explorer, falls while hunting (don’t ask). It won’t get you high, at least not like you’re used to, she tells Lee. He looks at her quizzically. I’m a medical doctor, she explains. I can spot a junkie from a mile away.

Daniel Craig leaves James Bond fully behind

She’s right about the yage, though perhaps not in the way Lee thought she meant. Of all the trips Lee has been on, this one is definitely different. Guadagnino leans into the druggy freakout, melding bodies, making skin translucent and glowing, perhaps giving Lee what he was looking for, perhaps giving him more than he bargained for.

At 2 hours and 17 minutes, the film is a little bloated, though the expansiveness and inventiveness of the filmmaking make that sound like complaining about too much dessert. Adding to it all is both the score, by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and the anachronistic soundtrack, with songs by Nirvana, among other bands. Kurt Cobain and Burroughs once collaborated on a project in one of those weird confluences of pop culture that feels right at home here.

What a trip.

'Queer' 4 stars

Fair ★★★ Bad ★★ Bomb ★

headline: These 3 Arizona cities were named among the best places to retire in the US. But are they?
fullText:
Arizona is commonly thought of as a golden place to spend your golden years, with many retirees moving here to take advantage of the relatively low cost of living and mild weather (excluding, of course, the summer).

But how do cities in Arizona actually stack up against other popular retirement locales? According to an analysis by USA TODAY, Arizona is actually the 15th most expensive state to retire in. For 25 years of retirement here, one would need to save at least $1.05 million.

Here's how Arizona cities ranked on the national level, according to two different lists that compiled the best places to retire in the United States.

Tucson outranks Phoenix as best place to retire

U.S. News & World Report looked at the most populous cities in the U.S. and ranked them by six categories: happiness, affordability, quality of health care, retiree taxes, general desirability and strength of the job market.

Each of the categories was calculated using a mix of relevant data sets. For example, "happiness" was scored based on the crime rate and air quality, among other factors.

Tucson was ranked No. 45 on the list of 150 cities, largely for its low cost of living, rich history and natural landscape.

Phoenix still ranked high for retirees

The greater Phoenix area was ranked the 52nd best place to retire by U.S. News & World Report. Phoenix's thriving job market, nice winter weather and low cost of living compared with coastal cities were all reasons for the ranking.

More: This is the wealthiest city in Arizona. Spoiler: It's not Scottsdale

Scottsdale also named 6th best place to retire

WalletHub analyzed 182 cities earlier this year and found that Scottsdale is the sixth best place to retire in the U.S., especially due to the high quality of life it offers.

Scottsdale, along with Pearl City, Hawaii, has the highest share of the population aged 65 and older. Scottsdale also outpaced other cities in the categories of quality of life, activities available, and health care quality, which earned the city a high spot in the list despite its poor performance in the affordability rank.

Scottsdale came in 110th for cost of living, making it one of the lowest-ranking states for that category.

Yet, Scottsdale offers higher quality health care and plenty of enjoyable activities for retirees compared to most U.S. cities, which is why WalletHub still named it among the top.

These Arizona cities were ranked among the worst places to retire

Of the 182 cities Wallethub analyzed, several Arizona cities were among the worst cities to retire.

Glendale was named the 64th, with low scores in affordability and access to health care. Mesa was ranked the 76th worst city to retire for similar reasons, according to Wallethub's analysis.

headline: Jose Feliciano on 'Feliz Navidad,' 'Light My Fire' and that national anthem
fullText:
Leer en español

Jose Feliciano had no intention of writing a holiday standard when he met with producer Rick Jarrard on a hot summer day in the singer’s LA home to discuss the track list for a Christmas album they were planning to record.

The Puerto Rican singer-guitarist had cracked the U.S. English-speaking market two years earlier when his distinctive reinvention of the Doors song “Light My Fire” peaked at No. 3 on Billboard’s Hot 100, fueling the success of 1968’s “Feliciano!” album, which hit No. 2.

It was Jarrard who suggested Feliciano try and come up with his own song for the Christmas album instead of just doing seasonal standards.

In a matter of minutes, Feliciano had written a holiday classic for the ages, “Feliz Navidad,” which made its way to No. 6 on Billboard’s Hot 100 in December 2020, 50 years after the single’s initial release and 10 years after its induction to the Grammy Hall of Fame.

We caught up with Feliciano in advance of a show that’s been billed as A Festive Evening of Feliz Navidad and his Classic Hits at the Celebrity Theatre in Phoenix to talk about the history of that classic song and more.

The story behind Jose Feliciano's hit 'Feliz Navidad'

Question: You're doing a show called A Festive Evening of Feliz Navidad. Could you talk a bit about the writing of that song and the feeling that inspired it?

Answer: You know, we really love that story about "Feliz Navidad" and how it came to be.

I was working on a Christmas album for RCA in 1970 with my producer, Rick Jarrard, who had produced my “Feliciano!" album with "Light My Fire" and "California Dreamin’." We were great friends, and one day, he was at our house in California working on a song list for a Christmas LP.  

We had a beautiful album in place that we felt recounted the “Greatest Story Ever Told," so to speak, and we wanted it to be just perfect.

Then he comes to me and says, “Jose, you know, you should really think about writing a new Christmas song for this album." And I remember thinking, “Oh Rick, I love you, but how do you expect me to compete with Irving Berlin or Brenda Lee? I mean, I don’t really think I could do that.” So he goes, “Just think about it; just give it a shot.” 

So, I sat down and started doodling a little bit, and a few minutes later, there was "Feliz Navidad." Just like that. I played it for him, and he said, “Jose, that’s just perfect. Thank you." I remember saying, “Oh, Rick, but it’s too simple; it’ll never go anywhere.” We always laughed when we talked about the day. 

Best Christmas songs of all time: 30 seasonal favorites for your holiday playlist

Q: You talked to NPR about missing your family and feeling very lonely when you wrote it, and yet it’s such a festive song. How did you manage to turn such melancholy feelings into such a happy song?

A: That’s a great question, but I have no idea. I guess it’s a little bit of who I am: a little of both when I can take what’s maybe melancholy and make the best of it, right?

Q: I’ve read that it was summer when you wrote it. How did you get in the Christmas spirit in an LA summer?

A: Yes, it was a hot July summer day; in fact during a heat wave. It was rough to bring some Christmas spirit into the room, but I think we did a good job. It’s a beautiful album, and I’m very proud of it to this day.Q: How did you manage to write it that quickly?

A: You know, it was one of those deals where the tune came to me, and I just sang along with it. I did a pass with some lyric,s and there was a little song. I had no idea, it just came to me.

Q: How did you decide to make it a bilingual song?

A: I didn’t decide anything. I started thinking, I started singing, I started playing, and there it was. That’s who I am, so I guess it was just a little bit of me reliving the feeling of my Christmas cultures as they’d merged together over the years.

Q: Did it feel like a seasonal standard when you finished writing it?

A: No, not necessarily. It was a nice song that we enjoyed putting together in the studio. Rick played the coronet. I played the bass and guitars while Paulinho (Magalhaes) played the drums and percussion. Rick put some festive horns on it and we were happy it went on the album, but you know, the business is fickle and you don’t know what’s going to catch.

Q: What was it like to see it grow into a Christmas standard?

A: I guess it was somewhere in the '80s where a German group called Boney M did a cover of it and I think it did quite well, so that was cool. I hadn't expected anything like that, but then it just happened. How does that feel? Well, you know, it feels pretty good, makes me quite happy. And very grateful.

Q: That song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2010. How did it feel to receive that honor 40 years after releasing the song?

A: I was surprised and very happy, but more than anything, very grateful.  Just grateful. God is good.

Q: So many artists have covered "Feliz Navidad." There was even an album’s worth of covers a few years back. Do any stand out in your mind as being particularly good or that made you especially happy or proud?

A: Oh no, not really,  I just love them all. You know, the little kids singing together in their school assemblies, the guys in the mall playing their instruments and making some happy noise, choirs in holiday pageants. Artists whom I also respect. It’s all good.Q: Are there other Christmas songs you especially enjoy performing at these holiday-themed concerts?

A: I particularly love "The Little Drummer Boy" That means a lot to me because I can relate to it. All I have to give, really, is my music.  I love "Silent Night." I do a verse in Spanish as well as, of course, in English. Then Rick wrote a song some years ago called "On This Christmas Night." I don’t perform it live. It’s almost too emotional for me to do so, as it’s so poignant. You can hear it on my website on Radio Feliz. It actually opens the collection on the music player. It’s just such a beautiful song. I love Christmas music.

'Light My Fire': The song that made Jose Feliciano famous

Q: You broke through in the ‘60s with your classic reinvention of the Doors song “Light My Fire.” Could you talk about what drew you to that song and how you went about making it your own?

A: Man, that’s another Rick story. I just came to LA from New York where I was signed by RCA. The label wanted to record me there. They set me up with a successful and talented staff producer, Richard Jarrard. Rick came to the Golden Bear in Huntington Beach, where I was playing, to listen to my set.

He didn’t want it to be an album of my performances, really, but there were a few songs, you know, from what I did on stage, that he wanted to record. So, towards the end of the session, he said, “Hey Jose, I love the way you do 'Light My Fire.' Why don’t you try that one? We’ve got some time left over, so why don’t you give it a shot?"

And here again, I balked a little. I said something like, “Oh Rick, you know, I mean, it was just a hit like a year ago, and I almost did it tongue-in-cheek, you know, slowing it down and making it more sensual compared to the way it was originally done.” 

And so he repeated that we had some time lef,t and he said, "I tell you, let’s just give it a shot.” And so there you go. That was another one of his ideas. 

Q: “Light My Fire” was the B-side of your single. Were you surprised that it became the hit instead of “California Dreamin’?”

A: Yeah, I feel that was a fluke. "Light My Fire" was the B-side to "California Dreamin’," which had started getting some significant airplay. That was very cool, but somebody up in Seattle turned the record over and started playing "Light My Fire" for his audience, and it took off. It really took off… all over the world.

"California Dreamin’" also did really well, but "Light My Fire" eclipsed everything else.

What happened when Jose Feliciano sang the national anthem?

Q: The same year you released that song, you were invited to sing the national anthem at the World Series. Could you talk a bit about the backlash that greeted your interpretation and how that felt?

A: I was playing in Las Vegas in October 1968, opening for Frank Sinatra, and I got a call from the Detroit Tigers, from a fellow by the name of Ernie Harwell — their play-by-play announcer, a Hall of Famer in his own right and really a wonderful guy. He had heard that I had an interesting version of the anthem and wanted me to come to Detroit to sing it.

So, I took the redeye after my last set in Vegas and Ernie met me at the airport in Detroit and brought me to the stadium.

I wasn’t expecting to be asked in what key I was going to do the anthem as I was to be accompanied by their band. I explained that I played my guitar alone and that I was fine, thank you. Then Ernie and I walked out onto the field.

I started playing and it was to me such an exhilarating moment to be able to say "thank you" to a country that had given my family and me a chance to survive.  We came from Puerto Rico, very poor, but we'd always squeak through somehow by those who helped Pop get a job or who helped with handouts for my brothers and my mom and dad and me.

God‘s hand was in it all the time and so this was my love song to a country that was so good to me.

When I finished, I heard applause and cheering like normal, you know, and that was wonderful, but there was an undertone, a rumbling that was disconcerting. It wasn’t long after that I realized that my intentions had been misconstrued, though I truly wasn’t trying to be disrespectful in any way or flippant. I'd had a record going up the charts at the time and it disappeared pretty much within hours.

My record career was essentially over for quite a while, and it was pretty awful. That went on for months and months and look, we're still talking about it today! It was the first time anything like that had ever happened, where the national anthem had been changed in any way whatsoever. They wanted to place a mandate restricting any changes, musically or lyrically, to the "Star-Spangled Banner" and so much more.

Lots of things went down, but, um, you know, I think after all these years, people finally understand my heart, and I am grateful for that.

Q: What did it mean to you to win the Best New Artist Grammy?

A: All of my 19 Grammy nominations and the nine Grammys that I’ve taken home have been a blessing to me, and they’re all my babies. I love them all.

Q: As the first Latin artist to cross over to the English-speaking market in a big way, how does it feel to see the inroads Latin music has made in recent years?

A: I’m just pleased that people appreciate my work, Spanish or English, because that’s who I am, naturally. Maybe it gave others the courage and inspiration to also do what they love in Latin music, as it's now a really important part of the American fabric.

headline: Politicians are using immigrants for political gain – including Democrats | Opinion
fullText:
New York Mayor Eric Adams now says he wants to deport those who are charged with a crime, even before they are convicted.

That’s clearly a move to thwart Donald Trump’s wrath.

I suspect other Democratic governors and mayors will do the same once Trump returns to the White House, where he can withhold federal funding to so-called “sanctuary” or immigrant-friendly states and cities.

Why haven’t authorities like Adams gone after criminals before? Are they letting violent criminals off the hook just because they’re here illegally?

Even Adams is using migrants for political gain

That’s what Trump and MAGA want Americans to believe, and it worked to get him elected again.

Immigration reality is something entirely different and much more complex. But most don’t want to deal with it and prefer the soundbites fed to them to spark fear and hate toward this population.  

Adams’ flip underscores politicians’ eagerness to use migrants as pawns for their personal political gains — just as Trump has done.

The Democratic mayor has complained about the financial strain that undocumented migrants put on his city. Yet he kept spending billions to house and feed them.

Why didn’t he at least target criminals for deportation then?

Why the newfound courage to ignore due process and simply kick them out of the country?

Trump sees all undocumented immigrants the same

Because of Trump, of course, and Adams’ own legal problems that include charges of bribery, wire fraud and secretly soliciting campaign contributions from overseas donors.

That’s what I abhor about some politicians of both parties. They’re transactional and always use the most vulnerable to get their way — and not necessarily for the benefit of the country.

Violent criminals — accused killers, rapists and thieves, for instance — are fair game for deportation. In Trump’s view, though, everyone is the same type of criminal just for crossing the border, including children.

Studies have consistently shown that migrants are less likely to commit crimes than those born in the U.S., but that doesn’t matter to Trump.

We can’t ignore those who commit crimes, of course.

But Trump has thrown every undocumented immigrant currently in the United States in the same dumpster fire and wants to round up every single one of them — including doctors, lawyers, teachers, farmworkers and others doing essential jobs.

He's using the 'Operation Wetback' playbook

Trump is using President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s deportation playbook, offensively called “Operation Wetback.”

Just like Eisenhower, Trump plans to carry out military-style immigration sweeps to round up migrants. What he does with them after the migrants are detained is not entirely clear.

“You look back in the 1950s, you look back at the Eisenhower administration, take a look at what they did, and it worked,” Trump told “60 Minutes” in 2015 during his first presidential bid.

No, it didn’t work. If it did, we wouldn’t be talking about another mass deportation operation, right?

The immigration challenges of the 1950s aren’t the same as those in today’s messy and dysfunctional immigration system.

Opinion: Why Trump must deport everyone at once

After World War II, the United States had strict immigration quotas, but farmers needed workers. As a result, the U.S. created the Bracero program for agricultural guest workers from Mexico.

But farmers preferred to hire undocumented workers because they entailed fewer regulations and were cheaper labor. Sound familiar?

To deal with that, Eisenhower carried out his “Operation Wetback,” sending migrants deep into Mexico because most of them were Mexican.

To what extent will cities, states help Trump?

But fewer Mexicans are crossing the border illegally today. Most now come from all over the world, including Latin America, Haiti, Venezuela, Cuba, Ukraine and other war-torn countries.

That’s a logistical nightmare for Trump’s mass deportation plan — unless border states like Texas and Arizona help.

Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has spent billions targeting migrants, is itching to lend a hand, reportedly with anything Trump may need, including manpower and land to build detention centers.

Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs has said she’ll work with Trump on border security but will oppose him on policies that hurt families, whatever that means.

And now, we’re beginning to see to what extent Democrat-run states and municipalities like New York City are willing to do to appease Trump.

It looks like they might not need much arm-twisting to go after criminals. But what about everyone else?

Migrants can't count on politicians for protection

Legally, Trump doesn’t need local authorities to round up migrants because immigration is a federal responsibility.

However, Trump knows he can’t do it alone and will try to force governors and mayors to do his bidding. How much they resist will depend on individual political vulnerabilities.

There will be plenty of time to write about ways to fix the broken immigration system to benefit America and the law-abiding migrants already here.

For now, hard-working, law-abiding migrants shouldn’t count on politicians for protection.

They’re on their own.

They’ll have to rely on each other, on civil rights groups and a few good souls who still see the financial and cultural benefit of a melting pot America.

Elvia Díaz is editorial page editor for The Arizona Republic and azcentral. Reach her at 602-444-8606 or elvia.diaz@arizonarepublic.com. Follow her on X, (formerly Twitter), @elviadiaz1.

headline: 5 reasons to remain optimistic about Cardinals amid losing skid
fullText:
After consecutive road losses, the Cardinals’ season has hit a snare. Two weeks ago, it looked as if the Cardinals might cruise to the playoffs. Now, this week’s game against Seattle is likely to be season-defining.

Based on multiple projection systems, the Cardinals would be better than a 50% chance to make the playoffs with a win. If they lose, that drops below 20%. For the Seahawks, the odds are roughly the same. It is the most impactful game in the NFL this week.

Ahead of that showdown, here are five reasons to remain optimistic about the Cardinals, despite the results of the past two weeks:

They outplayed the Vikings

In the locker room after the Cardinals’ loss to the Vikings, there was a stunned silence. Players reacted differently than they had after any of the five previous defeats. “This one hurts for sure,” Marvin Harrison Jr. said.

But for all the pain of a blown lead and a one-point loss, the Cardinals’ actual performance was encouraging. They went on the road against a 9-2 team and outgained them, 406-273. The Vikings had not been outgained by such a margin all season.

Simply measuring how the Cardinals played — and not the result — it may have been their best performance of the season.

Consider their other games against teams with winning records. They played well at Buffalo but needed a kickoff return touchdown to stay close in the second half. Their offense went silent against the Lions. They were destroyed by the Commanders and Packers. They beat the Chargers at home, but were outgained by 69 yards. They couldn’t get any offense going against the Seahawks in Seattle.

Last week’s loss hurts in the standings and it featured both a lack of discipline and poor coaching decisions. But it reflected a team ready for the stretch run.

Nick Rallis has transformed the defense

Excluding a pick-6 against Seattle, the Cardinals are allowing just 12 points per game over their past four games, while racking up 19 sacks in that span. Opponents are averaging just 3.5 yards per carry in those same games.

Imagine that back in September, when the Cardinals were projected as one of the league’s worst defenses.

The players, of course, deserve credit for the transformation. Garrett Williams has emerged as a star at nickel while Max Melton and Starling Thomas V have impressed at outside corner. Linebacker Mack Wilson Sr. was a gem of a find in free agency. Dante Stills, Roy Lopez and L.J. Collier have all made an impact on the defensive line.

But defensive coordinator Nick Rallis may be the biggest factor in the unit’s success. Opponents can’t seem to get a grasp on the Cardinals’ tendencies. They expect blitzes when the Cardinals drop seven defenders into coverage and look unprepared when the Cardinals do bring pressure.

Rallis has his players performing above their level, which should give the Cardinals a chance in each of their final five games.

Trey McBride is a star

Harrison’s lack of production has been a point of frustration among fans and analysts all season. The fourth overall pick has eclipsed 64 yards in just two of 12 games.

But in tight end Trey McBride, the Cardinals have a weapon to ease Harrison’s burden. If defenses take away the deep passing game to Harrison, McBride will exploit them underneath. Since Week 6, he’s averaging 7.6 catches and 86.6 yards per game. Over the past two weeks, he became the first tight end in NFL history to record 12 or more catches in consecutive games.

“Because of his skill set, because of how dynamic he is, he’s gonna be a person that’s at the top of our list in terms of how we design the passing game,” offensive coordinator Drew Petzing said. “We need to make sure that he's involved in the process.”

The Cardinals offense has lacked consistency this season, but McBride is a threat to have an impact in any game against any opponent.

The schedule gets easier

All of the above are reasons to be optimistic about how the Cardinals are playing. But who they play over their final five games is equally important.

They looked impressive heading into the bye week, in large part because they dominated the struggling Bears and Jets, both at home. They looked far less formidable over the past two weeks, on the road against 7-5 Seattle and 10-2 Minnesota.

Up next: Seahawks home, Patriots home, Panthers away, Rams away, 49ers home.

The Cardinals are unlikely to be more than a field goal underdog in any of those games, and they figure to be significant favorites against the Patriots and Panthers.

By combined winning percentage, the Cardinals’ remaining schedule is the NFL’s sixth-easiest, while the Seahawks’ remaining schedule is the ninth-hardest.

The Cardinals rebuild is ahead of schedule

It’s not what anyone wants to hear when a division title is within reach. But even if the Cardinals miss the playoffs, this season is likely to be a success.

"We've earned the right to play meaningful games in December," Cardinals coach Jonathan Gannon said. "So we're kinda right where we wanted to be when we set out for the season."

While the Cardinals never admitted to rebuilding, they have not acted like a contender with their roster moves.

They left themselves $91.9 million of cap space heading into free agency and did not part with significant draft capital at the trade deadline. Plus, general manager Monti Ossenfort has had only two offseasons to undo the damage done in the final years of Steve Keim’s tenure. And Kyler Murray is still just 27 years old, with plenty of time left in his prime.

Considering all those factors, 2025 has always been seen as the first year of their contention window under Gannon and Ossenfort. By getting significant growth from their young players — especially on defense — the 2024 Cardinals have only bolstered the future outlook, even if they fall short of the playoffs this season.

headline: Arizona's Stevie Nicks has a rare eye disorder. Here's what we know
fullText:
In a recent interview with Rolling Stone, Stevie Nicks revealed that she has been diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration, also known as AMD, a common eye disease that may result in blurred vision or blind spots.

Macular degeneration occurs when the macula, a small spot near the center of the retina that’s needed for sharp central vision and allows us to see objects that are straight ahead, begins to waste away.

AMD is the leading cause of vision loss in one or both eyes among people 50 and older.

Nicks is 76.

As AMD progresses, a blurred area near the center of vision is a common symptom. Over time, the blurred area may grow larger or you may develop blank spots in your central vision. Objects also may not appear to be as bright as they once were.

Does Stevie Nicks have macular degeneration?

Yes. There are two kinds of macular degeneration — dry and wet, or neovascular. Anywhere from 80% to 90% of the 20 million AMD sufferers in the U.S. have the dry variety.

Wet macular degeneration occurs when abnormal blood vessels develop underneath the retina and macula. Neovascular means pertaining to new vessels. Often, these blood vessels leak blood and fluid. Because of the fluid buildup, a bulge forms in the macula.

It is possible to have both dry and wet macular degeneration in the same eye, and either condition can appear first.

Nicks has wet macular degeneration, which is far more rare and serious and often progresses more quickly.

“I got diagnosed with this thing a year and a half ago called wet macular degeneration, and it is not a good thing,” the Phoenix-born singer revealed in Rolling Stone.

“I was seeing all these colors, big things of purple. I was having, like, acid trips. And I’m going, ‘I’m not taking any acid, so I don’t understand what this is.’ Now, every six, seven, eight, nine weeks, I have to have a shot in each one of my eyes. That’s going to be for the rest of my life.”

When Nicks was diagnosed with AMD, she decided it was time to focus on her visual art while she still could, telling Rolling Stone, “All of a sudden, I’m going like, ‘You know what? You need to finish these drawings, because what if you start to lose your sight?’ I haven’t drawn in years … but my drawings are as important to me as my songs.” 

Ultimate playlist: Stevie Nicks' 20 greatest songs of all time, ranked

What is the main cause of wet macular degeneration?

Age is a major risk factor for wet macular degeneration. The disease is most likely to occur after age 60, but it can occur earlier.

Other risk factors, according to the National Eye Institute, include:

  • Smoking. Research shows that smoking doubles the risk of AMD.
  • Race. AMD is more common among Caucasians than African-Americans or Hispanics/Latinos.
  • Family history and genetics. People with a family history of AMD are at higher risk. As of 2015, according to the National Eye Institute, researchers had identified nearly 20 genes that can affect the risk of developing AMD, and many more genetic risk factors are suspected. However, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends against routine genetic testing for AMD, and insurance generally does not cover such testing.

Behind the music: How Stevie Nicks and Tom Petty came to record 'Stop Draggin' My Heart Around'

Wet macular degeneration symptoms

AMD has few symptoms in the early and intermediate stages. Only a comprehensive dilated eye exam can detect AMD. If you are at risk because of age, family history or lifestyle, don't wait to experience changes in vision before getting checked for AMD.

People with late-stage AMD may experience blurry vision, dark spots or floaters, degraded color vision and other symptoms, according to the Cleveland Clinic. 

Not everyone with early AMD will develop late AMD. For people who have early AMD in one eye and no signs of AMD in the other eye, about 5 percent will develop advanced AMD after 10 years. For people who have early AMD in both eyes, about 14 percent will develop late AMD in at least one eye after 10 years.

With prompt detection there are steps you can take to reduce your risk of vision loss.

Wet macular degeneration treatment

The following treatments for wet macular degeneration are from information developed by the National Eye Institute.

One option to slow the progression of neovascular AMD is to inject drugs into the eye, such as Nicks is undergoing. With neovascular AMD, abnormally high levels of vascular endothelial growth factor are secreted in the eyes. VEGF is a protein that promotes the growth of new abnormal blood vessels. Anti-VEGF injection therapy blocks this growth.

This treatment may require multiple monthly injections. Several anti-VEGF drugs are available. They vary in cost and in how often they need to be injected.

Another option is photodynamic therapy. This involves laser treatment of select areas of the retina. First, a drug called verteporfin is injected into a vein in the patient’s arm. The drug is absorbed by new, growing blood vessels. The eye care professional then shines a laser beam into the patient’s eye to activate the drug in the new abnormal blood vessels, while sparing normal ones.

Once activated, the drug closes off the new blood vessels, slows their growth and slows the rate of vision loss. This procedure is less common than anti-VEGF injections and is often used in combination with them for specific types of neovascular AMD.

Some cases of wet macular degeneration are treated with laser surgery, though this is less common than other treatments. It involves aiming an intense “hot” laser at the abnormal blood vessels to destroy them.

This laser is not the same one used in photodynamic therapy, which may be referred to as a “cold” laser.

This treatment is more likely to be used when blood vessel growth is limited to a compact area in the eye, away from the center of the macula, that can be easily targeted with the laser.

Laser treatment may destroy surrounding healthy tissue, which often results in a small blind spot where the laser has scarred the retina. In some cases, vision immediately after the surgery may be worse than it was before. But the surgery may also help prevent more severe vision loss from occurring years later.

Dietary supplements may slow the progression in those who already have the disease.

headline: Amkor secured north Peoria land for its $2B complex. Here's what happens next
fullText:
After finalizing a sale for 56 acres of land in north Peoria, Amkor Technology Inc. is gearing up to construct its planned $2 billion facility, where it will assemble and test microchips for the semiconductor industry.

Notably, the plan will support companies like Apple Inc. and the nearby Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

When complete within the next decade, Amkor’s complex will be the largest of its kind in the nation and will create about 2,000 jobs in the northwest Valley.

Here’s what we know so far about Amkor’s plans to expand the footprint of the Silicon Desert.

What is Amkor, and what is it planning to do at its new complex?

Amkor, which is headquartered in Tempe, is an Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test Company, or OSAT.

Since launching in 1968 in South Korea, it’s become a leading provider of testing and packaging semiconductors for major companies like TSMC and Intel.

The company employs about 30,000 people in 11 countries, including South Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Portugal and Vietnam.

Semiconductor packaging for cell phones makes up half of Amkor’s overall revenue. Another 21% of its business comes from testing microchips for the automotive industry.

At its new campus, Amkor will test and package microchips that TSMC is producing at its north Phoenix complex for Apple.

In July, Amkor was awarded $600 million in CHIPS Act subsidies for the project.

When is Amkor starting construction?

In November, Amkor closed on 56 acres of property that the master-planned Vistancia Development community owned off Loop 303 and Lone Mountain Parkway, according to real estate database Vizzda.

It purchased the slice of Vistancia’s 320-acre commercial core called Five North at Vistancia for over $4.12 million.

About 6 acres of that were sold to Amkor. It was gifted the remaining 50 as part of the three-way development agreement it entered with the city of Peoria and Vistancia in February.

Now that Amkor owns the land, it must get construction going by the end of September 2025.

The first phase of the plant must be finished by Sept. 30, 2027. Failure to do so means Amkor will pay the city $5,000 daily until the phase one portion of the site is completed.

Amkor’s facility must be fully built by September 2034. Within that time frame, it also must have invested at least $700 million in site improvements and construction.

That includes $2.1 million in turn-lane improvements between Lone Mountain Parkway and Desert Cactus Lane, a requirement outlined in a subsequent three-way agreement with Peoria and Vistancia.

What types of jobs is Amkor looking to fill, and when?

As required in the initial development agreement, Amkor must meet a series of employment benchmarks throughout the facility’s construction.

By September 2029, it must employ at least 550 full-time workers.

Here’s how that must break down over the coming years:

  • 300 employees by Sept. 30, 2027.
  • 425 employees by Sept. 30, 2028.
  • 550 total employees by Sept. 30, 2029.

Another 300 employees must be working at the plant when it is fully open.

Failing to hire the minimum number of employees by the milestone dates would put the company on the hook for $5,000 a month, but not to exceed $2.4 million until it reaches the agreed-upon goal.

City officials have explained that while Amkor is responsible for creating 850 total jobs, that’s just the base. The company and the city have expressed confidence in surpassing that minimum as Amkor has touted the creation of about 2,000 jobs.

When the time comes to staff the facility, Amkor will look to hire a mix of roles, including engineers, technicians, operators and support staff.

According to Amkor officials, about a third of the jobs will comprise engineers with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

Another third will include technicians, most of whom will need an associate’s degree.

High school-level graduates with a background and interest in STEM education will round out the rest of the Amkor team in Peoria.

Where will all these new Amkor workers live?

Construction is underway to create more homes near Amkor’s and TSMC’s facilities in the north Valley.

Developers of a 6,500-home community called Saddleback broke ground last month near Loop 303 and Vistancia Boulevard. The 5,300-acre development will have 2,500 acres of open space and neighborhood parks.

A few miles east, off 83rd Avenue and Happy Valley Road, a 903-square-foot mixed-use project called The Trailhead is being built. It includes a shopping center with retail and restaurant space, a renovated church, and a 336-unit apartment complex.

Other developers are eyeing land directly around TSMC.

The Minnesota-based Roers Cos. applied to rezone a five-acre site for a 147-unit affordable housing complex near 30th Avenue and Deer Valley Road.

And Georgia-based homebuilder PulteGroup submitted applications to Phoenix to rezone about 6,300 acres for a proposed development that could include nearly 20,000 housing units, plus business parks, retail, and potentially, a resort.

Before PulteGroup can proceed with the development, it must first acquire the land through a public auction, as the state land department currently owns the property.

What are Peoria and Amkor doing to address water scarcity?

Under the initial development agreement, the city is committed to providing Amkor with a maximum of 980,000 gallons daily of reclaimed water during the project’s first phase and nearly 2 million gallons daily for both phases.

Over the next decade, Amkor will pay the city 50% of the costs to treat the reclaimed water. It also must return at least 80% of its wastewater after retreating it through an industrial pretreatment program the company must build.

The city and Amkor also agreed, “in principle,” to collaboratively design and construct a recycled water facility.

headline: Arizona's cold weather may bring a mix of rain, snow, hail and graupel
fullText:
Arizona is known more for its deserts than its rain and snow, but even in such a dry state, all types of precipitation are possible — especially during the winter. 

From rain to snow to freezing rain, Arizona winters can bring a mixed bag of weather conditions. 

A true wintery mix — well known to people from northern climes — is rare in the Phoenix area due to its warmer temperatures and lower elevation, but it has happened. 

Measurable snow has fallen a handful of times in central Phoenix since records began in 1896. In higher elevations bordering the metro area, snow, hail and sleet occur slightly more frequently. 

In Flagstaff and other high-elevation areas, precipitation is a key feature in Arizona winters — and the state’s water supply. 

“You can get sleet, freezing rain, snow and rain all from the same storm system,” said Erinanne Saffell, Arizona’s state climatologist. “That’s that wintery mix possibility, depending on what happens to those snowflakes. It depends on what’s happening with the temperature closer to the ground.” 

Here’s everything to know about Arizona’s winter precipitation — what’s most beneficial, what’s most dangerous and what’s that graupel stuff, anyway. 

What kind of winter precipitation falls in Arizona? 

To begin with, it rains in the winter. If temperatures reach 32 degrees and there is moisture in the atmosphere, water vapor freezes into small ice crystals as snow. But even if snow forms, it may not reach the ground. 

As ice crystals in a cloud stick together, they become snowflakes heavy enough to drop to the ground. If the temperatures stay at or below freezing as snow falls, it will remain as snow. 

“But as that snow is dropping from the cloud, it can land into other kinds of conditions,” Saffell said. 

If the snow hits a higher portion of the atmosphere where the temperature is above freezing, it will melt and turn into rain.

When rain hits ground that’s frozen, it will freeze on impact and create freezing rain. 

Once a snowflake melts in the air, it can’t turn back into a snowflake until it returns to the clouds as water vapor. It can refreeze, but it will not form another snowflake. 

Wintry mix: Why doesn't it snow in Phoenix? It can, but you have to be fast to catch it

You know about sleet and hail, but what is graupel?

Sometimes, winter precipitation turns seemingly solid, with frozen pellets battering cars and peppering the ground. While hail, sleet and the lesser-known graupel look the same, they’re all a little different. 

Sleet forms as rain that refreezes on its way to the ground, but hail takes shape within the clouds. 

Hail forms in the colder portions of clouds with strong updrafts.

“Inside that cloud, it’s freezing, a little bit of it melting, then it goes back up and freezes until finally, it’s so big it breaks suspension and drops down to the ground,” Saffell said. 

Hail tends to be larger and harder than sleet, though Arizona typically only gets small, pea-sized hail, according to Saffell. 

Graupel begins as snow that transforms when it hits a portion of a cloud with supercooled water. 

Supercooled water is liquid inside a cloud that’s below freezing but remains water. When a snowflake hits supercooled water, it rimes — when the supercooled water begins to freeze around the snowflake. 

It then drops down to the ground, where it will look like a pellet but isn’t hail or sleet. 

“When you pick up a piece of graupel, you can crush it with your fingers,” Saffell said. “It’s sometimes called soft hail.” 

Graupel can fall in the Phoenix area, Saffell said, but it’s usually limited to January and February.

Future runoff: How crews measure snow depth and water content

What is the most beneficial type of precipitation for Arizona?

While Arizona has two rainy seasons — summer and winter — winter precipitation brings the most measurable benefits to the state’s water supply. The arid region can’t be picky when it comes to precipitation, but one type is better than others. 

“We want our winter precipitation and we’ll take it in any form, but we prefer to have it as snow because then it will melt slowly and move into our aquifers more readily,” Saffell said. 

Scientists and water managers measure it through the snow-water equivalent, or how much water snow will provide after it melts. 

“The interesting thing about snow is that it’s mostly air. When we have snowflakes coming down, they’re mostly air pockets,” Saffell said. “On average, when we have about 10 inches of snow, that would melt down into about an inch of liquid water.” 

Rain can cause rapid runoff and flooding, but snow melts at higher elevations gradually and creates an extended release into rivers, streams and groundwater reserves. 

Rare weather: How a Pacific hurricane flooded Phoenix and why it could happen again

What is the most dangerous kind of precipitation?

Hail may be damaging to vehicles and private property, and accumulated snow can cause travel to be a headache, but Saffell considers freezing rain to be the most dangerous type of winter precipitation. 

“The dangerous precipitation that folks don’t realize a lot and we don’t get here in Phoenix is freezing rain,” she said. “You have that icing that will stick to the ground, and you can’t drive, people can’t move, and it can go into your roof and make it collapse.” 

Outlook: A weaker La Niña is expected this winter. What does that mean for Arizona?

How much winter precipitation will Arizona get this year?

Winter precipitation varies year to year due to a variety of factors like drought and climatological conditions. Some years are better than others, and Saffell expects slightly less than average this winter. 

The National Weather Service has issued a La Niña watch with a 57% chance it will emerge by the end of the year. La Niña is a climatological condition that is part of a natural cycle called the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO. 

La Niña events occur when the Pacific Ocean is cooler than normal, typically triggering abnormal weather events around the world. 

The Southwest tends to be drier and warmer than usual during a La Niña winter, but because this year’s event is shaping up to be a weak one, Arizona may not be extremely dry. 

“There could be a good amount of precipitation up in Colorado and the northern tier of the U.S., which would be great because ultimately having snow in the Colorado Basin, even in the upper basin, is helpful to our water supply,” Saffell said. 

Hayleigh Evans writes about extreme weather and related topics for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. Email her with story tips at hayleigh.evans@arizonarepublic.com.

headline: North Phoenix shopping center gets green light from city despite opposition
fullText:
A plan that will bring a grocery store and retail center to a north Phoenix neighborhood got the nod of approval from the Phoenix City Council on Wednesday, despite some lingering opposition from neighbors.

Vestar, the developer of Desert Ridge Marketplace, Tempe Marketplace and other open-air shopping centers around the Valley, is planning to build Black Mountain Village at Black Mountain Parkway and Deer Valley Road, directly north of Pinnacle High School.

The plan was unanimously approved by the Phoenix City Council, despite several community members urging them to deny the proposal.

Vestar is proposing a grocery-anchored shopping center totaling about 160,000 square feet of buildings on a 20-acre site. The plan includes the grocery store, along with attached ancillary retail and five standalone buildings.

The project was first proposed more than a year ago and received extensive opposition and support from the community. The process was paused but resumed in October 2024, when it was presented to the Desert View Village Planning Committee with some changes meant to address some concerns raised about the project.

The major changes to the plan included limiting the square footage of the grocery store to a maximum of 65,000 square feet, and prohibiting a gas station on the site, Ryan Ash, vice president of development for Vestar said. The Village Planning Committee, which serves as an advisory body to the City Council, also added a prohibition against car washes on the site, but Ash said there was never a plan to include a car wash.

However, some neighbors still staunchly oppose the project, calling it inappropriate for the site, which was zoned for single-family homes.

James Tuffin, who lives in the single-family neighborhood near the site, said the changes to the plan solve a problem that didn’t exist because the original submission to the city did not include a gas station or a grocery store larger than 65,000 feet. Later submissions did include a larger store and a gas station that could be built only if it were related to the grocery store.

Tuffin said he and others who oppose the project are concerned about the drive-thrus that are proposed on the site, and the traffic and litter that could come with them.

In recent meetings, he said, many people showed up in support of the project, saying they need a grocery store in the area. However, he said, many people were unaware that another project, CityNorth, located at Loop 101 and 56th Street, is also planning to include a grocery store. The site of CityNorth’s proposed grocery store is about three miles from the Black Mountain Village site.

Tuffin took issue with the messaging behind the support of the development, and said the change was a “grave injustice,” saying that the Arizona State Land Department and the city have failed to plan where they will need grocery stores, which requires this one will be added in an area he feels is inappropriate for it.

Eight members of the public spoke at the meeting, most expressed opposition to the project, citing concerns about the proximity to the school, and worry about students crossing the street with increased traffic. Three people spoke in favor of the project, saying it would enhance walkability in the neighborhood, and said they were glad Vestar had made changes to accommodate the neighbors’ concerns.  

Ash said Vestar would have preferred to find a site that was already zoned to allow the development, but there are only two sites in the area that fit the parameters and neither would be suitable for a retail center, and one is already planned for development into a storage building.

Both the Village Planning Committee and the Phoenix Planning Commission recommended that the council approve the project.

Vestar would still need to go through the public hearing process to receive permits for drive-thrus, Ash said, so residents will again have an opportunity to weigh in. It is too early in the process for Vestar to share the names of the businesses that could go into the center, Ash said, including which grocer is planned for the site.

The site is controlled by the Arizona State Land Department, and Vestar will have to bid on the land at a public auction in order to follow through with its plans. Ash said an auction for the land will be scheduled after the zoning change.

Construction on the site will likely begin in early 2026, Ash said, with businesses in the center expected to open in early 2028.

headline: Protecting Phoenix's historic Sunnyslope Rock Garden, a front yard folk art display
fullText:
The Sunnyslope Rock Garden, an imaginative folk-art display made of rock, pottery shards, colorful chipped glass and concrete, was designated historic by Phoenix City Council on Wednesday.

The rock garden is part of a modest Sunnyslope home near Cave Creek Road and Cheryl Drive, south of Peoria Avenue. It's bounded by a waist-high concrete wall colored turquoise. Inside, the environment includes "a mosaic interpretation of Seattle’s Space Needle, representations of Inca villages, towers, carved and cast figures, fountains, free-form masonry shapes, animals, people, houses, and decorative patterns," according to the application.

The castings and concrete structures extend from the edge of the property, abutting the sidewalk, to the front door, where it wraps around a pillar of the house. Some of the figures are miniature; others are life-sized.

The city said the property is significant because it's "a rare local example of a folk art environment. The sculptures possess high artistic value using a distinctive method of construction and materials."

It was built by Grover Cleveland Thompson, a machinist with no formal art training who was missing three fingers, according to Sunnyslope Historical Society president Julia Taggart. He moved to Arizona from Seattle and started on the garden in 1954. He worked on it until his death in 1977.

Thompson's daughter, Cloydene, sold the property the next year to Marion Blake, an art teacher from New York. Blake said she fell in love with the garden during a trip to visit her parents and immediately knew she had to leave New York to be with it.

"There was no way I could let anything happen to it," Blake told The Republic on Tuesday, the day before City Council approved the historic designation. She beamed with excitement as she shared different details of the garden. and gushed over Thompson's dedication to repetition in his artwork.

Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego plans to issue a proclamation honoring the Sunnyslope Rock Garden, as well as Thompson and Blake, according to spokesperson Arielle Devorah.

The Sunnyslope Rock Garden also referred to as the Thompson Rock Garden, will be the first rock garden in Arizona to receive historic status. The designation provides protection for the property against renovation and demolition. It also qualifies the property for city grants to help with upkeep or rehabilitation.

Taggart, who helped Blake apply for historic status, said she hopes the approval paves the way for other unique structures to receive historic designation. There's one other known rock garden in Phoenix, the Louis Lee Rock Garden, near Camelback Road and 40th Street.

The Sunnyslope Rock Garden is not currently open to visitors, but Blake is planning an open event on Jan. 1 at the garden to celebrate Thompson's birthday and achieve historic status.

Taggart said the Historical Society was also working with Blake to set up future tours. Interested visitors should go to SunnyslopeHistoricalSociety.org for information.

Historic designation after 40 years of trying, owner says

Blake bought the house in 1978 from Thompson's daughter and sought historic status since. For the last 40 years, Taggart said Blake has gathered hundreds of pages of signatures and submitted petitions to the city for historic status.

Blake said when she didn't hear back, she figured the city just didn't care. But that changed this year, when Taggart helped Blake submit a formal application. Taggart said Blake hadn't known about the form and no city official ever reached out to assist her. The fact Blake doesn't have wifi or use email further complicated things, Taggart said.

City spokespeople did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Blake's unanswered petitions.

It's possible the property would not have qualified for historic status in the past. City code typically requires properties be at least 50 years old, which at minimum would have barred eligibility until 2004.

But Taggart and Blake believe the Rock Garden has long been eligible because the code allows an exception to the 50-year requirement if the property has "achieved significance within the past fifty years" and it's "of exceptional importance."

The city first identified the rock garden as potentially historic in 1979. The Phoenix Historic Building Survey said the site wasn't yet 50 years old, but may still qualify for the National Register of Historic Places because it's "an unique example of folk art used in landscaping."

Taggart said she and Blake plan to pursue a spot on the National Register next.

Taylor Seely covers Phoenix for The Arizona Republic / azcentral.com. Reach her at tseely@arizonarepublic.com or by phone at 480-476-6116.

headline: AZ could soon resume executions after a nearly 2-year hiatus. What to know
fullText:
Executions could resume in Arizona next year, ending a moratorium that began nearly two years ago.

Upon taking office in January 2023, Gov. Katie Hobbs and Attorney General Kris Mayes, both Democrats, suspended capital punishment pending a review of Arizona's death penalty process.

Retired U.S. Magistrate Judge David Duncan was hired as a commissioner to undertake that review, the scope of which was laid out in an executive order that also called for a written report.

Last week, Hobbs ended Duncan's review, saying she had lost confidence in the effort.

Duncan, in an outline of his report, wrote “that lethal injection while theoretically achievable is, in actual practice, fundamentally unreliable, unworkable and unacceptably prone to errors." He said that opinion could change after speaking with medical personnel who were going to be involved in the state's next execution and watching "a complete rehearsal" of Arizona's lethal injection process.

Hobbs cited an "execution preparedness" review the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry sent her on Nov. 22 as proof the state is ready to proceed with putting prisoners to death.

On the day of Duncan's dismissal, Mayes said she would seek a death warrant for a prisoner in the coming weeks.

Here's what to know about capital punishment in Arizona.

How are executions carried out in Arizona?

Executions in Arizona may be carried out by lethal injection or gas chamber.

Arizona voters abolished the use of the gas chamber after a controversial execution in 1992. It took Donald Harding 11 minutes to die as he cursed and gestured at then-Attorney General Grant Woods. But Arizona law still lets inmates convicted of death penalty offenses before November 1992 choose how they want to die: gas or lethal injection.

The last inmate to opt for the gas chamber was Walter LaGrand in 1999.

In 2021, as the state prepared to resume executions, lawyers for condemned men said state officials purchased a different type of cyanide than the one called for in the state's newly published protocols for administering a gas chamber execution. Officials bought potassium cyanide instead of sodium cyanide.

Ryan Thornell, in his letter to Hobbs summarizing the Corrections Department review of execution procedures, did not mention gas chamber protocols, focusing only on the administration of lethal injections.

Arizona previously used a mixture of drugs to carry out lethal injections but now only uses a compounded form of pentobarbital.

The state has attempted to improperly import execution drugs at least twice, first in 2010 and then again in 2015. The second time, The Republic reported the state paid nearly $27,000 to import a drug that was stopped by federal officials at the airport.

Duncan reported being shown the state's pentobarbital supply in a safe within a Department of Corrections facility but said it was being stored in unmarked jars and that he was not able to verify where it came from.

What happened during Arizona's most recent executions?

After an eight-year pause, Arizona resumed executions in 2022, killing three men: Clarence Dixon, Frank Atwood and Murray Hooper. The state struggled to administer the lethal injection in all three cases.

Attorneys for Clarence Dixon, who was executed in May 2022, said his IV insertion process took 40 minutes. Dixon's execution team resorted to inserting an IV line into his femoral vein, which his legal team said caused him to experience pain and a media witness said resulted in a "fair amount of blood."

The execution team for the June 2022 execution of Frank Atwood also struggled to insert IVs, prompting technicians to consider the femoral vein. However, Atwood asked the team to try his arms again, eventually guiding them to successfully make the insertion into one of his hands.

During the November 2022 execution of Murray Hooper, Hooper turned and asked the viewing gallery, “Can you believe this?” as the execution team tried and failed repeatedly to insert IVs in his arms before inserting a catheter into his femoral vein.

The last execution before the spate in 2022 was conducted in 2014. It took two hours for the drugs to kill Joseph Wood. Witnesses reported watching Wood gasp for air hundreds of times during the execution.

How many people are on death row?

There are currently 111 people on Arizona's death row.

Twenty-five of the people on death row have exhausted all of their appeals, and the Attorney General's Office could seek a warrant for their execution, according to the Attorney General's Office.

The Attorney General's Office said those 25 people have completed the direct appeal of their conviction, their first state post-conviction proceeding and their first federal habeas proceeding, including appeals.

Who can request a death warrant?

The Arizona Supreme Court will decide whether only the attorney general can seek death warrants after Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell, a Republican, forced the issue.

Mitchell, dissatisfied with the suspension of the death penalty by Hobbs and Mayes, in June moved to seek a death warrant for prisoner Aaron Gunches. In response, Mayes said the authority to seek an execution rests solely with the attorney general.

The Supreme Court then, on its own motion, decided to resolve the dispute.

But on the day of Duncan's dismissal, Mayes said she would soon seek a death warrant for Gunches. Now, Mayes believes the conflict before the Supreme Court is moot, according to the representative of her office.

A spokesperson for Mitchell said the county attorney was "monitoring the situation to see what the Attorney General will do."

The death warrant authority issue has been fully briefed and will be placed on a conference calendar for the justices' consideration, a representative for the Supreme Court said.

"At that point, the justices will meet and decide any authority and mootness issues as necessary," said spokesperson Katie Fisher.

Gunches was sentenced to death for the 2002 murder of Price, a former longtime boyfriend of Gunches' girlfriend. Gunches kidnapped and shot Price multiple times in a desert area off the Beeline Highway. Gunches has advocated for his execution.

Republic reporter Robert Anglen and former Republic reporter Michael Kiefer contributed.

headline: Maricopa Community Colleges to offer one of Arizona’s first bachelor's degrees in AI
fullText:
The Maricopa County Community College District has unveiled a new bachelor’s degree in AI and machine learning, the latest expansion of artificial intelligence education in Arizona.

The newest program adds to the district's growing slate of bachelor’s degrees, which began after former Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey signed a bill in 2021 allowing the system to offer the courses. Starting next fall, three more degrees will be available, including artificial intelligence and machine learning as well as business administration degrees in accounting and management.

Leaders with the district said these new programs were chosen to support fast-growing industries seeing a significant need for workers. 

The bachelor's of science degree in AI and machine learning will be available at Chandler-Gilbert Community College. The college is also home to an AI Incubator Lab run in partnership with Dell, Intel and the state of Arizona.

A report released earlier this year showed more than half of business leaders are concerned about filling their roles in the coming years, with most showing a preference for candidates with AI skills.

That’s likely just one part of what’s to come for AI in the job market, said Gabriela Rosu, dean of instruction at CGCC.

“It’s here to stay,” Rosu said. “This is AI, the next internet.”

There’s been a rise in demand for AI courses among students as well, Rosu said. They often don’t fit the standard characteristics of first-time learners with many returning to school after receiving a bachelor’s or master’s degree. Earning credentials in AI has become a popular way to pivot career paths or change jobs altogether, she said.

"We have 18- to 40-year-olds," Rosu said.

Rosu expects graduates of the upcoming program to move on to a variety of fields, including manufacturing, information technology and semiconductor engineering. Students in the program will also complete a capstone project in partnership with local businesses looking for talent. School officials are also hoping to introduce dual-enrollment options for high school students looking to learn more about AI and possibly continue their studies at a college in the district.  

Arizona’s first AI and machine learning certificate program was launched in the district in 2020 as an associate degree track. The addition of the new bachelor’s degree will make Chandler-Gilbert Community College one of three community colleges in the country offering an AI program of its kind.

And the community college district isn’t alone in pushing for AI in the classroom. Three of Arizona State University's program requests this year were for AI-related degrees, including AI engineering and AI information technology. The University of Arizona offers a degree in applied computing, with an option to study AI.

Regardless, Rosu said higher education is still not meeting the moment when it comes to the upcoming expansion of AI in the workplace. That's something she expects will become more evident over the next several years as businesses identify where their needs are.

Nervousness around AI taking jobs away is an understandable concern, Rosu said, but the jobs the new technology will create will outweigh potential losses.

Learning about AI — and teaching it — also opens up a variety of ethical concerns surrounding a powerful and ever-expanding technology, she said. To combat that, each course students take incorporates ethics and respect of privacy.

“That's very important," Rosu said. "For us as an institution to have that really embedded into the students."

Bachelor’s programs at MCCCD are typically a third of the price compared with traditional programs, according to district officials. The district has enrolled nearly 5,000 students in its bachelor's degree programs.

“Our system continues to transform accessibility for thousands of Arizona students who may have thought college was outside their reach due to cost, acceptance rate, or location,” said Maricopa Community Colleges Chancellor Steven Gonzales in a release.

headline: Tempe has OK'd nearly 2,000 new apartment units close to ASU. Everything to know
fullText:
High-rise development in Tempe has historically clustered near Mill Avenue, east of Arizona State University, or along Tempe Town Lake, but a slew of newly approved and proposed apartments, all along a half-mile stretch of Rural Road, could bring more high-rises east.

The university is in the middle of its own major growth spurt on that side, with major developments underway in the Novus Innovation Corridor, which includes apartments, restaurants, corporate offices and hotels. The development will span more than 300 acres on land owned by the university, which will generate money for the university’s athletics programs.

But even outside of Novus, private development is coming in droves, with a hyper-focus on the stretch of Rural Road between University Drive and Apache Boulevard.

Here's a roundup:

What's Leo Tempe, the 20-story tower project near ASU?

The latest proposal to come to the Tempe City Council, a project at Rural and University, is called Leo Tempe, and will include two 20-story towers and a 10-story parking garage on a 3.7-acre site. The site includes a Chevron station, several restaurants, a tattoo shop and a strip retail center, all of which would be razed to develop the new building on the site. However, some of the businesses, including Gus’ New York Pizza, have expressed interest in keeping locations at the new development, Nick Wood, the zoning attorney representing the developer, Up Campus Student Housing, said at a Tempe City Council meeting. In total, the Leo would have 950 apartment units.

What is the 18-story project by Empire Group?

The site is just west of another proposed apartment building, which is planned to include two towers, the tallest reaching 18 stories. That project is planned by Scottsdale-based Aspirant Development, a division of Empire Group. The Tempe City Council approved that project in late 2023. That development is planned to include 539 apartment units.

Tempe approved demolishing a hotel, to be replaced with what?

On the southern end of the half-mile stretch, at Apache and Rural, developer Gilbane is planning to raze a hotel building, called Moxy Tempe, to build an apartment complex, Vale Student Housing. That project is not a high-rise, instead planned to reach eight stories. The project, which will keep the existing CVS Pharmacy on the site, was approved by the Tempe City Council in October. Gilbane is also the developer of the nearby Apollo apartment complex on Apache Boulevard and Terrace Road.

What is the 189-unit site being built just east of Moxy Tempe?

East of the Moxy site, another apartment complex, called the Marshall Tempe, is underway on construction. That project is not a high-rise, but is planned to reach seven stories with 189 apartment units, according to real estate database Vizzda.

Are there other apartment developments slated near ASU?

Another apartment complex had been proposed across Rural from the site where Vale Student Housing is planned, but that proposal, which was requesting a 21-story development, was withdrawn after a critical reception from the Tempe City Council.
