headline: Horne announces charter school expansion plan with federal funding
fullText:
Arizona Superintendent of Public Instruction Tom Horne announced plans Wednesday, Dec. 4, to expand charter schools in the state with $34.8 million in federal funding.

Horne said the money would be used to help open 24 new charter schools over the next three years and support 23 existing ones. He said the funds would help give Arizona students "as many school ... options as possible." The funding was granted through the U.S. Department of Education's Expanding Opportunities Through Quality Charter Schools Program.

Charter schools, which were approved by the Legislature in 1994, are publicly funded and privately operated. They are tuition-free. Arizona is the state with the largest percentage of public school students enrolled in charter schools, at 20%, compared to the U.S. average of 7%, according to 2021 data from the National Center for Education Statistics.

Charter school operators must apply for federal grant funding through the Arizona State Board for Charter Schools.

Grant recipients must be focused on serving "educationally disadvantaged" students, Horne said. At least 30% of students in the proposed school must be either "racially and ethnically diverse" students, economically disadvantaged students eligible for federal lunch program support, students with disabilities or English language learners, according to application guidelines. Applicants must be registered nonprofits.

"This grant also seeks to close achievement gaps in academic scores, provide technical assistance to educators to improve teaching and learning, and encourage dual or concurrent enrollment in college-level courses," Horne said.

Horne's announcement came as many public school districts in the Phoenix area are grappling with declining enrollment.

The Governing Board of south Phoenix's Roosevelt Elementary School District, which serves a high proportion of low-income students and whose student population is more than 90% Black or Hispanic, was set to vote Thursday on closing five schools due to declining enrollment. The district has attributed enrollment decline in part to competition from nearby charter schools. Since 2009, federal funding from the Quality Charter Schools Program has gone to at least nine charter schools located within Roosevelt's boundaries.

Rather than compete with public school districts, however, Horne said he thinks charter schools "complement" them.

"Even a good ... district school may not necessarily meet the needs of all the students," he said. "And so, the parents should have the ability to find a school that does meet those needs."

Charter school enrollment in Arizona has risen by nearly 50% over the past decade, while overall public school enrollment has remained stagnant, increasing by just over 1% since the 2013-14 school year, according to state data. Public school districts still serve the vast majority of Arizona’s public school students.

Money from the federal Expanding Opportunity Through Quality Charter Schools Program has been granted to dozens of charter schools across Arizona since the first round of funding was received by the state in 2009, including to schools in the charter networks Academies of Math and Science, Arizona Autism Charter Schools, ASU Preparatory, BASIS, Great Hearts Academies and Legacy Traditional Schools. The majority of schools that have received funding from the program have been in Maricopa County.

A 2022 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that between 2006 and 2020, charter schools that received grants through this federal program were slightly less likely to close within five years than schools that did not receive them. The report also found that about 14% of charter schools nationwide that received awards either closed or never opened.

Arizona is one of six states to receive funding through the program this year.

Horne announced the grant funding at a school in the Vista College Preparatory charter network located within the boundaries of a public school district facing steep enrollment declines, the Phoenix Elementary School District. He described Vista College Preparatory as among the "most successful charter schools in the state — one that serves the same type of underserved population this grant is designed to help."

"We need more schools like this in urban and rural settings," Horne said. "This grant will help do that."

The Vista College Preparatory school where Horne made his announcement received an 'A' letter grade this year. On the 2024 statewide assessments, 34% of its students passed in math and 42% of its students passed in English language arts, surpassing the neighboring district school on both measures.

headline: WM Phoenix Open chairman: Some changes, but 'fabric' of popular PGA Tour event intact
fullText:
The most noticeable change to the upcoming WM Phoenix Open, tournament chairman Matt Mooney said Wednesday, is the new entrance gate to TPC Scottsdale that will be set up at Greenway-Hayden Loop just past the Frank Lloyd Wright Boulevard intersection.

The gate will not open at exactly the same time as the main entrance to the tournament, but it should alleviate the foot traffic that became an issue during the rain and foul weather that hampered the experience for everyone at the Open in February of this year. 

"We'll still have the main entrance and so everyone who comes in on a shuttle or parks will still go through that main entrance," Mooney said from the WM Phoenix Tee-off Luncheon at Chase Field. "But to have this new entrance that essentially drops you off right at the 18th tee, one of the most amazing views on the course is above the 18th hole looking down at 17 and 16.

"And so one of the things that we've been planning for is how do we account for the fact that we think everybody is going to come in and want to take a selfie or a picture to look at that background, because it is really incredible."

The new entrance gate is among the improvements for the 2025 WM Open. The trouble at the 2024 tournament, largely due to weather, included overflow crowds, a lack of space on the cart paths and walkways, closed parking lots due to flooding, and players complaining about fans — intoxicated or not — being too close to the action.

In the end, conversations with players, primary sponsor Waste Management and the city of Scottsdale didn't bring about change to the nature of the tournament, only some adjustments to the course infrastructure.

Mooney and Thunderbirds executive director Chance Cozby flew to Southern California 36 hours after the 2024 WM Open to meet with members of the PGA Tour Players Advisory Council.

"The thing that we came away with was how much they all love this," Mooney said. "We were honestly surprised with how little they had in terms of recommendations or tweaks to the event. ...

"We want to find the right tweaks. But there's a reason this has been the five-time tournament of the year in the past decade and is the biggest event on the PGA Tour. So we're being really mindful not to change that fabric."

So the Thunderbirds looked to be better, not bigger, in 2025.

Other changes in 2025:

  • Removing general admission any-day tickets and having day-specific tickets, allowing organizers to control the crowd exactly to the number each day. "And then by going digital we know that we're going to be a lot more efficient at our entrance but also have better data about our users and more accountability with each user," Mooney said.
  • Infrastructure changes such as making the Taylor Morrison Fairway House and the Desert Oasis venues on the course open to all attendees. New landscaping on top of some small grassy hills on the course will allow fans to watch multiple holes of golf from a higher vantage point.

Some of those hilltops were roped off in the past, and people used one such hill to form a muddy slide in the rain this year.

The early-morning rush to the stadium hole at 16 will continue to be a staple of the WM Open. Mooney recalls thousands of fans lined up in 38-degree temperatures and rain, ready to make the mad dash.

"People travel from all over the world to do that," he said. "We love that moment, wouldn't want to go too far from that."

Also at Wednesday's luncheon, the Thunderbirds presented Arizona State men's golf team member Joséle Ballester with a sponsor's exemption for the WM Open in 2025. Ballester, of Spain, won the U.S. Amateur tournament this year.

National championship-winning football coach Nick Saban, now a media personality with ESPN, answered questions from Diamondbacks president Derrick Hall on Wednesday. Saban reiterated that ASU running back Cam Skattebo is his favorite college football player, as he said on ESPN's "College Gameday" last weekend.

Saban said he would pick ASU to beat Iowa State for the Big 12 championship on Saturday's show, which drew applause from the hundreds seated at the home of the DBacks.

Saban played in the 2024 Pro-Am tournament, calling it one of the most enjoyable events he's ever been a part of.

"What was interesting is, every SEC fan in that arena made sure I knew they were there," Saban said, recalling his tee shot at the 16th hole.

headline: Urban camping is now a crime in Tempe as city plans to enforce camping ordinances
fullText:
Urban camping is now a crime in Tempe punishable by jail time and thousands of dollars in fines, according to an announcement from the city saying it would enforce a ban on sleeping or setting up structures like tents in public spaces.

The rule itself isn’t anything new. Tempe’s “urban camping ordinance” was first passed in 1997 and “prohibits anyone from using public property as housing,” the city’s news release on Tuesday noted.

But that ban hadn’t been enforceable since at least 2018, when a federal court ruled that criminalizing homeless individuals for camping in public spaces constituted “cruel and unusual punishment” if they did not have access to alternative shelter. 

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned that decision June 28. Then on Nov. 5, Arizona voters passed Proposition 312, which made it possible for property owners to apply for a property tax refund if their cities don’t enforce existing bans on homeless camping in public spaces. 

Those two legal changes left Tempe with two options — repeal the 1997 ban or ramp up enforcement of criminal penalties against homeless camping in public spaces. Tempe opted for the latter.

Tempe is the latest city to reach that conclusion. Other cities, including Goodyear and Surprise, recently enacted bans after the passage of Proposition 312.

In 2022, Phoenix cleared "The Zone," the Valley's largest homeless encampment, paving the way for the passage of Proposition 312.

“Tempe is implementing strict enforcement of its urban camping ordinance,” the city wrote. “(The local ban) includes pitching tents or building shelters in places such as city parks, preserves, alleys, bus stops, schools or rights of way. It also bans activities such as making fires, storing personal belongings in public spaces and laying down bedding for sleeping.”

Ron Tapscott, a community activist from Tempe, criticized the city's move as a simplistic approach to a complex problem.

"Attempts to criminalize it have increased," said Tapscott, who is also a member of Tempe Neighborhoods Together and Tempe First. "But the issue has gotten a lot more nuanced and more complicated, and the city is not recognizing that."

Tempe will give one warning to those who violate the ordinance. 

The city’s announcement also said violators will be “offered outreach services.” It’s unclear whether Tempe’s existing system can accommodate all of the individuals who might get nabbed. 

After that warning, violators will be charged with a class 1 misdemeanor, which is the highest level of offense that can be prosecuted in municipal courts. The charge carries a fine of as much as $2,500 and up to six months in jail.

The surge in Tempe's rent prices has also seen a rise in people experiencing homelessness. Resources and funding have not been increased to mitigate that need, Tapscott said.

Shelter services available for Tempe's homeless are also limited, according to Tapscott. His concern is whether Tempe will have the resources to accommodate all of the individuals who need services.

"That means either the street or jail while they're waiting," Tapscott said.

“It is hoped that those in need of assistance will take the opportunity to get help,” Tempe wrote in its announcement. 

"We have just recommitted to our community that we will be enforcing that ordinance around urban camping that was already on our books in response to Proposition 312," said Tim Burch, director for Tempe's Department of Community Health and Human Services.

"This is a moral issue, but now it's also a political issue," Tapscott said.

Tempe’s announcement said residents can call the city’s CARE & HOPE Line at 480-350-8004 to report a homeless individual in need of assistance. Residents can also report an encampment online using Tempe’s reporting tool.

Reporter Sam Kmack covers Tempe, Scottsdale and Chandler. Follow him on X @KmackSam or reach him at sam.kmack@arizonarepublic.com.

headline: 'Great things happen': How ASU football's Shamari Simmons and Xavion Alford bonded
fullText:
Each Thursday before that weekend’s game, Arizona State cornerback Shamari Simmons makes his way to safety Xavion Alford’s house. With Simmons occupying the nickel cornerback position near the line of scrimmage and Alford roaming in the back at free safety, the dynamic between the two is a key piece to ASU’s secondary. 

The Sun Devils take on Iowa State in Saturday's Big 12 championship game, and ASU will need their best effort.

At those Thursday get-togethers, a bond has been built. Over many, many games of Call of Duty (Simmons is better, which Alford freely admits) and NBA 2K (Alford says he’s got Simmons beat there), stacks of wings and steakhouse visits, the two have formed a relationship that has become the backbone of one of the most important units for the Sun Devils. 

“We good friends,” Simmons said. “I’m going to remember him until I pass away.”

The two are hard-hitting players who seek out and invite the contact. They’re not the defensive backs who shy away from a big hit.

But they are polar opposites when it comes to one aspect of their game: being vocal. Alford is a talker, Simmons isn’t. 

That contrast is what makes everything work.

“Shamari’s not a big talker. He’s a more action guy. Xavion is the talker, but he’s about that action as well,” defensive backs coach Bryan Carrington said. “When you got two guys in between these white lines who are about that action, other guys can absorb it.

"It gives everybody that ‘Space Jam-drinking-Mike secret stuff’ so those guys are hitting on all cylinders. It spills over to every aspect of our defense.”

Alford, who gave himself the nickname “100-Yard Landlord” back in high school in 2020 once he saw that Name, Image and Likeness was about to become a thing, has been one of the leading safeties in the country this season. He has given up just seven receptions this year, the fourth-fewest in FBS. Alford has forced an incompletion 37.5% of the time when he’s targeted, which is best in FBS.

Simmons has been even more lights out. Among slot defenders, he’s one of 11 players in the country who hasn't allowed a touchdown while also playing the second-most snaps. Simmons’ 1.11 yards allowed per slot-coverage snap is the 25th-best total in FBS.

While both are enjoying great individual seasons, the two are like a levy system that depends on one another. 

“When I got a safety that’s back there behind me," Simmons said, "I feel confident when I’m playing man. He definitely gives me a lot of confidence."

Alford said building that trust allows the two to play more freely: “I just let him know, 'Hey, do your thing. I got you.' And vice versa.”

The pair hit it off when they first visited Tempe two years ago after entering the transfer portal. Simmons came over from Austin Peay in Tennessee while Alford had been at USC. They shared similar goals of playing at the next level and carried the same mindset. Southern roots, with Alford being from Texas and Simmons from Alabama, helped strengthen that bond.

Constructive criticism is what made the relationship blossom. They’re not afraid to call out each other.

“We kind of just matched,” Alford said. “We push each other. He holds me accountable whenever he needs to and I hold him accountable as well.”

Or as Simmons puts it: “We ain’t ever been too big-headed about each other. It’s just about work. We man enough to tell each other, not get in our feelings about it.”

There’s a lot going on right now with the ASU football team. The No. 15 Sun Devils are in the midst of a 10-2 season with an appearance in the Big 12 Conference championship game waiting, and potentially the College Football Playoff. However, the relationship between the two has not gone unnoticed by the coaching staff.

Carrington hopes that fellow players on the team see what they have done, and replicate it.

“Their relationship is probably the closest, as far as Xavion to Shamari, Shamari to Xavion," he said. "I don’t think anybody has exceeded their relationship. It’s unbelievable. Shamari being our team MVP last year, Xavion being more of the voice in that leadership role, to see those two guys on the field, the relationship they have, others should look up to it. Others should admire it.

"When you have a roster of people who believe in Coach’s vision – and we don’t have guys on the roster who are selfish, that have their own agenda – great things happen.”

Logan Stanley is a sports reporter with The Arizona Republic who primarily focuses on high school, ASU and Olympic sports. To suggest ideas for human-interest stories and other news, reach out to Stanley at logan.stanley@gannett.com or 707-293-7650. Follow him on X, formerly Twitter: @LSscribe.

headline: ‘Why would you take my child?’: Mercedes Vega's parents attend suspect's arraignment
fullText:
Leer en español

Erika and Tom Pillsbury sat seething with silent rage in a courtroom as they laid eyes on the man accused of torturing and murdering their daughter last year.

Clad in an orange jumpsuit with the words “MCSO Unsentenced” printed on the back, 22-year-old Sencere Hayes appeared in Maricopa County Superior Court Wednesday for his arraignment, where he pleaded not guilty to the murder of the Pillsburys' daughter, 22-year-old Mercedes Vega.

His court appearance came weeks after Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office homicide detectives arrested him in Tennessee before extraditing him to Arizona, where he faces multiple felony charges including first-degree murder and kidnapping.

‘Why would you take my child?’

Erika was surprised by how skinny Hayes was.

She said he didn’t look like the kind of person who could take down her daughter, who stood 5 feet 10 inches tall and worked out every day intending to become a personal trainer.

At one point, Erika said she locked eyes with Hayes as he turned around to sign some paperwork. She wanted him to answer the questions that had taken residence in her mind for nearly two years.

“Why would you take my child?” Erika asked while speaking with reporters after the hearing. “Why would you kill my beautiful baby girl?”

Tom said it took everything he had to stay quiet and seated as he watched Hayes stand a few feet away from him.

“It’s very hard for me to sit there and not want to reach over the counter and grab him and basically take his life,” Tom said. “It’s what we needed to do. But to know that this person is still on this planet and my daughter’s not — and this is the person that supposedly did this — is very hard to swallow.”

While Hayes’ court appearance lasted only a few minutes, Erika said it was important he knew Vega's parents were present and planned to witness the court proceedings personally.

“I just wanted him to feel our presence,” Erika said. “I wanted him to hear us breathing. I wanted him to know — to feel everything that we have to say to him even though we couldn’t say a word to him.”

Tom and Erika understood Hayes was entitled to due process under the law and was considered innocent until proven guilty, but that did little to assuage their frustration.

“He’s pleading not guilty, and he has a defense and that’s his right,” Erika said. “That’s our law, but it is frustrating. It’s frustrating to watch him receive rights when my daughter received nothing.”

Waiting for more arrests

While watching Hayes stand before a judge was a bittersweet moment for them, Erika and Tom said they were still waiting for a phone call from MCSO announcing detectives had arrested other people suspected of taking part in their daughter’s killing.

Tom and Erika believed at least three to four people were involved in Vega's killing given the level of coordination that would have been required to leave her in a burning car they abandoned in Tonopah.

“He had to figure out Mercedes, what she did, where she was at, where she lived and all that stuff, and there’s no way he could have figured that out without somebody helping him,” Tom said.

Firefighters discovered Vega’s body on April 17, 2023, after receiving reports of a car on fire about 10 miles west of the Tonopah exit off Interstate 10.

Vega's body was lying deceased in the backseat — roughly 60 miles west of her Tempe home.

A medical examiner report ruled Vega’s death as a homicide, citing cause of death due to burns she suffered and smoke inhalation, the latter of which meant she was still alive when the vehicle was set ablaze. She also suffered blunt-force trauma and gunshot wounds that contributed to her death, the report said.

Gloves and bleach were found in the front of the car, and lighter fluid was found in the backseat. Whoever torched the car likely left in another vehicle, given Tonopah’s remote location.

Vega's car was found illegally parked near Culinary Dropout in Tempe. Such a coordinated effort strongly suggests there were multiple actors, Tom said.

Makenzie Lockhart, a friend of Vega, also was convinced multiple people were involved in her friend’s killing and can't wait until every one of them is taken off the streets.

“I want everybody to be brought to justice,” Lockhart said. “So, as happy as I am over (Hayes') arrest, I’m not fully satisfied yet.”

Plea deadline for suspected armed robber weeks away

While Hayes’ court case is in its infancy, a man suspected of robbing Vega at gunpoint in 2020 has a few weeks left to decide whether to take a plea deal.

Vega was returning to her Phoenix apartment near Cambridge Avenue and 16th Street when a man, who police identified as then 24-year-old Cudjoe Young, approached her from behind while pointing a handgun at her and demanded she give him her bag, cellphone and car keys.

Court documents say Young demanded Vega unlock her phone for him, which she did by entering the password before Young ran away with her belongings.

Erika said her daughter had several thousand dollars in cash on her after completing a shift at the gentleman’s club Le Girls, where she was a dancer when she was robbed.

“Cudjoe had followed her home from work,” Erika said. “He knew she was one of the top earners, and it was a very successful, lucrative day for her.”

On Dec. 15, 2020, police arrested Young at his home in Tempe and brought him to Phoenix police headquarters. Vega identified Young in a photo lineup, after which officers booked him into jail on one count of aggravated assault and one count of armed robbery.

Arrest documents say Young denied robbing anyone and requested an attorney.

Documents said Young bonded out within days of being arrested and somehow went nine months without an ankle monitor installed despite that being a condition of his release. Pretrial services eventually noticed and rectified the issue.

Young was scheduled for a settlement conference Dec. 18 in Maricopa County Superior Court where he may or may not accept a plea deal. Should he reject the deal, he faces a trial scheduled to begin Jan. 13.

‘You change your pain a little bit’

Erika and Tom still struggle to understand why someone would target their daughter — much less torture her before leaving her to die in a burning car out in the middle of nowhere.

Lockhart said she wasn’t sure if Vega was killed to keep her from testifying at Young’s trial, or if it was simply revenge for helping put him behind bars in the first place.

She recalled spending hours exchanging theories with Erika on who would target Vega and their motivation for doing so. Lockhart said police haven’t said they’ve uncovered evidence directly linking Hayes and Young together, but she said various facts — including them living close to one another in Tennessee — was too much to be a coincidence.

“It is too many moving pieces, and these pieces somehow fit together,” Lockhart said.

As for Erika, she said it was somewhat satisfying to finally look Hayes in the eyes, but the pain of loss remained, albeit in a slightly different form.

“You change your pain a little bit,” Erika said. “It changes. It’s been a year and a half since she was murdered so horribly. And that was the main, main focus that I would think about all the time before I knew that somebody was going to be held accountable.”

Perry Vandell is a public safety and breaking news reporter at The Arizona Republic. He can be reached at perry.vandell@gannett.com or 602-444-2474. Follow him on X, formerly known as Twitter, @PerryVandell.

headline: Is deporting criminals really tough on crime?
fullText:
Morning. In today’s opinions newsletter: Deporting criminals and Arizona’s plans for execution.

President-elect Donald Trump has proposed “the largest deportation operation of illegal criminals, drug dealers, and human traffickers in American history.”

And as Elvia Díaz writes, even the Democratic mayor of New York City seems to be on board.

But what does that mean? Are we talking about deporting people who are already in prison for their crimes?

If so, I’m not cool with that.

If they’re dangerous enough to be in prison, legal or not, they should stay there until their sentence is up. (I guess Trump could try to send criminals to other countries’ prisons, though I doubt they’d take them. Or ensure they stayed in for their full term. And if not, then what happens to them?)

Furthermore, if we’re talking about deporting anyone who is accused but not yet convicted of crimes, as the New York City mayor says he supports, how do we know they won’t find their way back across the border to reoffend (it still has holes, after all)?

It might sound tough to say we’re kicking out the criminals. But given what little we know so far, it feels soft on crime to me.

headline: Emboldened GOP lawmakers plan attack on Arizona's most vulnerable | Opinion
fullText:
After expanding their control over the Arizona Legislature, Republican lawmakers are feeling emboldened.

They’re feeling tough, superior, invincible. Smug.

Given that, will they immediately go after human smugglers or fentanyl dealers? Will they join Attorney General Kris Mayes in the fight to protect Arizona water rights?

Will they take measures to make it easier for Arizonans to afford housing, bring down grocery prices, and create programs to retain and increase the number of teachers and nurses we need?

Um, maybe.

GOP ratchets up attacks on transgender kids

For now, however, some GOP stalwarts are planning first to use their newly expanded political superpowers to take down Arizona’s most vulnerable citizens: Transgender children.

Oh, the big dogs at the Capitol are pawing the ground and snarling.

Or, as state Sen. John Kavanagh, one of the GOP’s barking bully boys, put it, “I’m hoping that the governor and some of the Democrats have now learned their lesson from this election where, amongst other things, their uber wokeness was rebutted.”

Targeting innocent kids isn’t entirely new. It has reared its ugly head in states all over the country.

That includes Arizona, where more than a few attacks on transgender youngsters have found their way into the Arizona Legislature over the past couple of years.

The Arizona Republic reported on Tuesday on bills being proposed by Republican lawmakers aimed at making life even more difficult on transgender students, bills that ratchet up a notch the lack of humanity in bills from previous years.

Religious reasons to make a child more vulnerable?

For example, Senate Bill 1002, sponsored by Kavanagh, a proposal that would prohibit school employees from calling a student by a pronoun that differs from the student’s birth sex or by a name that isn’t listed on their official school record unless a parent provides written permission.

It also allows employees to refuse to use preferred pronouns even with parental permission on the grounds of religious or moral reasons.

Really? I am not a theological expert, but I cannot think of a single religious or moral reason to make a vulnerable child feel even more vulnerable.

Opinion: Senator handles transgender attacks with class

Particularly when you know — or should know — how much more at risk for harm transgender kids are than their classmates.

The American Academy of Pediatrics reported that 73% of transgender adolescents reported psychological abuse, 39% reported physical abuse, and 19% reported sexual abuse.

They make up a miniscule percentage of any school’s population, making them easy to isolate, easy to harass.

Rebutting 'uber wokeness' is simply bullying kids

The National Institutes of Health has reports indicating that 82% of transgender individuals have considered killing themselves and 40% have attempted suicide, with the highest percentage of suicidal thoughts, plans and gestures coming from transgender youth.

And it doesn’t get much better for them as they get older.

Studies, like one from the Williams Institute at the UCLA School of Law, found that transgender people are four times more likely than others to be victims of violence.

Gov. Katie Hobbs will veto any bills like these that cross her desk.

But they’ll still get introduced and probably will get passed. Tough-guy lawmakers like Kavanagh call that rebutting “uber wokeness.”

I guess that sounds better than bullying children.

headline: Who wins 6A football championship? The Arizona Republic's breakdown, pick
fullText:
The 6A state football championship game is filled with intriguing story lines between two teams that few thought would make it this far.

Peoria Centennial, in preseason, seemed destined for the Open Division playoffs not the 6A bracket. But an 0-4 start while waiting for transfer players to become eligible at midseason derailed those plans. Mesa Mountain View has long been forgotten as a championship contender since winning the last of its eight state titles in 2002.

But, the Coyotes and Toros prevailed and made it to the 6A championship game. Here's a closer look at Saturday's 1 p.m., final at ASU's Mountain America Stadium in Tempe:

6A championship

No. 14 Centennial (6-7) vs. No. 4 Mountain View (12-1)

Mountain View will be facing a highly motivated football team on a mission in the playoffs after going 3-7 in the regular season with the 45-17 loss to rival Peoria Liberty the final wake-up call. The Coyotes still made the 6A playoffs as the No. 14 seed, helped in part by four top 6A teams moving into the Open playoffs, which allowed other teams to move up and into the 16-team 6A playoff bracket.

Centennial has flipped the script in the playoffs and now, they're trying to make history as the first seven-loss team to win an AIA state football championship at any level.

It starts on defense, because, if the Coyotes don't get to Mountain View junior quarterback Brady Goodman, they'll get picked apart in the secondary. Goodman is still hobbled by an ankle sprain suffered in the final quarter of the Salpointe Catholic quarterfinal game. He's been in a walking boot since then, only taking it off for limited practice time and last week's semifinal game.

Once that boot comes off, and if he keeps getting clean pockets, watch out. Goodman is as good as any quarterback in the state dissecting defenses with a big, accurate arm and quick release. Especially with his playmakers. Mikey Sumko leads the team in receptions, but junior Talan Arnett now holds the single-season 6A state record for most TD receptions with 23. He caught two TD passes in the second half of last week's stunning 28-27 win over top-seeded Brophy Prep.

Goodman's ankle has responded well to therapy this week, so there may be more mobility. But this is a balanced offense with a big, strong line that can control the clock. Tailback Reese Bodily is very good, and outside linebacker and California-signee Beckham Barney can get rolling downhill out of the wildcat QB spot.

Both teams' seasons were jump-started after Liberty losses. Mountain View's only loss was humbling 49-20 setback to Liberty on Sept. 13. Since then, the Toros have won 10 in a row.

"We got on a roll and I think we all started to believe," Barney said.

The Toros' defense is tenacious, and they don't just tackle, they make statement tackles, burying backs into the turf.

Centennial will try to get tailback Owen Reynoso going between the tackles, but the Coyotes might need a lot of help from bullish sophomore back Derrion Bartholomew (5-foot-11, 225 pounds), who went for nearly 200 yards rushing two weeks ago in the 37-14 quarterfinal win over Casteel, while Reynoso was nursing an injury.

Quarterback Kainan Manna got used to two freshmen among his receiving corps the first half of the season, while waiting for dynamos Nikko Boncore and Shamar Berryhill to become eligible. Both of those seniors are in midseason form now, capable of changing the game on a dime with big plays after catches.

"Our thought process (after Liberty) was forget everything that's gone on before this," Boncore said. "We're 0-0. Our motto is to go 1-0 every game. We'll see what happens."

This could be the best of the four big-school state championship games Friday and Saturday at ASU. Fasten your seatbelts, this is going to be a thrill ride.

Prediction: Centennial 33, Mountain View 31

headline: ASU finds right Big 12 dance partner
fullText:
It is the headiest of days for Arizona State football fans.

The new national media darling has spent the week receiving all the attention and compliments — backhanded and otherwise — in the week leading up to the Big 12 Championship game (10 a.m. Saturday, ABC).

Meanwhile, Iowa State has been quietly idling by, like ASU's unknown "plus one" on the steps of a gala.

The difference is the Cyclones have actually been to this particular dance before. The Sun Devils are nouveau riche to this rarified air.

Facing Oklahoma in Arlington in 2020, ISU had perhaps the greatest season in its program history. Entering the game ranked No. 6 in the CFP, they already had a regular-season win over the Sooners in their back pocket.

The Cyclones fell behind 24-7 in the first half, and a second-half rally fell short in a 27-21 loss. Head coach Matt Campbell's pain hasn't faded. It informs the way he thinks ahead of Saturday's game.

"You always reflect back on the wins, but you reflect on the losses, you know, and obviously that game, that moment was a great learning opportunity for all of us," he told the media at his news conference Tuesday. "That one obviously stings just because you played pretty good football that day, but not good enough."

For ASU head coach Kenny Dillingham, a visit to Campbell before that historic season was part of his education as an assistant. He visited Ames, Iowa, in 2019 as an Auburn staffer.

"I thought they were overachieving at that time, early in his career, at a high level before he had built it up," Dillingham said at his Tuesday news conference, explaining why he went. "Now he's built it up. Now they're achieving at a high level consistently. And I wanted to go just study."

And study he did, with a coach and his staff who were making a surprising impact at a place not accustomed to big impacts — and still is.

Until last Saturday, the Cyclones had never had a double-digit-victory season. Campbell has won 63 games since 2016, the best stretch in program history.

ASU never reached the extended depths of despair ISU has — the Cyclones averaged 3.3 wins per year between 1980-99 — but the Devils know what climbing out of a deep hole feels like.

Given the program's state at the end of the 2022 season after a two-season, slow-motion implosion, the two teams meeting in the first year of the expanded Big 12 Conference make a good pair. Both teams are striving to raise their profile without losing a sense of where they came from — which is to say from a long distance.

When asked if ASU set the standard as the best program in the conference, Dillingham was as blunt as ever.

"I guess winning is the determining factor for the best teams, you know, but I think what our goal is to be the very best version of ourselves," Dillingham said. "I'm going to say that from now until forever, and then people are going to get really bored of asking those questions, because I'm going to say the same thing for a long time."

headline: Lori Vallow Daybell to face trial in ex-husband’s death after competency ruling
fullText:
Corrections & Clarifications: A prior version of this article incorrectly described Lori Vallow Daybell's relationship to Brandon Boudreaux.

Lori Vallow Daybell, the “Doomsday Mom,” was cleared Thursday to stand trial in the 2019 death of her ex-husband following a monthslong process to evaluate her competency in Maricopa County Superior Court.

After reviewing evaluations by two mental health experts who found her competent, Commissioner Travis Marderosian issued the ruling and set a status conference hearing in her case for Friday morning. 

A finding of competency means it was determined that Vallow Daybell could understand the purpose and nature of the proceedings and assist in her defense.

Vallow Daybell was convicted in Idaho in 2023 for the murders of her two children, Joshua “J.J.” Vallow, 7, and Tylee Ryan, 16. 

Their remains were discovered buried on the property of her husband, Chad Daybell, who was sentenced to death earlier this year for his role in the murders.

Her mental fitness was also an issue during her Idaho prosecution, where she underwent almost a year of treatment before being deemed fit for trial.

In Arizona, her competency became an issue after her former defense team requested a competency evaluation. When she changed lawyers, her team tried to withdraw the request because Vallow Daybell told the court that she wanted to represent herself.

The court has yet to decide whether Vallow Daybell will be allowed to represent herself.

Extradited to Arizona, Vallow Daybell faces charges of conspiracy to commit murder in connection with the shooting death of Charles Vallow and attempted murder of her niece's ex-husband, Brandon Boudreaux. 

Charles Vallow was fatally shot by Vallow Daybell’s brother, Alexander Cox, in 2019, who claimed self-defense. Cox died months later of natural causes.

headline: Arizona State, Iowa State to square off for Big 12 championship and CFP berth
fullText:
The hunt for a Big 12 title and a berth in the College Football Playoff takes center stage Saturday as Arizona State (10-2, 7-2) and Iowa State (10-2, 7-2) square off in the conference championship game at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas.

A deep dive into the numbers indicates it should be a close contest. The teams have the same record. ASU averages 422.6 yards total offense and 32.1 points while Iowa State is at 419.8 yards and 31.2 points. Defensively, the Sun Devils give up an average of 336.6 yards per game, the Cyclones 330.6.

They are one-two in time of possession, with Iowa State at 32:32 and ASU 32:22. Yes, they're that close.

Even the results against common opponents are comparable. Iowa State beat Central Florida 38-35, while ASU did so 35-31. The Cyclones beat Utah 31-28 while ASU won 27-19. Both defeated Kansas State, ASU to the tune of 24-14 and Iowa State doing so 29-12.

Both lost to Texas Tech. Iowa State's other loss was to Kansas, whom ASU defeated, while ASU lost to Cincinnati, a foe the Cyclones topped.

They are one spot apart in the latest CFP rankings.

It is a winner-take-all for what is expected to be the conference's only representative in the 12-team field.

Let's take a closer look at the contest:

Follow along: Iowa State vs Arizona State score updates, analysis for Big 12 championship game today

No. 15 Arizona State (10-2, 7-2) vs. No. 16 Iowa State (10-2, 7-2)

Time/site: 10 a.m. MST Saturday, AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas.

TV: ABC (Joe Tessitore, Jesse Palmer). Radio: Arizona Sports 98.7 FM (Tim Healey, Jeff Van Raaphorst).

Series history: This will be the first meeting between the schools.

Storyline

Both teams are exceeding expectations. ASU was picked last in the conference but it reached the 10-win plateau for the first time since 2014 while Iowa State hit 10 wins for the first time in the program’s 133-year history.

The Sun Devils have won five straight games, the last loss coming at Cincinnati 24-14 on Oct. 19 when ASU was without starting quarterback Sam Leavitt who was nursing a rib injury.

They go into the game without one of their premier playmakers in wide receiver Jordyn Tyson, who sustained a collarbone injury on Saturday against Arizona. Dillingham said the team draws some comfort knowing it has overcome the loss of key players in the past. There was that one game without Leavitt but the Sun Devils also defeated Central Florida without leading rusher Cam Skattebo.

Iowa State, which is making its second appearance in the Big 12 championship game, has won three straight games. The Cyclones were ranked as high as No. 11 before back-to-back losses in early November.

What channel is Big 12 championship on? How to watch Arizona State vs Iowa State

Coaching matchup

ASU: Kenny Dillingham (second year, 13-11), 34, is the youngest head coach in the FBS and came to ASU in November 2022 after serving as offensive coordinator at Oregon where he mentored eventual first-round draft pick Bo Nix. He is a local product, out of Chaparral, and served on staffs at Auburn, Memphis and Florida State.

Iowa State: Matt Campbell (ninth year, 63-50 at Iowa State, 98-65 overall), 45, came to Iowa State after five years at Toledo. He took over a program that had won eight combined games in the three prior seasons and made only eight bowl appearances since 2000. The Cyclones are now bowl-eligible in the seventh of his nine seasons. The Massillon, Ohio, native was a defensive end in his playing days at Mount Union (1999-2002).

Arizona State will win if . . .

It succeeds on fourth down: Fourth down is probably more important for ASU than any other school just because the Sun Devils don't have a strong option for field goals. The evidence of that was a miss from just 21 yards last week by Parker Lewis. ASU has converted only one of its past six field-goal attempts. ASU has converted 14 of 27 fourth-down tries (51.9%) and has had a reliable defense to back it up on the failed tries. Iowa State is second nationally on fourth down, converting 16 of 20 (80%).

It runs, runs, runs: If you don't have your star wide receiver, what better way to neutralize that loss than run the ball? ASU does that well anyway, averaging 195 yards per game, 24th nationally. The Cyclones also have been vulnerable against the run ranking 96th, giving up an average of 173.7 ypg. Iowa State knows ASU is down its star receiver so they could opt to put an extra defender in the box. If that is the case, hitting some short passes early will help.

It handles the big-game atmosphere: The Sun Devils have been up to the challenge and handled hostile environments all season but none have played on this big of a stage. They have been playing with house money for more than a month because expectations were relatively modest but now they have a chance to do something few have achieved, especially at ASU, and that's win a conference title.

Iowa State will win if . . .

It doesn't turn the ball over: QB Rocco Becht has thrown for 3,000 yards but also has eight interceptions and what Pro Football Focus calls 18 "turnover-worthy plays," a pass that has a high percentage chance to be intercepted or a poor job of taking care of the ball and fumbling." That is second-most in the conference. ASU has done good job of capitalizing on opponent mistakes so this will be a key.

Contains ASU run offense: This is one spot Iowa State has proven vulnerable, ranking 96th against the run (173.7 ypg). It has had several key injuries on defense and a couple of players have returned so that should help. It gave up 287 to Cincinnati three weeks ago and ASU ranks higher in rushing offense than does Cincinnati but was more successful last week in holding Kansas State to 144.

Get some pressure on the QB: Iowa State ranks last in the conference and 124th among FBS schools in sacks. Leavitt has proved to be a very accurate quarterback and he is a dangerous runner, so if the Cyclones don't offer some resistance they could be in for a long day.

Personnel notes

ASU: There could be players who see action in this game or a future CFP or bowl game because now postseason games do not count against a redshirt. The most prominent player to look for here is senior wide receiver Malik McClain, who came in late in the fall but was impressive in early practices. With Tyson (75 catches, 1,101 yards, 10 TDs) out and Jake Smith (hamstring) having missed recent games, McClain should be a major addition to that position group.

Others out for the season are DL Anthonie Cooper, RB Raleek Brown, WR Zechariah Sample, OL Jalen Klemm and DB Cole Martin.

Arizona State CFP scenarios: ASU fans should root for UNLV, Clemson

By the numbers

1 - Pro Football Focus ranking for ASU quarterback Sam Leavitt for freshman players. Among those with at least 500 snaps, Leavitt is the nation’s highest-graded freshman with a grade of 89.4. That's 5.2points higher than South Alabama’s Gio Lopez (84.2), who is second and he is 11.9 points better than Tennessee’s Nico Iamaleava for the highest freshman grade among Power 4 freshman quarterbacks (77.5). The grade is tied for the seventh-best among all FBS freshman quarterbacks in the PFF era since 2015 (min. 500 snaps played). Of the 7 players tied or ahead of him 6 have started an NFL game this season (Brock Purdy, Trevor Lawrence, Caleb Williams, Drake Maye, C.J. Stroud, Spencer Rattler).

4 - Number of 300-yard passing games for Iowa State sophomore QB Rocco Becht. He is one of five players in school history to achieve that in a season.

4 - Defensive touchdowns scored by ASU this season, two were fumble returns for touchdowns while two others were interceptions returns. That is fifth among all FBS schools, the only teams faring better being Notre Dame (6), Tulane (6), Coastal Carolina (5) and Oklahoma (5).

43 - Big 12 victories for Iowa State since 2017, the league’s most during that stretch.

44 - Consecutive games with a reception for Iowa State's Jaylin Noel, ISU’s longest-active streak and second-longest in school history.

245 - Yards needed for Cam Skattebo to break ASU's single-season rushing record of 1,642 yards set by Eno Benjamin in 2018. Skattebo, who is at 1,398, is currently sixth. The next player he can overtake is Freddie Williams who had 1,427 in 1974.

They said it

ASU coach Kenny Dillingham

"They're very well coached. They're physical. They tackle well. They're good at destructing blocks. Like they get off blocks well. The fundamentals of the game they do really well. That's usually what wins, the teams that do the little things well."

ASU QB Sam Leavitt

"I'm not worried about the nerves. I'm super excited. I get to go play on the stage. That's what you dream about when you're a little kid. You watch these games. Shoot, I watched the game last year for the Big 12 championship and now I'm going to be on that stage. I'm going to go out there, get hyped, embrace the moment and then get back in my bubble and in my zone and play the game."

Who will win and why

Iowa State 32, Arizona State 28: The Sun Devils are playing with house money at this point. They hardly expected to be in this position. They will be hard-pressed to overcome the loss of one of their premier playmakers, Jordyn Tyson. Championship games often come down to the small things, and the fact that ASU does not have a reliable kicker is no small thing.

headline: Longtime KTAR reporter Jim Cross leaving after 25 years. 'It's time for a change'
fullText:
Jim Cross, a morning news reporter at KTAR for 25 years, is retiring.

His last day is Friday, Dec. 6.

The decision "just came down to it's time for a change," Cross said. "Just seems like the right time. Loved my time here. And loved working with so many great people and Bonneville was a first-class outfit to work for."

While he's been at KTAR for 25 years, Cross has been in radio for about 45 years and is a member of the Arizona Broadcast Association Hall of Fame. Broadcast jobs tend to be itinerant in nature, so "25 years in one place is almost unheard of in this day and age," Cross said.

Cross is ready to relax

Now he's ready to relax.

"Not sure what the future holds," Cross said. "Pretty wide open, but not going to do anything for a few months. I’ll be 64 Saturday, so rest and relaxation sounds really, really good."

Especially when your shift started at 5 a.m. on weekdays for years. So, will Cross sleep in on Monday?

"Oh yes!" he said. "Well, at least that’s the plan."

headline: Maricopa County will ask courts to dismiss challenge to Proposition 479 transportation tax
fullText:
Maricopa County will ask the courts to dismiss the local Republican Party's lawsuit challenging the passage of Proposition 479, officials said.

Voters approved the measure last month to raise billions of dollars for the Valley's highways, roads and bus route.

Tom Liddy, chief of the civil division of the Maricopa County Attorney's Office, said the county's response is due Saturday and the county will seek dismissal of the complaint.

The request comes after the Maricopa County Republican Committee sued to challenge the certification of Proposition 479.

Attorney Bryan Blehm filed the complaint Nov. 30 in Maricopa County Superior Court, asserting the ballot measure only garnered 59.82% of the vote and should not stand because voters amended the Arizona Constitution in 2022 to "require all tax measures to receive at least 60% of the votes cast."

Blehm argued the courts should decertify the results because they fell short of the 60% threshold established by the passage of Proposition 132, which voters passed in 2022. The lawsuit names the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, which played a key role in certifying the results.

Blehm could not be reached for comment.

The court scheduled oral argument for Dec. 13.

Connect Maricopa, the campaign committee supporting Proposition 479, filed a motion to intervene on Wednesday, according to the Superior Court website. In it, the group rejects Blehm's claims that Proposition 479 was required to hit Proposition 132's 60% threshold.

Supporters of the regional transportation tax called the lawsuit misguided, arguing an overwhelming majority of voters passed the measure and that challenging it would be detrimental to the Valley's economy.

Marty Shultz, a chairman of Proposition 479's original predecessor, Proposition 300, said Blehm's central legal argument was faulty because the Proposition 132 burden only applies to constitutional amendments.

When lawmakers were debating this issue in 2023, they clarified that the requirement that tax measures need 60% voter approval applies only to constitutional matters. The transportation tax extension does not amend the constitution.

MAG: Transportation plan 'will be implemented on schedule'

Ed Zuercher, executive director of Maricopa Association of Governments, the quasi-governmental agency that creates the regional transportation spending plan, said the projects would continue as scheduled.

“The lawsuit is without merit. The regional transportation plan that was unanimously approved by MAG’s mayors, tribal and county leaders, and supported by business leaders and the voters, will be implemented on schedule. We have a 40-year track record of success, and we’re squarely focused on delivering the next generation of transportation investments.”

Proposition 479 asked voters to continue a half-cent sales tax for the next 20 years. Voters first approved it in 1985, then again in 2004. The tax provides revenue for the regional transportation plan approved by mayors across the Valley. The tax accounts for $14.9 billion of the $28.2 billion plan, so a little more than half.

It is set to fund freeways (40.5%), bus transit and bus rapid transit (33.5%), major roadways and regional transportation infrastructure (22.5%) and light rail maintenance (3.5%). But paired with other funding sources, it unlocks billions in federal matching funds that frees city revenue in Phoenix, Mesa and Tempe to expand the light rail 11.9 miles and the streetcar 4.4 miles.

Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego reacted Wednesday, saying, “Maricopa County voters overwhelmingly passed Prop. 479 because they understand that a strong transportation system isn’t political. It's critical to our future. This lawsuit is deeply flawed and misguided, and I hope the courts recognize its malignant intentions.”

'The economy ... doesn't just happen'

Shultz, a former APS lobbyist with decades of experience in politics, said he wasn't surprised by the GOP lawsuit but worried about ramifications.

"Hopefully this ill-conceived action will not subject 479 to any sanctions or reversal," Shultz said.

He repeated the campaign argument that such an investment is vital to the region's economic development.

"Our economic success over the decades has been based, in part, on the development of a comprehensive transportation system," he said."What the perpetrators of this lawsuit failed to understand is that the economy, that they say they believe in, doesn’t just happen," Shultz said.

"I intend to call key Republican leaders and members of the Republican Party and 'complain like hell' over this behavior. It’s inappropriate, sends the wrong signal, and it probably will fail in court."

headline: Will Devin Booker score 50-plus for third straight game at New Orleans? Phoenix Suns face Pelicans
fullText:
NEW ORLEANS – Devin Booker spent his high school years in the deep south of Mississippi, playing at Moss Point where his No. 2 jersey is retired and his dad, Melvin, also starred.

They’d make the little more than 90-minute drive to New Orleans to check out NBA games at Smoothie King Center. So, it feels like home when Booker returns to play against the Pelicans.

“It’s the atmosphere more than anything,” Booker said. “I feel comfortable in the South. There’s a southern drawl to it. If you’ve never lived in it, it’s kind of hard to explain, but these gyms have a special energy, a special culture to them.”

Lately, he’s been really comfortable at this arena. The Suns (12-8) begin a three-game road trip Thursday against the struggling, short-handed Pelicans (4-18).

Booker scored 52 points in each of his last two games in New Orleans earlier this year, on Jan. 19 and April 1 of last season, both double-digit victories for the Suns.

Having family and friends present brings out the beast in Booker.

“My family takes time out of their schedules to make the drive over here,'' Booker said. "They’ve been supporting me for the longest, since high school days. I always try to do something special for them.”

This hasn’t been just about having a heater in New Orleans against the Pelicans for Booker. He cooked the Pels for 58 points in a 118-114 victory Dec. 17, 2022, at Footprint Center.

Booker may have another scoring explosion Thursday in New Orleans.

Losers of their last nine games, the Pelicans are 28th in defensive rating and have the worst record in the Western Conference, but Booker isn’t underestimating them.

“Respecting your opponent, understanding what those guys are capable of,” Booker said. “I’ve been playing against (CJ McCollum) for the past 10 years. I know what he’s capable of. Obviously BI (Brandon Ingram) is a star. Dejounte (Murray) is a great player and I trust Willie Green a lot, too.”

Green was an assistant under Monty Williams when the Suns reached the 2021 finals.

“We know what they’re capable of,” Booker continued. “They’ve been having the injury bug all season, but I think a few of those guys are back.”

Pelicans forward Zion Williamson remains out with a left hamstring strain, but the Suns are down Kevin Durant for this three-game road trip that concludes with a weekend back-to-back against Miami (10-10) and Orlando (16-8).

Durant is back in Phoenix recovering from a left ankle sprain suffered in Tuesday’s win over San Antonio to cap a six-game homestand. He’s scheduled for a re-evaluation next week.

“Everyone has to give a little bit more,” Booker said. “Execution down the stretch is going to be a big part. He’s been carrying us in the clutch this year, but we all have to give a little bit more. He brings a lot on the defensive end that he doesn’t get credit for. We’re going to have to protect each other in the paint. Just communicate.”

Booker won’t have to worry about gathering up tickets for family and friends Thursday night. “I let my dad handle that,” Booker said. “It’s usually around 50 to 100.”

headline: Roommate sentenced to probation in beating death of Phoenix man
fullText:
A woman who photographed and delayed reporting deadly injuries to her friend and roommate — the man who officiated her wedding — will spend 3 years on probation for her role.

Shannon Marie Higgins, 38, and two others were charged in the 2023 death of 49-year-old Jake Kelly. On Wednesday, Dec. 4, 2024, she was sentenced for hindering the prosecution of that case, a felony charge she pleaded guilty to in October.

She is the first of the defendants to be sentenced. And in the mind of Kelly's mother, Jan Kelly, she deserved more punishment.

The 78-year-old moved from Texas to Arizona because of the court case and her commitment to seeking justice for her son. She spoke in court Wednesday about Higgins' betrayal.

"I’m not saying that Shannon had a hand in what happened to my son, but what I am saying is that she was there," Jan Kelly said. "They were friends, and she did nothing about it. And she never called for help. He laid there for 16 hours when he probably could have been saved. And no one helped. No one came to his aid.'

'She has just as much to do with him dying as they did," she said of the other two defendants. "She didn't get help. She didn’t do anything for her supposed friend.”

Victim beaten into a coma in driveway of Phoenix home

Higgins married Cory Scott Young, 45, who pled guilty to the same felony charge and is scheduled for sentencing in January. Higgins uses the last names, Young and Higgins-Young, according to court papers and testimony at her sentencing.

The third defendant, Angel Mullooly, 35, was charged with second-degree murder in the beating that occurred Aug. 27, 2023, in the driveway of a Phoenix home. Mullooly is awaiting trial.

Court records show Higgins and Cory Young falsely claimed to police that they did not know Jake Kelly was injured. Deputy County Attorney Brett George told the sentencing judge that the night Jake Kelly was beaten into a coma, Higgins and her husband took him inside and "put him in various places in the house" to take pictures of him. They took him to a hospital hours later.

Jan Kelly shared photographs of her son's injuries to the court and with The Arizona Republic. They show his face marked with bruising throughout, his eyes closed and blackened and a tube surgically inserted in his windpipe to help him breathe. Jake Kelly died at the hospital.

In an interview, Jan Kelly described the friendship between her son and Higgins. He moved into her home to help her with rent and would regularly get his mom on the phone to give the younger woman advice, Jan Kelly said. A cook by trade, Kelly regularly cooked for Higgins. For months, life was good for the pair.

Then Young entered their lives. “Did he see it coming? No, he didn't,” Jan Kelly said about the leadup to her son’s death.

Multiple court documents filed by police and defense attorneys and reviewed by The Republic do not indicate a clear motive for the beating. But Jan Kelly does not rule out that her son was targeted for being openly gay.

“We don't know why,” she said about a motive. “I probably won't ever know why, honestly. I’ve come to grips with that.”

Deputy County Attorney Brett George told the judge that given the “callousness and the depravity that Ms. Higgins showed," she should spend some time in jail at the start of her sentence.

Higgins asks judge for leniency at her sentencing

Higgins spoke to the judge on her own behalf asking for leniency, calling the situation a "nightmare" for herself and others. Her attorney, Katie Gipson-McLean, said evidence showed Higgins and others involved were intoxicated the night of the beating. Higgins no longer drinks, and has been remorseful since she was first taken into custody, Gipson-McLean said.

“There were decisions that were made that could have been different, and some that were out of my control to change, and things that I could have done differently but I can't change now," Higgins said.

"I made mistakes and take full responsibility for them," she added later in her brief statement. "Your honor, I do ask for leniency on my sentencing. I have a great job again in accounting, my own place to live and two little girls that would be devastated not to have me around. I do ask that you please allow me to continue this growth for my family and for myself."

In handing down the sentence, Maricopa County Superior Court Commissioner Monica Garfinkel said she considered the wishes of the Kelly family, and that Higgins already served 43 days in jail. She also noted Higgins' improvements to her life and the gravity of delaying the prosecution. She said it wasn't possible to know whether Jake Kelly would have lived had Higgins called police.

Higgins has prior nonviolent convictions, but from over a decade ago, and had undergone addiction treatment and gotten an education since then, Garfinkel said. She submitted dozens of letters from people supporting her, the judge said, and several attended the sentencing on her behalf.

Garfinkel gave Higgins three years of supervised probation, with a deferred jail term of 90 days to begin next year. Higgins may never serve that term if she obeys the probation order. Probation terms include completing treatment and relapse prevention, not using drugs or alcohol and having no contact with the Kelly family.

“Too many times, people get probation they think it’s a get out of jail free card, there's no consequences attached to that," Garfinkel said. "But there are. I want there to be a reminder that this is your punishment and you need to take it seriously and you need to make sure that you don’t slide back into the bad behavior.” 

With one case resolved, Jan Kelly plans to continue her pursuit of justice for her son's death. “This is my swan song," she said. "This is what I'm gonna do with the rest of my life.”

headline: 5A Championship: How Desert Edge, Cactus became heated high school football rivalry
fullText:
There was no handshake line Nov. 1, after Goodyear Desert Edge's 21-6 win over Glendale Cactus. Will there be one following Friday's 5A football championship game between the schools at Mountain America Stadium?

Jim Dean, assistant director of the Arizona Interscholastic Association, assures there will be a traditional handshake line following the final.

The issue stems from bad blood that formed last spring and led to the resignation of Desert Edge co-head coaches Marcus and Mark Carter. The twin brothers stepped down to keep the Scorpions from being placed on probation and banned from this fall's postseason.

It started with a social media post from a Cactus parent asking what a good school would be for their child to transfer. Mark Carter responded to it by promoting Desert Edge.

That turned into an alleged recruiting violation with the Agua Fria Union High School District, which suspended Mark Carter from coaching for a year in an effort to prevent the Arizona Interscholastic Association from placing the football program on probation. Marcus Carter was allowed to continue coaching.

That wasn't enough. The AIA placed the football team on probation, prompting the Carters to resign, which lifted the probation. Henri MacArthur, an assistant, was promoted to head coach.

The Scorpions came out fired up to beat Cactus in the November meeting.

Now, the same two schools will meet for the 5A Championship at 8 p.m. Friday, at Arizona State's Mountain America Stadium.

Both teams know they have to keep their cools and play with precision.

"The focus is on us," MacArthur said. "The opponent really doesn't matter as long as we play to our standard."

This is the second year in a row Desert Edge has made it to the 5A title game.

Last year, the Scorpions made a wild second-half comeback and appeared to have won the game in miraculous fashion with a two-point conversion with no time left over Gilbert Higley. But the Scorpions were called for holding on Deshawn Warner's run and the two points were taken off the board. Hezekiah Millender's subsequent two-point try on a pass was broken up in the end zone and Desert Edge lost 42-41.

That game was drama-filled with Desert Edge making a valiant effort after 16 of its players, some of those key starters, were ejected during a late first-half fight with players from both teams leaving the sideline.

"Play the right way," MacArthur said this week. "We don't need antics. That's just going to get you in trouble. Get to it and play football."

Desert Edge has made an incredible comeback in its first season under MacArthur, who has been involved in the Desert Edge program for 10 years. The Scorpions started the season losing three of their first four games. But the losses came against Open finalist Peoria Liberty, Scottsdale Notre Dame team before a litany of injuries derailed its season and Higley, which made it to the Open playoffs.

After the 17-10 regular-season finale loss to Buckeye Verrado, MacArthur appointed Nick Ludovico the full-time offensive coordinator. Changes to the offense and play-calling have been apparent in 42-19, 30-14 and 27-14 playoff wins.

The last one came in a revenge match with Verrado that has Desert Edge confident it can claim its second state football title, having won it in 2015.

Cactus, which lost to Higley in the 5A final two years ago, is seeking its first state title since 2009, when Larry Fetkenhier was the head coach and current head coach Brian Belles was the defensive coordinator. Cactus also won state titles in 2005 and 2006 and was state runner-up six times.

Cactus overcame a rough 2-2 start to this season, losing to 4A semifinalist Snowflake 31-14 and to Open qualifier Scottsdale Desert Mountain 44-0.

The Desert Mountain loss could have doomed most teams. But the Cobras have bounced back every time they had a bad game this year to get to this game, coming through with a 38-35 win over No. 1-seed ALA Gilbert North last week, when senior wide receiver JuJu Stubblefield had 11 catches for 216 yards.

In the Desert Edge loss, Stubblefield had just one catch for two yards.

"They're just really good defensively," Belles said.

When the brackets came out, Belles had a feeling it would be his team and Desert Edge in the end.

"We've got our work cut out for ourselves," he said. "We do every time we play those guys. They're just so talented."

In the 21-6 loss to Desert Edge, Cactus was penalized 13 times.

"It's a matter of maintaining discipline," Belles said. "When I played, it was Horizon and us when I was at St. Mary's. It's the same kind of deal, man. There wasn't a whole lot of love lost between the teams, but you do it in between the whistles and in between the white lines."
