headline: Donald Trump isn't in power yet and is already changing the world | Opinion
fullText:
One of the defining acts of modern global power occurred nearly five years ago on the other side of the world.

It left its signature as a burning ball of twisted steel. 

You can see a picture of it in a New York Times story from January 2020. The image is stark and has likely seared into the minds of world leaders. 

A U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone had swooped down and fired on a rolling convoy that was leaving Baghdad International Airport. Missiles killed Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani, top commander of security and military in Iran, and nine other people.

World leaders know what Trump is capable of

Had there been any doubt on who authorized the attack, The Times gave an instant clue in its dateline.

“West Palm Beach, Fla.” 

Then-President Donald Trump had ordered the strike near the end of his first administration. The Pentagon said Suleimani was targeted because he and his Quds Force were “responsible for the deaths of hundreds of American and coalition service members and the wounding of thousands more.” 

Iran’s Supreme Leader was furious. He called for vengeance. 

In western Europe, the London-based Economist magazine asked this question in a headline: “Qassim Suleimani’s killing — masterstroke or madness?”

Few national leaders would have ordered such a strike — to take out the top military general in a nation of 90 million people that has long been known as the chief exporter of global terrorism and is a soon-to-be nuclear power.

Trump did. 

And because he’s the kind of man who would, the world is already changing because he was elected president.

Trump's reelection is changing the Middle East

We are roughly six weeks away from the second Trump inauguration, and already world and national leaders and major corporations are scrambling to adapt.

Trump has already ordered Iran and its proxy army Hamas to release the remaining hundred or so hostages (including seven Americans) that it captured in the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist invasion of Israel.

“If the hostages are not released prior to Jan. 20, 2025, the date that I proudly assume office as president of the United States,” wrote Trump, “there will be all hell to pay in the Middle East, and for those in charge who perpetrated these atrocities against humanity.” 

Hamas and Iran will likely take seriously Trump’s threat. They saw what happened at Baghdad airport in 2020. They know Trump is capable of anything. 

It led to a ceasefire among Israel and Lebanon

“Strong America is back,” declared CNN’s Scott Jennings, who emerged as a conservative star on mainstream TV news this election cycle. 

“This is outrageous that these Americans were taken and murdered, and we’ve basically stood back and given lip service to both sides. ... It’s wrong and (these are) the wages of weakness.” 

Already Trump’s election victory on Nov. 5 has helped produce a ceasefire on Israel’s second front — the Lebanon border — where Israel has faced a possible land invasion by another Iran proxy, Hezbollah. 

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that Trump wants the war in Gaza to be over by the time Trump returns to Washington, and thus Netanyahu — who is closely aligned with Trump — is willing to upset his own base to get it done, argued Dennis Ross, writing in The Times of London.

Ross served as Middle East envoy to Democratic presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama.

Trump has emboldened populists in Europe

In Europe, populist-right movements are ascendent against the ruling liberal parties. Trump’s win has only emboldened them and put the establishment center-left on the defensive.

In France, President Emmanuel Macron, with the foundations of his government shaking, is sounding very Trump-like as he expresses a kind of EU version of America First.

“Our role here,” Macron said, “is to not comment on the election of Donald Trump, on whether it’s a good or bad thing. He has been elected by the American people, and he will defend the interests of Americans. ... The question is, are we prepared to defend the interests of Europeans?” 

If Europeans are feeling the need for change, so is Euro media.

The Economist, no friend to Trump and which endorsed his opponent Kamala Harris, scolded European nations in this week’s cover story:

“Mr. Trump rightly complains that European members of NATO are free riders on American defense spending. Either because Mr. Trump demands it or because he starts to withdraw from NATO, European countries will need to find a lot more money to spend on security.” 

Also getting the message that change is afoot, Ukrainian Prime Minister Volodymyr Zelensky has signaled he is prepared to negotiate anew an end to the war that started when Russia invaded his country in February 2022.

Canada, Mexico and Latin America are on edge

In North America, Trump set the Canadians and Mexicans on edge with promised 25% tariffs if they do not secure their borders and stop the flow of undocumented immigrants and illegal drugs across the U.S. border.

As the Canadian currency — the loonie — dropped to its lowest level since May 2020, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau scurried to Mar-a-Lago to demonstrate that Canada is willing to work with the new president. 

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, who is further to the left of her predecessor, populist Andrés Manuel López Obrador, may have less in common with Trump, according to journalists on the Washington Post podcast Impromptu.

But the government likely understands Trump’s transactional nature and will find ways to work with him, as in the past.

Further south, Latin America’s dictators are freaking out, writes Arturo McFields, a former journalist and former ambassador for the Organization for American States, writing in The Hill.

“The Trump effect is already underway,” he wrote. “In Venezuela, Nicolas Maduro’s dictatorship is releasing political prisoners. In Nicaragua, Daniel Ortega and his wife passed a radical constitutional reform consolidating power. In Cuba, the regime is amplifying its repression and surveillance over its citizens.”

Business execs are making peace with MAGA

Closer to home, business titans are beginning to make peace with the incoming administration.

Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, whom Republicans have regarded as a tool of the Biden censorship regime, has spoken positively of Donald Trump and had dinner with him at Mar-a-Lago. 

The Trump-Zuck relationship is warming, reports The (U.K.) Guardian, “as Zuckerberg seeks to influence tech policy in the incoming administration.” 

Large corporations are reaching out to the MAGA right in unconventional ways, The Wall Street Journal reports. They are trying to build bridges to the alternative media ecosphere conservatives built after they were denied access to mainstream media. 

“To break into the unusual circle of influence that surrounds Trump, chief executives are discussing whether to try to secure an appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast,” The Journal reports. 

Some Democrats are open to deportation

While a number of Democratic governors, including Arizona’s Katie Hobbs, have joined the resistance against Trump and his proposed mass deportations, he is getting unexpected friendly overtures from some major Democratic figures.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York City Mayor Eric Adams have both said they will work with the Trump administration to deport migrants who commit crimes in this country. 

“Someone breaks the law, I'll be the first one to call up ICE and say, ‘Get them out of here,’” Hochul said. “I don’t want them here. I don’t want anybody terrorizing my citizens.”

Hochul, however, draws the line at deporting immigrants who are law-abiding, she said. 

After Trump’s victory, Adams ended a controversial plan that provided prepaid debit cards to migrant families staying in city-funded hotels, ABC-7 in New York reported.

Like Hochul, he supports deporting migrants who have been charged with crimes, the New York Post reported. He also dared progressives to “cancel” him for it.

Further, he said he would like to meet with Trump’s incoming border czar, Tom Homan, “hear his thoughts on how we are going to address those who are harming our citizens.”

Adams said he wants to “find out what (Homan’s) plans are, where our common grounds are. We can work together.”

Democrats in Congress are bracing for a fight

Democrats in Congress are reacting to Trump’s victory in a different way. 

They’re moving out older, more sclerotic leadership to make way for the young lions in the caucus who “are proven fighters and can effectively push back on Republican priorities like harsh limits on legal immigration.” 

Among those moving aside is Arizona U.S. Rep. Raul Grijalva, 76, who announced this week that he would step down from the top Democratic spot on the Natural Resources Committee.

Opinion: Democrats will regret their social media retreat

Others on the way out of committee leadership include U.S. Rep. Jerry Nadler of New York, 77, from the Judiciary and U.S. Rep. David Scott of Georgia, 79, from Agriculture. 

“It’s akin to a mutiny, especially given Democrats’ typical deference to seniority in who leads panels,” Politico reported. “But party lawmakers are increasingly anxious about the incoming Trump administration and full GOP control of Congress.” 

Social justice advocates face a reckoning

Stung by an election won by the party hostile to their objectives, transgender activists have begun to take a hard look at their own smash-mouth politics, The New York Times reports. 

When Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts urged Democrats to allow discussion of such things as transgender women in women’s sports, he was accused of being a Nazi enabler, and activists showed up at his office to protest his “hate,” The Times reported. 

We can’t even talk about these issues in a civilized way, Moulton said. “Here we are calling Republicans weird, and we’re the party that makes people put pronouns in their email signature.” 

Transgender activists sympathetic to what Moulton and other critics have endured say it’s time to “rethink and recalibrate their confrontational ways, and are pushing back against the more all-or-nothing voices in their coalition,” The Times reported.

The Trump phenomenon can be a ball of flame that is all consuming, like the missiles that took out the Iranian general.

But it can also work — as we’ve seen in this country — like a wildfire that burns through the old growth to make room for green chutes to finally emerge. 

Phil Boas is an editorial columnist with The Arizona Republic. Email him at phil.boas@arizonarepublic.com.

headline: AZ pays opioid distributor share of settlement dollars, drawing ire of attorney general
fullText:
Pharmaceutical distributor Cardinal Health has paid the state of Arizona over $11 million so far as part of a settlement over the nation's opioid crisis, according to the Attorney General's Office.

And Arizona has paid the distributor about three times that amount back.

The state paid Cardinal Health over $33.8 million in opioid settlement dollars to provide services in prisons, a payment dashboard on the attorney general's website shows.

That money was for “Hepatitis C Pharmaceutical Expenses” during the state budget year that ended in June, according to the dashboard. Cardinal’s $11 million in payments to the state so far, which account for just a portion of its share of the opioid settlement, began in 2022, state records show. 

That an opioid distributor was paid with money meant to alleviate the damage of the opioid crisis has rekindled the ire of Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes.

"Every Arizonan affected by the opioid crisis has a right to be as outraged as I am," Mayes said in a statement. Mayes publicly opposed the use of the settlement money within prisons and lost a lawsuit earlier this year trying to stop it.

She said Cardinal Health, "a company that played a role in fueling this crisis," was being allowed to "recoup what it owed in the settlement."

Mayes revives political fight with Hobbs, GOP lawmakers

The state budget included the transfer of $115 million in opioid settlement money from accounts within Mayes' office to the Arizona prison system by early July. Mayes objected to using the money in that way, calling it a "blatant budget gimmick" as the state tried to backfill a shortfall. She feared it could violate the settlement agreement.

The budget negotiated by Republican legislative leaders and Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs' office made clear that money would be spent in Arizona prisons, including for hepatitis C treatment. Hobbs' office publicly criticized Mayes at the time, saying she was "flatly wrong" to object to using the money in prisons.

And ultimately a judge sided with Hobbs and GOP leaders Senate President Warren Petersen and House Speaker Ben Toma, affirming the use of the money.

But Mayes revived her concerns about the budget this week.

"The decision by Senator Petersen, Speaker Toma, and Governor Hobbs to allocate these funds for this purpose was wrong," she said. "Had the budget process been more open and transparent, it’s possible that funds meant to address the harm caused by the opioid epidemic would not have been funneled back to a company whose actions contributed to the suffering and deaths of Arizonans."

Mayes called for the state's contract with Cardinal Health to be canceled and the settlement money be "restored for appropriate uses in Arizona communities."

A spokesperson for Cardinal Health declined to comment on the record for this story.

The Arizona Republic reached out to the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry by phone and email multiple times for this story since Nov. 26. Questions about the department's arrangement with Cardinal Health, and the appearance of paying settlement money back to an opioid distributor, were sent on Wednesday. The department did not respond by deadline.

Petersen and Toma did not respond to text messages requesting comment Thursday.

Hobbs: Taxpayers would 'pay the price' for canceling contract

A spokesperson for Hobbs said canceling the state's contract with Cardinal Health, as Mayes wants, would drive up costs.

“The Governor does not agree with the Attorney General’s position because it will increase costs on taxpayers and disrupt the bulk purchasing of lifesaving medication by over 200 state agencies and local governments throughout the state by canceling a contract used by governments across the country," Hobbs' spokesperson Christian Slater said in an email.

Ohio-based Cardinal Health is one of the largest health care companies in the nation. It distributes pharmaceuticals and manufactures medical and laboratory products, among other services. It is publicly traded and reported a revenue of $228 billion to its shareholders in the most recent fiscal year, an increase of 11% over the prior year, its disclosures show.

The company and its subsidiaries provide pharmaceuticals for many Arizona government agencies, including corrections and the Arizona State Hospital, through a contract that has existed since at least 2019, state contract and financial records show.

The contract was competitively bid in a way that allows other states and government entities within Arizona to purchase pharmaceuticals from Cardinal Health without having to start a new contract process, state officials said.

Slater said ending that agreement would drive up costs for any entity that uses that contract. And for that reason, Hobbs disagrees with Mayes.

"Arizona taxpayers at every level will pay the price," he said. "Governor Hobbs is committed to being a smart steward of taxpayer dollars and delivering the cost-effective health care that working families expect from their state government.”

Cardinal Health and two other opioid distributors must pay the state of Arizona about $198 million over the course of 18 years under the terms of a national settlement agreement. Cardinal Health is on the hook for roughly a third of that money.

The settlements include a total $1.1 billion windfall for Arizona. Much of that money will support county and municipal governments, with just under $500 million going to the state, according to terms that were inked by former Attorney General Mark Brnovich, a Republican.

The settlements outline how the money can be used, and addressing addiction of people within the criminal justice system is one of them.

Testing and treatment of hepatitis C in Arizona prisons was mandated by a federal judge in 2023 as part of a nearly decade-old lawsuit trying to bring Arizona's prisons up to constitutional standards. That judge noted in a March order there were some improvements in hepatitis C treatment, but more broadly a "complete failure" to comply with her order for changes.

Hepatitis C is a bloodborne infection that can be deadly if untreated and is more common in prisons, where it can be spread by injecting drugs and tattooing, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It is also curable with antiviral medicines that cost tens of thousands of dollars each.

headline: The yin and yang of a worldwide Trump effect
fullText:

More than a month remains before President-elect Donald Trump is inaugurated.

headline: Copper Canyon OL John-Alexander Lopez makes school history signing with NAU
fullText:
John-Alexander Lopez was adopted when he was 2-days old. He grew up and learned to be an electrician, following his adoptive dad everywhere he went for jobs.

Now he's made Glendale Copper Canyon High School history.

On Wednesday, the 6-foot-5, 275-pound senior offensive lineman signed his national letter of intent with Northern Arizona University, making him the first football player in the 20-year history of the school to sign with a Division I college.

This was longtime Arizona high school football coach Rodger Schenks' first year around Lopez. He never was more impressed by a student athlete's conduct on and off the field.

"In the classroom, off the field, he's helped change the culture," Schenks said.

A 3.9 GPA student, Lopez, also a thrower in track and field, is quiet and humble, mature and accountable. He's involved in more than just sports at school.

Lopez said this latest achievement, signing with a Division I school, was just one more step to show how thankful he is to his parents, Nellie Granados and Juan Lopez.

"Honestly, it's a sign of how hard I've been working," he said. "I've always wanted to get somewhere in my life, because I always wanted to make my parents proud, to show them that all of their work of raising me after adopting me has led me to somewhere well."

Lopez was grateful that Nellie and Juan came into his life, after his blood mother was about to give him away to the state after his birth.

"I've never had problems with my baby," said Nellie Granados. "Every year he's an honors student. He's meant a lot to the schools, the middle school, the high school.

"He has had groups of elementary-age students that he would read to them."

Nellie was 45 when she and her husband Juan adopted John-Alexander 18 years ago. At the time, her youngest child was 9.

"I knew his (biological) mother, and she was very young and naive," Nellie said. "She was going to give him away to the system. Me knowing her, and, at that time, I was a teacher. I told her I would take the baby. She said, 'Well, he's Black.' I said, 'I was not brought up judging people by their skin color.'

"He was 2 days old. I brought him home from the hospital. I brought her home. Alex became part of our family. It was the best joy of my life. I was 45 and I had no thinking of having any children of my own anymore."

When John-Alexander was born, CPS was ready to take him, but his biological mother contacted Nellie.

"She told me, 'I had the baby this morning, and if you want the baby, you need to come to the hospital now, because CPS is here and they want me to sign over the documents to them and they're going to take him.' I said, 'No, no, no, you sign nothing. I'll be over.' I got up from my seat, I told the principal I had to go, emergency. And it all happened."

Nellie said she recognized the CPS worker at the hospital. They had gone to high school together.

"She couldn't believe it was me," Nellie said. "She said, 'There's not many Nellies in the world. I can't believe it's you.' She took my social (security number), my husband's social, they did a background check, and two days later I brought him home."

Juan Lopez, who has worked as an electrician for 30 years, found a helper in John-Alexander once he was old enough to go with him on jobs. John-Alexander learned the trade from him.

Now, when a classmate or teammate needs help at home with their electricity, they go to John-Alexander and the father-and-son team are on the job.

"It's part of the reason why I made my major in college, to go into construction management or civil engineering'' he said. "All of the work when I was younger with my dad inspired to get me to where I am now."

Recently, John-Alexander has been assisting his mother through several health challenges, including having a foot amputated.

"She's had issues the past couple of years, going through injuries and illness. But we've pushed through everything, helping her with the support of our entire family."

Nellie is hoping to get a prosthetic in time to be able to walk with her son during his graduation high school graduation ceremony in May.

"There are so many things coming his way, and I want to make sure that I'm there for him," Nellie said.

Richard Obert has been covering high school sports since the 1980s for The Arizona Republic. He also covers Grand Canyon University athletics and the Arizona Rattlers. headline: Is Milan Momcilovic an NBA prospect? Former Pewaukee standout is starring for Iowa State basketball; stats, rankings, brother, highlights
fullText:
Milan Momcilovic appears poised to take his game to the next level in 2024-25 at Iowa State.

The former Pewaukee High School basketball standout enters a huge non-conference showdown against Marquette on Wednesday night on the heels of an impressive showing in the Maui Invitational.

The former Wisconsin Mr. Basketball and three-time state champion scored a career-high in Iowa State's final game in Maui, helping the Cyclones go 2-1 in the high-profile event.

And if early returns are any indication, Momcilovic will continue to raise his NBA stock for an Iowa State team (5-1) that should get a lot of attention all season as it remains near the top of the college basketball rankings.

Marquette head coach Shaka Smart recruited Momcilovic and gave him an offer, but the Golden Eagles weren't one of his six finalists over two years ago.

Momcilovic's immediate connection to Iowa State head coach T.J. Otzelberger led him to Ames, Iowa, often a hub for Milwaukee area stars.

Here's the latest on Momcilovic:

Where did Milan Momcilovic go to high school?

Pewaukee High School.

He won three consecutive WIAA Division 2 state championships to complete his high school career from 2021-23. Momcilovic swept the postseason awards as a senior, winning Mr. Basketball, WBCA state player of the year and Gatorade state player of the year.

The Watt brothers, also Pewaukee HS graduates, were huge fans of Momcilovic's Pewaukee Pirates during their state title runs.

How many points does Milan Momcilovic average per game?

Momcilovic is Iowa State's third-leading scorer at 12.8 points per game through the team's first six games.

That's an improvement from the 10.9 points he averaged in 37 games, all starts, as a freshman.

Milan Momcilovic stats

Momcilovic has started from the time he arrived at Iowa State.

And he's produced from the jump. Momcilovic led the team in scoring in his first college game and never slowed down as he displayed the smooth shot he was known for in high school. He nailed a game-winning shot in the closing moments to defeat Houston early in the conference season, a moment that helped put him on the map.

Momcilovic earned a spot on the Big 12 Championship All-Tournament Team after leading the Cyclones to the Big 12 tourney title. His Cyclones were a No. 2 seed in the 2024 NCAA Tournament and advanced to the Sweet 16.

His stat line as a freshman: 37 games, 30.2 minutes, 10.9 points, 42% shooting, 35.9% from three-point range, 80.9% free throws, 3.1 rebounds, 1.2 assists, 0.4 blocks, 0.5 steals.

His stat line as a sophomore: 6 games, 26.7 minutes, 12.8 points, 51.9% shooting, 47.1% from three-point range, 71.4% free throws, 3.3 rebounds, 0.8 assists, 0.2 blocks, 0.2 steals.

Momcilovic's shooting has improved significantly. He scored a career-high 24 points in the Cyclones’ 99-71 victory over Colorado in the fifth-place game of the 2024 Maui Invitational last week. He shot 9 of 13 from the field, including 6 of 9 from three-point range.

Milan Momcilovic height, weight

Momcilovic is 6-feet-7 and weighs 225 pounds.

Milan Momcilovic NBA

Before the college basketball season began, Momcilovic slotted in as a second-round pick at No. 43 overall, according to ESPN's rankings.

Bleacher Report's most recent mock draft has the Iowa State star 52nd overall.

"Milan Momcilovic has quickly shown off the high-level shot-making skill that earned him looks last season. Some of the off-balance jumpers he's able to make rank high on the difficulty scale," Bleacher Report's analysis of Momcilovic notes. The sports website compares him to former first-round pick Rodney Hood.

Milan Momcilovic brother

Milan Momcilovic's brother, Luka, is a senior on the Pewaukee High School boys basketball team and a Division 1 recruit having committed to St. Thomas in Minnesota. Milan played the final two years of his high school career at Pewaukee with Luka.

Luka has a similar build to Milan, standing at 6-foot-7 and weighing 215 pounds.

Luka earned Division 2 All-State Honorable Mention honors last year after helping the Pirates to a state runner-up finish. Momcilovic was named to the Division 2 All-Tournament Team.

Milan Momcilovic 247 rankings

Milan Momcilovic was a four-star recruit from Rivals, ESPN and 247 Sports as a senior. Overall, he was ranked the 34th-best player in the country by 247 Sports in 2023, No. 42 by Rivals and No. 51 by ESPN. His ranking was the third-highest ever for an Iowa State recruit in modern era, his bio states.

headline: A $1 million Mega Millions ticket was sold at a Milwaukee food mart
fullText:
Someone who bought a lottery ticket at Milwaukee's El Rey Food Mart has earned a million-dollar prize.

The winning Mega Millions ticket was sold at the food mart, 1320 W. Burnham St., for Tuesday's drawing. The ticket matched five of five numbers, 52-60-61-66-67, but not the Mega Ball, which was 23.

Only three tickets sold for the drawing matched five of the five numbers. The other two tickets were sold in Ohio, according to a news release from Wisconsin Lottery.

Since the current Mega Millions jackpot run began Sept. 13, 38 tickets sold have won least $1 million, Wisconsin Lottery announced.

The jackpot is now an estimated $579 million for Friday's drawing.

In 2024, the Mega Millions jackpot has been won three times. Most recently, it has been won in Texas, where an $810 million winning ticket was sold.

In November, a Cedarburg man, Ethan Tews, won $1 million from a Bankroll scratch ticket purchased at a Madison Kwik Trip.

The odds of winning a million-dollar Mega Millions prize is one out of 12, 607,307 and the odds of winning the Mega Millions jackpot are 1 out of 302,575,350.

According to the Wisconsin Lottery website, since 1988, Wisconsin Lottery has generated more than $19.1 billion in total revenue. More than 93% of that revenue has been distributed to homeowners, winners and retailers.

Alcohol became available at Badgers football games this year. Then, arrests went down

Despite a disappointing Wisconsin football season, there was one bright spot at Camp Randall Stadium this year: arrests for underage drinking were the lowest they've been in four years.

It's a trend campus police noticed ever since the university started selling alcohol at its football games this August, writes reporter Eva Wen.

According to University of Wisconsin-Madison Police Department interim police chief Brent Plisch, alcohol-related police contacts decreased by about 25%, from 118 incidents in 2021 to 89 incidents this year.

Although it might seem counterintuitive, Plisch said this is a phenomenon across college athletics in general: After allowing alcohol to be served inside the stadiums, universities tend to see a reduction in police contacts for alcohol-related offenses.

Plisch said the reduction could be because people of legal drinking age no longer feel the need to pregame or drink excessively prior because they know they can buy alcohol at the stadium. headline: Mega-popular TikToker Alix Earle had 'best Thanksgiving ever' at Lambeau Field with 45 of her loved ones. What else did she do in Green Bay?
fullText:
Alix Earle had "the best Thanksgiving ever" in Green Bay, Wisconsin.

The mega-popular social media influencer shared that sentiment in a recent TikTok.

Earle, who has 7.1 million followers on the platform, spent the holiday with 45 of her loved ones in a Lambeau Field suite for the Green Bay Packers-Miami Dolphins game.

But not before swinging by Kopp's Frozen Custard on the way up and doing up Blackout Wednesday at a Green Bay country bar.

Why was Earle in town? Her boyfriend, Braxton Berrios, is a wide receiver for Miami, though he's out for the season due to injury. Earle's mom, Alisa, is from Wisconsin and her side of the family still lives here.

Here's a look at Earle's visit and the videos she made along the way:

How Alix Earle spent Blackout Wednesday in Green Bay, Wisconsin

It was two years ago on Thanksgiving Eve that Earle posed a question to her followers in a TikTok — and it went absolutely viral.

In the video, she was trying on different going-out fits. One of those: A Princess Polly plunging white corset top.

"Like, is this too much for a little like bar in New Jersey?" she asked. Her conclusion: "Definitely."

She decided on a different shirt and headed out, but would end up running back upstairs to change back into the white number.

This Blackout Wednesday, Earle was in Green Bay. But, still paid homage to that viral moment.

Since Earle and her family were going to the football game the next night, they celebrated Thanksgiving dinner on the eve, she shared in a "GRWM" (get ready with me) video.

"The night before Thanksgiving, I feel like everyone is just ready to go out 'cause all we're going to be doing is sitting and eating food tomorrow," she said.

But before all of that, she needed to know the coat situation.

"I know it's 20 degrees, but I'm like, do you wear it to a bar 'cause then where do you put it?" she asked.

Valid question, Alix. But, always a coat, yes.

In another video, she asked her followers to help pick out her outfit, which needed to work for both family dinner and going out.

She decided on a grey matching shorts set with tights that was giving corporate chic and NSFW all at the same time. She added a pair of black knee-high boots, an oversized black blazer and black purse.

"Like, is this too much for a little bar in Wisconsin?" she asked. "Definitely."

So, where did Earle and her posse end up going for BOW? Black Saddle Tavern & Oasis, 201 N. Washington St., she said in a later TikTok.

"We were having fun, we were dancing," she said.

When she goes out, the Earle girls — what her fans are called — want to party together, she said. But, her mom isn't used to the shoving, crowding and cameras.

"I'm always like: "Mom, just like please be nice to everyone," Earle said. "If my mom cursed you out last night, I'm so sorry."

The story behind Alix Earle spending Thanksgiving at the Packers-Dolphins game in Green Bay

Before the NFL schedule was released this year, Earle knew that the Packers were going to be playing the Dolphins, she shared in a video.

"My grandma called me and was like, 'We need to make this happen,'" she said.

When it was announced that it would be the Thanksgiving game, Earle booked 10 hotel rooms in Wisconsin and planned to get tickets to the game.

"It's extra special because my grandma had a tough year and we've never all spent Thanksgiving with everyone," she said in the video.

With a group of over 40 on board and the expectation that it would be cold, Earle started looking into suite options. Poppi — one of Earle's longtime brand partners, which she invested in — planned to deck it out, she said.

"I'm really, really excited because, apparently, Lambeau Field is like one of the coolest stadiums," she said. "I think it's the oldest stadium. So apparently, like the fans just go nuts. It's right in the middle of a residential area. And, everyone just says it's such an experience."

Sounds about right! Except for that Soldier Field, home of the Chicago Bears, is officially the oldest. Lambeau is second. The Bears gotta ruin everything, huh (still miss you, Simone).

Why wasn't Alix Earle's boyfriend, Miami Dolphin Braxton Berrios, in Green Bay for Thanksgiving?

While Berrios' family was supposed to travel to Green Bay and be in the suite as well, Berrios' injury prevented him from sitting on the sidelines and traveling, Earle explained in a TikTok.

"Honestly, I think my grandma's secretly probably happy because she's such a Packers fan," Earle said. "I was like: Grandma, you cannot root against Braxton. Like, you have to wear Dolphins stuff. And now, she's like: I can wear my Packers gear."

A glimpse at Alix Earle's time at the Packers-Dolphins Thanksgiving game at Lambeau Field in Green Bay

In true tailgate fashion, Earle layered the heck up.

"Happy game day!" she said in a TikTok. "Let's get dressed for a football game in Green Bay, Wisconsin — except it's 20 degrees."

She wore a black turtleneck and thick tights under her favorite pair of skinny jeans, a custom white Dolphins sweatshirt with "Berrios" on the hood and a vintage orange Dolphins bomber jacket. She added not one, but two pairs of socks under black boots.

She finished off the look with a white beanie embellished with her boyfriend's number and a Frame belt.

"Here we gooo into the cooold," she sang.

In her game day vlog, Earle and her 45 relatives and family friends got the party started in a party bus.

Later, at Lambeau, Earle was surprised by how many Dolphins fans there were among the sea of cheeseheads.

"But, we were definitely outnumbered," she added.

While Earle and her immediate family repped the Dolphins, the rest of her group sported the green and gold. (She made a funny TikTok about that, too).

The "massive" suite — "that Poppi got us," Earle said — was indeed decked out, with custom merch, sweaters, blankets, tumblers and buckets filled with cans of the prebiotic soda.

"Just when we thought it couldn't get any better, it started snowing," Earle said in her vlog. "And then, I started crying because I was just so happy to be there with my family. And, everyone was having so much fun."

There were fireworks and an elaborate spread of food, including truffle mac and cheese.

It was Earle's sister/fellow social media star Ashtin Earle's first NFL game. Earle's kid sister, Penelope, sat outside the whole game, locked in. On the other hand, little sister Izabel fell asleep on the floor inside the suite.

"It truly was just really magical," Earle said. "My family was having so much fun. It was the best Thanksgiving ever. I just kept crying."

Who is Alix Earle?

Besides being a successful TikToker, Earle is host of the "Hot Mess with Alix Earle" podcast, which is part of "Call Her Daddy" star Alex Cooper's Unwell Network.

Earle — who lives in Miami — is known for her "GRWM" videos in which she talks about what's going on in her life while she applies makeup and picks out a fit.

While jet-setting and sharing those glamorous moments, Earle also comes off as down-to-earth, goofy and relatable, opening up about what it's like being a 20-something and her own insecurities.

Earle was just in Wisconsin in June to surprise her grandma and introduce her to her beau. During that visit, she filmed a funny TikTok with her mom and grandma at the Harbor House, danced like nobody was watching — or filming — at RWB Milwaukee, swung by the Milwaukee Public Market and more.

She also came to town in the summer of 2023. During that trip, she went to Bradford Beach with family, partied at The Outsider, shopped 414Flea, and again, hit up Kopp's.

In a previous video, Earle said that she and Ashtin once spent a summer living in Milwaukee.

This year, the University of Miami alum was named to the Forbes 30 under 30 — social media list. She was also the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit's inaugural digital cover star and walked in the SI Swimsuit runway show for Miami Swim Week.

This past summer, however, Earle faced backlash after screenshots had been circulating online of her using a racial slur on her ask.fm account when she was 13, according to a USA TODAY report. She confirmed the screenshots were real and apologized for her ignorance as a teen.

"My platform has always focused on positivity, entertainment, and uplifting others, and will continue to do so. I am sincerely sorry to those I have offended," she shared, in part, on an Instagram story.

headline: 10 top winter Milwaukee concerts, from Tyler, The Creator to Rod Wave to Justin Timberlake
fullText:
There was a time when many major tours skipped over Milwaukee during the winter months — and who could blame them?

But not this winter.

Two of the biggest country stars in the world will play Fiserv Forum six days apart in January. Two of the biggest rappers in the world will play the Bucks arena two days apart in February. That same month, one of the biggest pop stars of the 20th century will be in town — and there are some highly promising theater and club gigs, too.

These are the 10 top concert options in Milwaukee this December through February, listed in order of occurrence.

Girl in Red

When touring starts to slow down each December, WLUM-FM (102.1) steps up in a big way with its Big Snow Show concert series, bringing exciting alt-rock up-and-comers and arena-level headliners to the Rave. The 18th year of concerts kicks off with Norwegian artist Girl in Red, who turned a catchy and cathartic debut album into opening slots on Taylor Swift’s historic “Eras Tour.”

When, where, how much: 8 p.m. Dec. 9, the Rave, 2401 W. Wisconsin Ave. $47 to $112 at the box office and therave.com.

Cage The Elephant

The Big Snow Show booking coup continues with blistering alt-rockers Cage The Elephant, onetime Milwaukee regulars who haven’t been to town in five years. And in that absence, the band has headlined arenas behind latest album “Neon Pill” and scored the prestigious opening slot for Oasis’ highly anticipated North American stadium tour next year.

When, where, how much: 8 p.m. Dec. 11, the Rave. $55 to $70.

Kelsea Ballerini

The country pop star, who unsurprisingly avoided curveballs in exchange for rising stardom, took an unexpected risk with her surprise 2023 EP “Rolling Up the Welcome Mat” that candidly dissected the end of her marriage to Morgan Evans. She’s continued the rejuvenation with recently released full-length “Patterns,” which marked her highest debut ever on the Billboard 200 and led into her first arena-headlining show in town.

When, where, how much: 7 p.m. Jan. 25, Fiserv Forum, 1111 N. Phillips Ave. $75.50 to $493 at the box office and fiservforum.com.

Kerry King

The mighty Slayer, one of the “big four” influential thrash metal bands (alongside Metallica, Megadeth and Anthrax) didn’t come to Milwaukee on its farewell tour. But Slayer guitarist Kerry King isn’t skipping Brew City this time as he tours behind debut solo album “From Hell I Rise” with a band that includes Slayer’s Paul Bostaph on drums.

When, where, how much: 7 p.m. Jan. 28, the Rave. $40 to $50.

Cody Johnson

Separating himself from his fellow country superstars with a pronounced reverence for traditionalists like fellow Texan George Strait, Johnson took a major artistic (and commercial) leap with last year’s double album “Leather,” which just won album of the year honors at the CMA Awards. Be smart and arrive early for Ashley McBryde; Drew Baldridge also opens.

When, where, how much: 7:30 p.m. Jan. 31, Fiserv Forum. $50 to $150.

Rod Wave

Taylor Swift may be a superstar in her own realm, but she has an equal in one regard: Rapper-singer Rod Wave and Swift are the only artists who had three different No. 1 albums on the Billboard 200 from 2021 to 2023. Wave just missed the mark with his latest album "Last Lap," which debuted at No. 2 this fall, but his powerful, trauma-processing catalog has a massive fan base, filling up Fiserv Forum for shows in 2022 and 2023. Sweetening the deal for his return (which was postponed from November) is another rapper who’s headlined Fiserv Forum in the past, Moneybagg Yo.

When, where, how much: 7 p.m. Feb. 4, Fiserv Forum. $54 to $382.

Tyler, The Creator

Rod Wave may have the first major Milwaukee hip-hop show of the year, but Tyler, The Creator has a good chance of putting on the best rap show in the city next year just two days later. His latest (and possibly greatest) album "Chromakopia" is a huge hit (No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for three weeks as of press time), and his intensely thoughtful presentation at his last Fiserv Forum concert — from huge, imaginative set pieces to carefully plotted blinking (yes blinking) was one of the best Milwaukee concerts of 2022. His return is highly anticipated for another reason: It will be just the second show of his world tour.

When, where, how much: 7:30 p.m. Feb. 6, Fiserv Forum. $164.50 to $545.50.

Goose

It was a blow to jam band fans in Milwaukee and beyond when Widespread Panic canceled its planned Riverside Theater residency this fall in the wake of guitarist Jimmy Herring’s cancer diagnosis (here’s hoping to a speedy recovery). But the city will be the host of a very special event for jam band fans in early 2025: the first scheduled shows of the year for one of the most exciting new star acts from the scene, Goose.

When, where, how much: 8 p.m. Feb. 6 to 8, Miller High Life Theatre, 500 W. Kilbourn Ave. $34.75 to $251.72, $135.75 to $238.50 for three-day pass, at the door, the Riverside Theater box office (116 W. Wisconsin Ave.) and pabsttheater.org.

Wallows

Until recently, Dylan Minnette probably was best known for being one of the stars of Netflix’s “13 Reasons Why,” while his friend Braeden Lemasters was best known for a role on TNT’s “Men of a Certain Age." But the actors' alt-rock act Wallows — with hints of the Strokes, but dreamier — is becoming their best-known outlet, leading to arena shows behind latest album “Model.” In Milwaukee, they'll play a more intimate setting.

When, where, how much: 7:30 p.m. Feb. 10, the Rave. $50.50 to $199.

Justin Timberlake

Fortunately, a bout of bronchitis and laryngitis didn't "ruin the tour." This fall, illness prompted Timberlake to postpone six tour dates, including one in Milwaukee, but he didn't outright cancel them, instead rescheduling them for February. And while the pop superstar has been saddled with "meh" reviews for his latest album "Everything I Thought I Was," his current tour, fueled by a huge catalog of hits, engaging personality and some very elaborate and impressive staging, has been getting rave reviews.

When, where, how much: 7:30 p.m. Feb. 22, Fiserv Forum. $60 to $500.

headline: Analysis of accidental shootings shows how they are charged in Wisconsin varies. What to know
fullText:
The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel conducted a first-of-its-kind analysis of accidental shootings where children are hurt or killed in Wisconsin, covering 2016 to December 2024. Here are some key findings: 

  • Wisconsin has a law designed to address accidental shootings of children as a misdemeanor, but prosecutors in Milwaukee County almost always opt instead to file felony child neglect charges, which can have impacts on defendants’ lives for years.
  • Outside Milwaukee, such cases are more often charged as a misdemeanor, including cases where a child has died. Only the most extreme cases have led to felony charges.
  • The number of accidental shootings involving children rose 30% during the pandemic and has been ticking down in the past two years. Milwaukee has the most cases in the state, roughly half of the 165 cases during the whole period.
  • Thirty-one children died in accidental shootings statewide, ranging from two in one year to seven deaths in 2022. Nineteen of the deaths occurred in Milwaukee County.
  • Relatives of the victims are typically the ones charged in such cases. Most often, it is the mother or father.
  • The majority of defendants charged in such cases do not have criminal histories. They typically receive probation or short jail terms. Longer sentences, however, have been handed down especially when a child dies and the defendant has a criminal record.

headline: 5 facts about accidental gun deaths in the U.S. and Wisconsin that may surprise you
fullText:
Accidental shootings are the most uncommon type of gun death in the U.S., accounting for about 1% of all shootings. Here are some facts about accidental gun deaths in the U.S. and Wisconsin:

  1. Accidental shooting deaths have been dropping nationwide, from 2,000 in 1979 to about 500 annually now. The share of child victims has risen, especially during the pandemic.
  2. Accidental gun deaths account for 5% of all gun deaths among children in the U.S. 
  3. Over time, children ages 1 to 4 have become more likely to be victims, and nationwide those toddlers are more often Black children.
  4. Victims in the age groups of 15- to 19-year-olds and 20- to 24-year-olds are tied for having the highest rate of unintentional gun deaths nationwide. The two single age groups with the highest rates are 3-year-olds and 21-year-olds.
  5. In Wisconsin, there were 123 unintentional gun deaths between 2004 and 2021, with the largest category being ages 18 to 29 with 36 deaths.

Sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data from 2018 through 2023; Wisconsin Department of Health Services data from 2004 to 2021 (the most recent available)

headline: Here’s the data and sources behind our investigation into accidental shootings in Wisconsin
fullText:
To investigate unintentional shootings involving children in Wisconsin, we had some simple goals: We wanted to be as complete as possible and we wanted to reveal something new that readers may not know.

We would like to think we accomplished both. Here is how we did it:

Data was key as we set out to figure out how often children are hurt or killed in accidental shootings and how those cases are handled in the criminal justice system.

We analyzed unintentional gun death data from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention over roughly 20 years. (It is important to note the CDC uses the term “unintentional” not “accidental” when referring to such cases to underscore the preventability of these incidents, a CDC spokeswoman said.)

We also searched media accounts using online search tools and the publicly available databases of two gun safety groups, Gun Violence Archive and Everytown for Gun Safety.

To learn how such cases are handled in the criminal justice system, we analyzed data from Wisconsin’s Consolidated Court Automation Programs (CCAP) with the assistance of Journal Sentinel data reporter Eva Wen and Branden DuPont, deputy director of analytics at Loyola University’s Center for Criminal Justice in Chicago. 

From CCAP, we extracted every case charged over the past 20 years under a 1991 statute created specifically to address accidental shootings. 

Reporter John Diedrich and former intern Ben Schultz collected every criminal complaint for about 50 cases and coded them for factors such as the defendant’s relationship to the victim, how the gun was stored and why the gun was purchased.

After Diedrich requested records from the Milwaukee County District Attorney’s Office and the Milwaukee Police Department, it became clear that unintentional shootings involving children are charged in different ways in different counties. In Milwaukee, the team found such cases are almost always charged as felonies under a different state law. 

The team sought to find every accidental shooting case through this layered approach. However, because the cases are charged differently, some cases were likely missed.

All told, the team examined roughly 130 criminal cases statewide dating back nearly 20 years, but results are based on data from 2016 to 2024 as that data is more complete. Through media accounts, the team also examined nearly 200 incidents, charged and uncharged, going back to 2005.

The team also examined unintentional shootings during gun hunting seasons, analyzing data from the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and assembled by Wen.

Diedrich attended more than a dozen court hearings and interviewed dozens of people including defendants, victims, firearms instructors, prosecutors, defense lawyers, public health researchers, elected officials and law enforcement officers. He and visual journalist Mike De Sisti attended gun training classes, a home safety tour and talked with families affected by charging decisions.

Reporter John Diedrich can be reached at jdiedrich@gannett.com.

About this project

Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporter John Diedrich examined the full extent of gun deaths in Wisconsin during a nine-month O’Brien Fellowship in Public Service Journalism at Marquette University.

The project reveals the full picture of gun deaths in the state and tells the stories of people affected by gun deaths and those trying to find solutions.

Marquette University and administrators of the program played no role in the reporting, editing or presentation of this project.

headline: Wisconsin lawmakers pit neighbor against neighbor with every school referendum | Opinion
fullText:
On election day, Wisconsinites across the state voted to raise the cost of their own housing in order to ensure that their communities could offer decent public education. A record number of school referendums were on the ballot, and a whopping 78% of them passed. Local taxpayers across the state granted their schools $3.4 billion out of their own pockets to cover necessary expenses.

But they shouldn’t have had to.

Like some James Bond movie villain, the Legislature has set up a diabolical game for its citizens to play every election cycle. We can have predictable and stable housing costs, or we can have adequately-funded schools, but we can’t have both. And we citizens have to fight each other on a regular basis to decide which will prevail. Lawmakers sit by idly and watch it all happen – cackling and petting a hairless cat, I imagine.   

Those additional property taxes are not mere inconveniences. It isn’t just “pain” for some of our neighbors. It isn’t just an additional “pinch” in the wallet. With one vote, the neighborhoods and the school districts where some folks have lived for decades have become unaffordable to them. 

Opinion: Your child may not be doing as well in school as you think. State lowered bar.

And for communities that voted down a school referendum, the results are no less devastating. A failed referendum often means that schools have to cut teachers, shut down electives and defer renovations to crumbling buildings. With one vote, the schools and communities where folks have hoped to raise their kids or spend their careers have become uninhabitable to them.

Wisconsin lawmakers did 3 things to put school funding into bind

Our state legislature has done three specific things to put us in this bind. 

First, it reneged on a 1993 promise to cover two-thirds of all public schooling costs in the state, which means local property taxes have to pick up the tab. 

Second, starting in 2009, it decoupled local taxation authority from the rate of inflation, which will force every district to referendum sooner or later. 

And third, it continues to dramatically underfund special education. That’s the big one.

Letters: State education budget proposal is a big win for students across Wisconsin

By law, special education is “categorical” aid, which means that the state funds it according to actualcosts rather than an estimated average. It also means that state money for special education is not capped by “revenue limits.” 

But because the state only reimburses one third of special-education expenditures – the worst rate in the nation – local school districts have to cover the balance with local property taxes and general state aids, which are restricted by revenue limits. 

Wisconsin districts are constantly having to drain their general funds to provide special education services because state support for those expenses is so stingy. And adding injury to insult, state law prohibits local districts from compensating for the state’s own dereliction without referendum approval. 

Current school funding structure pits neighbor against neighbor

That is what pits neighbor against neighbor, making affordable housing and adequate public schooling look like optional luxuries rather than basic necessities.

We do not have to live this way. The state has created this mess for us, and the state can clean it up any time it wants. 

How?

Mainly by increasing its own share of educational spending. The state doesn’t even need to levy additional taxes to do it. This year, the state of Wisconsin once again has a multi-billion dollar budget surplus (projected at more than $4 billion). That means it is already collecting vastly more taxes from its citizens than it is reinvesting in our communities. This is the third consecutive year of surpluses, with another projected in 2025. The state is curling itself around its mountain of gold like some JRR Tolkein dragon while local taxpayers fight each other over indispensable public goods.

The state could fully fund special education in Wisconsin without even breaking a sweat. Covering every dime of those expenditures across the state would leave roughly 70% of our budget surplus available to invest elsewhere. 

Policies to right this standing wrong are already circulating. The state superintendent recently announced a budget proposal that would shift more school funding responsibility toward the state. It includes explicit housing-cost protections for property owners. Rep. Robyn Vining’s “Save Our Schools” bill would also enshrine a 90% special-education reimbursement rate into state law, protecting homeowners from tax hikes and stabilizing school district budgets. 

Either major party would kill for the 60% vote share that school referendums got on November 5th. Funding public education while protecting homeowners is the easiest ‘W’ on the policy table. It’s not rocket science. Let’s get it done. 

Derek Gottlieb is an associate professor in the College of Education and Behavioral Sciences at the University of Northern Colorado.. He is the author of A Democratic Theory of Educational Accountability (2020), and the creator and host of the Wauwatosa podcast The Referenda.

headline: Moxy hotel plan to undergo a February Common Council review. A Milwaukee union opposes it
fullText:
A new hotel planned for downtown Milwaukee's Deer District is to undergo a city review in February − which will likely include union opposition.

The eight-story, 160-room Moxy Hotel is proposed for a site just off North Phillips Avenue between the FPC Live concert venue under construction and Fiserv Forum. The lot's official address is 430 W. State St., according to the Department of City Development.

An application for zoning approval has been filed with the department by the development team. That includes a Milwaukee Bucks affiliate which owns the site and Middleton-based hotel operator NCG Hospitality.

The project will need Common Council zoning approval. That process starts with a Plan Commission hearing, tentatively scheduled for Feb. 17, said Andy Inman, NCG Hospitality chief development officer.

NCG Hospitality also operates The Trade hotel, which opened in 2023 at 420 W. Juneau Ave., just north of Fiserv Forum on a Deer District parcel owned by a Bucks affiliate.

The main difference between The Trade and Moxy: the latter focuses on guests attracted by concerts and sports events, Inman said.

NCG Hospitality in April opened a Moxy in downtown Madison next to The Sylvee concert venue − also operated by FPC Live.

The developers plan to begin construction in late summer of 2025, with completion by mid-2027. There's no request for public financing.

Union attempting to organize workers at The Trade hotel

However, there were tax dollars devoted to Fiserv Forum's construction − which provides much of the impetus for the Moxy proposal, said Peter Rickman, president of Milwaukee Area Service and Hospitality Workers Organization.

MASH is trying to organize roughly 90 employees at The Trade.

Rickman said the National Labor Relations Board is investigating the group's claims that NCG Hospitality violated federal labor law in connection with a union representation election at The Trade in June.

The company denies those claims, and Inman said Moxy's ownership group differs from The Trade's owners.

Also, Inman and Bucks and Fiserv Forum President Peter Feigin both said Moxy would be built with union labor − which happened with The Trade.

Feigin said Moxy would be an investment of more than $70 million, adding to Milwaukee's property tax base while providing more patrons for nearby restaurants, taverns and other businesses.

Rickman plans to raise the union issue with Common Council members, Mayor Cavalier Johnson and other city officials in connection with NCG Hospitality's zoning application.

Both Johnson and Ald. Robert Bauman, whose district includes the site, declined to comment on the Moxy proposal.

headline: 10 tips to protect your home, whether you own a gun or not, according to safety experts
fullText:
Firearms instructors stress that a gun is the last line of defense against a home invasion. There are many things you could do to protect your home against burglaries and home invasions, whether you have a firearm or not.

  1. Add outside lighting. Static lights that stay on and lights that are activated by motion are both excellent deterrents.
  2. Make sure all windows and doors are locked; consider using longer screws in door hinges, ensuring they reach deep into the door jamb and the structural studs.
  3. Get a deadbolt for your doors. Double-key deadbolts are the best.
  4. Landscape with thorny or spiky bushes under your windows.
  5. Get a dog. The size is not as important as the bark.
  6. Never leave a key hidden on your porch or under a flower pot.
  7. Install a camera system; consider an alarm system.
  8. Make it appear like someone is home by setting lights on a timer when you are gone.
  9. Ask your neighbors to keep an eye on your place and offer to watch theirs.
  10. Don't leave a ladder next to your house. That gives burglars access to try second-story windows.

Sources: Home defense experts; law enforcement agencies; and the Insurance Information Institute.

headline: Here's what must happen before Red Arrow Park can open its ice skating rink for the season
fullText:
With winter weather now in full swing, Milwaukeeans may wonder when their favorite outdoor seasonal activities will kick off.

One popular attraction that remains closed is Red Arrow Park's Slice of Ice skating rink at 920 N. Water St. A representative from Milwaukee County Parks told the Journal Sentinel that the skating rink's opening date each year is weather-dependent.

Before the rink can open, "we need a few consecutive days below freezing without precipitation in order to get the ice filled in," she said.

Once Slice of Ice does open, the rink will offer free skating if you bring your own skates. Skate rentals are also available — $11 for adults and $8 for children 17 and under. You can rent skater support aids and ice sleds for those with mobility impairments. For hours and more information, visit the Slice of Ice website.

When does Red Arrow Park ice skating open?

The Parks representative said there isn't yet an opening date for Slice of Ice this year.

The rink usually opens in time for the Christmas and New Year's holidays. Some years, skating season has even started in late November. Last winter, unseasonably warm temperatures meant Slice of Ice couldn't open until Jan. 5, nearly a month later than usual.

Biggby Coffee is now open in Red Arrow Park

Skaters will notice one big change that's come to Red Arrow Park since last winter ― the former Starbucks next to the skating rink has been transformed into Biggby Coffee. The new café serves lattes, hot chocolate, cold brew coffee, smoothies, ready-to-go food items like breakfast sandwiches, cookies, muffins and bagels, and more.

The park's café space was vacant for about a year before Biggby opened its doors last week. Starbucks stood there for almost 20 years and closed at the end of last November. Milwaukee County Parks officials served skaters hot chocolate, coffee and treats after the Starbucks closure, and they quickly began searching for a new vendor for the space. Biggby was confirmed to be the successor in mid-December, and remodeling construction started in late September.

Where can I ice skate indoors in Milwaukee?

While you wait for Slice of Ice to kick off its season, you can hone your skating skills indoors at these Milwaukee-area rinks:

  • Pettit National Ice Center, 500 S. 84th St., offers public skating some afternoons and most evenings. Admission is $9 for adults, $8 for teens and seniors over 62, and $7 for kids 4-12. Children 3 and under skate free. Skate rentals are an additional $5. Visit the Pettit website for daily open skate hours and more information.
  • Wilson Ice Arena, 4001 S. 20th St., has afternoon public skate times almost every day throughout the year. Admission is $6.75 for adults and $5 for children 17 and under and seniors 60 and over. Skate rentals are $3.75 each. Groups of 10 or more receive discounted admission and skate rentals but must call and register in advance. Learn more and view the open skate schedule on the ice arena website.
  • Eble Park Ice Arena, 19400 W. Bluemound Road, Brookfield, has public skate hours most days. Admission is $7, and skate rentals are an additional $3. Visit the Waukesha County Park System website for the schedule of open skate times, updated regularly.
  • Naga-Waukee Ice Arena, 2699 Golf Road, Delafield, offers public skate times most days. General admission is $7, and admission is $6 for seniors 60 and over and military service members. Skate rentals are $3. Click on this link to visit the Google Calendar for public skate times each day. Visit the Waukesha County Park System website to learn more.
