headline: City of Brookfield residents could see an $8 million referendum on the April ballot
fullText:
Brookfield residents could vote this spring whether to raise their property taxes to avoid cuts to city services if officials decide to put an $8 million operating referendum question on the ballot.

The City of Brookfield’s Finance Committee voted 5-2 Tuesday to recommend the Common Council put a property tax levy referendum question with a $8 million amount on the April 2025 election ballot.

If approved, the measure would raise property taxes for the average Brookfield homeowner by an estimated $400 a year, according to Brookfield’s director of finance and administration Robert Scott.

Officials say Brookfield operating referendum is needed to avoid cuts to city services

The City of Brookfield is projected to face a major budget gap in the next five years.

Without a referendum, the city estimates an $11 million levy shortfall by 2032, according to projections Scott shared with members of the Finance Committee Tuesday. That could result in cuts to service provided by police and fire, the library, and streets to make ends meet, Scott said.

"With the $8 million amount, you basically buy yourself time through 2030," Scott told committee members, adding that a referendum wouldn't need to be revisited by council members for another five years if that amount passed.

The City of Brookfield has never held a property tax levy referendum, according to Scott. Residents last passed a school referendum for the Elmbrook School District in 2008, according to the district.

Elmbrook serves the City of Brookfield and Village of Elm Grove, as well as a small section of the City of New Berlin.

Finance Committee members were tasked with recommending a dollar amount and how to spend any excess funds to the Common Council. Members discussed higher and lower referendum amounts before the majority voted on the recommended $8 million.

Ald. Mike Hallquist, who supported the recommendation, had earlier suggested the committee consider an $8.6 million price tag that would earmark the extra $600,000 explicitly for street maintenance funds.

Ald. Rick Owen, who voted against the $8 million recommendation along with Ald. Jerry Mellone, wanted a lower number to limit residents' opposition. Owen said he'd support a $6 million referendum.

"Like everybody else is saying, you want to make sure this wins, and I think you've got to be very careful about your ask," Owen said.

How much would the average city of Brookfield property tax bill increase?

If voters approve an $8 million referendum, the estimated $400 property tax increase per homeowner is based on $460,000, the average assessed price of a home in Brookfield.

In comparison, the owner of an average house is currently paying a little under $400 less than they were paying 12 years ago, according to Scott. That's due mostly to monies in school-related credits and tightened tax levy limits, he said.

Why are municipalities turning to operating referendums?

Wisconsin municipalities can't raise their levies due to state-imposed revenue limits, making raising property taxes the main way to keep up with rising costs.

Other Milwaukee suburbs have turned to operating referendums recently to increase their tax levies.

Germantown, Port Washington, Cedarburg, Grafton and Saukville passed public safety referendums April 2 to increase funding for fire and police services.

In November, Madison voters passed a referendum to raise $22 million through property taxes in order to avoid service cuts, Wisconsin Public Radio reported.

Wisconsin school districts have also increasingly turned to referendums to raise more taxes for funding.

Brookfield, like other municipalities, can collect more money annually due to net new construction in the area.

Although Brookfield's growth in recent years is significant, money from that alone is nowhere near the amount needed to keep up with inflation or other rising costs that affect the city's budget, Scott said.

The previous legislature session's work to increase shared revenue — unrestricted aid provided by the state to counties and municipalities through several programs — for local governments, has helped slightly in Brookfield, but not enough, Scott said.

Brookfield received $1.3 million in shared revenue from the state in November 2024, according to the Department of Revenue.

Any extra funds could cover Brookfield road maintenance, city debts, depending on staff recommendations

The Finance Committee has spent nearly two years discussing how to address the anticipated budget gap, landing on the need for the referendum, Scott said.

Besides determining the dollar amount to request to the Common Council, the committee will make a suggestion for ways to use funds not immediately needed for the 2026 budget, Scott wrote in a letter to the committee.

The amount of those extra funds would depend on the referendum's dollar amount. Staff recommends they be used to replenish the vehicle and equipment replacement funds, pay off city debts, give a one-time boost for pavement maintenance, fire department budgeting and more.

Additionally, funds could be used to close another Tax Incremental District, or TID, and place its monies in an escrow to retire the remaining debt balance. Earlier this year, the City Council voted to close TID No. 5 and added about $325,000 in capacity to the levy for the 2025 budget, according to Scott's letter.

At its next meeting, the Finance Committee plans to discuss possible uses for any excess funds in order to make a recommendation to the Common Council.

Common Council needs to vote to put the referendum on the April 2025 ballot

A referendum is not a done deal.

The Brookfield Common Council must approve a referendum question before the statutory deadline of Jan. 21 in order to get it on the April 2025 ballot.

The council will vote on the question before Jan. 21, but the meeting has not yet been scheduled.

The council has already approved a roughly $71,000 agreement for Mueller Communications to lead a public education campaign in the event the city pursues a referendum.

Bridget Fogarty reports on Wauwatosa, Brookfield and Elm Grove for the Journal Sentinel. She can be reached at bfogarty@gannett.com

headline: Act 10 could take center stage in upcoming state Supreme Court election
fullText:
MADISON - The race for Wisconsin's Supreme Court is set to take center stage in 2025, and there could be a new issue on the justices' schedule: the overturn of the law known as Act 10, which removed bargaining rights from the majority of state employees.

Dane County Circuit Judge Jacob Frost on Monday overturned the law, which stripped the collective bargaining rights from public employees, consequently decimating the size and power of employee unions. Act 10 was heavily championed by then-Gov. Scott Walker, a Republican, who touted it as a way for the state and local governments to save money.

Walker, in a video posted to X shortly after Monday's ruling, said an appeal to the decision is likely to head to the Supreme Court and that Act 10 could be gutted by liberal justices if they maintain a majority on the court.

"My fear is, with the potential for a fourth political activist added to the Supreme Court next spring in Wisconsin, you could see this completely unraveled," he said in the video.

The ruling this week is likely to be challenged in lower courts before making its way to the state's highest court, and the candidates — liberal Dane County Judge Susan Crawford and Waukesha County Circuit Court Judge Brad Schimel, a former Republican attorney general — will face questions over how they would vote on the issue if it came before them.

"It tends to be the court where the big battles get fought out," said Barry Burden, a political science professor at University of Wisconsin-Madison and director of the university's Elections Research Center. "Without a kind of regularly functioning legislative branch and executive branch working together, the court is the venue where the hot items, big ticket items, are being decided."

State workers cited 'dire' workplaces in challenge to the law

The effort to overturn Act 10 started late last year, when several unions representing public employees filed the lawsuit, citing a "dire situation" in state workplaces, with issues including low pay, staffing shortages and poor working conditions.

In his ruling, Frost said the decision came down to how state employees were classified as either "public safety" employees or "general" employees. Public safety employees, like police officers, were exempt from the ban on bargaining, and their unions remained strong while others were dismantled.

The judge deemed that distinction unconstitutional, and said he couldn't remove the provisions outlining public safety employees or general employees while leaving the rest of Act 10 in place.

While unions and employees across the state are celebrating the victory, there is also awareness about the appeals that will likely be filed in the coming weeks. And the case is then likely to make its way to the state Supreme Court, setting the stage for a battle.

Liberals currently hold a 4-3 majority on the court, but that could change after liberal Justice Ann Walsh Bradley announced her retirement, opening up a seat.

That means once again, the ideological balance of the court is up to Wisconsin voters. And with state Supreme Court races garnering more attention, more money and more votes, that means that there will be more attention paid to the issues on which they could vote.

Abortion is expected to be another key issue in Supreme Court race

Of course, abortion is likely to be on the docket. Though a ruling in one of the abortion cases before the court could come before April election, it's still likely that the new court will find itself voting on other abortion-related cases. Then there are the cases involving the separation of powers, resulting from the lawsuits filed by Democratic Gov. Tony Evers against the Legislature in recent years, and maybe even some environmental issues as well.

But Act 10 is likely to play a central role in the messaging once the campaigns for Schimel and Crawford start in earnest.

Joe Oslund, the Democratic Party of Wisconsin communications director, said that while the race is going to be bigger than any one single issue, he expects voters to continue to reject the agenda of former Gov. Walker and Republicans who want to return Wisconsin to it. Schimel, who served as attorney general during Walker's time in office has already brought attention to Act 10 as an issue for this race.

"I think at the end of the day, Wisconsinites had enough of that," Oslund said. "That's evident in their rejection of Scott Walker in 2018 and I think we've moved on as a state, and it's time to kind of heal and unite and move forward."

And the right to have a voice in the workplace and the ability for employees to advocate for themselves is important not only to state workers, but all of those who are employed, Oslund said. Different classes of workers were being treated differently under Act 10, and it was being justified by Republicans as a cost-saving measure.

"We can make good fiscal decisions without attacking people's right to organize," he said.

Brandon Scholz, a former Republican strategist, said at this point, it's difficult to say how much of a role Act 10 will play in the campaign at this point, because it does affect a smaller group of people — state employees. But there will be interest from unions at large, which have historically advocated for political candidates.

But it still remains to be seen when and if Act 10 actually makes it to the Supreme Court.

"The question is, where will this appeal be, and what can the two candidates have to say about it?" he said.

Burden, the UW professor, said it's becoming commonplace for candidates for Supreme Court to talk more about the cases they could be a part of, a shift that's happened in recent years. Voters want to hear how the potential justices will vote, and how that aligns with their values and desires.

"Now we should just expect candidates to be quite frank about all of that, and it can be helpful for drawing out support of allied groups who are going to campaign on the candidates behalf, to put in money or to volunteer time," he said. "You can imagine the labor unions are going to be active in this next Supreme Court race, in a way they probably weren't in the past, because act 10 is at stake again, so this is likely to be another expensive, ideological battle for control of the Supreme Court."

Laura Schulte can be reached at leschulte@jrn.com and on X at @SchulteLaura.

headline: Policy Forum report: Wisconsin finances in good shape. Lawmakers cautioned against big moves
fullText:
MADISON - Heading into a year of crafting Wisconsin's next biennial budget, leaders may want to be more conservative than in years prior, according to a new report released Thursday.

The report, created by the nonpartisan Wisconsin Policy Forum, shows that while the state still has large reserves that put it in a strong financial position, officials may want to be cautious, especially in regards to tax cuts or big spending increases.

Here's what you should know about the study, and what it shows for the 2026-2028 budget, which will be put together next year.

How much will the state have in reserves?

The Policy Forum estimates that Wisconsin will have about $6 billion in total reserves. That number is $3 billion less than it was in 2023, but still puts Wisconsin in a better position than has been in in the past. For context, the report said, states averaged total reserves of 23.3% of general fund spending in 2024 compared to 26.9% for Wisconsin, according to the National Association of State Budget Officers.

But of course, with any predictions, there is uncertainty in regards to future state revenues and spending, the report said.

"The economy and state costs and tax collections could be affected by global events and federal policies on taxes, tariffs, and immigration," it said. "Those factors in turn could have big impacts on the state’s fiscal position."

Why did the surplus amount fall this year?

The combined forces of inflation and massive amounts of federal pandemic aid boosted state tax collections, the report said, and when paired with tight limits on spending, that created the huge surplus the state reported during the last budget session. The surplus helped to build up state reserves that remain large today.

Federal COVID funding has now run out, and there won't be any more coming to Wisconsin.

What does the study not include?

The study didn't look at additional funds to help pay for the rising costs of things such as Medicaid, K-12 schools, local governments, prisons, technical colleges, and the Universities of Wisconsin.

While Medicaid is expected to cost $1.1 billion over the next two years, the Legislature could use federal funds to expand the program. Republicans, however, have indicated they do not support such an expansion.

There could also be local impacts to reserves from the choosing to increase spending, or opting not to. For example, if the Legislature decides not to allow new revenue for school districts, the state may need to provide additional general aid, or school boards could decide to raise property taxes locally.

What options does the report lay out for the budget?

Lawmakers are going to have to consider how much budget positions have changed in the last few years, the report said. There isn't the opportunity for massive spending increases or tax cuts without the potential to impact future funding for programs and services offered by the state. To make up for the federal funding the state received in past years, officials may want to consider spending some of the current reserves, while still maintaining some of that money to "protect against unforeseen shocks."

"The influx of federal aid and a relatively strong economy helped protect the state’s finances in recent years despite the incredible turmoil of the pandemic. Yet there is no guarantee that the state’s good fortune will last," the report said.

"In future years, the state may have to rely less on outside assistance and more on the prudence of its own elected officials."

Laura Schulte can be reached at leschulte@jrn.com and on X at @SchulteLaura.

headline: Sterling Sharpe, a Hall of Fame finalist, was a fascinating part of Packers history
fullText:
(Editor's note: A version of this story first published in 2021)

"Pick a member of the Green Bay Packers who you thought of as indestructible," Milwaukee Journal columnist Michael Bauman wrote in late 1994. "Sterling Sharpe may not be the only answer, but he certainly is the most prominent one."

Sharpe has been a name on the lips of Packers fans around this time each season, when the NFL begins its machinations for the next Hall of Fame class.

Sharpe has reached the finalist stage for the Class of 2025, and he's in a pool of five former luminaries — including ex-Packers head coach Mike Holmgren — in consideration, from which three will be chosen.

When Bauman wrote that passage about Sharpe, news had just broken that the neck injury Sharpe had sustained late in the season was not only going to keep him out for the forthcoming NFL playoffs, but represented a serious threat to his standout career. 

Packers fans have often imagined the "what if" implications if Sharpe had been able to continue playing. The fusion surgery necessary on his C1 and C2 vertebrae after the 1994 season left him open to re-injury and with too little range of motion to function as a wide receiver in the NFL.

He was waived in March 1995, still a month away from his 30th birthday, and he never played again.

Sharpe was a fascinating figure in Packers history. The drama around his contract before the 1994 season — and how the team should handle his roster status before 1995 — served as a prequel of sorts to what the organization would later experience with his quarterback, Brett Favre. But Sharpe was also dynamite on the field, responsible for one of the greatest moments in Packers playoff history and setting numerous records during his tenure. Even with a shortened career, he has a strong case for the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Here's what you need to know about Packers great Sterling Sharpe:

Sharpe never missed a game until the end

There's a cruel irony to Sharpe's career ending because of injury; Sharpe constantly battled through ailments.

He played in all 112 regular-season games over seven years since the team drafted him in the first round of the 1988 NFL Draft out of South Carolina. That included the 1994 season finale, one game after he suffered the injury that would cut his career short, in which he finished the year (and, as it turned out, his career) with nine catches, 132 yards and three touchdowns to help Green Bay clinch a playoff berth.

Sharpe had been injured Dec. 18 against Atlanta when his head snapped back while blocking Brad Edwards. He lay motionless on the turf at Milwaukee County Stadium for 3½ minutes, but he eventually walked off under his own power and was quickly shown on the sideline smiling with the coaching staff.

But Sharpe re-injured himself against Tampa Bay.

"It was kind of a funny feeling in my right arm and I really didn't want to try to get up and maybe make it worse than it really was," Sharpe told Fox after the win.

The Packers were on the cusp of their first home playoff game in a non-strike season since the 1967 Ice Bowl, a game they would win against the Lions, 16-12, by famously holding Barry Sanders to negative-1 rushing yard.

During his career, Sharpe battled through broken ribs, a turf toe injury that required surgery and a hamstring injury, but that playoff game would be his first game in which he was sidelined.

He twice caught the most single-season passes in NFL history

Sharpe first set an NFL record for receptions in a season with 108 in 1992. His 112 in 1993 amended his own mark, though that was matched by Jerry Rice and surpassed by Cris Carter the following year. With Green Bay and Holmgren at the front end of the passing revolution in the NFL, there's no telling how high Sharpe's numbers ultimately would have climbed.

He finished his seven years with several Packers records, including most career pass receptions (595), most consecutive games with a reception (103), most consecutive seasons with 50 receptions (all seven), most touchdown receptions in a season (18) and most in a game (four, which he did twice, tied with Don Hutson).

Heck, Sharpe was the first Packer since Hutson to even catch 90 passes in a season. He also matched James Lofton with the most 1,000-yard receiving seasons (five). By the time his career ended, he was 14th all-time in NFL career receptions.

Sharpe's 1993 franchise record of 112 receptions in a single season stood until 2020, when Davante Adams finished the year with 115, and Adams tied Sharpe's 1994 mark of 18 touchdown catches. Adams caught 123 passes in 2021 to reset his own mark.

If we imagined that Sharpe conservatively played four more seasons at merely his career averages (85 catches, 1,162 yards, nine touchdowns per season), he would be ninth all-time in career NFL touchdown receptions (101) while top-25 in career receptions (24th, 935), and yards (23rd, 12,782).

His 40-yard touchdown catch in the 1993 playoffs with 55 seconds to go gave the Packers a thrilling playoff win over the Lions, the franchise's first playoff win since 1982 and the spark of the franchise's successful run. It was Sharpe's third touchdown of the memorable 28-24 win and the only playoff win of Sharpe's career.

He seldom spoke to reporters

Sharpe briefly chatted with the media after the playoff win, which appeared to take some coaxing and was a surprise considering Sharpe hadn't spoken to local media in four years.

Sharpe, who perhaps ironically later became an analyst for NFL Network, was famous for his refusal to speak to reporters.

"It's a motivational tool for me," Sharpe once told Bill Scott of WNFL Radio. "If I (have a great game), somebody in the media will want to talk to me. It's one way of me saying, 'Guys, for what you did to me way back when, I'm finally getting a chance to pay you back.' I chose not to do that after my first year because, I thought, from what I heard and read, I wasn't treated quite as fairly as I should have been."

Sharpe caught 55 passes for 791 yards as a rookie, with one touchdown. There was some criticism of his play as a first-round draft pick, although Sharpe himself had admitted in a 1989 interview that he came in 10 pounds overweight and ran "atrocious" routes.

"During the 1990 season, I had minimal success following two earnest attempts to interview him after games," Milwaukee Journal Packers writer Bob McGinn wrote, noting that he never had any sort of confrontation with Sharpe. "Periodically, I have asked him questions since then, and usually have received a monosyllabic reply or a blank stare. He does his job and I do mine."

His contract situation was under the microscope in 1994

Sharpe's willingness to sit out the season opener ruffled feathers at the outset of the 1994 season.

Sharpe had seven years left on a 10-year contract extension he signed in 1991, and the club had already amended some escalator clauses to make incentives easier to reach. But Sharpe wanted another restructuring, informing the team as much at the tail end of the exhibition season. 

The Saturday before the season opener in Minnesota, Sharpe told Holmgren he wouldn't play under the current contract. But an agreement was reached between 6 and 6:30 p.m. that night, Sharpe checked into the team hotel and wound up catching seven passes for 52 yards and a touchdown in a win over Minnesota on Sunday.

His contract now included language that promised him $1 million more than the highest-paid receiver in the league.

Sharpe's insistence makes more sense, given the hindsight of his career trajectory. But he wouldn't even get to enjoy the fruits of that non-guaranteed contract following the massive injury. 

It was uncertain if Sharpe would play again

It was clear Sharpe wouldn't play in 1995, but Sharpe's status was complicated by a statement from his surgeon, Craig Bingham of Charlotte, N.C., who indicated there was a 90% chance the new technology around the fusion would allow Sharpe to return in 1996.

Facing a deadline, Packers general manager Ron Wolf finally announced in spring of 1995 that the club would be waiving Sharpe.

"The severity of the neck injury Sterling suffered, and the fact that research indicates no player who has had that type of surgery has returned to the playing field along with the uncertainty of his future availability, literally left us with no alternative," Wolf said in a statement. "We therefore are terminating his contract, with reluctance."

Other tidbits

  • With Sharpe out for the playoffs, Robert Brooks moved into a prominent role, and the Packers promoted Bill Schroeder from the practice squad.
  • Packers offensive line coach Tom Lovat called Sharpe the finest downfield blocker he'd ever seen.
  • Sharpe was taken with the seventh pick in the 1988 draft; his draft class also included Hall of Fame receivers Tim Brown (No. 6) and Michael Irvin (No. 11).
  • Though not blessed with "'stopwatch speed,'" McGinn wrote, "Sharpe has been pivoting away from or running through defenders, including cornerbacks, safeties and linebackers. In many ways, Sharpe carries the ball like a running back, which often is how he is utilized in Holmgren's innovative schemes. He is a physical, elusive runner, just what the new staff desperately needed for the 49ers offense."

headline: How will Wisconsin's offense look in the future? Badgers coach Luke Fickell shares his vision.
fullText:
MADISON – Last month, one day after Luke Fickell fired Phil Longo as offensive coordinator, the Wisconsin football coach shared his vision of what the team’s offense will look like in the future.

He wasn’t too specific other than to note that spreading the field would remain important and that being able to provide a variety of looks would be key.

On Wednesday, Fickell took a break from talking about his 2025 recruiting class to talk about where his search for an offensive coordinator stands.  He also offered a few more details about what he’s looking for in an offense.

The first thing we learned is that the coordinator search is ongoing.

“I’d like to tell you in three days we’re going to be able to do this thing, but we have to do our due diligence and we can’t hastily jump into this,” he said. “Look I wanted it done yesterday. I wanted it done a week ago.”

Luke Fickell wants a pro-style attack

When Fickell hired Longo two years ago, the implementation of Longo’s Air Raid offense fueled a lot of the buzz the Badgers enjoyed that offseason. In practice the attack didn’t achieve the desired results.

The Badgers ranked 10th in the 18-team conference with 23.9 points per game and ninth with 363.1 yards per game when the change was made. Last season UW ranked seventh in points (23.5) and sixth in yards (381.2) per game when the conference featured 14 teams.

Fickell said he wants a pro-style attack moving forward.

“What does that mean? It doesn’t mean any more than we want to be multiple,” he said. “We want to be able to play in 11 personnel (one running back, one tight end, three receivers). We want to be able to play in 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends, two receivers). We have 13 personnel (one running back, three tight ends). If it’s possible 21 (two backs, one tight end, two receivers).

"We want to be in the gun. We want to do the things we’ve done out of the gun in the passing game, but we also want to be able to see ourselves under center for six, eight, 10 snaps a game.”

Yes, Badgers fans, Fickell said he would like to play more under center. One of the criticisms of the Air Raid from fans and former players was the use of the shotgun in short-yardage situations.

Wisconsin was actually a decent short-yardage team early in the season when those criticisms reached their height, but the visual of a Badgers offense in the shotgun for a short-yardage play was hard for some to swallow.

A goal Fickell said is to build on what the team was able to do out of the spread, while adding elements like play-action that work best from playing under center. And there would be, of course, the option of playing under center more in short-yardage situations.

“That’s what everyone wanted, right?” Fickell said. “Fourth and 1 against Alabama why aren’t you under center? That’s not the reason we got stopped, but I do think there are a lot of things that can help us and give us some different advantages if we do them in the right way.”

Fickell also noted that there is a possibility that he would hire an offensive coordinator as well as a quarterbacks coach. Longo held both roles.

Fickell wants to get bigger along defensive front

Fickell also touched on a tweak planned for the defense. He is looking to get bigger players up front, particularly at outside linebacker/defensive end on the short side of the field.

“That outside linebacker, defensive end into the boundary, to me the vision is that it has to be guys who are bigger,” Fickell said. “When you look across the board we might be interiorly this past year probably at least an inch or two and about 25, 20 pounds short, undersized, to the rest of our league.”

As Fickell tries to figure out what went wrong during the Badgers’ season-ending five-game losing streak, one issue he seems to have determined is was a wear-down factor up front defensively.

“I’m trying not to talk about it, but it is us," Fickell said about the losing streak that caused UW to miss a bowl game for the first time since 2001. "We have to pinpoint and try to say why, and we can say we got worn down, we got beat up, we got hurt. Some of that comes down to you’re going to have to get bigger. … Size isn’t everything, but it does help you stay healthy and some things like that.”

headline: I spent months investigating accidental child shootings in Wisconsin. I’m left without easy answers.
fullText:
I remember the stairs being steep, a slow climb to the second-floor apartment where a toddler had accidentally shot himself.

A general assignment intern for the Milwaukee Sentinel, I was there to interview the mother of the wounded boy and other family members. 

I had been to several shootings that summer, in 1992. This one felt different. 

It was an accident; nobody intentionally left the gun out. And yet adults responsible for the boy’s well-being, including his mother, had failed to protect him. They had been negligent and also were suffering, just as the boy, who survived the shooting, was suffering in the hospital.

I don’t remember much about the interview or what happened to the mother and others who were home at the time of the shooting. I recall leaving with conflicted emotions. As a 22-year-old reporter, I doubt I was able to bring much nuance to the piece I wrote.

I am trying to do that 32 years later.

The “Unintended” project examines what happens when children are hurt or killed after they get their hands on a gun. We have all seen the headlines, in Milwaukee and across the country. 

These are tragic and preventable. They are horrific and infuriating. And they are sad.

My goal was to examine this issue in a new way, looking at how often the cases happen across Wisconsin, learning what happens afterward, and seeing if there are ways to prevent them.

As with my 2023 "Behind the Gun" project, launched through the O’Brien Fellowship in Public Service Journalism at Marquette University, this effort centers on the people of Wisconsin and the real-life challenges they face. 

That project examined all firearms deaths across Wisconsin, including suicides, revealing the full measure of how people in every county in the state are affected.

As a follow-up, I wanted to delve into accidental shootings, to learn why a mother kept a loaded gun under her mattress, how a father would take the chance of getting a gun even though he is a felon, and why a Milwaukee County prosecutor charges these cases as he does.

My editor, Greg Borowski, and I took a chance on this project, forgoing snappy solutions and quick fixes, and leaning into the complexity. We invite you to grapple as we have.

What do we call these? How often do they happen? 

From the start, I wanted to be careful with language. I wrote about language usage in a reporter’s notebook I did for “Behind the Gun,” where I explained why I did not use phrases like “gun violence” or “responsible gun owner.”

These cases, like the one I covered in 1992, are often called “accidental shootings.” Some gun owners I interviewed call them “negligent shootings.” The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention terms them “unintentional shootings.”

I am following CDC’s guidance to use "unintentional" and also using “accidental,” as most people know them that way.

I started by examining how often unintentional shootings occur. They are the rarest type of shooting and are actually dropping, but children are more often the victims. Between 2018 and 2023, about 500 people have died annually nationwide from unintentional gunshot wounds, about 115 of them children, CDC data shows.

A death or so a day seems like a lot, especially because they are preventable, but we are a big country. It is important to note there are other accidental deaths that occur more often, such as unintentional drownings (eight times as often) and motor vehicle crashes (85 times more common), according to CDC data.

It is also important to note the majority of accidental shootings do not end in death, so these numbers are just part of the story.

Getting accurate non-fatal unintended shooting data is difficult, however, because law enforcement doesn’t tabulate those specifically. But groups like Gun Violence Archives and Everytown for Gun Safety track them through media accounts and other sources. 

As I began reporting, I asked people I knew to guess what percentage of shootings are accidental. 

Many said 25% or higher. That's 25 times higher than the actual figure.

I suspect part of the reason may be how we in the media cover these cases. When I set up a Google alert for "accidental gun deaths" and Wisconsin, there were lots of hits but most weren’t from Wisconsin. They occurred elsewhere and were picked up by media here.

In Wisconsin over the past eight years, there have been 15 to 20 unintentional shootings each year involving children, a handful of them fatal. The numbers jumped in the pandemic but have been trending down since.

Why were these guns there in the first place?

Another question I had: How are children getting these guns? 

To understand that, I think, requires understanding why people have firearms in the first place. 

This hit home when I was at a training event for new gun owners at Prince Hall Masonic Temple in Milwaukee in summer 2023. 

Firearms instructor Jieire Vance explained to the class that the Wisconsin Department of Justice suggests keeping all guns locked up, unloaded, and separated from ammunition. 

After a couple of seconds, several in the class laughed. One woman said she was in the class to learn how to defend her home quickly. That made me wonder whether the solutions being advanced are realistic for all people.

People told me about their concerns: Living in dangerous neighborhoods, worried about their children’s safety, being in fear of an abuser, and noting the sometimes slow police response.

Gun owners also told me they feel an almost shaming attitude at times from non-gun owners who may live in safer, more well-policed areas. 

Judgment seems especially strong when a child gets a gun. 

The irony here is that many gun owners I interviewed over the past two years are hyper-aware of safety and security. And it pains them to see such cases. 

These gun owners have ideas of how to prevent such shootings, which include secure storage. Many are skeptical of the cheap cable locks that come with new guns. They advocate getting a gun safe that makes the firearm available to the owner but inaccessible to anyone else.

I told my O’Brien colleague Lee Hawkins what I was hearing from gun owners. He said, “So it’s not by accident that some people are not having accidents with guns.”

Perspectives from all sides of this issue

With a handle on the frequency, I turned to what happens afterward. I found cases charged in Milwaukee County – which sees by far the most unintended gun deaths in Wisconsin — are often felonies. In other counties, prosecutors are more often charging misdemeanors. 

Deputy District Attorney Matthew Torbenson, who oversees such cases in Milwaukee County, explained his view of the cases and described how he had a hand in changing Wisconsin’s law, allowing them to be charged differently.

Wisconsin has a 1991 law for accidental shootings involving children that says they should be charged as misdemeanors, but Torbenson finds the law lacking. 

Torbenson has been a prosecutor about as long as I have been a reporter in Milwaukee and we spoke for hours about these cases. With passion, he said he owes it to these children and their loved one to charge these cases. 

“We have a responsibility to protect them,” he told me.

In interviews with several mothers and fathers charged, they shared regret for what happened. They acknowledged some punishment is appropriate, depending on the circumstances. Several also described how they are struggling with the after-effects of being charged with a felony.

“I'm not a bad mom,” BriOnna Givens, whose son shot himself in the hand, told me. “And that doesn't matter because this mistake happened.”

The cases continue. In just the past month, two more children in Milwaukee were injured in accidental shootings. Two mothers have been charged with a felony. That makes five such cases this year.

More than three decades after I left that apartment, I don’t have the tidy answers. 

But it has me thinking.

And now perhaps it has you thinking as well.

Reporter John Diedrich can be reached at jdiedrich@gannett.com.

headline: This Milwaukee firearms instructor helps students make a home defense plan — and a gun storage strategy
fullText:
With a folder and pen in hand, Jieire Vance stepped to the front door of the bungalow on Milwaukee’s north side. He looked like a remodeling contractor or maybe the cable guy.

But Vance was there for what could be a matter of life and death.

Vance, a firearms instructor, was helping a family develop a plan for what to do if an intruder breaks into their home and deadly force is needed.

It was the home of Mikieya Williams, who recently had taken a gun safety class. She already owned a gun but wanted better training and, most of all, guidance on how to create a home defense plan.

The free home evaluation is part of what Vance and his partner, Theron Rogers, offer to those who take their classes. The two are both former law enforcement officers and know it’s one thing to talk about gun safety and home defense in a classroom setting; it’s another in the home.

Over the past several years, the pair has taught thousands of new gun owners in Milwaukee, the majority of whom are Black women, through their company, Guaranteed Protection Services.

Students tell them they are getting guns for many reasons: because of an abusive ex-husband or partner, for protection because of crime in their neighborhood or a concern that police are busy and may be slow to respond when called.

Vance said female students tend to be very open to instruction. Most are deeply concerned about their children’s safety; that’s why, in part, they are buying the gun. 

At the class Williams attended, Vance and the other instructors highlighted what’s at stake when guns are not secured. They showed a slide of a boy who had been shot and is now forced to use a colostomy bag.

“Could you imagine being 7 years old and being attached to that? For the rest of your life?” said firearms instructor Eddie Silas, who works with the two and co-owns Prolific Arms gun shop in West Allis with Rogers. 

“Kids have a natural curiosity about things they don't understand. That same curiosity can lead to disaster. It can happen to any one of us if we’re being negligent.”

Instructors make it clear: A loaded gun can be kept readily available for home protection and at the same time be inaccessible to children. That is a must.

“I want people to be thinking about this in our community: How am I storing my gun? It is critical,” Silas said.

Williams, 34, said she got a gun in the past year because there is more violence in her neighborhood and the broader community. She is also keenly aware of protecting her children from the very gun she intends to protect them with. This may be in the form of an accidental shooting but also suicide and others risks from unsecured guns.

“Gun safety is essential to me, especially because I have children,” she said.

Make a home defense plan and practice it

On the day of his visit in May, Vance stands in the living room of Williams’ home and quickly assesses key factors:

A two-story home. Lines of sight to the front and back door from a hallway in the center of the home. Two parents live here along with a grandparent and three children — 12-year-old twins Tremiya and Trevante, and 3-year-old Timothy.

The family lives on the northwest side of Milwaukee where burglaries, robberies and aggravated assaults have been climbing over the past three years, according to Milwaukee Police Department crime data.

Vance’s first questions are quickly answered: Do the children know there is a gun in the house? Yes. And will they be part of the home defense plan? Yes, in part.

Security experts stress that a gun is not the first line of home defense; it is the final line.

Developing a home security plan starts with keeping doors and windows locked and reinforced, adding outside lighting, coordinating with neighbors to keep an eye out for each other, and considering cameras, an alarm system and a dog.

Vance is preparing this family for an event where those precautions fail. 

He explains to the 12-year-old twins that if there is a break-in their parents will be the only ones with guns. The children will have the vital job of calling 911.

Vance walks through the house to identify a hiding place where the children would go in an emergency. Then they role-play calling 911. He explains that if police officers come into the house, they will announce themselves. 

“Whenever there are shots fired, all the police know is that there's a gun involved and a bad guy,” Vance said to the children. “If you do not give a description of who you are, what you have on, and where you are, you can be easily mistaken.”

The home safety evaluations were welcome news to Milwaukee County Deputy District Attorney Matthew Torbenson when he learned about them from a reporter. Torbenson sees the gruesome results of what happens to children when guns are not stored securely.

“That's fantastic,” Torbenson said of the tours. “It’s proactive.”

Across the country, an estimated 1% of homes are burglarized each year, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. However, the risk varies based on geography. For instance, the burglary rate in the city of Milwaukee is, on average, double the national average and three times the rate across Wisconsin, according to FBI data. Still, home invasions are not a common event statistically.

Even as burglaries dropped with more people at home during the early stages of COVID, there was a surge in gun buying. An estimated 3% of U.S. adults, or 7.5 million people, became new gun owners between 2019 and late April 2021, according to research.

Williams said she has seen guns handled in an unsafe way, whether by young men at a nearby gas station or in a tragic case close by last year. A 3-year-old girl shot herself in the hand when the parents left a loaded gun on the floor of a bedroom closet.

Williams said there have been no break-ins at their home but she hears gunshots in the neighborhood fairly regularly.

“I would say it is 85% safe here, but that might be pushing it.”

Williams said she would get a safe, like the ones she learned about in Vance's class, to ensure her children can't get the gun.

“I want something that is secure and easily accessible.”

Gun storage invention comes from tragedy

California-born tech inventor Timmy Oh began his journey toward making gun storage safer a decade ago, when he heard his mother at the breakfast table mention a toddler shot himself after getting his parent's gun in Los Angeles.

As a 17-year-old, Oh thought, "How can this be happening with all the new technology in society today?" 

With an uncle on the Los Angeles Police Department, Oh already liked firearms and was determined to find a solution to stop children from getting access to loaded guns.

Oh's first attempt, as a student at the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in upstate New York, was a flop.

He developed a device he thought would stop the gun from firing — unless by the owner. The idea was to stop a bullet from exiting the firearm. But when gun owners reviewed the concept, they told Oh with this device the firearm would likely explode in the owner’s hand.

Oh didn’t give up. He vowed to spend enough time with gun owners to learn what would work and what they would use.

Oh created a biometric safe that looks a bit like a holster. It is called "Reach." The butt of the firearm is visible but the gun itself cannot be removed without the owner's fingerprint.

Oh said his product uses more advanced fingerprint technology that can progressively learn the owner’s print over time, making it more reliable. There would be the first impression and then further impressions, said Oh, whose company is called Vara Safety.

Oh, 28, is seeing an increased willingness by gun owners to spend more on safes, but there also remains skepticism.

“Some gun owners are like ‘I don't need safe storage. I just keep it on my nightstand or under my pillow,’” he said. “But I believe that is changing.”

Mallory O’Brien, an epidemiologist who has studied firearms injuries and deaths for decades in Milwaukee and now works at Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions in Baltimore, said inventions like Oh’s show how technology is racing ahead to improve safety.

“If you're investing in a firearm for personal safety, invest in the additional protection of storing it safely in one of those new devices,” she said. “Today, there are solutions.”

Chance to reframe guns in Black Milwaukee

As Vance wraps up the tour, he sits down with the family to talk about how the practice went and how stressful it was. One of the twins, Trevante, plays over in his mind how he wished he had done better. He promises he will next time. His mother says there will be more practice and they will involve their father next time.

“We’ll drill this,” said Williams, the mother of three. “I’m the type of person, if I teach you something, I want to make sure you got it.”

Vance, who is Black, turns the discussion to guns and the view of them in the Black community in Milwaukee. He asks what they think of when they hear the words “guns and kids.” Is it negative? The twins both nod their heads. 

“A lot of that negativity comes from what we see, and what's happening in our city and especially in our community,” Vance said. “A lot of it is negative, nobody's being safe and then there's a lot of heinous crime going on.”

Vance tells them that children their age elsewhere in Wisconsin routinely learn firearms safety through hunting and other activities. That is not happening as often in Milwaukee, but Vance and fellow trainers in the Black community would like to change that. 

His simple request to them: Forget what they have learned and seen about guns. They have been getting an education on television and movies, on music videos and even at the corner gas station, he said, but it was a bad education.

“Erase all of that today,” Vance said. “Everything moving forward is going to be either what your mom teaches you or what we teach you in class.”

As the hour-long visit wraps up, Williams is pleased she accepted the offer to get a safety tour. She said she always had the determination to defend her children; now she will have the knowledge.

“By myself, I have played it out all the time,” she said. “But I never actually sat down to come up with a plan, which is so essential. This is awesome.”

Reporter John Diedrich can be reached at jdiedrich@gannett.com.
