headline: AG Skrmetti: TN transgender minor care law is about regulation not discrimination | Opinion
fullText:
The United States Supreme Court heard oral arguments Wednesday in a case that strikes at the heart of our state's ability to protect its youngest residents.

United States v. Skrmetti isn't just another legal dispute — it's the first Supreme Court case to look at how the Constitution applies to gender identity issues.

At stake is whether Tennessee can protect kids from procedures that its legislature deems harmful.

As Tennesseans, we've always believed in putting children first. Our state legislature in 2023 passed legislation, Senate Bill 1 (S.B. 1), that requires people to wait until they reach adulthood before they can use drugs or surgery for the purpose of gender transition.

Puberty blockers, hormone treatments and sex-reassignment surgeries are off-limits to kids in Tennessee. That’s the same common-sense approach we take with tattoos, alcohol and tobacco purchases, and other consequential decisions. Yet now, the federal government argues this age-conscious protection amounts to illegal discrimination.

Recent studies in Europe should cause us pause

Let's be clear about what is before the court: This case will determine whether states can establish safeguards around life-altering medical procedures that can cause kids great and irreversible physical harm, including permanent loss of their ability to ever have children.

Leading medical authorities across Europe have recently restricted kids’ access to these same procedures. These European countries were once enthusiastic about the use of these interventions to treat kids with gender dysphoria — kids who struggle with a conflict between their sex and their self-perception.

But after careful review of the research, the medical communities that pioneered gender interventions for minors have pushed for restrictions because of new evidence.

And these concerns are all the more significant because the number of youth seeking these treatments has exploded.

Opinion: Attacks against transgender Tennesseans cause harm, Sen. Yager, not health care

One study in the U.K. showed a staggering 4,000% increase in the number of adolescent girls seeking gender transition treatment. This radical shift demands careful consideration, not a constitutional rule that would enshrine one side’s view of a contentious medical debate.

States should be ‘laboratories of democracy’ without federal overreach

The Biden Administration's argument would deny Tennessee a state’s traditional role in restricting risky medical procedures.

This represents a fundamental misunderstanding of our constitutional system, where states serve as “laboratories of democracy” and have particularly wide discretion to address areas of medical uncertainty.

Opinion: Supreme Court should uphold Tennessee law against transgender minor care

If some states want to take a different approach based on their values and interpretation of the evidence, they're free to do so. But the people of Tennessee, working through Gov. Bill Lee and a bipartisan supermajority of elected representatives, retain their right to protect kids from procedures deemed harmful by the legislature.

Constitution does not mandate medical experimentation

Critics have attempted to frame Tennessee’s protective measures as discrimination. This misleading characterization ignores the fundamental reality that age restrictions on medical procedures exist precisely because we recognize that kids need time to develop and mature before making life-changing decisions.

When the evidence supporting these life-altering interventions for kids is deemed weak by the legislature, the fundamental medical principle of “do no harm” supports Tennessee’s cautious approach.

Opinion: Walmart rolls back DEI policies. They should’ve let them evolve, instead.

The Constitution does not mandate medical experimentation on children.

Meanwhile, Tennessee has always had the right, and the solemn obligation, to protect its kids. S.B. 1 continues this vital tradition, ensuring that life-altering medical decisions with big risks are reserved for adults capable of giving informed consent.

Laws should protect minors while respecting their rights

As this case now awaits a ruling from the Supreme Court, Tennesseans should understand what we’re fighting for: Our right to protect Tennessee’s children and our ability to establish responsible healthcare regulations.

Half the states in our nation have already taken similar protective measures, recognizing that careful, evidence-based approaches to pediatric medicine best serve the interests of their kids.

The people of Tennessee elected their representatives to make these important decisions. We trust our state officials to carefully weigh medical evidence, consider ethical implications, and implement policies that protect children while respecting individual rights. We have the authority to hold our representatives accountable when they go astray.

The Biden Administration’s unprecedented reading of the Constitution threatens this essential allocation of power and would concentrate decision making in unaccountable judges in a way that undermines our ability to safeguard our most vulnerable citizens.

Jonathan Skrmetti has served as the Tennessee attorney general and reporter since 2022.

headline: Writers spar about Trump's power, Hunter Biden's pardon, TSU and transgender health care
fullText:
Greetings, readers:

After taking a break for Thanksgiving, the Tennessee Voices newsletter is back in your inbox.

The top read essays of this period have involved President-elect Donald Trump, the proposed school vouchers expansion statewide, Tennessee State University's finances and President Joe Biden's pardon of his son Hunter.

Many of these issues have also elicited rebuttals from both ordinary citizens and elected officials.

Presidential overreach

Middle Tennessee State University Professor John Vile wrote an essay titled "Trump will soon learn again that presidents aren't kings and aren't all-powerful."

In it, he argues that Trump, in his second term, will likely confront the same backlash to presidential overreach as his predecessors like Franklin Roosevelt or Lyndon Johnson.

Frequent letter writer Don Forte took issue with Vile and wrote: "The very reason that Trump needs to 'overreact,' as you call it is that the present administration has 'overacted' in getting this country in dire need of correcting a multitude of destructive policies."

School choice

On the school vouchers front, state Rep. Caleb Hemmer, D-Nashville wrote a critique of Gov. Bill Lee re-introducing his proposal during the 2025 legislative session to expand the Education Freedom Scholarship from just a few counties to the entire state. The legislation failed to pass in 2024.

"Once again, this new version is jam-packed with all kinds of seemingly nice things tacked on to try and distract people from the fact that this is all a scam designed to defund public education," Hemmer wrote

Tennessee Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, R-Franklin, took issue with Hemmer directly in a guest opinion essay: "Detractors, like Rep. Caleb Hemmer, D-Nashville, continue to misrepresent the intent and impact of this legislation."

Columnist Andrea Williams has been critical of the previous administration at Tennessee State University under former President Glenda Glover.

Save TSU Community Coalition member Rev. Dr. Christopher Jackson defended Glover and TSU.

"(Glover) is obviously a giver, not a taker. The real takers are the State of Tennessee who have systematically failed to pay TSU what they owe," he wrote.

Williams addressed his criticism in a response titled: "Tennessee State University is underfunded and was poorly run. Both can be true."

Biden's pardon of Hunter

Letter writer Phyllis Gobbell defended the president's decision: "When Trump keeps his promise to pardon the January 6 insurrectionists he calls “patriots,” who stormed the U.S. Capitol at his bidding, maybe the spotlight will turn from Hunter Biden, whose offenses don’t begin to rival Trump’s crimes against America."

I took a different view in my latest column, comparing Biden to a Roman emperor. Admittedly, I recently saw "Gladiator II." "But in the end, (the pardon) chipped away at the notion that the justice system is fair and equal. In other words, if you have a powerful parent or patron, you do not have to pay the piper," I wrote.

Gender affirming care for minors

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court heard oral arguments in the case of U.S. vs. Skrmetti concerning Tennessee's 2023 law that bans transgender health care for minors.

Jonathan Skrmetti is, of course, the Tennessee attorney general and he wrote a defense of the law in an essay published Wednesday evening. "The people of Tennessee, working through Gov. Bill Lee and a bipartisan supermajority of elected representatives, retain their right to protect kids from procedures deemed harmful by the legislature," he wrote.

Earlier in the week, Vanderbilt Professor Emeritus Malcolm Getz wrote an essay defending gender affirming care. He has a trans relative and has vocally spoken out for the rights of transgender citizens in Tennessee.

Agree or disagree? Or have a view on another topic entirely? Send a letter of 250 words or fewer to letters@tennessean.com. Include your full name, city/town, ZIP and contact information for verification. Thanks for adding to the public conversation.

Thanks for adding to the public conversation and keep in touch.

headline: After 5th straight loss, Nashville Predators on pace for worst season in franchise history
fullText:
At Scotiabank Arena on Wednesday night, the Nashville Predators held a 1-0 lead over the Toronto Maple Leafs through two periods.

Then Maple Leafs star Auston Matthews scored two goals in the first 2:29 of the third period.

In an instant, the Predators' lead evaporated.

Apparently, so are their chances at a competitive season.

The Predators, with the defeat to Toronto, have now lost five games in a row — oddly, their fourth straight by the same 3-2 score — and remain in seventh place in the Central Division. Their last win — an inexplicable 4-1 win over the Central-leading Winnipeg Jets — was nearly two weeks ago. They haven't strung together consecutive wins since before Halloween.

Now more than ever, it seems like this Predators season is lost.

Nashville Predators on pace for worst season in franchise history

With a record of 7-13-6, the Predators have 20 points and a points percentage of .385. Play that out over 82 games, and they would finish with about 63 points.

Going by points percentage, the two worst seasons in franchise history are 1998-99, the inaugural season (28-47-7, 63 points) and 2001-02, their fourth season (28-41-13-0, 69 points).

If things don't improve, this team could surpass both in ineptitude.

PENALTIES: Nashville Predators lead NHL in bench minor penalties: Coach Andrew Brunette explains

A quick reminder: The inaugural franchise expansion season was not expected to do much. It existed as a hockey team for 82 games, and that was enough.

The 2001-02 team had bad special teams and no offense — forward Denis Arkhipov led the team with 20 goals — though it was also Martin Erat's rookie season, so it wasn't a total loss.

But somehow this year's Predators team, with all of its star power, isn't even on pace to be better than either team. Through 26 games, the 1998-99 team had 10 wins, and the 2001-02 team had nine wins. This team has just seven.

Offense is this season's main issue, and that was apparent again vs. Toronto. The Predators scored two goals or fewer for the 17th time this season — they are now scoring 2.30 goals per game, worst in the NHL.

Even the 1998-99 team (2.32) and the 2001-02 team (2.39) had higher goals per game averages.

Nashville's next game in its march to unfortunate franchise history comes against the Montreal Canadiens on Thursday (6 p.m. CT, FanDuel Sports Network).

headline: Tennessee age verification law for adult websites challenged on free speech grounds
fullText:
A free speech advocacy group has filed a federal lawsuit against a new Tennessee law that requires websites with content deemed "harmful to minors" to age-verify users through an upload of a state ID or other means, claiming the law infringes on the First and Fourth amendments.

The Free Speech Coalition, a nonprofit trade association that represents adult entertainers in First Amendment cases, along with a number of plaintiffs including Nashville-based adult content creator MelRose Michaels, are claiming the state law, which was signed by the governor in June and is set to go into effect Jan. 1, is "censorship."

“Engaging in legal speech is not a criminal act,” Alison Boden, the executive director of Free Speech Coalition, said in a statement. “This law, and others like it, have effectively become state censorship, creating a massive chilling effect for those who deal in sex or sexuality, and creating significant privacy risk for Tennesseans who want to access sexual health information, adult content or any other controversial speech.” 

More: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee signs age-verification bill as First Amendment debate continues

The new law, known as the Protect Tennessee Minors Act, requires that websites with a 33% or more of content deemed "harmful to minors" must verify the age of each user who attempts to access the site every 60 minutes through uploading a state ID or other means, such as facial recognition, as well as retain seven years of anonymized data on users who access the site.

The demarcation of content as “harmful to minors” — a classification that is spelled out in the bill with an explicit list of sexual depictions and activities — has been used with increasing frequency at the state and local level to pass laws restricting drag performances, increase penalties on librarians, ease the removal of books from school libraries, block pride events and even ban public displays homosexuality.

It includes any content that “the average person, applying contemporary community standards … would find sexually explicit and harmful or inappropriate for minors or designed to appeal to or pander to the prurient interest.”

The lawsuit, filed last week, alleges that the law violates the First Amendment by imposing content-based restrictions on protected speech, as well as implementing an unconstitutional prior restraint on speech by forcing websites to self-censor and block access to content before it is deemed harmful.

Websites would have good reason to self-censor, should the law stand: while similar laws have passed in 19 other states and are under consideration in seven more, Tennessee is the only one with felony penalties.

Free Speech Coalition has challenged similar laws in Indiana, Montana, Texas, Louisiana and Utah. The Texas case, Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, will be heard by the U.S. Supreme Court in January.

The lawsuit also alleges that the Tennessee law violates the Fourth Amendment right to due process, due to its allegedly vague standards, as well as Section 230, which protects the independence of website hosting platforms from most legal liability regarding user content.

"Despite this long legacy of constitutional invalidity, the Tennessee Legislature enacted the law in April 2024, and the Governor signed it into law the next month, rendering it effective on January 1, 2025," the lawsuit states. "Now, providers (including plaintiffs) are in the untenable position of abiding by the Act’s terms and enduring the constitutional infringement, or violating them and risking ruinous civil and criminal liability."

The plaintiffs are seeking an expediated preliminary injunction to halt the law while the case is heard, in the end goal of having the law permanently blocked.

The Tennessee Attorney General's Office did not respond to a request for comment.

headline: How much snow will Nashville receive in December 2024? How will La Niña impact snowfall in Tennessee?
fullText:
Nashville saw its first snowfall of the holiday season on Tuesday night, but can it expect any more this year?

Narrowing down snow chances is difficult, said National Weather Service Meteorologist Krissy Hurley, but something that's for sure is that Music City and the Middle Tennessee area will experience above average temperatures throughout the end of the year, as previously forecasted by the Climate Prediction Center.

Through Dec. 13, Middle Tennessee will experience slightly (33-40%) above average temperatures. Then on Dec. 14-27, temperatures are expected to be 55- 60% above average. In December, Nashville experiences average highs of 52 and average lows of 33.

"So tentatively the pattern looks warmer than normal overall, but that doesn't necessarily mean we won't see instances of cold weather in that time frame," said Hurley in an email to the Tennessean.

Here is what else to know.

Will it snow in Middle Tennessee?

According to the weather service, Nashville's first measurable snow on average takes place on Dec. 23. Crossville however, normally experiences snowfall on Dec. 15 while Clarksville measures its first snow near the end of the year on Dec. 27.

Currently, the weather service is unable to predict exact snow quantities for the month of December.

Here is a look at the top five past snowstorms in Music City:

  1. March 1892: 17 inches
  2. February 1886: 16 inches
  3. February 1929: 15 inches
  4. December 1964: 10 inches
  5. January 1951: 10 inches

How will La Niña impact snowfall in Tennessee?

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, La Niña is most likely to emerge in October through December of 2024 and is expected to continue through March 2025.

During La Niña conditions, low pressure systems generally move north of the area which often keeps the Volunteer State in the area of warmer temperatures.

The probabilities for Tennessee to experience a major winter event like snow or ice are lower, however, extreme winter events shouldn't be ruled out, National Weather Service Meteorologist Ryan Husted previously told the Tennessean. For example, the La Niña winters of 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 both experienced above normal temperatures yet they still came with a "substantial" cold snap.

Based on previous snowfall events, Music City favors normal (4.7 inches) and below normal snowfall during La Niña winters.

The winters of 2020-2021, 2021-2022 and 2022-2023 were all La Niña winters, and they received 5.2 inches of snow (near normal), 9.5 inches of snow (above normal) and 1.2 inches of snow (below normal), respectively.

headline: How Amazon is fighting to match Pandora, Spotify -- and why it's using Nashville and country music to do it.
fullText:
It's 10 a.m. on a late October day. Rising country superstar Bailey Zimmerman gleefully grins with an over-caffeinated smile while surrounded by Warner Music Nashville executives on a performance stage in global broadcaster SiriusXM Radio's downtown Nashville studio outpost .

Zimmerman is receiving what could very well be the last of two-dozen plaques he's earned from the mega-popularity of the 24 singles he's released in the past three years.

He's receiving the plaque not because songs like "Religiously" and "Rock and a Hard Place" have been downloaded, sold and streamed to the tune of over 25 million in sales. Instead, it's because, via subscription-driven SiriusXM's Pandora service, he's been played 1 billion times.

The moment occurs after an interview with radio and television veteran Cody Alan on SiriusXM's The Highway channel. That talk feels like more of an Instagram reel-length snapshot into a conversation between the two because the pace at which their lives are moving is best defined by a statement Zimmerman candidly makes during their discussion.

"There's so much to learn and so much to do in so little time. All I'm trying to do is not half-a-- any of it."

'Moving at the speed of how people consume culture'

For two decades, terrestrial radio and broadcast television fans of popular music have decried satellite radio's "Wild West" approach to programming multiple stations with hit songs, deep cuts, studio recordings and live performances, all simultaneously available at one's fingertips.

Because of the lack of direct advertising on the platform, a sense is at play that you're hearing a radio personality's hand-curated tastes rather than something specifically dictated by non-human forces.

SiriusXM's 33 million subscribers would agree that such a uniquely bespoke listening experience is worthwhile and at the forefront of how music defines pop culture.

SiriusXM has over 150 channels in total, broadcasting a multitude of genres. Since 2010, Nashville has been the home of Channel 56, the modern country music channel The Highway. Nine months ago, SiriusXM moved its Nashville offices from Bridgestone Arena to space in the "Batman" building at 333 Commerce St.

Moving its Nashville headquarters into state-of-the-art space highlights how seriously the platform is taking how quickly demographic ages 18-49 have adapted to and are sustaining country music's surge as America's musical and pop cultural bellwether.

"The Highway is moving at the speed of how people consume culture and musical discovery via (interpersonal) connection is a leading how people's appetites for consumption are trending," Steve Blatter, SiriusXM's senior vice president and general manager of music programming, says to The Tennessean.

Competing in a broadening, restructuring marketplace

Streaming portals and terrestrial radio stations are achieving synergy between playlists and programming at an ever-quickening pace. In 2023, Spotify and YouTube launched radio-similar features curated to balance genre, artist frequency and the mix of chosen artists versus new recommendations.

Two years prior, MusicWatch reported that the number of streaming listeners had doubled that of terrestrial radio, continuing a trend going back to 2017.

What has emerged since is a marketplace that may not driven by "music" but more by "consumable content." That broadens the competitive reach to include digital online shorts via social media and YouTube, Amazon Music, Apple Music and Spotify as streaming platforms, terrestrial radio stations and what SiriusXM offers, coupled with its 2019-purchased streaming portal Pandora.

This system rewards hyper-performing, chart-topping artists but also fosters a thriving underbelly of performers whose ability to develop fanbases is slowly eating into the mainstream market share of other genres.

In short, the same market that developed the ability of artists like Shaboozey and Morgan Wallen to top Billboard's all-genre Hot 100 charts for a combined 12 months has also supported Jason Aldean, Zach Bryan, Luke Combs and Post Malone, plus Kelsea Ballerini, Kane Brown, Jelly Roll, Lainey Wilson and Zimmerman, among many others.

Developing a sustainable strategy

Blatter credits SiriusXM's successes in rock — a longtime country-friendly format — via their Alt-Nation channel for creating The Highway's successful template. In the early 2010s, reading the blogosphere and indie circuit like tea leaves saw the channel break pop-leaning outliers like Foster the People ("Pumped Up Kicks") and Grouplove ("Colours") to platinum-selling success.

The Alt-Nation strategy has proved bold yet rewarding in country music's mainstream.

Cross-mapping Nashville's perpetually diverse and fertile minor league baseball-style farm system of acts with how blog authors and indie tastemakers frequently worked against established standards a decade ago allowed Blatter to land on everything from Florida-Georgia Line's "Cruise" to Luke Combs' "Hurricane" four years later.

Blatter calls a programming process that often navigates around and beyond country's already lucrative and well-established expectations a "human and instinctual combination of art and science" that blends with over a dozen data points, including digital track sales, Pandora streams and first-hand, portal-to-user research regarding how songs are resonating with listeners.

"SiriusXM subscribers actively want their tastes engaged," says Alan, the SiriusXM host and broadcast television and radio veteran .

He highlights how the platform's ability to curate a passionate community within an already mega-popular yet insular one allows for a particular type of market testing that ensures that songs that become hits via SiriusXM have an assured place across all facets of country's format and entrenchment within pop culture at-large.

'What exists beyond their first taste of success'

Of those in Nashville worth having a conversation about how listeners respond to SiriusXM's streaming, nobody is better equipped than SiriusXM broadcast personality Buzz Brainard. The award-nominated broadcaster and voice talent (he has worked for Fox, the Disney Channel and the Travel Channel in his four-decade career) has worked at SiriusXM for over a decade.

Hundreds of SiriusXM The Highway fans have flooded Lower Broadway's Margaritaville bar for Brainard-hosted Friday evening, mini-concert-driven happy hours for nearly a decade.

"I receive the most-instant kind of feedback on country's growth," jokes the host about emceeing those festivities.

Brainard, 62, is a Michigan native old enough to understand the transformational power of what SiriusXM is accomplishing in Nashville. On the floor of their new studio's performance suite, a marker made of wood from the Ryman Auditorium's stage across the street is inlaid and points north to country music's Mother Church. Like country music and its roots as a culture and genre, the Ryman is nearly 10 times older than SiriusXM.

A mix of honesty that defines the future of what "three chords and the truth" looks like is happening next door to where that notion was birthed.

"Accepting that we have the most extensive potential reach of any country channel on the planet means that we're also accepting that we can expand country music's horizon of reach," Brainard says. "Everybody's looking everywhere for the next big hit. However, we're willing to find that hit artist and alongside getting them into regular rotation, we're talking to them and attempting to help cultivate what the bigger picture of what exists beyond their first taste of success can look like.

"We've gone from throwing artists into a den of wolves to allowing them to have a space where they can experience some level of comfort and pleasure as they (navigate through the industry)."

Doubling down on 'relatable music made by relatable people'

Over the past half-decade, since veteran SiriusXM host Ania Hammar and newcomer Macie Banks have been affiliated with the broadcaster, its ability to crest, then peak as a leading broadcaster highlights the value of trusting the work of curating country's future to the hands of a diverse few in aiding the broader health of the genre's surge.

Banks, 29, highlights that SiriusXM is cultivating a predominantly country music-defined future for her fellow millennials and Gen Z listeners where immediate and profound engagement can occur with artists who feel as if they're breaking by the second on social media platforms.

"Relatable music made by relatable people organically exists best beyond algorithms and numbers," she adds.

"Artists broken by The Highway now represent our format's stadium headliners," Hammar says about the potential for artists being "discovered" via the platform.

"Also, because our subscriber base highlights how broad the genre's most curious fanbase has become, we're allowed to define trends instead of chasing them."

A boundary-pushing future

SiriusXM's Blatter says the platform's programming is helping to inspire the quality of the genre's hits to reach "an all-time high."

Over a decade of successfully platforming country's traditional roots, modern hits and pop-ready outliers in a single format leaves the executive feeling accomplished yet motivated.

"Maintaining an open mind to the power of a diverse, well-crafted set of songs and stories allows for country's possibilities to push every boundary."

headline: Taylor Swift is a global star, but Nashville remains the heart of her empire
fullText:
NASHVILLE — Taylor Swift's record breaking Eras Tour is set to draw to a close Sunday in Vancouver, Canada. It’s one final, far-flung stop for the behemoth production that has landed on five continents over the last two years.

While the tour has undeniably been a worldwide phenomenon, it can still be argued that the show — and Swift’s empire —continues to revolve around Nashville.

Swift has close ties with a number of cities, including with London an ocean away and most recently with Kansas City, where her boyfriend Travis Kelce plays with the Chiefs.

But throughout the Eras Tour, Tennessee fans reported frequent sightings of her band, singers and dancers taking off from Nashville’s airport on their way to the next show. Many of Swift’s business enterprises are registered in Tennessee, as well. The state’s lack of an income tax may have something to do with that.

But perhaps the ties run deeper.

Swift’s bedazzled career grew out of her innate talent and considerable ambition, which were nurtured by mentors, peers and corporations in Nashville at the start of her career. The music industry here often compares itself to a family, however flawed, and in fact, Swift’s parents still live here.

Perfect Christmas gift for Swifties: Celebrate Taylor Swift's unprecedented Eras Tour with USA TODAY's enchanting book

It's been a lifetime coming

Swift started her career as an 11-year-old pacing the pavement of Music Row handing out demo CDs to the front desks of country music labels. At age 13, she almost signed a development deal with RCA Records but withdrew from the contract. She convinced her parents to relocate from Wyomissing, Pennsylvania, to Hendersonville in 2004.

"I was in my office in the summer, July of 2004, when a mother and daughter walked in to register," says Paul Decker, the former principal of Hendersonville High School. "I handed them the information we needed to have on file, and I asked, 'What brought you to Hendersonville?'"

Decker recounts how Swift's mom Andrea replied: "We're going to try to get Taylor in the music business."

The principal smiled. He knew the odds of a teenager making it.

"I hope it works out for you," he said.

It's a statement he remembers vividly and still laughs about considering every time he turns on the television, someone is talking about his former student.

"I haven't seen the Eras Tour," he says before making a quip. "I'm still waiting on a phone call from Taylor saying, 'Hey Mr. Decker, you want to come to one of my concerts?'"

Swift met her childhood best friend Abigail Anderson Berard in the Hendersonville High School halls and wrote songs in the back of math class. She fearlessly approached songwriter Liz Rose at an industry event and asked her to collaborate. Rose agreed to mentor the teen after school and "Tuesdays with Taylor" were born. The singer would help Rose nab her first Grammy, and Rose helped guide Swift on her debut, second, fourth and Christmas albums.

"She just called me and said, 'I have an idea, will you come to the studio so we can write this?' And she had the idea for 'White Horse,'" Rose says. Swift has been a Grammy contender ever since, racking up five nominations for her most recent album, "The Tortured Poets Department."

"She thinks different," Rose says. "There are a lot of great songwriters in the world, but she is one of a few. I know that she's the biggest star in the world, but she's a songwriter first."

As an eighth grader, the blue-eyed starlet with blond curls played an industry event at the Bluebird Cafe catching the eye of Scott Borchetta. The promotions executive in the midst of starting his own label Big Machine Records signed Swift in 2005. Before their business relationship came to an acrimonious end over the ownership of Swift's discography, his company produced her first six albums before their business relationship came to an acrimonious end over ownership of Swift's recordings.

But Tennessee has remained a strand of the singer's DNA. She shot the music video to "Love Story" at Castle Gwynn in Arrington, "You Belong With Me" at Pope John Paul II High School in Hendersonville and "The Story of Us" at Vanderbilt University.

Her bandmates joined her crew before she embarked on the 2009 "Fearless" tour. They include Nashville-based guitarist Paul Sidoti, bassist Amos Heller and Eras Tour bandleader Mike Meadows.

As the singer's career went into orbit, she transferred from Hendersonville High School her junior year into a program with Aaron Academy, a private Christian school that extended a homeschooling option. Swift received her diploma in the mail in 2008, the same year she filed her first company, Taylor Swift Productions Inc., with the Tennessee Secretary of State's office.

Swift registered other limited liability companies in the state including her travel, marketing and management agencies. Although she purchased properties in New York, California and Rhode Island, she continued to vote and house her businesses in her Tennessee home base.

When Swift dove into other genres — starting with pop music on her fourth album — she faced criticism and ostracism from parts of the country music capital. In 2020, Broadway bar Legends Corner caused an uproar when it replaced her image with Brad Paisley on a mural paying homage to country music singers.

A return to Nashville

But all of that changed when she returned to Nashville in May 2023 for three bedazzled nights of the Eras Tour. To welcome her back, then Mayor John Cooper tweeted about a new Taylor Swift bench in Centennial Park.

"As of today, you now have the perfect place to read at Centennial Park," the mayor wrote. "Nashville is READY for the weekend."

She chose to announce the rerecording of her third era, "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)," at her May 5, 2023 show in Nissan Stadium. The tens of thousands of Swifties packed inside the open-roofed stadium along the Cumberland River cheered at piercing levels. Even fans without a ticket danced on the nearby pedestrian bridge, peering into part of the venue to catch a glimpse of Swiftmania.

"I've been planning something for a while," Swift told the audience. "It's my love language with you. I plot. I scheme. I plan. And then I get to tell you about it."

During the May 7 show, a torrential downpour prompted a two-hour delay, but like in all cities she visited, come Monday morning Swift was the talk of the town.

Later that year, Swift donated $1 million to relief after tornadoes tore through Middle Tennessee, killing six.

"I still look at her and go, 'Wow,'" Rose says after flying to Miami to catch one of the last U.S. shows of the Eras Tour. "I'm just so proud of her. She's such an unbelievably great artist, person and songwriter."

The demand for tickets skyrocketed near the end of the tour with some going for north of $1,300 on StubHub. Tens of thousands of fans watched social media livestreams each show hoping the singer would make an album announcement, bring on a surprise guest or debut a music video. Influencers readied their laptops and phones hungry to pounce at any show changes. As she traversed the world, fans followed her every move.

Many Swifties have been anxiously awaiting the rerecord of her sixth album, "Reputation (Taylor's Version)."

But another rerecord remains to be heard: her first, eponymous album that she wrote on Music Row. Rose, for one, is looking forward to "Taylor Swift (Taylor's Version)" and Swift's return to Nashville and country music.

"She had such great songs," Rose says. "It's going to be as much fun for me as it is for everybody. I can't wait to hear what she puts on there from the vault."

headline: Lucinda Williams dives into the Beatles' catalog on a new album recorded at Abbey Road
fullText:
Lucinda Williams was 10 years old in 1963 and living in Santiago, Chile when she caught Beatlemania.

She listened to the band on the radio, tacked Beatles posters to her bedroom walls, pasted magazine cut-outs of the group in her scrapbook pages and crushed hard on Paul McCartney first, and then George Harrison.

"Was I one of those crazed fans? Yes, I was," the legendary Nashville singer-songwriter said. "I was infected with Beatlemania. Not infected — touched."

Williams, known for tracks "Fruits of My Labor," "Can't Let Go" and her genre-defying rock-country-folk sound, is channeling that fandom into an album of Beatles covers, a project that let her jump head first into the world of the iconic Liverpool pop band.

"Lucinda Williams Sings the Beatles From Abbey Road" arrives on Dec. 6 as the seventh volume of the "Lu's Jukebox" series, a collection of albums where Williams covers other artists' work.

As she sat in a hotel room in East Village, New York, Williams told The Tennessean about the new project and recalled her earliest memories of the Beatles.

Lucinda Williams takes on Abbey Road Studios

The 71-year-old musician started her jukebox series during the pandemic to keep busy, releasing six volumes since the project's launch. She's belted out Rolling Stones' hits, dove into the catalog of Bob Dylan and connected with the music of her late friend Tom Petty.

In 2020, Williams suffered a stroke that led to a five-week stay in a Nashville hospital and a long recovery journey. Though Williams can no longer play guitar due to the limited use of her left arm, years of physical therapy and resilience have gotten her back on track.

"I'm just so stubborn and hard-headed ... I didn't want to be waylaid by (the stroke)," Williams said. "The alternative didn't appeal to me."

Williams has continued to do what she does best: writing, touring and recording.

In 2023, she dropped her first studio album since the stroke, the lauded "Stories From a Rock N Roll Heart." Williams' Beatles record follows as her first jukebox album in almost four years.

More: Lucinda Williams leaves Nashville's Ryman Auditorium awestruck by career retrospective

She had already covered most of the major blues, country and rocks artists that she could think of, so she knew it was time to sing the tunes of one of her favorite childhood bands, the Beatles. Williams' husband and manager, Tom Overby, was on board — and he wanted to go big.

Since Williams would be in the U.K. for some shows, Overby suggested they record the album at Abbey Road Studios, the London studio the where the Beatles famously recorded many of their hits and crafted an album in its name.

If Williams were to record in Abbey Road, she would become the first major artist to sing the Beatles' hits within its walls since The Fab Four, a Beatles tribute band.

"I had to jump through hoops a little bit to get in over there because, you know, they weren't sure who I was at first," Williams said with a chuckle. "It's kind of funny, kind of endearing at the same time."

Williams had two days to record the 12 songs for her album — and the weight of creating a record in Abbey Road Studios was ever-present.

"I didn't know what to expect," she said. "I'd never been in there ... is it going to be sort of like an antique, leftover from that the '60s era?"

It was shockingly contemporary, she said, but she still was mesmerized.

"Just being in somewhere where the Beatles had been and recorded these iconic historical songs, I mean, that never left your head," she said. "I'd sit down in a chair ... did George maybe sit here before? I was kind of walking on eggshells a little bit at first."

But Williams and her band didn't have a whole lot of time for nerves to take over.

"We pretty much had to get in and get out, do our thing and move on," she said. "It was kind of good, in a way, for it to be like that because then you're not dwelling on things. You can't afford to do that."

Williams balances staying true to Beatles, making songs her own

The hardest part of the process actually came before recording the songs, Williams said. It was picking which songs to cover.

Out of the Beatles' catalog of over 200 songs, it was hard to narrow it down to just a dozen tracks. Williams initially gravitated toward ones from the early '60s, since that's when she discovered the band. She was a pre-teen then.

"I just remember as a kid listening to their music; it made me feel good, songs like 'Strawberry Fields Forever,'" Williams said.

But she says she can't quite pinpoint what it really was that made the Beatles so popular. It's something intangible, she thinks. "I just loved how I felt when I listened to a song."

Her favorite Beatles song, and the track she closes out her album with, is "The Long and Winding Road." The gorgeous melody and lyrics of the 1970 song have always spoken to Williams, but she found the tune tough to record.

Other songs on the record include "While My Guitar Gently Weeps," "Yer Blues" and "Let It Be." Quite a few of the Beatles songs, like "I'm So Tired," sounded simple but were deceivingly difficult to sing for Williams.

"I've heard them 1,000 times, but they weren't necessarily that easy to do," she said. "There'd be a song that would be quite a bit more complex and challenging then you can tell just by listening."

And though Williams wanted to make the songs her own, she didn't want to stray too far from the heart of the Beatles' tunes. She had to balance getting the songs right, not becoming a covers band, and being authentically Lucinda Williams.

Her band had a common understanding that they wouldn't try to copy every element of the songs. The drummer would count off and they'd play it live, just like a concert. That's how Williams kept it her own.

In that, a respectable balance was achieved. Williams' gravelly, weathered voice has its typical hypnotic effect, and, of course, the Beatles' melodies never get old.

"I found that I really enjoyed covering other people's songs. I like getting in there, just making them my own," she said.

"It's kind of like a little bag of mysteries — you never know what you're going to find."

  2. "I'm Looking Through You"
  3. "Can't Buy Me Love"
  4. "Rain"
  5. "While My Guitar Gently Weeps"

headline: NFHS permits video review in TSSAA football playoffs. Most coaches don't want it
fullText:
The nine 2024 TSSAA football championship games in Chattanooga this week will once again not include official video reviews, even as the method is catching on in other states. 

That’s fine with most Tennessee high school football coaches, who don't want video review in the TSSAA football playoffs.

The Tennessee Football Coaches Association wasn’t keen on adopting video replay when the TSSAA gauged its interest in 2023 and little has changed since then, TSSAA executive director Mark Reeves said Tuesday.  

“It hasn’t come up, honestly, to us,” Reeves said. “The last two or three or four years it seems like right around football championship time, it’s a question that comes up. But it hasn’t been what I would call a hot topic (this year).”  

The NFHS allows use of video review in football and basketball for the postseason and championships, with football being approved in 2019. At least 13 state high school athletic associations allow instant replay in football. Five states — Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Alabama, Georgia and North Dakota — allow replay for every playoff game. South Dakota, Nebraska, Wisconsin and Ohio allow it just during state championship games. Minnesota allows it during semifinal and championship games only if they’re played in an NFL stadium. 

The TSSAA has communicated with Alabama and Georgia about how they use the technology to be proactive in case the TSSAA adopts the method. If member schools aren’t interested in video review, though, it’s not something the TSSAA would push, Reeves said. 

From Page coach Charles Rathbone to Macon County's Kyle Shoulders, most coaches who were asked about video review during this week’s BlueCross Bowl media availability were largely neutral or opposed to the method, even if just used in the championship games. 

The TSSAA will meet with the TNFCA this week in Chattanooga as it does each year during the state championships, but it’s not known if video review is on the meeting agenda. 

More: Our experts pick all nine 2024 TSSAA football state champions and predict the scores

Oakland coach Kevin Creasy, whose team will face Houston in the Class 6A final this week, was on the fence. “I think it would be pretty neat,” he said, adding he’d be curious to know how it would work, such as if teams would be permitted to ask for a certain number of reviews. When controversial calls have gone against Oakland, “I definitely wanted replay, and when it went our way I was fine with it not being around.”

Houston coach James Thomas believes if regular season games don’t include review, the same should go for championship games.

Melrose coach Gerald Morrow isn't in favor of video review but wondered if replay could be useful during the final two minutes of games when calls can decide the outcome.

headline: Tennessee Titans vs Jacksonville Jaguars: Score prediction, playoff scenarios, betting odds
fullText:
The Tennessee Titans' exceedingly slim playoff hopes are on the line Sunday in yet another in the long history of late-season duels between the Titans and their rival Jacksonville Jaguars.

The Titans (3-9) host the Jaguars (2-10) at Nissan Stadium on Sunday (noon CT, CBS) with the home team's hopes of winning the AFC South and securing a playoff spot dangling by a thread. With the division-leading Houston Texans sitting at 8-5, a Titans loss or tie would make it mathematically impossible for them to win enough games in the final month of the season to catch up in the division standings. The Texans don't play this week, but if they win even one more time this season, that also will eliminate the Titans from the postseason.

For now, though, it's time for another Titans-Jaguars showdown. This matchup hearkens to the stretch of four straight years (2012-15) where both teams had losing records when they faced each other in December. With the Jaguars already eliminated from playoff contention and in line to earn the No. 1 pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, this game has much bigger implications on the offseason ahead than the season at hand, but that doesn't mean there won't be reasons to watch.

ESTES | What a brutal stretch for Nashville pro sports

Here are The Tennessean's scouting report and score prediction for Titans vs Jaguars.

Tennessee Titans vs Jaguars defense: Will Levis' chance to turn progress into points

The Jaguars' defense ranks last in the NFL in yards allowed per game and per play and passing yards allowed per game and per attempt. Only the Carolina Panthers are allowing more points per game than Jacksonville. For Titans quarterback Will Levis, this means the opportunity to capitalize on his four weeks of progress and turn that into actual scoring output.

In four games since returning from his shoulder injury, Levis is fifth in the NFL in passer rating. Despite this, among the 18 teams that have played four games in that stretch, the Titans are 13th in points scored and 17th in points differential.

The next step for the growth of this offense, and for Levis' growth as a passer, is to turn successful outcomes into points more often. Facing one of the NFL's worst defenses should present an opportunity to do so.

Titans vs Jaguars offense: Can Titans frazzle Mac Jones without Trevor Lawrence?

Quarterback Trevor Lawrence, who suffered a concussion in last week's game against the Texans after getting bombed by an illegal hit from former Titans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair, has been put on IR. (He reportedly also will have surgery on his AC joint in his non-throwing shoulder). That means backup Mac Jones will be behind center. Jones has started twice and appeared in five games this season, not enough to be qualified for the league's leaderboards. But if his per-game numbers were translated against the league's best, he'd come out as the NFL's third-worst quarterback by yards per attempt, second-worst by passer rating and worst by passing yards per game.

The Jaguars' offense is clearly limited without Lawrence — not that the offense is all that great with him, either. The Jaguars rank 31st in first downs per game and third-down conversion rate, and last in time of possession. The Titans' defense hasn't played particularly well lately. If that trend continues against this version of the Jaguars' offense, that's much more of an indictment of the Titans than it is a commentary on the Jaguars.

Titans vs Jaguars betting odds

The Titans are favored to win by 3.5 points per BetMGM. The Titans' moneyline is set at -200 and the Jaguars' moneyline is set at +165. The over-under points total is set at 39.5 points.

Score prediction: Titans 28, Jaguars 17

Here's a chance for the Titans to exorcise some frustration after last week's beatdown. The Titans aren't the safest team to count on, but Jacksonville is giving up almost 450 yards per game in its past five contests. The lanes will be open for the Titans to move the ball. Levis and company just need to make it happen.

headline: Azeez Al-Shaair's hit on Trevor Lawrence was a mistake, not a sign of a bad person | Estes
fullText:
The Tennessee Titans have missed linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair.

On the field, for sure, but more so away from it. Linebacker Otis Reese IV, after only one season together, still considers Al-Shaair “the best teammate that I’ve ever been around” at any level. Reese remembers Al-Shaair as a mentor, someone to emulate. Said he knew everyone who worked in the Titans building. That’s because he took the time to speak with them.

“I was blessed to have him last year as a rookie,” Reese said Wednesday.

Defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons knows Al-Shaair well, too. Loves the way he plays the game. Fast and physical and yet, “I know he wasn't intending to go out there and hurt no one,” Simmons said.

These two Titans players were vouching for the character of a former teammate they played alongside in 2023. Note that they were defending the person.

Neither defended what Al-Shaair did during this past Sunday’s game.

Surely by now, you’ve heard about or seen the hit that got Al-Shaair, now a member of the Houston Texans, ejected and subsequently suspended three games by the NFL.

Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence runs and slides. Al-Shaair crashes into him with a forearm raised. Lawrence falls back, his head striking the ground, a blow that left him in the “fencing posture” that can be indicative of a brain injury.

It was bad. It was scary.

It started a melee between the two AFC South rivals, and it sidelined Lawrence, who’ll miss Sunday’s game at Nissan Stadium against the Titans. The Jaguars placed him on injured reserve because of a concussion, perhaps ending his season.

Shouldn’t have happened.

“Him playing the game fast,” Simmons said of Al-Shaair, “that’s not an excuse. Because we all know the rules.”

That’s a defensive player saying that.

Yet when you ask the Titans’ quarterback: “You've got to understand how tough of a position he's in as a defender,” Will Levis said. “As a quarterback, I know it's crazy hearing me say that. But I get it.”

Opinions, as you can see, are all over the place. And everyone, it seems, is talking about it. Al-Shaair’s hit has made national headlines, becoming fodder on channels like CNN. Most folks are blaming Al-Shaair. Some want to talk about quarterbacks sliding late, as Lawrence did. Others are speaking about truly serious topics like head injuries and football safety.

Me? I’d just like for people to better know the person.

This linebacker who messed up, apologized (in a roundabout way) and has nonetheless become a national villain with the encouragement of the NFL, who while punishing Al-Shaair as a player also called into question his character as a human being.

The NFL could have just announced his suspension. Instead, it put out a lengthy statement that read like a petulant rant. It casually cited Al-Shaair’s “repeated violations of rules intended to protect the health and safety of players and promote sportsmanship” without specifying those past violations.

It included portions of a letter sent by Jon Runyan, the league’s vice president of football operations, to Al-Shaair that told him: “Your lack of sportsmanship and respect for the game of football and all those who play, coach and enjoy watching it is troubling and does not reflect the core values of the NFL.”

That line bothered me.

Because if Runyan knew anything about the person he was scolding as a player, he'd know how much Al-Shaair does reflect those core values.

Go read a wonderful, in-depth article The Tennessean’s Paul Skrbina authored last season about Al-Shaair and his background.

From 2023: Azeez Al-Shaair, the Tennessee Titans' 'unconquerable soul' no longer has to be 'invisible'

Here’s a guy who came from nothing. Wasn’t drafted out of college. Has made a nice career for himself and for his family because of how hard and aggressively he plays. As Reese said: “Some people play the game with a whole different mentality than other people.”

That menality is what got Al-Shaair in trouble Sunday. Not the first time, and he deserved the punishment. No excusing that hit on Lawrence.

But it’s unfortunate that the only thing so many will ever bother to know about Al-Shaair is how he was that dirty football player who took out Jacksonville’s quarterback. There’s more to appreciate.

“Nobody embodies our program more than Azeez,” a fired-up Texans general manager Nick Caserio told reporters in Houston. “What he's about, what he's been through. You all know his story. There's not a more selfless individual, more about the team, who's earned the respect, that represents everything we want this program to be about.”

A year ago, the Titans’ leadership would have said the same thing about Al-Shaair.

Still don’t know why they didn’t re-sign him.

headline: TSSAA football playoffs live updates: CPA captures second straight DII-AA state championship
fullText:
CPA held off a rally attempt from BGA to capture the program's second straight Division II-AA BlueCross Bowl state championship, beating the Wildcats, 38-26, Thursday at Finley Stadium in Chattanooga.

BGA recovered two straight onside kicks and scored twice late in the fourth quarter to give CPA a scare. But Rawls Patterson's 336 yards rushing and four touchdowns was too much for the Wildcats' defense as CPA finishes the season 14-0.

Lions coach Ingle Martin captures his fifth state title with the program while CPA won the program's seventh title overall.

Stream HS Football in Tennessee with the NFHS Network

BGA wideout Arnett Hayes broke a state championship record with 260 yards receiving and nearly tied another mark with 15 receptions. His state record broke the mark set by former Giles County star Zach Bailey (212 yards in 2009) and his 15 receptions was just one shy of tying Lee Mayhall, of USJ, set in 2011.

Patterson's 336 yards was just 58 yards short of former Beech great Jalen Hurd's set record of 394 yards set in 2012.

The Rawls Patterson show continues for CPA

The junior running back has 336 yards rushing with four touchdowns as CPA takes full control of this Division II-AA state championship game against BGA with a 38-13 lead. Patterson's 12-yard scoring run with 4:22 left in the game was his fourth of contest.

Patterson is closing in on a TSSAA state championship game rushing record, held by former Beech great Jalen Hurd who ran for 394 yards against Columbia in 2012.

CPA extends lead with touchdown pass in 4Q

Division II-AA Mr. Football candidate Hutson Chance rifled a pass to Owen Cabell early in the fourth quarter for a 7-yard touchdown to extend CPA's lead to 31-13 with 11:03 left in the game. Chance is 9-of-13 for 74 yards. It was the third reception for Cabell.

End of 4th quarter: CPA 24, BGA 13

The total yards between CPA and BGA are almost even, but CPA's ability to control the game with its run game has been the difference as the Lions have rushed for 254 yards. Rawls Patterson has rushed 23 times for 250 yards and three touchdowns.

BGA has been impressive through the air with 199 yards passing, compared to just 62 from CPA. Arnett Hayes has caught 12 passes for 174 yards. The state record for receptions in a title game is 16 (Lee Mayhall, USJ, 2011)

CPA answers as Rawls Patterson continues dominance

After BGA drew within 17-13 midway through the third quarter with a 32-yard field goal, CPA promptly went back down the field for its own touchdown. Rawls Patterson's 35-yard run pushed the Lions' lead to 24-13 as Patterson continues to haunt BGA's defense. Patterson currently has 240 yards rushing and three touchdowns.

BGA inches closer midway through third quarter

Syrus Harr's 32-yard field goal adds another three points to BGA's total as the Wildcats draw closer but still trailing CPA, 17-13, with 7:54 left in the third quarter. Arnett Hayes caught passes of 22 and 23 yards on the drive.

Halftime: CPA 17, BGA 10

Arnett Hayes goes 40 yards on a screen pass from Kaedyn Marable to set up a 33-yard field goal as time expired to give BGA some momentum going into halftime against CPA, trailing 17-10.

CPA took control late in the half after Rawls Patterson's second touchdown run of the game, a 3-yard plunge with 41 seconds left. Patterson has 166 yards on 16 carries, punishing the middle of BGA's defense. The Lions' defense held BGA on two fourth-down plays in the second quarter and forced a first-quarter Wildcats field goal in the first quarter despite BGA having a 1st and goal.

Hayes has 121 yards receiving on nine receptions.

CPA takes control with a 17-7 lead

Rawls Patterson scores for the second time in the first half, this time from 3 yards out as CPA takes control of the DII-AA state championship game against BGA with 41 seconds left. Patterson has 166 yards rushing on 16 carries in the first half

Rawls Patterson chewing up BGA's defense

CPA's running back has carried the bulk of the Lions offense in the first half, eating up chunks of yards in the teeth of BGA's defense. He had 101 yards in the first quarter and has 158 yards with a touchdown as CPA continues to hold a 10-7 lead with 54 seconds left before the half.

Patterson missed most of first meeting between the two schools Sept. 19, a 49-16 CPA win.

CPA forces turnover on downs

The game's first fourth-down play went incomplete as BGA's Kaedyn Marable scrambled on a 4th and 9 near midfield. Marable was forced to throw it away against CPA's pressure early in the second quarter.

End of 1Q: CPA 10, BGA 7

CPA ran for 102 yards in the first quarter and Rawls Patterson already has 101 yards on just nine carries as the defending Division II-AA state champs hold a three-point lead against BGA after the first quarter.

BGA's Arnett Hayes has six receptions for 67 yards but the Wildcats have been penalized seven times for 70 yards.

CPA's Rawls Patterson gives Lions lead late in first quarter

Patterson carried the ball the final six plays of CPA's scoring drive, capped by his 5-yard scoring run as the Lions claim a 10-7 lead with 1:25 left in the first quarter.

BGA's defense holds inside its own 10 yard line

CPA was poised to tie the game after a 27-yard run from Rawls Patterson and a 29-yard pass from Hutson Chance to Weston Parker. But BGA's defense held despite CPA staring at a 1st and goal from the 9 yard line. The Lions settle for a field goal as BGA still leads 7-3 with 6:45 left in the opening quarter.

BGA takes early lead on first possession

BGA running back Ethan Kellum powers his way for a 9-yard touchdown run as the Wildcats score on its first possession of the game with 9:43 left in the first quarter. BGA's Arnett Hayes caught a 30-yard pass from Kaedyn Marable that led to Kellum's TD and a 7-0 lead.

headline: Josh Heupel sounds right message, while I examine curse of Tennessee's CFP seed
fullText:
Welcome to SEC Unfiltered, the USA TODAY NETWORK's newsletter on SEC sports. Look for this newsletter in your inbox Monday through Thursday. Today, national college football columnist Blake Toppmeyer takes over:

Josh Heupel wisely approached a question Wednesday about College Football Playoff seedings. The Tennessee coach said the Vols must embrace a mindset “of anyone, anywhere, anytime” unless they intend to exit the playoff after “a cup of coffee.”

Bingo.

CFP committee chairman Warde Manuel and his cohorts within the selection group wouldn’t be moved by Heupel’s rhetoric anyway, so he might as well focus his efforts on getting Tennessee mentally prepared for the possibility of first-round road trip to Ohio State.

Let fans, athletics directors, conference commissioners and media types do the squabbling, but coaches must get their guys to believe: Anytime, anyplace.

As a sports columnist, though, it’s not my role to promote that mindset, freeing me up to say that I think this projected No. 9 seed for Tennessee ranks as maybe the worst possible spot for the Vols in the playoff bracket.

Tennessee would be set up for a brutal gantlet if the bracket the committee set up Tuesday holds true after this weekend’s conference championship games.

 Now, you might be thinking, Hey, knucklehead, how is the No. 9 seed worse than the Nos. 10, 11 or 12 seeds?

Let me explain.

The No. 9 seed will be on the road at the No. 8 seed, which currently is set up to be Ohio State – and facing the Buckeyes presents as no prize.

Yes, Ohio State looked as appealing as spoiled cottage cheese in a 13-10 loss to Michigan last weekend, but until that game, which annually haunts Ryan Day, the Buckeyes had played like a top contender for the national championship.

Ohio State built arguably the nation’s most talented (and expensive) roster, and even after losing to Michigan, oddsmakers list Ohio State with the third-best odds to win the national title.

Other teams that could host first-round games include Notre Dame, Penn State, Georgia or Texas (depending on which team wins the SEC championship game). If I’m Tennessee, I might rather play any of those teams than Ohio State.

The Buckeyes beat Penn State in Happy Valley, proving on that day, at least, that Ohio State is better than James Franklin’s squad. Tennessee already lost to Georgia, but there’s that whole idea of it being tough to beat the same team twice. Notre Dame and Texas might be great, or they might be overrated. Given their forgiving schedules, it’s hard to know.

To face one of those teams, though, Tennessee would need to be seeded no better than No. 10 within the current bracket.

But, it’s not just the potential first-round opponent that makes me think the Vols might draw a bracket boobytrap with the No. 9 seed. Regardless of first-round opponent, the winner of the No. 8-9 matchup will advance into a quarterfinal game against the No. 1 seed.

Right now, that team would be Oregon, the nation’s only undefeated team.

If you’re seeded No. 12 and happen to upset No. 5, the prize is a quarterfinal game against the No. 4 seed, which could be Boise State, the playoff’s Group of Five representative.

The winner of No. 6 vs. No. 11 will advance to play the No. 3 seed, currently set up to be SMU.

The winner of No. 7 vs. No. 10 would play the quarterfinal against the No. 2 seed, which right now is Texas.

At every turn, that No. 9 seed looks unappealing, but the bracket order might change again on Sunday. And, anyway, No. 9 is at least a lot better than the No. 13 seed. Ask Miami about that.

headline: Tim Hortons launch in Tennessee scores new locations. Where are they, when could they open
fullText:
An area business owner plans to open two more Tim Hortons restaurants in Lebanon after making earlier announcements to open two of the Canadian-based coffee and bakery franchises in Mt. Juliet and Donelson.

Naren Patel will open one Tim Hortons franchise at 1459 West Main Street in Lebanon. The other planned location is on the corner of South Hartmann Drive and Franklin Road and will be part of a future commercial development named Franklin Corner, according to plans submitted to Lebanon officials.

Tim Hortons is known for coffee, specialty drinks and baked foods.

The West Main Street location will replace an old car wash. A “minor” site plan that only requires Lebanon planning staff approval is under review, according to Planner Joshua Stahle. The site plan is considered minor since the new proposed building is largely contained within the footprint of the former car wash.

The Franklin Road location's site plan is already approved.

Franklin Corner will include Teriyaki Madness, Dosbros Fresh Mexican Grill, a liquor store and a BP gas station at 1500 Franklin Road, Patel said.

One of the Tim Hortons restaurants to be built in Mt. Juliet is a free-standing building on the same lot where the refurbished Golden Bear market and gas station is at 10576 Lebanon Road that Patel also owns on Mt. Juliet’s north side. The other future Tim Hortons is at 5120 Beckwith Road near the TriStar Mt. Juliet ER medical building on the city’s south side. A gas station is also part of the Beckwith Road development.

Patel also announced a Tim Hortons to be built in Davidson County's Donelson that will replace a former Krystal restaurant at 2527 Lebanon Pike.

He tentatively plans to start work on the Donelson location before the end of the year with hopes to open in February. Work on the Wilson County locations is expected to start next year. Opening estimates for the Wilson County locations are:

  • 1459 West Main Street, Lebanon: Second quarter 2025
  • 1500 Franklin Road, Lebanon: Third quarter 2025
  • 10576 Lebanon Road, Mt. Juliet: Second quarter 2025

headline: Why TSSAA football teams can't use electronic helmet communication devices similar to NFL
fullText:
A memo sent to TSSAA member schools in October was sent as a reminder to Tennessee high school football coaches. However, it was one that caught their attention.

There are National Federation of State High School Associations rules in place regarding the use of electronic communication devices. The penalty if a team is caught using those devices, including ejections, a $500 fine and a suspension for the following game.

The NFHS rule is not a new one. High school football isn't college or the NFL. The NFHS passed regulations in 2015 that permitted the use of communication devices during "authorized conferences outside the nine-yard marks, on the sidelines and during halftime." But use of communication devices by players except for those conferences continues to be prohibited.

What isn't permitted, though, is having electronic devices where communication between coaches and players can take place on the field during a game.

Rule 1.6.2 of the NFHS Football Rules Book states: “Electronic communication devices, including but not limited to audio recorder, Local Area Network (LAN) phones and/or headsets, mobile phones, still photograph(s), film, analog or digital video(s) and/or Internet depictions may be used by coaches and nonplayers.”

Coach-to-player communication on the field is not allowed during the game with an active player on the field.

Coaches can talk to players on the sideline. They can share plays on tablets. They can give athletes a headset and have them talk directly to coaches in the press box. They can even pull a position group in front of a large screen TV and go over plays from a previous drive.

But all of that is done on the sideline when those players are not active in the game.

What happened during Trinity Christian-Riverside game

During a TSSAA non-region football game on Sept. 26 between Riverside and Trinity Christian Academy, a member of TCA's chain crew saw a Riverside player cover the earholes of his helmet, similar to how NFL and college football players look when trying to hear the in-helmet communications with coaches. The chain crew members also saw what appeared to be a walkie-talkie device used by a Riverside assistant coach.

TCA coach Darren Bowling said he addressed what was seen with the game officials. In the conversation, Bowling said that Riverside admitted to having a device in the helmets, but said they were for recording video. There were no penalties given to Riverside and no one was ejected from the game.

In a statement to The Jackson Sun, Decatur County Schools director of schools Chris Villaflor acknowledged the incident and explained what happened following.

“Officials had a conversation with the football staff about the use of electronic communication devices,” Villaflor wrote in the statement. “There were no penalties assessed to our team. When Decatur County Schools heard of these allegations, we immediately began our own investigation to ensure that we are in compliance with TSSAA rules.

"In October, TSSAA announced to all schools that there are new, clear penalties for any coaches and players using electronic devices. We have reviewed this new policy and taken steps to ensure that our football program is in compliance. We consider this matter to be closed and have no further comment.”

In that October memo, TSSAA executive director Mark Reeves wrote that the high school association was "aware of some situations within the state where electronic communication devices may have been used between coaches and players in football contests." He referred to the NFHS rules book.

"We will be communicating with local official associations on the appropriate penalty if a team is caught using electronic communication during a contest," Reeves wrote in the memo. "If this happens, the players involved and the head coach will be issued a flagrant unsportsmanlike penalty, resulting in their ejection. TSSAA bylaws state that the ejection of a coach results in a $500 fine and suspension from the next contest. A subsequent ejection results in a $1000 fine and a suspension for the next two contests.  A repeated offense such as this could also result in additional disciplinary action to the football program."

Electronic devices in football

The NFL has utilized coach-to-player communications since 1994. Coaches speak directly to the quarterback with in-helmet electronic devices. In 2008, the NFL adjusted the system to include a defensive player. Communication devices, however, are new to college football as the sport adopted it this season, after experimenting with it during bowl games last season.

In a game, the player who receives coach-to-player communication is designated with a green dot on the midline on the back of his helmet. Communication is cut off with 15 seconds left on the play clock or when the ball is snapped, whichever comes first.

The device itself is a one-way speaker near the earhole of the helmet so the designated player can hear what’s being spoken.

How does TSSAA regulate electronic communication devices?

The TSSAA operates under NFHS rules and works with the guidelines set by the organization. Reeves said that the TSSAA cannot examine and investigate every cheating accusation.

“We as an association can't go back and investigate playing rules,” Reeves said. “We can't go back and review film in a baseball game to try to determine whether or not a kid was using Vaseline on the tip of his cap because curveball was breaking 18 inches. If we open up that Pandora's Box … there's no way that we can do that.”

If a penalty had been called during the Riverside-TCA game when the devices were found, there could have been a further investigation, Reeves added.

TSSAA assistant director Richard McWhirter, who was until recently the chairman of the NFHS rules committee for football and oversees the rules committee for the TSSAA, said that the NFHS has been in conversation about electronic devices for three or four years.

McWhirter said electronic devices are a long way from being permitted because there is not enough structure in terms of funding and setup in the stadiums for some of the smaller programs that would struggle to pay for the necessities.

“What has more of a chance of passing than (in-helmet communication) is maybe the companies with wristbands where you can say what the play is (and) type out (a play),” MrWhirter said. “Right now there’s a wristband with 28 plays or whatever written on there and they’re signaling something in. They wouldn’t signal anything in with this, it would be typed in straight to the wristband. You’ve probably got something like that with a better chance of passing, because you can’t run down the field looking at your wristband.”

Milan coach Wade Comer, who guided McKenzie to three appearances in the state championship game and the 2022 Class 1A championship, said that it’s a matter of keeping the game fair.

“They need to make sure everybody’s playing by the same rules,” said Comer, who led Milan to the Class 2A BlueCross Bowl championship game this season. “That’s their job, they should enforce rules and make sure everybody’s abiding by them.”

What TSSAA coaches are saying about communication devices

Ensworth coach Tim Hasselbeck played in the NFL from 2001-07 and worked as an analyst for Fox Sports and ESPN from 2007-23 before taking over for the Tigers this season.

Hasselbeck said that there are benefits and drawbacks to having communication devices and that the only way to make it work is to outfit all the stadiums with the capabilities of having the devices.

“We’re doing fine without it,” he said. “We’re very fortunate to be a well-resourced school and not every school has the opportunities that we have. I think it sounds good, but it would be hard because there’s infrastructure you’d need in the stadiums.”

Hasselbeck added that there’s a part of the game that is a help to the players and communication devices could affect that.

“We want our kids to grow up through this game,” Hasselbeck said. “Part of growing up through this game is when they are out there, they are the ones playing and it’s on them to make good decisions.”

What other TSSAA football coaches are saying

  • “You see things like that trickle down from each league," Riverdale coach Will Kriesky said. "I could see that coming down to us. You look at baseball now. They’re able to use electronic devices. It wouldn’t surprise me in a few years.”
  • “It’s not going to change my game,” Bowling said. “My game’s old and that’s fine.”
  • "It's not high on my priority list, but if it was adopted it would have to be something that we'd have to look into and figure out the pluses and minuses of it," said Lamar Brown, who coached Knoxville West to back-to-back 5A state titles in 2022 and 2023. "I think the minus would be giving the quarterback too much information sometimes and not letting him just play. It could benefit high school football, but the biggest thing would be you have to have a way to enforce the rules."
  • “I'm not really for it at this moment," Beech coach Anthony Crabtree said. "It's probably coming. I would just like to try to keep the game as pure as possible for right now. There's going to be things that go along with that. I like the purity of high school football.”
  • "For small schools that don't have a lot of coaches on its staff, I think it could be a great tool to talk directly to your QB," said East Robertson coach Chase Brooks, whose team lost to Riverside, 13-7, in the Class 2A state championship game last year. "But it would need to be like college where they cut the communication off after a certain amount of time. But I'm for any way we can get information to a kid quickly without that kid having to constantly run to the sideline to get a play."

Austin Chastain is a sports writer covering West Tennessee high schools. Reach him by email at  achastain@gannett.com or on X, formerly known as Twitter, at @ChastainAJ.
