headline: WNBA expansion draft is Friday. Who will Fever protect, make available for Golden State?
fullText:
Find out who the Indiana Fever lost in the expansion draft to the Golden State Valkyries by clicking here.

'My mouth dropped.' Indiana Fever fans vent after Golden State Valkyries pick Temi Fagbenle

INDIANAPOLIS — The WNBA expansion draft is Friday, and the Indiana Fever may have to say goodbye to one of their players.

Or, maybe they won’t.

The expansion draft for the Golden State Valkyries will air 6:30 p.m. on ESPN where the newest franchise in the league will have the chance to pick one player from each team to make up its 2025 roster. But just because the Valkyries have the ability to pick a player from each team doesn’t mean they will.

Clarkonomics: Dissecting complexity of paying Fever star what she's really worth

Fever 2025 schedule takeaways: WNBA leans into Sky rivalry, bigger arenas

There are multiple ways the expansion draft can shake out for the Fever: Golden State can pick one of Indiana’s players, or the Fever and Valkyries can work out a pre-expansion draft trade that could give Indiana more autonomy in which player leaves the franchise, or Golden State won’t pick a player from Indiana’s roster at all.

We’ll find out the specifics Friday. Before then, here’s what you can expect on how the expansion draft works:

How does WNBA expansion draft affect Indiana Fever?

Golden State will start constructing its team with the expansion draft, getting up to 13 players from the draft before free agency even begins. In its most basic form, Golden State will be able to pick one unprotected player from each team as well as one unrestricted free agent who has not yet used all of their core years.

The Valkyries will then need to use their core designation (a max one-year salary in exchange for exclusive negotiating rights) on the unrestricted free agent they pick. Players who have already used up their core seasons — including players like Brittney Griner, DeWanna Bonner and Brionna Jones — aren’t eligible to be picked, so they don’t need to be protected by their teams. 

Each existing team can protect up to six players on their roster, which includes outgoing unrestricted free agents that are eligible to be cored and players they have the rights to but are not currently in the league. Then, Golden State can pick from the unprotected list.

Golden State can also opt to negotiate a trade with different teams — they could pick a player from one team and trade them to another team, whether it be for cap space or yet another player, or the Valkyries can negotiate with a team to pick a specific player from their roster.

The Valkyries can also opt to not pick a player from a team at all. There are only 12 roster spots on each WNBA team, and Golden State would come out with 13 players if they picked one player from each team and a UFA. With free agency starting in January too, the Valkyries may not want to fill up their roster that quickly. 

Predicting Fever's WNBA expansion draft protected list

Emphasis on predicted, as the league did not release the protected lists of any team.

  • Caitlin Clark
  • Kelsey Mitchell
  • Aliyah Boston
  • Lexie Hull
  • NaLyssa Smith
  • Temi Fagbenle

The top three are all but guaranteed: Clark and Boston, the past two No. 1 picks with four and three more years of control under the Fever, respectively, are no-brainers. Indiana also plans to core Kelsey Mitchell, which means they need to protect her as well. 

Lexie Hull worked her way into the starting lineup and was a pivotal player in the second half of the season, making it likely the Fever don’t want to give her up. Temi Fagbenle, who is a restricted free agent, was an essential part of the roster when she was healthy as well. Fagbenle missed 22 games with various injuries, but was a crucial veteran voice both on and off the court.

NaLyssa Smith is the sticking point — she was a starter for most of the season, but her minutes dwindled in favor of Fagbenle at times, especially during the postseason. Smith was vocal about her dissatisfaction with her playing time this past season, but that may have been directed at the previous coaching staff. Smith reposted the announcement of Stephanie White becoming the Fever’s new coach in November after Christie Sides was fired.

Indiana could protect Smith in hopes they could trade her later in the offseason and get another player in exchange for the former No. 2 overall pick. Or they could be planning to keep her for 2025 and hope a new system brings out the best in her. 

Golden State’s potential options from the Fever

Katie Lou Samuelson, Grace Berger, Damiris Dantas, Victaria Saxton and Kristy Wallace will all likely be unprotected from the Fever’s roster. Erica Wheeler, the final player on Indiana’s roster, will be an unrestricted free agent this season.

Of those, I believe Berger or Samuelson would be the most likely picked by Golden State. 

Berger, an IU alum, just finished her second season with the Fever. She had a lot of usage in her rookie year in 2023, playing in 36 games and averaging 14.2 minutes and 4.6 points. Her spot in the rotation fell off in 2024, though, as she only appeared in 11 games with an average of 9.3 minutes per game.

Berger is a versatile and quick player who made the WNBA All-Rookie team in 2023. She has a lethal midrange shot, which could open up some options on a new team. On top of that, she’s relatively cheap — her salary, which is unprotected, would be $80,000 for 2025.

Samuelson, on the other hand, is a veteran player who could bring some experience to a completely new franchise. She was drafted No. 4 overall out of UConn in 2019 and has bounced around a bit, playing with Chicago, Los Angeles, Seattle and now Indiana. Going to Golden State could be somewhat of a homecoming, as she is from Huntington Beach, Calif. 

The five-year WNBA veteran did have a difficult season in 2024, with it being her first after having her daughter in summer 2023. She played in 37 games, mostly coming off the bench after beginning the year as a starter, and averaged 4.3 points per game in 18.2. minutes. This year, with having a full offseason of training, Samuelson could be primed for a bounce-back year. 

The thing that could turn Golden State away from Samuelson, though, is her hefty $180,000 salary owed to her in 2025. That salary is protected, so Golden State would be on the hook even if they eventually released her. 

Other options for the Valkyries, of course, include a trade with the Fever so Indiana could agree to specific terms with a return for the player they are giving up.

headline: Steve Alford just made DI basketball coaching history with record-shattering feat
fullText:
It's 8:30 a.m. Wednesday and Steve Alford has woken up as a 60-year-old man for the 11th straight day. He's in his office at the University of Nevada joking that the monumental coaching record he recently set "just means I'm getting old."

But there have been plenty of 60-year-old coaches before him in Division I basketball, hundreds before him, yet Alford is only the second in the history of DI college hoops to accomplish this feat: Winning at least 100 games at four different schools.

156 at Iowa. 155 at New Mexico. 124 at UCLA. And now 102 at Nevada.

That puts Alford alongside the late legendary Lefty Driesell, the coach known for starting Midnight Madness, but also the first coach in history to win his 100th game at his fourth school in 2002 with Georgia State. Driesell also accumulated at least 100 wins at Davidson (176), Maryland (348) and James Madison (159). He retired in January 2003, in the middle of his 41st season, with a career record of 786-394, which at the time made him the fourth winningest DI men's basketball coach behind only Dean Smith, Adolph Rupp and Bob Knight.

Being talked about in the same breath as Driesell is an honor, Alford says, a coach he never played against but one he had followed through his career.

The Steve Alford story, Part 1: 'Everything coach Knight promised me, it all came true'

Alford's 100th win at Nevada came Nov. 16 at home with an 85-59 victory over Santa Clara. Since that game, the team has won two more, putting Alford at 102 wins with Nevada and a 6-2 record for the season.

With a 687-357 overall record, Alford is the 11th winningest active DI coach. Still, as he talked about his 100-wins feat to IndyStar on Wednesday, Alford gave much of the credit to his fellow coaches and players throughout his 34-year career.

"I've been with incredible staffs at all the stops and win, lose, or draw, those were the people I wanted to go through that, those challenges with, the celebrations with," he said. "And then, obviously, the players that those staffs recruited, just high character guys. And that doesn't mean we won all of our games or didn't have any speed bumps along the way, but just incredible players."

Alford, who played his college career under Knight at IU, winning a national title in 1987, spent four years in the NBA after being drafted 26th overall by the Dallas Mavericks. He also played for the Golden State Warriors before leaving pro basketball in 1991.

"And I tell people all the time, I had no idea the journey I was going to go on when I got out of playing. I was only 26 years old when I got into this business and Manchester College hired me," Alford said. "I had no idea what my career was going to look like."

At Manchester, Alford finished with a 78-29 record in four years before moving to Southwest Missouri State where he compiled a 78-48 record the next four years. Once at Iowa, his 100-plus wins began.

"I'm very blessed that every school, every place, every city, every community has been incredible. And in every stop, something really cool has happened with our family," Alford said. "And you know those are really the only things you can hope for when you're a husband, a father and, yeah, you know now a grandfather."

Yes, Alford and his wife, Tanya, are grandparents, and he said it's every bit as wonderful as he'd heard it would be.

A.J. is two and a half years old and the son of Bryce Alford and his wife, Ali. Bryce is now an assistant coach for the Oklahoma City Blue of the NBA G League. Kai is a little over a year old and the son of Kory Alford and his wife, Haley. Kory is the head coach at Huntington University.

"I'm just so blessed that basketball has been so good to our family," Alford said.

As for setting this historical record? "You know, I don't think anybody ever wins enough, but I think the communities appreciated how we went about it, the culture that we were trying to build in basketball."

The Steve Alford Series

The Steve Alford story, Part 1: 'Everything coach Knight promised me, it all came true'

The Steve Alford story, Part 2: Learning from Bob Knight — the hard way

The Steve Alford story, Part 3: Defeated for the first time, he brings Indiana to Nevada

Steve Alford: The early years

  • Alford was born in Franklin, Indiana, on Nov. 23, 1964. 
  • He played for New Castle High School, where his father, Sam, was his coach.
  • Alford became the all-time single-game and career scoring leader for New Castle.
  • He scored 57 points in the 1983 semi-state game and had 2,116 career points, which puts him 33rd on Indiana’s list of top scorers.
  • He was 1983 Indiana Mr. Basketball.
  • The Steve Alford Inn in New Castle pays tribute to him and stays current: A giant shoe is repainted to the colors of the team he’s currently coaching. 

Follow IndyStar sports reporter Dana Benbow on X: @DanaBenbow. Reach her via email: dbenbow@indystar.com

headline: IU football roster breakdown defense: How will Hoosiers use transfer portal to fill holes
fullText:
BLOOMINGTON – Curt Cignetti and his staff must cross an important bridge between Wednesday's signing day and College Football Playoff preparation in the next two weeks.

Their players now focused on the upcoming challenge of whomever Indiana might draw in the Playoff bracket Sunday, Cignetti must also concern himself with replacing many of them. Cignetti and his coaches rebuilt their roster a season ago around a nucleus of experienced players without much eligibility left, knowing they’d need to hit the transfer portal again in 2024. Now, that time has come. The portal officially opens Monday, Dec. 9.

How IU's success impacted recruiting: 'Everything is on the up-and-up.'

In his own words: Why Davion Chandler signed with IU.

Today, we’ll look at where the Hoosiers are likely to attack their roster weakness once portal recruiting begins in earnest. Let’s dig in on defense.

Note: This breakdown will not take into account possible future transfers out. Players might be mentioned that later elect to move on. Such is the danger of modern college sports. Onward.

Edge rusher

This will be one of the keys to IU’s offseason defensively, at least in terms of personnel.

Mikail Kamara has a decision to make. The first-team All-Big Ten selection’s draft stock has never been higher, but that could also earn him significant financial opportunity if he remains in college for one more year. He walked at senior day, but he can return.

Lanell Carr technically cannot, but if Zach Horton has a narrowly tailored case for another year based on limited playing time in a large number of games in a season earlier in his career, Carr does too. For now, we’ll assume he’s gone, along with Jacob Mangum-Farrar.

Indiana has some interesting young players coming through, including TaDerius Collins, Venson Sneed and Daniel Ndukwe. But they will almost certainly need to add for impact here. If Kamara departs, even more so.

Projected adds: 2-4

Defensive Tackle

IU’s top two tackles, James Carpenter and CJ West, are gone after this year. The cupboard is not entirely bare, provided players like Marcus Burris and Mario Landino remain and continue developing.

Tyrique Tucker, one of the few younger JMU transfers from last winter, had a very good season in a reserve role at tackle, and should be in line for more snaps in 2025. But West’s departure leaves a hole at nose tackle, and depth is likely a concern. Indiana needs to add.

Projected adds: 2-3.

IU Insider: Get your Hoosiers fix direct to your inbox

Linebacker

Maybe the most stable position on the defense, provided no one leaves unexpectedly.

First-team All-Big Ten linebacker Aiden Fisher has a year left. Indiana did an excellent job bleeding Isaiah Jones beside Fisher and Jailin Walker across the course of the fall. And true freshman Rolijah Hardy earned more and more of his coaches’ trust as the season wore on.

Make no mistake: Walker will need replacing. He was among the most versatile and disruptive linebackers in the league this season, just as important to Indiana’s defensive success as Fisher (or any player save perhaps Kamara). But this is one of those positions where there’s at least less to do, and that’s working under the assumption the staff doesn’t feel it has a Walker replacement already on roster.

Projected adds: 1-2.

Cornerback

The secondary is a two-sided coin for Cignetti. Corner is the good side.

Provided no unexpected attrition, Indiana should return starters D’Angelo Ponds and Jamier Johnson, with JoJo Johnson and Jamari Sharpe behind them. If someone does transfer, there are promising young corners on roster in Dontrae Henderson and Josh Philostin, and Indiana signed multiple players at the position Wednesday.

This might be one area where fresh NIL resources are necessary to keep good players where they are. Someone like Ponds, for example, who spent this season proving his value at the Power Four level, could command significant attention once again.

But there are at least birds in hand here for Indiana. That’s helpful.

Projected adds: 1-2.

Safety

Primarily because there are precious few such options here.

IU leaned on four safeties primarily this season: Shawn Asbury, Amare Ferrell, Terry Jones Jr. and Josh Sanguinetti. All but Ferrell are gone after this year.

Ferrell might be the pick of the bunch, as one of the highest-graded safeties in the conference this season per Pro Football Focus. He’s also versatile enough to switch between playing deep and at the hybrid nickel spot.

He will need help though. Bryson Bonds has another year if he wants to use it. Jah Jah Boyd flipped from James Madison to IU to some fanfare a year ago out of high school. Beyond that, Indiana needs both depth and impact. Expect the Hoosiers to pursue starters, plural, at the back end.

Projected adds: 2-4

Punter

This one is pretty straightforward. James Evans is out of eligibility after this year. Alejandro Quintero can handle both and is listed as a punter, but the bulk of his career game work has been kicking, not punting, duty.

Long term, IU might address this position via a young player brought in and developed. For now, replacing Evans with a transfer looks likely.

Projected adds: 1.

Punt return

Myles Price handled the bulk of this work for Indiana in 2024, with Ke’Shawn Williams filling in behind him. Both will need replaced.

Having said that, those were players recruited to more substantial roles whose skillsets also naturally fit at punt return, rather than returners who eventually found a home somewhere else in the two-deep.

The Hoosiers’ next No. 1 punt returner will probably be recruited for a bigger job, and tack this one. We’ll call for a couple adds here, but understand we’re probably talking about someone joining at another position and simply including this in their overall role.

Projected adds: 1-2.

Listen to Mind Your Banners, our IU Athletics-centric podcast, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

headline: IU football roster breakdown offense: How will Hoosiers use transfer portal to fill holes
fullText:
BLOOMINGTON – Curt Cignetti and his staff must cross an important bridge between Wednesday's signing day and College Football Playoff preparation in the next two weeks.

Their players now focused on the upcoming challenge of whomever Indiana might draw in the Playoff bracket Sunday, Cignetti must also concern himself with replacing many of them. Cignetti and his coaches rebuilt their roster a season ago around a nucleus of experienced players without much eligibility left, knowing they’d need to hit the transfer portal again in 2024. Now, that time has come. The portal officially opens Monday, Dec. 9.

Today, we’ll look at where the Hoosiers are likely to attack their roster weakness once portal recruiting begins in earnest. First, we review the offensive side of the ball.

In his own words: Why Davion Chandler signed with IU.

How IU success impacted recruiting: 'Everything is on the up-and-up.'

Note: This breakdown will not take into account possible future transfers out. Players might be mentioned that later elect to move on. Such is the danger of modern college sports. Onward.

Quarterback

Kurtis Rourke was the latest in a string of transfer quarterbacks who thrived in Cignetti’s offense. After Jordan McCloud won Sun Belt offensive player of the year in 2023, Rourke’s success grew so substantial it won him All-Big Ten honors and briefly inserted his name into the Heisman discussion.

Provided Cignetti and his staff want another veteran signal caller competing at the top end of the two-deep next year (they could put the job in Tayven Jackson’s hands), the sell should not be difficult.

The other question, if Cignetti does want a portal QB, will be one of distributing scholarships through the classes. Does Jackson want to fight out another quarterback competition? Do either of IU’s redshirting freshmen, Alberto Mendoza or Tyler Cherry, cast an eye afield?

These are good problems to have. But they are still part of the calculus in recruiting this position.

Projected adds: 1

Running back

Justice Ellison and Ty Son Lawton, Indiana’s top two backs this fall, will both exhaust their eligibility following this season. But the cupboard is not necessarily bare.

Redshirt juniors Elijah Green and Kaelon Black combined for 75 carries, 452 yards and seven touchdowns this season, in spot duty behind their more veteran teammates. Black, a James Madison transfer, showed good power while Green — albeit in limited snaps — displayed excellent burst.

Cignetti and running backs coach John Miller could attempt to add over top of those two players or build around them, perhaps reinforcing the room with depth and counting more heavily on redshirting freshman Khobie Martin.

With 1,445 rushing yards and 22 touchdowns exiting the top of the depth chart, and one out-and-out running back in the high school class, the Hoosiers will need to add here one way or another.

Projected adds: 2-3.

Tight end

Much as the staff would love to keep Zach Horton around, he looks bound for the exit door. Horton has a bit of a narrow argument for getting a year back, but at this point it looks unlikely.

Trey Walker is also out the door, and James Bomba, who has a year left, is undecided, which means most or all of IU’s experience at tight end will need replacing.

Indiana has taken some intriguing tight ends from the high school ranks in recent years, including Brody Foley, Sam West and Brody Kosin. West in particular has flashed in moments during spring practices. Could any of them be ready for the step up?

Cignetti will want to be absolutely certain. Competent perimeter blocking is a crucial component of his pass offense, and IU relied heavily on Horton in that area this fall. If none of those players is ready for the step up, the Hoosiers will need at least one tight end from the portal.

Projected adds: 0-1.

Wide receiver

Indiana will probably need to allocate extra resources to tying down Omar Cooper and Elijah Sarratt, but in those two it has solid foundations at the boundaries. The slot needs work.

The staff will have known that for awhile, having stocked that position with transfers (Myles Price, Miles Cross, Ke’Shawn Williams) it knew had just one year of eligibility remaining. Still, even if a younger player like Charlie Becker is ready for a move up, or a freshman can step in right away, impact adds are a must at those inside receiver spots that are so important in this offense.

Andison Coby is likely gone after this year too, and Donaven McCulley and E.J. Williams already left for the portal. Indiana must address depth on the outside. The good news for Cignetti is that in an offense that rotates receivers so much, that’s not a tough sell.

Projected adds: 3-4.

Offensive line

Indiana’s actually in decent shape here as long as it keeps the bulk of what it has together.

Carter Smith (LT), Drew Evans (LG) and Bray Lynch (RG) are all back. Trey Wedig (LT) and Mike Katic (C) will need replaced positionally, and as leaders more broadly, but provided Evans can make a full recovery from his Achilles injury, the Hoosiers should get a comfortable chunk of its line back, with decent young depth behind it.

Three questions worth asking: 1) Is there a readymade replacement on roster for center (or another position should IU shift a starter over), 2) same for left tackle and 3) does Nick Kidwell try to get the year back he lost to his preseason injury? If the answer to all three is yes, Indiana has a number of the pieces it needs here and might just focus on depth. If no to either, that’s when the question of hitting the portal for a starter looms larger.

Projected adds: 2-4.

Kicker

Derek McCormick will be gone, but Quinn Warren looked good deputizing for him earlier this season, so IU might feel it has its kickoff specialist already on roster.

And unless there’s some unspoken doubt over Nicolas Radicic, placekicker is in good hands. As things stand, IU doesn’t need much here.

Projected adds: 0.

Kickoff return

The question will be whether Cignetti feels he has a clear replacement for Solomon Vanhorse on roster already.

One of those insurance adds from James Madison, Vanhorse wasn’t called upon to do too much this season, but he was a steady hand at the wheel returning kicks. Does Indiana need to dip into the portal for this, or simply promote from within?

Projected adds: 0-1.

Listen to Mind Your Banners, our IU Athletics-centric podcast, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

headline: Three observations on Pacers: Season-worst offensive half dooms them vs Nets
fullText:
After rallying back from a 24-point deficit to get within two points of the Raptors before ultimately fading to a double-digit loss on Tuesday night, the Pacers came back from a 21-point deficit on Wednesday night to tie the game but then gave up a 10-0 run and still fell 99-90 to the Nets in Brooklyn.

The Pacers dropped their fourth straight game and their eighth straight road game, falling to 9-14 overall and 2-10 on the road on the year. Meanwhile the Nets improved to 10-13.

The Pacers started the game with their two worst offensive quarters of the season and finished with their second-worst offensive game of the season. The Pacers showed some signs of progress on the defensive end and better overall effort than they did on Tuesday in many cases, but they also had extended stretches when they looked more lost than they have at any time in the last three seasons.

"This is a difficult stretch, tough time," coach Rick Carlisle said. "We are making progress in some areas. ... Some of this growth is difficult because wins are hard to come by. It's been a rough stretch, but we have to look for positives."

Here are three observations. For this game, five weren't necessary.

For extended periods, the Pacers' offense looked hopeless

The last time the Pacers had 35 points or fewer in a half, Tyrese Haliburton wasn't on the team. It was a 92-84 loss to the Knicks on Nov. 15, 2021 when the Pacers scored all of 10 points in the fourth quarter and 35 in the second half. The last time they had fewer than 35 in a first half was Feb. 10, 2021 against the Nets when Kevin Durant, James Harden and Kyrie Irving were still on Brooklyn's roster and the Pacers were starting Jeremy Lamb and Justin Holiday. That group scored 30 points in the first half but managed 32 in both the third and the fourth quarters that night in a 104-94 loss.

The Pacers' offense in the Haliburton era hasn't been brilliant every single night, but it's rarely been too feeble to score fewer than 45 points in a half. As recently as Sunday it scored 45 points in a quarter and last season its 123.3 points per game were more than any team had averaged in an NBA regular season in 40 years. They've always found ways to at least put points on the board.

But in Wednesday's first half they truly seemed to have no answers for the problems Brooklyn's defense presented. The Nets pressured the ball, walled off the paint, took away drives and made sure All-Star forward Pascal Siakam was usually dealing with multiple bodies. They dared the Pacers to move the ball around the perimeter and shoot 3s. As a result, the Pacers mostly settled for jump shots and mostly missed them.

In the first quarter they made just 7 of 23 field goals including 1 of 11 3-pointers for 17 points, their lowest scoring quarter of the year. They didn't turn the ball over that quarter but they gave it away 12 times in the second quarter when they scored 18 points on 6 of 16 shooting and managed just two points in the paint after scoring 10 in the first quarter.

The Pacers rebounded with 35 points in the third quarter on 12 of 19 shooting including 4 of 8 from 3-point range, but they then scored just 20 points in the fourth quarter including just 10 after they tied the game at 80 in the game's last 8:06 with just three field goals in that time frame. All told they shot 42.7% from the floor and 8 of 33 from 3-point range and had their second-lowest points-in-the-paint output of the season with 36.

Carlisle has repeatedly made the point that with wings Aaron Nesmith and Ben Sheppard out and guard Andrew Nembhard finally coming back from knee tendinitis -- he sat out Wednesday's game on the second night of a back-to-back -- the Pacers are simply not the same team they were a year ago and they have to develop a different identity.

It seems like they should have fewer problems getting it together on offense than defense because they still have their four leading scorers available in Haliburton, Siakam, Myles Turner and Bennedict Mathurin, plus two efficient off-the-bench scorers in veteran backup point guard T.J. McConnell and rim-running forward Obi Toppin. But as a collective unit, they don't seem to have come to any conclusions on how to best operate and they find themselves more and more frequently relying on individual talent and shot making rather than the brand of random "organized chaos" as Haliburton called it last season that allowed them to play fast and free and score easily. Their level of offensive cohesion seems to be regressing rather than progressing.

The Pacers have slipped to 14th in the league in scoring (113.4 points per game), eighth in field goal percentage (.482), seventh in points in the paint and 10th in assists after leading the NBA in all four categories last year. They're also 14th in 3-point percentage and 21st in 3-pointers made. They've fallen from second to 21st in offensive rating with 111.2 points per 100 possessions compared to 120.5 last year. The Pacers could certainly use Nesmith and Sheppard to run the floor and space it and they could use Nembhard back to make life easier on Haliburton, but the Pacers seem to have deeper problems those men might not be enough to fix.

There was some defensive progress, but not enough

Haliburton said after Tuesday's loss to Toronto that the Pacers needed to "look in the mirror" and have a "reality check" and understand that their level of effort, especially on the defensive end, was not acceptable.

There were, in fact, some moments that the Pacers could look at on the defensive end and be proud but they had breakdowns at some of the most inopportune times, and considering the Nets rank 22nd in the NBA in scoring and were missing their leading scorer in Cam Thomas, they can only take so much pride in those.

The Pacers kept themselves in striking distance in spite of their abysmal offensive first half by holding the Nets to 51 first-half points on 18 of 47 shooting. They didn't allow more than 27 points in a quarter and held the Nets to manageable figures of 43.2% overall shooting, 44 points in the paint and 12 of 36 (33.3%) shooting from beyond the arc. They blocked 10 shots with Turner swatting four.

But they kept losing veteran Nets wing Cameron Johnson who scored 26 points on seven 3-pointers. Most of those were at least somewhat contested but the Pacers were in most cases just slow enough either in fighting off screens or closing out in rotation to allow Johnson to get in rhythm.

By their standards -- which aren't very high -- the Pacers didn't give up a ton of easy layups with the Nets finishing with 44 points in the paint on Wednesday. However, the easy ones they gave up were very untimely. Immediately after Pascal Siakam tied the game at 80, the Nets took the lead on an alley-oop dunk from Shake Milton to Ben Simmons because Toppin left Simmons to prepare to double-team Day'Ron Sharpe, even though Sharpe never got the ball. Nets forward Jalen WIlson drove for a few easy layups after that and once the Nets went on a 10-0 run the Pacers were in too big of a hole to dig out again.

Johnny Furphy helped keep the Pacers in it

The Pacers weren't expecting to rely on rookie wing Johnny Furphy this year. At the end of camp, which he missed almost entirely with ankle injuries, Carlisle said he would likely see a lot of time with the Mad Ants.

However, Furphy hasn't played a G League game yet and on Wednesday, he found himself as the Pacers' only reliable outside shooting option and also their best bet for guarding point guards.

In the first half, Furphy hit one of the Pacers' four 3-pointers and he also grabbed six rebounds, so Carlisle started him in the second half instead of Quenton Jackson. Furphy guarded Dennis Schroeder and was part of the reason he shot 2 of 11. On offense, he hit three more 3-pointers in the third quarter and was the Pacers' leading scorer at the time before finishing with 14 points on 4 of 8 shooting from 3-point range. He finished with seven rebounds and also blocked a shot, playing a season-high 25 minutes.

"His young looks belie his toughness," Carlisle said. "He's solid. He's smart. He knows how to play the game. He's a ball-mover. He's an energy-giver. He did a lot of good things in this game and we needed it. We were looking for a spark wherever we could get it."

headline: Doctor testifies man's death in Indianapolis police custody was caused by THC
fullText:
The trial of two Indianapolis officers charged in the death of Herman Whitfield III continues Thursday.

Whitfield, a 39-year-old gifted pianist, died after police responded to a 911 call from his parents — Gladys Whitfield and Herman Whitfield Jr. — for a mental health emergency about 3:20 a.m. April 25, 2022. Five officers and one recruit trainee responded. Whitfield was shocked, handcuffed and restrained chest-down before falling unresponsive and losing a pulse. He was pronounced dead at a hospital.

The Marion County Coroner's Office ruled Whitfield's death a homicide caused, in part, by being shocked and restrained by law enforcement. The autopsy noted obesity and hypertensive cardiovascular disease as contributing conditions. Toxicology tests showed cannabinoids, including Delta-9 and THC, in Whitfield’s system. There were no signs of alcohol or other medication. 

Whitfield's death sparked demands for police accountability and clinician-led mental health emergency response from Indianapolis' Black faith community. It also renewed calls to defund the police from Indy10 Black Lives Matter.

Adam Ahmad and Steven Sanchez, who have attended trial each day in police uniform, were indicted by a grand jury on charges including reckless homicide, involuntary manslaughter, battery, battery resulting in moderate bodily injury and battery resulting in severe bodily injury. Both remain on paid administrative duty with the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department.

Testimony came to an end around 4 p.m. as both sides said they were done calling witnesses.

Closing arguments will begin Friday morning.

State's rebuttal witness refutes defense experts

On Wednesday, the defense asked expert witness Mark Kroll if he agreed with the opinions of cardiologist Dr. Alon Steinberg. He said he did not.

The reason for that line of questioning wasn’t clear until Thursday, when the state called Steinberg as a rebuttal witness.

The prone position is dangerous, Steinberg said, especially for people with heavier bodies. The position makes it harder to ventilate – not just to breathe in oxygen, but also to expel toxic carbon dioxide. This can be catastrophic for people who’ve recently been exerting themselves, Steinberg explained, because their bodies need more oxygen.

Whitfield’s sweating and heavy breathing suggested that he was in acidosis when police arrived, Steinberg said. But when he was put into the prone position, Whitfield’s acid level became so high that “his heart could no longer contract, and his electricity got wiped out, and he went into asystole.”

Steinberg said he thinks Whitfield went into cardiac arrest between five and seven seconds before the handcuffs were locked.

Whitfield had a “huge opportunity” to survive the cardiac arrest, Steinberg said. He was young and he was in the presence of people who knew CPR. But because he was kept prone, nobody knew he’d stopped breathing.

Steinberg said he disagrees with the defense witness testimony that Whitfield died from THC arrythmia.

“Besides it being extremely rare,” Steinberg said, “there seems to be a logical reason for him to die.”

He pointed out that Whitfield was under the influence of THC for the entire time officers were in the home, and only died once he was in prone restraint.

Among all of the fatal cases of THC-induced arrythmia in the case reports the defense witness referenced, people had died because their nervous systems were too relaxed, Steinberg explained. That’s the opposite of what Whitfield was experiencing when he was restrained.

In a fiery cross-examination, defense attorney John Kautzman asked Steinberg if arrestees throughout the country should be “dropping like flies” from prone restraint.

“Most people who are placed in a prone restraint position survive. It’s very rare,” Steinberg acknowledged. He said Whitfield’s death occurred because of a confluence of factors, including his prior agitation, weight and enlarged heart.

If the cardiac arrest had been triggered by Whitfield’s thickened heart, Steinberg said, his heart would have gone into a shockable rhythm – not asystole.

Kautzman also confronted Steinberg’s lack of peer-reviewed research, pointing out that the doctor's testimony was based on two of his own articles.

Day 3 trial testimony: Officer on trial in death of Herman Whitfield testifies he didn't know victim stopped breathing

Forensic physician says Herman Whitfield III died from THC

Dr. William Smock has studied in-custody deaths as a Louisville-based forensic physician. He served as one of the prosecution’s witnesses in the trial of Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer convicted of killing George Floyd.

Whitfield’s death was “absolutely not” from positional asphyxia, Smock testified. The body-worn camera footage showed Whitfield suddenly stopped struggling and talking, consistent with a sudden cardiac arrest and not asphyxia. Smock said his review of the bodycam footage led him to conclude that Whitfield died 20 seconds before the handcuffs were locked.

Smock told the jury that Whitfield died from THC-induced arrythmia when a high level of cannabinoids interacted with his enlarged heart and physical exertion.

Nothing the officers did caused Whitfield’s death, and they were doing what they were trained to do, according to Smock’s testimony.

On Wednesday, medical examiner Dr. Zachary O’Neill testified that THC wasn’t implicated in Whitfield’s death, explaining that medical literature on THC-related deaths is sparse. Smock said the opposite.

There’s been “study after study after study” linking THC with cardiac complications, he said. On the stand, Smock referenced several case reports, but no studies.

Whitfield had at least one bad reaction to THC before his death, medical records show. On May 1, 2020, he was taken to a Florida hospital by police for “bizarre, abnormal behavior.”

He was diagnosed with “psychosis followed by THC use.” Whitfield returned to normal once he sobered up. When Whitfield’s father picked his son up from the hospital, he should have been told about that diagnosis, Smock said.

Among the case studies of 36 patients with THC-induced cardiac arrythmia, six had died. None were in prone restraint, and several had alcohol or other drugs in their system.

Daniel Cicchini, who is lead prosecutor on the case, pointed out that according to a report from Whitfield’s 2020 interaction with police, he was also agitated after taking THC. He wasn’t put into prone restraint, and he survived that encounter, Smock agreed.

Whitfield was going to die from THC on April 25, 2022 even if he hadn’t interacted with law enforcement, Smock said.

“He died because he elected to take marijuana knowing that he had adverse reactions,” Smock said. “He caused his own death.”       

The defense rested its case after Smock's testimony.

Smock was later recalled to the stand to rebut cardiologist Dr. Alon Steinberg testimony. Smock said that in his experience as an emergency physician, he has never seen a patient recover from asystole.

That throws a wrench into Steinberg’s contention that Whitfield could have been saved if he’d been taken out of the prone position immediately after handcuffing.

Indianapolis officer Adam Ahmad explains his thought process

Ahmad testified that before Whitfield was handcuffed, he alternated between manic and unresponsive states with “no rhyme or reason.” Ahmad thought Whitfield was catatonic, not unconscious, when he was in the prone position.The jury saw a compilation of five officers’ synchronized body-worn camera footage, though only the audio from Ahmad’s perspective was played.

Ahmad said that when he told Sanchez to “stay on his head,” he was asking the other officer to pay attention to Whitfield’s head – not to physically touch or press it. That’s consistent with Sanchez’s testimony from Wednesday.

Also in line with Sanchez’s account, Ahmad said that Whitfield wasn’t fully prone because his head was turned to the side and one of his shoulders was elevated. Ahmad said he “constantly checked” Whitfield’s face to make sure that it stayed turned to the side.

Defense attorney John Kautzman asked Ahmad if he believed it was safe, feasible and appropriate to roll Whitfield onto his side, called the recovery position. Ahmad said he did not believe it was because Whitfield could become manic again. There was “no reason to put ourselves back at square one,” he said. The floor was covered in broken glass, he added.All of the actions he took on April 25, 2022 were in accordance with his training and objectively reasonably, Ahmad testified.  On cross-examination, deputy prosecuting attorney Janna Skelton asked Ahmad if Whitfield was still a threat after he was handcuffed. After some tense back-and-forth, Ahmad acknowledged Whitfield wasn’t a threat.

Indianapolis police department regulations state that officers must remove someone from the prone position as soon as it is “safe, appropriate and feasible.” The jury asked which of those conditions – safe, appropriate, or feasible – stopped officers from rolling Whitfield over.

Skelton followed up after Ahmad didn’t point to a specific reason Whitfield was kept prone.

“Was it not safe to roll him?” she asked.

“No,” Ahmad said.

“Was it not appropriate to roll him?”

“No.”

“Was it not feasible to roll him?”

“No.”

Ahmad was then dismissed from the stand.

headline: Meet IndyStar politics reporter Brittany Carloni
fullText:
It takes a staff of dedicated journalists to bring you the news from around Central Indiana. In this feature, the Indianapolis Star introduces readers to our newsroom staff — or, rather, we let them introduce themselves. Up this week is Brittany Carloni.

What's your job title?

State and federal politics reporter

When did you join IndyStar?

May 2021

What's your favorite part of your job?

I love being able to take a reader inside an important event or moment they might not easily have access to every day. For example, this summer I covered Indiana's delegation at the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee.

Why journalism?

When I graduated from high school and told friends and family I wanted to study journalism, I got a lot of feedback that my decision might be a poor choice because the news industry was dying. But I had a mentor in college who told me journalism is challenging but worth it and that he believed I could be successful. Once I pushed away the doubts, I found he was absolutely right.

What's your favorite Indy area restaurant or hidden gem?

My new favorite spot is Borage over in Speedway.

What do you do to unwind from a job that can be stressful?

I try to get outside and go on walks with my dog, Atticus. We live in an area with a lot of fellow dog owners, and there is no better stress reliever than dogs.

What are you reading or streaming?

I just finished "A Fever in the Heartland" by Timothy Egan, which has been on my TBR book list for a long time.

What song do you shamelessly jam out to in the car?  

Anything CCR (Creedence Clearwater Revival). My dad has a playlist with a bunch of “oldies” songs we would sing in the car when I was a kid and CCR’s “Down on the Corner” and “Have You Ever Seen The Rain” are two of my favorites to jam to when I’m on a road trip.

What’s the best piece of advice you ever received? 

Breathe. My mom gave me a decorative sign reminding me to breathe whenever I am stressed.

Do you prefer dogs or cats?

I love both. Sometimes it seems like my dog Atticus is part dog and cat.

What’s something people would be surprised to learn about you?  

I played the cello and took 10 years of private piano lessons. I credit my musical talents to my mom, who taught music in a Wisconsin school district for 40 years and encouraged me and my siblings to learn an instrument.

How did you earn your first dollar?

Unofficially, babysitting. Officially, I scanned tickets at the entrance gates for people who attended Summerfest, an annual music festival in Milwaukee.

headline: Braun should target income taxes, not property taxes | Letters
fullText:
Our governor-to-be, Mike Braun, is looking to lower Indiana residents' tax burden. While I applaud his efforts, I encourage him to look at reducing or eliminating the state income tax as opposed to limiting local taxing authorities' property taxes.

Hicks: Indiana's regressive tax system burdens the poorest Hoosiers

Property taxes are one of the few sources of local income that is controlled by the locality. The state budgeting formula for providing funds is inherently unfair. In some cases, cities are adversely affected; in some cases rural communities are under-funded.

One of Braun's stated goals is to increase the talented workforce in Indiana and to emulate states like Texas and Florida. One of the big drivers to those other states is the absence of a state income tax. With Indiana continuing to run budget surpluses, it is financially easier for the state to take the hit on tax revenue than it is for already struggling local communities.

Mike Morley lives in Carmel.

headline: 6 ways Governor-elect Mike Braun plans to change Indiana, from taxes to immigration
fullText:
Gov.-elect Mike Braun has unveiled his top priorities for Indiana in 2025, setting the tone for his first term.

Some require cooperation from the state legislature, including reforming property taxes and implementing universal school choice in Indiana. But others are entirely within his purview: Reorganizing the executive branch of state government, for example, and being a willing partner in the federal government's anticipated illegal immigration crackdown.

Here are Braun's top six issues for 2025:

Reduce property taxes

Braun made this a central part of his campaign platform, and it's remaining at the top of his list as governor-elect.

His vision is to provide significant property tax relief for homeowners in light of historic COVID-era increases in assessed values, which really started to skyrocket in 2022. A task force of state lawmakers that studied tax reform came out with vague recommendations last month that had a far greater emphasis on business property taxes over homestead taxes, but the Braun administration is trying to keep homesteads in the discussion.

More: How did property taxes become a top issue in the Indiana governor's race?

Specifically, he wants to:

  • Reset homeowner property tax bills to pre-COVID levels.
  • Cap annual property tax increases at 2-3% for homeowners and farmers.
  • Eliminate state tax on retirement income, including pensions, 401(k)s and IRA distributions.
  • Create tax-advantaged Farm Savings Accounts to help stabilize farm income.
  • Institute sales tax holidays for back-to-school supplies, outdoor recreation equipment and youth sports gear.
  • Update the farmland base rate formula to provide targeted relief for agricultural communities.

Reorganize and slim down state government

Braun has already started to reorganize the executive branch so that the governor's cabinet has eight clearly defined secretaries who oversee a set number of related agencies. He's even started to name some of these secretaries.

The goal is to improve efficiency and lines of communication. Currently, there are dozens of state agencies with their own directors and not a clear path of reporting above them or coordination among them. Braun hopes a reorganization will translate to improving people-facing government services.

A number of other efficiency-oriented priorities include:

  • Review every state agency and eliminate outdated regulations.
  • Digitize certain state government services, such as:
    • Processing documents with the BMV that currently require an in-person wait.
    • Automatically notifying veterans when they are eligible for benefits.
    • Providing an online "one-stop shop" for farmers to access state services, similar to the existing one-stop shop for businesses.
  • Fix the Medicaid budget gap.

Adopt universal school choice and workforce initiatives

Most Hoosier families already qualify for Indiana's school voucher program. Braun, like the Republican-controlled legislature, wants to remove all remaining income barriers to this program.

Here are his other education and workforce-related proposals:

  • Increase teacher base pay and establish performance-based compensation.
  • Create a new Office of School Safety to help schools enhance their security measures.
  • Create a "Workforce Investment" tax credit.
  • Restructure the Indiana Economic Development Corporation and enhance regional efforts on job creation.
  • Improve reading literacy and math outcomes in schools.

Drive down the cost of health care

This is one of Braun's tentpole issues. He often relates his self-insuring his company, Meyer Distributing, saving his employees from premium increases over the last 16 years and, as he puts it, solving the health care cost crisis in a microcosm.

More: Mike Braun is leading the race for governor. But is his record a liability or benefit?

Here are his proposals for reforming Indiana's health care market:

  • Drive down costs by requiring greater price transparency, regulating pharmacy benefit managers and reforming the prior authorization system.
  • Expand access in rural areas, including to obstetrics, by offering new incentives for rural health care facilities and improving telehealth coverage.
  • Protect coverage for pre-existing conditions.
  • Create a "Primary Care Access Revolving Fund" to support new medical facilities.
  • Reform mental health treatment to reduce the burden on the criminal justice system.

Enhance public safety and stem illegal immigration

Braun is taking a decidedly tough-on-crime, pro-law enforcement stance that stands to support the immigration-focused agenda of the incoming Trump administration.

Specifically, he proposes:

  • Addressing illegal immigration by enforcing sanctuary city bans, cooperating with federal authorities on their enforcement efforts and preparing the Indiana National Guard to deploy to the border.
  • Supporting law enforcement with competitive salaries, training opportunities, protecting qualified immunity and establishing minimum bail requirements for violent crimes.
  • Combating drug trafficking by stiffening penalties for distributing fentanyl and methamphetamine, enhancing state police's power to intercept drugs, and supporting prevention and recovery programs.

Diversify energy policy to lower utility bills

A plethora of new, tech-heavy development in Indiana is placing ever greater demand on the state's energy grid. Meanwhile, Hoosiers' electricity bills have increased more than national averages.

Braun talks often about an "all of the above" energy policy, meaning the state should pursue a variety of energy sources, including fossil fuels, renewables and nuclear.

He proposes:

  • Establishing a commission to develop energy and water plans for the state.
  • Cutting red tape for utilities, with the aim of passing savings to consumers.
  • Making Indiana a leading state in developing nuclear energy over the next decade.

Contact IndyStar state government and politics reporter Kayla Dwyer at kdwyer@indystar.com or follow her on Twitter @kayla_dwyer17.

headline: President Biden is culpable for Hunter's problems | Opinion
fullText:
President Biden is glossing over an uncomfortable truth: His thirst for the presidency caused terrible consequences for his son.

Biden is blaming President-elect Trump for Hunter Biden's problems — and not without reason. Republicans' embarrassing, bad-faith mission to connect Hunter's troubled life to nonexistent crimes by the president made Biden's son collateral damage. Biden cited Republicans' strategy while defending his choice to pardon Hunter in a statement.

"It is clear that Hunter was treated differently," Biden said. "The charges in his cases came about only after several of my political opponents in Congress instigated them to attack me and oppose my election."

Briggs: The media didn't normalize Trump. Reality did.

But the charges also came about only after Biden sought the presidency for the third time in 2020 while knowing full well his ambition would subject his son to a microscope. Hunter is not an innocent victim here. He was found guilty on a litany of charges, including failing to pay taxes between 2016 and 2019 and lying to purchase a gun while addicted to drugs.

If we're going to talk about how Republicans targeted Hunter, then we also must acknowledge Hunter cashed in on the Biden name to reap millions of dollars, which he blew on drugs and other unsavory activities.

President Biden knew his son was mired in cycles of vice. He also knew his political pursuits could exacerbate his son's struggles. He chose to run for president anyway.

Is it unfair that Biden had to weigh the presidency against his fragile son? Sure. But, for most normal people, it wouldn't have been a difficult choice. Most people would protect their children.

It takes a certain level of narcissism to pursue political power. Campaigning even for local office puts strain on families. The greater your ambition, the brighter the spotlight you shine on everyone around you. When you rise to the level of running for president, the media becomes interested in your cousin and your former teachers.

Biden knows how it works. His hero syndrome led him to believe that he was so uniquely well suited to lead America that winning the presidency was worth any cost to his family. Once the toll on Hunter added up, though, Biden betrayed his rhetoric over democratic norms and disgraced his office by freeing his son of consequences for his actions.

We can play whataboutism with Trump, another abuser of the office. Actually, let's. Trump's ascent to the presidency in 2016 caused a long list of Trump associates to face greater scrutiny and, ultimately, legal consequences for actions that otherwise might have flown under the radar if Trump had not been president. No one is shedding tears for them. Nor should they.

Trump, of course, pardoned some of his cronies and is likely to pardon more of them once he takes office.

Biden promised to be better than Trump and said he would not pardon Hunter. Then he blamed Republicans for making him break his promise. The more likely explanation is one that goes unspoken in the president's statement. 

Biden knows Hunter probably would not have faced prison time if he had not become president. It's not Biden's sense of justice that led to the pardon. It's his sense of guilt.

headline: Pianist Michael Davidman finds 'inner connection' to whatever he plays in Indy contest
fullText:
As a finalist for the 2021 American Piano Awards, Michael Davidman brought his charisma and penchant for finding personal connections to repertoire to Indianapolis stages. Almost four years later, he's back — this time with what he calls a deeper awareness of the music he performs.

"I've just become more aware of going farther into what I'm able to do and what kind of sounds I can create and the way I play certain pieces and different repertoire for sure," said Davidman, 27.

Audiences will hear the fruits of the pianist's musical growth when he performs with the Indianapolis Chamber Orchestra at 3:30 p.m. Sunday at the Indiana History Center, 450 W. Ohio St. Tickets, which are $40 for adults and $20 for students and seniors, can be purchased at pianoawards.org.

Davidman is the third of five finalists to visit Indianapolis for the first leg of the 2025 American Piano Awards classical competition, which will culminate in the final rounds between March 31 and April 5. Over the past four years, he's added quite a few pieces and accomplishments to his resume.

The pianist has a newly minted artist diploma from the International Center for Music at Park University near Kansas City and is now studying at the Escuela Superior de Música Reina Sofía in Madrid. He previously earned a bachelor's degree from the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia and a master's from the Juilliard School in New York City.

Davidman won third prize at the 2022 Long-Thibaud International Piano Competition, first prize in the 2018 New York International Piano Competition chamber ensemble, and was co-winner of the 2019 Juilliard Gina Bachauer Competition. Davidman has played solo and with ensembles in the U.S. and abroad. 

No matter where he performs, the pianist said he finds his own way into pieces like J.S. Bach's Toccata in D Major; César Franck's Prelude, Chorale and Fugue; and Vladimir Horowitz's arrangement of Camille Saint-Saëns’ "Danse Macabre" — all of which appear on Sunday's program.

"You still always have to maintain that inner connection no matter what," said Davidman, who splits his time between Madrid and New York, where he grew up.

'My instincts are mine': Pianist Sasha Kasman Laude brings her own style to Indy contest

The pianist also finds inspiration for his new musical ideas in old opera and other rare recordings, which he shares on his PucciniMD YouTube channel. He was especially moved by a 1947 "Madame Butterfly" performance in Geneva starring Mafalda Favero, which he sought out after reading a book of interviews with 20th-century prima donnas.

Favero's interpretation offered a perspective of the now-famous opera that expanded Davidman's understanding of the work.

"I'm half Italian, so going back to people that my grandma and great-grandma were listening to and that culture ... it brings this kind of vitality to it and this inspiration of the past and my own musical heritage in a way," he said.

headline: 'Coach let us have it': Teri Moren challenges Indiana women in comeback win vs USI
fullText:
BLOOMINGTON -- There were a lot of adjectives Shay Ciezki and Lilly Meister could use to describe IU women's basketball coach Teri Moren's talk at halftime.

"Loud," Ciezki simply said. "Loudly."

"Loud," Meister affirmed. "Direct, stern."

But the Hoosiers' first-half play, Meister said, required that type of halftime chat. Indiana went into the locker room trailing by 13 points to Ohio Valley Conference member University of Southern Indiana.

"Coach Moren came in at halftime and let us have it, and we deserved it, rightfully so," Meister said. "We were daring them to shoot, giving them wide open shots, and a team like Southern Indiana, whose an in-state opponent, they're gonna knock those down, and they did. So coach let us have it, and we took it to heart."

To their credit, Indiana came out of the locker room looking like a different team. In the second half, the Hoosiers outscored the Screaming Eagles by 17 points, scraping through the night with a 67-63 win. Indiana is now 6-3 heading into Big Ten play.

Indiana women's basketball score: Indiana women's basketball erases double-digit deficit to edge Southern Indiana

Still, there are some things they need to address. First off: that first half. There were multiple aspects that went wrong, including eight turnovers, shooting 31% from the field and a general lack of effort.

"I was obviously disappointed in our effort," Moren said of the first half. "I didn't think we were focused, I didn't think we were locked in to executing the game plan at the level we needed to, I didn't think we fought, I didn't think we were playing with much pride, all things that they know, right, that they have to do to in order to win basketball."

One of Moren's most frustrating moments came near the end of the second quarter, as the Hoosiers were desperately trying to cut into what became a 13-point deficit. As the Hoosiers raced down the court, Penn State transfer Shay Ciezki called for a screen, twice, but it never came.

With the shot clock running down, Chloe Moore-McNeil instead shot a 3-pointer, which airballed, and Moren threw her arm up in frustration while turning to walk back to the bench.

"It's poor decisions on our part, and I'll take the responsibility for that," Moren said. "I have to make sure that in those situations, in those scenarios, when the shot clock is running down, what a good shot looks like for us. And Chloe knows better, you know, we either want to attack at the rim ... whether that's a layup in or a foul, and not settle for a step-back 'we hope it goes in' kind of shot like that."

Some of it comes down to experience, too, Moren said. With Ciezki transferring in from Penn State this offseason, it's the first season she and Moore-McNeil are running the backcourt together, and they're still learning how to play off each other. On top of that, the two switch off who is running point, taking the ball up the court and calling plays, which can sometimes add to the complexity.

In that instance, it's a learning moment. Something that can hopefully help them as they get into Big Ten play this week.

"It's a great moment that we'll have in film to be able to go back and talk about, 'Look, in these scenarios, it happens often, where the shot clock is running down, what can we jump into that will at least give us a high percentage shot?'" Moren said. "Or a shot that we can live with, instead of looking like we had no plan."

The only problem is that those learning opportunities before Big Ten play are dwindling by the day.

Indiana opens Big Ten play on the road against Penn State on Saturday. Then, the Hoosiers have two more nonconference games before conference play resumes for the rest of the season. In less than a month, No. 1 UCLA is coming to Assembly Hall. Weeks after that, No. 6 USC will be making the trip, as well.

IU is running out of time to improve — especially in their post play.

The Hoosiers had a dominant post in Mackenzie Holmes for five years, taking the conference by storm with the defensive juggernaut. Now, as Holmes exhausted her eligibility and was picked by the Seattle Storm in the 2024 draft, IU is searching for a new identity.

The Hoosiers have Lilly Meister, who backed up Holmes for two years, and Tennessee transfer Karoline Striplin sharing time at the post, but Moren isn't sure if it'll be enough for the dominant posts in the Big Ten.

"I was disappointed in our post play," Moren said of the game against USI. "I thought Lilly and Strip were just okay offensively, defensively. I think about some of the post player that we're going to see in the Big Ten, right ... we're going to play against some of the best post player in the country, and we've got to be able to respond much better, and we got to help them as a staff."

headline: Before 'Slaughterhouse-Five,' Kurt Vonnegut made a board game. Now you can play it
fullText:
Before Indiana author Kurt Vonnegut was well-known, he was looking for a project to support his growing family. He pitched a board game in the 1950s.

It was rejected.

Avid Vonnegut fans have heard of GHQ, short for General Headquarters, but until recently, the game didn't see the light of day. Owing to a collaboration between the Indiana University Lilly Library, the Vonnegut family and one particularly passionate fan and board game enthusiast, the public can now purchase the long-lost tabletop war game.

At the time, Vonnegut believed GHQ had the potential to become “the third popular checkerboard game." The original GHQ rules, sketches and related correspondence were in a sealed collection at IU. With permission from the Vonnegut family, board game enthusiast Geoff Englestein worked with archivists to turn the ideas into a real game.

“He was still in the process of coming to grips with his attitude towards war, his experience with the war, his time in Dresden,” Engelstein told The Herald-Times. “That this was an unabashed war game was really intriguing.”

headline: Hoosier Survey shows majority support for legal marijuana, first-trimester abortion
fullText:
Hoosiers in 2024 largely support legalized marijuana, according to the results of this year’s Hoosier Survey from Ball State’s Bowen Center for Public Affairs.  

The nonpartisan Hoosier Survey is conducted annually and asks Indiana residents about key social and political issues, including abortion rights, immigration and gun policies. The survey also asked about what issues Hoosiers find most important for Governor-elect Mike Braun to tackle starting next year.  

The Bowen Center for Public Affairs surveyed 615 adults between Nov. 6 and 7. Here is what the survey found:  

Do Indiana residents support legalized marijuana?  

Support for marijuana legalization remains high among Hoosiers, despite limited action at the Indiana Statehouse.  

Kevin Smith, the interim director of the Bowen Center for Public Affairs said the support among Hoosiers “reflects national trends” on marijuana legalization.  

Weed about it: Will marijuana laws change this year in Indiana? These bills have been introduced.

According to the 2024 Hoosier Survey:  

  • 62% of Hoosiers believe marijuana should be legal for recreational and medicinal use 
  • 25% believe marijuana should be legal only for medicinal use 
  • 13% believe marijuana should not be legal 

How Hoosiers view abortion 

The 2024 Hoosier Survey found that more than 80% of respondents believe abortion should be legal when there are threats to the mother’s life, if rape or incest caused the pregnancy or if there is a lethal fetal anomaly. That support reflects Indiana’s near-total abortion ban that was signed into law in 2022 and went into effect last year.  

The Hoosier Survey also found that support for legal access to abortion splits by trimester with about 66% supporting the procedure during the first trimester. The majority of respondents opposed abortion in later stages of pregnancy, according to the survey results.  

What Hoosiers think about immigration 

About 70% of survey respondents said that “undocumented immigration” is a serious issue for Indiana right now.  

Survey respondents were also asked their thoughts on legal immigration in the U.S.:  

  • 19% said legal immigration should be stopped.
  • 31% said legal immigration should be decreased.
  • 42% said legal immigration should be “kept at present level.” 
  • 8% said legal immigration should be increased.

Do Hoosiers support permitless carry? 

The Hoosier Survey asked respondents' views on several gun policies including permitless carry, banning assault weapons and allowing teachers to carry guns in schools.  

  • 58% said they opposed allowing people to carry a gun without a permit, while about 31% support it.  
  • Nearly 60% support banning assault-style weapons with about 23% opposing bans. 
  • 45% support allowing teachers and other administrators to carry guns in schools with about 36% in opposition.  

What issues Mike Braun should address first 

Survey respondents ranked school safety, public safety and health care as the top three most important priorities for the next governor.

headline: 'I look better, too': Josef Newgarden reflects on back-to-back Indy 500 wins
fullText:
INDIANAPOLIS -- 366 days as a defending Indianapolis 500 winner – the chaotic, sometimes demanding schedule, the raucous celebrations, the hunger to win again and unique stresses that April and May 2024 delivered – aged Josef Newgarden in ways the Team Penske driver perhaps only realized Wednesday evening, nearly 200 days later.

Those wrinkles, along with the evidence of a more low-key celebratory romp through downtown Indianapolis’ night life, will now live in sterling silver on the Borg-Warner Trophy.

Because like only five of the 800 drivers to have raced in the 500 in its 113-year history, Newgarden went back-to-back in the Greatest Spectacle in Racing this May. The 110-pound Borg-Warner Trophy now carries 111 different faces and stands more than five feet tall. But like only Wilbur Shaw (1939, 1940), Mauri Rose (1947, 1948), Bill Vukovich (1953, 1954), Al Unser Sr. (1970, 1971) and Helio Castroneves (2001, 2002), Newgarden’s successes are now displayed side-by-side on the Borg, offering an opportunity for comparisons between the emotions of those two historic days, the lessons learned and the gargantuan challenge that still lies ahead.

“Oh wow, there are more wrinkles!” Newgarden exclaimed as the black sheet was removed from the base of the trophy near the end of Wednesday evening’s intimate ceremony at COHatch Polk Stables near downtown Indianapolis. “But I like the hair a little better. You don’t always get the same thing. You kinda just guess, and man, it does look better in 2024.

“I love that the details are different. You can tell I was a little different on the day. I’d had a different night. When you win it the first time, things go a little differently.”

Doyel: Newgarden edges O'Ward in classy duel for second straight Indy 500 win

Even to the naked eye and the casual observer, those faint details are clear in an up-close glance at the work of renowned sculptor Will Behrends, who’s crafted each face on the Trophy since 1990. On Newgarden’s Ken Doll-like figure, the faint wrinkles around his eyes pop as the light catches the sterling silver mold, just as it reveals notably taller, coiffed hair.

To the latter, Newgarden notes this May he “had a better morning, which means I had a better night.”

“I was a little more ‘professional’ the second time around, shall we say,” he continues. “The first time around, it’s a lot. You go with the flow, and then you realize that you have to wake up at 7 a.m. the next morning, and I said I wouldn’t do that again, so I was more prepared for the aftermath the second time around, and I think that reflects that.

“I definitely look slightly older, but I think I look better, too.”

It’s no doubt Newgarden appears more relaxed, more comfortable in his own skin this second time around. A year ago, the IndyCar veteran was eliminating distractions and extraneous social and business ventures – including his still young media company and his popular YouTube series with teammate Scott McLaughlin – in an effort to direct his attention, talent, time and energy to the things that mattered most to him. As he got a glimpse of his face on the Borg-Warner Trophy for the first time last year, he masked an inner turmoil from the frustrations of an otherwise disappointing 2023 IndyCar campaign.

For a dozen years, Newgarden had chased this dream. Then, just as he’d detached himself from winning the 500, the accomplishment came in a flash. For a driver famous for never being satisfied, the path forward as the newest member of the 500 winners’ fraternity was muddied.

Insider: How Newgarden simplifying his life turned the Bus Bros into just teammates

Twelve months later, with another winner’s ring in his trophy case and another Baby Borg on its way, there’s a jovialness to the soon-to-be 34-year-old. Wednesday night, he cracked jokes – about his transition to being a veteran driver and being unafraid to admit his confidence in what would be an historic three-peat in the 500 next May.

“I think the (victory tour) the second time around is certainly more enjoyable than the first, if you can believe it,” Newgarden told IndyStar on Wednesday. “You know how to go through it and savor it a little more than just drinking through a firehose.

“The second win is different in a lot of ways. The first one, you’ve never won it, and I was in a palace where I was kinda okay with the fact that I may never win it. And then you break through, and there’s that emotion. This time around, it’s more contentment.”

To kick off Wednesday’s ceremony, the two-time series champ joked with IMS president Doug Boles about off-handed conversations they’ve had about the unique, historic way the Racing Capital of the World might celebrate the first driver to win the 500 in three straight years. 

From May: Newgarden doesn't want to be IndyCar's superhero or black hat. He's both.

“It’s kinda crazy to think that it hasn’t been done before. It’s a unique position for us, with this race being over 100 years old,” Newgarden said. “The (odds are) certainly against us but ... I don’t think we’re going to be shy about how we have a great opportunity to win it. We’ll do the same things we always do, and it would be really significant if we can get it done.”

Newgarden has begun petitioning BorgWarner executives to make a special prize if he were to do the unthinkable. Since 1995, the namesake of racing’s most famous trophy has offered a rolling jackpot to the defending 500 winner, if they were to repeat. Before this year, only Castroneves had claimed the prize, which started at $20,000 in its first year and added an additional $20,000 each year until the Brazilian took home $160,000 in 2002.

A record-setting payday: Josef Newgarden's earns $4.288 million Indy 500 grand prize

The prize pool then reset in 2003, just as it has for Newgarden for next year, meaning that after taking home a nearly half-million-dollar bonus this year ($440,000) to create a record-setting grand-prize of $4.288 million, a theoretical third-straight win in 2025 to capture perhaps American open-wheel racing’s most famous untouched feat would deliver a relatively meager $20,000 bonus.

“I don’t want to sound unappreciative of the $20,000, but can we make a three-peat challenge?” Newgarden joked on-stage Wednesday evening with BorgWarner’s global director of marketing and PR, Michelle Collins. “(BorgWarner CEO Frederic Lissalde) loves a good deal. We can insure it! Insurance companies love this kind of stuff.”

Later, Newgarden was a tad more introspective.

“I joke about it, having that extra prize money for winning three years in a row, but winning three years in a row in itself, no amount of prize money can buy the significance of that,” Newgarden told IndyStar. “It will just be significant for all of us if we can get it done.”

headline: Katie Jenner will continue to head the state's education department under Braun
fullText:
Indiana’s Secretary of Education Katie Jenner will continue to lead the state’s education department when governor-elect Mike Braun takes office in January.

Braun’s transition team announced Thursday that he plans to keep Jenner in the position that oversees the state’s K-12 education system.

Jenner was appointed to her position in 2021 and is the state’s first secretary of education, which the state legislature changed to being an appointed position rather than elected position in 2017.

Since Gov. Eric Holcomb appointed Jenner, she has been tasked with leading the state out of the severe drop in proficiency scores seen in the wake of the pandemic, continued struggles with chronic absenteeism in schools, the continuous decline of early literacy scores and the recent initiative of “reinventing” the high school experience.

More on the reinventing high school: As final feedback period ends on Indiana's high school diploma redesign, concerns remain

"Dr. Jenner's proven track record of elevating Indiana's education system makes her the ideal choice to continue leading our state's academic initiatives," said Braun in a statement. "Her focus on literacy, STEM education, and workforce readiness aligns perfectly with our vision for Indiana's future."

Braun has already said his priorities for education will include a heavy emphasis on school choice, and his desire to remove any remaining income barriers for families to access the state’s private school voucher program.

Jenner said she was grateful to Braun for the opportunity to continue to serve in her position.

“Over the past several years, we have made significant strides in expanding educational opportunities and ensuring our students are prepared for success in the classroom and beyond,” said Jenner in a statement. “Working together with Governor-elect Braun, our dedicated teachers, school leaders, the General Assembly and stakeholders across the state, we will build upon this progress while addressing the evolving needs of our education system.”

Jenner holds a doctorate in education from the University of Kentucky and an MBA from Indiana State University. She chairs the state board of education and previously served as the vice president of K-12 initiatives and statewide partnerships for Ivy Tech Community College.
