headline: IU football loses one coach to Big Ten coordinator job, but all other assistants get new deals
fullText:
BLOOMINGTON – Tino Sunseri, IU’s quarterbacks coach/co-offensive coordinator, is expected to leave Indiana for the open coordinator position at UCLA.

A source confirmed Sunseri’s expected departure for Westwood on Thursday afternoon, though he will stay through the Hoosiers' College Football Playoff run.

The remaining nine assistant coaches on Curt Cignetti’s staff, as well as football’s director of athletic performance, Derek Owings, have all signed new multiyear contracts with Indiana, IndyStar confirmed.

Cignetti not only one getting a raise. Assistant salary pool now among highest in FBS.

Insider: What IU's financial commitment to Curt Cignetti means

Sunseri’s impending move comes as little surprise. The Pitt alum was considered a rising star when he coached under Cignetti at James Madison, and Sunseri’s work this season alongside co-OC and play caller Mike Shanahan helped the Hoosiers build one of America’s most productive offenses.

Sunseri was crucial in the recruitment and development of Ohio transfer quarterback Kurtis Rourke, whose all-conference performances this season have played a key role in the Hoosiers’ rise into the College Football Playoff. Rourke led the country in passer rating in 2024, per CFBStats.com, and his 27 touchdowns and 9.9 yards per attempt were either first or tied for first in the Big Ten. His 70.4% completion rate would be a single-season program record if it holds up through the postseason.

Sunseri added co-coordinator to his title when he made the move from Harrisonburg to Bloomington last winter, making his move west now a natural step up. UCLA parted ways with coordinator Eric Bienemy earlier Thursday, after an inconsistent offense paved the road to a 5-7 record in head coach DeShaun Foster’s first season leading the Bruins.

Foster will be familiar with Sunseri thanks in part to his time with the Carolina Panthers. Foster was a running back in Carolina from 2002-07, overlapping with Sal Sunseri, Tino’s father and the Panthers’ defensive line coach from 2002-08.

It’s not yet clear who Cignetti might target to replace Sunseri, but Sunseri is expected to stay with Indiana’s staff through the balance of the Hoosiers’ run through the Playoff.

While Sunseri’s departure leaves a key role unfilled on Cignetti’s offensive staff, the retention of the rest of his assistants will be a significant boost for a coach who has often credited staff continuity as key to success.

Cignetti will keep both of his play callers, Shanahan and two-time Broyles Award semifinalist defensive coordinator Bryant Haines, in place. Cignetti will retain the offensive and defensive line staffs that helped author substantial turnarounds at the line of scrimmage for IU this winter. And Cignetti will hold onto Owings, a strength and conditioning coach in whom Cignetti places substantial faith and responsibility.

Details of the fresh terms for remaining staffers were not immediately available. But it stands to reason an assistant-coaching salary pool that was roughly doubled by commitments included in Cignetti’s own new contract, confirmed last month, helped the Hoosiers keep the bulk of a staff that oversaw the most successful season in program history in place.

No. 9 in the latest College Football Playoff selection committee top 25, Indiana will learn its official Playoff fate Sunday afternoon, when the final post-conference championship rankings are released. The Hoosiers appear locked into an at-large berth, and likely to go on the road for their first-round game later this month.

headline: Jim Banks supports Pete Hegseth for Defense. What does Indiana's other senator think?
fullText:
Jim Banks, Indiana's incoming U.S. senator, supports Pete Hegseth, he said Thursday after meeting with President-elect Donald Trump’s embattled choice to lead the Department of Defense.

“Pete Hegseth is a decorated veteran and a patriot who will always put America first,” Banks said in a statement. “Pete is focused on what I’m focused on, which is getting wokeness out of the military and making our Department of Defense lethal again.”  

Trump in November nominated Hegseth, a former Fox News anchor, to lead the Department of Defense, which oversees the country’s military. Hegseth is a veteran of the Army National Guard.  

Hegseth has faced controversies over his nomination, including an allegation of sexual assault.  

The role requires confirmation by the U.S. Senate, which will include Indiana Republicans Todd Young and Banks. A spokesperson for Young’s office said the senator and Hegseth have not met yet, but plan to “in the near future.” 

Subscribe to our Checks and Balances newsletter for more Indiana political news

Jim Banks’ views on Pete Hegseth

It comes as no surprise that Banks, a fervent supporter of Trump, is publicly endorsing Hegseth. Banks also said last month he would vote to confirm Florida Republican Matt Gaetz as attorney general prior to Gaetz withdrawing from consideration following allegations of sexual misconduct between Gaetz and a minor. 

Hegseth’s nomination, too, has been followed by controversies. USA TODAY reported that Hegseth was involved in a sexual assault allegation in 2017, but no charges were filed. News outlets have also reported allegations of misconduct and intoxication while Hegseth led a veterans nonprofit, which his lawyer has denied.

Banks, who is also a veteran, has been publicly supportive of Hegseth since Trump announced him as his Defense pick last month.  

In a statement Thursday, Banks said that Hegseth “won’t back down from the media, or from the bureaucracy and he won’t back down from China, Iran or Russia.”  

Both Banks and Hegseth posted photos of their meeting on X Thursday.  

“Thank you for your time and support Senator @Jim_Banks,” Hegseth wrote on X. “I look forward to putting lethality back at the center of DoD’s mission.”  

What is Todd Young’s view of Pete Hegseth? 

Young, who served in the Marines, has not issued any public statements about Hegseth although he has publicly supported some of Trump’s other cabinet picks, including Florida Sen. Marco Rubio for secretary of state and former Georgia Sen. Kelly Loeffler to lead the Small Business Administration.  

IndyStar asked Young’s office in November about the senator’s view of Hegseth and then-Attorney General nominee Gaetz.  

“Senator Young has voiced his support for the nominees he has worked with and knows well,” a spokesperson said then. “For the nominees he doesn’t know well, he looks forward to learning more about their backgrounds and vision for the office in the coming months.”

Noblesville lost that No. 1 vs. No. 2 battle, 49-47, and Fishers went on to win the Class 4A state championship. Noblesville’s only other loss came during the regular season to Westfield, through the Millers avenged that in a big way in the sectional semifinal with a 28-point victory. Other wins included Carmel, Crispus Attucks, Zionsville, Hamilton Southeastern, Mt. Vernon and Brownsburg.

So far this season: Noblesville is 2-0 with victories over Hamilton Heights (76-38) and Franklin (59-41).

Coach: Scott McClelland is 56-21 in his fourth season at Noblesville and 302-190 overall in his 22nd season with stops at Morristown (twice), Brebeuf Jesuit and Western Boone. He led Morristown to a Class A state championship in 2017-18. Noblesville won a sectional title in 2022-23.

Sectional 8: The six-team sectional at Carmel is arguably (maybe inarguably) the toughest in the state. The other teams are defending 4A champion Fishers, Carmel, Westfield, Hamilton Southeastern and Zionsville.

Key returnees: Justin Curry, 6-3, Jr. (10.1 ppg, 4.1 rebounds, 1.4 assists); Baron Walker, 6-3, Jr. (7.0 ppg, 2.1 rebounds, 2.0 assists); T.J. Davidson, 6-0, Sr. (5.0 ppg, 1.7 rebounds, 1.6 assists); Aiden Brewer, 6-4, Sr. (4.0 ppg, 3.0 rebounds); Ryan Vetor, 6-3, Sr. (2.0 ppg, 1.6 rebounds)

Key newcomers: Adam Fine, 6-0, Jr. (played in 21 games last season); Max Miller, 6-3, Sr. (played in 13 games last season); Luke Davis, 5-11, Sr. (played in 18 games last season); Max Flanagan, 6-3, Jr.

Key losses: Aaron Fine (17.9 ppg, 3.5 rebounds, 3.4 assists); Hunter Walston (12.4 ppg, 5.7 rebounds, 3.0 assists, 2.0 steals); Will Smits (3.3 ppg, 2.7 rebounds); Luke Etchison (2.2 ppg, 1.2 rebounds)

Outlook: Noblesville was certainly capable of winning a state championship last season but ran into a Fishers’ team that ended up winning it in the sectional final in a classic game. The Millers lose their top two scorers from that team in Fine and Walston but there is plenty of talent returning, including two players – Curry and Walker – who could be Junior All-Stars. There are not a lot of missing pieces here other than size. But Brewer, who will be a Division I tight end, plays bigger than his height and Curry and Walker are bigger guards. Beyond the projected starting five, there is some inexperience. But the Millers have taken care of business in the first two games of the season.

From McClelland:

On building on success of last season into this year: “First and foremost, I think our culture right now is really good with our basketball program. We’ve got some experience back. Obviously we’ve got to replace some pieces with the graduation of Aaron and Hunter especially but our role guys Will and Luke are going to be some areas we have to concentrate trying to fill their roles they did such a good job in. We’ve got some guys back in Baron Walker and Justin Curry who both started last year. T.J. Davidson started some as well. Aiden Brewer started. We feel good about the pieces we return. Right now, it’s just finding out who we are and cleaning up some of our mishaps and mistakes from two games and just continue to try build and improve as we work towards March.”

On filling the roles of Fine and Walston: “I don’t know if you totally replace them. I think you try to adjust the guys who are coming back in their roles and try to put them in positions to be successful. I think Baron and Justin, you start there first probably. Obviously, Baron shot over 50% from the 3-point line and Justin was a double figures scorer for us last year. A.B. has started for two years so he’ll be a three-year starter. T.J. played in some big minutes last year and I anticipate Ryan Vetor playing a big role – we think in some ways similar to Hunter. Adam Fine will play a bigger role and we’re just trying to figure out who seven, eight and nine will be and go from there.”

On how you prepare for Sectional 8: “Maybe see if the 76ers and Pacers want to play. It’s the best of the best. You aren’t outcoaching anyone. Everyone is that good and everybody has a best player that is equal to, in some way, the next-best player on the other team. Winning a sectional, regardless of class, is never easy. It’s a very difficult thing to do. And then you magnify ours by a thousand when you look at the teams, how hard they play, how organized they are and how good the coaches are, not just the head coaches but the staffs of Carmel, Westfield, Zionsville, Fishers and HSE. It makes it fun, but it makes it challenging as well. You just have great basketball players. I fully anticipate this being as difficult as any other year.”

Why the Millers could be higher: This team is tested, experienced and tough. Who knows how things would have worked out if Noblesville had knocked off Fishers in the sectional championship, but it's certainly not a stretch to believe the Millers could have won 4A. And players like Walker and Curry should be better players than a year ago.

Why the Millers could be lower: The graduation of Fine and Walston does leave a major void. This team might not be as deep as a year ago or will at least be unproven going into the season. The sectional is as tough as ever and the schedule will test the Millers.

Prediction: This team could have a similar record to last going into the sectional, maybe something in the neighborhood of 19-3. We will get a better sense of how both teams stand after the meet in Noblesville on Friday, but you have to give the slight advantage to Fishers at this point to win the sectional.

headline: Pacers get disabled player exceptions for Isaiah Jackson, James Wiseman; what's it mean?
fullText:
INDIANAPOLIS -- The Pacers have been granted disabled player exceptions worth $2.2 million and $1.2 million for injured centers Isaiah Jackson and James Wiseman respectively, league sources confirmed to the IndyStar on Thursday. The news was first reported by Bobby Marks of ESPN.

A disabled player exception does not open up a roster spot, so the Pacers are still at their full allotment of 15 full-time players and three players on two-way contracts after the recent addition of center Moses Brown. However the exception does allow a team to take on salary in transactions that doesn't count against its salary cap total. That could be useful later in the season, particularly at the trade deadline, with the Pacers now well over the NBA's salary cap and close to the luxury tax threshold.

For a disabled player exception to be granted, a team must submit an application before Jan. 15 and an NBA designated physician must determine that a player is "substantially more likely than not" to be unable to return to play before June 15 of that league year. Jackson and Wiseman both suffered Achilles tendon tears in the first month of the season and they have not formally been ruled out for the year, but their likelihood of returning to the floor this year isn't very high. A team has until March 10 to use the exception, which is well after the trade deadline of Feb. 6.

How does a disabled player exception work in the NBA?

The money granted in the exceptions represents either 50% of the salary of the injured player or the non-taxpayer mid-level exception -- which is $12.8 million this season -- whichever is lower. Jackson is making $4.4 million this season and Wiseman about $2.3 million. It's not much, but the Pacers are right at the NBA's luxury tax threshold with a total salary of about $170.8 million this season with about $5 million worth of room before the restrictive first tax apron so anything could help in trade season. Salaries are prorated, so a player on a veteran minimum contract would fit in each exception after the midway point of the season.

What are the limits on a disabled player exception?

There are limits to the additions the designated player exception can cover. A free agent signed using a designated player exception can only be signed for the rest of the season, not for a multi-year deal. A player acquired in a trade must be on an expiring contract for the designated player exception to be used.

The exception can't be spread across multiple players and it can't be combined, so each exception can be applied to one player.

Still, if the Pacers do decide to shake up the roster at deadline, the exceptions can be helpful tools for them to add without going in to the luxury tax.

headline: Cadillac F1 hires former Manor Marussia team executive Graeme Lowdon as team principal
fullText:
Graeme Lowdon, the ex-F1 team boss for the now-defunct Manor team, has been hired as Cadillac F1's team principal, the team announced Thursday. Lowdon has spent the past two years as a team advisor, helping current and former team CEO's Dan Towriss and Michael Andretti hire and mold the team that will work from Fishers, Ind.; Warren, Mich.; Charlotte, N.C.; and Silverstone, England.

More: Cadillac F1 approved as F1's expansion team, Andretti family takes backseat

At the time of the team's initial denial for entry by Formula One Management in January of this year, it had made roughly 120 hires. It now reportedly has just under 300 people working on the expansion effort -- a number well under half the size of F1's longest tenured teams.

"I’m truly honored to be appointed as the team principal of this exciting new team and I would like to thank everyone involved for placing their trust in me,” Lowdon said in a release. “I believe that Formula 1 is the greatest team sport in the world, and teams are all about people. This is a team with a real love for, and desire to go, racing, and we have the experience and expertise to do just that.

"Racing is at the very heart of everything that we do. This is what I want to see in a team, and I really want to be part of it. I don’t underestimate the task ahead, and I have the utmost respect for the competition. I look forward to the challenge of racing. In the meantime, our work continues at pace.”

Mario Andretti: Cadillac F1 board director on team's approval, Michael Andretti’s exit

Added Towriss, who last week was named the CEO of TWG Global's motorsports division, which owns all of Andretti Global's properties (including Wayne Taylor Racing) and owns a stake in Spire's NASCAR team: "Graeme has been advising our team for the last two years as we have built out our operations; his experience on both the technical and managerial sides of Formula 1 and other motorsports ventures will serve him well as he builds the Cadillac Formula 1 team."

Lowdon joins a list of publicized Cadillac F1 hires made since Andretti added General Motors to its F1 aspirations that includes:

  • Rob White, chief operating officer (who worked as Alpine's operations director as well as its chief engine tech
  • Pat Symonds, executive engineering consultant (who previously served as technical director for the Benetton, Renault and Williams F1 teams as well as the series at-large)
  • Nick Chester, technical director (who held engineering and technical director roles for the Arrows and Renault F1 teams, as well as the Mercedes and McLaren Formula E teams)
  • Jon Tomlinson, head of aerodynamics (who worked in aerodynamics for the Jordan, Renault and Williams F1 teams, as well as the Mercedes Formula E team)
  • John McQuillam, chief designer (who worked in a similar role with the Jordan and Marussia F1 teams)

Herta? Bottas? Russell?: A look at Cadillac F1's 2026 driver options

Andretti Global also introduced this week at its Indianapolis shop the new chief performance officer of TWG Global's motorsports division Doug Duchardt, as well as new TWG Global motorsports chief operations officer Jill Gregory, who will also serve as Andretti Global's team president.

As Andretti Global's new sprawling race shop nears completion, with a targeted early-March 2025 grand-opening, TWG Global is expected to formally roll-out further team branding and leadership updates in the coming weeks.

Last week, Cadillac F1 team board member Mario Andretti told IndyStar that pending a proper 2025 IndyCar championship finish that would qualify him for an F1 super license, Colton Herta is still expected to fill one of Cadillac F1's two open seats for its 2026 F1 grid debut.

headline: This little piggy went to ... Beech Grove? Pot-bellied pig chases postal worker
fullText:
Pig jokes were flying in the comment section of a post on social media Thursday afternoon after images of what looked like a dark spotted pot-bellied pig were captured in Beech Grove.

"Anyone missing a pig?" Samantha White posted. "He's chasing the poor mail lady around my neighborhood." White said the woman was working for USPS and she contacted Animal Care Services to pick the animal up.

Animal Care Services confirmed they did capture the pig at North 25th Avenue and Troy Street near Perkins Avenue in Beech Grove. It was considered a stray and if there is an owner who can come forward they have four business days to claim the animal before the pig will be sent to a rescue.

"I hope this piggy finds his way back home," White told IndyStar.

It hasn't been confirmed if the pig was male or female.

Do we have wild pigs in Indiana? Are they wreaking havoc like everywhere else?

Beech Grove Mayor James W. Coffman commends the work of their animal patrol officer for capturing the pig.

"Whether it be a dog or a cat or a chicken or a pig, it's about ensuring the safety of everybody around and making sure those animals if they are pets can get home safely," Coffman said.

Are pigs allowed in Beech Grove?

According to the city's ordinance it's unlawful for anybody to own or harbor any swine, horses, ponies, poultry or other domestic farm animal in Beech Grove.

The only exception is a pot-bellied pig and no more than six hens.

Beech Grove law also states no owner should fail to exercise proper care and control of his or her animals to prevent them from becoming a public nuisance.

What counts as being a public nuisance?

Excessive, continuous, or untimely barking, molesting passersby, chasing vehicles, habitually attacking other domestic animals, trespassing upon school grounds, or trespassing on private property that leads to damaged property is deemed a nuisance.

This isn't a first for Beech Grove

Back in 2018, an eight year old female 14-foot Burmese Python named "Vine" escaped from his owners in Beech Grove, causing hysteria from residents and neighbors. Vine's owner, Benny Tarplee, didn't report the snake missing for five days.

He believes Vine left because it was too hot in the house and someone left the door cage unlocked during cleaning day.

Tarplee asked people not to kill Vine and assured that as long as Beech Grove residents didn't touch her, she wouldn't harm them.

During the search, Vine became a local legend, spawning a Twitter account and a petition to change the mascot of Beech Grove schools to pythons.

Vine was eventually found under Tarplee's shed.

headline: Vivek Ramaswamy once called Elon Musk a 'circus monkey.' Now they're coworkers and friends
fullText:
Biotech billionaire, former Republican presidential candidate and Cincinnati-area native Vivek Ramaswamy didn't always have nice things to say about his new co-worker, Elon Musk.

In fact, Ramaswamy in May 2023 compared Musk, his co-director for the newly formed Department of Government Efficiency, to a "circus monkey" for China, CNN first reported on Wednesday.

“I have no reason to think Elon won’t jump like a circus monkey when Xi Jinping calls in the hour of need,” Ramaswamy said on the May 8, 2023 episode of his podcast.

Jinping is the general secretary of the Communist Party. Ramaswamy was discussing how he sees American business leaders, including Musk, as beholden to China

Evidently, Ramaswamy has warmed to Musk. In a statement sent to The Enquirer and CNN, he said the past comments are "water under the bridge."

What is the DOGE?

President-elect Donald Trump tapped both of them to head his new advisory commission called the Department of Government Efficiency, also known by its acronym "DOGE." While it's still not clear how the DOGE will operate, Trump's description indicated it will operate as an advisory group and not as a formal federal agency. Ramaswamy and Musk will work together to propose where the incoming administration can cut government spending and departments.

Why are the comments coming to light?

CNN's KFile investigative team looked at Ramaswamy's past comments on Musk to gauge how the two might work together. In addition to the aforementioned podcast, Ramaswamy told a Fox News podcast in 2022 that Musk changes his politics "based on the favors that he gets to be able to do business in China."

'I love him and respect the hell out of him'

The Enquirer reached out to Ramaswamy, who sent the same statement he sent to CNN, saying the comments were made before he met Musk. They now know each other well, Ramaswamy said.

"I love him and respect the hell out of him, and I'm proud to call him a friend," Ramaswamy said in the statement. "The only country he puts first is the same one I do: the United States of America.”

Ramaswamy grew up in Evendale, a suburban village just outside of Cincinnati, and graduated from St. Xavier High School as valedictorian in 2003 before making millions founding a pharmaceutical company and asset management firm. He later sought the Republican nomination for president in 2024 before dropping out.

headline: Which teams are The Enquirer's picks to win 2024 high school state football championships?
fullText:
Greater Cincinnati could have a rare bounty of state championships on the gridiron this weekend.

Five local high schools, two from Southwest Ohio and three from Northern Kentucky, will play for state titles. Here is a look at their matchups and our predictions.

OHSAA Division I: Moeller Crusaders vs. Powell Olentangy Liberty Patriots

This is a matchup of Mr. Football finalists, as Moeller (14-1) junior quarterback Matt Ponatoski will go up against Liberty (13-2) senior quarterback Andrew Leonard.

Leonard is leading his program to its first state championship game, while Moeller is playing for its 10th state title, the first since 2013.

Leonard, the Central District Offensive Player of the Year, completed 199 of 282 passes for 2,915 yards and 36 touchdowns with just five interceptions while rushing for 678 yards and five touchdowns. Running back Jake Struck is a multi-sport athlete who can do most anything on the football field. He has 1,666 yards from scrimmage and 27 touchdowns. He also had five goals against St. Xavier in the state lacrosse final. Liberty has several other targets who can make big plays.

On the Moeller side, Liberty head coach John Sansbury said Ponatoski is the best QB his team has seen all season. Ponatoski has had a record-setting campaign with 4,075 yards and 56 TD passes against only three interceptions, including 431 yards and six TD passes to six different receivers in last week’s state semifinals.

Liberty’s defense allows 12 points per game, 15 or fewer in 12 of its 15 games. Moeller head coach Bert Bathiany said the Patriots’ defense limits big plays and forces turnovers, especially at crucial moments in the playoffs. If Ponatoski and the Crusaders' offense can play as well as they have been and limit mistakes, then the question will be whether the Patriots' offense can keep up.

Prediction – Moeller 35, Liberty 21.

OHSAA Division II: Anderson Raptors vs. Avon Eagles

This is the only matchup of unbeaten 15-0 teams on the seven-game slate of state football finals in Canton, and the only matchup where the names of both schools begin and end with the same letter.

Like the Division I final, this will be a matchup of Mr. Football caliber quarterbacks. Avon senior Nolan Good was one of the eight Mr. Football finalists, while Anderson senior Justice Burnam could have been a contender in most years. Ponatoski and Ohio State commit Tavien St. Clair from Bellefontaine were the Mr. Football nominees from the Southwest District.

Avon head coach Mike Elder said his team hasn’t played a team with an explosive spread offense like Anderson’s, or a receiver with numbers like Trace Jallick’s (1,882 yards, 20 TDs). But their defense has been strong against a tough schedule, allowing 12.7 points per game, and 14 or fewer in 12 of 15 games.

Elder said his team has a strong and experienced front seven, and Anderson head coach Evan Dreyer believes that group is one of the best in the state. Avon has a lot of speed in the secondary led by Jakob Weatherspoon, who has a lot of offers from elite Division I programs.

On the other side, Nolan Good, a Kent State commit, has thrown for 3,142 yards on the season with 28 TDs and eight interceptions in 302 attempts. Good also has 712 yards rushing with 11 more TDs, leading the offense to average 40 points a game. He has several targets with productive numbers, led by Matt Maxey with 84 catches, 1,272 yards and 10 TDs. University of Cincinnati commit Jeremiah Kelly anchors the offensive line.

After breezing through most of their schedule, Anderson has shown mental toughness the last two weeks, scoring touchdowns at the end of the game against La Salle and Big Walnut to advance to the finals. Last week, Anderson committed four turnovers and survived, which they will be unlikely to repeat against a talented Avon team. Dreyer said the Eagles force a lot of turnovers and the Raptors will need to be at their best and toughest to bring home their second title.  

Prediction – Anderson 28, Avon 27.  

KHSAA Class 2A: Beechwood Tigers vs. Owensboro Catholic Aces

The Tigers (13-1) will play for their fourth trophy in the last five years when they go up against the Aces (14-0) on Friday at 4 p.m.

Owensboro Catholic quarterback Brady Atwell is one of the top passers in the state. He has the fourth-most yards (3,406) and touchdowns (47), and the fifth-highest completion percentage (69.2). Waryn Ebelhar, Dereon Crowe, Cameron Woodward, Xavier Maddox and Miles Edge all have over 300 receiving yards this season.

Atwell is also the real deal on the ground as he has 563 rushing yards and 18 touchdowns. Edge and Crowe have combined for 1,107 rushing yards and seven touchdowns.

Vince Carrico is the top defender on Beechwood’s scouting report. He leads the team with 111 tackles while also contributing four sacks, two fumble recoveries and an interception.

Beechwood rode its home-field advantage to a 44-24 state semifinal win over Lexington Christian, a game many thought would be closer than it was.

The Tigers’ offense will attack from every direction. Clay Hayden has averaged 212 passing yards in four postseason games, but Chase Flaherty has 12 of the team’s 16 rushing touchdowns in four postseason games. Flaherty has been dealing with a sprained ankle since last Friday but should be good to go against Owensboro Catholic.

The Tigers and Aces have only played once before, a 16-0 Beechwood win back in 1999. With two explosive offenses, this is expected to be one of the higher-scoring games of the weekend.

Prediction – Beechwood 49, Owensboro Catholic 44

KHSAA Class 5A: Cooper Jaguars vs. Bowling Green Purples

Cooper’s (14-0) season has been made possible by their 2023 campaign. Facing almost the same schedule allowed the Jaguars to not only go undefeated but largely dominate their opponents.

They have the third-highest scoring offense in the state at 46 points per game, and the sixth-best average margin of victory at 30.6 points per game. Isaiah Johnson is one of the top receivers in the state, but even if he is not having the best game, Cam O’Hara can depend on Austin Alexander, Jaidan Combs and Malachi Ewell. The Jaguars proved their depth in the backfield last week as Ryker Campbell stepped up in place of an injured Keagan Maher.

While Cooper has the offense to compete with any team in the state, the defense has stepped up throughout the playoffs. The Jaguars returned an interception for a touchdown in each of their first three postseason games, and they forced a total of 14 turnovers in their last two games. Cooper has the most interceptions of any team playing this weekend (25).

While the Jaguars are playing for their first state championship, Bowling Green (12-2) is hunting for its ninth trophy. Two of those have come against Cooper (2012, 2023).

The Purples return quarterback Deuce Bailey, who has thrown for 3,033 yards and 45 touchdowns. Leading rusher Jaxen Smith (441 yards, six touchdowns) and receiver Trevy Barber (1,222 yards and 22 touchdowns) are also back.

In the trenches, Cooper will have its hands full with Montrez Trussel, Brandon Gurley and Malik Coburn, who have combined for 33 sacks. The Purples are second in the state with 49 sacks as a team.

The Jaguars and Purples play in the final state championship game, kicking off at 8 p.m. Saturday.

Prediction – Cooper 55, Bowling Green 35

KHSAA Class 6A: Ryle Raiders vs. Trinity Shamrocks

The Raiders (12-2) and Shamrocks (12-2) have two of the most impressive defenses in the state.

Ryle has induced a running clock in each game of its current eight-game winning streak. Trinity has shut out six of its last seven opponents and has allowed 24 total points in its last eight games. Saturday’s state title game, scheduled to kick off at 4 p.m., will be a hard-nosed, grind-it-out affair.

Some of the Raiders’ most historic seasons have ended against Trinity, including their runs to the 2006 title game and the 2010 state semifinals. Now they will try to become the first non-Louisville team to beat the Shamrocks in the state championship game.

In his first full season at quarterback, Nathan Verax has thrown for 2,105 yards and 27 touchdowns. He has thrown 10 interceptions, but just two of those have come in the last eight games. Jacob Savage will be a major factor in this game. He has run for 1,006 yards and 22 touchdowns and made 134 tackles with three sacks. University of Louisville commit Dillon Smith leads the team with 8.5 sacks while Dylan Lee has six interceptions.

In Trinity’s state semifinal win over Frederick Douglass, the Shamrocks allowed just 152 yards of total offense. They forced four turnovers and recorded four sacks. Jack DeBellis, Nicholas Lococo, Caleb Ricks, Bailey Vance and John Wilson lead on defense. Myles Howze is a turnover specialist with five interceptions and two fumble recoveries.

The Shamrocks aren’t one of the more formidable offenses in the state, but there is still firepower in quarterback Zane Johnson (1,806 yards and 16 touchdowns), leading rushers Christopher Wilson and Jamaurion Berry (1,461 total yards and 18 touchdowns), and leading receiver Jeremiah Lynn (519 yards and five touchdowns).

Prediction – Trinity 20, Ryle 16

headline: Beechwood, Ryle, Cooper hope to turn NKY into 'title town' with football state crowns
fullText:
For the first time since 2014, Northern Kentucky has three football teams playing in the Kentucky High School Athletic Association state championships.

Beechwood, Ryle and Cooper are all coming off dominant state semifinal wins and are playing their best football of the season.

While Beechwood and Owensboro Catholic are meeting for the first time in 25 years, Ryle will face Trinity, a team that beat the Raiders in the 2006 state championship. Cooper is facing Bowling Green in the state final for the third time (2012, 2023).

Here's what you need to know before this weekend's games. Team previews are listed in order of game times.

How does Beechwood match up against Owensboro Catholic?

The Beechwood Tigers will bring a tradition of excellence to the field as they take on Owensboro Catholic Friday in their 23rd state championship appearance.

"I know they're going to have high energy, high emotions playing in a state championship, getting back there for the first time in a couple years. We're just going to try to keep everything very similar to what we do whether it's a home game or away game," head coach Jay Volker said.

One of the state's top passers, Brady Atwell leads the Aces, having completed 69.2 percent of his passes for 3,406 yards and 47 touchdowns.

Beechwood is studying film from the Tigers' 35-23 win over Simon Kenton to prepare for the Aces. The Pioneers played an uptempo spread offense this season. Brady Lee threw for 284 yards and three touchdowns against the Tigers. The majority of those yards went to receivers Grayson Harris and Tysin Weaver. Lee is one of only three quarterbacks to throw for more than 200 yards against the Tigers this season.

"(Atwell) is really big and he's really good. He can make every single throw. He's going to be a challenge to stop and we're going to have to come up with everything possible to be able to stop him," Volker said.

Stopping Atwell will be a full team effort, but Luke Erdman, Tyler Fryman, James Cusick, Nathan Pabst and Caleb Arrasmith are more than up to the task. Those five have combined for 12 interceptions. On offense, the corps has 2,273 receiving yards and 36 touchdowns.

"As a (defensive back), you kind of want games like this. O-Cath is a heavy pass team and we haven't really had that this year because the motto against us has always been, 'Run it, run it, run it.' Our (defensive backs) are athletic and we can fly, so I think it's gonna be exciting," Erdman said.

Those numbers are made possible by Jordan Franks, a former wide receiver for the University of Central Florida, the Kansas City Chiefs and the Cincinnati Bengals. He is in his second year at Beechwood and is more than just the wide receivers coach. He worked with the skill players during the offseason to help them become the best version of themselves.

"He's allowed us to really expand our play style. Everything that he brings to the offense and how we approach it is something I'm truly grateful for," Erdman said.

Containing Atwell is certainly Beechwood's top priority, but they will also be focused on the turnover battle. The Tigers have two fumbles in the postseason and Clay Hayden has thrown two interceptions. By comparison, the Aces have one fumble and backup quarterback Dremail Carothers threw their lone interception in a blowout.

"It's going to be a close game. It's going to go for four quarters. Who's gonna win the turnover battle will eventually be the determining factor," Volker said.

Before the state semifinal, Volker kept getting messages asking if the game was sold out. He joked that he doesn't think Beechwood will ever sell out a game simply because there is so much space surrounding the stadium. The stands were full but additional onlookers gathered on the walkway above the west end zone, in the athletic center's weight rooms and in the cafeteria.

"People love good football around here and they know where to go to see it," Volker said.

Beechwood is also continuing a tradition of not having school on the day of the state championship game. It allows the students to make the trip to Lexington in time for the 4 p.m. kickoff and lets the players focus on the final game of the season. Erdman and Chase Flaherty, both seniors, know what's at stake on Friday night.

"Obviously, as seniors, we have a little bit more want for this one. This is our last chance," Flaherty said.

Ryle hopes to continue domination in Class 6A title game

The Raiders have one of the most unique streaks in the state. They have forced a running clock in each of their last eight games. Doing so this Saturday against 28-time state champion Trinity won't be impossible, but it's still something they want to do.

"I don't think there's a single person on our team that doesn't believe we can't beat them," junior Jacob Savage said.

Head coach Mike Engler responded: "A running clock might be a stretch. I'll take a one-point win."

The Raiders have been waiting for this moment for years. They've won six straight regular-season district titles but this title game appearance is the result of years of hard work by the upperclassmen.

"Out of all the Ryle teams I've been on, I think this is definitely the closest. With our juniors and seniors having so much success earlier in our football careers, we both had great football teams and I think that ultimately leads to where we are today," senior Dillon Smith said.

Only four teams have ever won a Class 6A state title. Scott County is the only non-Louisville team to ever win one. Of all the teams Trinity could have faced, Ryle may actually be the best matchup.

"We're actually very similar teams. When you look at us, defensive lines are really good on both sides, offensive lines are really good on both sides. Both have really good quarterbacks. Both have really good running backs. I think it's an evenly matched football game," Engler said.

The Shamrocks have shut out six of their last seven opponents. Engler noted a majority of points Ryle has given up on its eight-game winning streak were scored in garbage time when junior varsity players were on the field. If the Raiders wanted to shut out some of those opponents, they could have.

Junior quarterback Nathan Verax has also been key to the Raiders' success. He has completed 61.2 percent of his passes for 2,105 yards and 27 touchdowns. He has thrown just two interceptions in the last eight games.

Even though it hasn't happened since 2014, Northern Kentucky has a history of sending teams in close proximity to the state championships in the same year. Beechwood and Covington Catholic have won state championships in the same year four times. Highlands and Newport Central Catholic have done it twice.

Ryle and Cooper have a fierce rivalry on the field but outside the lines, both are happy to see the other succeed. The two schools in Union don't have a lot of state championship history but aren't taking this opportunity for granted.

"It's funny to be in the same city. Hopefully, they start calling us 'title town.' Cooper's got a good program. Randy does a great job. If we both win it, that'd be great," Engler said.

Cooper ready for a state championship after another breakthrough season

Is the third time a charm for the Jaguars state championship hopes?

They aren't thinking of it like that, but more like how this season could be a more successful sequel to the 2023 campaign.

"Now it's more like straight business. We know what it's like to play under the lights at UK. We know what it's like to play in huge, packed-out games. It's really doing what we do and business this year rather than just seeing what could happen like last year," senior Austin Alexander said.

Cooper has matured in every sense of the word. This season really started in January, and head coach Randy Borchers said their commitment has been "second to none."

The Jaguars have improved their scoring output from 34.8 points per game in 2023 to 46 points per game this year, and their average margin of victory has grown from 19 points to 30.6 points per game. In preparation for each week, they have learned that they are playing kids their own age and are no longer intimidated by certain schools.

In last year's state championship, they made early mistakes against Bowling Green and couldn't overcome a 14-point deficit. Last week, they were down 10 points at halftime but regrouped and scored 54 points in the second half.

Sure, the offense has been flashy, but its real redeeming quality has been its ability to keep Cooper rolling in times of trouble.

"They just make plays. Even in practice, some of the catches that our guys make are unreal. It's funny because, when we're in practice, we don't want those kids to do anything to get injured. We've got some of these guys diving for balls and we're like, 'Woah, woah, woah.' We don't want those guys doing it in practice but it's just the competitiveness coming out here," Borchers said.

On the field, the offense has been the show. Behind the scenes, it's senior tight end and edge rusher Austin Alexander. Who he's been this season is a culmination of what he's learned throughout his career.

"Just growing up every year, I feel like I've learned something from each football season. After freshman year, I was like, 'Man, I need to start getting to know some more of my guys.' Then after sophomore year, it was like, 'I need to be more of a vocal leader.' This year is just putting it all together, coming out here and attempting to lead not only on the field but off the field," Alexander said.

On Saturday night against Bowling Green, Borchers believes the key to a Cooper victory will be minimizing its mistakes and capitalizing on the Purples' miscues, things they didn't do last season.

The Jaguars have quickly ascended to the top of the Northern Kentucky football scene and are on their way to becoming a perennial powerhouse. Thanks to Alexander's commitment to the University of North Carolina and back-to-back championship appearances, more people are starting to learn about the Jaguars.

"We've been throughout the state where people have asked us in years past, 'Where is Cooper? We've never heard of Cooper.' Now when we travel, people say, 'Man, your football team is really good.' People are starting to take notice, which is a really cool place to be," Borchers said.

headline: Grandmother needs help caring for granddaughters after family tragedy | Wish List
fullText:
The Enquirer and United Way of Greater Cincinnati have joined forces for the 38th year to help families in need with the Wish List program. After wishes are granted, remaining funds assist people with similar needs throughout the year. This is the third of eight stories.

Andretta Owens’ nightmare began very early on the morning of June 7 when she was awakened by a phone call. Her 35-year-old daughter, Tyler Owens, died shortly after a car crash in Avondale.

Tyler was the mother of three girls: Ja’Nilah, 17; Ke’Ziah, 13; and Ter’Riah, 11.

“She was a very good mother,” Andretta said through tears. “She really tried hard to make ends meet. She loved her girls.”

Andretta loves them, too. Her granddaughters were uprooted from their home and now live with her part of the year; she shares caregiving with other family members.

“We’re trying to make sure we’re part of their lives and we meet their needs,” Andretta said. “Everybody’s trying to learn how to adjust to a new life. We have days we’re sad; we have days we’re angry. We’re getting adjusted to being without Tyler. It’s a process.”

On a nearby table, a photo of Tyler adorns a vase filled with roses, hydrangeas and irises. They’re all yellow, which was her favorite color. “My daughter loved fresh flowers,” Andretta said.

Less than five weeks after Tyler’s death, the family endured more trauma.

About 7:30 a.m. July 10, Andretta and Ke’Ziah were reading the Bible in the kitchen of the two-story Silverton house where Andretta has lived since she was a teen. They heard a loud crack. Just as they stood, a large tree crashed through the roof. Fortunately, they were not hurt, nor were Andretta’s two brothers who were upstairs.

A fire official told them it’s likely the tree was weakened by a previous lightning strike.

As she recounted the incident, Andretta began to sob. “This is all too much,” she said.

She composed herself, then added: “I have to get myself together in order to be there for (the girls). We have to get ourselves together. We have to take the next steps.”

As they take those steps, Andretta is grateful for the support they have received from family members; from her coworkers at Cincinnati’s Ronald McDonald House, where she is a housekeeper; and from Ladies of Leadership, which nominated the family for the Wish List. Andretta enrolled her granddaughters in the mentoring organization for girls last year.

Andretta moved into a rental home until her house can be repaired. She has insurance, but it’s not yet clear what her out-of-pocket expenses will be. Regardless, she needs help providing for her three granddaughters.

“We had tragedies,” Andretta said. “I want my girls to be able to overcome it – I’m not saying to forget – but to be able to move forward and reach their goals.”

Andretta's wish: Items for her three grandchildren, including bedroom furniture; clothes and shoes; laptop computers.

Estimated cost: $5,000.

How to help

Donations can be made online at www.uwgc.org/wishlist. You can also mail donations to: United Way of Greater Cincinnati, Attn: Wish List Pledge Processing, P.O. Box 632840, Cincinnati, OH 45263-2840. Please include “Wish List” in the memo line on checks.

John Johnston is the content writer at United Way and a former Enquirer reporter.

headline: Can AI help mental health crisis? Nearly 100 students, parents and clinicians weigh in
fullText:
As part of our yearlong reporting project on how schools are using artificial intelligence to identify students with mental health issues, The Enquirer heard from nearly 100 people in the Cincinnati community.

Here's more on who they are and how they felt.

Most were students, parents, mental health clinicians and youth workers. Close to 80 people filled out our survey, while around 20 attended our library listening session, which was open to the public, to share their thoughts. 

Cincinnatians expressed everything from cautious optimism to uncertainty and worry about having AI used to help determine whether someone is suicidal, depressed, anxious. Many said their biggest concerns about using AI this way were protecting students from privacy violations and biased results.

“My concern would be that once AI said a student was a danger, they would be treated as such,” shared one school administrator. “But, I also see the helpful aspect of it bringing up someone who may have slipped through the cracks.”

Over half think AI can help youth mental health crisis

People who thought AI would help solve the youth mental health crisis eked out a narrow majority – 54% – over people who disagreed or were not sure. This larger group agreed or strongly agreed that an AI-powered app that detects signs of distress could help address the youth mental health crisis.

51% said that AI would make schools safer. 

And some clinicians who attended our listening session saw value in using AI to predict suicide attempts.

“We’re really, really, really bad at predicting human behavior,” said Paul Crosby, a psychiatrist and the president of the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health center in Mason. “I understand why solutions like this are being sought because we haven’t come up with good ones ourselves.”

Isaac Trice, a clinical counselor at Talbert House in Western Hills, said that algorithms are already playing a role in mental health diagnosis for his clients. 

“Clients come in and say, well, TikTok told me that I’m a narcissist,” he said. “So I do think that it's important for us to be on the cutting edge and to use these tools.”

Still, every AI-related question on the survey resulted in 30% or more of respondents responding with “neutral” or “not sure”, indicating a clear uncertainty among many about using AI to help detect mental health issues.

Gharrie Hoffman, who has a master's degree in community counseling, doesn’t love the idea of using AI but felt she doesn’t “know enough about it.” She wants to see results proving it works before making a judgment call.

1 in 3 feel comfortable with AI recording therapy sessions, most people concerned about bias

The question that created the most even split among respondents asked whether respondents were OK with AI listening to their therapy sessions: 33% of respondents said they felt comfortable with it, while 27% said they didn’t. 

Owen Kovacic, an undergraduate at the University of Cincinnati, described having AI listen to therapy sessions as “intrusive and terrible for trust.”

Recent Oak Hills High grad Quinn Merriss is worried that using AI to detect mental health issues could lead to kids being involuntarily hospitalized in cases where it's not necessary.

Merriss also wondered whether therapists using AI would discourage students from seeking help. “How many kids are gonna stop talking, period, because they don’t want it involved?” they asked. 

The question that produced the clearest majority asked about bias. Nearly 60% of respondents said that using AI to check language for mental health or safety risks might lead to biased results or unexpected issues, while 10% said it wouldn’t. 

“When it comes to AI it can be made biased due to the information it is fed,” said Awa Bolling, an undergraduate at UC, a sentiment echoed by at least two other students.

Some people expressed doubts about using technology like AI to try to solve a mental health crisis that may have been caused by an excess of screen time in the first place.

Trice, the clinical counselor at Talbert House, put it this way: “When it comes to AI, are we chasing one pill with another?” 

People agree we need more clinicians, disagree on how to make schools safer

Students from high school to graduate school expressed widespread agreement on the need for more accessible mental health services. 

Increasing the availability of mental health clinicians, decreasing the cost of therapy, and giving students more time during the day to dedicate to their mental health, they said, were ways to get more students help. Awa Bolling, the undergraduate at UC, said that “more leeway with academic success” could take pressure off of stressed students. 

Respondents agreed that schools could be safer but differed in their opinions about what that should look like. 

A handful of people suggested increasing the number of police officers on campus. Still others felt that security equipment such as door locks and metal detectors were important.

More than one person identified hallways as areas that need to be monitored for bullying. According to one student from Taft High School, having adults in hallways “protecting students from bullies” and “escorting the victim to class” would make a difference. 

As the director of the Trauma Recovery Center at The Neighborhood House, Sheila Nared helps youth victims of violent crime process their trauma and practice resilience.

Nared believes that giving communities most affected by violence a say in decision making is key to preventing violence in the first place. 

“Those closest to the problem are those closest to the solution,” said Nared, but also “farthest from the resources and the power.”

What gives people hope? Hope Squad helps

Listening session attendees cited young people talking about their mental health as a sign that the stigma is decreasing, as well as increased access to mental health clinicians. 

Carlie Yersky, a clinical counselor for Greater Cincinnati Behavioral Health, said she draws hope from the access that students have to trained mental health clinicians within their schools. 

“When I was a kid, we did not have therapists in school,” said Yersky. “Now every school in Cincinnati is partnering with some mental health agency.”

Other attendees emphasized the importance of human and community-centered solutions to the mental health crisis.

“Create a culture of people caring about other people,” suggested Olive Weaver, a senior at Mason High, “rather than delegating any of the work to AI.” 

Weaver and other listening session attendees pointed to Hope Squad, a peer-to-peer suicide prevention program implemented in hundreds of schools around Ohio, as one example.

At Mason High School, Hope Squad is a class with an enrollment of over 80 students. Each grade has their own Hope Squad team, led by a teacher adviser, which meets four days a week. Hope Squad members are charged with keeping an eye out for peers who are struggling and connecting them to a teacher or counselor if they need help. 

“Often our kids see the issues well before the adults do,” said Beth Celenza, one of the school’s four Hope Squad advisers, so the class is about “empowering the students to be able to do something with that information.” 

Prior to the implementation of Hope Squad in 2017, the school district averaged one suicide per year, said district spokesperson Tracey Carson. 

It’s just one of the interventions the district established since then, said Carson, but together, the interventions seem to be working.

“I haven’t had a suicide since.”

How we did this

The Enquirer spent the past year reporting on how schools are using artificial intelligence to identify students with mental health issues. As part of our project, we took a two-pronged approach to hearing from the community. 

First we released a survey that we distributed online and in person, in areas with high foot traffic such as The University of Cincinnati, Findlay Market, and The Neighborhood House, a social services organization in the West End. Next, we hosted a listening session at the Cincinnati and Hamilton County Public Library main branch downtown, open to anyone. 

The result was that we heard from a large and diverse group of Cincinnatians who ranged from teens to those over 60 years old. 

The breakdown of survey respondents consisted of 64% students, and 23% were parents. Another 9% were mental health providers and 7% worked with kids in schools or community organizations. Most parent respondents had high school-aged kids or younger and lived in areas that stretched from Fort Mitchell, Kentucky, to Cincinnati suburbs like West Chester Township. 

The racial breakdown: 37% of respondents were Black, 37% were white, and 23% were Asian. Other respondents were Hispanic or Latino, Middle Eastern, North African or mixed race.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, help is available 24/7. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

Betsy Kim reported this story while participating in the USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism’s 2024 National Fellowship Kristy Hammam Fund for Health Journalism and received engagement mentoring and funding.

headline: Daniel Carter Beard Bridge repairs: What's next and why's it taking so long?
fullText:
Despite traffic tangles and slow commutes caused by the partial closure of the Daniel Carter Beard Bridge, “everything’s falling into place” for a March reopening, officials said Wednesday. 

Damaged portions of Interstate 471, leading to the bridge from Ohio, are gone. Weather permitting, crews start building new cement pads under the bridge Thursday. 

Here’s what's ahead in the coming weeks, as the Ohio Department of Transportation fixes what a Nov. 1 fire under the bridge destroyed. 

The plan for December 

Last Friday, workers began removing concrete from the deck of I-471 along with some steel beams, both warped by the fire. They completed that work Wednesday, removing about 7,600 square feet of concrete from two different spans on the interstate. 

An L-shaped hunk of the highway is out. “We’re saving what we can,” said Kathleen Fuller, a department spokesperson. 

Absent wet weather, workers will start pouring concrete footers under the bridge Thursday. The pads will be located just south of the 1000 Hands Playground, the Sawyer Point Park site that erupted in fire around 3:30 a.m. on Nov. 1. 

When the footers are complete, on Monday or just after, workers will move four shoring towers atop them. The towers had been supporting the damaged part of I-471. In their new locations, they’ll support the rebuilding of the roadway. 

Work on the northbound span of I-471 will also start next week. Crews will replace about 70 feet of the left wall, just north of the bridge, whose outer side was charred by fire. When that’s complete, in late December, the state will reopen the left lane, restoring all four lanes of traffic from Kentucky into Ohio. 

The plan for January 

The state expects contractors to deliver steel girders to the site by mid-January. Nucor Steel of Charlotte, North Carolina, is supplying the steel to Stupp Bridge, of Bowling Green, Kentucky, which will fabricate the steel into needed components in December. 

The state picked suppliers who could move quickly, Fuller said. “That was one of the assurances, that yes, they have the materials,” she said. 

Late January and February 

Steel parts will go up just after delivery, Fuller said. “Once the girders arrive they’ll start the install immediately,” she said. 

Workers will pour concrete for the new I-471 decks after that. Concrete walls will follow.

By March 

Officials can’t yet say the exact date southbound I-471 and southbound Daniel Carter Beard will be back in operation. Once the decks and sides are complete, workers will need to add pavement markings and signs. 

Costs to repair the Big Mac Bridge

The state of Ohio will pay for the repairs, then apply for some level of federal reimbursement. Officials don’t yet know the price tag. 

Squeezing 3 years of construction into 5 months

A job as big as this one would normally take three years from design through construction, state transportation officials said. Ohio’s contractors are aiming to complete it in five months. 

“Obviously this is an emergency situation,” Fuller said. 

Still, officials know “there’s a huge impact to a significant number of people,” she said, noting that the bridge normally carries about 100,000 vehicles a day. 

By comparison, the state closed a bridge near New Philadelphia in Ohio’s Belmont County in August because it was deteriorating and won’t even start its reconstruction until 2027, added Matt Bruning, another transportation spokesman. 

“The public generally doesn’t know about projects until groundbreaking,” he said.  

Most projects include months or even years of advanced planning. 

The cause

Officials of the Cincinnati Fire Department continue to investigate the cause of the fire.

headline: Who is Garrett Crochet? Lefty goes from White Sox to Red Sox in Winter Meetings trade
fullText:
Chicago White Sox left-handed pitcher Garrett Crochet had 209 strikeouts in 146 innings in 2024 and was a first-time American League All-Star, making him one of the most sought-after young arms in MLB.

On Wednesday, the Boston Red Sox traded for the talented southpaw, sending catcher Kyle Teel, outfielder Braden Montgomery, infielder Chase Meidroth and right-handed pitcher Wikelman González to the White Sox.

Jon Morosi reported last week that the Cincinnati Reds and Chicago Cubs were among teams interested in Crochet, who posted a 6-12 record, 3.58 ERA and 1.07 WHIP in 32 starts for the White Sox last season.

The Los Angeles Dodgers and Baltimore Orioles also were mentioned in recent Crochet trade talks.

What to know about the 6-foot-6 Crochet, who turned 25 years old in June:

Crochet was a first-round pick (11th overall) in the 2020 MLB draft.

Crochet's 5.9 WAR is the best among 2020 first-rounders.

One pick after the White Sox selected Crochet, the Reds took outfielder Austin Hendrick 12th overall.

Hendrick has yet to reach the majors. In 2024, he hit .188 with 173 strikeouts in 474 plate appearances for the Double-A Chattanooga Lookouts.

Crochet made his big-league debut against the Reds at Great American Ball Park.

On September 18, 2020, in Cincinnati, Crochet struck out two of the three batters he faced in an inning of relief.

Two days later, he pitched another scoreless inning at GABP in his second career outing.

He made one start against the Reds last season, allowing five earned runs on four hits, three walks and a hit-by-pitch with 10 strikeouts in 4 2/3 innings in a 5-0 Cincinnati win in Chicago on April 13.

Crochet won the American League Comeback Player of the Year award in 2024.

Crochet returned late in the 2023 season from extended rehab after undergoing Tommy John surgery that cost him the 2022 season.

He entered the 2024 season having tossed just 73 MLB innings over 72 relief appearances in three seasons.

Crochet didn't have a start that lasted more than four innings after June 30, but last season alone, he doubled his total number of innings pitched between 2020 and 2023.

The White Sox would've had Crochet under team control through 2026.

Chicago could've opted to hang onto Crochet, but their 2024 record of 41-121 suggested the White Sox needed much more than the talented young arm to rebuild.

Crochet reportedly made it known he wants a contract extension if traded.

Crochet earned $800,000 last season.

headline: Meet the Cincinnati Bearcats football new signees
fullText:
The University of Cincinnati Bearcats announced their latest football signing class on Wednesday as they attempt to improve personnel after falling short of a bowl bid Saturday vs. TCU.

Out of the high school ranks, the Bearcats took four offensive linemen, four defensive linemen, two tight ends, two linebackers, two safeties, a quarterback, a running back, a receiver, a cornerback and a "star" (hybrid defensive back). That's 19 new faces in the fold with many, if not all starting their conditioning work in January with Director of Football Performance Niko Palazeti.

"We want to win the trenches through high school," UC general manager Zach Grant said of signing eight linemen. "Typically, those are the hardest positions to acquire in the portal, Big people are hard to find in the country."

Grant says UC looks for trench players with broad shoulders and long arms.

Wednesday afternoon, UC head coach Scott Satterfield and general manager Zach Grant spoke about the new additions and upcoming portal plans.

Cincinnati Bearcats arrivals

Zebulin Kinsey – quarterback, 6'3", 215, Toronto High School, Wellsville, Ohio

Consensus three-star prospect and Top 30 quarterback according to On3. ESPN's No. 20 dual-threat quarterback prospect. Kinsey was Ohio Division IV Co-Offensive Player of the Year. Chose UC over other Power Four programs including Oklahoma State and West Virginia.

"He can run, he's got great size," Satterfield said. "He's got a really good strong arm. He's got a big upside I think. We don't need him to come have to play next year. It's come in, see where you are and continue to develop and grow."

Zion Johnson – running back, 5'8", 180, Newton High School, Covington, Georgia

Consensus three-star recruit and ranked among Top 40 running back recruits in the nation by ESPN and On3. Ran for 5,130 yards and 44 touchdowns in his prep career including 2,078 this season with 16 touchdowns. Chose UC over other Power Four programs including Tennessee, Ole Miss and Kentucky.

Giyahni Kontosis – wide receiver, 6'1", 195, Riverdale Baptist, Beltsville, Maryland

Consensus three-star prospect and Top 20 recruit in Maryland. Ranked among Top 100 receivers by 247Sports, ESPN and Rivals. Chose UC over other Power Four programs including Indiana, Pitt and Boston College.

Ka'Mauri Smith –tight end, 6'5", 200, Wayne High School, Dayton, Ohio

Consensus three-star prospect and Top 75 Ohio recruit. Ranked ESPN's No. 52 best tight end prospect. Chose UC over Power Four programs including Kentucky, Pitt, Purdue and Rutgers.

DaMari Witherspoon – tight end, 6'5", 220, East Palding High School, Dallas, Georgia

Had 17 catches for 255 yards and five touchdowns as a senior. Considered an under-the-radar prospect.

Jeremiah Kelly – offensive line, 6'3", 315, Avon High School, Avon, Ohio

Consensus three-star prospect and Ohio Top 100 player. Rated By ESPN as the nation's NO. 44 guard. Helped Avon to a 15-0 record and will play vs. Anderson Thursday night in the OHSAA Division II state title game in Canton.

Marcus McGregor – offensive line, 6'3", 280, Valley High School, West Des Moines, Iowa

Consensus three-star prospect and Top 20 recruit in Iowa according to On3.

Cray Paich – offensive line, 6'6", 290, Glenbrook North High School, Northbrook, Illinois

Consensus three-star prospect and Top 35 player in Illinois. Chose UC over Army and Navy among others.

Zach Taylor – offensive line, 6'4", 300, Camden County High School, Kingsland, Georgia

Listed as a three-star prospect by Rivals. He played nose guard and tackle for Camden County and was named All-Region First Team.

Tim Griffin – defensive line, 6'5", 255, Alcovy High School, Covington, Georgia

A four-star recruit and the nation's No. 21 defensive end prospect according to Rivals. Chose UC over Alabama, Florida State and Ole Miss among others.

James Early – defensive line, 6'6", 230, North Side High School, Fort Wayne, Indiana

Consensus three-star recruit and Top 35 player in Indiana. Chose UC over several FBS offers.

C.D. McFee –defensive line, 6'5", 296, Elkhart High School, Elkhart, Indiana

Consensus three-star recruit and No. 16 prospect in Indiana according to On3. Chose UC over several FBS offers.

Kamron Neal –defensive line, 6'4", 245, Campbell High School (Georgia), Fort Myers, Florida

Consensus three-star prospect and among the Top 60 edge recruits according to On3.

Myles Harrison – linebacker, 6'3", 210, Pickerington Central, Pickerington, Ohio

A three-star recruit by 247Sports and On 3 and Top 75 in Ohio according to On3. Had 50 tackles, 16 tackles for loss and nine sacks for Pickerington Central this season.

Terrell Holcomb – linebacker, 6'3", 205, Gahanna Lincoln, Gahanna, Ohio

Consensus three-star prospect and Ohio's No. 34 recruit by On3. He was the Ohio Capital Conference Defensive Player of the Year with 85 tackles, seven sacks, an interception and two blocked field goals.

Patrick Williams – cornerback, 5'10", 160, Rabun Gap-Nacoochee High School, Greenville, South Carolina

Consensus three-star recruit who helped his team to the NCISAA (North Carolina Independent Schools Athletic Association) championship. He was named NCISAA Division I First Team All-State.

Jamari Johnson –safety, 6', 165, Pell City High School, Birmingham, Alabama

Listed as a three-star recruit by On3 and 247Sports and a top 100 prospect in Alabama. Chose UC over several FBS offers including Troy.

C.J. Jones – safety, 5'11", 180, Bolingbrook, Chicago, Illinois

Consensus three-star recruit and Top 35 prospect in Illinois. Rated No. 72 cornerback in nation according to On3. Chose UC over Boston College among others.

C.J. Crite –star (defensive back), 6'1", 195, Lincoln County High School, Lincoln, Georgia

A consensus three-star recruit and Top 50 linebacker prospect according to On3. ESPN ranked him as the nation's No. 20 inside linebacker prospect. Had 119 tackles, three tackles for loss, three interceptions and two forced fumbles as a senior. Chose UC over several FBS offers including Western Kentucky and USF.

Cincinnati Bearcats portal plans

In addition to re-recruiting their current players, UC like many schools will be active in a transfer portal that's as busy as a new interstate Buc-ee's.

"Receiver is a big need," Grant said. "We need to help the pass rush, then cover players. We're going to be as aggressive as we can be."

Satterfield likes the current quarterback room but says they could add a portal running back to replace workhorse Corey Kiner. He sees big-play runner Evan Pryor with an increased role. The biggest need though as Grant mentioned is playmakers at wide receiver.

Cincinnati Bearcats de-commitments

Over the past year, UC has had highly-rated commits, flip to other schools, and likewise have had players flip to them. Wednesday, four-start cornerback Jahmari DeLoatch was swayed to his home state Virginia Tech Hokies. The Bearcats have had several top commitments move on leaving them with nothing but the fact they were in on some top players for most of the process.

"They've got so many directions they're getting pulled," Satterfield said of the recruits. "From coaches to family members, they have a lot of options out there. Some of the guys that were on the fence still loved us and could see themselves playing here. We don't burn any bridges with any of these guys. Look at it Corey Kiner, he was at LSU. Look at Joe Royer, he was right up the street (Ohio State) and now he's here."

Satterfield mentioned in current college football, you re-evaluate your team every six months. After the current portal session ends this month, another one begins after spring football for 10 days between April 16-25.

"You're battling these schools that have been at the Power Five level for a long time," Satterfield said. "They have 100,000-seat stadiums that have indoor (facilities) that are ready, great football facilities that are already in place. We're building a new facility that will be up and ready this summer. We're going to get our share."

Cincinnati Bearcats departures

As the revolving door of Division I football goes, the Bearcats have already lost several players to the portal. The following scholarship players will not be wearing a C-Paw next season. Their upcoming class status is listed.

Kalen Caroll, redshirt junior, cornerback –The Indianapolis Cedar Grove product started the first 10 game then made his exit.

D.J. Taylor, safety, redshirt senior –Taylor from Arizona State, walked on Senior Night. He played in two games this season.

Carter Brown, kicker, senior – The starting kicker for Scott Satterfield in 203, was benched after the Pitt game. Brown came from Arizona State. He lost his job in week two after a crucial missed field goal in the first half against the Panthers. He was 3-for-5 this season and 15-for-19 in 2023. Including his one season at Arizona State, he has made all 71 of his PATs.

Aaron Turner, wide receiver, senior – Taylor walked on Senior Night vs. TCU. He played in five games with five catches with one start vs. Miami University. Mid-season the plans were to try and get him a medical redshirt.

Sterling Berkhalter, wide receiver, redshirt senior – Berkhalter from Princeton High returned home for two seasons. He had 11 catches and a touchdown against Towson in the opener.

Caleb Schmitz, tight end, redshirt senior – Schmitz made his intentions to leave before the season ended. He had one career catch in 2023 at Oklahoma State.

Garrison Butler, defensive lineman, redshirt freshman – Butler did not see action for the Bearcats.

headline: NFL Network's Daniel Jeremiah: Lions OC Ben Johnson should wait to work with Joe Burrow
fullText:
Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson is expected to be a top candidate for NFL head-coaching vacancies.

During an appearance on "This Is Football," NFL Network's Daniel Jeremiah suggested that Johnson keep an eye on what the Cincinnati Bengals do with head coach Zac Taylor, in the event that an opportunity to work with quarterback Joe Burrow presents itself.

"My Ben Johnson take is a little different than everybody else," Jeremiah said. "It would be like - I don't want to say stalking. Maybe that's not the right word. I don't want to ever see anybody get fired. But if I'm Ben Johnson, I'm keeping an eye on Cincinnati and going, 'I would rather stay in Detroit and wait two years, three years for that opportunity to open up.' Because if you want to take what I've done to another level. The only quarterback who can run the stuff that I'm doing better than Jared Goff is the guy in Cincinnati."

Host Kevin Clark joked that Bengals owner Mike Brown would be unlikely to give Johnson "a five-year, $100 million contract."

"If you're Ben Johnson, do you care?" Jeremiah replied. "You could be there throughout the rest of this guy's career and go win a Super Bowl. And then hey, if I miss out on a couple million dollars at the end of my life, is that gonna make it drastically different? No."
