headline: FBI confirms investigation, search at home of Indiana pickleball entrepreneur
fullText:
This story has been updated with additional information.

The FBI confirmed that agents executed a federal search warrant today at the Brookville home of former Pickleball Rocks owner Rodney Grubbs who is accused of operating an alleged $50 million Ponzi scheme.

News of the federal agents presence at Grubbs' home in the 300 block of East 11th Street began to circulate among his investors early Wednesday morning. IndyStar has reached out to Grubbs for comment. He has yet to respond. Grubbs has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Attorney Paul Vink, who represented Grubbs in an investigation brought by the Indiana Securities Division, said via email that he no longer represents the embattled pickleball entrepreneur.

Meanwhile, the FBI says it wants to speak with people who have invested money with Grubbs.

Dubbed sport's 'ultimate ambassador': Pickleball apparel CEO accused of Ponzi scheme

A federal bankruptcy court forced Grubbs into bankruptcy earlier this year after investors accused him of defrauding them out of millions of dollars in an alleged Ponzi scheme involving real estate and pickleball ventures he promoted over the course of several decades.

More than 335 creditors, overwhelmingly couples and individuals, have since come forward in the bankruptcy case, alleging that Grubbs collectively owes them roughly $57 million. Grubbs has denied any wrongdoing, but by his own admission he's admitted to owing creditors at least $47 million.

Hundreds of people from across the U.S., Portugal, and Canada say Grubbs told them they could have the last available slot among for a small circle of investors if they put forth at least $25,000. They were told the money would be used to grow Pickleball Rocks as a business and fulfill new contracts. He gave a similar pitch for real estate investors, according to court records.

Grubbs guaranteed his pickleball investors a 12% interest rate compounded monthly, and a lump sum repayment after 18 months. Investors would receive an increased interest rate of 18% if he defaulted. He routinely did but convinced some investors to roll over their loans.

The Securities Division of the Indiana Secretary of State issued Grubbs a cease and desist order because he wasn't registered to offer short-term, high-interest promissory notes. The office called the activities an alleged fraudulent investment scheme. At the time, investors had stepped forward to say they struggled to get Grubbs to return their money. Many have since advocated for Grubbs to be criminally prosecuted.

Some of his investors have launched adversary proceedings to prevent the discharging of his bankruptcy case.

It's unclear what exactly what evidence the federal agents were seeking to find at Grubbs' home today or if anything has been removed as few details are available so far. Bridget Hayes, president of the Brookville Town Council, said the FBI notified the Brookville Police Department about the search warrant early Wednesday. The local department provided security around the perimeter of the scene, she said, adding that local officers did not go into the house.

Both local town and Franklin County sheriff officers were at the scene. An advisory from the sheriff's department alerted users to the closure of a portion of 11th Street between John Street and Fairfield Avenue.

"Some very dear friends of mine have been investors, and it has been a very trying time for a lot of people in town that did invest," Hayes said.

The Franklin County Observer, a local news organization, also posted photos showing Grubbs and agents wearing black vests with the letter F.B.I written in yellow on its Facebook page. In the photos, Grubbs is seen in leisurewear descending the steps to the house and standing in the street.

In a statement on its website, the FBI’s Indianapolis Division said it's seeking to identify potential victims who invested with Grubbs.

"The FBI is legally mandated to identify victims of federal crimes it investigates. Victims may be eligible for certain services, restitution, and rights under federal and/or state law," the statement said. "Your responses are voluntary but may be useful in the federal investigation and to identify you as a potential victim. Based on the responses provided, you may be contacted by the FBI and asked to provide additional information. All identities of victims will be kept confidential."

People coming forward as victims should fill out a form at the FBI's website.

The agency said it was assisted by the IRS-Criminal Investigation, the Indiana Secretary of State’s Office, the Brookville Police Department, and the Franklin County Sheriff’s Department.

Contact IndyStar investigative reporter Alexandria Burris at aburris@gannett.com. Follow her on X, formerly Twitter, at @allyburris.

headline: UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson killed in NYC: Casings had messages, reports say
fullText:
Police in New York City continued searching Thursday for the person who shot and killed UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in a "targeted attack" outside the hotel where the company was hosting an investor conference.

The 50-year-old executive, who arrived in the city from Minnesota on Monday, was shot by a masked shooter who appeared to be waiting for Thompson outside the hotel for several minutes Wednesday morning. The person walked behind Thompson and shot him in the back around 6:45 a.m.

The incident, captured on video, shows the moment the shooter approaches Thompson from behind and fires into his back. A woman a few feet from Thompson runs away as the shooter appears to clear a jam in the gun before stepping closer to Thompson, who was then on the ground, and firing again.

New York City Police Department officials said they were still working to find the shooter, who was last seen riding an e-bike into Central Park. In an alley near the Hilton hotel, investigators discovered a cellphone they will analyze forensically, as well as three shell casings.

Here's what we know so far about the shooting, the investigation and threats against Thompson:

Reports: Police identify writing on the shell casings

Investigators discovered writing on the shell casings discovered at the scene of the fatal shooting, ABC News and NBC News reported, citing police sources with knowledge on the investigation.

The words discovered written on the shell casings were “deny,” “defend” and “depose,” the sources told the outlets.

In addition to the shells, police discovered a water bottle and a candy wrapper in the area where the shooter was waiting for Thompson, ABC reported, adding that the evidence, as well as the cellphone, are believed to be linked to the shooter.

Shooter last seen riding e-bike into Central Park

After the gunman shot Thompson, police say he hid in an alleyway before boarding an e-bike and riding into Central Park, where he was last seen.

Police released several images of the shooter in which the gunman can be seen wearing a dark-colored jacket with a hood over his head, a black facemask, black-and-white sneakers and a distinctive gray backpack.

The NYPD has announced up to $10,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the shooter.

Thompson had received threats, wife says

Thompson's wife, Paulette Thompson, told NBC News her husband had been the target of threats, but she didn't know their nature or from whom.

"I don’t know, a lack of coverage? I don’t know details," she told the news outlet. "I just know that he said there were some people that had been threatening him."

Additionally, UnitedHealth Group, the parent company of UnitedHealthcare, was aware of concerning threats against its executives, CNN reported, citing a source with knowledge of the investigation. The company did not immediately respond to USA TODAY's request for comment.

Contributing: Jorge L. Ortiz, Nick Penzenstadler, USA TODAY

headline: VP-elect JD Vance picks Middletown school band for presidential inauguration
fullText:
Vice President-elect and Middletown native JD Vance has selected Middletown High School’s marching band to perform at the Inaugural Parade in Washington D.C.

It will be held on Monday, Jan. 20.

Ohio Senator George Lang, R-West Chester Township, confirms he extended the invitation to the Middie Marching Band on Wednesday after a member of Vance’s team reached out to him.

“JD is excited to have the Middies there,” said Middletown High School Principal Carmela Cotter. “We are very excited to go and have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for our kids to participate in the inaugural parade. It’s wonderful!”

“During the Inaugural Parade, the newly-sworn president and vice president will make their way to the East Front steps of the Capitol where they will review military troops before leading a procession of ceremonial military regiments, citizens’ groups, marching bands, and floats down Pennsylvania Avenue to the White House.”

Butler County sheriff, Ohio Senator George Lang help fund Middie Marching Band's trip to DC

All students who can attend were asked to notify the school by this Friday.

The school district will cover the cost of travel to Washington, D.C., “so students and staff can participate in this extraordinary event,” according to a district release.

High school officials were crunching the numbers Thursday morning to determine how much it would cost to send all 116 band members and 32 cheerleaders without burdening them and their families with the cost, especially given that it was so close to the holiday season.

“We are working through that now,” the principal told FOX19 NOW. “Certainly, if anyone wanted to help us, that would be great. It came up so quickly, and with the holidays coming, that has been a concern.”

More: Did JD Vance's hometown vote for him?

Butler County Sheriff Richard Jones said he saw the story about the trip on the FOX19 NOW app and is giving the school a $10,000 check from his campaign fund to cover the trip’s expenses so all band members and cheerleaders can attend.

The longtime sheriff just won his sixth term in office, his third unopposed race.

“When I went to school, I didn’t have any money and definitely couldn’t afford a trip to Washington D.C. So, I’m making sure these kids can participate in an experience of a lifetime,” Sheriff Jones said in a press release.

Sheriff Jones is requesting local businesses to make a donation, big or small, to support these local students so they can make this trip.

When does Donald Trump take office in 20 Everything to know about Inauguration Day

Ohio Senator George Lang (R-West Chester Township) confirms he extended the invitation to the Middie Marching Band this week after a member of Vance’s team contacted him.

“It is a tremendous honor for Middletown and all of Butler County that the Middletown High School Marching Band will be performing in the Trump-Vance inaugural parade next month,” Senator Lang tells FOX19 NOW. “It will be a special day to see one of our own sworn in as Vice President. I’m thrilled that JD has chosen to have his hometown represented on the national stage.”

Senator Lang said he and his wife, Debbie, are donating $1,000. Upon hearing that the sheriff has pledged $10,000, Lang told FOX19 NOW: “He is the best. I love our sheriff. America’s Best Sheriff.”

How you can help support Middletown High School’s marching band

Donations to support the Middie Marching Band’s trip can be made by checks payable to the Middletown City School District and delivered two ways:

  • Mail them to the school district’s central office at 1 Donham Plaza, 4th Floor, Middletown, OH 45042. Please write “Inaugural Parade” in the memo line.
  • In-Person: Drop checks off at the district’s central office during regular business hours.

For questions about other ways to support the band, please get in touch with Middletown City School District at 513-423-0781.

Students and staff will be traveling in buses to Washington D.C., according to the principal.

“We just got confirmation yesterday. It’s been a very quick turnaround. We are thrilled!” she tells FOX19 NOW. “It’s always exciting when one of our own gets to do anything exciting and this is such a rarity to have someone in the White House that attended our school not so long ago. We are all just so excited. The kids are excited. The staff is excited! It’s a good thing!”

Facts about VP-Elect JD Vance

Vance, 40, was born in Middletown in 1984 and was elected vice president of his senior class. He graduated from Middletown High School in 2003 with an honors diploma.

He rose to national prominence in 2016 with the publication of his best-selling memoir “Hillbilly Elegy,” which was adapted into a Netflix film in 2020.

He was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 2022 and began representing the State of Ohio in January 2023.

Vance and his wife, Usha, live in eastern Cincinnati and are the parents of three young children.

  • Vance will become the third-youngest vice president. He is the youngest since 1953, when Richard M. Nixon, who celebrated his 40th birthday just days before the inauguration, was sworn in as Dwight D. Eisenhower’s vice president. John C. Breckinridge, who was 36 when he assumed office in 1857 as James Buchanan’s vice president, holds the record for the nation’s youngest vice president.
  • Vance will be the first millennial vice president
  • He will be the first vice president to have served in the Marine Corps

Facts about Ohio-born vice presidents

Before Vance, the last Ohio-born vice president was Charles Dawes, from Marietta, who served from 1925 to 1929 under President Calvin Coolidge. Before that, there was Charles Fairbanks from Unionville Center, who served from 1905 to 1909, under President Theodore Roosevelt, and Thomas Hendricks from Fultonham, who served in 1885, under President Grover Cleveland from March until his death in November.

While Dawes, Fairbanks, and Hendricks were all born in Ohio, they built their political careers elsewhere before becoming vice president.

Facts about US presidents from Ohio

Ohio is sometimes referred to as the “Mother of Presidents” since seven U.S. presidents were born there:

  • Ulysses S. Grant: Born in Point Pleasant
  • Rutherford Birchard Hayes: Born in Delaware
  • James Abram Garfield: Born in Orange Township, now Moreland Hills
  • Benjamin Harrison: Born in North Bend
  • William McKinley: Born in Niles
  • William Howard Taft: Born in Cincinnati
  • Warren Gamaliel Harding: Born in Corsica, now Blooming Grove
  • William Henry Harrison: Born in Virginia, but settled in Ohio

Enquirer media partner Fox19 provided this report.

headline: Juvenile sentenced for firing gun on North College Hill school grounds
fullText:
(This story has been updated to add comments from the teen's attorney.)

A teen was ordered to spend several years at a youth detention facility for firing guns at North College Hill City Schools in September.

North College Hill police said in a news release Thursday that the male juvenile was ordered last week to remain in a detention facility until his 21st birthday by Hamilton County Juvenile Court Judge Stacey DeGraffenreid.

The juvenile was 17 when the crimes occurred, according to court documents.

Special report: Ohio's juvenile detention system struggles with violence, neglect

The first incident happened on Sept. 6 when gunfire caused a school football game to end early, police said. The second shots-fired call was reported during school dismissal on Sept. 13, the same day the juvenile was arrested.

The teen initially faced seven charges: felonious assault, tampering with evidence, obstructing official business, carrying a concealed weapon, improperly discharging a firearm in a school zone and two counts of receiving stolen property.

He was adjudicated delinquent, which is similar to being found guilty in adult court, for felonious assault, carrying a concealed weapon and one count of receiving stolen property. The other charges were dismissed at the request of the prosecutor as part of the plea agreement.

Court documents state the teen had at one time possessed two different stolen Glock handguns and had run from police officers in addition to firing the weapons.

Prosecutors had filed to have the case moved to adult court, but those motions were withdrawn at the time of the teen's plea.

Hal Arenstein, the teen's attorney, said his client was a North College Hill City Schools student.

Arenstein said he wasn't surprised prosecutors sought to transfer the case to adult court, given the teen was just months from turning 18 at the time of the offenses.

"The evidence was pretty strong against him," Arenstein said, adding that the teen faced a minimum five-year sentence in an adult prison versus the three years he'll spend in a youth facility.

"You don't want a young man like that to be housed with a bunch of adults," he added.

The teen's arrest was not connected with a Sept. 20 shooting during North College Hill High School's football matchup against Woodward.

While police initially said no one was injured in that incident, a Woodward parent told Enquirer media partner Fox19 that his son was grazed by gunfire during the game.

headline: Hazardous leaks happen all the time. Here are 10 Cincinnati-area communities with the most
fullText:
After a railcar leaking the chemical styrene forced an evacuation in Whitewater Township in September, residents started asking questions about the hazardous materials that pass through their community every day.

One of the big questions: How often do chemicals like this leak?

The short answer is it happens a lot. An Enquirer review of U.S. Department of Transportation incident reports found 3,220 reports of hazardous material spills or leaks in the past decade in the Ohio and Kentucky counties of Hamilton, Butler, Warren, Clermont, Kenton, Boone and Campbell.

But that total comes with some big caveats. Incidents that prompt evacuations, like the one in Whitewater Township, or that cause injuries or damage account for about 1% of the total.

The Enquirer’s review found 36 incidents that transportation officials classified as “serious,” with a total cost in damages of about $1.5 million. No severe injuries or deaths were reported in any of those incidents.

According to the reports, most leaks and spills happen during traffic accidents involving trucks carrying hazardous materials, or when containers crack or leak during packing, unloading or transportation by highway, rail or air.

It’s not a surprise, then, that the Cincinnati-area communities with the most hazardous material incidents during the past decade also tend to be transportation hubs.

Here are the 10 communities with the most incidents:

Independence – 1,031

Cincinnati – 582

Erlanger – 392

West Chester Township – 390

Walton – 182

Sharonville – 178

Fairfield – 143

Lebanon – 116

Hamilton – 43

Hebron – 34

Independence tops the list mainly because it’s home to a big Federal Express facility, which handles large numbers of freight and packages every day. It’s a similar story in Walton  (UPS), Erlanger (DHL), Hebron (Federal Express), Hamilton (UPS), Fairfield (Federal Express), Lebanon (Federal Express) and Sharonville (UPS). In West Chester Township and Cincinnati, truck freight terminals and truck accidents on highways appear to be the source of most incidents.

In all those places, the sheer volume of material passing through every day increases the likelihood that, on occasion, something breaks or leaks or gets mishandled. In almost all cases, according to the reports, the material was cleaned up on site without impacting people in the community.

Ground transportation is by far the most likely source of a spill or leak. Incidents involving air travel are mostly limited to facilities in Independence and Hebron, which handle freight from the airport.

As for railcar leaks like the one in Whitewater Township, those are the least common. The Enquirer found rail transportation accounted for 23 incidents, or 0.7% of the total.

Rail incidents, though, were more likely to be expensive.

The data reviewed by The Enquirer only went through Sept. 1 of this year, so it didn’t include damages from the Whitewater Township leak, which still are being determined. But even without it, rail incidents cost almost $400,000 in damages, or about 15% of all damages for all modes of transportation.

headline: Scouting report: Xavier Musketeers gets first road test against TCU Horned Frogs
fullText:
After losing its AP Top 25 ranking, Xavier will get its first taste of playing inside an opponent's home venue when the Musketeers visit the TCU Horned Frogs Thursday in Fort Worth, Texas.

It's the final edition of the Big East-Big 12 Battle as the scheduling alliance between the two conferences expires after this year. Xavier has been great in the event, compiling a 4-1 overall record.

Xavier at TCU

Tip: Thursday, 8 p.m., Schollmaier Arena (8,500)

TV/Radio: ESPN+/700 WLW

Ratings: Xavier is No. 65 in KenPom and TCU is No. 82. In the NCAA's NET Rankings, Xavier is No. 87 and TCU is No. 104. The Musketeers are a 1.5-point favorite over the Horned Frogs, according to BetMGM.

History: Xavier leads the all-time series, 2-1. In the inaugural Big East-Big 12 Battle in Dec. 2019, Xavier pulled out a 67-59 road win over the Horned Frogs.

TCU Horned Frogs scouting report

Record: 4-3

Head coach: Jamie Dixon (164-113 at TCU, ninth season)

Offense: 72.4 PPG

Defense: 64.3 PPG

Overview: TCU has won 20-plus games and gone to the NCAA Tournament in three consecutive seasons under Dixon, but the Horned Frogs lost three November games for the first time since 2009. TCU didn't lose its third game last season until Jan. 6.

Following a 3-0 start, TCU lost on the road to Michigan and went 0-2 with losses to Santa Clara and Colorado State last week in the Acrisure Invitational in Palm Springs, California.

TCU lost three players through the portal but added a half-dozen in a transfer class that ranked in the top 30 in the nation, according to 247Sports.

TCU's biggest get was UNC Wilmington's Trazarien White, but he's gotten off to a slow start offensively at just 9.9 points per game while shooting 42.4% from the field. Leading scorer Frankie Collins (11.3 points per game) is an Arizona State transfer.

Projected lineup

(Pos., Height, Stats)

Frankie Collins (G, 6'1", 11.3 PPG)

Noah Reynolds (G, 6'3", 9.7 PPG)

Brendan Wenzel (G, 6'7", 8.4 PPG)

Trazarien White (F, 6'6", 9.9 PPG)

Ernest Udeh (C, 6'11", 7.8 ppg)

Xavier Musketeers scouting report

Record: 7-1

Head coach: Sean Miller (170-76 at Xavier, eighth season)

Offense: 77.5 PPG

Defense: 66.6 PPG

Projected lineup

(Pos., Height, Stats)

Dayvion McKnight (G, 6'0", 11.4 PPG)

Ryan Conwell (G, 6'4", 16.5 PPG)

Marcus Foster (G, 6'5", 7.5 PPG)

Dailyn Swain (G/F, 6'8", 8 PPG)

Zach Freemantle (F, 6'9", 15.6 PPG)

Players to watch

Jerome Hunter

Leave it to one of the most experienced Musketeers to come up big off the bench. Xavier has struggled with bench production thus far and Sean Miller had seen enough in Sunday's win over South Carolina State.

Dante Maddox Jr. played just one minute in the second half; John Hugley played just six first-half minutes and Trey Green sat the entire second half until coming in cold to help Xavier ice the game at the free-throw line.

"I really feel like you can almost be baited into a false sense of how deep your team is because you're around guy every day and have a good, older group, which we do," Miller said.

Hunter was a different story as he played 27 minutes and finished with 10 points on 5-of-6 shooting and 3 rebounds.

"It was great to see him (Hunter) take that step forward," Miller said. "I think Jerome has separated himself from the guys that don't start. Maybe we start to look at the possibility of starting him. He's gonna play starter's minutes."

Keys to a Xavier victory over TCU

Go back to Dayton

Xavier's only experience on the road this year was a masterclass, it's just too bad it didn't count. Over a month ago, Xavier went to UD Arena in front of over 13,000 fans and beat Dayton in a charity exhibition, 98-74.

On that night, Xavier shot nearly 60% from the field, buried 12 three-pointers and had six players, including three off the bench, go for double figures.

Xavier can ill-afford to be fazed by the bright lights in a game that could turn into a Quadrant 1 win down the road. But it's a tall task. TCU is 4-0 at home so far and 41-12 since the start of the 2021-22 season.

Xavier's ball security will be tested again

If there's one paramount concern for Xavier over the last two games, it's been turnovers. The Musketeers have committed 35 over the last two games and it has thrown off an offense that had previously been trending in the right direction.

TCU's offense has struggled thus far but the defense can still get stops. The Horned Frogs are No. 32 in KenPom in defensive efficiency and have thrived with takeaways, ranking No. 34 in turnover percentage. Xavier wants to play fast and free, but if they can't do it cleanly, it throws a wrench in the offensive gameplan.

headline: JD Vance's mother asked Middletown to honor him. Not everyone is on board
fullText:
JD Vance's mother wants her son's hometown to show him some recognition – a proposal that drew both support and skepticism from the city council.

Beverly Aikins, Vance's mother, addressed Middletown City Council on Tuesday night and asked the city to put up a sign to publicly recognize her son as the vice president-elect.

"I am just here because I am JD Vance's mother and as you know he is our new vice president-elect and he thinks of Middletown as his home," Aikins said during the meeting's public comment. "I still live here and his sister still lives in Middletown. He's got two nieces who live here and I just think it would be really nice if we could acknowledge that this is his hometown and put up some signs."

"He graduated from Middletown High School," she added. "He comes back here frequently to visit me and take me to dinner, and I humbly request that."

Some Middletown leaders want 'Hillbilly Elegy' author to be honored

Vance graduated from Middletown High School in 2003. He wrote about his upbringing in the southwestern Ohio city in "Hillbilly Elegy."

Scotty Robertson, vice president of the Middletown Area Ministerial Alliance, said he also wanted to see city recognition for Vance.

"Any time someone from our hometown is elected to such a high office, that's something to celebrate," he said.

Robertson acknowledged "there are many that have been made nervous and afraid" by Vance and Donald Trump winning the election, such as immigrants and those in the LGBTQ community, and said their "voices need to be heard," too.

What Middletown city leaders said about Vance

Council, which is made up of five nonpartisan members, was divided on the issue. Councilman Paul Lolli agreed there should be a sign or street named after Vance. He said the city's communication team should have recognized Vance weeks ago on its official social media pages.

The city's school district made a post about Vance becoming the next vice president hours after the election results were finalized.

In response, the city's official Facebook page posted a statement congratulating Vance on Wednesday.

Councilman Steve West, who attended Vance's Middletown campaign rally in July, said it was "unacceptable" that Vance hadn't been publicly recognized by the city since Vance and Donald Trump won the election.

What if Vance and Trump create 'havoc?'

Councilwoman Jennifer Carter, who previously told The Enquirer she doesn't like Vance's polices, said the vice president-elect should have to prove himself before a sign or street is named after him, as other Middletown natives have done.

"Why can't we wait and see what he does?" she said. "If he gets into office and creates havoc, with him and Trump sending people out of the country... all of the things they said they wanted to do. If all of these things happen, we're still saying yay?"

Councilman Paul Horn agreed with recognizing Vance as a Middletown native.

"What if he really does bad things? That's how you remove signs – when people screw up," he said.

Mayor Elizabeth Slamka acknowledged the issue is polarizing, but said plans for signs recognizing Vance are "in the works," as well as a feature on him in the city's January newsletter.

A majority of Middletown voters, 62%, supported Vance and Trump in November.

  • White: 78.4% (80.6%).
  • Black: 11.8% (13.4%).
  • Asian: 0.8% (2.8%).
  • Hispanic: 4.3% (4.8%).
  • Foreign-born: 2.9% (4.9%).
  • Home ownership rate: 53% (66.8%).
  • Median home value: $135,200 ($183,300).
  • Bachelor's degree or higher: 16.1% (30.4%).
  • Median household income: $50,457 ($66,990).
  • Persons in poverty: 19.2% (13.4%).

headline: One of Southern Living's cutest Christmas towns is within driving distance of Cincinnati
fullText:
A picturesque, winter wonderland is just a short drive away from Cincinnati.

Danville, Kentucky was listed this week among "The 18 Cutest Christmas Towns In The South," by Southern Living.

The magazine recognized Danville, known for its historic firsts, for its plentiful historic destinations, festive displays, and holiday activities. Southern Living highlighted the city for its "Small Town Christmas," a low-cost holiday event that all families can enjoy.

Here's everything you need to know to plan your Kentucky getaway.

How far is Danville from Cincinnati?

Danville, "The City of Firsts," is approximately 37 miles south of Lexington.

Just over 120 miles away, the historic city is about a 2-hour drive from Cincinnati.

Where to stay during your Danville, getaway

These historic hotels are fit for a charming weekend stay.

  • Historic Boone Tavern Hotel and Restaurant: This historic hotel was built in 1909. The Boone Tavern was based on designs by the New York architectural firm of Cady & See. boonetavernhotel.com. 100 Main St., Berea.
  • Beaumont Inn: The historical home includes award-winning culinary experiences. beaumontinn.com. 638 Beaumont Inn Drive, Harrodsburg.
  • The Inn at Shaker Village: Named as a top hidden travel destination by BBC News, guests can stay in rooms, suites and cottages. shakervillageky.org. 3501 Lexington Road, Harrodsburg.

Add these holiday events to your Danville itinerary

  • Jacobs Hall Museum Christmas Tours, Dec. 13 and Dec. 14. Take a candle-lit tour of Jacobs Hall Museum. Tickets are required. 303 S. Second St., Danville.
  • A Merry Christmas with Brass, Dec. 12 at 10 a.m. and 7 p.m. The Dallas Brass will perform Christmas tunes along with the Boyle County High School Band behind images of colored lights and snowy landscapes. 315 Cunningham Way, Danville.
  • Jingle Through Junction City Christmas Parade, Dec. 14 at 5 p.m. Kick off the holiday season at the Junction City Christmas Parade. The festive afternoon will be packed with holiday cheer, including colorful floats, local vendors and family-friendly fun. 726 West Shelby Street, Junction City.

  • Danville Boyle County Humane Society Holiday Party, Dec. 12 at 5 p.m. Join the local humane society for an evening partying with the pooches. 778 N Danville Bypass, Danville.

headline: What should you do if you lose power in the cold? What to do during a winter power outage
fullText:
Frigid temperatures, cold and snowfall left thousands of Ohioans without power in parts of Akron, Cleveland, and other parts of Northeast Ohio Thursday morning.

The National Weather Service issued a lake-effect snow warning this week for several Northeast Ohio counties. The forecast calls for cold temperatures, winds as high as 50 mph, and snow accumulations between 6 and 10 inches. Power outages from the weather have already hit thousands of residents throughout the state. FirstEnergy, AEP and Duke Energy power outage maps all show customers without power this morning.

Here's what to do if you lose power during severe winter weather.

Lose power? These Ohio outage maps will tell when the lights will be back. How to check

Report the power outage to your electric company

Ohio Public Utilities Commission advises residents to call your servicer if you don't have power. It's still possible to report an outage without speaking with a live person. You can also head to the electric company's website to send an online report. Some companies offer live outage maps to track when power should be restored.

Keep warm if you lose power in cold weather

During a power outage, close doors and windows, dress in layers, and bundle up with blankets to stay warm. Don't use gas stoves or ovens, kerosene space heaters, grills, or other open-flame heat sources for warmth, as it presents the risk of carbon monoxide gas, which is deadly and odorless. The Weather Channel suggests keeping certain heating elements (generators, camp stoves or charcoal grills) outdoors and used at least 20 feet from windows and doors.

Don't leave lit candles unattended, and keep them out of reach of children and pets.

Unplug major appliances, electronics during a cold weather power outage

Computers and televisions should be unplugged to avoid a power surge once power is restored. The Weather Channel says to leave one lamp on so that you know when the power comes back on.

The site also recommends preserving your cell phone battery and texting instead of calling to ensure your phone lines remain open.

Know the signs of cold weather-related medical emergencies

Knowing the signs of frostbite and hypothermia is important during a winter power outage:

  • Frostbite: Losing feeling and color in the fingers, earlobes and the tip of the nose.
  • Hypothermia: Uncontrollable shivering, memory loss, disorientation, slurred speech, and drowsiness.

Call 911 if someone is displaying these symptoms.

The best way to handle outages in the wintertime is to stay prepared year-round. Plan for winter weather ahead of time, invest in an emergency supply kit, and inspect your home thoroughly.

headline: 'I'm reminded of him every single day.' Moeller football honors Gerry Faust in title quest
fullText:
Archbishop Moeller High School head coach Bert Bathiany has a painting of legendary coach Gerry Faust in his office, one of many memorabilia honoring him at the school.

Faust, who died in November, won the first five state championships in the school's history, winning them in six years from 1975-80. That was part of a legendary 19-season career in which his teams won 178 games against only 23 losses.

“I’m reminded of him every single day,” Bathiany said of Faust. “He exemplifies everything we want from our students here. He’s the ultimate Man of Moeller. Man of faith. You can’t talk about Gerry Faust without saying how strong his faith is.”

Bathiany, seeking his first state title as head coach, has faith in his Crusaders, who will try to bring home the 10th state championship in team history, the first since 2013. They will face Powell Olentangy Liberty (13-2) in the Ohio High School Athletic Association Division I state title game at 7:30 p.m. Friday at Canton’s Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium.

More: Reactions: Gerry Faust remembered as legend, coach at Moeller HS, Notre Dame and Akron

Several of Faust’s family members are expected to attend the game Friday night.

“Our guys know about Coach Faust,” Bathiany said. “But even in his passing, one positive out of this is we get to talk about him again and really remind our guys that he laid the foundation. He laid the foundation for this football program and we're reaping the benefits of it.”

Olentangy Liberty is located in Powell, which is a northern suburb of the Columbus area. To beat Olentangy Liberty, the Crusaders will try to make new history with one of the best quarterbacks in Ohio.

More: Here's how Anderson's football team matches up with Avon in DII state championship game

Who is Mr. Football finalist Matt Ponatoski?

Liberty head coach John Sansbury said his team has not faced an offense like Moeller’s or a quarterback like Matt Ponatoski since last season.

Ponatoski is one of eight finalists for this year’s Ohio Mr. Football award, which is decided and voted on by the Ohio Prep Sports Media Association and will be announced Thursday afternoon. A top Division I recruit in football and baseball, the junior quarterback is one of two underclassmen on the list.

“He has complete control of this offense,” Bathiany said. “He has a complete understanding of this offense. In the offseason, the message to him was we want you to be Peyton Manning. We want you to be Tom Brady. The offense goes through you and you're going to have a lot of say in where the ball is going to go. He makes a lot of decisions on the field and we just put the ball in his hands. And we trust him. We trust him fully.”

Ponatoski has had a record-setting campaign with 4,075 passing yards and 56 touchdowns, including 431 yards and six TD passes to six different receivers in last week’s state semifinals. He has only thrown three interceptions and completed 70.7 percent of his passes.

Five times he has thrown for five TDs or more, and eight times he has thrown for 300 yards or more. Last week’s 431 is a season high.

Ponatoski is the fifth Southwest Ohio quarterback to throw for 4,000 yards in a season. Entering the season, that mark had been reached 33 times in Ohio history.

Entering the season, 13 QBs in Ohio history have thrown for more than 56 TDs in a season, making Ponatoski currently tied for 14th. He has tied Western Brown’s Drew Novak (2021) for the most by any Southwest Ohio passer in a season.

“The cool thing is when we get to the sideline, he's on the headset right away,” Bathiany said. “Usually he's seeing something and he's right on point. When we talk about something on the headset, about something we want to adjust to, he's already thinking about that. There's always a lot of communication, a lot of conversation about what he likes. Plays that he likes to run and we give him a lot of responsibility.”

Ponatoski threw a 99-yard TD pass to Jovan Love last week, marking the fourth time a Cincinnati duo has accomplished that, the first time since 2007.  That was one of five TDs Moeller scored on the first play of a drive, as the Crusaders had several pass plays of more than 50 yards.

“It’s a huge challenge for our team,” Sansbury said. “Obviously at this point, every team's going to be good, but their offense especially has been explosive. You know the quarterback's outstanding. They’ve got big, tall receivers and tight ends. They got a big offensive line, they got a strong running back, so it's a complete offense and we're going to have our hands full for sure. We’ve definitely played some good quarterbacks this year, but this kid’s pretty special.”

Who are Moeller QB Matt Ponatoski's top targets?

Moeller’s receiving corps is as deep and diverse as any team in the state, if not more.

Deep threats Jovan Love (54 catches, 934 yards, 13 TDs) and Matthew Fogler (39, 884, 16) are two top targets on the outside. Bruising, athletic tight ends Cooper McCutchan (32, 534, 7) and Sam Hamilton (22, 272, 5) are big targets getting Division I offers. Roman Mason (38, 376, 3), Carson Khayo (37, 438, 3) and Landen Adams (27, 333, 6) can play inside but get big gains, too.

Tyler Josleyn (754 rushing yards, 8 TDs) leads a running back corps by committee that has effectively filled the void left by 2023 Mr. Football Jordan Marshall, now a freshman returning kickoffs for the Michigan Wolverines. Moeller rushes for 130 yards per game on 4.6 yards per attempt.

Moeller has six senior offensive linemen with a lot of starting experience.

“Matt gets so much attention all the time, but our offensive line has been unbelievable this year,” Bathiany said. “They’ve kept him clean throughout the year. Big running lanes. I can't even count how many times we haven't had any sacks in the game, which has been huge. All of that goes to the offensive line and Matt making good decisions, but Matt gives credit to them all the time.”

The Olentangy Liberty defense has been strong this year

Liberty’s defense allows 12 points per game, 15 or fewer in 12 of its 15 games. Bathiany said the Patriots’ defense limits big plays and forces turnovers, especially at crucial moments in the playoffs.

“I think they do a really good job of putting their players in a position where they can just play fast, which I think is the No. 1 job as a coach,” Bathiany said. “I really admire their effort, their attitude, their swagger. They have an edge to them that I really appreciate, so we’ve got our work cut out for us.”

Who are Powell Olentangy Liberty football's top players on offense?

Sansbury said his Patriots have 31 seniors, many of whom have contributed to the varsity program since they were sophomores.

One of them is senior quarterback Andrew Leonard, who is also a Mr. Football finalist.

Leonard, the Central District Offensive Player of the Year, completed 199 of 282 passes for 2,915 yards and 36 touchdowns with just five interceptions while also rushing for 678 yards and five touchdowns. A three-year starter, he also led the school’s baseball and hockey teams to the regional tournament and has been recruited by smaller Division I programs.

Liberty has several star players who played baseball and/or hockey or on the DI state-champion lacrosse team last spring.

Bathiany said Leonard can make things happen at QB and the Patriots have targets who can make explosive plays.

Running back Jake Struck is a multi-sport athlete who can do almost anything on the football field. He has 1,666 total yards from scrimmage and 27 touchdowns. An Ohio State University commit in lacrosse, he had five goals against St. Xavier in the 2024 state final.

“We're going to try and give (Struck) as many opportunities to get the ball, especially in space,” Sansbury said. “He's essential to our offense. You know, as all of our players are, but he can make some special things happen.”

Moeller allows 17 points per game. Northwestern signee Jonah Hayes and Jacob Cravens are the leading tacklers. Roman Mason has five of the team’s 20 interceptions. The Crusaders' defense has bent at times, but they've had more flexibility with Moeller's explosive offense.

headline: Zac Taylor provides injury updates ahead of Bengals at Cowboys
fullText:
Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor provided an injury update on several players ahead of the team’s next game against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday night.

The Bengals placed kicker Evan McPherson on injured reserve and linebacker Logan Wilson is also expected to land on IR after undergoing a procedure on his knee on Thursday.

Evan McPherson Bengals injury update

Taylor provided further explanation of when McPherson and Wilson got hurt and what led to the decision to end their respective seasons with five games to play. McPherson came out of Cincinnati’s most recent loss with a sore groin. When they underwent further evaluation the next day, it was apparent the injury was more severe.

“You know, it just felt sore during the game,” Taylor said of McPherson. “But again, nothing that a lot of guys don’t feel. So just felt like keep it warm, keep going. Then the next morning, it turned out to be more significant.”

Logan Wilson Bengals injury update

As for Wilson, the knee injury has been lingering. Taylor explained Wilson was dealing with knee soreness prior to the bye week and hoped he would feel better with a week of rest. That didn’t prove to be the case and that’s why he was unable to play against the Steelers. The Bengals’ medical staff and Wilson then decided the best course of action moving forward was a surgical procedure that will likely end his season.

“He came out of the bye week and thought it would feel better,” Taylor said. “And it didn’t. With a week of rest, he was really hopeful that, ‘I’ll be much better.’ Then came back that Monday, really that weekend, and it wasn’t feeling like it should. And then got to the week and didn’t get any better, last week, even with giving him time off. So, we sat him out and then this is where we’re at.”

Orlando Brown Jr. Bengals injury update

Starting left tackle Orlando Brown Jr. is unlikely to play against the Cowboys as he continues to deal with a knee/fibula injury. Taylor wouldn’t rule Brown Jr. out to return this season but it doesn’t sound like it will happen any time soon.

With Brown Jr. out for the Bengals’ upcoming game in Dallas, Cody Ford will swing back out to start at left tackle and Cordell Volson will resume his starting job at left guard. Taylor opted to start Ford in place of Volson last week in the loss to the Steelers.

At 4-8 riding a three-game losing streak, the Bengals are hoping to turn their season around against the Cowboys on "Monday Night Football."

“So it's a tough test for our guys and exciting to be on Monday Night Football, and I think that's what this team needs right now,” Taylor said. “Put us back in the spotlight, have an opportunity to overcome and find a win and get on the right stretch here.”

headline: Who is Jared Isaacman? Career, net worth of Donald Trump's pick to head NASA
fullText:
High school dropout turned billionaire Jared Isaacman has collaborated twice with SpaceX to go on missions to outer space—but for a good cause. Now he could be the next head of NASA under President Donald Trump.

Who is Jared Isaacman? Here’s what to know. 

Who is Jared Isaacman?

Jared Isaacman is the CEO of Shift4, a retail payment processing company, according to the Polaris Program. 

In September, Isaacman teamed with SpaceX to perform the first private spacewalk, a high-risk endeavor reserved for professional astronauts, according to the Associated Press. 

Isaacman is an experienced pilot and astronaut with enough flight hours earned to be able to fly fighter jets, according to Forbes. He raised more than $100 million for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital to fight childhood cancer, according to the website NASA Space Flight. 

What is Jared Isaacman’s net worth? How did he get so rich?

According to Forbes, Isaacman’s net worth hit $1.4 billion after he took Shift4 public. The publication estimates he has a $1.7 billion fortune now.

Where is Jared Isaacman from?

Isaacman is from New Jersey. He attended high school in Far Hills in Somerset County, New Jersey, but later dropped out at 16 to pursue a full-time job in computer technical support and repairs, Forbes writes. 

How did Jared Isaacman’s career begin? Shift4 Payments, Draken International founder

In 1999, Isaacman founded his retail payment processing company in his parents’ basement. Over the years, his company's name evolved from United Bank Card to Harbortouch and, finally, Shift4Payments. 

By 2020, Shift4Payments processed $200 billion in payments annually for over a third of the US’s hotels and restaurants. 

Additionally, Isaacman co-founded aerospace and defense company Draken International, essentially a private air force that trains pilots for the United States Armed Forces, per Forbes. He later sold that company to Blackstone, a real estate, investing and private equity firm with a commitment to serving veterans.
