headline: Losing to Michigan was big. Ohio State football winning national title would be bigger
fullText:
Dispatch sports editor Brian White perfectly captured the mood of Ohio State fans Saturday when he wrote that the OSU football season did not die at the hands of Michigan, but it sure felt like it.

Totally agree. But while eulogizing the first season (the 11 games before playing the Wolverines) and lowering the casket on the second (the one-game season that is Michigan) OSU fans also should remember to pray for the third season that begins on Dec. 20 or 21.

The pre-Michigan regular season died Nov. 23 with a win against Indiana, making the Buckeyes 10-1. The lone loss was to Oregon, by one point in rowdy Autzen Stadium. Time to offer condolences, agreeing it lived a good life. Not perfect, but worthy of admiration.

The Michigan single-game season passed away at 3:32 pm Saturday with an embarrassing 13-10 loss in shell-shocked Ohio Stadium, which doubled as a funeral home. “We gather here to remember …” What? That the Buckeyes were too talented to bite the dust? That they did not deserve to perish in a hail of horrible play calling? That it was a crying shame that an offense once so vibrant looked so withered at the end? 

Now comes the 12-team playoff third season, in which OSU has yet to kick the bucket, even if more than a few fans have buried the Buckeyes alive. Granted, the prognosis may not be all rainbows and lollipops, but a remarkable recovery is possible. 

Ohio State football: Day takes responsibility for Michigan loss, looks ahead to CFP

The question I pose to Ohio State fans: Which season matters most? I contend the correct answer is No. 3, at least historically speaking, which means fans should stop bellyaching and begin embracing the immediate future. 

Hear me out. The Michigan game is huge, no doubt about it. Winning it brings a yearlong right to brag and boast. Defeating the Wolverines, something that has not happened since 2019, puts a bounce in the step of those for whom scarlet and gray are more than colors. They are the hue and tone of cultural identity. Scarlet and gray represent winning, except for the past four Saturdays of Thanksgiving week, which is more than can be said for the brown and orange and black and orange of Ohio’s two NFL teams. Not that you can’t wear those colors proudly, but no one currently will confuse you for a winner if you do. 

But Michigan is not the end-all. Not anymore. It used to be that beating UM meant a trip to the Rose Bowl. Later, as college football diversified, which is a nice way of saying it got greedier, beating the Wolverines usually was a prerequisite to playing in a better bowl. The creation of a playoff and then expansion whittled away at the beat-Michigan-or-bust reality. The Buckeyes made the four-team playoff in 2022 after losing to UM and are about to qualify for the 12-team field despite the debacle that saw them upset by a 19.5-point underdog.

So while Ohio State can say its No. 1 goal is beating Michigan, and certainly beating Blue remains a high priority, in the long view it is not as important as winning a national championship.

Want proof? Without using Google, which team won the 1956 Ohio State-Michigan game? Don’t know? Can’t remember? How about 1966? Don’t care? (Answer: OSU lost both). But what happened in 1957 and 1968? The Buckeyes won national titles that still get talked about. Ditto 1942, 1954, 2002 and 2014. The point? National championships resonate across generations. They last.

What does that have to do with OSU losing to Michigan on Saturday? Just this: In 50 years, few fans will recall that Will Howard threw two interceptions against the Wolverines and coach Ryan Day and offensive coordinator Chip Kelly spit the bit with their play calling. But everyone will remember where they were if Ohio State wins the next four games to claim the national championship. 

Flip it to when Ohio State won the rivalry game. The Buckeyes outlasting Michigan 14-9 in 2002 and outslugging the Wolverines 42-28 in 2014 was fun stuff, but did it give OSU fans a greater sense of satisfaction than upsetting Miami in the BCS title game and Oregon for the CFP championship? Truth serum says no.

Don’t misunderstand. Losing to Michigan should not be downplayed, but a bigger prize that brings longer-lasting joy to fans remains within reach. Will Ohio State win it all? Maybe, maybe not. But the Buckeyes still can win it all. And to wish they won’t, in hopes that the school fires Day, is as foolish as running the ball into the strength of Michigan’s defense.

Season One is dead and buried. Season Two got swallowed up by the grave Saturday. There is plenty of time to grieve it, but not while Season Three remains alive. Instead, jump on the playoff bandwagon. It sure beats following a hearse.

headline: Ohio House passes bill to protect unconscious patients from abuse after Dispatch series
fullText:
Legislation to better protect patients that was introduced as a result of sexually abusive doctors is a step closer to becoming law.

The Ohio House of Representatives on Wednesday passed House Bill 89, sending it to the state Senate for consideration. Eighty representatives voted in favor of the bill, none voted against it and 19 representatives did not cast a vote.

If passed by the legislature's upper chamber and signed into law by the governor, the bill would prohibit medical providers from conducting intimate exams unless medically necessary or for certain other exceptions.

Read More: State medical board failed to protect Ohioans from doctors' sexual misconduct

While most patients may be unaware, such exams have in the past been allowed to occur at teaching hospitals, said state Rep. Brett Hudson Hillyer, a Republican from Uhrichsville who co-sponsored the bill alongside state Rep. Munira Abdullahi, a Columbus Democrat.

"This is an intimate exam and should be therefore appropriately consented to," Hillyer said.

By voting to pass the bill, Abdullahi said representatives signaled they would "take a stand for patients' rights." She went on to say the bill protects the trust and dignity of patients in Ohio's health care system.

"These are deeply personal and invasive procedures, and patients deserve to have their bodily autonomy respected, even when they are unable to speak for themselves," Abdullahi said.

House Bill 89 was introduced after The Dispatch's "Preying On Patients" investigation into how the State Medical Board of Ohio handled accusations of sexual misconduct by medical professionals.

The Dispatch launched its investigation after it was revealed the medical board had previously failed to take action against Dr. Richard Strauss, an Ohio State University physician accused of sexually abusing at least 177 former students and athletes during his time there.

The Dispatch investigation found that Strauss was no outlier in his abuse.

From 1980 through 2022, at least 256 Ohio doctors have faced disciplinary action for sexual misconduct. Of those doctors, 199 sexually abused or harassed 449 patients, The Dispatch found.

Those figures don't include an unknown number of victims who have never come forward or complaints that in the past were not fully investigated.

Another bill designed to safeguard patients that was reintroduced after The Dispatch's investigation was unanimously passed by the Ohio Senate earlier this year.

Senate Bill 109, proposed by State Sen. Bob Hackett, R-London, and approved by Ohio senators on April 24, would require doctors on probation for sexual misconduct to notify their patients in writing. It would also allow the State Medical Board of Ohio to act more quickly when a physician is accused of sexual misconduct and would require prosecuting attorneys to notify the board if a doctor is convicted or pleads guilty to a specific felony or misdemeanor in court.

Senate Bill 109 had its fourth hearing before the Ohio House's Criminal Justice Committee on Tuesday.

"Ohioans were not happy with what happened with Dr. Strauss and so we gave the medical board more authority on this," Hackett previously told The Dispatch. "Everybody knows it's a situation where we need to move quicker. Dr. Strauss abused a number of citizens, and we definitely don't want that to happen again."

headline: Columbus, Franklin County face tighter budgets in 2025 as federal COVID dollars dry up
fullText:
The Columbus city budget next year will be tighter than it has been in over a decade, warns Nick Bankston, chair of the Columbus City Council Finance Committee.

Bankston told The Dispatch Wednesday before the council's first hearing on the 2025 general fund budget that this could mean less city funding for things like nonprofits serving residents and the city not filling as many staff vacancies.

For the first time since 2009, Mayor Andrew J. Ginther's proposed $1.23-billion budget for next year doesn't include any money for the city's rainy day fund or the 27th pay period fund (meant for when there is an extra pay period as happens about every 11 years).

Ginther's proposed spending plan also calls for using all $19.5 million in the city's basic services fund, which has previously been used to cover city functions when unexpected expenses arise throughout the year.

According to Bankston, this crunch is due to multiple factors: federal COVID pandemic relief dollars are going away, three of the city's major unions (including police and fire) negotiated new contracts this year with raises, costs for everything are up and income tax revenue (about 80% of the city's revenue) has not increased as much as it has in previous years.

These challenges are not unique to Columbus, Bankston said. He said he doesn't want to be alarmist but wants to be transparent about the tough decisions that lie ahead.

"This is not doom and gloom," Bankston said. "The city of Columbus is doing fine."

Despite tight budget, Columbus City Council to vote on creating 'weed fund' to separate marijuana tax revenue from general fund

The city will collect an estimated 2.3% more in income tax revenue in 2024 than it did last year. But that's not keeping pace with the growing city's rising costs as it has in past years, Bankston said. In 2023, tax revenue increased by 5.2% and in 2022, it went up by 4.4%.

During the pandemic, the city received a windfall of about $510 million in federal recovery dollars. The city used those dollars to substitute revenue, to support nonprofits and to create programs for youth and violence prevention.

For example, this year, the city gave $9.4 million in federal dollars to the Community Shelter Board, which operates the county's homeless shelters, on top of the $5.5 million allocated in the 2024 budget. Unless revenue outperforms estimates, Bankston said the shelter board will not receive as much in 2025.

More city news: Columbus plans to clear six homeless camps

Even without adding to it, the city's rainy day fund will have an estimated $105 million at the end of 2025. The 27th pay period fund has $14.5 million and the next year with 27 pay periods is 2032. This would be the first year since the fund was established in 1994 that the city has not added to it.

The City Council will vote early next year on the 2025 budget. Bankston said his goal is to vote on the final budget in February.

Before then, the city could face even more budget headwinds if the Ohio Senate passes legislation to require cities to pay more into police pensions. A bill passed the Ohio House Wednesday.

Franklin County also returning to 'fiscal normalcy'

Franklin County is also being forced to tighten its belt a bit. The county commissioners are currently weighing county Administrator Kenneth N. Wilson's proposed $2.2-billion budget for the county.

Wilson told The Dispatch that the community will have to adjust to a return to fiscal normalcy now that the federal COVID dollars are gone. The county received about $430 million in federal pandemic funds. All federal COVID money must be appropriated by the end of this year, although it can be spent next year.

Unlike the city, the county didn't use COVID money to cover salaries or ongoing expenses. Wilson said the county tried to use the dollars on one-time capital improvement projects like donating $7 million to the Mid-Ohio Food Collective for more freezers. The commissioners stressed to nonprofits receiving COVID dollars these funds would not be available going forward, although some likely used the money for salaries.

"We tried to have as much impact with those dollars as we could because it was a once-in-a-generation infusion of money," Wilson said.

headline: 6 takeaways: Devin Royal, Ohio State looking for answers after decisive loss at Maryland
fullText:
COLLEGE PARK, Md. – The thumping beat of “Rock And Roll (Part 2)” pulsed through the deafening speakers at the Xfinity Center. The longtime staple of jock jams and sporting events for longer than anyone in Maryland’s student section has been alive, more commonly known as “The Hey Song,” was among the last things Ohio State’s players heard as they made their way to the court.

The undulating crowd of students, enjoying the free white T-shirts given out as part of a whiteout push for the Big Ten opener, added a PG-rated threat to the instrumental refrain.

“We’re gonna beat the (bleep) outta you,” they chanted.

The bleeped word rhymes with bell, but insert any curse word in its place and it would have accurately summarized what was to come. In an arena that has been downright disrespectful to the Buckeyes since the Terrapins joined the Big Ten, Maryland turned what was expected to be a litmus test between two conference higher-ups into a laugher by halftime. By the time Micah Parrish and Ja’Kobi Gillespie traded missed 3-pointers to close the half, the Terrapins held a commanding 50-17 lead that was every bit as decisive as the 33-point margin.

The second half was better for the Buckeyes. They fell behind by 40 in the first five minutes after halftime but outscored the Terrapins 42-33 in the final 20 minutes to make the final score look more respectable. Officially, it’s an 83-59 loss for Ohio State, but it’s hard to make too much of the Buckeyes closing the game by outscoring their hosts 36-20 in the final 15 minutes.

Maryland never trailed. It led by double figures for the final 33:04 and by 20 points for the final 26:39 while handing the Buckeyes a second consecutive loss. And unlike in last Friday’s 91-90 home overtime loss to Pitt, this one was never particularly close.

“I think we prepared very well,” sophomore forward Devin Royal told The Dispatch outside the visitors’ locker room. “We knew what they was going to do. We knew what coming out was going to happen, but we just didn’t play hard enough. We didn’t come out early enough and play hard enough. We didn’t have that aggressiveness that Ohio State plays with. Second half, we did better, but first half, we just came out very lackadaisical. They was making they shots and we wasn’t taking accountability.

“I feel like it’s just aggressiveness. We didn’t have the aggressiveness that we should’ve, but second half we did come out with more aggressiveness but it was such a big lead.”

Here are six takeaways from Ohio State’s latest loss at Maryland.

Ohio State Buckeyes: Join the Ohio State Sports Insider text group with Bill Rabinowitz, Joey Kaufman Adam Jardy

Ohio State was never in this game

Not exactly a groundbreaking statement, but this was never really a game. At the first media timeout, Maryland already held a 12-6 lead thanks to a 3-for-3 start from 3-point range. The Terrapins’ shots weren’t necessarily contested, a sign of what was to come.

“I thought we lacked real urgency and pressure defensively,” coach Jake Diebler said. “It was uncharacteristic of who we’ve been. They were able to look at us and hit some early 3s that gave them some momentum, and really there wasn’t even any action ran or anything to get those shots. We’ve got to be much better pressuring the ball, which we’ve worked on.”

Maryland would go 4 for 22 (18.2%) from 3 the rest of the way, but it didn’t matter. The Terrapins shot 55.9% during the first half, nearly making as many shots (19 for 34) as Ohio State attempted (6 for 21, 28.6%).

By the time the Buckeyes tried to draw any sort of line in the sand, the final outcome was decided. Both Royal and Diebler said nothing was amiss in the preparation leading into the game, or at least anything that would portend such a dreadful start to the game.

“The disappointing thing was we practiced really well these last couple days, and we came out and we just weren’t playing with the same urgency that we had been playing with really all season and practicing with,” Diebler said. “And it took too long to get it back. We tried different lineups, tried different guys to give us some energy and give us a little pop, but then we were turning it over too much and it’s hard to keep pace when you’re turning it over.”

Turnovers were again a problem

It’s not a secret that Maryland likes to pressure and turn teams over. The Terrapins entered the game with a 99-point advantage in points off turnovers, the second-highest margin among power conference teams.

At halftime, the Terrapins had forced 12 Ohio State turnovers, committed only two of their own and held an 18-0 advantage in points off of turnovers. All eight Buckeyes to play at least two first-half minutes had at least one turnover with Meechie Johnson, Bruce Thornton and Royal all committing two apiece.

“I thought our turnovers and our ability to pressure the ball and keep the ball out of the paint on the other side was a bigger issue tonight,” Diebler said. “That’s disappointing because I think we’ve been better at that.”

Ohio State’s depth is lacking

When his first full roster was assembled, Diebler pointed to Ohio State’s overall depth as a critical component to his team’s chances for success this year. Technically, the Buckeyes have 14 scholarship players, with sixth-year transfer guard Ques Glover a late addition as a walk-on whose scholarship costs are being paid by an NIL deal with THE Foundation.

He watched his fifth straight game from the bench after suffering an ankle injury in the Nov. 15 loss at Texas A&M. He was questionable for a few games but has been listed as out on the last two pregame availability reports. For this game, he was again joined by freshman Colin White, who suffered an ankle injury on a hard foul late in the Nov. 25 home win against Green Bay and has now missed two straight games.

Sophomore center Aaron Bradshaw is still not participating in team activities as the university investigates an alleged domestic incident at his off-campus apartment, marking the fourth straight game the Buckeyes have been without their projected starting center.

Royal, who led the Buckeyes with 18 points and nine rebounds in 24:40, had to leave the game with a cramping issue that also impacted him against Pitt. Freshman John Mobley Jr., who had all 15 of his points after halftime, exited the game in visible pain with 50 seconds remaining.

“That’s probably been the bigger issue for us is some of these kind of nagging injuries,” Diebler said. “Some of the sickness that guys have been dealing with. We’ve got an unbelievable medical staff and they’re working so hard to help guys get back to feeling really good, and I think our guys deserve some credit for battling through some stuff. We’ll get a thorough evaluation of where we’re at before practice (Thursday). We need to get healthy, because we need everybody.

“The strength of this team heading into the start of the season was our depth, and it’s being tested and challenged right now. We’ll get it figured out. We have to.”

Devin Royal was the lone positive

One player seemed to execute Ohio State’s gameplan during the first half, and that was the sophomore power forward from Pickerington. In 14:36, Royal had 10 first-half points on 4-of-5 shooting.

The rest of the Buckeyes were 2 for 16 from the floor and combined for seven points. Was he trying to set an example for his teammates?

“Yeah, I was,” he said. “I was trying to get the team back to where we need to be, trying to talk to them. At the end of the day, you’ve got to get out of your own self’s head. Me doing that, being aggressive, only does so much. Once everybody gets out of each other’s head, we’ll be good.”

By the end, Royal had a team-high 18 points on 8-of-14 (57.1%) shooting. Ohio State’s other eight players to attempt a shot were a combined 14 for 44 (31.8%). The cramping issue prevented Royal from posting a double-double as he finished with nine rebounds.

He’s now scored in double figures in five straight games, averaging 16.6 points and 8.6 rebounds during that stretch.

“(He brought) aggressiveness and physicality,” Diebler said. “I thought he executed the game plan well. We talked about driving them and getting into the paint, and he did it. We wanted to play inside-out by driving it and I thought he did a really good job. He was one of the best in the first half of attacking their press with aggressiveness. I think Devin now has been really consistent and it’s going to be really important for him that he continues to do that.”

The Xfinity Center is kryptonite to Ohio State

Regardless of preseason expectations, current rankings or point in the season, Ohio State has enjoyed virtually no success on Maryland’s home court. Starting with a 100-65 loss on Jan. 16, 2016, the Buckeyes are now 1-7 in this building since the Terrapins entered the league, and the one win came with no fans in the stands while playing through the COVID-19 pandemic.

In those seven losses, Ohio State has trailed for 239:12 of 280 possible minutes of playing time. Twice, the Buckeyes have never led, including Wednesday night. The average margin of defeat has been 16.4 points per game. Just one of those seven losses has been by single digits, and that was a nine-point loss.

Ohio State has trailed for 85.4% of the time it has played in this arena with fans in the stands.

Things don’t get easier anytime soon

Saddled with a two-game losing streak, Ohio State will host Rutgers Saturday in its first home conference game of the year. The Scarlet Knights are also 5-3 and riding a two-game losing streak, but they are led by two projected top-five NBA draft picks next year in freshmen Ace Bailey and Dylan Harper.

Then, after a week’s break for final exams, the Buckeyes will go to Atlanta to face Auburn for a neutral-site game. The Tigers are No. 2 in this week’s Associated Press poll.

headline: Columbus City Council to vote on creating 'weed fund' to collect marijuana tax revenue
fullText:
The city of Columbus could soon establish a separate "weed fund" to manage its income from the tax on marijuana sales, a new revenue source the City Council welcomes.

Columbus City Auditor Megan N. Kilgore said she conservatively estimates the city will bring in $8 million from marijuana sale tax receipts in the first year that the drug was legalized for recreational use in Ohio. Speaking at a City Council budget hearing on Wednesday, Kilgore said the revenue could be even more.

Columbus City Council will vote at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 16 on an ordinance to establish what Council member Nick Bankston called the "weed fund." The fund's actual working title is the "Cannabis Host Community Special Revenue Fund."

Bankston, chair of the council's Finance Committee, told The Dispatch that the council plans to keep this revenue out of the general fund, despite the budget being tight this year, so they can use the dollars for equity initiatives. He said they want to acknowledge that the previous criminalization of marijuana contributed to inequities. But the council has not determined what exactly that looks like.

The city only receives tax revenue money from sales in the city, Bankston said.

"If you do partake, whether recreationally or medically, we encourage you to buy within the city limits," Bankston said during Wednesday's budget hearing.

The 10% tax collected on marijuana sales goes to the state and 36% of that is supposed to get sent to the municipalities where the sales were made, said Matt Erickson, director of the Council's Legislative Research Office. He said the city won't see a dollar of this until around July.

headline: New NCAA roster rules: More scholarships, fewer athletes for Ohio State Buckeyes
fullText:
As Buckeyes fans watched Wednesday morning to see which members of Ohio State football's 2025 recruiting class would sign to officially join the team ahead of next season, it was also a first look at how the team could shake out under new proposed NCAA roster limits.

The changes come as a result of the House vs. NCAA settlement, a deal that will fundamentally transform college sports by permitting Division I schools to start paying athletes directly for use of their name, image and likeness.

More: Ohio State athletic director Ross Bjork issues open letter on House vs. NCAA settlement

In addition to a required $2.8 billion in backpay to former NCAA athletes over a 10-year period, the House settlement also allows schools to opt into revenue sharing going forward. Those schools can share up to 22% of their average athletic revenues. For Ohio State, that's about $20.5 million annually, The Dispatch previously reported.

While NIL deals and revenue sharing have been the top headlines, the House settlement will also make changes to athletic scholarships and roster limits. Schools that opt into revenue sharing are required to follow new roster limits.

Previously, the only restriction to NCAA rosters was related to scholarships. Sports like football and basketball require full scholarships for any student-athletes receiving a scholarship, but teams could still include non-scholarship walk-on athletes to their rosters. While FBS college football teams are currently limited to 85 scholarships, the average roster has about 128 players. 

But under the House settlement, scholarship restrictions are no more. Every student-athlete can receive up to a full scholarship. In turn, the NCAA will impose new roster limits beginning in fall 2025.

Ohio State Athletic Director Ross Bjork said in an open letter to Buckeyes fans about the House settlement last month that the university would add 91 new scholarships across both women’s and men’s sports.

Another result of the settlement is a reduction in roster sizes, so although the Buckeyes are adding scholarships, the total number of Ohio State athletes will drop by approximately 150, even as the university intends to maintain all 36 of its programs, according to a November news release.

While many teams could see a bump to their team's rosters, others will have to make cuts. Fourteen Ohio State programs, including football and men's basketball, have larger teams this season than next year's new limits will allow. Buckeye baseball would be most dramatically affected, with a roster limit of 34 compared to a current roster of 55. Football has a roster of 123, but would be limited to 105 players under the rules.

Though the changes won't go into effect for almost a year, some schools are already feeling the effects. According to a Yahoo! Sports report in late October, some schools have already eliminated roster spots and, for some, rescinded scholarship offers once promised to student-athletes. Several dozen current college athletes reported being notified that they are no longer part of their teams — some of the notifications arrived after the fall semester even began, according to the article.

Both Bjork and Ohio State President Ted Carter have affirmed that college athletics will be a facet of the university's 10-year strategic plan.

Currently, most Ohio State student-athletes do not receive a full scholarship and 30% receive no athletic aid, according to the university.

"As the department transitions from scholarship limits to roster limits, the number of student-athletes provided full or partial scholarships is expected to increase for most sports," Ohio State said in a news release. "All varsity sports will continue to offer scholarship opportunities."

Sheridan Hendrix is a higher education reporter for The Columbus Dispatch. Sign up for Extra Credit, her education newsletter, here.

headline: Columbus single mothers to get monthly payments in new, first-of-its-kind income program
fullText:
Thirty-two Ohio mothers will receive the first of 12 payments of $500 this week.

The payments, funded by the nonprofits RISE Together Innovation Institute and UpTogether, are part of what organizers say is the first unconditional guaranteed income program in the city.

Called Ohio Mothers Trust, the initiative is intended to aid single mothers with an income at or below 80% of the area median, according to organizers. That would be $74,400 for a family of three, according to the city.

“Ohio Mothers Trust aims to show that providing unconditional cash support to mothers can significantly boost the financial stability and overall well-being of families,” Danielle Sydnor, CEO of RISE Together, an organization that works to end poverty in Columbus, said in a statement.

Universal basic income? New Columbus program to give some residents monthly payments

It can also be an investment for Franklin County, as childhood poverty cost the county $5.2 billion in lost economic activity in 2021, Sydnor said.

That loss comes from reduced earnings, crime, health and child welfare impacts, according to a December 2023 RISE Together report.

“Providing families the resources they need is an investment in their future and the future health of our community," Sydnor said.

Where is the money coming from?

Motherful, a grassroots collective of some 600 single mothers in the Columbus area, identified and selected the participants from members of its collective who applied for the program. They will be routinely surveyed to learn about how the program impacts their lives.

"A lot of single moms don't have resources they can depend on," said Lisa Woodward, co-founder and co-director of Motherful. "They need cash because it's not a two-income household."

The $500 payments are money they can count on, without hoops to jump through or strings attached, she said.

"You just have to be a single mom," Woodward said. "Be a sister in our community."

67 years without a birth certificate? How a Columbus woman lived without a birth record

Motherful was founded in 2018 and has a resource garage and food pantry available to members at its Gahanna location. It works to support, empower and nurture single-mother families in various ways, including by providing community, education, resources and more.

It started when Woodward and fellow single mother Heidi Howes met and wanted to create a list of resources for single moms and found there weren't any. So, they created Motherful.

"Ever since the beginning, we always knew getting money to moms is an important thing," Woodward said. "We operate with no boundaries. ... We want moms to just get the money and feel free."

RISE Together and UpTogether are both funding the initiative, which costs $211,200. UpTogether is a national change organization originally founded under the name Family Independence Initiative in Oakland, California, in 2001.

Since 2020, UpTogether has given out more than $210 million to more than 200,000 people through managed direct cash programs nationwide.

Though Ohio Mothers Trust is a pilot program, the concept has been tested with other types of recipients, Woodward said.

"It does work," she said. "Direct cash works. I feel like we're giving dreams away."

VANISHED event: Dispatch to host Community Conversation on Dec. 11 about missing people in Ohio

Ohio Mothers Trust is investing in mothers, said Astar Herndon, UpTogether’s Midwest Partnership director, and trusting them to make the best choices for their families.

"Moms, after all, know what their families need,” Herndon said.

Woodward said there's more Motherful wants to do, including future cohorts of women getting cash support.

"It's just the start," she said. "We intend to use the results of this initiative to advocate for broader, unrestricted cash investments for families across Franklin County."

'A great opportunity'

Angelique Scales joined Motherful years ago as a volunteer, helping other moms.

Today, the 37-year-old is the one who needs resources after going through a divorce.

The single mother of three who lives on Columbus' North Side is one of the 32 mothers who will get help through the Ohio Mothers Trust.

"I'm very, very grateful," Scales said of being a recipient of the trust. "It's just helping me get back on my feet, as a stepping stool."

Scales, who is a self-employed creative director and consultant, hopes to use some of the money to invest in herself and her business so she can be a better mother. Just getting more money toward her family's bills helps her do that, she said.

"This initiative means I can actually knock off some major goals for myself," Scales said.

But it's more than the money. Scales also feels understood and supported as a single mom — an identity she said comes with some stigma.

"It's a great opportunity to pour back into us," she said. "They're really supportive of us getting what we need as single moms."

headline: A prayer for churches
fullText:
It might be time to offer a prayer for central Ohio churches. One, Summit on 16th United Methodist Church, has just been demolished to make way for apartments (see below) while another, the University Baptist Church on Lane, is facing the same fate. This isn't like losing a house. Churches bring a bit of architectural majesty to our streets. Yes, church needs evolve (no doubt far fewer OSU students attend church today than they did in the past), but how refreshing when the buildings themselves can find new uses. Think of the Bluestone event space in a former Baptist church on East Broad Street, or the Refectory restaurant, or CAPA's plans to convert a former Presbyterian church Downtown into performance space, or plans to revive the Holy Rosary Church on East Main, or my favorite, the Stauf's coffee shop in an 1880s Presbyterian church on Neil Avenue. Just as you can't plant a 100-year-old tree, you can't build a 100-year-old church.

Church goers

The Chicago development firm Up Campus Student Living has started work on Blume on 16th apartment complex, on the former site of Summit on 16th United Methodist Church. The five-story complex will include 74 apartments and 325 bedrooms in two- to six-bedroom layouts. Like other student-housing complexes, Blume on 16th will rent by the bedroom. Up Campus has not released rent rates.

Bridge Park finale?

The development firm Crawford Hoying has submitted plans for the final empty spot in its Bridge Park footprint. Plans call for condos, offices, a restaurant and a parking garage on the site, bordered by Dale Drive, Bridge Park Avenue, Banker Street and Wendy's headquarters. The plans mark a milestone for Bridge Park, a $600-million development that has transformed Dublin and served as a model for many suburbs seeking to create a dense downtown. While the plans would fill the last vacant space in the original Bridge Park footprint, it's still possible the footprint could expand to the south, or, with another developer, to the north.

Microsoft heads to Pataskala

Microsoft paid $11.4 million for 43 acres at Etna Parkway and Refugee Road in Pataskala, next to 289 acres the company bought last fall for $30.65 million. The tech giant is mum on its plans for the site, but I'm going to take a wild shot in a dark and guess a data center complex. Microsoft has already announced plans to invest $1 billion in three data center campuses elsewhere in Licking County.

New Albany facelift

A 30-year-old New Albany homes has hit the market after a thorough renovation. The home, on a 1.7-acre wooded lot, is listed by the Thomas ❘ Riddle Group with New Albany Realty for $3.495 million.

Property transfers

The Dayton-based home-rental company Vinebrook continues to refinance its central Ohio portfolio, as noted in this week's property transfers.

And that's the development wrap for the week. If you like what you see, subscribe for more.

headline: What is wind chill? How cold does it make you feel?
fullText:
It has been a cold and gusty week in Columbus, and the area's wind chill has been trending steadily downwards.

You have likely heard wind chill mentioned in passing in water cooler conversations or on a weather broadcast, but do you know what it really is?

Wonder no longer. Here is what you need to know about wind chill.

What is wind chill?

Wind chill is how cold people and animals feel outside, even if the air temperature is slightly warmer. 

How does wind chill work?

As wind increases, it draws more heat from the body, driving down body and skin temperature, according to the National Weather Service.

How to calculate wind chill

Prepare to use your middle school math knowledge.

The formula for calculating wind chill in degrees Fahrenheit, when T is the air temperature, and V is the wind speed, is:

Wind chill=35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16).

If you cannot be bothered to do your math homework, here is a helpful graphic of wind chill temperatures from the NWS.

Keep in mind that bright sunshine may reduce the effect of wind chill by 10 to 18 degrees.

Also, the NWS only calculates wind chill at temperatures of 50 degrees or lower and with winds of 3 mph or faster.

How does wind chill affect temperature?

It technically does not affect air temperature at all. The wind chill is how cold it feels to people and animals, but a thermometer reading in high and low wind chill conditions would be the same.

Inanimate objects, like car radiators, will only cool down to the air temperature, the NWS says. For example, if the air temperature is above freezing but the wind chill is below freezing, a glass of water left outside will not freeze.

Can you get frostbite from wind chill if it's below freezing but the temperature is above freezing?

No, you cannot. You can only get frostbite if the air temperature, not the wind chill, is below freezing, according to the NWS. You could still get hypothermia, however.

headline: Chi-Chi's restaurants to re-open 20 years after closure. Are they coming to Ohio?
fullText:
The 1990s really are back. A Mexican restaurant chain that peaked in popularity back when "Friends" was airing new episodes plans to return in 2025.

Will it come back to Ohio?

Chi-Chi's restaurant announced an agreement on Tuesday with Hormel Foods, an Austin, Minnesota, based global food company that owns Chi-Chi's trademarks, the release said.

The agreement will grant Michael McDermott, son of the Chi-Chi's founder Marno McDermott, use of the Chi-Chi's name on restaurant locations expected to open in 2025, the restaurant chain said.

"I still have fond memories of growing up in the Chi-Chi's restaurants that my father built throughout their time, instilling in me the passion and determination to pursue my own career in the restaurant industry," Michael McDermott, founder of Chi-Chi's Restaurants, said in a statement. "We have seen the impact our restaurant has had on individuals and families across the country and believe there is a strong opportunity to bring the brand back in a way that resonates with today's consumer—an updated dining experience with the same great taste and Mexican flavor."

McDermott added that he is determined to keep his family’s legacy alive “by combining the classic Chi-Chi's restaurant experience with modern influences."

Here is what we know about Chi-Chi’s restaurant return.

Chi-Chi's restaurant plans to open first new locations in Minnesota

The full details of the Chi-Chi restaurants that will open in 2025 are still pending. However, the restaurant chain’s owner did confirm that two locations are set to open next year.

“While we are currently in the early stages of planning by securing funding, we can say the first two stores will be opened in Minnesota in 2025,” Michael McDermott said in a statement. “Our goal is to explore the original development path Chi Chi’s took, through both company and franchised opportunities within the Midwest and East Coast.”

Will new Chi-Chi's restaurants open in Ohio?

While Chi-Chi's plan includes location in the Midwest, it isn't known if those plans include Ohio.

How many Chi-Chi's were in Ohio?

If a list posted on Fandom.com is accurate, Chi-Chi's operated 28 restaurants in Ohio during its heyday. The website allows users to create Wikipedia-style articles on whatever interests them—film, television, video games or, in this case, Chi-Chi's restaurants.

headline: How COVID-19 continues to challenge children learning in our schools

headline: Union sues John Glenn Columbus airport to allow Scabby the Rat, protest at groundbreaking
fullText:
A local construction union association filed a lawsuit against John Glenn Columbus International Airport and the Columbus Regional Airport Authority Wednesday, saying the airport is unlawfully restricting the union's free speech by not permitting a "Scabby the Rat" display and small protest at an upcoming terminal groundbreaking.

The Columbus Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council—representing local construction unions—plans to display the large inflatable rat commonly seen at labor protests and banners highlighting the group's ongoing dispute with the airport in a grassy area near the blue lot during the new terminal's groundbreaking on Dec. 9.

The trades council filed an application for the display with CRAA legal counsel on Nov. 25. The council did not receive a response within seven business days, meaning that according to airport policy, its application was denied, according to the lawsuit.

The council filed a lawsuit on Dec. 4 in the U.S. District Court Southern District of Ohio in Columbus, asking the court to require the airport to permit the Scabby the Rat display and protest and for the council's costs and attorney's fees.

What is the dispute about?

The planned protest stems from an ongoing dispute between the council, CRAA and the construction manager hired to build the new $2 billion terminal, Colorado-based Hensel Phelps Construction Company.

The council wants CRAA and Hensel Phelps to agree to a legally binding Community Benefits Agreement that outlines wage, health insurance and retirement benefit requirements for construction workers building the new terminal. 

The agreement would also "promote the use of a local and diverse workforce" and "guarantee that all construction workers performing covered work enjoy equal rights and treatment on the job site," and allow workers access to a grievance and arbitration procedure. Union-sponsored strikes or other activities that might delay construction or drive up costs are prohibited under the agreement, according to the lawsuit.

The council initially negotiated with Hensel Phelps directly in 2023, but negotiations soured when Hensel Phelps proposed a version of the CBA that would allow all contractors and sub-contractors to opt out of it.

The council then attended a CRAA Board of Directors meeting in Jan. 2024, asking them to ensure the CBA would cover all stakeholders. 

On Feb. 12, the CRAA modified its position on the CBA, asking the council to exempt Disadvantaged Business Enterprises—small businesses owned by socially or economically disadvantaged people who contract with the U.S. Department of Transportation—and diversity business partners from the agreement and its requirements, according to the lawsuit.

The council refused to agree to a CBA that exempts those businesses, and CRAA refused to modify its position. The last negotiating session occurred on May 22. No agreement has been signed or agreed to.

The council and its unions have been able to strike similar agreements with other projects in the region, including Intel's $28 billion semiconductor plant in Licking County, the $3.5 billion electric vehicle battery plant that Honda and LG Energy are building in Jeffersonville, the Hollywood Casino hotel project on the West Side, the Franklin County jail and other projects, labor leaders told The Dispatch in July.

In the summer of 2024, The Columbus Regional Airport Authority said it made significant efforts to collaborate with trade unions, The Dispatch previously reported.

"Despite our comprehensive proposals, the Columbus/Central Ohio Building & Construction Trades Council has rejected all offers," the airport said in a statement.

In a similar statement from the summer, the company said, "Hensel Phelps has offered numerous compromise proposals to the (trade unions), who have rejected all offers."

The council, CRAA and Hensel Phelps did not respond to requests for comment at the time of publication.

headline: Court says Columbus can shutter Downtown nightclub where fatal shooting occurred
fullText:
The City of Columbus obtained a court order allowing it to shutter a troubled downtown nightclub that was the site of a fatal shooting in June.

Columbus City Attorney Zack Klein said Thursday a Franklin County Municipal Court environmental court ordered The Avalon nightclub at 205 N 5th Street to close for one year.

Between January 23 and August, Columbus police were called to the property 78 times for incidents, including fights and guns being stolen from vehicles. There were at least six reports of assaults, fights or shootings at the club, including a June 14 shooting in which two people died and two others suffered injuries.

Police were called to the property for a shots fired report in November, Klein said. The city has said the club ignored previous court orders and refused to allow inspections.

"I want Columbus to have a vibrant nightlife, but it needs to be safe," Klein said in a Facebook post. "Owners cannot violate court orders, continue to see violence and criminal activity, and expect us to allow it."

Klein said the city may also submit an objection to future liquor permit applications by the business to the Ohio Division of Liquor Control.

headline: Anthony Pierson, prosecutor in Adam Coy case, leaving Franklin County Prosecutor's Office
fullText:
The lead prosecutor in the case against a former Columbus police officer found guilty of murdering an unarmed Black man is leaving the Franklin County Prosecutor's Office.

Deputy Chief Counsel Anthony Pierson is expected to leave the office Dec. 20, First Assistant Prosecutor Ed Leonard confirmed Thursday to The Dispatch. Pierson's departure marks the end of his third stint at the prosecutor's office.

Pierson submitted his resignation letter to Franklin County Prosecutor Gary Tyack on Oct. 31, according to a copy of the letter provided to The Dispatch.

The letter did not specify why Pierson was leaving, but Pierson told The Dispatch via text message on Thursday that he is going into private practice.

Pierson was the lead prosecutor in the criminal case against former Columbus police officer Adam Coy, who was found guilty by a jury Nov. 5 of murder, felonious assault and reckless homicide in the December 2020 shooting death of 47-year-old Andre Hill, who was unarmed.

Coy was scheduled to be sentenced Nov. 25, but a Franklin County judge delayed it after Coy's attorneys asked for a hearing to determine if the prosecution violated Coy's right to a fair trial by failing to disclose that it spoke to an expert witness whose opinion reportedly did not line up with the prosecution position.

Pierson was originally going to leave his position on Dec. 2, but was asked to stay to work on a few matters, including, but not limited to, the conviction of Coy.

Leonard said it was unclear who would take over the Coy case after Pierson's departure should a judge or appeals court determine Coy has a right to a retrial.

Earlier this year, Pierson lost a close Democratic primary race for county prosecutor to Columbus City Councilmember Shayla Favor. Pierson was backed by retiring county Prosecutor Gary Tyack. Favor won the general election in November over Republican John Rutan and will take over as county prosecutor in January.

Prior to his current stint at the prosecutor's office, Pierson most recently worked in Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost’s office as the lead prosecutor on all officer-involved shooting cases.

headline: 5 finalists honored, 1 named 2024 Everyday Kindness Hero
fullText:
"Everyone's a winner tonight," Jane Jacquemin-Clark said to the room filled with teary, attentive faces the evening of Dec. 4 at the Everyday Kindness Heroes award ceremony held at COSI.

Just moments before she was to be named from among five central Ohio finalists as the 2024 Everyday Kindness Hero Champion — and given a $5,000 award from the Columbus Foundation's Center for HumanKindness — Jacquemin-Clark acknowledged the other four finalists and 13 semifinalists, along with what inspires her.

Everyday Kindness Heroes: Meet 5 Columbus-area residents who bring good to the community

The four other finalists, who included Lisa Woodward, Ric Grubaugh, Nicole Hebert-Ford and Tracy Davidson, were each given a $1,000 award from the Center for HumanKindness.

Organized by the Columbus Dispatch, Columbus Monthly and Columbus CEO magazines, the event was sponsored by the Center for HumanKindness at the Columbus Foundation, AEP Ohio, COSI and the United Way of Central Ohio.

A panel of six judges including representatives from program sponsors and The Dispatch/Dispatch Magazines voted on who would be the final winner, a decision that was kept a secret to all but The Dispatch's marketing promotions and community affairs manager, Eric Wygle, who tallied the votes.

The five finalists donned the podium to share their stories of working for kindness in the Columbus community, with Woodward recognizing her own mother as she described her nonprofit to support single mothers, Motherful.

Grubaugh, a retired Columbus teacher, said his work at Star House serving homeless youth inspired him as he was mourning the loss of his wife, explaining the selflessness of kids experiencing unimaginable hardship helped him through his own.

Davidson described the way her community came together behind her to create The Big Bus, a mobile classroom in Westerville City School District. These six community members were "all-in since day one," she said, after she discovered a need to provide extra help to immigrant communities in the district.

As she acknowledged her fellow finalists and semifinalists, Jacquemin-Clark described how her own cancer journey led her to starting Hope Hollow along with her husband, Kevin Clark, to provide lodging to people traveling to Columbus for cancer treatment.

Hebert-Ford, the founder of a nonprofit created to help students with unmet needs, Student Success Stores, said her mission extends beyond providing students with the things they need.

Last year, Student Success Stores provided 43,368 basic-need items to over 2,000 different students in grades 6-12. However, on a greater scale, it is a mission of hope.

Spotlight: Student Success Stores take care of basic but important teen needs in Columbus, Whitehall

"Hope is what we try to provide to kids. Hope is greater than SAT scores and ACT scores," Hebert-Ford said.

"Students who have higher levels of hope are more likely to graduate, are more likely to succeed academically and so for us, it’s more than a pair of shoes. It’s more than a backpack. It’s providing hope to kids.”

The Dispatch's executive editor, Michael Shearer, reflected on Hebert-Ford's words right as he joined the director for the Center for HumanKindness, Kate Oliphint, to open an envelope revealing the kindness champion.

He noted that hope was the goal of the coverage on stories of kindness and the Dec. 4 event. Earlier in the evening, Shearer opened the night referencing The Dispatch's Dec. 1 cover story on the five finalists.

Shearer explained that if the story hadn't been planned in advance, the cover story would have naturally been the brawl between Ohio State and Michigan football players at The Game the previous Saturday, pointing to the power in the intentionality of kindness and the need for it in the community.

The 13 semifinalists were also recognized, along with a therapy dog, Fiona. Each semifinalist was awarded a $250 grant to an eligible nonprofit of his or her choice

Along with the kind canine, the 2024 semifinalists included Cody Ballard, Renny Tyson, Dottie Odrosky, Jill Cottone, Rick and Lisa Gawronski, Margaret “Peggy” Kasten, Jim Burns and Mary Casey, Mike Uetrecht, Chet Ridenour, Denise Kilgore and Fiona's owner, Sally Malaret.

headline: Gov. Mike DeWine wants all Ohio drivers to take training before getting a license
fullText:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio – Gov. Mike DeWine called on the state Legislature to require driving training for all Ohioans seeking a license, not just those under 18 years old.

Ohio law currently does not require driving training for residents over 18 years old who apply for a license.

"Whatever age you are, if you're getting your license for the first time, you need to take driver's training. To say that once you turn 18, you don't have to take any training just does not, frankly, make any sense at all," DeWine said Thursday.

Currently, anyone younger than 18 must complete a driver education class at a licensed driver training school, which includes 24 hours of classroom or online instruction and eight hours of driving time. They also must complete 50 hours of driving, with at least 10 hours of night driving, in addition to the driver education requirements.

Adults who fail the first attempt at the maneuverability or road portion of the state driving test are required to take an abbreviated adult driver training course.

Springfield getting simulators to help immigrant drivers

The governor's comments came as part of an announcement on driving simulators that will be available throughout Springfield, a central Ohio city grappling with a recent influx of Haitian immigrants that have caused traffic accidents.

Tension over immigration in Springfield escalated after Haitian immigrant Hermanio Joseph struck a school bus in 2023. 11-year-old Aiden Clark died and 20 other students were injured in the crash. Joseph was found guilty of involuntary manslaughter and vehicular homicide and sentenced to a minimum of nine years in prison.

Clark's father pleaded with people to stop using his son's death as a political tool at a Springfield City Commission meeting in September.

DeWine said issues with driving are understandable, given that the laws and norms in Haiti are different.

Ten simulators will be available around Springfield, each with a translator and instructor. The simulators give residents a chance to get familiar with road signs, lane marking and other rules of the road.

DeWine stressed that the simulators are available for any residents, not only immigrants

Dom and Terri Tiberi donated five simulators. The couple started the Maria Tiberi Foundation to prevent distracted driving 11 years ago after their daughter died in a car crash.

In addition to the simulators, there is a Creole translation of the Ohio driver's manual now available for Haitians.

DeWine noted other resources for Springfield residents, including mobile health clinics, ESL classes and a baby formula bank at a Springfield food pantry.

Andy Wilson, director of the Ohio Department of Public Safety, said the simulators are part of an effort to drive down some of the rhetoric associated with those crashes.

Where can Springfield residents find the driving simulators?

There will be 10 new simulators installed at six different locations here in Springfield:

  • High Street Church of the Nazarene.
  • Clark County Department of Job and Family Services.
  • Clark State College.
  • Springfield, Clark Career Technology Center.
  • First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield.
  • Life in Christ Community Church

Erin Glynn is a reporter for the USA TODAY Network Ohio Bureau, which serves the Columbus Dispatch, Cincinnati Enquirer, Akron Beacon Journal and 18 other affiliated news organizations across Ohio.

headline: Ohio State researcher, graduate sue President Ted Carter for Palestine protest arrests
fullText:
Two individuals arrested at Ohio State University in April after an Israel-Hamas war protest are now suing Ohio State President Ted Carter.

The plaintiffs filed separate complaints in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio Thursday, listing Carter and OSU police department detective Susan Liu as defendants, alleging the two violated their civil rights when they were arrested.

More: 'It is traumatizing' 3 Ohio State educators recount arrests at Israel-Hamas war protest

Sumaya Hamadmad, a research scientist in the Department of Ophthalmology and Vision Science at the Ohio State's College of Medicine, and Curtis Peace, a 2021 Ohio State graduate, were on the South Oval on the morning of April 25 around the same time a group gathered to protest the ongoing Israel-Hamas war.

The group of about 25 pro-Palestine demonstrators gathered in the early morning hours that Thursday to begin constructing an encampment on the South Oval, The Dispatch previously reported. Organizers with the Students for Justice in Palestine called it the "Ohio State Gaza Encampment."

University police officers told protesters to take down their tents later that morning because tent camping is not allowed on the lawn without prior approval, according to OSU's space rules. The tents were eventually removed.

According to Hamadmad's lawsuit, she was sitting in the grass on the South Oval and was not involved in the protest, but was arrested by officers anyway. Hamadmad believed she was "stereotyped because she was wearing a headscarf," according to the lawsuit.

Peace, according to his lawsuit, had complied with all police orders so far that day and was standing 50 yards away from the previous protest location when he was arrested while filming a group of police officers with his phone.

"It is illegal for a public university to squelch speech which the university is hostile to, whether they have expressed that speech or are assumed to have expressed that speech," Ed Forman, a civil right attorney with Marshall Forman and Schlein, said in a press release about the lawsuits. "Such conduct violates the First Amendment. The arrests of Hamadmad and Peace were illegal and without probable cause."

Ohio State spokesperson Ben Johnson said the university does not comment on pending litigation.

headline: Urban Meyer shuts down speculation about return to Ohio State football
fullText:
Former Ohio State football coach Urban Meyer on Thursday shut down speculation about a possible return to the school.

In a statement shared on his podcast, “The Triple Option,” Meyer offered support for Ryan Day, his former offensive coordinator who has faced questions about his job security in the aftermath of a fourth straight loss to archrival Michigan.

“It has come to my attention that there are reports speculating my return to the sidelines in Columbus,” Meyer said. “While I thoroughly enjoyed my seven seasons as head coach at THE Ohio State University, I have no interest in coaching again.

“I will always be a Buckeye and have full confidence in Ryan Day, his staff, and every player that puts on the Scarlet and Gray.”

Meyer was 83-9, including winning the first College Football Playoff, as he led the Buckeyes from 2012-18.  He was also 7-0 against the Wolverines.

He came out of retirement in 2021 to coach the Jacksonville Jaguars in the NFL before he was fired after only 13 games. He was 2-11 in Jacksonville. In recent years, Meyer has maintained he has no plans to return to coaching.

The 60-year-old Meyer is currently analyst with FOX Sports, appearing on the network’s Big Noon Kickoff pregame show that airs Saturdays.

Despite speculation about Day’s future in Columbus, he has received public backing from athletic director Ross Bjork and said Wednesday that he expects to continue to be at the helm of the football program next year.

Day is 66-10 overall and has the Buckeyes in position to appear in the College Football Playoff later this month after they finished 10-2 during the regular season.

headline: Thousands of patients in limbo as Ohio State, Anthem insurance contract deadline nears
fullText:
Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield members soon may no longer be in-network with one of the top cancer treatment facilities in the country, as Ohio State's health system and the health insurance carrier battle down to the wire over another contract.

Patients covered by Anthem were notified by Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center Wednesday that if Anthem and OSU's health system, including Ohio State Comprehensive Cancer Center, also referred to as "the James", can't reach a new contract agreement, any services, physicians, clinicians and facilities will be out of Anthem’s network Jan. 1, 2025.

After that date, tens of thousands of central Ohio patients would have to pay out-of-network prices for any services from OSU. The university health system said more than 100,000 Anthem patients have used their services in the past two years.

More: Anthem, OSU terminate contract, leaving Medicare Advantage patients out of network

"We are doing everything we can to stay in network with Anthem so you can keep accessing the high-quality care you depend on," OSU said in a release to patients, noting that it has been "working in good faith" with Anthem for over a year to renew the contract.

Anthem also expressed interest in maintaining the contract, but conveyed trepidation over OSU's demands.

"We are optimistic an agreement will be reached. However, we are concerned that OSU wants to increase its prices for patients and their employers at rates three times higher than inflation," said Jeff Blunt, a spokesperson for Anthem. "... Ohio’s consumers and employers who would pay these cost increases cannot afford these extreme price hikes."

More: Mount Carmel patients with Aetna insurance could be out of network come Jan. 1

OSU, however, said in a statement that Anthem is "mischaracterizing our negotiations" in "an attempt to confuse patients and employers." The health system stated that Anthem has underpaid them for the past few years, denies claims more than any other insurance carrier, and has not kept up with inflation while "consistently" raising employer and member premiums.

"Unlike other insurance providers, Anthem has refused to consider appropriate rate adjustments so the health care providers their members trust can cover expenses. Instead of paying for patient care, Anthem is keeping their members’ money," the health system said in a statement.

Narrowing negotiation window plagues other systems, too

This isn't OSU's first announcement of troubled contract negotiations with Anthem. Last month, OSU told Medicare Advantage patients using Anthem that they would no longer be in-network with the health system starting Jan. 1, citing an inability to come to that new, fair agreement. The change will affect around 11,000 Central Ohioans, according to Anthem.

More: Anthem, OSU terminate contract, leaving Medicare Advantage patients out of network

Mount Carmel Health System also recently alerted its patients that if they could not reach an agreement with Aetna, another major health insurance carrier, any patients using Aetna would be out-of-network in their system come Jan. 1.

I have Anthem insurance. Now what?

Negotiations between Anthem and OSU are still ongoing, so a change in care next year isn't set in stone.

OSU is asking patients to keep all scheduled appointment and procedures with them in the meantime. Patients with certain health conditions or undergoing active courses of treatment may qualify for Continuity of Care benefits. Those benefits would allow patients to continue receiving care at in-network prices, even if the contract ends, such as cancer-related care and pregnancy after the first trimester, among others.

Patients are urged to call the number on the back of their Anthem insurance card for more details on continuing care.

For further information and the latest updates on negotiations, you can visit Anthem's webpage on the situation as well as OSU's webpage.

Samantha Hendrickson is The Dispatch's medical business and health care reporter. She can be reached at shendrickson@dispatch.com

headline: Woman told Columbus police fatally shot man in self defense; domestic violence possible
fullText:
A woman detained in a shooting on Columbus' Northeast Side said she shot the man in self defense, police say.

The woman told police she was the person who shot Gerald Jackson, 38, when officers responded to a report of a shooting at about 4:50 p.m. in the 3400 block of Nutcreek Court, a cul-de-sace of a half-dozen duplex homes off Woodsedge Road in the Walnut Creek neighborhood.

The woman, who police have not identified, was detained at the scene. In a news release, the department said she is cooperating with the investigation.

Responding officers found Jackson suffering from a gunshot wound at one of the residences at the back of the cul-de-sac.

He was transported to a local hospital in critical condition, where he was pronounced dead at 5:28 p.m., according to a Columbus police dispatcher.

The woman told police she shot Jackson after he threatened her. Police said domestic violence may have been involved, but have not disclosed whether the woman and Jackson had a relationship.

headline: Darren Rizzi's North Jersey return as Saints coach means family, friends and NFL football
fullText:
Darren Rizzi has fond memories of the New York Giants growing up.

“I remember the strike year in 1982 where the Giants actually held practice on our [youth football] field in Hillsdale,” Rizzi said in an interview with NorthJersey.com two weeks ago.

“I was 11 years old and I could walk down to the bottom of the hill and watch the Giants practice. It was awesome.”

Rizzi, now 2-1 as the interim head coach of the New Orleans Saints, will get an even closer look Sunday when he brings his team in to face the struggling Giants at MetLife Stadium.

It will be a huge homecoming for the Bergen Catholic grad who has climbed multiple steps up the coaching ladder to get here.

“It will be a surreal experience,” Rizzi said.

Rizzi still has deep connections in North Jersey. His best friends from high school and his family will be there Sunday. They’ve coordinated a pre-game get together, and arranged for travel for his mother, Phylis, for the game.

Like any worried mother, Phylis is, well, a worried mother. She will be at MetLife too, praying at every snap and trying to keep a low profile.

“I am almost going to try to go incognito,” Phylis said. “I want to be able to be with my family. I just pray that he is safe and happy and secure.”

Ben Tonon is a Bergen Catholic graduate, and part of the Rizzi inner ‘triangle’ of best friends that includes Kurt Karcich.

Tonon is coming up from South Carolina to cheer for the Saints, natch, and support Rizzi.

“We’ve all been following Darren and his path to this point since he was at Rutgers and at Rhode Island and with the Dolphins,” Tonon said. “His ability to get the players to play hard, his relationship with his players is remarkable. I would run through a brick wall for him.”

Karcich is a St. Joseph Regional graduate and the son of Green Knights legendary coach Tony Karcich. Kurt lined up against Rizzi in the state championship game in 1987 - and won 7-0, not that he brings that up much.

The pair met at some shared Catholic school functions and hit it off immediately. They owned a love of family and football, and the friendship blossomed.

“I am ecstatic, this is long overdue,” said Kurt, now the principal at Point Pleasant High School. “He has all the qualities I think you want in a head coach. I have been with him on many recruiting trips when he was in the college ranks, and with the Dolphins and the Saints. He has a natural ability to lead people and command respect.”  

The Rizzi Storyline is the biggest entering Sunday's game - although the possibility of a former Don Bosco quarterback, Tommy DeVito for the Giants, facing a Bergen Catholic coach is fun too.

The Giants (2-10) have lost seven in a row and there are grumblings from fans about the job head coach Brian Daboll and GM Joe Schoen have done.

The Saints (4-8) just lost versatile star Taysom Hill to a season-ending knee injury in a loss to the Rams last week.

Tickets can be had for $10 on StubHub, so this isn’t exactly a marquee NFL matchup, but for Rizzi’s friends and family, this moment is priceless.

“You can say this, I have been a Giants fan since birth, but I hope they lose by 140 points,” laughed Tonon. “Both teams are struggling, but the product the Saints have put on the field has been incredible. I think everyone in New Orleans is seeing the product is something to go root for.”

“I’m rooting for the Saints,” Kurt said. “I’m a lifelong Giants fan, but I won’t even hesitate, I am rooting for my boy.”

According to Phylis, Darren originally was a Rams fan - Darren’s brother, Daniel, was a Cowboys fan, so Darren said he always hated the Cowboys - but when the Giants rose up in the late 80s, Darren switched to cheering for them.

It’s not lost on Darren’s friends that those Giants were led by a Bergen County native named Bill Parcells.

You never know how things might work out in the NFL (all indications are the Saints are happy with Rizzi), but it’s an easy leap that Giants fans could be looking at their future head coach on the opposing sidelines Sunday.

“I can imagine him being the coach of the Giants,” Tonon said. “That would be a dream come true.”

Quoting a source not connected with the club, Kay said the call with Fried “supposedly went very well,’’ and there were plans for a follow-up discussion with team officials.

As mentioned on ‘The Michael Kay Show,’ the Yankees diligence could be part of a Plan B pivot should Soto sign what’s expected to be a record contract with another club.

During Tuesday’s Dodgers press conference to formally announce lefty starter Blake Snell’s five-year, $182 million free agent deal with Los Angeles, agent Scott Boras offered that Soto had begun the process of eliminating teams.

Yankees’ owner Hal Steinbrenner’s quest to keep Soto in pinstripes has him competing with the Mets, Red Sox, Blue Jays and Dodgers, and the price tag could well exceed $600 million.

Soto’s decision could arrive at or before MLB’s annual Winter Meetings, set to begin Sunday night at Dallas.

Naturally, the Yankees have cast a wide net on a potential free agent and trade targets, and they’ll have a lot more work to do if Soto, 26, takes his impact offensive talent to another team.

With question marks at the corner infield spots, Willy Adames, Alex Bregman and Christian Walker have been linked to Yankees’ interest, while Cubs’ outfielder-first baseman Cody Bellinger is a potential target.

Though the Yankees have six ready starters, they could use Nestor Cortes and/or Marcus Stroman in a trade and pursue Fried or Corbin Burnes, the top two remaining free agent starters.

Of course, the Yankees are already paying Gerrit Cole $36 million annually through 2028, while lefty Carlos Rodon is earning $27 million per year through 2028.

Fried, 30, made two All-Star teams with the Atlanta Braves and twice finished among the top five in the NL Cy Young Award balloting.

During his eight-season Atlanta tenure, Fried posted a 73-36 record and 3.07 ERA, with a 1.164 WHIP. In 29 starts last year, Fried went 11-10 with a 3.25 ERA, and 166 strikeouts vs. 57 walks in 174.1 innings.

headline: Paterson remains a city of champions. These achievers prove it | Opinion
fullText:
There are plenty of positive people in Paterson and so many success stories in our city that need to be told. My mission as mayor is make sure to tell them.

In recent weeks, our city has made historic and heartwarming headlines. Paterson has been in the news for noteworthy achievements in education, sports and community development. All inspiring stories that help put our city back on the map, and stories I am eager and elated to share in the subsequent paragraphs.

Shadasia Green graduated from the famed Eastside High School and received a whole host of full scholarship offers from a number of colleges. She ultimately selected Old Dominion University, where she played basketball and earned a bachelor’s degree in science. Although she excelled in basketball, Shadasia started boxing to diversify and intensify her training regimen. A few weeks ago on the undercard of the Mike Tyson-Jake Paul fight, Shadasia Green won the WBO Super Middleweight Championship. Consequently, she became the first woman from Paterson and from New Jersey to win a world title in the history of boxing.

Rodney Addison is a renaissance man. He is an entrepreneur, civic leader, nutritionist and bodybuilder. He plays a pivotal role in helping us save lives through our RealFix program which was designed to address drug addiction in Paterson. Moreover, he is the founder of Deliberate Nutri, a sports supplement company focused on holistic health and peak athletic performance. Just recently, Rodney won the prestigious “Mr. America” bodybuilding championship and became the first Patersonian to win the award in the 85-year history of the national competition.

Bob Guarasci was not born in Paterson, but he has quickly become one of our city’s favorite adopted sons. Thirty years ago, he founded the New Jersey Community Development Corporation and chose Paterson as the place to serve as his organization’s home. NJCDC’s mission has been to create opportunities to transform lives. Since 1994, the nonprofit organization has built affordable housing for individuals with chronic medical conditions or developmental disabilities and children who age out of foster care. Moreover, NJCDC has built 10 playgrounds and created five community gardens. Earlier this month, Bob Guarasci was inducted into the New Jersey Hall of Fame for doing God’s work in Paterson.

Nancy Castro started her educational career in 1992. She has been a substitute teacher, instructional assistant, classroom teacher, substance abuse coordinator and vice principal, and she is currently the principal of the No. 1 elementary school and grammar school in New Jersey, according to U.S. News & World Report. This is the second time the school has earned this remarkable distinction under her leadership.

Andre Sayegh: Paterson is a city that seizes opportunities

The aforementioned individuals are now a part of the pantheon of Patersonians who exemplify excellence. Our city boasts a champion in almost every sport: Victor Cruz in football, Essence Carson in basketball, Kendall Holt in boxing, Derrick Etienne Jr. in soccer and Larry Doby in baseball. The recent achievements highlighted in this column solidify Paterson as a bona fide “City of Champions,” and thankfully, there are more champions emerging in Paterson and more success stories that will continue to be told.

Andre Sayegh is the mayor of Paterson.

headline: Tree lightings, seasonal festivities, live music: Things to do in North Jersey, Dec. 5-8
fullText:

  • Friday: Sunny, with a high in the mid-30s. Mostly clear at night with a low in the mid-20s.
  • Saturday: Partly sunny, with a high in the upper 30s. Partly cloudy at night, with a low in the mid-20s.
  • Sunday: Mostly sunny, with a high around 40. Partly cloudy at night, with a low around 30.

Fort Lee holiday tree lighting

Go: Mistletoe Market at Turkey Brook Park in Mount Olive is open 5 to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday. The tree lighting is 6 p.m. Friday. mountolivetwpnj.org.

Christmas tree lighting in River Vale
