headline: Girls swimming: North Jersey team-by-team previews for 2024-25 season
fullText:
Take a team-by-team look at the North Jersey girls swimming teams heading into the 2024-25 season.

Big North American

Demarest (2-6): The Norsewomen are aiming for a top-10 finish at the Bergen County meet after adding a talented freshman class led by Sooa Tani and Lauren Szukics. Senior Trianha Puente and sophomore Kristen Liu pave the way as experienced scorers.

Indian Hills (7-2): The Braves head into the season as defending league champions and with a superstar senior in six-time county champion Katie Lawrence. The NC State commit will share the middle lanes with sophomore standouts Riley Horgan, Olivia de los Reyes and Camila Bazan.

Mahwah (2-7): With only two seniors to replace, the Thunderbirds have the potential to be a faster squad. Sophomore Lovy Lee is a rising star in the butterfly and works alongside senior Elie Meizys.

Ramapo (0-8): The Raiders got a much-needed boost from the freshman class with club swimmers Naya Snono, Maya Los and Grace Turano all coming on board. The speed of junior Sam Oring will be another plus in the program's upward climb.

Ramsey (4-5-1): The Rams have a good mix of young and old after taking second at the Big North American meet last winter and welcoming in a very large freshman class. Everyone from their division-winning medley relay is back led by senior Keely McGhee and junior Cameron Burns.

Big North Freedom

Hackensack/Teaneck: The classic football rivals formed a new merger in the pool, giving longtime Comets coach Scott Davis a much larger roster this year. Senior Leticia Laynez and sophomore Rebecca Ortiz anchor the lineup and senior sprinter Leena Cobo adds value for two schools looking to shake off losing seasons.

Northern Highlands (6-4): The Highlanders are always on the hunt for a sectional title and snapping a streak of eight straight last year will only add motivation. Junior Jessie Wolf is back as an All-North Jersey sprinter, freshman Taylor Leishman will contend for major titles and seniors Grace McKenna and Zainab Mahrach bolster the lineup.

Ridgewood (7-2): The Maroons are riding high after capturing league and sectional titles a year ago. While Isabel Lee is off to Columbia, the rest of the county champion 400 medley relay is back: namely, seniors Emma Briganti and Esme Hendrikse and junior Josie Marino.

River Dell/Westwood (6-6): Coach Chris Armen kicks off his 20th year with a goal of qualifying for the state tournament and making a competitive run in the division race. Seniors Ava Perrino, Stephie Perez and Noa Kizhnerman will be integral in that quest.

Big North Liberty

Clifton (4-7): The Mustangs are pushing for a better record under new coach Michael Velez after improving their win total in back-to-back seasons. Senior Renata Chyshkevych is a big asset in the backstroke and sophomores Antonina Kiszkiel and Amanda Pinnock will play key roles.

Lakeland/West Milford (6-6): Turnout might be the biggest strength for coach Patty Kebrdle, whose team is vying for a winning record after back-to-back .500 seasons. Senior Emily Kebrdle will be a focal point as a three-time county champ and sophomores Amanda Magee and Emily Orsato are returning medalists.

Pascack Regional (9-1): The co-op took a huge step forward last year in coach Shawn Buchanan's return, finishing fourth at the Bergen County meet and sweeping its league rivals in dual competition. Amanda Bramley and Rianna Kirkorian make up a strong 1-2 punch again as individual division champs and Phoebe Garretson adds backstroke speed for a roster made up primarily of underclassmen.

Passaic (0-11): Although the elusive win never came last year, the Indians showed progress with their highest scoring average in over a decade. With Passaic County silver medalist Zariah Townsend back as a junior, the program continues to strive for more.

Passaic Tech (9-3): The Bulldogs will be favored to win a seventh straight Passaic County title with the return of all three individual champions: juniors Francesca Cordero and Danna Tapia and sophomore Charlize Macaranas. Julia Lo also returns as the reigning league champ in the butterfly.

Big North Patriot

Old Tappan (5-3): The Golden Knights will be a contender with the return of three Patriot first-teamers: Julia Fila, Coco O'Connell and Zoey Aydin. With only two seniors, Aydin will be thurst into the spotlight as a sophomore having already won league titles in the backstroke and breaststroke.

Paramus (4-3): The Spartans start a new era under Todd Colombo, who spent eight years as a head coach in Hudson County. Among the building blocks are seniors Angelia Choi, Adriana Coccaro and Subora Muca.

Tenafly (8-1-1): One year after going unbeaten in the regular season, the Tigers are on the hunt for a sectional crown with a deep and versatile lineup. Senior Emelia Lan and junior Sienna Plutzer help the cause as division champions and sophomore Sophie Kakuda is back as a county qualifier.

Wayne Hills (7-2-1): After back-to-back titles at the Big North Patriot meet, longtime coach Mike Shale will have some rebuilding to do with a roster of 11. Seniors Rebecca Siuffe and Sasha Wunej will be critical to their success.

Wayne Valley (3-6): State backstroke champion Sarah Rodrigues will take centerstage as a senior in her final season before heading down to swim at Texas. With classmates Avery Derstine and Urvi Sinha featured prominently in the supporting cast, the Indians will draw strength from the relays.

Big North United

Immaculate Heart (11-0): The Blue Eagles will chase after another Triple Crown behind an impressive group of veterans led by senior state medalist Kayla Rodriguez in the breaststroke. She'll chase after her fourth straight county title in that event while racing alongside juniors Mariana Builes and seniors Isabella Piccinich and Madison Assanah.

Paramus Catholic (2-6): Second-year coach Kristina Sajnoska will lean on junior Juliann LoCicero while trying to get the Paladins in the right direction. Freshman Alexa Broggi looks like an important addition.

NJIC

Garfield/Hasbrouck Heights (7-3): Coach Laura Mielke's team has turned in three straight winning season, but needs to rebuild a bit with a smaller lineup. Senior Lucia Lopez and sophomore Natasha Duran-Gonzalez will be go-to scorers after bringing home conference silver medals in the backstroke and butterfly, respectively.

Leonia/Palisades Park (9-2): The Lions will be hard to stop with state medalists Rebekah Jung and Iris Kim leading the chase for a 10th straight conference meet title. Seniors Sophie Dahiya and Sophia Lazarou add to an experienced lineup looking to get over the hump after falling three points short of its first sectional title.

Lyndhurst/North Arlington (3-5): The Golden Bears have improved their record over the last two seasons and the return of junior Evangelise Amaya is an important step in keeping that trend alive. Keep an eye on freshman Isabella DeCoro as well.

Rutherford (9-3): The Bulldogs have the speed to stay near the top of the conference after bringing back their four leading scorers from the NJIC meet. Seniors Ava Stadler, Grace Farnum and Salma El Sherbiny headline a solid top-to-bottom roster.

Secaucus (4-5): The Patriots turn to new coach Nicole Hernandez, who believes the team's endurance and competitive fire will translate to strong results. Sophomore Abigail Montero will be counted on in the freestyle and seniors Ryanne Abuhadba and Marie-Sophia Buenafe return as captains.

Weehawken (1-12): Personal growth will a focus this year for the Indians with eight swimmers on the roster. Sophomore Inez Pratt will be a bright spot and sophomore Katherine Neri has shown promise.

headline: Will daylight saving time become permanent? NJ lawmakers give it a try
fullText:
It’s been weeks now, and I still feel discombobulated.

Once upon a timepiece, it took me a mere three days to adjust to the disappearance (and reappearance) of daylight saving time. But the older I get, the less resilient I seem to be. 

I “fell back” to Eastern Standard Time in November, and I’ve been an unholy mess ever since.

And I’m not the only one. 

Two weeks ago, at a family gathering, I glanced down at my phone and asked the other guests what time they thought it was. 

Answers ranged from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. — and it was barely 5:45.

When I told them the actual time they stared at me in disbelief. Responses included “No!” “That can’t be!” And: “You’re kidding! I’m ready for bed!”

That last one didn’t surprise me, though. I’m pushing 70. And I’m always ready for bed.

Sometimes I wake up in the morning, shower, have coffee, take a few deep, fortifying breaths and then, you know …

Go back to bed.

Which brings me to another “fall back” lament: nightly sleep disruption.

About two weeks after the time change, my friend Tom announced, “I don’t know what’s wrong with me, but I’ve been waking up every morning at 3 a.m.”

“Me, too!” I yelled into the phone. “What’s going on?”

Two other friends told me the same thing.

I could see waking up an hour earlier or later than usual, depending on the time of year. But so many people waking up at 3 a.m. — and staring out the window like zombies?

It sounded like a “Twilight Zone” episode. We wake up in the middle of the night and stare up at the sky because we’re waiting for the spaceship to come and get us, so we can get onboard their craft, interact with intergalactic space visitors and, you know … 

Go to bed.

“Why do these earthlings sleep so much?”

“I have no idea. Maybe it’s because of their tiny heads.”

All of this clock-changing business was designed to save energy. But it seems to have the opposite effect on our bodies.

Dr. Adam Spira, a sleep expert on the Johns Hopkins University website, recently said, “The scientific evidence points to an acute increase in adverse health consequences from changing the clocks, including heart attack and stroke.”

Other effects can include mood disturbances and what the Johns Hopkins website refers to as “an elevated production of inflammatory markers in response to stress.”

Are all of these things intensified when you get older? Of course, they are.

Aging most definitely affects our internal body clocks the same way it affects those $19.99 kitchen wall clocks that I used to buy at Bed Bath & Beyond. They work fine for two or three years. Then they start losing five minutes here, 10 minutes there. Before you know it, they’re an hour behind, their hands are moving backward and their batteries start leaking. It’s a nightmare.

Our internal clock — also known as our natural circadian rhythm — takes longer to adjust to time changes as we age. In addition to creating new health problems, these changes can exacerbate existing ones, like insomnia.

All of this brings to mind a notion that’s been floating around for decades: Should we keep daylight saving time year-round?

Earlier this year, New Jersey lawmakers put forward a bill in the state Senate —  S1510 — that would put the state on daylight saving time permanently if Congress gives its approval. But that measure is still pending in the Legislature.

If you ask them, most folks will probably tell you they prefer daylight saving time. But not Dr. Spira. He says the extra daylight we get with DST throws off our natural clocks and makes the switch back to standard time more difficult.

Last week, I woke up, called my friend Tom and told him how tired I was: “The clock says eight, but it feels like 10 and I don’t feel doing anything. But at least it’s Saturday.”

He told me it was Thursday.

THURSDAY?

I’m a mess.

headline: Mehmet Oz has no business running the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services | Opinion
fullText:
President-elect Donald Trump has proposed unsuccessful Pennsylvania Senate candidate Dr. Mehmet Oz to run the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services — that’s the same Dr. Oz of television fame. Though he was trained as a cardiothoracic surgeon, his reliability regarding medical advice went off the rails years ago.

A profile of Oz in The New Yorker reviewed his televised claims and stated that “Oz has been criticized by scientists for relying on flimsy or incomplete data, distorting the results, and wielding his vast influence in ways that threaten the health of anyone who watches the show.” Putting Oz in charge of Medicare and Medicaid? What’s next? Perhaps Trump wants to appoint Mike Lindell, who sells “MyPillow” on late-night cable television, as surgeon general?

The voters of Pennsylvania wisely kept Oz out of the U.S. Senate. Of course, it didn’t help his campaign that he was a resident of New Jersey and quickly obtained a Pennsylvania address to run for Senate. Regarding giving Oz the consolation prize of a federal job, let’s consider some objective data.

Scientists at Canada’s University of Alberta medical school studied medical recommendations made on Oz’s television show. Most recommendations concerned general medical and dietary advice and how to lose weight. They studied whether there was any scientific evidence to support his recommendations and published their findings in 2014 in the British Medical Journal. There was “believable or somewhat believable” scientific evidence supporting the medical advice dispensed on “The Dr. Oz Show” only 33% of the time. I take care of children with cancer, and I never met a patient or their parents who wants a doctor whose advice is believable or somewhat believable one time out of every three. 

The researchers also reported that Oz recommended that his viewers consult a health care professional only 9% of the time — in contrast to another television advice-dispensing show called “The Doctors,” where the show recommended consulting a health care professional 33% of the time. Where I went to medical school, we were taught that standard practice involved obtaining expert advice from a doctor who had personally taken a patient’s medical history, performed a physical examination and reviewed the relevant X-rays and laboratory results. Maybe television’s Oz missed that lesson? 

Oz and his television show guests failed to disclose financial conflicts, said an article in the American Medical Association’s Journal of Ethics. The article concluded, “Oz is a dangerous rogue … He has told mothers that there were dangerous levels of arsenic in their child’s apple juice (there weren’t) and suggested that green coffee is a ‘miracle’ cure for obesity. Federal regulators discovered altered data in hyped coffee bean evidence … Dr. Oz also featured two guests on his show who claimed that genetically modified foods were cancer-causing (despite repeated safety reports that found no adverse effects).”

On the show about genetically modified foods, Oz identified his guest as “a scientist” when, in fact, he had no scientific degrees or experience in genetics or agriculture.

In the operating room, Oz was known for encouraging and practicing Reiki, a Japanese art of laying on the hands based on the groundless assertion that a nonexistent source of energy flows through our bodies.

In a 2014 congressional hearing, then-U.S. Sen. Claire McCaskill told Oz, “I don’t get why you have to say this stuff, because you know it’s not true … So why, when you have this amazing megaphone and this amazing ability to communicate, why would you cheapen your show by saying things like that?”

Opinion: Time's up on celebrity impunity: Power cannot hide sexual exploitation

Oz held a faculty appointment at Columbia University’s medical school. Several years ago, 10 prominent physicians wrote to Columbia’s dean. They said Oz was endangering public health and had demonstrated contempt for medical and scientific evidence. They recommended that his faculty appointment be revoked. In 2022, Columbia quietly changed Oz’s faculty appointment to emeritus status. 

A respected New York surgeon told The New Yorker that he stopped referring patients to Oz years ago. “Mehmet is an entertainer … Mehmet will entertain wacky ideas — particularly if they are wacky and have entertainment value.”

An editorial in the Journal of the Missouri State Medical Association described Oz’s promotion of useless homeopathic remedies, how he frequently had guests on his show who claimed they were psychics able to communicate with the dead and spirits, and that he hosted guests espousing the unscientific claim that sections of the eye’s iris correspond to parts of the body and that a person’s health can be diagnosed by examining regions of the iris. The editorial writer pointed out that the risks created by Oz were of “great harm by preventing or delaying proper diagnosis, providing false hope, and encouraging people to waste money on useless treatments.” "Dr. Oz's Five Wackiest Medical Beliefs” appeared in Forbes magazine. A professor of genetics at the Scripps Research Institute, Eric Topol, described many of Oz’s claims as “simple lunacy.” This is not medicine, Topol said, “it’s more like medutainment.”

Those Americans dependent on Medicare and Medicaid deserve a reliable manager at the helm of the system, not medutainment. Oz publicly forfeited a claim to reliability long ago on television for all to see.

Edward C. Halperin, M.D., M.A., teaches history of medicine at New York Medical College and is a pediatric radiation oncologist. He is also chancellor and CEO of the college. This essay represents his opinion and not that of the college.

headline: Paterson schools weigh adding staff to fix how it handles sex abuse claims
fullText:
PATERSON — City education officials are trying to figure out whether they need to hire additional employees to fix the way Paterson Public Schools handles sexual harassment complaints.

District officials said they are “assessing the resources” they need to address the findings of an investigation by the federal Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights that uncovered problems with Paterson’s system for addressing sexual harassment in schools.

After the civil rights office findings were announced Monday, Paterson Press asked the city district whether it required additional funding or staff members to comply with a 15-page plan for adhering to the federal law regarding sexual harassment in schools.

Story continues below photo gallery.

“Specific staffing and funding decisions are still under review as we work to align with the agreement’s goals,” said district spokesperson Aida Rosario.

“We will address the requirements through policy updates, enhanced training for staff, improved recordkeeping practices, and increased communication with students, families, and staff about their rights and available support,” Rosario added.

School board members said they were waiting to get a plan from the district’s administration for resolving the problem. Several board members said they were unaware that the district’s sexual harassment program was under scrutiny until news of the federal review broke on Monday.

The U.S. Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights sent Paterson Superintendent Laurie Newell a 20-page letter on Monday detailing the district’s failures over a five-year period starting in 2017.

“The district generally failed to respond equitably to allegations of sexual harassment, including sexual assault,” said the letter.

Four incidents not in district's reports

The civil rights office cited four instances in which its investigators learned of sexual harassment allegations involving school employees and students that were not included in the district’s compliant reports:

  • A high school case in which a teacher was involved in a sexual relationship with a student. The district fired the teacher and notified the Prosecutor’s Office but did not alert the Office for Civil Rights.
  • Another instance of a high school teacher and student being involved in “an inappropriate relationship.” Again, police were contacted but Paterson did not notify the U.S. Education Department.
  • An elementary school student who reported that an employee inappropriately touched her. The district investigated and determined that the allegation was “unfounded.” But the district did not file reports with the civil rights office.
  • A high school student who complained that a teacher touched her breasts while reaching across her. The district determined that the complaint was unfounded but did not submit a report to the federal Education Department.

The letter from federal officials to Newell cited many systemic problems, such as a lack of training and failures to inform staff and students about how sexual harassment should be addressed.

The agreement to rectify the problem includes numerous deadlines that Paterson school officials must meet to avoid further intervention from the federal government.

The agreement sets time frames for when Paterson schools must inform all students and staff members about sexual harassment protocols, for when training must be provided, and for when policies need to be revised.

headline: These NJ towns were named among the nation's most desirable eco-friendly suburbs
fullText:
When deciding on the best towns to put down roots, choosing one that offers eco-friendly living has become a growing priority for many people. And according to a recent report, three of the nation's most desired sustainable suburbs are located right here in the Garden State.

Solar Insure, a solar energy company based in California, surveyed 3,000 participants on the greenest towns they'd most like to move to for an eco-friendly lifestyle. With the results, the company compiled a ranked list of the 120 most desired sustainable suburbs across the country.

The communities selected all offer the charm and amenities that are a trademark of suburban living, but also focus on energy efficiency, green initiatives and reducing their overall environmental footprint.

NJ's most desirable sustainable suburbs

The New Jersey towns of Montclair, Princeton Junction and Maplewood were all named among the nation's most desirable sustainable suburbs.

The highest on the list for the Garden State, No. 36 Montclair's walkable neighborhoods and easily accessible public transit system contributed to its ranking, minimizing car dependency for the town's residents. Montclair also has a designated Office of Sustainability, showcasing the town's dedication to being eco-friendly through a comprehensive recycling program, community gardens and green building codes, among other things. Farmers' markets and local food initiatives that promote sustainability in Montclair were also cited in the report.

Princeton Junction, which ranked 43rd, was highlighted in the report for its green building standards, extensive recycling and sustainable landscaping practices. The town is also known for its abundance of parks and trails, hosting farmers' markets to support local agriculture and offering a convenient public transit system that minimizes car dependency, according to the report.

No. 65 Maplewood was named for promoting its recycling and composting programs, encouraging walkability with a pedestrian-friendly downtown and offering an abundance of green spaces, according to the report. The town is also known for supporting green building practices, energy-efficient upgrades and several other sustainability initiatives.

Other desirable eco-friendly suburbs in the tri-state area

Several other suburban communities in the New York metropolitan area were named among the nation's most desirable eco-friendly suburbs, including one that broke the ranking's top 10.

Brooklyn, specifically the Prospect Park area, was named the sixth most desirable eco-friendly community, according to the report. Integrating green infrastructure, bike lanes and a variety of public transit options in the borough contributed to its ranking, and the Prospect Park area was highlighted for having energy-efficient buildings, community gardens and waste reduction programs.

No. 26 Fairfield, Connecticut; No. 39 Rye, New York; No. 51 Scarsdale, New York; and No. 89 Pelham, New York made up the remaining communities named from the tri-state area.

And the top five most desirable sustainable suburbs, according to the report, are Coral Gables, Florida; Kailua, Hawaii; Santa Monica, California; Weston, Florida; and Hilo, Hawaii.

headline: NJ port workers' contract talks stuck over adding automation as January deadline nears
fullText:
Talks between the United States Maritime Alliance and the International Longshoremen’s Association have broken down in recent weeks over the issue of introducing more automation at East Coast ports, including the Port of New York and New Jersey, just a month and a half ahead of a new deadline — and potential new strike. 

A longshoremen's strike in October lasted 72 hours, shutting down 36 ports from Maine to Texas. More than 47,000 dock workers — represented by the ILA, a union based in North Bergen — walked off the job at the start of the month, including 4,500 from New York and New Jersey.

They agreed to return to the job with pay increases and a new deadline to iron out other contract details, including the automation issue, by Jan. 15, 2025. 

Story continues below photo gallery.

Union members fear that port automation could mean job cuts and want to negotiate the use of any such technology by marine operators. 

Leaders at the ILA had cut off contract talks in June after learning that a form of automation had been introduced at the Port of Mobile in Alabama, an action they said violated their existing contract. 

“Automation, whether full or semi, replaces jobs and erodes the historic work functions that the ILA fought hard to protect,” union President Harold Daggett said in a Dec. 3 statement on Facebook. “The ILA is prepared to strike again if an agreement is not reached.” 

The Lyndhurst-based shipping alliance, also known as USMX, represents shipping companies and port terminal operators. 

More: NJ ports have been slow to modernize. Will they take the leap to control costs?

“Port operations must evolve, and embracing modern technology is critical to this evolution," USMX said in a Dec. 3 statement promoting automation. "It means improving performance to move more cargo more efficiently through existing facilities advancements that are crucial for U.S. workers, consumers and companies.”

“Due to the lack of available new land in most ports, the only way for U.S. East and Gulf Coast ports to handle more volume is to densify terminals — enabling the movement of more cargo through their existing footprints," USMX said. "It has been proven this can be accomplished while delivering benefits to both USMX members and to the ILA.” 

Strike could upend global supply chain

A strike has the potential to upend the global supply chain and the national economy. The October strike generated fears that it could have disrupted the busy 2024 holiday shopping season. 

While the effect of the October strike was short-lived, shoppers engaged in panic buying for water bottles and paper goods, including toilet paper, even though most toilet paper is produced in the U.S. 

The economic activity in ports affects many types of businesses, such as warehousing and transport, which could see a fallout from work stoppages and put more than 100,000 employees out of work, according to news reports.

Story continues below photo gallery.

A port strike's far-reaching impacts on businesses and consumers extends even to the kitchen table.

Consumers would first notice shortages of perishable products, as grocery aisles could be bare of popular fruits like bananas within weeks, given that about two-thirds of bananas in the U.S. arrive at East Coast ports.

Ultimately, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which oversees the ports in both states, said it took less than a week to clear the backlog of goods after the October strike. 

In New York and New Jersey, the economic impact on the 19 counties that surround the ports of both states was $250 million to $300 million for every day of the strike, Port Authority officials said.

This story contains material from USA Today.

headline: North Jersey woman sues Dunkin' over spill of 'excessively hot' coffee
fullText:
HAWTHORNE — An Essex County woman is suing Dunkin’ after she said a scalding beverage spilled on her at a local coffee shop.

Zina Lewis, of East Orange, filed a six-count complaint against the fast-food titan in state Superior Court in Newark, claiming a worker was negligent by failing to secure the plastic lid to the top of her cup of coffee and that the liquid was too hot.

In fact, the lawsuit says, it was so “excessively hot” that it was unsafe for the public to consume. It was “heated beyond industry standards,” the complaint states.

Passaic County: Mom sues school district over bullying after her daughter attempts suicide

Because the lid did not fit on her cup, Lewis says, the coffee easily poured out. As a result, she endured permanent injuries, she says, while spending an unspecified amount of money on doctor bills.

The alleged incident occurred on July 15 at the Dunkin’ restaurant at 84 Goffle Road — less than 300 yards from the Prospect Park border.

The 12-page suit asks a judge to award damages and interest.

Dunkin’, a $13.3 billion brand with more than 13,700 restaurants in 38 countries, did not respond to an inquiry about the allegations. The suit identifies only the corporate entity as a defendant.

The Massachusetts-based chain retooled its image in January 2019 when it officially abbreviated its time-honored moniker. It was acquired less than two years later by Inspire Brands, a limited liability company that also owns Arby’s, Baskin-Robbins and Jimmy John’s, among other major players in the industry.

Court cases involving hot coffee have been famously satirized by TV sitcoms.

A September 1995 episode of “Seinfeld” parodied a widely publicized incident that occurred three years earlier when an elderly customer spilled coffee on her lap after purchasing it at a McDonald’s drive-thru in Albuquerque, New Mexico. A jury awarded the real woman, who was severely burned, almost $2.9 million, though news reports indicate that sum was reduced by the trial judge overseeing the case.

headline: These North Jersey restaurants are open on Christmas Day 2024
fullText:
Andy Williams was a multi-platinum recording artist. He sold over 11 million records in the U.S. alone, and had an estimated $45 million net worth at his time of death.

So, when Christmas rolled around each December and he crooned "It's the most wonderful time of the year!," he wasn't thinking about the weeks of shopping, days in the kitchen and hours of stringing lights that it took to make the holidays transpire.

Because he was Andy Williams. He had people for that.

This season, I can't help you hire a maid, decor company or personal shopper, but I can certainly alleviate the stress of preparing a five-course meal for your in-laws — and have you one step closer to singing along to those festive lyrics.

With chefs ready and eager to assume your culinary workload, then, here are eight local restaurants open on Christmas Day.

Blue Morel, Morristown

Special occasion dining is an everyday thing at Blue Morel, as the upscale restaurant is nestled inside Morristown's four-starred Westin Governor Morris. Featuring a menu of elevated eats prepared with seasonal flair, the lush hotel spot — which is currently turning out foie gras with apple, for example — is a comfortable-yet-impressive place to enjoy any meal; let alone a Christmas one.

This holiday, spoil your family with a dinner of pan seared salmon and crisp-edged crab cakes. As you traverse the Westin lobby, passing chandeliers and colorful couches on your way to the restaurant, you'll feel as though you stepped into The Plaza scene from Home Alone 2.

When/where: 11:30 a.m. to 6 p.m at 2 Whippany Rd., Morristown; 973-451-2619, bluemorel.com.

Cheng Du 23, Wayne

Nothing says Christmas like Chinese food (thanks, A Christmas Story), and no local Chinese restaurant compares to Cheng Du 23. Whereas tiny hole-in-the-walls offer fantastic eats, and larger pan-Asian restaurants wow with stunning ornamental vibes, the Wayne spot is one of the only around to nail both the gastronomic and atmospheric components of dining.

Order a plate of Crispy Whole Fish and enjoy a seasoned chef's specialty against a back drop of linen tablecloths and painted artwork, or opt for the Spicy Cumin Lamb and savor Sichuan flavors served by waiters in dapper black attire.

For a truly memorable experience, however, select the Peking Duck — because, unlike the one in A Christmas Story, it's served head off, cooked to the proper temperature (the Parkers' looked so dry I'm surprised it even made the scene) and accompanied by soft pancakes and sweet hoisin sauce.

When/where: 11:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. (closed 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m.) at 6 Willowbrook Blvd., Wayne; 973-812-2800, chengdu23.com.

RP Prime, Fair Lawn & Mahwah

Prime Filet Mignon, West Coast Oysters and a Chilled Colossal Seafood Platter for Two — there's not a dish on RP Prime's menu that doesn't scream extravagance.

Hungry for an American classic? Go for a medium-rare Porterhouse. More of a fish person? Try the Scottish salmon with champagne mustard. And, if you're a vegetarian? Porcini ravioli with fresh-shaved truffles have your name on them.

From the appetizers (think popcorn shrimp tempura) to the desserts (picture a four-scoop "Serendipity" ice cream sundae), every creation at the contemporary steakhouse is perfect for the most over-the-top day of the year.

When/where: Noon to 10 p.m. at 209 Ramapo Valley Road in Mahwah & 41-11 Route 4 in Fair Lawn; rpprime.com.

Sofia, Englewood

A sleek Italian steakhouse with elevated cocktails and a notable seafood selection, Sofia in Englewood is known for:

  1. Reliably serving great food
  2. Reliably being open

Simultaneously boasting house-made pasta (with 1.5 pounds of lobster) and hours until 1 a.m. (or later), the elegant spot is one of the only places you can go for a luxurious meal at 11:28 p.m.

Keeping with the trend, the restaurant will operate as usual on Christmas. To acknowledge the occasion, holiday specials will be offered alongside its traditional dinner menu.

When/where: 11:30 a.m. to 1 a.m. at 36 Engle St., Englewood; 201-541-8530, sofiaenglewood.com.

Meat Moot, Paterson

Christmas dinner is often associated with ham, but, after the honey-glazed pink meat, lamb might be the next most festive protein. The reason it doesn't take center stage (especially in a modern era), though, is likely because it's so challenging to cook. Leave a rack of chops over the heat for too long, and you're looking at a platter of leather boots on a stick.

Whether neck, shoulder or ribs, however, you'll never see overcooked lamb at Meat Moot.

Utilizing a multi-day smoking process, the team slow-cooks its meats to irresistible, fall-off-the-bone consistency.

And, when each cut is plated to order? It comes with nine sauces and six family-style sides.

When/where: Noon to 11 p.m. at 1068 Main St., Paterson; 646-804-8818, meatmoot.com.tr.

The 'Champagne Chalets' at Crystal Springs Resort, Hamburg

Imagine celebrating Christmas in a heated glass Champagne Chalet. Visualize magnificent views, floral decor and cozy wooden tables. Then put yourself at a romantic coursed dinner, or an evening with family, tucked in your own private suite on the stunning terrace of a four-diamond lodge.

As Stevie Wonder once sung, "That's what Christmas means to me, my love!"

When/where: The private glass Champagne Chalets are open from December 22-26 at 1 Wild Turkey Way, Hamburg. Call 844-205-1857 for availability. If booked, the festive hotel has multiple other lavish restaurants on its property; crystalgolfresort.com/dine.

The Highlawn, West Orange

If a prix fixe meal is what you're after this holiday season, The Highlawn has you covered. For Christmas, the tinsel-adorned restaurant — which probably has more lights than Clark Griswold's mansion — is offering a coursed lunch and dinner menu themed around the flavors of December.

Though the cost of the prix fixe is yet to be announced, the team promises "seasonal classics" like prime rib, roasted veal osso bucco and seared duck. Herbed popovers will accompany main courses, and desserts are sure to be à la mode.

When/where: 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. (lunch) and 5 to 9 p.m. (dinner) at 1 Crest Dr., West Orange; 973-731-3463, highlawn.com.

Flaming Grill & Modern Buffet, East Hanover

Because the only thing as exciting as waking up on Christmas is an all-you-can-eat Chinese buffet.

When/where: 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. at 240 Route 10 (Suite 10), East Hanover; 973-887-8888, fgmbuffet.com.

Kara VanDooijeweert is a food writer for NorthJersey.com and The Record. If you can't find her in Jersey's best restaurants, she's probably off running a race course in the mountains. headline: On Hunter's pardon, we shouldn't pan Joe Biden for doing his job as a dad | Opinion
fullText:
Everybody seems to be dumping on President Joe Biden these days because he erred on the side of mercy and pardoned his bad-boy son, Hunter.

Good for Joe. 

Biden will likely go down in history now as a so-so president. But he’ll always be a first-class dad.

Let’s not dump on him for that.

Children who step beyond the straight and narrow paths of life are difficult — and that’s an understatement. Plenty of parents know that. Some give up and disown their perpetually bad kids — and, frankly, who can blame such parents? Some kids never take responsibility, never clean up their act. 

But plenty of other parents never kick their kids to life's curb, allowing them to languish in an emotional gutter. They never close the doors to their home, even when rational neighbors and relatives tell them they should. I have come to believe that such parents are life’s unsung heroes. I’m blessed to know plenty.

Many of these parents spend decades of sleepless nights worrying about their kids. They write checks to cover the costs at addiction centers. They drive their kids to visits with psychotherapists and tutors. They pay off their kids' credit cards and all manner of other unpaid bills. They show up for court hearings, even prison visits. In short, they never give up, even when it hurts. They understand a difficult fact of life — that to be a parent is to know life is about second chances, maybe even third and fourth and fifth chances.

Biden could not divorce his role as a dad from politics

So it was with Joe Biden and his son.  

Biden never cut off his ties to his errant son. Yes, Hunter Biden was a drug addict. And yes, Hunter played a sleazy game of business when he traded on his father’s reputation and good name to secure million-dollar deals with a Ukrainian energy company. 

Yes, Hunter bought a gun illegally — and then made false statements. He delayed paying his taxes. A jury convicted him on the gun violations. Hunter pleaded guilty on the tax charges. He was likely heading to prison. And, to top off Hunter’s creepy rap sheet of moral and legal transgressions, he had a romantic fling with his dead brother’s wife, explaining that both were in mourning and needed some comfort.

Yes, the ick factor with Hunter was awesome to behold. And there is more — plenty more. 

When Joe Biden pardoned his son, the moral police who now dominate public dialogue across America, especially on social media, erupted in volcanic fashion. And why not?

Didn’t Biden promise in a televised interview just a few months ago that he would never pardon Hunter? (Well, yes.) And hasn’t Biden always proclaimed that America should trust his word “as a Biden”? (Yes again.) And isn’t Biden, as president, supposed to respect the rule of law? (Of course.) And wasn’t Biden deceitful, underhanded and more than a bit disingenuous in waiting until after the election to pardon his kid? (Good point.)

Looking at this issue from yet another legitimate point of view, consider the fact that Hunter Biden is allowed to go free now with an unusually wide-ranging presidential pardon while plenty of poor Black kids who don’t have access to good lawyers and a powerful father end up in jail for long sentences because they were caught with an illegal handgun. Or perhaps they smoked too much weed.

Indeed, Hunter Biden’s pardon has sparked a cottage industry of what-about-ism counterarguments. And rightly so. 

For instance, one argument, largely from MAGA world, suggests that if Biden pardons his son, why not also absolve Donald Trump of his alleged crimes? (Good point.) Or, if Hunter walks free, why not open the prison cells that hold hundreds of protesters after they were found guilty of crimes when they attacked the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021? (Another good point.)

As a Trump supporter who regularly emails me noted: “Are you happy that the disgusting liar YOU support lied about pardoning his criminal son????” (Note the extra capital letters and question marks.)

But MAGA world’s Trump supporters are not alone in their outrage. The uber-liberal “Pod Save America” podcast gang said Biden made the Democratic Party look “stupid.” And Vanity Fair magazine proclaimed that Biden’s pardon was a “stunning act of hypocrisy.” 

Opinion: By selfishly pardoning his son Hunter, Joe Biden flat-out destroyed his legacy

Opinion: Biden was right to pardon his son. Trump would have made Hunter a target

Can we learn from the lesson of the prodigal son?

I could go on and on. The anger from all directions on the political spectrum is not only understandable; it’s justified on many levels. Simply put: As a political and presidential decision, Biden’s pardon is riddled with duplicity and the kind of hoodwinking that voters despise in elected officials.

But Joe Biden is more than just a politician and a president. He’s a father. Balancing those roles — the professional and the personal — is extraordinarily difficult, maybe impossible in this case. Especially when you reverse course in such a public way.

Mercy and forgiveness are not always clean, especially when such virtues involve a long-suffering parent and a bad kid. In some instances, mercy and forgiveness — indeed, changing your mind and reversing course — can be downright clumsy.

Historians are already predicting that Biden’s political legacy will be forever tarnished. Some even predict that it will take years to redeem the nation’s respect for the rule of law, especially now that Donald Trump promises to clean up the so-called "deep state."

Maybe so. But when President Gerald Ford pardoned Richard Nixon in 1974, the nation did not dissolve into puddles of disillusion. The same was true when Bill Clinton pardoned the fugitive financier Marc Rich. Or when Barack Obama commuted 395 life sentences of criminals who had been sent to prison. Or when Trump pardoned Charles Kushner and Roger Stone. Or even when Abraham Lincoln, in summoning America's “better angels” after a bitter and bloody Civil War, did not opt to send Confederate traitors Robert E. Lee and Jefferson Davis to the gallows. 

Again, I could go on and on. 

Hunter Biden is a real-life version of the “prodigal son” in the famous parable that Jesus of Nazareth told as a lesson about mercy and forgiveness. Critics of Joe Biden might want to take a few minutes to read that tale in the Christian Gospel of Luke. It’s less than 600 words, but it speaks volumes.

The heart of the story depicts a father welcoming his misbehaving, ne’er-do-well “prodigal son” back to his home. The kid was shiftless, irresponsible –— basically a low-life jerk who rejected his father and demanded an early installment on his inheritance. The father gave the kid plenty of money. But the kid squandered it. And when the kid returned as a failure, the father not only opened the doors of his home, he threw a party, proclaiming that a son who was "lost" has now been "found." 

The story takes on an even more complicated philosophical and moral twist, however. The father’s other son — a good boy who played by the rules and worked hard for his father — complains about being ignored and asks a series of “what-about-me?” questions, pointing out how unfair the father’s mercy and forgiveness seems. You can almost hear the good son asking: "Why are we celebrating this jackass brother? Don't I count for something? What about justice for me?"

The essential beauty of the "prodigal son" story is that you can understand all sides — the bad son's need for help; the good son's desire for fairness; the father's longing to just love his kids as best he can. Indeed, each side makes good points.

In the end, the father opts for mercy and forgiveness. Such a decision might seem unfair to some. But it was right.

That’s what Joe Biden did. Maybe he wasn’t fair when he changed his mind. But he was right.  

Good for him.

headline: NJ companies stockpiling imports to avoid Trump's promised China tariffs
fullText:
From an apparel maker in Newark to an electrical distribution manufacturer in Kearny, the prospect of tariffs in a Trump administration has left New Jersey businesses facing uncertain prospects.

For some, it’s a “wait and see” approach, said Peter Connolly, director and chief executive officer of the New Jersey Manufacturers Extension Program. “They want to wait and see what he actually implements,” Connolly said of President-elect Donald Trump.

Others are not waiting around. 

Trump has promised he will quickly enact 25% tariffs on goods coming from Mexico and Canada, and additional 10% tariffs on anything coming from China; he previously promised 60% tariffs on goods coming from China. 

Story continues below photo gallery.

While some North Jersey companies manufacture their products in the U.S., some still import their raw materials from China, including Kearny-based Mac Products, which makes electrical distribution and transmission products, said owner Eddie Russnow. 

Russnow said Mac Products is “ordering forward" with its Chinese suppliers for the steel and copper used for many of Mac’s components. 

The plan going forward is to see where the raw materials can be sourced domestically, Russnow said, but the expectation is that Mac will take a hit to its profits, since any new tariffs against China will make the imported raw material he needs more costly, and the company can't raise prices. 

More: Trump threatens tariffs on Canada, Mexico, China imports. Here's what NJ gets from them

“If [companies] have an increase in their costs because of the tariffs, they’re either going to increase the cost to the customer, take a hit internally or reduce their profit,” said Tom Bracken, president of the New Jersey Chamber of Commerce.

The last option means finding “savings in other places,” Bracken said — usually through job cuts.

Why does Trump want tariffs?

Trump’s stated goal with tariffs is to shift more manufacturing domestically to the U.S. Many economists have criticized that notion, saying tariffs would trigger a trade war that would create obstacles for U.S. businesses to export their products overseas, and cause prices to rises on consumer goods on American store shelves.

“Despite Trump’s assertions to the contrary, tariffs are paid by the companies or entities importing goods and not by the countries themselves,” said Neil Saunders, a retail analyst and managing director of GlobalData.

“This means the cost of buying products from overseas, whether directly or as an input for manufacturing, would rise sharply,” he said. 

Most of the costs of tariffs would be borne by consumers, ultimately triggering more inflation and eating into the national gross domestic product, said Parul Jain, who teaches finance at Rutgers Business School in Newark. 

“Smaller manufacturers, conceivably, could be extra challenged by transition costs,” said a recent post by the New Jersey Business and Industry Association. “Larger manufacturers, also conceivably, might find tariffs an opportunity to rebuild their supply networks."

Tariffs, automation could make NJ-made more competitive

At Unionwear, a Newark-based company that produces apparel such as hats with the “Made in USA” logo on them, CEO Mitch Cahn is optimistic that the combination of tariffs and automation will make his products more competitive with imported goods. 

Still, Cahn said the company is expecting the automation machinery at the end of January and is in the process of pushing the delivery up ahead of Trump’s inauguration day, which is Jan. 20.

Cahn said there will be demands for “Made in USA” products thanks to the combination of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026, the 2026 World Cup being hosted in several U.S. stadiums, including MetLife in the Meadowlands, and the 2028 Summer Olympics being held in Los Angeles. 

“Tariffs will increase the cost of imported bags by 10% to 25%,” Cahn said. “Automation will reduce the cost of domestic bags by 75% by enabling the same labor to produce three times as much as they currently produce. These two together will significantly close the gap between import and domestic prices.”

Daniel Munoz covers business, consumer affairs, labor and the economy for NorthJersey.com and The Record.

headline: One family has owned this 117-acre NJ farm since the 1950s. Now it's listed for sale
fullText:
Gathered around the table in the kitchen of their family's Andover Township home — on a 117-acre property known as Blind Brook Farm — Cece Pattison and her children Kathy and David, as well as Jack via phone, reminisced about some of their fondest memories.

There was the time Cece and her late husband, Bill, brought their first horse to the farm in the 1950s, traveling from New Hampshire with the animal loaded on the back of a pickup truck. Or when Kathy would ride her childhood pony, Gingersnap — who loved to swim — bareback into the farm's pond on a summer day. Or the years they raised sheep alongside the neighborhood kids as part of the Sussex Shepherds 4-H Club, which Cece led for more than two decades.

"I remember when we first moved to the farm, getting up earlier than we even needed to, but we just thought that's what you did when you lived on a farm," Jack said. "It was still dark out, and we'd be carrying water buckets to the chickens or whatever it was, well before sunrise. Farming has always just held a special place in my heart."

All of these memories, and an endless list of others, are ingrained in the story of 70 Goodale Road in Andover Township. The property became part of the Pattison family in 1954 when Bill's parents, Henry and Mary, purchased it as a weekend retreat. It was then passed on in 1967 to Bill and Cece, whose family has called it home ever since.

"It's been an incredibly special and experiential thing. It's even a little hard to describe," Kathy said. "We actually get very emotional when we think about our family's connection to this place."

But the 117 acres of Blind Brook Farm were recently listed for sale, officially marking the end of an era for the Pattison family. Listed for $2.2 million by Marjorie Morville of Coldwell Banker Realty, the property is being sold to help fund Cece's transition to assisted living.

Kathy and David said their goal is to be able to pay for their mother's stay at a local assisted living facility in Sussex County to ensure that she remains part of the community she's spent so much of her life involved in.

"We've obviously been anchored here at the farm, but the farm is part of this larger community in Sussex County, and mom is like a mayor," Kathy said. "Everybody in the county knows her, because she's just been involved in so many activities and communities that are just intertwined with the farm."

Cece's community involvement included being a member of the Andover Township Land Use Board and the Agricultural Committee board, and a more than 40-year member of the board of the Sussex County Farm & Horse Show Association. She also helped open the Newton True Value Hardware store in 1980 alongside her husband, Bill; it operated for nearly 20 years.

What it was like living on the farm

Though New Jersey is known for its rich agriculture and abundance of farmland, it's not necessarily common for children in the Garden State to grow up on a working farm. Kathy said it's something that has helped set her and her siblings apart.

"I think it differentiates us. I now live in Boston, and I've raised my kids in the city. I work in high-tech startups, and I'm very proud of my farm girl roots," she said. "You have grit. I can manage animals, and I can get my hands dirty. I owe that to growing up on a farm."

She said it was always all hands on deck, regardless of how old the kids were. Between stacking hay bales, raising animals and helping build or restore farm structures, she said, the hard work helped shape who they are.

This was echoed by David, who not only grew up on the farm but also moved back after their father died in 2014. He said that for him, one of the best parts has been being able to see the farm in some of the most beautiful instances over the years.

"It's just the random moments when nature puts it on full display," he said. "It's when wild animals come to visit, or when there's rainbows, sunsets or even huge snowstorms."

About the property at 70 Goodale Road in Andover Township

This expansive property features the four-bedroom, three-bathroom main farmhouse, complete with original wide pine flooring, a spacious eat-in kitchen with a wood stove, a living room with built-in bookcases and a fireplace, a sunroom, and a basement with a full workshop. There's also the three-bedroom, two-bathroom guest home, which currently houses a long-term tenant, as well as a lakefront cabin with a private dock on Lake Aeroflex and a 1-acre buildable lot for an additional residential dwelling.

As for the farm, you'll find two barns with five stalls each, tack rooms, feed rooms, hay lofts and lambing pens. There also are covered utility and equipment garages, a three-car tandem garage, a chicken coop, a pond, a brook and four spacious pastures. Morville, of Coldwell Banker, said all of the farm equipment and shop equipment can be negotiated into the sale as well.

The property is also protected through the New Jersey Farmland Preservation Program, meaning whoever buys it must maintain it as it currently stands. Kathy said this was particularly important to her parents in order to preserve the beauty and serenity of their family farm.

The property is surrounded by state land of Kittatinny Valley State Park. Lake Aeroflex is stocked with landlocked salmon and trout for those looking to fish, and the property has easy access to the Kittatinny park rail-trails for horseback riding.

"This is history, heart and soul. We get very choked up when we think about it not being in our family anymore," Kathy said. "I think we do have this ideal buyer in mind, which is someone who will love it the same way we did."

headline: North Jersey Male Athlete of the Week scripts perfect ending to record-breaking career
fullText:
The video has been pulled up time and time again on JJ Ruehlemann's phone.

The one where the Waldwick senior lives out a childhood dream in the final and most important match of his high school soccer career. The clip starts with a long ball into the box and ends with Ruehlemann corralling it between two defenders and chipping a shot over the opposing goalie.

Then he runs over to his sideline, shrugs to a few nearby cameras and scans the crowd.

Of all the highlights in a legendary career, none can top what transpired on his game-winner with less than two minutes to go in the Group 1 final.

"I would be lying if I said I've seen it less than 10 or 20 times," Ruehlemann said.

If his deadpan reaction made it seem like Ruehlemann has been there before, it is not entirely wrong. No one in the state scored more goals this year than Ruehlemann, who broke a single-season school record with 40 on his last shot in blue and white.

Plus by now, the Williams College commit has a full bingo card of experiences as a two-time captain, three-time starter and four-year varsity player. The Warriors won a state title back in 2021, although his vantage point was a little different in that final as a freshman stapled to the bench.

This time, Ruehlemann never came off the field until the job was finished in a 2-1 win over Haddon Township.

"I have him as a student and he's top five in the class," coach Jon Noschese said. "He's very cerebral and intelligent. You could talk the most trash to him and say whatever and it bounces off him. I mean it. When it comes to pressure, he sees the world differently, in a good way."

What made the state championship a little extra special was sharing it with his older brother, Lucas, a senior forward at Wesleyan who made the trip down from Connecticut to watch Waldwick for the first time this season. Separated by two hours, the Ruehlemann brothers have kept tabs on each other throughout the season by livestreaming games.

For JJ, seeing his older sibling's success impacted two major decisions back in middle school. The first was to drop basketball around sixth grade to focus his attention on soccer. The second was to play year-round for the same club team, World Class FC, when other options were available.

"I considered switching clubs to an MLS Next, where high school [soccer] wouldn't be an option," Ruehlemann said. "But then I reconsidered and I said I really want to represent my high school. I'm glad I did."

His Waldwick teammates are just as glad. Ruehlemann led Bergen County in goals in back-to-back years and became the first to hit 40 in one year since Wallington's Nick Zielonka in 2019.

The challenge for the Warriors' forward was that the more he cracked the box score, the more attention he received from opponents. A 5-4 start this season provided another mental hurdle for Ruehlemann and everyone around him.

“I think it came down to us being more friends off the field,” said Ruehlemann, whose team lost once thereafter. “Going to each other's houses after games. Having pasta parties. Being connected. We hit that little bump in the road and decided it's time to go. We grouped together and figured it out. I think our game after that was Wallington. And in that game, it was like, all right guys this is do-or-die.”

As for his college decision, Ruehlemann picked up a couple of Division I offers, but turned them down because of the coaches, campus and high academics at D-III Williams, which accepts between seven and 10 percent of applicants.

Long after he graduates from the Massachusetts school, he'll still have the memory of scoring twice in the second half in his final game at Waldwick. Not to mention, the video to prove it.

"I think the entire season we've been down in games and come back," Ruehlemann said. "At halftime, we knew exactly that. We knew that we were controlling the tempo and we can get those chances. We just need to put it in the back of the net.”

Julian Ruehlemann

Sport: Soccer

School: Waldwick

Class: Senior. Age: 17

Accomplishment: Ruehlemann scored both goals in Waldwick's 2-1 win over Haddon Township in the Group 1 boys soccer final on Nov. 24.

Also nominated: Dez Jones of DePaul and Dylan Thornton of Hackensack for football.

headline: Officials investigate Lyndhurst house fire that resulted in multiple rescues
fullText:
Officials are investigating a fire that damaged a house in Lyndhurst early Thursday morning, resulting in multiple rescues and leaving one person in critical condition.

The Lyndhurst Fire Department responded to a house fire on Jay Avenue just after 5:30 a.m. on Thursday, according to a post on the Lyndhurst Fire Department's Facebook page. Upon arrival, responders found heavy smoke showing from the second floor of the building as well as a "well involved basement fire."

Lyndhurst police officers deployed a tactical ladder and removed one resident from a lower roof, according to the post. As additional fire companies arrived, a second person was rescued from the second-floor roof and a third person "leaped to safety" from a second story window.

Firefighters initiated "an aggressive interior attack and primary search," attempting to locate the fourth and unaccounted for person.

"Crews were met with heavy fire conditions in the basement as well as zero visibility and high heat on the floors above," says the post. "Shortly thereafter, ex-chiefs Steven Passamano and Nicholas Haggerty located the fourth unaccounted for occupant, just outside of his bedroom, where he was unresponsive and lifeless."

The victim was removed from the fire and CPR was immediately initiated, according to the post. He was taken to a local hospital where he was resuscitated, and was listed in critical but stable condition.

The fire was under control by 9 a.m. Thursday. There were no firefighter injuries, and the residence has been deemed uninhabitable by the Lyndhurst Building Department. The American Red Cross was dispatched to the scene to provide disaster relief to the displaced residents, according to the post.

The fire is under investigation by the Bergen County Prosecutor's Office Arson Squad and the local fire prevention office.

headline: Feds sign off on $10B Manhattan Port Authority bus terminal project
fullText:
Transportation officials from New Jersey and New York received the federal sign-off to go ahead with an auspicious $10 billion Manhattan bus terminal transformation in Midtown.

The bi-state Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates the existing terminal, said Wednesday that the Federal Transit Administration issued a “Record of Decision” following an “exhaustive” environmental review of the project’s environmental impact statement. 

The project’s $271 million first phase entails constructing two new roadway decks over areas of Dyer Avenue and the Lincoln Tunnel Expressway in Manhattan, which is slated to start early next year, according to a press announcement. 

Story continues below photo gallery

A July approval by the Port Authority’s board of commissioners hinged on the federal approval. 

The current terminal is used by NJ Transit buses, as well as Coach, Greyhound, Megabus, Peter Pan, Rockland Coaches and other bus lines.

Port Authority officials are racing to get federal loan approval while President Joe Biden is still in office, according to a report last month by Gothamist. 

During the press question and answer following last month’s board session, Port Authority Board Chair Kevin O’Toole and Executive Director Rick Cotton did not address the specifics of the news report. 

“I think speculating on hypotheticals doesn’t serve any cause,” Cotton said. “We are going to pursue that application and we’ll make any further decisions we need to as the [U.S Department of Transportation] handles the application.” 

Transportation officials have been trying for the past decade and discussing for even longer the process of replacing the 73-year-old bus terminal, which serves as a hub for commuters and travelers entering and leaving Manhattan.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said that over 250,000 people use the terminal on any given weekday. 

“This project will help us meet our projected ridership growth while also reducing congestion on our streets and providing an improved travel experience for our commuters,” she said Wednesday. 

The project includes building a new facility to stage and store buses, which will house customers during certain portions of construction. The project will overhaul the current bus terminal on 8th Avenue between West 40th and 42nd streets, rebuild the ramps that connect to the Lincoln Tunnel, and build as many as three new developments above or near the terminal.

“By replacing outdated infrastructure, we will deliver the modern, safe, and reliable transit infrastructure that New Jerseyans deserve,” Gov. Phil Murphy said Wednesday in a statement.

headline: Newark-based Prudential Financial promotes Andrew Sullivan to be next CEO
fullText:
Prudential Financial named one of its executives, Andrew Sullivan, to take on the role of CEO effective March 31, 2025, after the current head, Charles Lowrey, steps down from the post.

Lowrey will remain as the board executive chairman for 18 months, until late 2026, Prudential said on Wednesday. 

As of Thursday morning, Prudential, a Fortune 500 company, was selling at roughly $126 a share. 

According to Prudential, Sullivan was previously a nuclear submarine officer aboard the USS Nebraska. 

Sullivan, now the executive vice president and head of Prudential’s international business, joined the insurance firm in 2011. He was previously senior vice president at CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield, and an executive at Cigna. 

“I look forward to working with Prudential’s leadership team and employees to advance our strategy and expand Prudential’s position as a leader in investing, insurance, and retirement security,” Sullivan said in a prepared statement Wednesday. 

Under Lowrey, the firm laid off more than 600 people this year, and last year laid off 243 staff members, all in senior leadership positions, amid a $200 million restructuring in the fourth quarter. 

Wall Street ratings agency Moody’s reported that Prudential faces an increased risk in the commercial real estate lending sector. 

That along with “alternative investments” and junk bonds “could weaken capital if there is an economic downtown,” Moody’s said.

More broadly, some of the world’s largest banks and financial institutions have cut their head counts to tighten budgets amid uncertain economic times. 

In 2019, Prudential bought tech insurance startup Assurance IQ for $2.35 billion, but Prudential ultimately shuttered it earlier this year. Assurance's CEO reported to Sullivan in his role as head of Prudential's U.S. businesses.

“Families and educators in many school districts have been eager to establish new, high-quality preschool programs in their community,” Dehmer said. “This funding provides the resources to build, expand, or renovate school facilities specifically for preschool students.”

The initiative prioritizes increasing preschool seats by at least 10%, expanding classroom capacity, enhancing facilities with features such as restrooms, and converting half-day programs into full-day options.

headline: Probe into brutal attack at Paterson's JFK High complicated by gang links
fullText:
PATERSON — Authorities have not yet made any arrests in the brutal stomping, kicking, and punching attack on a student in the hallway at Paterson’s John F. Kennedy High School on Nov. 26.

Police sources said the probe has been hampered by a lack of cooperation from the victim in a case which they said has been complicated by gang affiliations.

Video recordings of the attack provided to Paterson Press show four young men inflicting more than 20 blows on the victim — many of them kicks and stomps to his head area — during the assault that went on for about 20 seconds while more than two dozen other students watched.

It’s not clear whether police investigators have seen those videos, or any recordings of the attack captured by school security cameras.

A police department spokesperson said the investigation into the assault is still ongoing.

School district sources said city educators have identified the attackers and imposed suspensions on them. But Paterson Public Schools officials have not revealed details of that discipline.

headline: Football: Final New Jersey Super 25 rankings for 2024 season
fullText:
After crowning seven state champions over the last week, the 2024 high school football season is in the books.

Four public-school champions − Glassboro, Rumson-Fair Haven, Toms River North and Winslow − completed undefeated seasons, while the fifth, Old Tappan, avenged its only loss of the season in the state semifinals.

Both non-public champions − Bergen Catholic and DePaul − finished with one loss. Bergen Catholic's came against national power IMG Academy in Week 0, and DePaul's came by one point in overtime against Delbarton.

Here are the final New Jersey Super 25 rankings.

25. St. Thomas Aquinas (8-3)

Final non-public ranking: 8

The Trojans scored a Big Central Conference-best 42 points per game and won by at least two touchdowns in all eight of their wins. Both of St. Thomas Aquinas’ in-state losses were thrillers, falling to Paramus Catholic 35-34 in overtime and to Holy Spirit 35-31 in the Non-Public B state quarterfinals. Chukwuma Odoh (1,418 rushing yards) and Josiah Zayas (1,063 receiving yards, seven interceptions) each scored 17 touchdowns.

24. Ridge (8-2)

Final public ranking: 17

The Red Devils graduated several top players and lost in Week 1, but quickly regrouped to win eight straight and reach the North 1, Group 4 sectional semifinals, losing to eventual sectional champ Ramapo, 28-27. Ridge’s fun offense averaged 35 points a game as Aidan Stieglitz rushed for 1,311 yards and 22 touchdowns and Ryan Turner amassed more than 1,000 combined rushing and receiving yards with 13 scores.

23. Rancocas Valley (9-3)

Final public ranking: 16

The Red Devils increased their win total for the third consecutive season, reaching nine victories for the first time since 2018. RV won six games in a row until a 42-27 setback to Toms River North in the South Group 5 sectional final. The Red Devils averaged 32.5 points per game and produced more than 4,600 yards of offense.

22. Camden (9-3)

Final public ranking: 15

The Panthers clinched the West Jersey Football League Colonial Division title outright with an 8-0 win over crosstown rival Eastside. After consecutive 10-win seasons that included sectional crowns, Camden lost a chance at a three-peat with a 15-7 loss to Point Pleasant Borough.

21. Morris Knolls (10-1)

Final public ranking: 14

The Golden Eagles won 10 straight games in their first season under coach Bryan Gallagher before falling to Ramapo in the North 1, Group 4 sectional final. Morris Knolls rushed as a team for 3,747 yards and 45 rushing touchdowns, led by senior Bobby Brickner's 1,366 yards. Morris Knolls went unbeaten in the SFC Liberty White division, which featured five playoff teams.

20. Ramapo (8-4)

Final public ranking: 13

The Green Raiders repeated as a sectional champion before losing in the Group 4 state semifinals to Phillipsburg, 35-6. Under first-year coach Nick Guttuso, a young team rebounded from an 0-3 start. Junior Casey Grusser threw for 2,267 yards and 17 TDs, and ran for 685 yards and eight scores. Junior Liam Hayward rushed for 816 yards and 10 scores.  

19. Point Pleasant Borough (10-3)

Final public ranking: 12

The Panthers won the South Group 2 sectional championship, their first sectional title since 2021, with a 15-7 win over two-time defending sectional champ Camden. They were then defeated by Rumson-Fair Haven in the Group 2 semifinal. Point Borough’s only defeats came to Rumson-Fair Haven (twice) and 24-21 to Toms River North in a game in which it led 14-0 in the first half and 21-14 in the fourth quarter.

18. Pascack Valley (10-2)

Final public ranking: 11

The Panthers earned their first sectional title since 2014 before losing in the Group 3 state semifinals, 43-14, to eventual state champion Old Tappan. Junior Adam Shaw passed and ran for more than 2,300 combined yards and 28 TDs on the season. Senior Kevin Regula amassed more than 1,400 yards rushing and receiving, and scored 19 touchdowns.

17. Union City (11-2)

Final public ranking: 10

The Soaring Eagles’ first trip to a state final ended in a 41-14 loss to three-time champion Toms River North in the Group 5 state final. Senior Mark Boyd ran for 61 yards, including an 11-yard TD run in the third quarter to cut the deficit to 20-7. Junior Xavien Rodriguez threw a 22-yard score to junior Khalil Sutton in the fourth quarter to pull within 26-14.

16. Somerville (12-1)

Final public ranking: 9

The Pioneers’ dominant season included winning the Central Group 3 section title, their first sectional crown since 2017. Somerville, which lost to Mainland, 36-35 in overtime, in the Group 3 state semifinals, averaged 34.6 points per game and gave up 10 points per game – both top five in the Big Central Conference. Brenden Pacheco threw for 1,742 yards and 27 touchdowns, and explosive Terrell Mitchell (Wake Forest) rushed for 1,406 yards with 18 touchdowns.

15. Mainland (10-4)

Final public ranking: 8

The Mustangs made a return trip to Rutgers, but couldn’t finish off their title defense as they suffered a 28-16 loss to Old Tappan in the Group 3 state final. Mainland completed its third straight season with double-digit wins, compiling a 34-6 record over the stretch. Junior quarterback John Franchini has thrown for 4,299 career yards, and junior wideout Jake Blum caught 15 touchdown passes this season – both Mainland records.

14. Phillipsburg (11-3)

Final public ranking: 7

The Stateliners ended a hex by winning the North 2, Group 4 sectional title in memorable fashion after falling in two previous finals. Phillipsburg drove 46 yards in 20 seconds and Alexie Moreira drilled a 46-yard field goal as time expired for a 13-11 win over Northern Highlands. Phillipsburg then beat Ramapo, 35-6, in the Group 4 state semifinals before losing to Winslow in the state championship game. 

13. Glassboro (13-0)

Final public ranking: 6

The Bulldogs finished off the sixth undefeated season in program history and the first in 16 years with a 56-14 win over Cedar Grove in the Group 1 state final. Senior Kenny Smith ran wild, rushing for 402 yards and four touchdowns, including a pair of 80-yard TDs. Smith finished his career with 5,283 yards, the second highest total in South Jersey history behind Glassboro grad and former Philadelphia Eagle Corey Clement (6,245 in 2012).

12. Delbarton (7-3)

Final non-public ranking: 7

The Green Wave suffered a setback in the first round of the Non-Public A state playoffs with a narrow loss to St. Augustine. Delbarton went undefeated on the road in 2024 with key victories at St. Peter's Prep, DePaul and Paramus Catholic. Quarterback Jadon Prinzivalli threw for 2,083 yards and 16 touchdowns in his senior season as Delbarton won the SFC United White division title.

11. Millville (10-3)

Final public ranking: 5

The Thunderbolts closed out their season with a 42-7 win at Vineland, tying the all-time series that began in 1893 at 67-67-19. Senior Lotzeir Brooks, an Alabama commit, finished his scholastic career with three catches for 72 yards and a touchdown. He set state records for career receiving yards (4,615) and touchdown catches (67). Jamal Wallace Jr. rushed for a career-high 156 yards and four touchdowns, eclipsing the 1,000-yard mark for the season. Millville has compiled a 44-8 record over the last four seasons.

10. St. Augustine (7-4)

Final non-public ranking: 6

The Hermits won a playoff game for the sixth consecutive season, knocking off Delbarton, 9-7, in this year’s postseason. St. Augustine fell to Don Bosco, 35-14, in the semifinal round. St. Augustine finished 3-1 in the West Jersey Football League American Division, one of the toughest in the state, with its only divisional loss to Winslow. Senior Julian Turney rushed for more than 1,000 yards for the second consecutive season and his 3,342 career yards rank third in program history.

9. Holy Spirit (10-2)

Final non-public ranking: 5

After back-to-back nine-win seasons, the Spartans hit double digits with their 10th win thanks to a 37-8 victory over Atlantic City on Thanksgiving. Jachere “Pops” Ward rushed 24 times for 156 yards and a touchdown. Holy Spirit captured two wins in the Non-Public B state tournament, bowing to DePaul in the semifinal round.

8. Old Tappan (12-1)

Final public ranking: 4

The Golden Knights secured their second Group 3 state title in three years with a 28-16 win over Mainland. Senior Alex Orecchio caught a TD pass, ran for a score, threw a TD pass and kicked four extra points. Sophomore Zach Miceli threw for 201 yards, including a game-opening 18-yard TD pass to Orecchio. Senior Nick Rossi ran for 81 yards and a TD.

7. St. Joseph (Montvale) (6-5)

Final non-public ranking: 4

The Green Knights’ season ended with a 20-14 overtime loss at Bergen Catholic in the Non-Public A state semifinals. Junior Lamar Best, who missed several games with a broken collarbone, and junior Mason Geis combined to throw for more than 2,000 yards this season in Augie Hoffmann’s first year of his second stint coaching his alma mater.

6. Rumson-Fair Haven (13-0)

Final public ranking: 3

Junior running back Kellen Murray ran for 170 yards and three TDs as the Bulldogs rallied from a 10-point deficit and beat Shabazz, 26-24, in the Group 2 state championship game. The win gave Rumson-Fair Haven its first state championship after falling by a combined five points in the last two Group 2 state finals. The Bulldogs concluded their first unbeaten season since going 7-0 in 1959. Owel O'Toole finished his career with 7,099 passing yards, the second quarterback in Shore Conference history to throw for more than 7,000 yards. 

5. Don Bosco (8-4)

Final non-public ranking: 3

The Ironmen lost for the second time this season to rival Bergen Catholic, 25-7, in the Non-Public A championship game. Junior Dante DeLuca rushed for 52 yards, including a 20-yard TD in the first quarter to tie the score, 7-7. Senior Deven Sisler threw for 183 yards, completing passes to six receivers, and he ran for 39 yards. 

4. Toms River North (14-0)

Final public ranking: 2

The Mariners are still the only program to win the Group 5 championship in the three years since the NJSIAA starting playing down to public-school group champions. They won their third straight with a 41-14 romp over Union City. Senior quarterback T.J. Valerio threw four TD passes – three to senior running back Mordecai Ford and one to senior receiver Nasir Jackson. Toms River North has the state’s longest winning streak at 19, and has won 39 in a row against public schools. The Mariners are 40-2 over the last three seasons.

3. DePaul (11-1)

Final non-public ranking: 2

The high-octane Spartans secured their second Non-Public B state championship in three years with a 33-21 victory over Pope John. Senior Nolan James rushed for 244 yards and two TDs. Junior Derek Zammit threw for 116 yards, including a 15-yard score to senior Elijah Burress in the third quarter for 26-15 lead, and ran for two scores. 

2. Winslow (14-0)

Final public ranking: 1

The Eagles completed their first undefeated season with a 35-0 rout of Phillipsburg in the Group 4 state final. It’s the program’s second undefeated season, joining the 1969 squad that went 9-0 when the school was known as Edgewood. Sophomore quarterback Jalen Parker threw for 238 yards and two scores in the title game. He finished with a program single-season record of 2,916 yards and 43 touchdowns. Winslow’s shutout was the team’s fifth of the season.

1. Bergen Catholic (11-1)

Final non-public ranking: 1

The Crusaders captured a school-record fourth consecutive state title with a 25-7 win over Don Bosco in the Non-Public A state final. Sophomore Bryan Porter ran for fourth-quarter TDs of 48 and 26 yards to extend an 11-7 lead and put the game out of reach. Bergen Catholic registered back-to-back safeties, one on a blocked punt by senior Ethan Cohall and another on a tackle in the end zone by senior David Matesic.
