headline: Deny, defend, depose: What UnitedHealthcare CEO killer wrote on bullets
fullText:
A manhunt is underway for a shooting suspect that left behind what may be a cryptic message found on the shell casings at the scene: the words deny, defend, depose.

UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson was fatally shot in what appeared to be a targeted, execution-style killing on Wednesday morning in front of the Hilton Hotel in busy Midtown Manhattan.

The suspect left behind three live rounds and three spent shell casings from the shooting that had the words “deny,” “defend,” and “depose” written on them, according to officials.

These words are very similar to the title of a 2010 book,  “Delay Deny Defend,” whose subtitle is “Why insurance companies don’t pay claims and what you can do about it.”

Thompson’s company, a subdivision of UnitedHealth Group, is the largest private health insurance payer in the United States, providing health insurance to more than 49 million people. It has faced much controversy over its relatively high rate of denial of health-care claims.

News reports cite Thompson's company shift to "value-based care" and their plan to start denying payment for what it deemed non-critical visits to hospital emergency rooms in recent years.

Who shot Brian Thompson?

The suspected shooter was masked, wearing a black hoodie, black pants and carrying a gray backpack. He ran off after the shooting, before getting on an electric bike and riding into Central Park where he was last reportedly seen.

Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said the suspect arrived at the scene about five minutes before the shooting and fired a shot at Thompson’s back as he walked by, according to news reports.

"The shooter then walks toward the victim and continues to shoot. It appears that the gun malfunctions as he clears the jam and begins to fire again," he said.

The police believe the suspect used a firearm with a silencer.

Why was Brian Thompson killed?

Brian Thompson was on his way to speak at UnitedHealth Group's investor conference when the gunman approached him from behind and started shooting.

NBC News reported the victim's wife Paulette Thompson said that he had been receiving threats, "There had been some threats," she said in a phone call to the news outlet. "Basically, I don’t know, a lack of coverage? I don’t know details. I just know that he said there were some people that had been threatening him."

“I can’t really give a thoughtful response right now. I just found this out and I’m trying to console my children,” she told the news outlet.

According to Thompson's professional biography on UnitedHealth Group's website, he was named chief executive officer for UnitedHealthcare in April 2021. Prior to this role, he served as CEO of UnitedHealthcare government programs including Medicare & Retirement and Community & State. Before leading government programs, Thompson served as CEO of UnitedHealthcare Medicare & Retirement.

UnitedHealthcare is the country’s largest health insurance company, covering millions of people across all 50 states.

headline: Gov. Murphy convenes with federal officials to discuss reported drone sightings in NJ
fullText:

Phil Murphy said Thursday that he convened a briefing with Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, senior officials from the Department of Homeland Security, the New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness, and New Jersey State Police to discuss the situation. Members of New Jersey’s congressional delegation also participated.

“We are actively monitoring the situation and are in close coordination with our federal and law enforcement partners on this matter,” Murphy said in a statement on X, adding that there is currently no indication of any threat to public safety.

The sightings, which began in Morris County just before Thanksgiving, have since been reported in Sussex, Somerset, and Warren counties, as well as other areas in North Jersey. Residents have taken to social media to share their accounts, with several users in a Sparta Facebook group claiming they saw drones flying through the town Tuesday night and early Wednesday morning.

Authorities have yet to determine the origin or intent of the drones. While some sightings may be legitimate, officials caution that others could be cases of misidentified objects or hoaxes.

The mysterious appearances have left many residents concerned, with questions about who is operating the drones and why they are concentrated in the region.

The New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness and other agencies have not provided additional details but encouraged residents to report drone sightings to local authorities.

The investigation remains ongoing, and officials are urging the public to stay vigilant. Updates will be provided as new information becomes available.

headline: Judge doesn't dismiss indictment against former Paterson mayor Torres
fullText:
PATERSON — Convicted former Mayor Jose "Joey" Torres has failed to convince a judge to dismiss an indictment pending against him, setting up a possible trial on a criminal charge that comes with a maximum 18-month prison sentence.

In a ruling made public on Thursday, Superior Court Judge Marilyn Clark determined that there was sufficient probable cause for the indictment, which accuses Torres of violating his 2017 guilty plea by trying to submit a nominating petition to run for mayor in 2022 after he was already banned from holding public office.

“I reach this legal conclusion and cite the state’s argument that it is disingenuous for Jose Torres to assert that he knew he could not hold public office again but was not prohibited from gathering over 1,100 signatures on the petition, and then presenting same to the City Clerk for filing, thereby placing him on the mayoral ballot in the general election,” Clark said in her ruling.

Story continues below photo gallery.

“The state further argued that it is disingenuous to seek a public office that he could not hold, and thereby disenfranchise voters who had supported him,” Clark wrote.

Torres declined to comment on Clark’s decision after a court session on Thursday. The judge scheduled a follow-up “pretrial” court conference for the Torres case for Dec. 19.

Are Torres lawyers negotiating a plea deal?

Political figures who have been following the latest Torres case speculated that the lawyers involved may be negotiating a plea agreement that would allow the former mayor to avoid going to prison a second time.

Torres in 2017 pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit official misconduct by paying three city Public Works Department employees overtime with taxpayers’ dollars for doing renovations on a private business owned by the then-mayor’s family members. Torres spent 13 months in prison because of that conviction.

But in 2021, he and his supporters mounted a campaign for him to run for mayor again in Paterson’s 2022 election.

Clark’s decision pointed out that state authorities had sent Torres a letter in October 2021 warning him that he would be violating the court order from his 2017 guilty plea if he ran for mayor.

“This court further notes that the Office of the Attorney General did not immediately seek to arrest or indict Torres when it initially became aware of his possible intentions,” the judge said in her ruling.

Applying for a job different than running for office?

Torres and his lawyer, Mike DeMarco, repeatedly have noted that the plea agreement order said the convicted mayor could not apply for public employment. They have contended that applying for a job is different from running for elected office.

Clark’s ruling emphasized that she was not deciding on Torres’ guilt or innocence.

“The state may present the argument to a jury that Jose Torres knew that he was already disqualified and could not assume office, and thereby knew that he was violating the provisions of the order,” Clark wrote. “Jose Torres may argue that he reasonably interpreted the order differently.”

“Under all of these circumstances, this court concludes that there is probable cause for the issuance of the indictment,” Clark said. “Again, if there is no resolution, the outcome of this matter will be determined by a jury trial.”

headline: Say goodbye to NY: Luis Severino agrees to 3-year deal with Athletics, reports say
fullText:
One of the New York Mets' top starting pitchers throughout the 2024 season has a new home.

Luis Severino has agreed to a three-year, $67 million deal with the Athletics, according to reports. ESPN's Jeff Passan was the first to report the news. The deal includes an opt-out after the 2026 season.

Severino, who has spent his entire career in New York, will now headline an Athletics' rotation as they enter a new era in Sacramento. It is the largest guaranteed deal in the history of the franchise.

After nine seasons with the Yankees, the 30-year-old right-hander resurrected his career on a one-year, $14 million deal with the Mets in 2024.

For the first time since 2018, Severino started at least 30 games. He finished with an 11-7 record with a 3.91 ERA and 161 strikeouts in 182 innings in helping lead the Mets to the playoffs, where they reached the NLCS for the first time since 2015.

It was also the first season since 2018 when Severino avoided major injury after being hampered by shoulder, elbow and lat injuries over his final five seasons with the Yankees. His resurgence and health was partially attributed to a better sleep regimen, a newfound willingness to pitch to contact with his sinker and a careful rest schedule.

What's next for the Mets?

The Mets now move forward without one of their top two arms from last season's rotation. Sean Manaea and Jose Quintana both remain on the free agent market. Manaea turned down his player option and $21.05 million qualifying offer to explore his options in free agency.

The team's rotation is now led by Kodai Senga, who is coming off an injury-ravaged 2024 when he only made one start; David Peterson, who had a career season on the heels of hip surgery; and Frankie Montas, who offically signed a two-year, $34 million deal to join the Mets on Wednesday.

It would appear that the Mets have at least one or two more voids to fill in their starting rotation, with Tylor Megill, Jose Butto and Paul Blackburn lingering as options to occupy the back end of the unit.

headline: Police find 200 partying at Paterson warehouse used as illegal nightclub
fullText:
PATERSON — Detectives allegedly found more than 200 people partying this weekend inside a warehouse that authorities say was converted into an illegal night club, officials said.

The raid late Saturday night at 1 Erie Street in Paterson’s Bunker Hill industrial area represented the latest enforcement action by the Paterson police department’s Nightlife Task Force.

Officer in Charge Patrick Murray said the detectives at the scene arrested 12 people on various charges accusing them of operating the club illegally.

Murray said the nightlife task force not only addresses quality of life problems that afflict Paterson residents, but the group targets businesses that tend to be breeding grounds for violent crimes.

Fifteen percent of Paterson’s shootings have some connection to illegal clubs, he said. Several times in the past decade, there have been homicides inside illegal clubs.

Since its inception in February, the nightlife task force has made 192 arrests involving 791 criminal charges and 197 municipal ordinance violations, police officials said. The special unit has shut down 20 illegal businesses and has 42 under surveillance, officials said.

headline: Drones have been spotted in 8 NJ counties. See which towns on our interactive map
fullText:
Federal, state and local authorities convened Wednesday to discuss an uptick in reported drone activity across North and Central Jersey as residents continue to flood the FBI tip website and take to social media to report the mysterious objects.

Residents in eight counties in the upper portion of the Garden State have purportedly seen the unmanned aerial vehicles travel overhead as the skies darken each evening. Reported sightings of the unusual activity have been seen as far west as High Point Monument in Sussex County and across North Jersey toward Garfield in Bergen County. In Central Jersey, many residents have reported suspicious activity in the skies from as far south as Delaware Township in Hunterdon County and west across Somerset County.

The map below shows the areas in which drone activity has been reported by either law enforcement or residents, via official statement, social media posts or through in-person discussions.

More: NJ drone sightings have residents watching the skies. Should you believe social media?

When did alleged drone activity first appear?

Residents were first to spot the alleged drones the week before Thanksgiving, with initial sightings centered in Morris County. Since then, the FBI has assisted local law enforcement with investigating a purported uptick in drone activity across county lines, including a "possible fixed-wing aircraft" flying along the Raritan River on Tuesday. The federal agency did not confirm where the object was spotted on the river, which stretches across Somerset County not far from Trump's private golf resort in Bedminster.

Florham Park police chief: Drones appear to be 'nefarious in nature'

Florham Park Police Chief Joseph Orlando said in a Facebook post Wednesday evening Morris County law enforcement has been working with state and federal partners to determine the launch point and landing location of the purported drones, "as well as the people or entities responsible for their presence in our airspace."

Drones have been spotted "above critical infrastructure such as water reservoirs, electric transmission lines, rail stations, police departments and military installations," he said, adding that local law enforcement has been pushing for answers from state and federal partners.

"While we currently have no evidence or information to indicate these drones pose an imminent threat at this time, their presence appears nefarious in nature," he added.

Related: What are the different types of drones, and what might people be seeing in North Jersey?

Gov. Murphy, senior officials meet

Gov. Phil Murphy convened Wednesday in a briefing call with U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, senior officials from federal and state homeland security and state police to discuss the suspected drone activity, he said in a post on X. Murphy indicated there was no immediate threat to public safety. The meeting was also attended by members of New Jersey's congressional delegation.

headline: Shore football champs Rumson, Toms River North would be great matchup. Why they didn't play
fullText:
PISCATAWAY - An exciting and outstanding Shore Conference football season concluded Wednesday night with Rumson-Fair Haven’s hard-earned 26-24 win over a talented, fast and physical Shabazz team in the NJSIAA Group 2 championship game at Rutgers University’s SHI Stadium.

It was Rumson-Fair Haven’s first overall state group championship after defeats by a combined five points to 13-0 Caldwell and Westwood teams in the Group 2 championship game the last two seasons.

Toms River North won its third straight Group 5 championship last Friday with an emphatic 41-14 win over Union City at MetLife Stadium

However, there was one thing missing from the season: A matchup between 13-0 Rumson-Fair Haven and 14-0 and Group 5 champion Toms River North.

"It would have been a fun game to prepare for,'' Toms River North coach Dave Oizerowitz said Wednesday night. "They have a great staff and program.''

The two programs have been the only Shore Conference public school programs to advance to Group championship games in the three seasons the NJSIAA has played out to overall public school group champions.

Toms River North has gone 40-2 since the start of the 2022 season, won 15 straight playoff games and 39 straight against public schools. Rumson-Fair Haven has gone 29-10 since the start of the 2022 season and 13-2 in playoff games.  

More: Group 2 NJ football state championship: Rumson-Fair Haven beats Shabazz

“I know a lot of people want to see that game, and we would love to play them, too,” said Rumson-Fair Haven junior running back Kellen Murray, who rushed for 170 yards and three TDs on 28 carries Wednesday night. “They’re a tough team - they’re always great competitors and we love playing against them.”

Toms River North and Rumson-Fair Haven have a recent history

The two programs had met the last four full seasons from 2019-23, They did not meet in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season because the Shore Conference went to a geographical-based schedule.

Three of those seasons, the two teams met, they were in the same division – the power-packed American Division. That’s when the Shore Conference aligned its divisions by strength of program without an emphasis on geography.

The other time two met was in a season-opening game showcase at SHI Stadium in 2022 season. That was the varsity debut of current Rumson-Fair Haven senior quarterback Owen O’Toole, who Wednesday night became the second Shore Conference quarterback to surpass 7,000 passing yards in a career

Toms River North won three of the four games, but all its wins were in games that were extremeley competitive.

Why Rumson-Fair Haven and Toms River North did not meet this season

Part of the reason, Rumson-Fair Haven and Toms River North did not meet this season is because they were placed in different divisions as the Shore Conference went to a more geographical alignment for its divisions in addition to evaluating the strength of program.

Rumson-Fair Haven was in Class A North, which was the power division in Monmouth County. Toms River North was in Class A South, which consisted of Ocean County’s power five programs and Group 5 Monmouth County school Howell.

More: Dad's love for football was passed to championship Rumson coach: 'I think of him all the time'

Each school had three nondivisional games against Shore Conference teams during the regular season.

Two of Toms River North's out of division slots were taken up by games against its sister schools - Toms River East and Toms River South. Those are games the Toms River Regional schools district administration wants to be played. The Toms River North-Toms River South rivalry is one of the Shore Conference's most historic. Toms River North and Toms River East were long-time Thanksgiving rivals.

The Mariners' other nondivisional game was against Southern - a team it was in the same division with for many years.

Rumson-Fair Haven's nondivisional games were against Point Pleasant Borough - the team it also beat in the Group 2 semifinal, Manchester and Donovan Catholic.

More: Live updates: Rumson-Fair Haven beats. Shabazz, wins NJ state Group 2 championship

Long-time Shore Conference schedule-maker Nick Pizzulli does a great job - with help from certain requests from member schools on who they would like to play - in making the conference's schedule, But, in 20/20 hindsight, and admittedly, this is a second guess after the fact, the easy switch this year would have been for the teams to have met Oct. 18.

That's the night Toms River North beat Southern 35-32 and Rumson-Fair Haven won a 56-32 shootout over Donovan Catholic in a game that was highly competitive for three quarters. A Southern and Donovan Catholic matchup would have been a good one. A TRN-RFH meeting could have been elite.

A game that needs to be played every year

The reasons why Rumson-Fair Haven and Toms River North did not meet this season are understandable and nobody's fault.

However, starting next season, even if the two teams are in different divisions, it is a matchup the Shore Conference needs to schedule. The programs are too good not to meet.

It is a matchup scholastic football fans want to see and deserve to see.

Knowing how the two coaching staffs love to see their teams challenged by playing the best, it is a game they would love compete in, too.

headline: Dad's love for football was passed to championship Rumson coach: 'I think of him all the time'
fullText:
PISCATAWAY – The joyous celebration spilled from the sideline onto the field as the final seconds wound off the clock at SHI Stadium Wednesday night, the sea of purple signifying the culmination of a 15-year climb to the pinnacle of New Jersey high school football for Rumson-Fair Haven.

Head coach Jeremy Schulte said throughout the game he couldn’t help but think about his father, Jerry, so much a part of what’s happened in this perfect season. He would have loved the program he played such a big part in building winning its first NJSIAA Group 2 championship, after losing in the final the past two season.

And he certainly would have been proud of his son, who took the Bulldogs’ program to new heights this season.

Jerry Schulte, who spent 50 seasons coaching high school football in the area, died March 1, but he was as responsible as anyone for the 13-0 season that culminated with Wednesday night’s 26-24 victory over Malcom X. Shabazz. The Bulldogs went unbeaten for the first time since 1959, their only other perfect season.

“I think of him all the time during games,” Jeremy Schulte said. “I got to spend a lot of years with him so it kind of got taught into me, but yes, throughout the entire game I’m always thinking about him.”

The season’s been dedicated to his memory, and it couldn’t have been a more fitting conclusion

The elder Schulte was a defensive coordinator when Rumson won its first-ever sectional title in 2010, forming the foundation for what was to come. It included the Bulldogs becoming just the third Shore Conference program to win four straight sectional championships (2013-16), which Schulte taking over as head coach from 2016 through 2021, winning a pair of sectional crowns.

More: Rumson-Fair Haven-Toms River North football matchup would have been great for all to see

More: Group 2 NJ football state championship: Rumson-Fair Haven beats Shabazz

Jeremy Schulte's father served as assistant coach for two years

The past two seasons he served on his son’s coaching staff, and was part of eight sectional championships in all.

“This year we wanted to do it for his dad,” quarterback Owen O’Toole said. “We wear a ‘JS’ sticker on the back of our helmet. He’s on our mind all the time. We miss him every day. This one is for him.”

And while Rumson was unable to finish the job the past two seasons, including last year’s overtime loss to Westwood, this year the Bulldogs built a 10-point second half lead and survived a Shabazz TD in the final minute, recovering an onside kick.

“This team had a a chip on it shoulder,” running back Kellen Murray said. “It was a tough loss for Coach Schulte and we knew we had to come back here, especially after those losses the last two years. This senior class was really tight.”

Now Jeremy Schulte is well on his way towards forging his own coaching legacy, with the Bulldogs rising to new heights this season. They’re the second Shore Conference public school to win a group title since the playoffs were expanded in 2022.

““It’s incredible. The job Coach Schulte does as the head coach, it’s just like we didn’t skip a beat,” O'Toole said. “He’s everything. He’s like a father figure, an older brother figure to us, and so is every coach.”

In this game, Jeremy Schule made several key decisions - going for a pair of critical fourth downs that resulted in touchdowns, including a second quarter drive that put them in the lead for good.

When the game was wide open in the first half, Rumson held its own against speedy Shabazz. And when it turned into a defensive struggle over the final two quarters, the Bulldogs were ready for that, too.

And in the end, it was a victory, a championship, that Jerry Schulte’s fingerprints were all over.

Stephen Edelson is a USA TODAY NETWORK New Jersey sports columnist who has been covering athletics in the state and at the Jersey Shore for over 35 years. Contact him at: @SteveEdelsonAPP; sedelson@gannettnj.com.

headline: Seton Hall basketball: Prince Aligbe leads win over NJIT
fullText:
NEWARK – Since he arrived on campus in June, Prince Aligbe has been a leader off the court for Seton Hall basketball.

On Wednesday, with the young season at a low point, he finally took charge on the court.

The Boston College transfer put together his best game as a Pirate to push the struggling Hall past NJIT 67-56 before a crowd of no more than 3,000 at the Prudential Center.

The junior forward tallied 19 points, seven rebounds and three assists while shooting 8-of-11 from the field as Seton Hall (5-4) moved past Saturday’s historically bad loss to winless Monmouth.

“This is kind of what I envisioned Prince being," Hall coach Shaheen Holloway said. "Obviously 19 points is really good, but him being a double-double guy or close. He had it tough going. Prince is a great person, but he overanalyzes everything. Just play through it. Tonight he did a good job of playing through it.”

Aligbe entered the game shooting just 26 percent from the field. He exited with a career high in scoring.

“Obviously it feels good to play well,” Aligbe said. “I was just doing the little things: Telling myself run the floor hard, crash the boards, play for my teammates and let the game come to me.”

NJIT (1-9) got little production outside of star guard Tariq Francis (23 points), but stymied the Pirates with a zone and hung around for 32 minutes after a slow start.

"I was disappointed, in the biggest way," Holloway said. "I thought we played a good 15 minutes in the first half and that was it. We came out with juice, we came out with energy, and then it kind of just dropped. We go into the locker room and our guys are worried about them(selves) and not us winning. So that’s something we’ve got to clean up. I’ve got to do a really, really, really good job of making people understand what playing at Seton Hall is all about.”

FIVE TAKEAWAYS

1. 'I'll take the bullets'

With the schedule about to ratchet up in quality – Oklahoma State comes in Sunday, followed a trip to Rutgers Dec. 14 and then the Big East opener at Villanova Dec. 17 – the status quo is obviously untenable.

When asked what he most needs to see out of this group going forward, Holloway didn't mince words.

"Being together," he said. "Stop worrying about what everybody is saying and what they’re reading."

Then he went into detail.

"I told the group, it’s tough because there’s only one guy who’s from around here and that’s Dylan (Addae-Wusu, a New Yorker), so they’re not used to this type of pressure and used to this type of noise," Holloway said. "It’s getting to them. I told them, stop worrying about that. Let me handle that. I’ll take the bullets – I don’t care. You know it’s funny. People think, like I forgot how to coach because of how things are going. Alright, sure, whatever."

Clearly, Holloway is referencing anonymous posts on message boards and/or social media. No one with an ounce of credibility has questioned his overall fitness as a head coach -- the guy took Saint Peter's to an Elite Eight and just guided Seton Hall to a 25-win season -- although specific critiques are inevitable when the team is playing as badly as his Pirates have been.

“We’re going through a little slide, but tonight I thought was a good sign with some guys breaking out of certain slumps – I wouldn’t call them slumps, but certain things," he said. "Moving forward, everyone has to be on the same page. We need the guys who can score to score, the guys who can defend to defend, the guys who can rebound to rebound. Once we do that, we’ve still got a good chance of being a good team.”

Aligbe also alluded to the difficulty of dealing with negativity.

“When adversity hits who are we going to be?" he said. "Are we going to bawl or are we going to act like we’ve been here before? That was the main message the last couple of days.”

2. Grant Billmeier returns

Shortly before tip-off, he walked out of the tunnel to cheers.

For Grant Billmeier, this will always be home.

The former Pirate center and assistant, now in his second year at the NJIT’s helm, brought his program to the Rock for the first time and received the warm welcome of a favorite son.

"I think they're happy I wasn't representing Seton Hall because as a player they booed me a lot," he said with a laugh about the cheers. "Honestly, I spent 15 amazing years at Seton Hall. It's a very special place in my heart. I'm fully committed to turning around NJIT's basketball program. But 15 of my 40 years were spent on that campus and I have tremendous memories from my time there."

Billmeier is one of five former Pirates who hold head-coaching gigs in Division I. He’ll face another, his old teammate Donald Copeland, when the Highlanders visit Wagner Dec. 14.

"Grant is a great guy," Holloway said. "Proud of Grant. He does a good job. His team plays hard for him, they run good stuff. He's got a bright future in coaching."

Billmeier expects Seton Hall-NJIT to become an annual fixture on the schedule.

"I definitely think so," he said. "It makes sense."

3. The Tariq Francis show

NJIT has a big-time player in Francis, a sophomore who came in averaging 19.7 points, 4.4 rebounds and 4.2 assists. The Pirates simply could not stay with the Pittsburgh native, who is a nephew of Rutgers associate head coach Brandin Knight. He shot 9-of-20 from the field, including 5-of-12 from 3-point range.

"Man, Tariq, super proud of him," Holloway said. "I watched him grow up, he’s like my little nephew. A lot of the shots he took, we knew he was going to take those shots. Obviously no one on our team is like him so you can’t really (simulate). He made some tough shots."

It was a performance reminiscent of Saturday’s torching by Monmouth guard Abdi Bashir, who lit up the Hall for 28 points. Afterward Hawks coach King Rice issued a public plea to other coaches to wait until the season ends to contact Bashir about transferring.

That resonated with Billmeier.

“Everyone kind of knows tampering goes on, but I agree with King, be respectful fellas,” Billmeier said earlier in the week. “Let the kid enjoy the moment, let the kid get better, let him have a great year, and in the springtime things will play out the way they’re supposed to.”

4. Lineup notes: some good, some bad

Holloway inserted junior Manny Okorafor at starting center for freshman Godswill Erheriene, and the Pirates jumped out to a 19-5 lead. Okorafor is slowly improving after missing the entire month of October due to a severe dehydration episode – but seems far from ready for the hand-to-hand combat of the Big East.

Postgrad guard Dylan Addae-Wusu returned after missing the Monmouth game while recovering from the flu and came off the bench. He chipped in 12 points, three boards and two assists.

Trimming his rotation to nine, Holloway did not call on sophomore forward David Tubek, freshman center Gus Yalden or freshman guard Jahseem Felton. Backup point guard Zion Harmon was not in attendance, missing a sixth straight contest due to personal reasons. He’s still on the roster but there is no indication when or if he’ll return to action.

The Pirates finally got a productive game from point guard Garwey Dual (11 points, 2 assists), which is a start. But Scotty Middleton and Yacine Toumi struggled to contribute against NJIT. Isaiah Coleman hardly touched the ball in the first half. And Chaunce Jenkins suffered a second straight ice-cold game – he’s getting the defense tilted against him regularly now, and has to adjust. The Pirates desperately need his scoring.

5. Historically small crowd

A pretty good student contingent showed up – the university ran a Greek Night promotion, which is always an inducement – but the total crowd was the Pirates’ smallest in recent memory at the Prudential Center.

But no one booed, so that's an improvement.

Jerry Carino has covered the New Jersey sports scene since 1996 and the college basketball beat since 2003. Contact him at jcarino@gannettnj.com.

headline: Colts Neck horse farm sold at auction to mystery buyer after 55 years in one family
fullText:
COLTS NECK - Overbrook Farm, which was the birthplace of the Graded stakes-winning racehorse Irish War Cry, sold for $6.1 million at auction. 

Max Spann, president and owner of Max Spann Real Estate & Auction Co., said he can’t disclose any information about the buyer, but that the 235-acre farm drew “over 15 qualified bidders with funds” and “over 100 preregistrations for the auction.” 

The farm, which has been in the Bailey family for over 55 years, has served as a breeding and training farm with a half-mile racetrack on the property. 

Richard E. Bailey, a sports television executive, bought Margate Farm in 1969, according to an Asbury Park Press article.

Colts Neck news: Cops seek help after crash leaves one dead on Route 537

Overbrook found the spotlight in 2017 when one of its own, Irish War Cry, chalked up a win in the Wood Memorial and finished second in the Belmont Stakes. The colt was owned by Isabelle de Tomaso, the daughter of Monmouth Park founder Amory Haskell.

While many farms have been turned into suburban neighborhoods, mixed-use apartment buildings or warehouse complexes, Overbrook Farm was chosen for preservation due to its proximity to Naval Weapons Station Earle. 

Under the federal Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration (REPI) program, the farm would be preserved for farmland use to “avoid land-use conflicts near military installations, address environmental restrictions that limit military activities and increase resilience to climate change,” according to the Department of Defense website. 

The Navy, Monmouth County and Colts Neck paid over $7.3 million to place a conservation easement on the farm, allowing only farm and agricultural uses in the future. 

Spann said, “We do sell a lot of preserved farms with this type of restriction. … There’s a strong market for preserved farms. It doesn’t completely mitigate the value of the farm by preserving it and there’s a lot of people that really appreciate a farm and the beauty that it has by itself.”

Spann said many farm owners choose to put their properties up for auction because “it gives them price discovery; they get to see the true market value of their farm.” 

He said auctions also allow owners to control the timing and the terms and conditions of the sale. 

In addition to the half-mile racetrack, the 235-acre farm has two main houses, labor houses, barns and paddocks.

headline: DNA software in Caneiro murder case ignores basic engineering standards: Expert
fullText:
FREEHOLD — When Nathaniel Adams went to a lawyer's office in Ohio to inspect the source code for computer software increasingly being used to analyze DNA evidence in criminal cases in New Jersey and the nation, he soon hit a roadblock.

"I got to the beginning of the program, but it was halted - it required a license,'' Adams, a software engineering expert consulting for the defense team of Paul Caneiro, testified Wednesday.

So, Adams said he asked the lawyer representing the developer of the computer software known as STRmix for the license and was told the person who had set up the computer he was working on had already left. 

"He said, 'he's not coming back,'"Adams said.

As a result, his planned inspection to ensure the source code he was looking at was the same version as that used to process DNA evidence against Caneiro in the murders of four of his family members "couldn't be accomplished,'' Adams said.

That inspection took place in November 2022 under a highly restrictive protective order signed by a judge after many months of talks between lawyers for STRmix, prosecutors and defense attorneys. The inspection was a precursor to an ongoing pretrial hearing on a challenge by Caneiro's lawyers to the to admissibility of the DNA evidence STRmix produced in the case.

Caneiro, 57, of Ocean Township, is expected to go on trial next year in the murders of his brother, Keith, 50; sister-in-law Jennifer, 45; niece Sophia, 8; and nephew Jesse, 11, whose bodies were discovered at Keith Caniero's Colts Neck mansion Nov. 21, 2018, by emergency workers responding to a slow-burning fire at the residence.

Keith Caneiro had been shot four times in the head and once in the back. Jennifer Caneiro and the two children were repeatedly stabbed and badly burned. Jennifer Caneiro also was shot in the head.

DNA that the STRmix program determined to be a mixture from Paul and Sophia Caneiro, and another mixture to which Jesse was deemed to be a contributor, was later found on clothing recovered from the defendant's basement.

The outcome of the pretrial hearing before Superior Court Judge Marc C. LeMieux will determine not only if the DNA evidence can be used against Caneiro at his upcoming trial. It also will have implications on the future use of STRmix in New Jersey.

The Pubic Defender's Office is seeking to block its use going forward, asserting the method it uses to analyze DNA is not generally acceptable in the scientific community. 

The challenge in the Caneiro case represents the first time a court in New Jersey will rule on the validity of the STRmix software, which uses a method known as probabilistic genotyping to analyze DNA, deviating from traditional methods of DNA analysis that have been in use for decades.

Prosecutors are looking to have the STRmix evidence admitted at Caneiro's trial and clear the way for the state police to continue using the software in its DNA lab.

Adams, who works for Forensic Biomedical Services, a consulting firm in Dayton, Ohio, was the third defense expert to testify at Caneiro's pretrial hearing about what he perceived to be shortcomings of the software.

He echoed the sentiments of Mats Neimdahl, head of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Minnesota, who testified Tuesday about what he said was the lack of adequate documentation the STRmix software had been properly tested and verified.

Adams said documentation that was available did not show that any tests that were performed were connected to the computer program's specifications detailing what it is supposed to accomplish.

"These are fundamental software engineering concepts that they've failed to adhere to,'' Adams testified.

Adams said he once was sent a "cease and desist'' letter from STRmix's lawyer after he testified about STRmix in a case in the state of Washington in 2016.

The lawyer threatened a lawsuit and "accused me of disclosing confidential information about STRmix during my testimony and claimed I had caused irreparable financial harm to the STRmix organization,'' Adams said. 

Adams' firm had to hire a lawyer and expend a lot of time, money and energy to resolve the matter, he said.

Sometime following his inspection of the STRmix software on Caneiro's behalf in November 2022, Adams said he was again contacted by the Public Defender's Office to inspect a more recent version of the software, which was used to develop additional DNA evidence against Caneiro. Adams said he declined and explained why.

"The actual review itself, not being able to take place as intended, is practically difficult in this instance, but it also affects the conversation more broadly,'' he said.

STRmix claims it has been used in 500,000 criminal investigations and that its code has been reviewed four to five times, Adams said. 

"If these reviews cannot be effective, cannot be accomplished, and I can't discuss them after the fact, then that's misinformation going out in the world that at some level, I feel complicit with if I continue to engage in a very limited partial (review) of the system,'' he said.

Kathleen Hopkins, a reporter in New Jersey since 1985, covers crime, court cases, legal issues and just about every major murder trial to hit Monmouth and Ocean counties. Contact her at khopkins@app.com.

headline: Giving Tree brings cardboard art to Asbury Park Convention Hall Holiday Bazaar
fullText:
ASBURY PARK - For some at the Jersey Shore, creating art is preferable to cutting down a tree to celebrate the holidays, and now that abstract idea is gradually turning into a boardwalk tradition.

The Asbury Park Boardwalk and the Wooden Walls Project want the public to enjoy the fourth annual artistic holiday sculpture known as The Giving Tree in the Grand Arcade at the historic Convention Hall. The Giving Tree is available for viewing from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. through Dec. 30.

Local artists Michael LaVallee, aka Porkchop, and Bradley Hoffer collaborated to create the cardboard abstract display in the outline of a traditional Christmas tree, complete with custom lighting. The lighting scheme, created by Jason Dermer of Asbury Audio, helps to turn the Grand Arcade into a winter wonderland for all to gather and share the holiday art experience.

"I think what people don't get about it is (the artists) are two people that design it, spend weeks cutting it with a boxcutter, it is crazy. It is 16 feet tall," said Jenn Hampton, the founder and curator of Wooden Walls Project, a nonprofit organization based at the Asbury Park Boardwalk.

Dining in style: These Shore restaurants go all out with holiday decorations

Hampton said the mission of the nonprofit is to bring art and art experiences to people.

"A lot of experiences aren't free anymore, so we try to do as much as we can to ensure that art is available to everyone," she said.

2020 was first year the nonprofit collaborated with the Asbury Park Boardwalk. The first tree was nicknamed "the Giving Tree" and the name stuck as the idea became an annual tradition.

She added that the novelty of the Giving Tree also symbolizes the "importance of connectedness, shining a light on the Boardwalk’s conscious effort to support local arts and charities, and as the centerpiece for the Asbury Park Holiday Bazaar, the Boardwalk’s commitment to provide a platform for local makers and musicians."

The Asbury Park Holiday Bazaar runs Fridays through Sundays in December. The seasonal pop-up marketplace features local and regional handcrafted and vintage goods, art, photography, live music, workshops, kids art classes, food and libations.

Charity tables are setup around the tree, allowing local nonprofits to utilize the space around the tree.

Every weekend, Santa Claus appears at the tree and partners with the Asbury Park Toy Drive so people can bring a toy or make a donation to kids in need around Asbury Park. The Asbury Park Toy Drive hopes to help over 700 families this year. Adjacent to Santa are the Asbury Park Historical Society, the Asbury Park African American Music Project, the Asbury Park Music Foundation, and the Asbury Park Arts Council.

Holiday lights: See what's new at this year's Holiday in the Park at Six Flags Great Adventure

Hampton wants to make sure people know that Asbury Park is more than just music.

"Visual art and art experiences; people just assume that it happens. I want to make a real impact, and I think making an art tree as this symbol of our community speaks volumes. We accept that Asbury Park is a little different, it is unique and special. We do things differently here," Hampton said.

She admitted there "are tons of people who hate (the Giving Tree)" because it isn't a traditional Christmas tree, but now there is a sense of pride about the unique work of art.

"It becomes this talking point and even that talking point connects us. My goal is help them see things differently. The whole project on the boardwalk is about perception, how we see things, how we connect," Hampton said. "That makes it feel like we are not so divided, we can all agree on one thing; we like art."

headline: Howell wiped out plan for 200,000-square-foot warehouse complex; now it's getting sued
fullText:
HOWELL - The developer proposing to construct over 200,000 square feet of warehousing and offices on Victory Road is suing the Township Planning Board months after the application was unanimously denied.

The applicant, AAVRHW Property LLC (Victory Road) and Stavola Realty Co., sought preliminary and final major site plan approval to cut down a large portion of the existing woods and construct a 203,802-square-foot warehouse/office building on Victory Road across the street from Squankum Brook Farm.

The Township Planning Board unanimously denied the application at the Sept. 19 meeting, and the denial received applause from the public in attendance.

The lawsuit, filed on Nov. 27, is requesting preliminary and final major site plan approval with design waiver relief from the board and states that "the board's denial of the application was arbitrary, capricious, unreasonable, contrary to law and unsupported by the record."

You can read a full copy of the lawsuit at the bottom of this story.

Not just Christmas: Howell Rutgers student collects thousands of toys for kids in hospitals

The proposed development would have consisted of 193,802 square feet of warehouse space and two separate office spaces totaling 10,000 square feet. The developer also proposed 25 loading dock spaces, 35 trailer parking spaces and 72 passenger vehicle parking spaces, four of which would be equipped with electric charging stations, according to the lawsuit.

According to the lawsuit, the board "improperly considered evidence presented by, and on behalf of, members of the public that had no sufficient factual or legal basis" and "improperly relied on off-site conditions to deny the application."

The lawsuit alleges the board improperly based denying the application on "off-site traffic and circulation impacts" and "improperly relied on considerations that were outside its jurisdiction."

'A motorhead's dream': Raceway Park's wild history revealed by long-hidden photos, movies

According to the lawsuit, at the time the application was deemed complete, the property was located in the Township’s Special Economic Development (SED) Zone and prior to that filing the property was the subject of a solar panel ground-mount installation development application, which was denied by the zoning board.

Betty Lou Velez-Gimbel, who has lived at Squankum Brook Farm on Victory Road with her husband for the past two decades, reached out to neighbors to inform them about the project and organized meetings in their homes to plan a fight against it that included hiring a lawyer, Zoe Ferguson.

Velez-Gimbel advocated to township officials and the council that the warehouse property should be rezoned to residential to be consistent with the residential zoning on Victory Road. In November, she ran an unsuccessful independent campaign for the township council.

headline: Derek Simpson, former Rutgers guard, has found a fit at Saint Joseph's
fullText:
PHILADELPHIA – Derek Simpson deflected a pass on the perimeter, leapt onto the floor for the loose ball, corralled it, and passed ahead to a teammate in one furious swoop.

That kind of hustle is a familiar sight for Rutgers basketball fans, who appreciated it for the two years Simpson played on the banks. Now it’s endearing the Lenape High School grad to his new program, Saint Joseph’s, and their fans who gave the effort a thunderous applause during Tuesday’s showdown with Princeton.

“Joy, energy, unselfishness – Derek brings those things every day,” Saint Joseph’s coach Billy Lange said. “It’s great to have him here.”

Princton won the game 77-69, but Simpson put his best foot forward, scoring 13 points and handing out six assists while committing just two turnovers in 35 full-throttle minutes. On this night the junior was the best guard for the Hawks, who are 5-3 with wins over Villanova and Texas Tech.

Simpson said his time at Rutgers gave him a “a high-level mindset” on how to compete in college.

“I got to guard some great people in the Big Ten,” he said. “There were humbling experiences, guarding people who were really good and are playing in the NBA right now. It only helped me get better. I loved my experience at Rutgers, it was nothing but a blessing to compete at that level, but new beginnings happen.”

The Mount Laurel native was an impact sub as a freshman at Rutgers, but got thrust into the lead guard role unexpectedly as a sophomore after Cam Spencer and Paul Mulcahy made late departures via the transfer portal. The Scarlet Knights struggled all around last season and, like many programs, experienced an offseason exodus. Of the key players who transferred out, Simpson arguably has found the best fit.

Whereas Cliff Omoruyi is platooning at center for Alabama and Mawot Mag and Gavin Griffiths are barely contributing at BYU and Nebraska, respectively, Simpson is averaging 8.9 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.7 assists in 32 minutes per game. He is Saint Joseph’s top perimeter defender and shares lockdown tips gleaned from a certain former teammate with his new backcourt mates.  

“The big person I got my advice from is Caleb McConnell,” he said of the Scarlet Knights’ former Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year. “I think about some of the things he’s taught me, how he watches people’s hip movements. Little things like that I try to pass on to these guys.”

Saint Joseph’s sports one of the top backcourts in the Atlantic-10 Conference with Erik Reynolds, Xzayvier Brown and Simpson, an explosive trio that is still learning to play together.  

“Defense, with us, it’s not a weakness, but we can really improve on it,” Simpson said. “I try to motivate the guys about that.”

Saint Joseph’s takes on La Salle Saturday in the Big 5 Classic championship game at the Wells Fargo Center. As always, Simpson will have family in attendance. When it came time to transfer, the pull to stay local was strong.

“I knew I couldn’t go that far,” he said. “Had to have grandma, mom, dad, my sister come to the games.”

Lange recruited him hard out of Lenape High. Simpson is older and wiser now, but the happy warrior mindset is still there, evident each time he hits the floor for a loose ball.  

“He plays with great swagger, he’s got a burst and I just love who he is as a human being,” Lange said. “He’s a great kid.”

Jerry Carino has covered the New Jersey sports scene since 1996 and the college basketball beat since 2003. Contact him at jcarino@gannettnj.com.

headline: Toms River schools hope Trenton will offer more money, but might have to sell land instead
fullText:
TOMS RIVER - Toms River Regional schools are still in funding limbo as the district waits to see if pending legislation could help close a $12.4 million budget gap, or if it might have to turn to a real estate sale.

"We're waiting and being as hopeful as we can," Superintendent Mike Citta said.

Toms River Regional has also completed appraisals on 27 acres of district-owned property by the Joseph A. Citta School, as well as land by High School East for a possible sale to raise money.

The school board voted 6 to 3 to approve a 9.9% tax increase in June, but only if the state coughed up an additional $12.4 million in aid. When no additional aid was offered, the board voted against the spending plan, which left the district without a budget and forced the state to put the budget with the tax increase in place. Interim Ocean County Schools superintendent said she had no choice but to order that initial budget implemented, with the tax increase.

New BID boss Downtown Toms River gets new boss after previous chief clashed with mayor

The district sued the state in October in Ocean County Superior Court, claiming New Jersey's aid cuts have made it impossible for Toms River Regional to provide a "thorough and efficient" education as required by the state constitution. The state has not yet replied to the district's lawsuit.

A bill introduced by state Sens. Anthony M. Bucco, R-Morris, and Declan J. O'Scanlon Jr., R-Monmouth, would shift $64.9 million in budget appropriations to help fund schools, including more than $40 million from arts programs. The bill and a companion bill in the Assembly, would add a supplemental $145 million to schools; the measures so far have only received Republican support.

Another bill, introduced in the Senate by Carmen F. Amato Jr., R-Ocean, would allow districts facing budget shortfalls to apply for loans, as has previously been permitted.

Assemblyman Alex Sauickie, R-Ocean, has introduced a bill to provide $106.5 million in supplemental school aid to districts that have been allocated an amount of aid that is less than the schools' adequacy budget, as defined by the state (the amount required for a thorough and efficient education under the state's constitution) and have per pupil spending of $19,000 or less.

Toms River homeless camp emptying: This is why their lawyer credits the mayor

It is unclear whether any of these bills, which are all before the education committees in the Senate and Assembly, can gain approval before the end of the year and would be supported by Gov. Phil Murphy. Murphy is a Democrat, and the state Legislature is controlled by Democrats.

Toms River and other districts at the Shore, including Asbury Park, Neptune, Jackson, Middletown and Brick, have lost state funding under S2, the education aid formula that redistributes money from districts that have lost student population, to those that are adding students.

"We are in neutral and waiting," Citta said.

headline: Girls basketball preseason Top 20 Shore team rankings
fullText:
Heated gyms, buzzer beaters, comebacks efforts, defending champs and everything in between when it comes to high school girls basketball is almost upon us.

More: Top NJ high school girls basketball players head to 'The Fort' for summer league: takeaways

Here are our presesason team rankings:

1. Red Bank Catholic (Last season: 26-5)

Last year the Caseys finished their season only losing one game to a Shore Conference team (Manasquan), won a sectional title, and won a Non-Public A State Championship--the scary part is most of that roster was underclassmen. Now they have a transfer in Scarlet LeVake, a versatile 6-foot-2 in from Paul VI of Virginia, who'll add to their already talented team. Junior Addison Nyemchek is a nationally ranked player (No. 51) boosted by her play over the summer, Monmouth commit Tessa Carman is returning for her senior year and Navy commit Christina Liggio is also returning to add to the talented back court. Adding more depth to this team has made them a scare to look at. Don't be surprised if this team begins to receive national attention. Head coach Joe Montano will have this team playing full court press from the tip-off till the final buzzer. If they're able to capitalize on their tough schedule against teams such as Morris Catholic, Rutgers Prep and Long Island Lutheran (NY) then they're nearly a shoo-in to go back-to-back on state titles.

More: Red Bank Catholic girls basketball wins section title; St. Rose falls to Rutgers Prep

2. St. John Vianney (22-8)

The Lancers had a good group of highly talented players, but inexperience played a role against top teams, this year should be different. SJV still managed to win their fourth straight Shore Conference Tournament title last season. The twin towers in 6-foot-4 Taylor Sofilkanich (No. 38 in ESPN's 2026) and 6-foot-1 Stella Lockhart, both juniors, have another year of experience under their belt. The two have been making noise over the summer playing against the top players in the nation and holding their own. They'll be without Daniella Matus, who transferred back to Morris Catholic, and sharpshooter Julia Karpell, who's now at Fairfield. Aleena Dinker and Saint Michael's commit Brooklyn Taylor will each be seniors and likely to be key in the back court, although SJV always manages to have a surprise transfer who's a contributer. Dawn Karpell will make sure her team is ready, and with them losing to RBC last season in the playoffs, the Lancers have something to prove this year.

More: St John Vianney Girls Basketball squeezes by Trinity Hall 57-53

3. St. Rose (19-10)

The Purple Roses have the luxury of Jada Lynch being on their roster. The 5-foot-10 junior guard led the team in every category but three-pointers last season. She's spent the summer playing overseas and can play and defend every position on the floor. Last season St. Rose was hindered with injuries, but still was a dangerous team that made a South Non-Public B finals appearance (lost to Rutgers Prep). Senior guard and Tampa commit Cassidy Kruesi is a deep shooter who led the team in three's as a junior. Kruesi is also another player on the Purple Roses that can defend the multiple positions. Junior Brooke Missry is a developing guard who can knock down shots, Misericordia University commit Lizzy Mitchell is returning from injury, and Christina Hatfield enters her second year as head coach after a successful first year. The Purple Roses are back.

More: St. Rose Girls Basketball pulls off OT win over Trinity Hall

4. Ranney (15-11)

By the time the season was coming to a close last year, Ranney put the Shore Conference on notice that it will be one of the best soon. A close defeat to St. Rose in the Non-Public B Semifinals was a showcase of how dangerous this team can be. Senior and Lafayette commit Haley Poser is a 5-foot-8 guard with a high IQ and feel for the game. Sophomore and 6-foot-3 forward Ashley Kreiger has been getting Division I offers and is only getting better. Thomas Jefferson University commit Michelle Steele is transferring over from Holmdel. This team has shooters, size, defenders and playoff experience. They'll have their moments to prove themselves with games against St. Thomas Aquinas, St. Rose and Manasuqan. You saw it here first, Ranney will be a strong team in the Shore Conference.

East Stroudsburg commit and senior forward Lilly Riggi has solid skills and can defend the paint with the best of them, junior Grace Feeney is a stretch-forward that can knock down the long ball, and freshman Allison McAndrew may be able to contribute early in her career. The Monarchs roster is filled with players with decent height and are able to switch out on any position because of it. If head coach Matt McCarthy is able to continue to build on what he had last season then this team can be dangerous.

The Bulldogs are typically always known for having a good basketball team, and this year should be no different. They'll be without Raquel Guidetti, Abby Boyle, and Ella Mason this year, but they still have some scorers on the roster. Sylvie Notine and Erin Reid will likely be the leaders on the team and carry a heavy work load. Head coach Dave Callahan has been running a summer league at The Fort and is hopeful of the accomplishments his team can reach this season. They'll play the best the Shore Conference has to offer with two games against RBC and SJV, plus other good squads. The ceiling for this team is unknown for now, but they deserve their respect.

Last year the Rebels went on a historic run and won their first basketball section title (Central Jersey, Group 4) in school history - boys or girls. 6-foot forward and East Stroudsburg commit Kiera McKown averaged a double-double last year as a junior. McKown will be the clear leading scorer, rebounder, and blocker for the Rebels this season. Sophomore Kylee Beam had some impressive games as a freshman. Whether they'll be able to win another section title will yet to be seen, but they've announced themselves as one of the favorites to win another section title.

The Jaguars only graduated two seniors from last years roster and will look to build on an impressive season. Sophomore Cali Brown will likely be given the keys to the offense at the guard position. Brown, Avery Brooks, and Kaylee Ambos are all long range shooters with at least another year of high school hoops after this season. headline: County officials: Monmouth Executive Airport owner restricted our on-site inspection
fullText:
WALL - The county says it will attempt to make a third site visit to Monmouth Executive Airport, after their aviation consultant complained they were restricted by its owner to “just two hours to inspect more than three miles of runway and taxiway, in the middle of the night.”

Merchant Aviation, a Summit-based aviation firm, has been appointed by the Monmouth County Board of Commissioners to evaluate whether New Jersey’s largest privately-owned airport could be better run and maintained under public ownership by the county.

Alan Antaki, who owns the 740-acre complex off Route 34 — which has a longer runway than LaGuardia Airport in New York — said through an attorney that he has no intention of selling his property for any price.

Antaki and his legal team said that Commissioner Director Thomas A. Arnone, director of the Board of Commissioners, has already invoked eminent domain in forcing his way onto Antaki’s private property for the county’s latest airport site visit on Nov. 22. An earlier visit last spring included Arnone and Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden, who is also chairman of the Monmouth County GOP.

“Upon receiving a number of reports concerning the airport’s safety, it became our duty to ensure it is in top shape for all who use it,” Arnone said in a statement this week. “If the property owner has nothing to hide, our experts would have been granted the time needed to properly assess the property. Our team complied with all of the property owner’s requirements, and we hope next time, he’ll comply with ours.”

Matt Dolan, an attorney representing Antaki, said the county has no jurisdiction over airport operations or airport safety.

“That is the province of the New Jersey Department of Transportation or — in some cases — the Federal Aviation Administration,” Dolan said.

In fact, the state Transportation Department just licensed the airport for another year after recently completing its annual inspection of the complex and its two runways, Dolan said.

County officials said that their Nov. 22 inspection — which was conducted between 1 a.m. to 3 a.m. — presented challenges for their own representatives from Merchant Aviation.

Officials were told they could not continue to visually inspect the runway and taxiways beyond the two-hour window permitted by the owner, nor could they separate into smaller groups to be more efficient.

“Mr. Arnone continues to cling to the fiction that his interest in seizing the airport is necessary to protect the people who use the facility that I own and operate,” Antaki said. “His claims are a deception to hide his real reasons for wanting my property.”

Antaki said the county’s interest in his airport is all about its appetite for more money and power.

“Tom Arnone’s ongoing false narrative regarding ‘concerns over safety’ is designed solely to harm the airport and its ongoing operations in furtherance of Arnone’s self-stated ‘pet peeve’ about wanting to own an airport because three other counties in New Jersey do,” Dolan said.

Arnone has said the board is responding to complaints received about current safety conditions at the airport — which was built in the 1930s and maintains much of its original character. However, the county has acknowledged that there are no written complaints in their possession and that the reports they have heard are “anecdotal.”

County representatives have pointed to a recent letter to the editor published in The Coast Star from former state Assemblyman Ned Thomson, R-Monmouth, who recently raised his own concerns about the airport.

In order to address those reports, county officials argue that a public inspection of the airport is required to alleviate the safety concerns expressed to the county commissioners.

To do that, the county said it needs greater accommodation to professionally inspect two miles of runway and taxiway, as well as dozens of on-site buildings.

Antaki and his lawyers reject the accusation that the Nov. 22 inspection of the airport was obstructed.

Dolan said that the county’s statement was “another desperate attempt by the county commissioners to mislead the public, denigrate Mr. Antaki, and spin a false narrative as the commissioners fumble for plausible reasons to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to take the airport from its rightful owner.”

The county did not object to the time or the duration of the inspection when it was agreed to in November, Dolan said.

“The county’s attorneys and consultants willingly accepted the time that was allotted to inspect the airport,” he said. “It was not an issue in November; now in December it is an issue. Why? What transpired over the past two weeks that has the county commissioners concerned?”

Edmond J. Harrison, director of commercial development and revenue management of Merchant Aviation, said that the company hoped to have unrestricted on-site access “to give a fair and complete evaluation of the conditions of Monmouth Executive Airport for Monmouth County residents.

“We hope that with a second visit, our analysis will be more forthcoming,” Harrison said.

Antaki’s attorneys said they have received no letter from the county counsel notifying them that their consultant is seeking an additional visit to the airport this year.

“Mr. Arnone is setting a dangerous precedent for property owners in Monmouth County, suggesting that county government has a duty to inspect private property to confirm it remains in ‘top shape,’” Dolan said.

headline: Jackson Memorial High School hockey team rebounds after year of setbacks. Here's how
fullText:
JACKSON — Jackson Memorial High School's hockey players are back on the ice after a year of disappointing struggles and a season with no team.

The team was defunded last year as officials at the Jackson School District were faced with years of declining state aid and cut costs to balance its budget.

The result left Jackson Memorial students and parents searching and failing to find a partner team before the winter season launched a year ago.

But this year, 16-year-old Andrew Brockman, a sophomore at Jackson Memorial, is excited to be back on the ice.

"I missed my freshman year (playing hockey)," he recalled. "I wanted something more to do. I wanted to have more friends. I had just moved here. I was only here for a year, and I wanted to be around more people, and hockey was that community I loved."

Brockman and the other Jackson players have found that community alongside high school hockey players from Robbinsville and Allentown. With Jackson's five members, the combined team has 26 players, said Head Coach Dan Bergan.

Administrators and athletic directors from the three schools worked together to ensure all the players would be back on the ice this season, Bergan said.

"My (Jackson) Jaguars have been revitalized," he said, sporting patches for Jackson Memorial and Allentown on his Robbinsville jacket.

One year ago: Jackson hockey players desperately hunt for co-op team days before season starts

Co-op and triple partnerships like Robbinsville-Allentown-Jackson Memorial are becoming more common, Bergan said.

"The difficulty nowadays is hockey is getting harder and harder to find a partner (team)," he said Tuesday after the players practiced at the Mercer County Skating Rink in West Windsor. "Hockey is getting so expensive that you're getting fewer and fewer players.

The costs for equipment and ice time have increased dramatically in just a few years, he said.

Numerous hockey teams across the region have formed co-op teams. Jackson Liberty players have joined this season with Red Bank Regional's team while Point Pleasant Beach and Manasquan players have also formed their own team, according to the New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association, or NJSIAA.

Other districts at the Jersey Shore have also adopted the three-school approach to forming a hockey team: including Freehold Borough-Raritan-Colts Neck and Ocean Township-Shore Regional-Monmouth Regional, according to the NJSIAA.

"Our coach Dan Bergan welcomes us (Jackson players) in with open arms, treats us like his own (Robbinsville) kids," said Robert Tignini, a 17-year-old Jackson Memorial senior. "The players on the team treat us like brothers."

Even when hockey players like Jackson's are self-funded, rather than school-funded, these public school partnerships open the game to students whose families cannot afford expensive, private travel hockey teams, Bergan said. A private travel hockey team can cost a parent a few thousand dollars for the year, he said.

Fundraisers and raffles will help pay for the roughly $1,000 season cost for each Jackson and Allentown player, he said. Robbinsville players' costs are supported by their school district, the coach added.

Jackson junior Ryan Bartlett, 16, said the tri-team partnership has been a great opportunity for the Jackson players.

"I've learned so much from this program that I never had before in hockey," he said.

Jackson junior Nate Rachunok, 16, said he was also glad to be back playing hockey with his classmates once again.

"I'm just feeling way better," he said. "There's something in my life again… just hopping on the ice with all the boys, having fun."

Amanda Oglesby is an Ocean County native who covers education and the environment. She has worked for the Press for more than 16 years. Reach her at @OglesbyAPP, aoglesby@gannettnj.com or 732-557-5701.

headline: Sickles Market looks to reopen after bankruptcy; here are plans for back wages, gift cards
fullText:
LITTLE SILVER — Sickles Market hopes to return by next summer.

In a statement posted on social media Thursday morning, investment group 1663 Partners LLC, who will become the new owners of Sickles Market, said they are focusing on pulling Sickles Market out of bankruptcy.

A reorganization plan filed in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in November includes plans to pay employees back wages in full and include two weeks of severance for former employees. Also, the company will honor outstanding Sickles Markets gift cards "over time," the statement said. Gift cards are typically wiped clean by the bankruptcy process.

Sickles Market in Little Silver closed in March, part of a series of financial difficulties that took down one of Monmouth County's most storied family businesses.

A century-old business failed: The inside story of how Sickles Market collapsed

Its owner, Bob Sickles Jr. of Rumson, and AHS Realty LLC, his business which holds the land of the Little Silver store and his Rumson home, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in May. Sickles listed $10.9 million in assets and $7.5 million in liabilities, court papers state.

1663 Partners LLC came forward with a willingness to reopen Sickles Market and hire Sickles, his two daughters, and a former employee to run the store. The group also is sponsoring Sickles' Chapter 11 plan of reorganization, court papers said.

"Efforts are now focused on concluding the bankruptcy process and preparing the market for a targeted reopening by summer 2025," 1663 Partners said in the post. "This will include a comprehensive business plan aimed at revitalizing the market's legacy while maintaining its reputation for quality produce, plants, gourmet goods and more.

"The Sickles family and 1663 Partners deeply value the trust and dedication of the market's loyal customers, exceptional vendors and supportive community," the post states. "These partnerships are integral to the market's success, and we look forward to continuing them in this new chapter."

Financial problems at Sickles Market, a 116-year-old family business, became evident after the abrupt closure of Sickles in Red Bank in February and then Sickles Market, its landmark homebase on Harrison Street in Little Silver, in March. A sister store in Red Bank, Bottles by Sickles, closed in April after eviction proceedings.

It resulted in lawsuits from vendors and suppliers. Sickles' other debts include about $800,000 in unpaid sales tax and $300,000 in back wages, court papers state.

In a certification filed in bankruptcy court in May, Sickles pointed to the poor performance of Sickles Market's 2020 expansion into Red Bank's West Side, the COVID lockdown and its aftermath and effects on sales at the Little Silver market for the company's troubles.

headline: Pedestrian suffering from life-threatening injuries after being struck in Howell
fullText:
FREEHOLD – A pedestrian has suffered life-threatening injuries after she was struck by a car Tuesday in Howell, and the investigation into the cause of incident is underway, authorities said.

At 5:17 p.m., Howell Township Police responded to Route 9 and Lanes Mill Road for a vehicle versus pedestrian crash, Monmouth County Prosecutor Raymond S. Santiago said.

An initial investigation found that a female driver was traveling north in the left lane of Route 9, and as she approached the intersection near Lanes Mill Road, a collision with a 45-year-old woman from Lakewood occurred, Santiago said. As a result, the pedestrian was taken to a local hospital, where she is being treated for life-threatening injuries.

The driver remained on scene, Santiago said. The identities of the driver and the pedestrian were not released.

An investigation involving members of the Monmouth County Prosecutor’s Office, Monmouth County Serious Collision Analysis Response Team (SCART), and the Howell Township Police Department remains active and ongoing, Santiago said. Anyone with information about this matter is being asked to contact MCPO Detective Nicolas Logothetis at 800-533-7443 or Howell Township Police Department Patrolman Daniel Scherbinski at 732-938-4111.

No charges or summonses have been issued with regard to the incident at this time, according to the prosecutor.

headline: The best coaster in the country is in New Jersey … and doesn’t exist anymore
fullText:
Great Adventure’s Kingda Ka has long been the gold standard for thrill seekers.

It’s so imposing that PlayNJ.com, a New Jersey-based gambling analysis site, just gave Kingda Ka a perfect score in its ranking of top daredevil coasters.

The site tauts Kingda Ka’s gut-clenching specs.

It runs more than 3,000 feet of track.

It tops 125 mph.

It stands at 456 feet tall.

It also stands completely idle.

Six Flags, the parks’ parent company, shut down the ride early last month, ending its nearly 20-year run of terror.

What is the best coaster in the country?

PlayNJ.com this week named Kingda Ka the ultimate daredevil rollercoaster in the country. 

The gambling analysis site said it looked at 434 coasters at 113 U.S. theme parks.

Kingda Ka earned a perfect score of 100 from PlayNJ.com, surpassing North Carolina’s Fury 325 — the longest coaster in the study at 6,602 feet — as well as Ohio’s Millennium Force, Orion, and Top Thrill 2; Virginia’s Project 305; California’s Superman: Escape from Krypton and Goliath; and Texas’s Titan.

What happened to Kingda Ka?

Great Adventure’s towering coaster debuted in 2005 and quickly became a must-ride for casual coaster fans and enthusiasts.

But, insiders had been suggesting for months that Six Flags, the park’s parent firm, was planning Kingda Ka’s demise.

As October came to a close, coaster fans flocked to the park to ride Kingda Ka and started posting videos of “last rides.”

A few days later, Six Flags confirmed the park’s most-famous ride was no longer running. It shut down Kingda Ka and is retiring the Green Lantern rollercoaster as part of an expansion project already in the works.

An unnamed ride should be ready for the 2026 season, and will come after the 2025 debut of The Flash: Vertical Velocity, which Six Flags Great Adventure is calling North America's first super-boomerang coaster.

headline: Shore native artist named to 2025 Forbes 30 Under 30 list for Art & Style
fullText:
Qualeasha Wood is celebrating a big honor.

According to Forbes, she took on over $20,000 in credit card debt to fund her machine-woven tapestries.

More: Whoopi Goldberg ready to return to stage as 'wonderfully odd' Miss Hannigan in 'Annie'

"Inspired by a familial relationship to textiles, queer craft, Microsoft Paint and internet avatars, Wood's tufted and tapestry pieces mesh traditional craft and contemporary technological materials," according to her website.

“My practice has kind of been all pushing boundaries,” Wood told Forbes.

Forbes says her art uses digital imagery to illustrate themes touching on her identity as a queer Black woman.

“I’m making work for that little girl who once upon a time hated art and didn't feel welcomed in that space," Wood told Forbes.

In 2021, Wood became one of the youngest artists ever to have work shown in and acquired by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Her work has also been purchased by producer Swizz Beatz, currently displayed at the Brooklyn Museum.

Her works also have been seen at the Harvey B. Gantt Center for African-American Art + Culture, the Art Institute of Chicago, Spelman College Museum of Fine Art, the Pippy Houldsworth Gallery in London and more.
