headline: College Football Playoffs odds: Who will win national championship? We handicap the field
fullText:
We will find out on Sunday who is in the first College Football Playoff 12-team field, including the top seeds.

But who is going to come out on top after all the playoff games are played? Who will be the champion of this 12-team jumble? Who is the team whose fans can say - with no arguments - that it is No. 1?

We asked noted oddsmaker Danny Sheridan to handicap the field and here are his odds against winning the CFP national title:

More: Miami Hurricanes were lock for ACC title game, CFP; then they reverted to form

Oregon Ducks 4:1

It's no surprise Oregon tops this list. The Ducks (12-0) have been No. 1 in every poll released so far.

While quarterback Dillon Gabriel has no chance at winning the Heisman Trophy, the sixth-year senior has led this Pacific Northwest team to an undefeated season heading into Saturday's Big Ten Championship Game. The Big Ten Offensive Player of the Year passed for 3,275 yards and 24 touchdowns while tossing only 6 interceptions. He also added 175 rushing yards and 7 rushing touchdowns. 

Texas Longhorns 9:2

In their first season in the SEC, Texas (11-1) has proven it belongs and now has a chance at a national title. First, the Longhorns have a rematch against Georgia for the SEC championship Saturday in Atlanta. The Bulldogs handed the Longhorns their only defeat, 30-15, in Austin in October. But the outcome was more emphatic than the final score; Georgia led 23-0 at halftime.

Ohio State Buckeyes 5:1

Forget the collapse against arch-rival Michigan and the post-game melee; THE Ohio State University can still win the big one.

The Buckeyes have talent across the board - adding to that on Wednesday - and can play with anyone. Ohio State handed No. 4 Penn State and No. 10 Indiana their only losses. Ohio State lost to Oregon by one point and that game was played in Eugene.

Georgia Bulldogs 6:1

People are still talking about the marathon win over Georgia Tech, but the Dawgs are right in the hunt.

Georgia quarterback Carson Beck has had an up and down season, but he threw for five touchdowns off 297 yards on 28-for-43 passing vs. Georgia Tech.

Notre Dame Fighting Irish 10:1

It would only be fitting that the school that has 11 national titles on its football resume should win this year's title.

Quarterback Riley Leonard, a semifinalist for Comeback Player of the Year, has led the Irish to an 11-win season, including 4-0 vs. ranked teams. The former Duke Blue Devil suffered multiple injuries last season but has rebounded to score14 rushing touchdowns, fifth among all quarterbacks.

Penn State Nittany Lions 10:1

Can the Nittany Lions upset the Ducks for the Big Ten championship? Of course, they can. Two of their key players are Tyler Warren, who has caught more passes (81) than any tight end in Big Ten history, and edge rusher Abdul Carter, who has 10 sacks on the season and was named Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year.

Alabama Crimson Tide 15:1

How can a team with three losses still be in the picture for the national championship? Well, it helps when your name is Alabama. It's hard to put that inexplicable loss to Vanderbilt out of one's mind, but Alabama has gone toe-to-toe with the SEC heavyweights and done well, including a 3-1 record against current Top 25 teams.

Tennessee Volunteers 20:1

Another SEC team that cannot be overlooked. The Vols, who beat Vanderbilt 36-23, are ready for the playoffs.

"If you are not of the mindset going into this thing of anyone, anywhere, anytime," head coach Josh Heupel said, "then you are just there to have a cup of coffee anyways."

Best of the rest ...

SMU is 40:1, Indiana 50:1 and Clemson 75:1 so don't count on any of this trio making it to the top.

headline: Miami Dolphins' Tua Tagovailoa won't face Azeez Al-Shaair, and let's all be glad | Habib
fullText:
MIAMI GARDENS — The NFL has stepped in, thankfully, allowing us to avoid a situation in which the league’s admitted poster child for concussions, Miami Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, doesn’t come face-to-face with the league’s newest villain, Houston linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair.

That’s what awaited us next week when the Dolphins visit the Texans. Alas, the NFL did what it had to do, suspending Al-Shaair for the shot heard ‘round the league when he hammered Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence, knocking him out of the game and probably the season.

Al-Shaair, from Florida Atlantic, was slapped with a three-game suspension for the vicious hit on a sliding Lawrence. His appeal failed, meaning that with the Texans on a bye this weekend, he won't suit up against the Dolphins on Dec. 15.

Probably best for all concerned, you have to say. Imagine the reaction by Miami’s offensive linemen if Al-Shaair, cast in the role of heel more befitting of the WWE, took the slightest liberties around Tagovailoa, whose history of concussions need not be explained here. Powder keg isn’t a strong enough term.

More: Miami Dolphins rookie Chop Robinson: Practicing with Bradley Chubb 'crazy,' 'a dream'

As it is, the result of the hit is ugly for all involved. The Jaguars placed Lawrence on injured reserve, and at 2-10, it’d be pointless to bring him back for the season finale. The three paychecks Al-Shaair is out are just the start of his problems as his playing style is under attack. That’s not entirely without reason, unlike the Islamophobic ugliness he’s receiving, which absolutely is.

Tagovailoa said Wednesday that the buzz among teammates alerted him to the hit. As soon as he saw it, his reaction was what you’d expect from a reasonable person not connected with the Texans.

"I thought that was crazy," Tagovailoa said. "He was giving himself up and you know, defensive guy came and smoked him. I don't know the reaction time with being a defender, trying to go and make a play on a guy. So I don't know all the logistics with that. But I felt like he did have time to sort of – even if he was going to launch – he could have launched out of the way, knowing that Trevor was giving himself up."

Tua Tagovailoa blames himself for leaving Dolphins 'out to dry'

This isn’t, as you’d expect, one of Tagovailoa’s favorite topics. If any quarterback knows the risks involved with scrambling for yardage or even simply operating within the pocket, he does. Back in Week 2, he scrambled for the line to gain on a fourth-down play, collided with Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin, suffered a concussion, and the Dolphins still haven’t recovered. They’re 5-7, including a 1-3 slump in games Tagovailoa missed.

Result: He’s blaming himself for trying to do his job.

"Nobody else will say it but me, and I feel like this has a lot to do with myself, obviously putting myself in harm's way in the second game, going down, basically leaving my guys out to dry," Tagovailoa said. "That's what I would say. And anyone can have an opinion about like, it's football, it's this, it's that. I do take heart to that as well. And still don't want to do that to my guys again."

The difference here is that Al-Shaair initiated a hit that was 1) brutal and 2) unnecessary. The moment Lawrence began his slide, the play was over. Or should have been.

The proper response when one of your own commits such an act is to be contrite, show concern, then shut the (bleep) up. Which is not what the Texans did. GM Nick Caserio alternately was defensive of his linebacker, then offensive on the entire situation. He said, “Nobody embodies our program more than Azeez.” Even if you somehow don’t find Caserio’s timing strange, you have to wonder how many in the Texans’ “program” quietly take exception to Al-Shaair being held up as representative of the group. Caserio then went on a whatabout rant naming illegal hits in games not involving the Texans that did not result in a suspension. 

What Caserio apparently overlooked – but the league didn’t – is this isn’t Al-Shaair’s first offense. As a member of the 49ers, he grabbed Bucs QB Tom Brady by the throat. He punched a Bears running back and took a cheap shot on a Titans back.

That’s evidence of the type of player Al-Shaair is. What it isn’t: a green light to go after Al-Shaair limitlessly on a personal level, particularly when it comes to religion. Apparently in the eyes of online critics, Al-Shaair opened the door to such hate by writing “All Praise to Allah” atop an apology to Lawrence he posted on social media. Would it have mattered if, say, he instead wrote “Praise Jesus” or “All Glory to God”? Why?

“To Trevor I genuinely apologize to you for what ended up happening,” he wrote. “Before the game we spoke and I told you how it was great to see you back on the field and wished you well. I would never want to see any player hurt because of a hit I put on them especially one that’s deemed ‘late’ or ‘unnecessary.’ ”

Azeez Al-Shaair was once a team leader at FAU

Six years ago, Al-Shaair was a 21-year-old senior at FAU who merely hoped he had a future in the NFL. What he did know was the world – and life – isn’t always fair.

“Everybody knows I am Muslim just from my name,” he told The Palm Beach Post.

He’d become an Owls team leader through his words and the kind of maturity one is force-fed after watching his family’s home burn to the ground before his sophomore year of high school. With the family living in a motel, Azeez was forced to take two-hour bus rides to Hillsborough High in Tampa. Football became his release.

“It was kind of the one time where I felt like I was good at something, or was worth something,” he said.

Al-Shaair could stop running backs, all right. Hurtful words were a different animal altogether.

“I can’t be the person that’s going to stop that, but what I can say is that anybody who meets me, whether it be Muslim or whatever, the same way I might meet somebody and they might be something – I just need to know who that person is first,” he said. “And if I don’t know you, I can’t judge you.”

He hoped that those who did take the time to know him were glad they did.

“You understand the type of person I am, and I’m a good person,” he said.

And he credited his faith with becoming who he’d become: “When you have something to believe in, when you have values, it stops you from doing things that might come into your head. Negative things. You see people shooting up schools and killing different people. When you don’t have any type of guidance or a foundation of things that you go by, and morals, it really can create chaos.”

Lightening the mood, Al-Shaair joked about what he’d do if he landed an NFL contract: “I don’t know. Go get something to eat, maybe.”

Six years later, here we are. His background does nothing to forgive his actions on the field any more than the attacks by bigots warrant forgiveness.

Forgiveness is tough to come by, at least for the time being. We can all hope healing, for Trevor Lawrence, is not.

fullText:
Interested in that Margaritaville specialty license plate the Florida Legislature approved this year to honor the late singer and businessman Jimmy Buffet? Or the one to let other drivers know that in The Villages, "Dreams Come True"?

You might want to hurry. New specialty plates in Florida must get at least 3,000 presales before the first one comes off the press, and there's a limited time to do it.

In October, the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles deauthorized 15 different specialty license plates for not reaching their presale limit. One plate, for the Florida State Beekeepers Association, was given a one-year extension and can be presold until July 1, according to a FLHSMV release.

Once approved, specialty license plates in Florida "have 2 years to reach the 3,000-voucher requirement," FLHSMV spokesperson Molly Best said in an email.

The FLHSMV also discontinued some specialty plates that people have already been driving around with. Florida law requires approved specialty plates to be discontinued if the number of registrations for them drops below 3,000 for at least 12 consecutive months.

Specialty license plates are plates for your registered vehicle that feature different artwork than the standard Florida white, orange and green plates to let you add a colorful personal touch for your ride. headline: Cardinal Newman football player signs with Illinois after transformation of body, spirit
fullText:
When it comes to the Fighting Illini, Cardinal Newman's Dylan Frechette embodies the "fight" of what it takes to be a successful college football player.

And what it takes to be a great person, as well.

The Crusaders' top offensive lineman officially signed with Illinois on early signing day, the stroke of his pen symbolizing the beginning of the next chapter in a story of bravery, perseverance and victory.

Frechette lost his mom, Stephanie, in October 2022 following a three-month illness.

National Signing Day: A look at where top local recruits are headed

Watch Florida high school football live on NFHS Network

The father of a former Newman player reached out to tell Crusaders head coach Jack Daniels about Frechette.

Daniels and the Cardinal Newman staff brought him down from Rhode Island during Christmas break in 2022 for an introduction, which led to an unexpected but perfect fit for everyone involved.

"We went out to Denny's, had breakfast, talked, obviously really fell in love with the kid at that moment," Daniels said. "We were still trying to find out how he could transition down here. We were at a Cardinal Newman fishing tournament talking about him and the guy that owned the boat overhead us talking."

That man and his family, the Marvins, took him into their home after Frechette moved to South Florida from Rhode Island, and he committed himself wholly to the sport of football, dropping 100 pounds in the process of becoming one of the state's top offensive linemen.

In body and mind, Frechette reinvented himself on the gridiron – and as a person as well.

"He was 400 pounds," Daniels said. "He's lost 100 pounds. He's a whole different guy. I told him if he lost his weight: 'You'll be a Power Five kid. You'll get a full scholarship.' He's worked and earned it."

It's an incredible change for a great player, but as Daniels says, he's "an even better person."

No, this isn't "The Blind Side," the 2009 rendition of Michael Oher's journey by John Lee Hancock.

But he's heard people reference the movie many times before when they hear about his background and the passing of his mom.

"That really motivated me to continue with this football stuff because I always told her I was going to be great," Frechette said. "So that's my plan. I was 397 at my highest weight, and now I'm sitting at 295 and feeling good. It took a lot of work, sweat, blood and tears."

He's always been known as "The Big Island," hailing from Rhode Island. There's just a little else emphasis on the "big" now.

It's still a nickname appropriate for his dynamic play.

For most people, perhaps including his new fan base of Illinois football fans, knowledge of his story centers on the growing list of pancake blocks and decidedly small number of sacks his quarterback has taken.

But really, what they'll be getting is a stellar player and an even better person.

To his mom, Frechette has a simple message.

"This is for you," he said. "This is for you."

headline: Boca manicurist who threatened Donald Trump after 'watching too much MSNBC' sent to prison
fullText:
WEST PALM BEACH — A 60-year-old manicurist with no criminal history will spend a year in federal prison for threatening to kill President-elect Donald Trump — a crime her attorney blamed on exposure to too much cable news.

Martha Jane Schoenfeld left voicemails in June threatening to detonate bombs at two of Trump's properties in Florida and Nevada. In exchange for her guilty plea, prosecutors recommended she be sentenced to one year of probation in lieu of prison.

Schoenfeld and her attorney agreed. Trump, notified of the plea bargain like all federal crime victims are supposed to be, did too.

The judge did not.

U.S. District Judge Raag Singhal took the rare step Tuesday of exceeding prosecutors' recommended penalty. Made wary by the two assassination attempts on Trump that followed Schoenfeld's arrest, he sentenced the Boca Raton woman to 13 months in federal prison instead.

Boca Raton manicurist denied, then admitted, making Trump bomb threats

Schoenfeld apologized Tuesday for the bomb threats, which she said she had neither the means nor the desire to carry out. According to prosecutors, Schoenfeld made the threats in voicemails to the Trump International Golf Club in suburban West Palm Beach and Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas on June 6.

"There is a bomb I left on the site," she said in one. "Hopefully you will get everyone evacuated, except for Trump."

Members of the Secret Service traced the call back to Schoenfeld, a wife and mother of two adult children, within hours. A federal agent and Boca Raton police officer arrived at her condominium the same day, and she invited them inside.

Schoenfeld initially denied knowing about the bomb threat but backtracked when told that investigators could trace where the call came from.

Investigators learned of a second bomb threat made to the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas shortly after departing from Schoenfeld's home. The Secret Service agent called Schoenfeld, who again denied knowing about the threat before admitting that she had made it.

She added that she left a threatening voicemail with U.S. Sen Marco Rubio of Florida around the same time, an admission which did not culminate in a separate charge.

Arrested shortly thereafter, Schoenfeld made her first appearance in federal court on July 12 — one day before the first failed assassination attempt on Trump during a campaign rally in Pennsylvania.

Faced with the possibility of 20 years in federal prison, Schoenfeld pleaded guilty to one of two threat-related charges in September — forgoing her right to a trial by jury but ensuring that prosecutors would recommend she be spared from prison.

"This was a lady in a condo that was watching too much MSNBC and got carried away," her defense attorney Mark McMann said Wednesday. "We agreed the probation and the embarrassment was enough. She's been through enough."

McMann added that the probation recommendation was even green-lighted by the Secret Service and Trump. Under the federal Victims' Rights and Restitution Act, prosecutors have an obligation to inform victims or their representatives of any plea bargain, as well as their right to appear in court.

Neither Trump nor his representative attended Tuesday's sentencing hearing, McMann said.

McMann said the hearing was the third time in his 35-year career that he's seen a judge sentence a defendant to more time in prison than prosecutors recommended. He attributed the surprise outcome to a combination of factors, including the heightened rhetoric about Trump and the two assassination attempts.

"It was just an environment where the judge didn't want to be too lenient," he said.

Schoenfeld, free on a $25,000 bond, must surrender herself back into federal custody by Jan. 15. With good gain time, McMann said she may be able to shave 60 days off of her 13-month sentence.

Once she is released, she must complete a year of probation.

headline: Miami Dolphins' Anthony Weaver explains why 'soft' defense wasn't problem in Green Bay
fullText:
MIAMI GARDENS — It wasn't the cold. And they weren't soft.

Those are the conclusions of Miami Dolphins defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver after reviewing defensive film of Miami's loss at Green Bay on Thanksgiving night.

After the loss, Dolphins linebacker Jordyn Brooks said the defense's performance was soft.

Weaver prides himself on a tough, physical, aggressive approach.

So what did Weaver think of Brooks' comments?

OUR PICKS: Dolphins predictions vs woeful Jets: Palm Beach Post experts' Week 14 picks

"It's one of those things when you're talking after the game, you're reacting purely off emotion," Weaver said. "And I'm sure that once he watched the tape, I wouldn't be surprised if he changes tune. Because that game, the missed tackles could, you could say are, they kind of equate to softness in the moment, but when you see the why they occurred, you would see that softness had nothing to do with it. I give credit to the Green Bay Packers for just making plays and making us miss."

The Dolphins missed 20 tackles last Thursday.

This week, coach Mike McDaniel said players stopped their feet. But he did not believe they turned down tackles or loafed.

Is it possible the frigid conditions affected the Dolphins' technique and fundamentals?

"No," Weaver said. "It's one of those things where as a coach you're always trying to predict what's going to happen in the game. Our poor tackling in this showing was certainly one I didn't see coming. Was it the cold? Who knows. Was it playing on a Thursday? Who knows.

"It could be a variety of things. You've got to give credit to them, right? Just in terms of breaking tackles. Josh Jacobs is not an easy guy to bring down. Do we need to be better with our technique and fundamentals in wrapping up, driving our feet, not diving off the diving board? Absolutely. But I certainly wouldn't attribute that to the cold. I coached in Houston or we've gone to Green Bay And we've won a number of places where it hasn't been a concern so I certainly wouldn't put that on the weather."

headline: Miami Dolphins may have short-yardage answer in new backup QB Tyler Huntley.
fullText:
MIAMI GARDENS — The Miami Dolphins moved Tyler Huntley into the backup quarterback position this week, ahead of Skylar Thompson.

What is it about Tyler "Snoop" Huntley that the Dolphins like as Tua Tagovailoa's backup?

"We just felt that Snoop right now with what he was able to bring and a certain area of also his mobility on playing outside of extending plays is also something that is always good," Dolphins offensive coordinator Frank Smith said Thursday. "Especially when your starter has a certain skill set in the pocket and your backup has a different skill set."

Huntley was 1-2 as a starter in Tua Tagovailoa's absence.

Huntley had 1 touchdown, 1 interception and 67 rushing yards.

"If we didn't have turnovers in the Indy game, we feel that the game could have gone into our favor because of the way we were running the football," Smith said of a Huntleys start." A couple of little miscues, but ultimately when Snoop was in there, we were operating efficiently. His ability to execute and distribute, we just feel like it was a good addition."

The Dolphins could use Huntley on 3rd-and-1 or 4th-and-1 situations, as they once did when Jacoby Brissett was Tua's backup quarterback.

Miami Dolphins schedule: Could Tyler Huntley solve short-yardage woes?

Miami has struggled in short yardage for years.

"I mean, it's not outside the realm of possibility," Smith said of Huntley in short yardage. "Ultimately we're just going to use the guys that are available and what is necessary to make sure that we are core principle, maximizing efficiency of our offensive production score points. points. So all options are always on the table."

Huntley said this week that there's not a "Snoop" package.

But, obviously he could be sent into the game in short yardage at any time.

The Dolphins will likely continue to limit quarterback sneaks with Tagovailoa, in part, due to his concussion history.

Miami Dolphins news: Tyler Huntley is Tua Tagovailoa backup

Huntley missed time with a sprained AC joint in his throwing shoulder. But he says he's fully healthy.

"We got a couple weeks under my belt," Huntley said of studying the offense even more while he was rehabilitating. "So I feel pretty good about it."

How does Snoop view his role now?

"Just being there for Tua, you know, just making sure he's got all the keys going into the game, and just being the biggest supporter to my team," Huntley said. "Just being there for every step, and just being ready to step in when it's called on."

headline: Dolphins' playoff odds are long now | Schad
fullText:
MIAMI GARDENS — The Dolphins have only an 11 percent chance to make the NFL Playoffs, according to projections by The Athletic.

So you're saying there's a chance.

Look, it's really unlikely.

At this point, going from 5-7 to 8-9 or 9-8 is most likely.

And, yes, that will be an overall disappointment.

And, yes, everyone will say they would have made it if not for injury to Tua Tagovailoa.

Here is the percentage chance The Athletic says Miami has in each remaining game:

vs. Jets: 70 percent

at Texans 36 percent

vs. 49ers: 51 percent

at Browns: 53 percent

at Jets: 55 percent

If Miami is able to win out, and finish 10-7, after a 2-5 start, we will say this was a successful season.

If Miami is then able to stay very competitive in a playoff loss at Buffalo, Kansas City or Pittsburgh, yes, it would be a successful season.

Anything short of all that, no, it won't be.

The Dolphins are the subject of national scorn and criticism right now.

They can't beat good teams. They can't win in the cold. They're soft.

They hear it.

headline: Delray-area man, 90, dies four days after head-on crash along Jog Road near Boynton Beach
fullText:
BOYNTON BEACH — A 90-year-old man has died from injuries he sustained over the weekend in a head-on crash in suburban Boynton Beach, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said.

Nathaneal Rossin of suburban Delray Beach died Thursday, Dec. 5, four days after medics took him to Delray Medical Center with serious injuries sustained in a Dec. 1 wreck at South Jog and Flavor Pict roads.

Investigators say Rossin's 2024 Honda Accord collided with another vehicle shortly after 10:30 a.m. that day. He was driving north on Jog approaching Flavor Pict when the driver of a southbound 2015 Toyota SUV attempted to make a left turn at the intersection and failed to yield the right of way.

West Palm fatal: Police ID man who died after box truck, SUV collide on South Dixie Highway

The driver of the Toyota, identified as a 75-year-old suburban Boynton Beach man, sustained minor injuries and also received care at Delray Medical Center.

Neither alcohol nor drugs were considered to be a factor in the crash, and both drivers were using seat belts, the sheriff's office said.

The crash report did not indicate whether any charges or citations are pending. It also did not say how fast the vehicles were traveling when the wreck happened.

headline: West Boca Raton football star Javian Mallory a 'game-time decision' for state semifinal
fullText:
West Boca High’s first-ever appearance in the FHSAA 6A semifinals Friday against Miami Southridge could come down to a battle between supreme defensive-tackle tandems.

It’s a matchup John Madden would cherish.

Top-seeded, unbeaten West Boca, during its magical 13-0 season, has boasted a brilliant defense led by the tackle duo of junior Xavier Reid and sophomore Jamar Thompson.

Southridge, full of football tradition, also boasts two ravenous DTs in Spencer Voss and Ryan Miret.

West Boca coach Dylan Potts, who has drastically turned around a second-rate football program in his three seasons, believes there is no better interior pairing in Florida.

The Bulls’ DT duo has spearheaded a defense that has allowed 14 or fewer points seven times and posted a 17-0 shoutout last Friday in the FHSAA 6A regional finals over Wiregrass Ranch.

High school football: West Boca claims Class 6A-Region 3 championship

“The defense as a whole starts with Xavier and Jamar Thompson," Potts said. “Those two are our heart and soul and gets everything going for our defense. That’s the best 'DTackle' tandem in the state and it’s not even close."

Southridge coach Pierre Senatus begs to differ.

“I think ours are better," Senatus said.

Friday’s semifinal winner on the Boca Raton field will face either Buchholz or Osceola in the state championship game on Dec. 13 at Florida International.

Unlike West Boca, which had won just two playoff games total before this season’s gallant march into December, Southridge is rich in football history.

The Miami Heights school won three state titles (1991 1993, 2016) and has sent nearly two dozen players to the NFL. The latest Southridge alumni on NFL rosters are Justin McCray, DiCaprio Bootle, Tyrique Stevenson and the Davis brothers of Iowa State were Heisman Trophy finalists.

But that was then and this is now.

“They’re an outstanding team," Senatus said of West Boca. “They’ve put a collection of talent together."

“I think it’s going to be decided in the trenches," Senatus added. “The battle between the lines. Who can dominate the line of scrimmage. They want ball control and smashmouth and win down the middle. But we believe we have a strong center (defense) too that will be difficult to displace."

All this semifinal needs to make it full-blown old-school is a snowstorm, and that’s not happening in Boca.

“We need to play our style of football," Potts said. “We play defense like we’ve done the past couple of years, it’s the heartbeat of our team. If we play defense like that and our offense gets the running game going, we feel comfortable we can play with anyone in the state."

Grant Edmond and Xavier’s younger brother, linebacker Maxwell Reid, are also West Boca defensive standouts. Xavier (seven sacks) is mulling nine college offers, including two from the Ivy League, and Thompson, considered a Power Five prospect, has received five.

“What separates (our defense) from a lot of teams is they have such a mentality to attack the ball," Potts said. “They’re always lined up right, communicating. We play fast without thinking what they need to do. They’ve been trained to see these looks 100 million times."

The defense is so staunch it sometimes overshadows a potent offense led by sophomore running back Jayden Lockhart, who has picked up the load because of the unspecified absence of junior star Javian Mallory, who had previously dealt with hamstring issues.

West Boca has rolled this postseason despite the absence of Mallory. Potts said he’s a “game-time decision." When asked why he’s been out, Potts called it “a coach’s decision."

A slash runner, Lockhart piled up 113 yards in the regional final victory last week. He has seven touchdowns on the season. If Mallory plays, it only gets tougher for Miami Southridge as Mallory averaged 96 yards in the regular season.

“He does a great job of one cut and getting downhill," Potts said of Lockhart. “Over the last two years, he understands the scheme. That’s what separates him. His vision has allowed him to have more success along with his work ethic and being a 4.0 student."

West Boca still is going with a rotation at quarterback of junior Mason Mallory and sophomore Trey Moran because it works. Mason has thrown for over 1,500 yards with 18 total touchdowns (rushing, passing).

Meanwhile, Moran has passed more than 1,000 yards, 250 rushing yards and 21 total touchdowns with just three interceptions.

 Call them “The M & M Boys." “They’re having big-time seasons," Potts said.

The receiving corps of Mark Hanniford (nine TD catches) and Bill Clancy (seven TDs) has been stellar.

“They’re sound on the offensive line, their running backs are special," Senatus said. “They have a lot on offense from receivers to the backfield."

Fourth-seeded Miami Southridge has offensive weapons aplenty also, led by sophomore quarterback James Perone and receiver Darius Clements as well as a highly ranked rushing attack. 

“We know it’s a tall task in front of us," Potts said. “Miami Southridge has a history of great football. It’s going to be tough Friday but we’re good, too."

Last season, West Boca upset Atlantic in the first round for its first playoff win since 2006. Now the Bulls are two wins from a first-ever state title with a squad mostly composed of juniors and sophomores.

“We expected to be here," Potts said. “This isn’t a surprise to us or our kids. We had the intention before the year if we did what we’re supposed to do, we’d be in this position. We’re here."

headline: Miami Dolphins soft? 'If the shoe fits,' assistant head coach Jon Embree says
fullText:
MIAMI GARDENS — Jon Embree, the Miami Dolphins’ assistant head coach and tight ends coach, never has been one to sugarcoat, as he proved again Thursday.

Embree was asked the appropriate ways to measure whether a team is soft – a question based, of course, on recent comments by players, analysts and reporters that the 5-7 Dolphins are just that. The question was framed on whether domination in the trenches, offensively and defensively, is a fair way of objectively determining softness.

“I know offensively, we need to be better in short-yardage situations,” he said. “So if that’s the definition, then right now, if the shoe fits, we have to wear it until we prove otherwise.

headline: New-to-Austin liver tumor treatment liquifies cancer before doctor's eyes
fullText:
Cheri Roper felt the lump in her breast. She had waited to get her annual mammogram because as a woman with dense breasts, her mammogram would get flagged and she would need to get an ultrasound to be cleared of cancer.

"It was constant panic," she said, but the testing never found anything. So, she just skipped the mammogram. "My answer wasn't the best," she said.

The 76-year-old retired math teacher from Georgetown, though, had it confirmed in April. She had a fast-growing breast cancer that had spread to her liver and lymphnodes.

Chemotherapy successfully got rid of the cancer in her lymph nodes and her breast, but that pesky liver cancer was not going away. It had shrunk, but it would need more than chemotherapy and the immunotherapy medications Roper will continue to take.

Roper's prayer partner saw a story on cable news about a new technique for getting rid of the liver tumor: histotripsy.

The technique uses robot-guided, targeted ultrasound waves to destroy the tumor. The body then reabsorbs the dead tumor cells. It doesn't require any surgical cuts, but the person has to be anesthetized to allow for controlled shallowed breathing because the liver is close to the diaphragm and moves with every breath.

It was a technique that Dr. Shaun McKenzie of Texas Oncology Surgical Specialists and St. David’s Medical Center had been interested in and was working on getting the specialized machine in Austin.

Roper did some internet research into histotripsy and learned that it was FDA-approved for liver tumors. She asked her oncologist to get her a referral to a doctor who was doing histotripsies, and figured she'd probably be sent to Houston's MD Anderson, where she had received a second opinion previously, or Dallas or San Antonio.

She was surprised when McKenzie's office in Round Rock called. McKenzie had been looking for the right patient to be the first patient to have a histotripsy done at St. David's Medical Center. He looked at Roper's imaging of her liver tumor and saw that she would be a good candidate to use histotripsy instead of surgically removing the tumor.

Learn more: 'Dramatic responses': St. David's bringing liver cancer innovations to Austin

Roper met with McKenzie and agreed to have the histotripsy done by McKenzie. On Oct. 4, she was taken into the operating room. For 20 minutes, McKenzie positioned the device over the tumor in the liver and watched it deaden before his eyes with the intense ultrasound waves. The tumor turned into liquid inside an outer shell.

Over time the body will absorb the dead cancer cells and leave a hole in the liver. The liver will then lay down healthy tissue in its place. Because the tumor cells are dead, they do not spread cancer. There is a theory that by absorbing the dead tumor cells, the body might actually have an immune response to the tumor, helping the body better respond to the cancer in the future, McKenzie said, but that hasn't been proven officially, he said.

Roper thinks that's the coolest part of having this procedure: not only is her tumor gone, but it might help her body fight the cancer in the future.

"I just believe I'm going to be completely well," Roper said.

Histotripsy is an outpatient procedure.

A traditional surgery would have removed part of the liver, which would grow back, but it would be a much harder recovery. It also would require a hospital stay.

Roper only had some fatigue and some nausea caused by pancreatitis because her tumor was so close to her pancreas and the histotripsy irritated that organ.

Other patients who have since had the procedure done by McKenzie have not had their tumor so close to the pancreas and have not had the nausea, just the fatigue, McKenzie said.

Histotripsy is only FDA-approved for tumors of the liver. It has an 85% to 95% success rate in clinical trials, according to Johns Hopkins University. It is being studied in the kidney and the prostate, which are solid tissue organs like the liver.

Roper is now done with chemotherapy and just will continue to take two immunotherapy injections throughout her life to stave off a recurrence.

A scan now shows that she has no evidence of cancer. "It's very exciting to me that they can do this," Roper said of the histotripsy.

headline: Flu is back in Austin. Here's what you need to do now to avoid getting sick
fullText:
"We have been seeing an uptick in respiratory viruses, including the flu," said Elora Jiskra, a nurse practitioner with the American Family Care Urgent Care clinic on William Cannon Drive in South Austin.

Locally and nationally, the flu trackers at Austin Public Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also reflect that increase. The number of flu cases in Austin remains moderate but has been steadily climbing since the third week of November. Nationally, the flu burden is still considered low but is increasing with each week.

Why is flu back?

It's the season for flu. Families have been traveling since Thanksgiving week, adding new germs to the local mix. People are also more likely to be inside for more hours in the day as temperatures drop and rain or snow (in northern areas) begins to fall.

What type of flu is being seen?

Jiskra mostly has seen influenza B in her urgent care, with a few cases of influenza A. Typically flu A is more common and hits earlier in the year, and flu B hits after the holidays. Flu A mutates more rapidly than flu B. Flu A also causes more hospitalizations and death, but flu B is more severe in children.

What are the symptoms of flu?

Either version of flu typically has these symptoms:

  • Sore throat
  • Runny or stuffy nose
  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Chest congestion
  • Headache
  • Muscle aches
  • Feeling very tired
  • Sweating and chills
  • Nausea
  • Diarrhea
  • Stomach pain

The stomach issues are more common in children than adults.

This year, Jiskra is seeing a lot of people test positive for the flu without having a fever. If they have any of the symptoms, she'll do a flu, COVID-19 and/or strep test. In children, she'll also test for RSV.

Read more: What kind of cedar fever season will Austin have this year? Plan now before it starts.

What can you do to prevent the flu?

Now is the perfect time to get a flu shot. Shots are available for anyone 6 months or older. Children younger than 8 who have never had a flu shot will need two shots a month apart.

Most insurance covers flu shots at no cost to the patient.

You can get a flu shot at any pharmacy, through your doctor or through one of the mobile vaccination clinics from Austin Public Health. American Family Care Urgent Care clinics also have the vaccines.

In addition to vaccines, you can do the typical things you need to do to stay healthy, including washing your hands often, wearing a mask in crowded spaces or around sick people, getting plenty of rest and eating healthy food.

Which flu shot is right for you?: When should you get new COVID, flu shot in Austin? Here's what to know and where to go.

If I get a flu shot, can I still get the flu?

Yes. You can't get the flu from the flu shot because the vaccine is not a live virus. You can, though, still get the flu from what's circulating around and from those with whom you come in contact. Your symptoms typically are lessened by having the flu shot, and the duration also can be shortened.

People who have conditions such as asthma, an autoimmune disease or anything that would make them more likely to have a bad outcome if exposed to the flu should not put off their vaccination.

Flu shots help keep people out of the hospital and prevent death.

Learn more: How having the flu could damage your heart, increase risk for attack or disease

Why do I need a flu shot every year?

Flu shots reach their maximum efficacy two weeks after they are injected and between six and nine months after the injection. Then the protection starts to wane.

The flu also mutates each year. The annual flu shot is based on predictions of which strain of flu will emerge and what strain was present in the Southern Hemisphere earlier in the year.

What happens if I get the flu?

Get tested right away. Your doctor can prescribe antiviral medications such as Tamiflu, which work best within the first 48 hours, to lessen the effects of the flu and keep you out of the hospital.

Stay home. To prevent the spread of the flu, stay home until you are fever free for 24 hours and your symptoms have eased.

headline: Deaths in first years of Texas' abortion bans should be studied, not skipped | Opinion
fullText:
Before their names became etched on tombstones, Porsha Ngumezi and Nevaeh Crain were excited mothers-to-be. Ngumezi, a charter school finance manager in the Houston area, hoped to give her two sons a baby sister. Crain, a recent high school graduate who lived in East Texas, was expecting her first child.

But these women had the deadly misfortune of suffering miscarriages in 2023, after Texas’ strict abortion bans went into effect and doctors and hospitals became hesitant to provide standard miscarriage care.

Ngumezi’s heart stopped in June 2023 after hours of heavy bleeding that wasn’t properly treated. Crain, ravaged by infection, died of organ failure that October, despite pleading for help in three trips to hospital emergency rooms over a 20-hour period.

Recent reporting by ProPublica brought their stories to light. Yet their cases — and who knows how many others from 2022 and 2023 — will never appear in the official review by Texas’ Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Review Committee, the state panel tasked with studying serious complications and pregnancy-related deaths in order to inform lawmakers.

The stated reasons are frustratingly bureaucratic. Buried in a yearslong backlog, the committee decided to drop all 2022 and 2023 cases. Its next report, slated to be published by September 2026, will contain the 2021 cases already under review, then jump ahead to 2024 cases.

“We just need to move forward, to have the most recent, the most actionable information that the review committee can make,” Chris Van Deusen, a spokesman for the Texas Department of State Health Services, told me after The Washington Post first reported the committee's decision last week.

He noted the report published by the committee this year covered cases from 2019 and 2020, providing data that now feels out-of-date. “We can't be as far behind as we have been,” Van Deusen said.

The backlog is real, but this solution is deeply troubling. Skipping over 2022 and 2023 erases an essential study of the earliest years under Texas’ abortion bans.

At best, it deprives lawmakers of a key review to help them improve their policies. At worst, it quietly absolves those who championed Texas’ abortion bans by keeping two years’ worth of the collateral damage out of view.

Van Deusen said skipping over 2022 and 2023 “had nothing to do with the abortion issue, or trying to hide that or suppress that in any way.”

But you can see why others are skeptical.

“We just have to read all the stories out there about women who have not received all the necessary treatment for complications in pregnancy,” state Rep. Donna Howard, D-Austin, who chairs the Texas Women’s Health Caucus in the Texas House, told me this week. “It’s clear there is politically damaging information that would be discovered if those cases were analyzed.”

Even if you take the committee at its word, this is the wrong approach. If Texas has so many dangerous and deadly pregnancies that researchers are struggling to keep up, we should be studying more of this problem, not less of it.

Instead, as my colleague Bayliss Wagner reported earlier this year, Texas law prohibits the Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Review Committee from examining any deaths involving a person who recently had an abortion.

And now, in skipping all other cases from 2022 and 2023, the committee is looking away from Ngumezi, Crain and who knows how many others like them — women who were carrying much-wanted pregnancies, only to suffer complications or die because they couldn’t get the miscarriage care they needed.

Plus, going forward, the committee will no longer review all cases of maternal complications and deaths, but a representative sample. Other states use this approach, handling annual reviews swiftly so the committee doesn’t get backlogged again.

Had the new sampling methodology been in place for the last report, epidemiologist Savannah Larimore told the committee in September, it would have taken only nine months (instead of 27) to review 2019 cases, and only 12 months (instead of 32) to review 2020 cases.

But we sacrifice the full picture — a study of all cases — in the process.

Each legislative session brings new laws that reach further into the lives of pregnant Texans, sometimes fatefully so. Yet instead of finding ways to examine the full impact — by bringing more researchers on board, for instance — Texas is paring back its reviews.

A deadly problem grows, and our official documentation of it shrinks.

Grumet is the Statesman’s Metro columnist. Her column, ATX in Context, contains her opinions. Share yours via email at bgrumet@statesman.com, or via X or Bluesky at @bgrumet. Find her previous work at statesman.com/opinion/columns.

headline: Proposed Texas bill would ban sale of all THC products, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick says
fullText:
If passed, a Texas bill could ban the sale of all THC products in the state, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick announced Wednesday.

Patrick is launching an effort to pass Senate Bill 3, which would ban all forms of consumable tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) from being sold, according to a news release from his office. As president of the Senate, Patrick has strong influence over which legislation is heard. The bill's low number suggests it will be among the first to be debated in the next legislative session.

The commercialization of hemp products with trace amount of non-intoxicating Delta 9 THC was legalized by House Bill 1325, with the intention of strengthening Texas agriculture. The law allows the production, manufacture, retail sale, and inspection of industrial hemp crops and products in Texas, granted that they stay at 0.3% or less delta-9 THC level. This also includes products for consumable hemp products that contain cannabidiol (CBD), as well as other edible parts of the hemp plant.

People are also reading: Marijuana laws in Texas are confusing. Here's a guide to know what is and isn't legal

Patrick now argues retailers used a loophole to sell dangerous products to adults and children alike.

"Dangerously, retailers exploited the agriculture law to sell life-threatening, unregulated forms of THC to the public and made them easily accessible. These stores not only sold to adults, but they targeted Texas children and exposed them to dangerous levels of THC," Patrick's statement says. "Since 2023, thousands of stores selling hazardous THC products have popped up in communities across the state, and many sell products, including beverages, that have three to four times the THC content which might be found in marijuana purchased from a drug dealer."

Senator Charles Perry, R-Lubbock, will sponsor the bill to "keep these unsafe products off our streets."

"We are not going to allow these retailers to circumvent the law and put Texans’ lives in danger," Patrick continues in his statement. "This bill will have broad bipartisan support in the Senate, and I trust the House will also see the danger of these products and pass this bill with overwhelming support so it can become law immediately."

The Texas Department of State Health Services lists the following examples of consumable hemp products (CHP):

  • Cannabidiol (CBD) oil
  • CBD gummy bears
  • Food and drinks infused with CBD
  • Over-the-counter drugs containing CBD
  • Topical lotions and cosmetics that contain CBD

What does Texas law say about cannabis?

The Lone Star State has not broadly legalized cannabis in any form. While recreational marijuana remains illegal, medical marijuana is permissible in certain circumstances.

In 2015, Texas passed the Compassionate-Use Act, which allowed the first legal use of low-THC cannabis products in the state for patients with intractable epilepsy. It was expanded in 2019 and 2021 to include other conditions.

Chapter 169 of the Texas Occupations Code states that patients suffering from the following are allowed to use low-THC cannabis products: 

  • epilepsy
  • seizure disorders
  • multiple sclerosis
  • spasticity
  • amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
  • autism
  • cancer
  • post-traumatic stress disorder
  • an incurable neurodegenerative disease

Marijuana remains illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act (CSA). It is listed as a Schedule I controlled substance, under strict regulations by the federal government, and has "no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse."

Read more: These 2 marijuana stocks could surge under Trump's second term

Texas AG sues cities over cannabis decriminalization

Patrick's announcement of Senate Bill 3 comes amid other disputes over Texas cannabis regulations. At the end of November, Dallas joined a list of cities being sued by Attorney General Ken Paxton over the decriminalization of cannabis.

The lawsuit, filed just weeks after 67% of Dallas voters approved Proposition R, also known as the "Dallas Freedom Act," challenges the city's move to amend its charter and prevent police from arresting or citing individuals for possessing up to 4 ounces of cannabis, except in cases involving felony investigations tied to violence or narcotics.

The measure would also prohibit officers from using the smell of cannabis as probable cause for searches or seizures and restrict city funds and resources from being used to test cannabis-related substances to determine whether they meet the legal definition of cannabis.

Paxton's lawsuit argues that the decriminalization is unconstitutional, as the state of Texas enforces harsher penalties for cannabis possession. THC is classified under Penalty Group 2 of the Texas Controlled Substances Act, and the possession and distribution of cannabis are criminal offenses under Sections 81.120 and 481.121.

"Cities cannot pick and choose which State laws they follow," Paxton said in a statement. "The City of Dallas has no authority to override Texas drug laws or prohibit the police from enforcing them."

Recreational cannabis use has been legalized in 24 U.S. states, and 38 states allow it for medical use.

— The Texas Tribune contributed to this report.

headline: College Corner: Your A student is not exceptional
fullText:
My first year in the classroom was 2001. During the first weeks of school, I assigned my "college prep" ninth grade English students to write an informal paper, asking them about themselves and their backgrounds. This was a "no right or wrong answers" task, and I eagerly awaited their responses.

A few days later, their handiwork was on my desk. I found nonsensical phrases, chicken scratchings, paragraphs that went on for rambling pages, and a few with no sentences or punctuation at all. Beside myself, I walked down the hallway to my department chair, and asked very simply, “How in the world am I supposed to grade these? Almost none of them resemble an essay!” She replied with a knowing smile, “They must like you. They wrote a lot."

These were not disadvantaged students in an underfunded district, but average suburban ninth graders.

The lesson I learned that school year was nearly impossible for me to swallow. I needed to begin as if they had never taken an English class before. Woe was me to think that they had prior knowledge of sentence structure, capitalization and punctuation. With a few exceptions, the question loomed in my mind: “How on Earth did some of these kids pass middle school English?” I was forced to lower my expectations, and my liberal arts soul died a little bit. Although I did not realize it at the time, this was an example of a budding trend in American education. Grade inflation is a serious issue that questions the validity and uniformity of what a high school diploma really means.

In 2022, 89% of students earned an A or B in English, social science, math and science across the board. This, juxtaposed with the decline in basic math, reading and critical thinking skills, should be enough to give college admissions officers and hiring managers pause. According to the National Assessment of Educational Progress Transcript Study in 2019, national grade point averages, high school credits earned, and advanced/AP/IB courses taken are all on the rise. Yet, standardized test scores in 12th grade math assessments have significantly decreased. Why? Grade inflation.

When students have opportunities to turn in late assignments or retake tests until a “B” is achieved, the rigor of what is expected in the classroom inevitably declines. More than ever, parents and students are boldly self-advocating, which can be a good thing in some instances. But when teachers feel browbeaten by administrators and parents to give students infinite chances and to assign students higher marks than they earn, it sends a clear message that students do not, indeed, need to try very hard. The organizational, time management, study/soft skills needed to succeed when high school is complete are woefully inadequate for some recentgraduates, and colleges/employers are paying the price.

For families who have highly selective colleges in mind for their children, there is one very important thing to keep in mind: Your A student is not exceptional or gifted. Simply earning a 4.0 GPA does not signal what it used to, and while this level of GPA is table stakes for highly selective colleges and universities, in today’s admissions landscape, it isn’t nearly enough.

Parents, just because your student has earned a 4.2 GPA in high school does not mean that they will be a competitive applicant for selective college admissions. Test scores are making a comeback, and they are more important than ever for majors such as business, engineering,nursing, computer science and STEM disciplines. Wisely chosen, directed extracurricular experiences that relate to a student’s major of choice are paramount, as are rigorous coursework and excellent essays. I implore you to look at your student realistically and adjust your strategy and expectations accordingly. No student wants to be made to feel like a failurebecause their parents expect Ivy League acceptances.

Other elements of the college application picture, such as test scores, class rank, essays and extracurricular activities are an integral part of showcasing who a student really is. Access College America can help with that.

headline: Iowa State basketball fends off Marquette in battle of top-5 teams
fullText:
AMES — Score one for the Big 12 and Cyclone Nation.

In a clash of top-5 heavyweights, No. 5 Iowa State basketball fended off a late push by No. 4 Marquette in the latest edition of the Big 12-Big East battle, 81-70, on Wednesday night at Hilton Coliseum.

Curtis Jones hit a fast-break layup to cap off a game-sealing 14-0 run to give the Cyclones a 75-61 lead, with 3:36 remaining.

Just before that, though, the Cyclones hit a second-half drought. They went more than six minutes without a made shot, which allowed Marquette to creep back into the game.

Until that point, they were leading by as much as 13 after Milan Momcilovic had a basket to make it 54-41, with 16:20 left in the game.

Marquette went on a 10-0 run to tie things up at 61 apiece until Keshon Gilbert finally broke the dry spell and scored four-straight points for the Cyclones to reclaim the lead. Jones followed up with a 3-pointer, before later finishing off the game.

Gilbert led the Cyclones with 24 points and seven assists. He had 18 of his game-high 24 points in the first half. He was hit by an elbow that led to a bloody nose, and he briefly exited the game, before returning to action in a No. 51 jersey to close the game.

Joshua Jefferson finished with a 15-point, 12-rebound double-double. Dishon Jackson added 11 points and seven rebounds.

The Cyclones buckled down defensively in the second half. Outside of Marquette's run to tie the game, the Golden Eagles shot just 12-of-36 (33.3%) and 4-of-15 (26.7%) from long range after halftime.

Iowa State led Marquette, 46-37, at the break.

The Cyclones went on an early 14-2 run that propelled them in front. Jones and Momcilovic made back-to-back deep shots to start the run, then Gilbert topped off the scoring spurt with a pair of free throws to make it 16-7, with 13:05 left in the first half.

Marquette entered as the sixth-best team in the country for defensive efficiency, according to KenPom. The Golden Eagles also boasted the third-highest turnover rate (25.3%) and the nation's best steal rate (17.1%). Iowa State stayed poised against Shaka Smart's trademark 'havoc' defense. The Cyclones only posted 12 turnovers on the night and enjoyed a strong shooting performance in the first half, knocking down 18-of-28 (64.3%) shots and 4-of-7 (57.1%) from 3-point range.

The Cyclones briefly pushed their lead into double figures in the opening 20 minutes, but Marquette hit a few baskets to keep the game within reach heading into the break.

Marquette had four players finish in double figures. Royce Parham had 17 points. Kam Jones, who entered Wednesday night averaging a team-best 19.6 points per game, finished with 14 points on 6-of-21 shooting, with eight rebounds and nine assists. Stevie Mitchell finished with 13 points, while Demarius Owens had 11 points.

The Golden Eagles shot 27-of-70 (38.6%) overall and 11-of-31 (35.5%) from the 3-point line.

Iowa State improves to 6-1 overall. The Cyclones will return to action on Sunday against Jackson State. Tip-off is scheduled for 5 p.m. CT at Hilton Coliseum.

headline: Off Hours: Create new holiday traditions in Des Moines with our entertainment editor
fullText:
Off Hours, your free weekly newsletter from the Des Moines Register, showcases all things fun you can do in central Iowa. Recently, we've written about karaoke bars, where to go thrifting, where to buy crafts, Black-owned businesses, vegan restaurants, gluten-free options, the Amana Colonies and where to buy plants.

Hi, Des Moines, it’s your favorite entertainment editor at the Des Moines Register back with another edition of Off Hours. When I was growing up in Eldridge, Iowa, we used to drive to my grandparents’ house in Lyons, Nebraska, every Christmas. That meant Santa came early to the Stapletons. Usually we’d go out for dinner that night, usually around Dec. 20 or 21, and come home to presents under the tree. When I was older, I always tried to figure out how my parents did it while letting my brother still believe in the magic of Santa Claus. How did your family celebrate the holidays?

The Deal

Here’s the deal: Aside from an early Christmas every year, we really didn’t have any traditions for the holidays when I was a kid. I never learned how to ice skate. We sometimes baked. We didn’t have a traditional meal we made every year. We did have a big family gathering at Bestamor’s house (she was my great great grandparents’ the first child born in the United States after the family moved to Cozad, Nebraska, from Denmark). She was a sweet woman and still spoke Danish.

My parents would play pinochle and 500 with my grandparents, and we were stuck watching one of three TV stations back then. We always drove home on Christmas Day and no restaurants were open for that five-hour trip back to Eldridge, just north of Davenport.

So I’ve tried to come up with some of my own traditions as an adult. For a while, my mom would do this fun stocking stuffer ball with gifts wrapped between layers of Saran Wrap. The first person starts unwrapping the ball until the next person rolls doubles with a pair of dice. Then you keep handing the ball off to the next person. You keep all of the things that come out while you’re unwrapping. The trick is to put plenty of candy or gum in so the kids want to trade for the hand lotion or face masks they will never use.

My mom and I started going to Christmas Eve service at Westminster Presbyterian Church in Beaverdale for the children’s service. The kids dress up as angels and shepherds and such while the minister delivers the service. It’s really cute. The highlight for me is singing “Silent Night” while holding candles as the lights are dimmed in the nave. We like the lanterns that light up the sidewalks in front of the church.

Afterward, we like to do some drives around Des Moines to see the holiday lights. I love how the neighbors along Ashby Avenue and Wallace Lane off Beaver Avenue go to the nines to decorate their homes.

We also love the Charles Gabus Memorial Tree Park in Urbandale, where the park is decorated with more than 80,000 holiday lights and includes a custom-built train, larger-than-life ornamental displays, a gingerbread house, an ice-skating rink, and holiday-themed events.

What are your favorite things to do for the holiday season in Des Moines? Shoot me an email at sstapleton@gannett.com with your favorite activities.

My Top Three Things I Want to Do for the Holidays in Des Moines

This year, I want to try some new things with my mom. Here are a few that caught my attention:

1. Holiday Promenade: Every Friday night, the shops and restaurants in the East Village stay open with their windows decorated. Each Friday includes different activities, and this one offers a chance to find Elf of a Shelf dolls hidden throughout the neighborhood. Find one and get a prize. I love dining in the East Village, too, so try Lucca, Bar Nico, Alba or Clyde’s Fine Diner, which has become one of my favorites in 2024.

2. “The Nutcracker”: In Las Vegas, I used to go to “The Nutcracker” performed by Nevada Ballet every season, so I want to reignite that tradition this year with the performance by the Ballet Des Moines at Hoyt Sherman Place. The enchanting production brings the story of Clara, her Nutcracker, and her dreamy journey, all on pointe. Tickets range from $35 to $114 for shows Dec. 12-15.

3. A night at Noce: I took my mom to "Voix de Ville" this fall and want to return for one of Max Wellman’s MANY holiday-inspired evenings with a backdrop of jazz and American standards. Count me in to hear Wellman perform “It's the Most Wonderful Time Of The Year,” “The Christmas Song,” and “Sleigh Ride” during the 15th Annual “Home for the Holidays.” Wellman performs again Sunday night and Dec. 16, with tickets starting at $25.

Eat This, Drink That

Homemade Pop Tarts, $3.99: These sweet treats look more like Toaster Strudel than Pop Tarts, but who cares what they’re called. When I dined here, the restaurant offered strawberry (good) and brown sugar (must-order). It was the perfect “appetizer” for a breakfast.

Get it: The new It’s My Jam Café in Ankeny, or just south of it, was jam packed on the Saturday morning I went. Find it at 7015 N.E. 14th St., Ankeny. Go between 6 a.m. and 2 p.m. daily.

Sugar Cookie Martini, $10: Vanilla vodka, Rumchata and amaretto come together with a frosting-coated martini glass rim with jimmies in green and red décor. It felt like drinking a sugar cookie.

Get it: I love it when a restaurant goes all out with holiday décor, and the new Merll’s Pub & Patio in Waukee went all out with Santa suits covering the bar stools, ornaments hanging from the ceiling, Christmas trees, and even wreaths on the kegs above the bar. Find it at 788 W. Hickman Road, Waukee.

48 Hours Off

Thursday night: Comedian and television host Chelsea Handler heads to Des Moines to bring her brand of comedy to the Des Moines Civic Center, 221 Walnut St., Des Moines. Her latest book, “I’ll Have What She’s Having,” comes out Feb. 25, 2025. See the 7 p.m. show for $49.50 to $99.50.

Friday afternoon: Experience a German-inspired Christmas market at Principal Park, 1 Line Drive, Des Moines. Christkindlmarket from the Iowa European Cultural Connection celebrates a 750-year-old European tradition of showcasing hand-crafted products as well as polka music, traditional dance and choirs. Participants will find children's activities, the warm mulled wine Glühwein, and European beer. Stop by on Friday and Saturday from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. or Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Friday night: Catch “Erma Bombeck: At Wit’s End” at the Temple Theater, 1011 Locust St., Des Moines. This quick-witted story captures the life of American columnist and humorist Erma Bombeck, who gave women nationwide a dose of humor as she dispensed with her warm-hearted comedy spanning being a daughter, mother, and wife. Former Des Moines Register writers Allison Engel and Margaret Engel wrote this bio about the syndicated columnist. Tickets start at $20 for the 7 p.m. show. Various times through Dec. 21.

Friday night: “All That Jazz” and more take over the Des Moines Civic Center, 221 Walnut St., Des Moines, with the final Des Moines performance of “Chicago.” The tale of fame and fortune during Chicago’s Jazz Age follows two of the Cook County Jail’s most notorious murderesses — the vaudeville star Velma Kelly and chorus girl Roxie Hart — as they compete for fame. Tickets start at $40 for this show at 7:30 p.m. Also Saturday and Sunday.

Saturday afternoon: Get in the holiday spirit when the Des Moines Gay Men’s Chorus performs “Thankful,” a show that includes “songs of Santa, snow globes, and ugly sweaters, and deeper reflections on gratitude, love, and community.” The 2 p.m. show at Hoyt Sherman Place, 1501 Woodland Ave., Des Moines, goes for $35, with a second performance at 7 p.m.

My Day Job

Thanks for reading! I’ve been working on some People to Watch features for the end of the year. I recently wrote about the hottest new restaurants in the metro (I’d love to hear some of your new favorites) and five great things I ate at Prime & Providence in West Des Moines. What are some of your favorite dishes in Des Moines?

Want to follow me? You can find me on Facebook, Twitter, or Instagram, or drop me a line at sstapleton@gannett.com.Did someone forward you this? Subscribe to have the Off Hours newsletter delivered to your inbox each Thursday morning for free. 

Interested in writing an Off Hours about the things you love to do during your time off? Drop us a line at sstapleton@gannett.com.

And don't forget to follow Off Hours on Instagram!

headline: Iowa State football recruiting grades: How Cyclones' 2025 signing day class stacks up
fullText:
Early signing day for Iowa State football is in the books and the 2025 recruiting class looks to have come together in a similar style to what coach Matt Campbell has done in Ames throughout his tenure.

“We’re really excited about the class coming in,” Campbell said in a press release. “The staples, and what we’ve always believed in, we didn’t waiver from those. This class has guys that are winners, that come from great high school football programs and our coaches did a great job recruiting within a six hour radius of our doorstep. We wanted to continue to find guys that fit what Iowa State is about and I think we did that.”

Here's a brief rundown of how the class shapes up and grades for each position.

More: Iowa State signing day live updates: Latest signing news, recruiting rankings

Iowa State football recruiting grades by position

Quarterback - A

Before suffering an injury late in the high school season, Algona star QB Alex Manske was torching the state with 18 touchdowns, zero interceptions and a 68.5% completion percentage to go along with eight rushing touchdowns. There are likely still a couple more years with Rocco Becht at the helm of the offense, but a depth chart with Connor Moberly, JJ Kohl and Manske on it should make Cyclone fans excited for the future.

Running back - B

Running back isn't a major position of need given the depth the Cyclones have, but Ryver Peppers (three-star by 247Sports) adds more depth. He rushed for 4,268 yards in his high school career and averaged more than seven yards a carry.

Wide receiver - B

The Cyclones added three wide receivers to the roster: Zay Robinson, Karon Brookins and Dyllan Malone. All three are three-star prospects. Brookins (6-foot-4) and Malone (6-foot-3) bring elite size to the position group. Robinson, a multi-sport star at Valley, is an incredible athlete who had a knack for making the big play for the Tigers.

More: Iowa State vs Arizona State prediction, picks, betting odds: Who wins Big 12 championship?

Tight end - NA

Offensive line - B

Size is the one word you can use to describe the four guys Iowa State signed Wednesday. Will Tompkins (6-foot-5, 270 pounds), Kuol Kuol (6-foot-6, 260 pounds) and Sione Perkins (6-foot-9, 260) bring huge frames at offensive tackle. Once they hit the weight room, they should be next in line to develop into solid players for ISU.

Vaea Ikakoula (three-star from Utah) at 6-foot-3, 315, brings college-ready size in the interior of the offensive line as well.

Defensive line - C

Iowa State has struggled to rush the passer in the past two seasons and added a trio of three-star edge rushers in Will Limbaugh (Algona, Iowa), Trey Verdon (Hamilton, Ohio) and Charlie Woleben (De Soto Kansas). Alongside them, defensive tackle Ka'Mori Moore (Lee Summit, Missouri) rounds out a solid haul of prospects for the Cyclones to develop, but there is not a standout prospect here that looks like an immediate fix to ISU's pass-pressure issues.

Another player, BJ Carter (Middleburg, Florida, three-star recruit), has publicly committed to Iowa State but was not announced by the Cyclones on Wednesday.

Linebacker - A

Anyone who watched Iowa high school football knows how good Will Hawthorne is. A four-star recruit by 247Sports, he rushed for more than 2,000 yards and was the leader on defense for a Gilbert team that fell just short of the UNI-Dome.

More: Can the Iowa State football defense slow down Arizona State star running back Cam Skattebo?

Defensive backs - B

The Cyclones added four guys, three of whom are safeties — Sprit Lake's Ethan Stecker, Joshua Patterson (Jacksonville, Florida) and Mason Ellens (Glen Ellyn, Illinois). LeMarcus Hicks II (Des Plaines, Illinois) rounds out the secondary additions at cornerback, giving the Cyclones a quartet of three-star commits for the unit.

Iowa State will lose a few key players from a strong secondary to graduation shortly, so added depth is a plus for the class.

Iowa State football recruiting class grade

This is a fairly standard recruiting class for the Cyclones, with overall rankings and types of prospects similar to that of other classes Campbell put together at Iowa State. Nothing that blows fans away, but it's the type of class that helped the Cyclones build a winning program and reach the Big 12 title game this year.

If Manske lives up to his billing, along with finding a few other diamonds in the rough, that could go a long way in making this class shine.

headline: Will Iowa State football be in CFP? The case against Cyclones making playoff bracket
fullText:
It's postseason time for college football, and Iowa State football controls its own destiny.

With a Big 12 Conference championship game against Arizona State and potential College Football Playoff berth, the Cyclones have a chance at the best overall season in program history. But there's also a chance that coach Matt Campbell's group finishes in disappointment and without a chance at a national title, especially after a 7-0 start to the season.

The final CFP rankings/bracket will be released Sunday. Here's where ISU stands in the CFP bracket race after Tuesday's rankings release and how the Cyclones might miss the 12-team cutoff:

Iowa State CFP predictions

More: Iowa State football: Where the Cyclones stand in latest College Football Playoff rankings

Why Iowa State won't make College Football Playoff

Simply put, Iowa State is highly unlikely to make the CFP if it doesn't win the Big 12 championship.

Had the Cyclones remained undefeated entering the matchup against ASU, they would certainly be in consideration for one of the top-12 spots even without a conference title. But ISU's consecutive losses to Texas Tech and Kansas to begin November probably eliminated the team from a chance at an at-large bid.

The 45-36 defeat against the Jayhawks was particularly harmful to the Cyclones' resume. Not being a member of the Big Ten or SEC also hinders Iowa State's likelihood for an at-large bid.

The good news is that if ISU beats Arizona State on Saturday, the Cyclones are virtually guaranteed to be in the College Football Playoff.

headline: What's the best temperature to set your furnace this winter? Here's what Iowans said
fullText:
The age-old debate is settled (sort of).

This fall, we asked readers to vote in an informal survey asking the classic question: At what temperature should you set your heat?

About 56% of Iowans have a heater in their home, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, compared to the rest of the U.S. at only 34%.

So what is the temperature sweet spot to keep everyone in your family comfortable? Here's what Iowans said:

What temperature do most Iowans set the heat to?

Setting the furnace to 68 degrees in the winter was the most popular temperature, according to the poll, with about 26% selecting that option. In second place was 70 degrees with 16% of the votes. A cozy 72 degrees came in third place with 13% of the votes.

About half of readers set their furnaces to a temperature between 68 and 70 degrees.

Here's how Iowans voted in total:

  • 68 degrees: 26%
  • 70 degrees: 16%
  • 72 degrees: 13%
  • 69 degrees: 9%
  • 67 degrees: 7%
  • 66 degrees: 6%
  • 65 degrees: 4%
  • 71 degrees: 4%
  • 63 or colder: 3%
  • 74 degrees: 3%
  • 73 degrees: 3%
  • 64 degrees: 2%
  • 75 degrees: 1%
  • 76 degrees: 1%
  • 77 or warmer: 1%

(Note: Totals may not add up to 100% due to rounding)

In the summer, 74 degrees was the most popular temperature, according to an informal Register survey. About 18% of online respondents selected that temperature. About half of respondents selected a temperature between 72 and 75 degrees.

What do the professionals say about thermostat temperatures?

Lowering your thermostat 5 to 8 degrees during the winter can make a big difference on your bill, MidAmerican Energy said online, noting that 68 degrees in the winter should be your typical setting.

Similarly, the Iowa Utilities Commission estimates that you can save as much as 10% a year on heating and cooling by turning your thermostat back 7 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit for eight hours a day from its normal setting.

The federal Department of Energy recommends setting the temperature to what you find comfortable. It reminds people that the smaller the difference between indoor and outdoor temperatures, the lower the overall heating bill will be.

headline: Introducing the Des Moines Register's 2024 All-Iowa high school volleyball team

The 2024 Iowa high school volleyball season lived up to the hype.

Ankeny Christian (1A), Denver (2A), Mount Vernon (3A), Bishop Heelan (4A) and Pleasant Valley (5A) capped off their seasons with state championships.

It was a year filled with non-stop action. Standouts bolstered their resumes while emerging players solidified their place among the state's best.

The Des Moines Register is pleased to announce its 2024 All-Iowa high school volleyball team. The selections feature an Elite Team group as well as first teams for all five classes. The players chosen for the Elite Team automatically earn first-team honors in their respective classes.

All athletes are listed in alphabetical order by last name:

Elite Team

Carli Cline, Sr., West Burlington

Count on Cline to keep the ball in play. She had a stellar senior season, leading the state in digs (746) and averaging seven of them per set. Despite missing the state tournament, the defensive specialist helped West Burlington to 37 wins this season, marking their fourth-straight season with over 30 victories.

Maliyah Hacker, Sr., Bishop Heelan

As Bishop Heelan's top striker, Hacker led Class 4A with 426 kills on her resume. The outside hitter also finished in the top five in serve aces (60) and serve successes (432).

Hacker was named to 4A all-tournament team. She totaled 20 kills and 10 digs in Bishop Heelan's 4A state title victory over Pella.

Isabelle Kremer, Jr., Pleasant Valley

Kremer was instrumental in Pleasant Valley's Class 5A state title victory over Waukee Northwest. The 6-foot-2 outside hitter led the way with 24 kills and tacked on four digs against the Wolves.

Kremer finished her junior season with the second-best kill efficiency rate (.394) in 5A.

Meester was named captain in the 3A all-tournament team at the Iowa high school state volleyball tournament.

The Louisville commit led Mount Vernon with 16 kills during its state title victory over Western Christian. Meester finished her senior season with the third-most kills (575) in the state.

Naeve, a versatile outside hitter, led the state with 753 kills this season. She averaged 7.5 kills per set on a .320 kill efficiency rate.
