headline: Iowa State basketball: 3 takeaways from the Cyclones' win over No. 4 Marquette
fullText:
AMES − Iowa State men's basketball picked up a marquee win Wednesday night.

The No. 5 Cyclones fended off a late push by fourth-ranked Marquette to win, 81-70, during the Big 12-Big East Battle at Hilton Coliseum.

Marquette, who trailed for the majority of the game, had a game-tying 10-0 run midway through the second half. But the Cyclones responded with a 14-0 run to pull away and ice the game.

Keshon Gilbert had a game-high 24 points, with seven assists. Joshua Jefferson had a 15-point, 12-rebound double-double. Curtis Jones had 14 points and five boards, while Dishon Jackson chipped in 11 points and seven rebounds.

Here are three takeaways from Wednesday's win:

More: Iowa State vs Marquette recap of Cyclones' victory over Golden Eagles

Iowa State learns from its past mistakes, closes out against Marquette

Iowa State, once again, proved it belonged with the top teams in college basketball. But it didn't show up on Wednesday just for a moral victory.

The Cyclones let a game slip away against Auburn, squandering an 18-point lead, and losing to the Tigers on a last-second tip-in during the Maui Invitational.

"We just learned from our mistakes and maybe move on, build on the past," Jefferson said. "Don't continue to make the same mistakes. I think we just continue to do better every single day."

For a moment, it looked like there might be a case of deja vu, as Marquette stormed back into the game and tied things up, 61-61, with 9:07 remaining.

The Cyclones shook off a six-minute stretch where they didn't make any shots and responded with a crucial 14-0 run to reclaim the lead and seal the game. There was no letdown this time around.

"We were in a similar position in the Auburn game, when we were up, and then they came back and we reclaimed the lead -- which is hard to do -- and then we weren't able to finish," said coach T.J. Otzelberger. "Our guys, from that experience, know that good teams are going to keep coming.

"I felt like we had a more concerted effort defensively, guard the dribble, keep it out of the paint. ... Our guys, there's a mental focus that we're able to dial into at that point to put ourselves in a good position."

Keshon Gilbert continues his hot, tough play

Despite taking two hard blows to the face that drew blood over the last week, Gilbert remained a leading force for the Cyclones.

He took a hard hit to the face during the Maui Invitational, and an elbow to the face Wednesday night. This time, it required him to leave the game for a few minutes late in the second half.

Despite that, he returned and still produced down the stretch, providing a statistical and emotional boost.

"I hate for him to keep taking those type of shots," Otzelberger said. "... When he came back from that locker room and had his nose taped up and came in our huddle, all of our guys erupted. There was a smile on their faces.

"They were all cheering and clapping, just innately and that says so much about Keshon. It says how much they think about him, how much he means to our team, how important he is, and how much we all recognize how quickly something like that happens -- he bounces back and has such great focus on the task at hand."

More: Iowa State basketball fends off Marquette in battle of top-5 teams

Gilbert has recorded 20-point games in three of his last four outings. Since the start of the Maui Invitational, he's shot a combined 26-of-41 (63.4%) overall and 4-of-8 (50.0%) from long range. He is also 30-for-33 (90.9%) from the free-throw line and is averaging 4.5 assists per game in that four-game stretch.

"Just being aggressive, finding gaps," Gilbert said. "My teammates found me in transition, so we had it rolling."

Cyclones' defense by Heise, 'banged up' Lipsey key in win

Outside of Marquette's comeback run, the Golden Eagles had a hard time operating against the Cyclones' defense.

Iowa State limited Marquette to shooting 27-of-70 (38.6%) and 11-of-31 (35.5%) from 3-point range.

In the second half, the Cyclones held the Golden Eagles to 12-of-36 (33.3%) overall and 4-for-15 (26.7%) from deep.

Kam Jones and Stevie Mitchell entered Wednesday's contest as the Golden Eagles' leading scorers. They combined for an average of 35.5 points per game.

Jones had 14 points, eight rebounds and nine assists, but shot just 6-for-21 (28.6%). Joplin had just eight points on 3-of-13 shooting (23.1%).

"There was great focus most of the first half," Otzelberger said of his team's defensive execution. "There was a couple of shots they got late in the first half that we could have been more dialed in on. They had some stretches where they went on runs, and Kam Jones was great making plays and setting guys up.

"Ultimately, Nate Heise, the job he did defensively in the second half, specifically guarding Jones, he was phenomenal. He was physical. He was competitive. I thought Nate was a big-time difference maker for us defensively down the stretch."

Tamin Lipsey, despite being banged up and only scoring one point, was an impact player defensively.

"His defense, I'll put him against anybody in the country," Otzelberger said of Lipsey. "His competitive spirit, his focus, truly special that way. ... When he's out there he just has a command and a demeanor, a veteran experience how he carries himself. He's banged up right now. He's not anywhere near 100%, and he lays it on the line and does whatever we need to be effective.

"I thought he did great tonight. You can't look at the stats and say, 'Oh he had one point or four assists, didn't have to do with anything.' He is a very impactful player. the confidence he gives our other guys, the plays that he makes -- hopefully we can get him healthy so he can be the player that we all know he can be and perform at that level."

headline: Des Moines man in chase, standoff gets 40-year sentence for drug dealing
fullText:
A man who engaged Des Moines police in an hourslong June standoff has been sentenced to up to 40 years in prison on related gun and drug charges.

Cody Radke, 39, pleaded guilty to two separate charges of possession of methamphetamine with intent to deliver and another of felon in possession of a firearm. At Radke's Nov. 26 sentencing, Judge Scott Beattie ordered him to serve consecutive prison terms of 25, 10 and five years for a maximum total of 40.

According to the sentencing order, Radke must serve at least 5 1/2 years before he will be eligible to seek parole.

Radke's charges stem from an October 2023 search of his home in which officers found a pistol, large quantities of methamphetamine and other drugs and several thousand dollars in cash. Radke, who was ineligible to possess a gun due to a prior felony, agreed to cooperate with police in other investigations but failed to complete his side of the deal, leading to charges being filed in February, according to court filings.

More: Des Moines man sentenced to 15 years in prison for shooting at police officer during chase

On June 24, an Iowa State Patrol officer spotted Radke driving on the northeast side of Des Moines and attempted to stop him on multiple outstanding warrants. Radke fled from pursuit, at times travelling more than 70 mph into oncoming lanes of traffic on Hubbell Avenue, and eventually returned to his home and barricaded himself inside, police wrote in a report. He surrendered about three hours later and investigators found more methamphetamine, apparently packaged for distribution, in his vehicle.

Radke's attorney, Jesse Macro, declined to comment after the sentencing.

headline: Waukee has its own natural gas utility. Voters will be asked in March whether to sell it.
fullText:
Waukee voters will vote in a special election next year whether the city should continue to operate its natural gas utility system — a rare arrangement in the Des Moines metro and unusual in Iowa.

Waukee residents are concerned they pay too much for gas to heat their homes and power their appliances. And the city expects it will be a challenge to keep its gas rate competitive as natural gas prices in Asia, Europe and North America keep rising.

Waukee City Council members on Monday approved a special election on March 4, 2025. It will ask voters whether the city should sell its municipal gas utility, which serves more than 10,000 customer accounts and owns and operates more than 175 miles of gas mains.

Waukee is the only city in the metro that operates its own gas utility and one of only 51 in the state.

Waukee City Administrator Brad Deets said that Cedar Falls has the largest municipally owned and operated gas system in Iowa, followed by Waukee.

Deets said when Waukee established its system in 1966 the city was much smaller and was not connected to the rest of the Des Moines metro, so it made sense for the city to have its own gas system.

But it's become increasingly difficult for the city to remain competitive on gas rates — and many residents have complained about the costs.

"It's a common theme," Deets said of concerns the mayor and City Council members have raised, received or seen on social media in recent years.

Global trends, local growth are challenges to city's gas rate

The short of it is that Waukee is not a big enough player in the natural gas market to have sufficient leverage over the prices it pays for gas. And local demand is only expected to grow from a surging population.

The city buys its natural gas from Omaha-based Northern Natural Gas in advance, based on expected use estimates. If there's a cold snap that drives up demand, Waukee purchases "spot gas" to meet it, according to the city.

Spot prices fluctuate and "quickly respond to changes in weather or availability of supply," according to the American Gas Association.

Deets said spot gas is typically more expensive than contracted gas. And that was brought home by a cold snap from Feb. 13 to 17, 2021, that Deets said first raised concerns about the sustainability of the city's utility.

While frigid temperatures and ice caused widespread power outages in Texas, Waukee used its entire natural gas budget for a typical winter in that one week. Deets said the city had enough cash reserves to cover the costs, but those costs were passed on to Waukee utility customers and significantly drove up their monthly bills.

Other pressures on the spot price of natural gas also increase costs.

Russia's expanded invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 caused global gas prices to spike. As Russia also cut off gas supplies to the rest of Europe, the U.S. stepped in as an exporter and became the world's largest liquefied natural gas exporter in the first half of 2022, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

The spot price of natural gas has come down since its most recent peak in August 2022. But according to the latest energy outlook from the Energy Information Administration, continued growth in U.S. natural gas exports through 2050 is expected to increase the spot price — though not beyond the 2022 spike.

Waukee leaders also note that more unpredictability in weather patterns caused by climate change — fueled by greenhouse gas emissions, including from the burning of fossil fuels such as natural gas — has presented its own challenges.

More: What are those giant new poles in West Des Moines? And no, it's not another Topgolf.

Deets said the past couple of winters have been warmer than expected, which is a disadvantage for the city because it doesn't get all its money back when it sells back unused gas.

The city can pay to store some gas, but it has limited capacity, Deets said. "We're a small fish in a big pond" when it comes to gas providers, he said.

And this is all as Waukee continues to rapidly grow. Projections earlier this year from the Des Moines Metropolitan Planning Organization anticipate Waukee will grow 75% through 2050, to a population of almost 45,550 people.

The city made changes in 2022, including to its gas rate structure, but Waukee's month-to-month gas rates have remained higher than in neighboring cities.

A Waukee homeowner who did not wish to be identified provided the Register with a copy of their most recent municipal bill. The residential rate listed for service from Oct. 22 to Nov. 22 was described as "$11.25 plus $0.015375 per cubic foot plus local option sales tax." There was also a total listed for a "gas tax."

Deets said the city's cubic foot charge ranged over the past year from $0.002810 to $0.015996 — calculated each month based upon costs to the city.

That range also matches the cubic foot rates the Waukee homeowner shared with the Register after reviewing their monthly bills from the year to date.

It's not necessarily easy to immediately make a comparison to another city's rates by just looking at a gas supply competitor's bill.

A Register reporter's most recent bill from MidAmerican Energy Co. — for gas service from Oct. 8 to Nov. 6 to a rented apartment in West Des Moines — illustrates that MidAmerican calculates its rate differently.

MidAmerican took the cubic feet of gas used and multiplied by values for "Pressure" and "BTU Factor" to get a figure in "therms." That therm figure was then separately multiplied by charges for gas supply, delivery and energy efficiency, and those costs were then added up with a $10 basic service charge, a meter class charge, a "rate case cost recovery fee" and the local franchise fee charge.

Deets said Waukee's rates have been 20% to 50% higher than in neighboring communities, which, based on his own family's recent gas bill, means a difference of about $30 or $40 for a month.

Applied to the bill that the Waukee homeowner shared with the Register, 20% to 50% would mean a difference of about $14 to $35 for that month of service.

What would happen if voters choose to sell the gas system?

No third-party utilities have been interested in operating Waukee's gas utility if the city still owned it, according to the city.

If voters approve a sale, the city expects to be rid of its utility by the end of next year. The new owner would set gas rates, control operations and send instructions to account holders about setting up new accounts and making payments.

Deets said city staff who operate the gas system — five people in Public Works and another three who handle billing — would still work for the city, in large part because Waukee's growth would keep them needed in other roles.

The value of the city's municipal gas utility system is estimated at about $19.3 million.

Deets said the City Council and mayor have not made any decisions about what to do with the proceeds from a potential sale.

If voters do not approve the sale, it would be at least four years before it would appear on ballots again.

headline: Hines: Keshon Gilbert emerging as a star for Iowa State basketball
fullText:
AMES – It’s still the first week of December. The college basketball season is only seven games old for Iowa State. We’re more than three weeks away from the start of Big 12 play. 

A couple things, though, are coming into focus. 

The Cyclones are just as good – and maybe better - as their preseason top-10 ranking suggested, and Keshon Gilbert is an early All-American candidate. 

Those two things are likely not unrelated. 

“He’s the engine that’s driving us right now,” Iowa State coach T.J. Otzelberger said. 

Gilbert’s excellence and Iowa State’s elite status were both readily apparent Wednesday as the guard scored 24 points in the No. 5 Cyclones’ 81-70 victory over No. 4 Marquette at Hilton Coliseum. 

More: Iowa State basketball fends off Marquette in battle of top-5 teams

“Gilbert was phenomenal all game long,” Golden Eagles coach Shaka Smart said. 

The UNLV transfer was good last season for Iowa State, but he was a piece of the puzzle for a team that relied on the sum of the parts being greater than the whole. He was a guy, along with a bunch of other guys, who made the Cyclones the Sweet 16 team they became. 

This year, though, Gilbert looks like The Guy. 

He’s averaging 16.5 points, 5.3 assists, 2.5 rebounds and 1.7 steals while shooting 54.4% from the floor. The eye test, too, backs up the stats. The 6-foot-4 St. Louis native is more aggressive, more efficient and playmaking more. 

He’s playing at nothing short of an All-American level this season. 

“I can’t say enough about how every day at practice and every night (in games) he’s showing up for us in a major way,” Otzelberger said. “It’s great to see.” 

Gilbert was at his best in the first half against the previously unbeaten Golden Eagles when he scored 18 points on 5 of 8 shooting from the floor while going 6 of 6 from the line.  

“Just being aggressive, finding gaps, getting fouled,” Gilbert said of his first-half success. “My teammates was finding me in transition, so we had it all rolling.” 

More: Hines: Iowa State basketball returning home from a successful week at Maui Invitational

The scoring is what stood out throughout much of the game against Marquette, but Gilbert’s ability to create for others this season has been spectacular as well. He finished with seven assists against Marquette, and his assist rate this season is up from 25% last year to 33% now. 

He’s not a totally different player than he was last season, but he’s a turbocharged version of it.  

“A lot of times last year I maybe made a bad play and I’d be stuck on the play,” Gilbert said. “I understand mistakes happen. It is what it is. Life goes on so you’ve got to move on and get to the next play.” 

And if that's not enough to endear Gilbert to the Iowa State faithful, coming back into the game after his face was gushing blood following an elbow to the nose certainly will. That's the stuff of legend, really.

"How can you not love pulling for that guy?" Otzelberger asked. "The energy, leaving it on the court. What he does every single game is phenomenal."

Even as The Guy, though, Gilbert isn’t alone, and that’s what makes this Iowa State team a national title contender. 

After shredding Marquette in the first half, Gilbert was bottled up more in the second half by the Golden Eagles. 

Without his scoring, Iowa State got big contributions offensively from Joshua Jefferson and Curtis Jones. Nate Heise was big on the defensive end. Brandton Chatfield contributed on the glass. Tamin Lipsey locked up Marquette star Kam Jones. 

There’s still a long way to go and sustaining success can sometimes be harder than finding it in the first place, but, so far, Iowa State is delivering on the hype and expectation of the offseason. 

Gilbert, though, is absolutely exceeding it.

headline: Two Iowa cities ranked in the top 100 in the US for singles. See which cities.
fullText:
Getting dumped is not fun, but if you live in one of these two Iowa cities, chances are good that there are single residents out there looking for love.

WalletHub compared and scored nearly 200 cities across the United States to find the best city for singles. While no Iowa city cracked the top 25, Des Moines and Cedar Rapids both made it in the top 100.

How did WalletHub determine the best cities for singles?

WalletHub compared 182 cities — including the 150 most populated U.S. cities and at least two of the most populated cities in each state — across three categories:

  1. Economics
  2. Fun and recreation
  3. Dating opportunities.

The cities were ranked using metrics such as average meal costs, nightlife options per capita, and total single population. Each metric was graded on a 100-point scale, with a score of 100 indicating the best.

More: The hottest new restaurants from Arcadia to What Dak in Des Moines, November 2024

How did Iowa cities rank among the best U.S. cities for singles?

Des Moines ranked 58th out of 182 with a score of 52.5, and Cedar Rapids came in at 71st with a score of 51.7.

Both cities scored high in economic possibilities, with Des Moines ranking 12th and Cedar Rapids 34th out of 182 cities, performing higher in this category than communities like Tallahassee, Florida and Virginia Beach, Virginia.

More: Iowa has the lowest housing costs. That earned it a top 20 spot for best states to live.

What are the top 5 best cities for singles?

Here are the top five cities for singles in the U.S., according to WalletHub:

  1. Atlanta
  2. Las Vegas
  3. Seattle
  4. Pittsburgh
  5. Tampa

"Atlanta has an extremely high number of attractions, restaurants, and nightlife activities, giving people a wide variety of venues for dates," WalletHub wrote. "Living in Atlanta gives you a deeper dating pool to swim in compared to other cities — Over 69% of the city’s population is single, the eighth-highest percentage in the country."

headline: Advocacy groups oppose Iowa-backed lawsuit over federal nursing home staffing levels
fullText:
A group of nonprofit advocacy organizations is seeking to intervene in a lawsuit that challenges new, federally mandated staffing levels in nursing homes.

The National Association of Local Long-Term Care Ombudsmen is among seven organizations hoping to ask a federal judge to deny a request made by the nursing home industry and 20 state attorneys general – including Iowa’s Brenna Bird — for an injunction that would block implementation of the new staffing requirements.

The organizations have not yet been authorized to file their “friend of the court” brief, but approval in such circumstances is normally granted.

The injunction is being sought in a lawsuit filed eight weeks ago in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa, and seeks to block implementation of the Biden administration’s new staffing requirements. The lawsuit was filed by Bird and the attorneys general of 19 other states along with 19 industry organizations who argue the new requirements are cost prohibitive and will result in nursing homes closing.

Joining NALTCO in the fight against the attorneys general are the nonprofit organizations known as the Center for Medicare Advocacy, the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care, the Long-Term Care Community Coalition, California Advocates for Nursing Home Reform, Justice in Aging, and the Michigan Elder Justice Initiative.

NALTCO’s role in the case is particularly noteworthy in that the organization comprises members of each state’s Long Term Care Ombudsman’s Office, which were created by Congress in 1978 to serve as independent advocates for nursing home residents.

Typically, each office, including that of Iowa’s Long-Term Care Ombudsman, operates within an arm of their respective state government. The result is that the ombudsmen’s national organization is now opposing the legal efforts of Republican attorneys general in states where many of those ombudsmen now work.

In October, Bird said she was leading the court challenge of the staffing mandates to ward off a “mass shutdown of nursing homes” and to “stop the Biden-Harris attack on senior care that will force nursing homes out of business.”

In November 2023, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds publicly announced her opposition to the new staffing rule, joining 14 other Republican governors in signing a letter to President Joe Biden in which they argued the rule was “unrealistic” and would “harm the seniors, elderly and disabled it’s designed to help.”

According to data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, 14% of Iowa’s 422 nursing facilities were cited for insufficient staffing in fiscal year 2023, before the new requirements were enacted. That’s more than double the national average, which was 5.9%.

Only five other states – Hawaii, Michigan, Montana, New Mexico and Oregon — had a worse record of compliance with the staffing requirements in place at that time.

Advocates for nursing home residents cite ‘excessive profits’

In their court brief, the advocacy groups argue that understaffing of nursing homes has been a decades-long problem leading to widespread injuries and death inside taxpayer-supported, profit-generating nursing homes that collect Medicare and Medicaid dollars to pay for resident care.

For decades, the government has required only that nursing homes provide “sufficient” staff to meet residents’ needs but has left it to owners to define “sufficient.” The new standards establish specific, minimum nurse-staffing requirements, such as the around-the-clock presence of at least one registered nurse.

Federal data indicates many nursing homes already meet some of the new standards, and, on average, those that operate as nonprofits exceed the newly mandated staffing ratios. The advocacy groups argue the new standards are voluntary in that they apply only to those nursing facilities that choose to accept Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement for resident care. They also argue that the research that led to the formulation of the new mandates suggests they could save 13,000 lives per year.

“The public interest favors prompt implementation of the staffing rule,” the groups state in their brief. “The public has a compelling interest in having vulnerable nursing home residents – their family members, friends, neighbors – receive appropriate care and in having their tax dollars spent on resident care, not on excessive private profit for owners and operators.”

Among the 46,520 comments received by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Advocacy in response to the proposed rule were comments submitted by front-line caregivers working in nursing homes – some of which are included in the advocacy groups’ brief to the court.

One registered dietitian reported that in the facility where she worked, staffing shortages were so severe the nurses would periodically declare a “med holiday” and throw away all the medications intended for residents on one shift because they didn’t have time to pass them out.

Other commenters referenced their colleagues being unable to provide toileting assistance, baths or food for residents. Others wrote of residents wearing the same clothes for a full week because there wasn’t enough staff on hand to help them change clothes.

Industry officials have argued that CMS lacks the authority to dictate staffing levels at privately owned nursing homes. The advocacy groups say otherwise and claim the congressionally approved Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 states the federal government has a “duty and responsibility” to ensure that standards of care are adequate to protect residents, and that the law expressly provides that nursing facilities must meet any requirements the federal government “may find necessary.”

The groups also cite a recent study that found that some nursing home owners are hiding their profits through a practice called “tunneling,” in which they pay other companies that they own inflated prices for resident care. One 2024 study found that care facilities in Illinois hid 63% of their profits by paying inflated prices to related entities. In New York, a study found that owners there spent more than $1 billion — 16% of their operating expenses — on payments to related parties.

The Iowa-led lawsuit is one of two currently working their way through the federal court system. The other lawsuit, filed in Texas, was initiated by the American Health Care Association, a lobbying organization that primarily represents for-profit nursing homes.

Some observers say the litigation will have little impact on the fate of the staffing mandates since the Trump administration is expected to do away with the requirements once the president-elect take office in January 2025.

headline: Union of Concerned Scientists pushes for Midwest wetland protections in Farm Bill
fullText:
A new report from the Union of Concerned Scientists found wetlands in the Upper Midwest region are “in peril” due to recent legal challenges and a lack of state-level regulation. The report looks to a new farm bill as a vessel to protect wetlands. 

The report, authored by Stacy Woods, the research director for the Food & Environment program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said industrial agriculture has inflicted “devastating damage” on wetlands across the country and that Iowa has more than 640,000 acres of wetland. 

These wetlands, along with those in states across the Upper Midwest region, act as “natural barriers” to flooding. The report found this flood protection equates to nearly $23 billion in annual residential flood protection. Iowa’s wetlands alone could mitigate $477 million worth of flood damage to residential areas. 

These estimates in the report are extrapolated from a 2022 study that found one acre of wetland was the equivalent to $745 in benefits from prevented flood damage. 

The report alleges the Supreme Court decision in Sackett v. the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency “stripped” Clean Water Act protections from wetlands that are not connected to federally recognized bodies of water. 

The new interpretation of the law, combined with the “absence of state-level wetland protections” in Iowa and other Upper Midwestern states makes wetlands “particularly vulnerable” to pollution or drainage, the report found.

Chapter 456B of Iowa Code says a protected wetland cannot be drained without a permit from the Department of Natural Resources and the wetland must no longer meet the criteria of a protected wetland, or be replaced by a “wetland of equal or greater value.”

According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, in 2020, the Conservation Reserve Program had restored more than 3 million wetland acres across the country since the program started in 1985. The same program has restored over 118,000 acres of wetland in Iowa and enrolled 66,000 acres as “buffer” in farmable wetlands, according to data collected by Environmental Working Group.

A hope for Farm Bill protections

The report looks at the Farm Bill as a place to implement wetland regulations to stop “large-scale commodity growers and corporate agribusiness interests” that “exploit wetlands for agricultural expansion.” 

Farm bills in the past have established protections for wetlands, including the Conservation Reserve Program and the “swampbuster” provision that linked a landowner’s eligibility for USDA incentive programs to their preservation of wetlands. 

An Iowa landowner recently sued the USDA over the provision and several groups including Iowa Environmental Council, Iowa Farmers Union, Dakota Rural Action and Food & Water Watch, sought to intervene in the lawsuit, which a federal judge of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa approved Tuesday. 

The lawsuit alleges swampbusters created an unconstitutional condition for a farmer to receive USDA benefits, while the now-approved intervenors say without the law, there would be little to no protections for wetlands from farmers seeking to expand their croplands. 

In addition to swampbuster, the report details other Farm Bill provisions that have protected wetlands, including conservation and wetland easement programs and the Environmental Quality Incentives Program, or EQIP, which “enhance(s) wetlands” by promoting soil and water conservation.

The report calls for the next Farm Bill, which Congress has been unable to agree on and pass for more than two sessions now, to “enhance” existing conservation programs and implement new incentives that “foster soil and water health.”

These suggestions include: increasing the Conservation Reserve Program acres to 45 million acres; increasing funding for the Conservation Stewardship Program from $1 billion to $4 billion annually; expanding funding to historically underserved, disadvantaged and new farmers, and to link the Federal Crop Insurance Program to a farmer’s participation in conservation practices. 

According to the report, investments from these recommendations constitute “only a fraction of the significant annual value wetlands deliver.” 

“Integrating these initiatives into the next food and Farm Bill will fortify USDA programs that safeguard wetlands from industrial agriculture, ensuring these vital ecosystems thrive and continue to mitigate flooding, purify water, and support our communities and our climate,” the report said. 

Groups across the country and political parties, including Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, have urged Congress to reauthorize the Farm Bill, rather than extend the 2018 bill for a second time.

headline: xBk annex, multicultural bookstore coming to historic Des Moines firehouse near Drake
fullText:
The historic Fire House No. 11 in in Des Moines' Drake Dogtown neighborhood will soon be home to an annex of music venue xBk Live and a multicultural bookstore.

The adjacent xBk will take over one side of the ground floor of the firehouse at 1163 24th St., creating a space for smaller events, community gatherings and merchandise sales. In the other half, online bookstore Nos Books — nos meaning "us" in Spanish — will open its first location.

Luis Luján has been selling books for two years at farmers' market pop-ups and other events across the Des Moines metro. At the firehouse, he told the Des Moines Register, he plans to offer a variety of fiction, non-fiction, poetry, history and cookbooks written by or about people of color, and he'll have Spanish-language editions stocked as well.

More: 'We're not invisible': Independent bookstore stocks books with diverse stories, characters

"It's exciting, a little terrifying and a very humbling," said Luján. "My hope was always that we would see enough interest that we could transition Nos Books into a brick and mortar."

Tobi Parks, who opened xBk in 2019, bought the firehouse from J&M Investments for $400,000 in 2021. As she planned to expand into the space, Parks said, she heard about Luján from a friend who had purchased books from him. She reached out and offered him the chance to be neighbors.

Setting down roots in the Drake neighborhood, which hasn't had its own independent bookstore in years, made sense to Luján. The firehouse, too, was alluring, he said.

"As soon as I walked in, I fell in love," he said. "A space like that, with the high ceilings and the history, you can see yourself bringing new life to that."

Nos Books is expected to open in February. Luján hopes to host a pop-up event at the firehouse the weekend of Dec. 14.

Did the firehouse need a lot of work?

The two-story brick structure was built in 1890. Most recently, it had been occupied by the office of attorney Valerie Cramer.

Parks received nearly $55,000 from Des Moines' Neighborhood Commercial Revitalization fund to make improvements to the building's façade, replace windows and doors, repair the roof and install an energy-efficient heating and air conditioning system. The total project cost $629,000.

Yes, the fire pole is intact, though it isn't functional.

Parks told the Des Moines Register in an email that she's also aiming to open XBK's ancillary space in February. The city's Board of Adjustment will review a request from Parks to allow the sale and consumption of alcohol in the firehouse at 1 p.m. Dec. 18 at the Richard A. Clark Municipal Service Center, 1551 E. Martin Luther King Jr. Parkway.

headline: Who was Brian Thompson, the UnitedHealthCare CEO, Iowa native murdered in New York City?
fullText:
Brian Thompson, 50, the UnitedHealthCare CEO killed Wednesday in what authorities said was a targeted attack in New York City, had deep ties to Iowa.

Here's what to know about him.

Where did Brian Thompson live?

UnitedHealthCare has its headquarters in the Minneapolis metro, where Thompson lived in the suburb of Maple Grove with wife, Paulette, a doctor, and their two sons.

More: What is UnitedHealthcare? Company's CEO fatally shot in Manhattan Wednesday morning

Brian Thompson grew up in Jewell, Iowa

Thompson grew up in Jewell, in Hamilton County north of Ames, the son of Pat and the late Dennis Thompson. His father attended Ellsworth Community College and Iowa State University and was employed at grain elevators.

Brian Thompson had one brother, who lives in Chicago, according to his father's obituary.

Who is Brian Thompson's wife?

Thompson's wife, who goes by Pauley, also grew up in Iowa, where her late father was a doctor in Webster City and later moved to Des Moines.

Thompson's four sisters-in-law include Des Moines-area resident Maria Reveiz, who is a non-practicing physician, a yoga instructor and a co-founder of the downtown Noce jazz club.

Brian Thompson remembered as 'outstanding student' at South Hamilton High School

Thompson graduated in 1993 from South Hamilton High School in Jewell. He was an "outstanding student," according to Principal Todd Coy, then a health and physical education teacher.

His achievements included being an athlete and homecoming king, class president and valedictorian.

UnitedHealthCare CEO Brian Thompson studied accounting at the University of Iowa

According to the Business Record, Thompson also was valedictorian when he graduated from the University of Iowa in 1997 with a bachelor's in business administration, majoring in accounting.

His LinkedIn profile says he was a Collegiate, Carver, State of Iowa and Faculty scholar and was named outstanding accounting student in his junior and senior years.

Brian Thompson's career included work at PwC and 20 years at UnitedHealthCare

After graduating, Thompson moved to Minneapolis to work as a CPA for the accounting firm PwC. There, he was a manager in auditing and later, transaction advisory services.

In 2004, Thompson joined UnitedHealthCare, one of the largest Fortune 500 companies, as director of corporate development. He became a vice president, then chief financial officer over increasingly important sectors of the business before being named CEO of UnitedHealthCare Medicare & Retirement in 2017. In 2019, he became CEO of the company's government programs.

In 2021, he was chosen to be overall CEO, overseeing a global workforce of 140,000.

Family, business leaders remember UnitedHealthCare CEO Brian Thompson as 'loving' and 'generous'

"Brian was an incredibly loving, generous, talented man who truly lived life to the fullest and touched so many lives. Most importantly, Brian was an incredibly loving father to our two sons and will be greatly missed." — Paulette Thompson, wife, in a statement to Fox News

"He was a wonderful person and a wonderful father, and we are heartbroken and shocked.” — Maria Reveiz of Des Moines, sister-in-law

"He was a good person, and I am so sad." — Elena Reveiz of Omaha, Nebraska, sister-in-law, speaking to the New York Times

"He was a devoted father, a good friend to many and a refreshingly candid colleague and leader.” — Mike Tuffin, president and CEO of commercial health insurance trade group AHIP

"Brian was an outstanding student. Held his academics as high as any student I’ve been around. Missing a question on a test was something that frustrated him. He was just a great kid to all.” — Todd Coy, principal, South Hamilton High School

"His achievements and character left a meaningful legacy within our schools and community." — South Hamilton School District statement

"This is horrifying news and a terrible loss for the business and health care community in Minnesota. Minnesota is sending our prayers to Brian’s family and the UnitedHealthcare team." — Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz

"He was just an incredible guy — nice, resourceful. This is just a total tragedy." — Steve Parente, a former Trump administration health care official who worked with Thompson, to the Minneapolis Star Tribune

“I knew him to be a visionary leader who developed innovative ideas to take on some of the nation’s greatest challenges. His death is a great loss for our country and for the health care industry.” — Kim Keck, the chief executive of the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, to the New York Times

headline: Brooks Brothers plant closure delivers imporant economics lesson | Opinion
fullText:
Many people would rather get their teeth drilled than discuss economics. If you are one of them, dial up your dentist, because today’s topic probably will make you uncomfortable.

Some politicians like to talk about other countries “stealing” the jobs of American workers. The politicians would have us believe these countries are snatching jobs right from under the noses of unwilling, and unwitting, employers in the United States.

A menswear writer named Derek Guy recently provided an important dose of context for American consumers. That context shows politicians have not been completely candid with consumers about the economic realities behind this trend.

I will leave the discussion of the politics of this for another day and another person. Instead, I want to share Guy’s knowledge and analysis. He posted about this on social media.

The peg for Guy’s discussion of manufacturing economics was the closure and auction of the machines and other contents of what for 70 years was known as the Garland Shirt Factory. The plant was named for Garland, North Carolina, a town of about 600 people where 150 men and women made an American fashion icon, the Brooks Brothers button-down oxford shirts. 

For generations, these high-quality shirts were chosen by the upwardly mobile men in boardrooms, banks and businesses throughout the United States. “They were a popular perennial,” Guy wrote of the Brooks Brothers’ shirts.

“But over time, Brooks Brothers fell into a common problem: the burden of expansion,” Guy wrote. “In 1971, they had just 11 locations. In 2001, there were 155 stores and outlets in the U.S. and Japan.”

During this expansion, the company’s real estate costs grew. The company was locked into long-term leases. So, executives looked for other ways to offset those expenses. One way was reducing the cost of making the shirts sold in their stores. Another was to turn to discounting to sell even more shirts.

Brooks Brothers moved its production to other countries, where labor costs were dramatically lower.

Traditionally, Brooks Brothers shirts rarely went on sale, Guy wrote. When they did, it was once a year and only after Christmas. But by 2010, Brooks Brothers shirts were available at discount during mid-season sales, at end-of-season sales, at Christmas sales, “4 for $249” sales, and “select shirts for just $39” sales.

While that discounting led to more shirts being sold, it also made the economics of producing shirts at a profit in Garland more difficult, even with the factory also sewing for other companies besides Brooks Brothers.

Guy explained this shirt-making reality in his social media post: “When Brooks Brothers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, I interviewed a number of their executives. I asked, How is it possible that the company that invented the oxford cloth button-down, one of the most iconic American designs, is not able to charge a premium over stuff found on

Amazon?”Here are some shirt-making economics:

“The simple reason is because at $10-$14/hour wages, a shirt is expensive,” Guy wrote. “At such prices, a company might buy a shirt from Garland at $40, sell it to a store for $80, and then the store sells it to you for about $150.

“But people don’t want to pay $150 for a shirt. Ultimately, consumers want cheap clothes,” Guy wrote.

What has occurred in Garland has occurred in many other American communities where textile companies have cut jobs and stopped cutting and sewing shirts — and suits, blouses, slacks and dresses — over the past several decades.

The U.S. International Trade Commission reported in September that the United States is the largest apparel importer in the world, bringing into the U.S. $79 billion worth of clothes each year, mostly from Asia.

A report by Statista, a data analysis company, provides a statistical foundation for why clothing manufacturing has shifted overseas, primarily to countries in Asia. While workers in Garland might have earned $10 to $14 per hour, garment workers in China are paid the equivalent of about $220 *per month*, Statista reported. In Cambodia, they receive about $190 per month. In Bangladesh, the pay is about $95 per month, according to Statista. 

American employees have no desire to work for wages found in developing countries. And economists remind us that tariffs will simply increase the cost to American consumers for those button-down shirts Brooks Brothers now sells that are made overseas.

Kenneth Ragland, who last managed the Garland operation, summed up the challenge bluntly in an interview with North Carolina’s Sampson Independent newspaper: “Lots of people talk about Made in the USA as being so necessary, but when the rubber meets the road, most Americans want cheap goods, which do not make it easy for U.S. firms to survive.”

Randy Evans is a retired journalist.

headline: EPA: Japanese company to pay $460,000 fine for hazardous chemical releases in Eddyville
fullText:
Ajinomoto Health & Nutrition North America will pay a nearly $460,000 fine and add protective equipment to resolve alleged violations tied to the Japanese company's release of hazardous chemicals at its Eddyville operations in southeast Iowa.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announcement Wednesday is tied to an inspection that agency officials conducted after the Eddyville facilities accidentally released hazardous chemicals in 2021 and 2022. The releases allegedly violated the federal Clean Air Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act.

A consent agreement Ajinomoto reached with the EPA said the company released 177,256 pounds of hydrochloric acid in 2021 when a storage tank valve failed, resulting in employee evacuations and a shelter-in-place order for Eddyville. In 2022, the company released about 973 pounds of chlorine gas, prompting employees to evacuate or shelter in place. About 15 were treated at a nearby hospital.

Chlorine gas is considered a hazardous chemical. It has a pungent, irritating odor and can be fatal when inhaled, or lead to chronic lung conditions through exposure.

“Ajinomoto’s operations presented a significant risk to its workers and the surrounding community,” David Cozad, EPA Region 7 enforcement and compliance division director, said in a statement. “This settlement, including the installation of an anhydrous ammonia containment system, will reduce the risk to workers and residents.”

Eddyville is a city of about 950 people, about 70 miles southeast of Des Moines.

Ajinomoto said the safety of its "employees and the community is our top priority."

"We have invested in our facility to address EPA recommendations, reinforcing our commitment to safety, quality, and environmental responsibility in our daily operations,” Leora Coleman-Fire, Ajinomoto Health & Nutrition's vice president and general counsel, said in a statement. 

The company owns and operates two amino acid manufacturing facilities, one for food and beverage industries and the other for animal nutrition products. The facilities use several chemicals in their processes, including anhydrous ammonia, hydrochloric acid and phosphoric acid, the EPA said in a statement.

The agency identifies the chemicals as “extremely hazardous substances” because they are known to cause serious adverse effects to the environment and human health, including injury and death.

As outlined in the agreement, the EPA alleges that Ajinomoto violated multiple legal requirements, including failure to:

  • Identify potential hazards that may result from accidental releases.
  • Design and maintain safe facilities that provide the steps necessary to prevent hazardous substance releases.
  • Adequately complete analyses to detect potential releases of hazardous substances and address them.
  • Comply with mechanical integrity requirements to prevent releases.
  • Adequately coordinate with local emergency planning and response organizations to make them aware of the chemicals used at the facilities and the risks presented.
  • Report the use of hazardous chemicals at the facility to local response authorities.

In addition to paying the $458,265 civil fine, Ajinomoto agreed to install $227,589 in equipment at one facility, designed to contain and reduce the potential for anhydrous ammonia releases to the surrounding area. Ajinomoto also conducted a compliance audit at its facilities to evaluate and address any outstanding noncompliance with federal law.

Facilities that use hazardous, toxic and flammable substances are required to comply with the Clean Air Act. The law requires facilities to develop plans that identify the potential effects of a chemical accident, how to prevent an accident and how to respond.

Federal law also requires that facilities help communities plan for chemical emergencies and potential risks.

headline: Des Moines botanical garden extends Dome for the Holidays hours after high demand
fullText:
The Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden has extended its hours due to high demand for Dome for the Holidays.

The local botanical garden transforms into a tropical light oasis during the new attraction. Dome for the Holidays has sold out since opening on Nov. 16, according to a news release from the Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden. So organizers decided to expand the opportunities for people to visit the holiday event.

What is Dome for the Holidays at the Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden?

Dome for the Holidays features the botanical garden dressed in thousands of lights, accompanied by a collection of blown glass sculptures and festive music. You can sip on refreshments while checking out the train display and hunting for gnomes.

The holiday train display even has a new look and theme this year, according to the botanical garden's website.

More: Where to find giant holiday light displays across the Des Moines metro in 2024

What are the new hours for the Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden's Dome for the Holidays?

The Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden offers tickets for the special holiday event starting at 5 p.m. every Wednesday through Sunday. The final entry to the event is 8 p.m. The garden closes at 9 p.m. and the attraction will be available through Dec. 31.

The general daily admission to the Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden will shift to 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tuesday through Friday during December.

How much are tickets to the Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden's Dome for the Holidays?

Tickets to the Dome for the Holidays must be purchased in advance. Visitors select a 30-minute entry window and spend about 45-70 minutes at the event. Botanical garden members receive a $3 discount on each ticket price.

  • Adults: $15
  • Children 13 years old and younger: $9
  • 1 year and under are free

Tickets can be purchased at the Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden's website.

headline: Joni Ernst eyes federal work-from-home policies as head of new DOGE Caucus
fullText:
U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst is proposing to move federal agency headquarters out of Washington, D.C., sell off unused real estate and enact sweeping changes to telework policies that emphasize tracking remote workers' productivity.

She's set to make the recommendations Thursday during her first meeting as head of the Senate's Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, Caucus.

“For years, I have been tracking down bureaucrats relaxing in bubble baths, playing golf, getting arrested, and doing just about everything besides their job,” Ernst said in a statement provided to the Des Moines Register. “It would almost be funny if it wasn’t happening on the taxpayers’ dime and at the expense of veterans, seniors, small business owners, and Americans in need of competent service from government agencies. Federal employees need to return to work, but if they don’t want to, I will make their wish come true.”

The Department of Government Efficiency, launched by President-elect Donald Trump, is headed by billionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Ohio biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy. Though it's not an actual government department, Musk and Ramaswamy will serve as volunteers to advise Trump on ways to slash spending and reduce regulations.

Ernst, as head of the Senate arm partnering with the group, previously identified about $1 trillion in potential federal spending cuts she pitched in a letter to Musk and Ramaswamy.

Ernst has been a vocal critic of post-pandemic work-from-home policies for government workers.

In the 60-page report, her office says that prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, just 3% of federal workers worked from home, while today nearly one-third are entirely remote with just 6% reporting working in-person on a full-time basis.

She said those changes mean the government must establish better oversight and productivity tracking of those employees.

But it also means the federal government should move agency headquarters to other parts of the country and close down unused office space. According to the report, government buildings average an occupancy rate of 12%.

"Tracking employees' locations and work products — like the private sector does — can identify poor performers and improve management," the report says.

Musk and Ramaswamy are also set to meet more widely with congressional Republicans on Thursday.

Here's a look at Ernst's report.

headline: Truck driver faces eluding charge after Iowa troopers followed him for 75 miles on I-80
fullText:
Editor's note: Joseariel Rosa Rivera pleaded guilty April 1 to eluding police and has been fined $430. No other charges have been filed against him in relation to the December 2024 pursuit.

Original article:

A 30-year-old truck driver from New Jersey is facing charges of eluding after leading police on a 75-mile pursuit on Tuesday.

According to a search warrant, Joseariel Rosa Rivera had bloodshot and watery eyes, constricted pupils, visible body tremors, an elevated resting pulse rate and repeatedly stated “Jesus Christ is coming” to law enforcement and medical personnel. A blood sample was collected from Rosa Rivera and will be taken to the Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation Crime Lab for analysis.

Rosa Rivera was driving a semi tractor trailer dragging a chain and creating sparks on Interstate 80 near Underwood in western Iowa at about 6:30 a.m., said Sgt. Alex Dinkla, spokesperson with the Iowa State Patrol. Troopers attempted to pull the Rosa Rivera over at the 40 mile marker but the driver allegedly ignored the lights and sirens, Dinkla said.

Various agencies deployed stop sticks, which are tire deflation devices, that deflated several of the trailer's tires, Dinkla said. But Rosa Rivera continued to operate the truck on the tire's rims eastbound toward the Des Moines metro.

The driver eventually pulled into the Dallas County weigh station, located near the 115 mile marker, and was taken into custody. The driver was transported to a Des Moines hospital for evaluation.

Troopers pursued the semi for about 75 miles before the driver pulled over.

The pursuit shut down Interstate 235 for about 25 minutes during the morning commute Tuesday.

(This story was updated to add a video.)

headline: 'The best is yet to come': Gov. Kim Reynolds touts Iowa tax cuts while accepting award
fullText:
Gov. Kim Reynolds touted her realignment of Iowa's tax system on Thursday while accepting an award from the Iowa Taxpayers Association, promising "the best is yet to come."

"Iowa’s journey to tax competitiveness, it wasn’t a matter of a few modest tweaks," Reynolds told a crowd Thursday at the association's annual symposium in Altoona. "It was a complete, top-to-bottom transformation that couldn’t have happened without an outstanding team of legislators, advocates, business leaders and others that were behind me."

Reynolds received the association's Linda S. Weindruch Award. The annual award "recognizes outstanding accomplishments and contributions in promoting and protecting the principles and policies of fair business taxation," according to the association's website.

In a speech after she accepted the award, Reynolds recapped the series of tax cuts she has signed into law since she became governor, taking Iowa's top individual income tax rate from 8.98% in 2018 to what will be a 3.8% flat income tax rate beginning in January.

Reynolds signed the cut dropping Iowa to a flat rate earlier this year. The law speeds up an earlier tax cut signed by Reynolds that would have brought Iowa to a 3.9% flat income tax by 2026.

Reynolds also has signed corporate tax cuts that will eventually lower the state's corporate tax rate to 5.5%.

And, working with Republicans in the Iowa Legislature, she has signed laws eliminating taxes on retirement income, getting rid of Iowa's inheritance tax and cutting property taxes.

More: Iowa Republicans have been cutting income tax for years. See how your bill has changed:

In all, the tax cuts will result in Iowans paying $24 billion less in taxes over a decade, Reynolds said.

"There’s no more complexity and there’s no more gimmicks," she said of Iowa's tax system. "What you see is what you get. Low taxes, low spending and more money in the pockets of citizens and businesses who truly create prosperity."

Reynolds' critics have said the cuts will harm the state's ability to pay for services.

A state panel in October estimated that Iowa will take in $1 billion less in revenue over the next two years, largely because of the tax cuts.

In her speech, Reynolds said she and Republicans in the Iowa Legislature have worked together to keep state spending well below the amount of money Iowa takes in each year. This has led to more money in Iowa's reserves and billions in the Taxpayer Relief Fund, which must be used on further tax cuts.

The award from the Iowa Taxpayers Association is one of a string of tax and budget-related awards Reynolds has received this year.

Last month, Reynolds received the 2024 Distinguished Service Award at the Tax Foundation's 2024 Tax Prom in Washington, D.C.

She also received an "A" grade from the conservative Cato Institute in the think tank's biennial Fiscal Policy Report Card on America's Governors. Reynolds was one of six governors to receive the highest grade.

More: What's in Iowa's $8.9 billion state budget for the coming year? We break it down:

Republicans intend to pass property tax cuts in 2025 legislative session

While Reynolds and Republicans in the Iowa Legislature have said they hope to eventually eliminate Iowa's income tax, their focus in January will be on property tax cuts.

Sen. Mike Bousselot, R-Ankeny, said Tuesday at a legislative forum sponsored by the Greater Des Moines Partnership that he expects lawmakers to pass some type of property tax cut next year.

"Iowans loud and clear have said property taxes are making it unaffordable for them to live in our communities," he said.

Speaking at the same forum, House Minority Leader Jennifer Konfrst, D-Windsor Heights, emphasized the importance of including local governments in any decisions about property tax changes.

"When we’re talking about taxes and property taxes, we want to make sure we’re talking to local communities as well to make sure you don’t get left high and dry when the time comes to pay for the roads in your community," Konfrst said. "We want to make sure that we’re having a community conversation about this, not a top down approach."

headline: Ryan Walters says he'll try to change Oklahoma law to require elections for superintendents
fullText:
In his latest headline-making move, Oklahoma schools Superintendent Ryan Walters announced that he will attempt to craft a new state law to require public school superintendents to be elected by voters.

The state's top education official said late Wednesday that he wants to move away from the current model — in which superintendents are hired by voter-elected school boards — to a new system where voters would choose superintendents directly. He said the switch would make school leaders accountable to voters.

It's unclear, however, how Walters' proposal might become law. He does not have the power to change the law himself. The state Legislature writes and passes laws, and Walters did not say whether any state lawmakers were willing to sponsor his proposal in the upcoming legislative session, scheduled to start in February.

As of Wednesday evening, no bill containing Walters' proposal had been filed for consideration in either the Oklahoma House or Senate.

While Walters used attention-grabbing language in announcing the proposal to elect district superintendents, he provided few specifics about how it would work.

"We have seen rogue administrators ignore the will of the parents and taxpayers in their district to inject pornography into schools, cover up the sexual misconduct of teachers, allow students to lick each other's toes, and even be arrested by public intoxication on school grounds," Walters said.

Several legislators, including at least two members of Walters' own Republican Party, quickly raised questions about the idea.

Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, a member of the House Appropriations and Budget subcommittee on education, called the suggestion "another example of Ryan Walters’ desire to get clicks instead of improving student outcomes.

"School boards are elected, and they pick the superintendent for their district," Osburn said. "Rather than focusing on outcomes, he’s just trying to sow seeds of conflict with hard-working superintendents, which is simply and unnecessarily disruptive. None of this will bring us up from dead last in the nation in ACT scores and student outcomes. I wish he would focus on the job he was elected to, rather than trying to score political points for who knows what. The voters of Oklahoma and their kids deserve better."

Rep. Melissa Provenzano, D-Tulsa, a member of the House's Common Education Committee and a former public school principal, also criticized the proposal. "This is a sad attempt by the superintendent to say whatever sensational thing comes to his mind in order to keep the spotlight on himself instead of supporting our kids," she said.

Another Democrat on the House education committee, Rep. Jacob Rosecrants of Norman — who, like Provenzano, is a former educator — said the idea of electing district superintendents has been "catching on" in states under Republican control, such as Oklahoma, which has a GOP supermajority in both legislative chambers. He said conservative national lobbying groups have prepared so-called "model" bills toward that end.

"It's similar to the idea of moving local school board elections to November," Rosecrants said. "These ideas weaken local control and will only further politicize our public schools when we need to do all we can to de-politicize them."

Rep. Danny Sterling, R-Tecumseh, said he viewed Walters' proposal as a solution to a problem that doesn't exist. He said the process of selecting a school superintendent is complex, and an elected candidate might not even have the credentials, knowledge or experience in the educational system.

"Currently, when a superintendent is employed by a school district, more times than not, they are vetted by the school board, a teacher’s committee, etc., to make sure they will be both qualified for the job and would be a good fit for that district," said Sterling, who's also a member of the House Education Committee and a former high school principal. "This is not necessarily a 'one size fits all' position."

Sen. Adam Pugh, R-Edmond, the chair of that body's Education Committee, declined to comment through a Senate spokesman.

In announcing the proposal, Walters said he believes many Oklahoma superintendents "continue to defy reforms implemented under conservative leadership."

Though he did not provide examples of such defiance, many school administrators decided in November to ignore a directive issued by Walters. He had instructed superintendents to show students a video announcing the new Office of Religious Liberty and Patriotism inside the Oklahoma State Department of Education, which he leads. In the video, Walters touts the office, then invites students to join him in a prayer for President-elect Donald Trump.

Most school leaders have also ignored a Bible-teaching mandate he issued earlier this year. Attorney General Gentner Drummond's office has said Walters had no legal authority to show the video or enforce the Bible mandate. The mandate has drawn at least two lawsuits, including one in the Oklahoma Supreme Court.

More: Sen. Markwayne Mullin questions Ryan Walters' Bible mandate, calling it a 'slippery slope'

"Parents are rightfully horrified by this kind of misconduct, and it's time to put parents in control over their neighborhood schools by giving voters a direct way to hold superintendents accountable," Walters said.

Walters said his proposal for electing superintendents would cover election dates, eligibility requirements, pay levels and other details.

Mid-Del Schools Superintendent Rick Cobb, who has previously clashed with Walters, said he'd want to see any potential bill to learn what Walters has in mind. "Generally, though, we already have accountability through locally elected school boards who select and evaluate superintendents," Cobb said.

The announcement comes amid weeks of political, attention-grabbing initiatives by Walters surrounding Trump's election. He announced in November he had directed the purchase of more than 500 Bibles for Oklahoma public schools at a cost of nearly $25,000.

(This story was updated to add new information.)

headline: How OU football QB Jett Niu went from committed to Oklahoma State to signing with Sooners
fullText:
Jett Niu had to scramble Tuesday.

Finding OU gear in Utah isn’t exactly easy.

Luckily for Niu, a local sporting goods store at least had a Sooners’ sweatshirt and flag.

“I’m still trying to find a hat right now,” Niu told The Oklahoman on Wednesday morning before his signing ceremony at Lehi High. “It was just so late, I don’t think you could get one here on time.”

It’s been a whirlwind of a last few days for Niu, a quarterback who had been committed to Oklahoma State since September.

But Wednesday, Niu instead signed with OU, marking the first recruiting impact in Norman for new offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle.

More: Why OU football OL recruit Michael Fasusi enters signing day still committed to Sooners

Niu wasn’t even thinking of OU being a possibility until offensive lineman Darius Afalava reached out to him Friday, asking if he was open to possibilities beyond the Cowboys.

Afalava and Niu have known each other for years, playing against each other in Lehi, which sits between Salt Lake City and Provo.

“I’m open if they wanna call,” Niu told Afalava, who had been committed to the Sooners since June and who also signed with OU on Wednesday.

Monday night, not long after solidifying Arbuckle as the Sooners’ new offensive coordinator, Niu’s phone rang.

It was Brent Venables.

“He was just really laying out the format for me because he said they’d lost a QB commit and he said he would love me over there,” Niu said. 

During his initial recruitment, Niu had developed a strong relationship with Arbuckle, who was then the offensive coordinator at Washington State.

The Cougars were one of Niu’s first Division I offers.

“This offense really, really fits the style of offense I played in high school,” Niu said. “He also does really good with quarterbacks and he develops them a lot. He’s developed Cam Ward and John Mateer and he was one of the really good quarterbacks this year. 

“I think he can really develop me and get me to my best potential.”

More: Examining each OU football 2025 recruiting class signee

Niu threw for 2,857 yards and 29 touchdowns as a senior and rushed for 66 yards and three touchdowns, helping Lehi to the state semifinals.

“He’s a really skilled, developed quarterback," Venables said. "He’s got a great frame, will continue to put some weight on him but his mechanics and fundamentals are exceptional, the way he climbs the pocket, his accuracy, his ability to push the ball down field, his instincts. Incredible quickness in his release and great communication, leadership qualities."

The Sooners were sent into a bit of a scramble when Kevin Sperry, who had been committed since March 2023, flipped to Florida State on Nov. 21.

With little certainty over the direction of the offense in 2025 and beyond, the Sooners had to wait before pulling the trigger at the position.

But they knew they didn’t want to go without.

“Really felt like we needed, foundationally, to have a freshman quarterback in the room,” Venables said.

When Venables decided on Arbuckle, that door was open for OU to grab OSU’s quarterback commit.

The relationship with Arbuckle was established. The relationship with Venables was not.

“That was actually the first time talking to him,” Niu said of the Monday conversation. “Then we talked again that morning and me and my dad talked to him and it just felt different. We knew that he was a good guy."

By Tuesday, Niu had decided to flip.

“I think there’s a trust, knowing what he was signing up for and who would be mentoring and tutoring (him),” Venables said. “Once I was able to bridge the gap with Jett and his family with what our program is all about, things that are important to us — standards, expectations, values, beliefs, how we do what we do, all those types of things — it was a slam dunk for both sides.”

More: Washington State QB John Mateer plans to enter transfer portal. Could he land with OU?

That didn’t make the decision easy, though.

Niu developed strong relationships in Stillwater, particularly with quarterbacks coach Tim Rattay. 

“It was super tough,” Niu said. “That call is never easy but I just kind of told him that I think this is the pathway for me and he understood. He was bummed out about it.”

Now, Niu is preparing to move in a few weeks to a state he’s visited before but to a city and university where he has not been.

“I’m definitely going in blind,” Niu said. “But I’m trusting in God and that he has a plan for me and I’m definitely excited.”

headline: What is Thunder's motivation to win NBA Cup? OKC 'doing it for JWill' to get prize money
fullText:
Until just moments before he stepped to the postgame podium Tuesday night, Cason Wallace hadn’t known that the Spurs and Suns could alter his team’s reality. 

Wallace might be better off. He was oblivious to all the NBA Cup’s multiversal realities, to its web of outcomes that were no longer in OKC’s hands once it won Tuesday. 

“I don’t really know much about the Cup or how it works,” Wallace said. “I’m just tryna win.” 

After the Thunder's 133-106 win against the Jazz on Tuesday, as well as Phoenix’s win over San Antonio, the Thunder clinched West Group B, advancing to a quarterfinal game in Oklahoma City against the Mavericks next Tuesday at 8:30 p.m.

Somewhere in between the Thunder’s advancement and the idea of being on the Las Vegas strip in December, Gilgeous-Alexander lost track, too. 

“It’s all too confusing,” he said. 

More: Lu Dort injury update: OKC Thunder guard playing through 'mallet finger' on shooting hand

The NBA Cup hasn’t exactly gripped people the way the NCAA Tournament has. Its intrigue and complexity is similar to that of a Rubik’s Cube — though more people might be into the cube than the bracket at the moment. 

Daigneault seemingly has better things to do. Before the Suns downed the Spurs, Daigneault claimed he wouldn’t devote an extra second to the outcome. 

“No, I'm gonna go home and hug my wife,” he replied, probably tongue-in-cheek, when asked if he’d watch the game. 

Daigneault’s priorities felt clear once OKC opened the fourth quarter with a hefty lead. Four of his five starters never saw the floor in the final period. Any thought of point differential was dead to Daigneault. 

“Zero,” Daigneault said, asked how much he’d thought about playing starters late. “No. 1, because of player health. Imagine if it’s an NBA Cup game, and we’re up by 30, and I run a 35-minute player out there, and god forbid something happens because I’m chasing a point differential — that would be really bad for the league. And for the team. 

“I don’t love the design, because it’s incentivizing that. Or running the score up on an opponent. There’s a certain grace that you win with, (and) they’ve created an incentive that flips that on its head.

“I just know what it feels like to be in the games, and you’ve got the angel and the devil on your shoulder. But we’re going with the angel. We’re going to go with player health.” 

More: 2024 NBA Cup knockout round: Time, TV schedule and prize money

Amid the pool of confusion and distaste was at least one wide smile. That's typical of Jaylin Williams. But Williams, who’s yet to play this season, apparently psyched his teammates up on Tuesday ahead of the Cup game. And via text messages ahead of previous Cup games. It’s about more than winning. Or a trip to Vegas.

Jaylin Williams has money on his mind. 

“(Jaylin) has been adamant about winning the money,” said Jalen, who concluded that he might buy a Lamborghini with his potential $500,000 in earnings. “So, (we’re) doing it for JWill.” 

Added Gilgeous-Alexander: “He made sure across the locker room that we understood how important this game was. And, like, all day. Every chance he got.”
