headline: New Oklahoma chancellor sworn in by father, a retired federal judge, at regents' meeting
fullText:
The state’s new chancellor, Sean Burrage, and his father, retired federal judge Michael Burrage, shared a special moment Thursday morning when the father swore in the son as the 10th person to lead Oklahoma’s higher education system.

The two men embraced immediately after Sean Burrage took the oath of office.

“A president told me once that a father’s responsibility is to create memories,” said Dennis Casey, of Morrison, the chair of the nine-person board for the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education. “That was a pretty good memory right there.”

One of the regents, former Oklahoma Supreme Court Chief Justice Steven Taylor, introduced Michael Burrage at the start of the regents’ meeting as a former classmate at the University of Oklahoma College of Law and a longtime friend.

Former U.S. President Bill Clinton nominated Michael Burrage in 1994 to be a U.S. district judge, and Burrage went on to serve in all three U.S. federal court districts in Oklahoma, making him one of the nation’s first First American federal judges. He retired from the federal bench in 2001 to re-enter private law practice. Michael Burrage was inducted into the Oklahoma Hall of Fame in 2016.

“Congratulations on this opportunity and this achievement in your career,” Michael Burrage told his son. Michael Burrage then turned to the regents and thanked them for giving his son the chance to serve as chancellor, then administered the oath of office.

Sean Burrage, who’s also a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, served two terms as a Democratic state senator, representing parts of Rogers County and Mayes County, from November 2006 until June 2014. He spent part of that time as the minority floor leader. After leaving the Senate, he became the president at Southeastern Oklahoma State University in Durant, after being chosen by the regents of the Regional University System of Oklahoma.

After a little more than five years at Southeastern, he left in October 2019 to join executive leadership at the University of Oklahoma, where he served as OU President Joseph Harroz’s chief of staff and vice president of executive affairs until last month. Burrage succeeds Allison Garrett, whose retirement became effective Sunday.

Harroz was one of five current presidents at the state’s 25 higher-education institutions to attend the ceremony, joining Thomas Newsom, of Southeastern, Kyle Stafford, of Northeastern Oklahoma A&M College in Miami, Lana Reynolds, of Seminole State College in Seminole, and Janet Wansick, of Eastern Oklahoma State College in Wilburton.

Glen Johnson, a former Oklahoma House Speaker who later became the state’s chancellor, also was present, as was the current RUSO executive director, Brandon Tatum.

Burrage acknowledged the uniqueness of having his father being able to administer the oath of office. He thanked numerous people in his remarks after the ceremony, including former OU President David Boren, former state Senate President Pro Tempore Stratton Taylor and Garrett.

“Our goal is to ensure that more Oklahomans earn college degrees,” Sean Burrage said. “That’s it. Everything that we do is to make sure that more people get educations. Public education is how my family got where they are and I believe in it at the K-12 level, I believe in it in higher education, and that’s why I took this job.

“Higher education is necessary, but not sufficient, for the entire state to be successful. I pledge that we will do our part, on behalf of all the institutions here in Oklahoma, to do what we can, to do the necessary work to create an educated and a healthy workforce for our state to drive the economy.”

headline: OKC officer charged with aggravated assault after incident with 71-year-old man
fullText:
An Oklahoma City police officer has been charged with aggravated assault and battery following a viral use-of-force incident with a 71-year-old man, county officials announced Thursday.

The incident drew scrutiny nationwide after the department released body camera footage on Nov. 8 showing the interaction between Sgt. Joseph Gibson, 28, and 71-year-old Lich Vu after an Oct. 27 vehicle collision near NW 39 and Meridian Avenue.

Gibson appears to throw Vu to the ground during an argument in which Vu refused to sign a ticket for an alleged improper U-turn.

According to a news release from Oklahoma County District Attorney Vicki Behenna's office, the situation escalated to the point where Gibson performed a “takedown” on Vu, which caused Vu to fall headfirst on the pavement. The news release said Vu sustained significant injuries including an orbital fracture, neck fracture and a brain bleed.

Vu was still in the hospital as of Thursday, the DA's office said.

Following an internal investigation, Gibson was charged with one count of aggravated assault and battery, a felony.

“The Oklahoma County District Attorney’s Office takes all use-of-force incidents very seriously,” Behenna said in the news release. “We evaluate the law and the facts in each individual case, and in this particular case determined the Officer’s actions were an unreasonable use-of-force."

If convicted, the range of punishment for aggravated assault and battery is up to five years in prison or up to a year in the county jail and/or a fine of up to $500, according to the news release.

headline: Dewar dominates Laverne in second half, captures Class B-I football state championship
fullText:
EDMOND — Dewar couldn’t have had a much worse start to its Class B-I championship game against Laverne. 

Laverne star senior Felix Teal fielded the opening kickoff and showed why he’s considered one of the state’s best players in eight-man football, scoring a 91-yard touchdown. 

Just one play into the matchup, Laverne had made a huge statement. 

But Dewar didn’t get rattled. 

The Dragons quickly responded and put together a touchdown drive that ended with a 24-yard touchdown pass from sophomore Peyton Kilhoffer to senior Ben Atoigue. 

More: Months after devastating tornado, Sulphur High School playing for state title, community

From then on, Dewar slowly started to overpower Laverne with its superior size and physicality. And by the second half, it wasn’t even close. 

Class B-I fifth-ranked Dewar defeated No. 2 Laverne 44-12 on Thursday afternoon at the University of Central Oklahoma’s Chad Richison Stadium, claiming its second football title and first since 2020. 

Junior running back Braelin Lewis, an Okmulgee transfer and the son of former OU standout Ronnell Lewis, was one of the main leaders of a Dewar offense that had 463 rushing yards on 62 attempts. 

Lewis finished with 35 carries for 279 yards and one touchdown, while Kilhoffer had 17 attempts for 160 yards and three scores and also had two touchdown passes. 

“We’re probably all going to cry here in a minute all together in the locker room,” Lewis said. “It’s just an unreal feeling. I mean, coming from an 0-10 season at Okmulgee, just to experience this my first year here it’s unreal.” 

Dewar (12-1) had just a 16-12 lead at halftime against Laverne (12-2) but pulled away in the third as Kilhoffer had touchdown runs of 35 and 36 yards. 

More: The Oklahoman's high school football picks for every state title, semifinal game in Week 14

The Dragons added to that in the fourth as Lewis scored on a 1-yard run and Kilhoffer hit senior Naea Corbin on a 12-yard touchdown pass. 

“Just how physical we played,” Kilhoffer said of what the biggest key was on Thursday. “Our linemen just dominated theirs.” 

Dewar had a banner that read “put a ring on it” as the players trotted onto the field.  

Dewar isn’t a big school, but the Dragons felt the love Thursday. 

“Whenever I turned around coming onto the sidelines, I see our whole town supporting us,” Lewis said. “That’s the biggest thing that I came to Dewar for is the entire fans that come out and support us, the pride that they have in Dewar is unreal here. It’s absolutely crazy.” 

For Kilhoffer, the victory is something he’ll never forget.

“Best feeling in the world,” Kilhoffer said. “Never felt anything greater.”

More: How OU football landed trio of Carl Albert signees: 'We're all gonna do big things'

Three and out

Player of the game: Braelin Lewis. The junior tailback had one of his best games of the season while leading Dewar to its second state title. Lewis rushed 35 times for 279 yards and a touchdown while having two additional scores reversed due to penalties.

Key moment: As Dewar led by four at halftime, sophomore quarterback Peyton Kilhoffer opened the second half with a 35-yard touchdown run to extend Dewar’s lead to 12. Kilhoffer pretty much sealed the victory toward the end of the third quarter, scoring again off of a 36-yard touchdown run as Laverne was held scoreless in the second half.

Read option: Kilhoffer had a stellar day, scoring four total touchdowns in Dewar’s state title win. He finished with 17 rushes for 162 yards and two touchdowns while going 4-of-11 passing for 49 yards and two additional scores.

—Jordan Davis, Staff writer

headline: Will Tennessee be nation's No. 1 team under Rick Barnes after losses by Kansas, Auburn?
fullText:
Tennessee basketball could be the nation's new No. 1 team when the next polls are released.

The No. 3 Vols moved to 8-0 on Tuesday, and the next day, the two teams ranked ahead of them lost: No. 1 Kansas was upset by Creighton 76-63 and No. 2 Auburn lost 84-78 at Duke. Both the Jayhawks and Tigers are 7-1.

If UT is ranked No. 1 on Monday, it would be the third time in program history and the earliest in the season it has held the top spot.

The Vols were ranked No. 1 for one week in the 2007-08 season, but they lost at Vanderbilt in their next game and fell from the top spot.

headline: What Kim Caldwell's grandma texted her after Lady Vols blew lead against Florida State
fullText:
Kim Caldwell had someone back home to answer to after Lady Vols basketball blew an 18-point lead against Florida State on Wednesday.

Her grandmother.

"Not a great win, but we'll take it. Nothing like blowing an 18-point lead," the first-year Tennessee coach said. "My grandma texted and said, 'What happened?' And I said, 'It was a terrible halftime speech.' "

Tennessee (6-0) may have blown the lead, but it won the game 79-77 over Florida State in the SEC/ACC Challenge. The Lady Vols led by as many as 20 points near the end of the second quarter and led 45-27 at halftime at Food City Center.

But their defense couldn't stop the Seminoles (8-2) coming out of halftime and UT got outscored 30-12 in the third quarter. The game was tied 57-57 going into the fourth.

"We have a lot to learn from this one," Caldwell said. "I think we needed it. We needed a test, and the more you can get tested early, the better you'll be going into conference. And that's what all of your nonconference schedule is about."

Talaysia Cooper led Tennessee with 22 points; FSU guard Ta'Niya Latson scored a game-high 38 points.

"That's a really good team," Caldwell said. "In my opinion, it's a top-25 team. They have had big wins, they have three great players surrounded by a great cast. So we're happy to get out of here with a win."

headline: Knoxville couple volunteer to help remote community after flooding from Hurricane Helene
fullText:
More than 20 large trees shut down a dirt road in the remote community of Butler, Tennessee, which is somewhere near Johnson City.

There was one house at the end of that road, well off the grid, that was inhabited by an old man. A neighbor posted a message on the Facebook page “Hurricane Helene Volunteering in East Tennessee Area.” She was concerned about the man’s welfare.

“I’m a firm believer in, ‘If you want to have an opinion, you better be ready to back it up,” said Halls resident Nora Taylor. “I’ve always been a giving person. My boyfriend [Jay Waters] is a tree cutter [with Davey Tree]. I thought he could use his skill to help.”

Taylor and Waters know that area well because he has family there. In the first week after the hurricane hit in late September, Taylor and Waters made three trips with donated food and clothes, and another to volunteer.

Along with a large contingent of people, Taylor and Waters helped clear the road. They knocked on the door of the house but got no answer.

“We didn’t want to break in the house (to check on the man), because we didn’t know what to expect,” Taylor said.

They went to the neighbor’s house and urged her to make contact. While there, the group removed a tree from the neighbor’s shed.

“She was so happy for the help that she started crying,” Taylor said. “That made us feel good.”

More trips will be needed

Bottled water and hygiene supplies were the primary items taken to the devastated area. Taylor, a 2009 Fulton High School graduate, is convinced the folks there will be in need for quite a while. 

And she doesn’t plan to curtail her trips anytime soon.

“Whenever someone points out a need, there’s a group addressing it,” Taylor said. “That’s what struck me. It doesn’t matter where people are coming from, there’s a job to be done and they do it.

“It was amazing, seeing the devastation. … You see the broken roads. You see the bridge out. It’s hard to believe.”

Positive vibes come from area

In the midst of the debris, Taylor said she can’t help but sense the positive nature of the volunteers and the people who are experiencing the love. 

“Just seeing so many people jump in and do what they can,” she said. “It helps you appreciate what you already have. 

“When you’re there and come home, you appreciate what it means to have electricity and a hot shower. 

"Then you start to thinking, ‘Am I doing enough?’ This is going to go on for a long time. There’s so much work to be done to help these people rebuild their lives.”

Taylor said she’s going to continue to collect items and make her trips to the affected area.

“There’s still so much I want to do,” she said. “I’ll find those small areas and help people shovel mud out of their houses.”

To help Taylor, contact her on Facebook.

headline: Ambulances in Knoxville arrived late 224 times, and not at all at least once, in October
fullText:
American Medical Response, Knox County's ambulance provider, was fined almost $100,000 in October for failing to respond to emergency calls from sick and injured people quickly enough.

In one instance, a Knoxville Fire Department paramedic and battalion chief rushed a "profusely" bleeding patient to the hospital in a KFD SUV because first responders were worried he would die before an ambulance arrived.

It's the first time since July that AMR has fallen below the target response times laid out in its contract with the county. AMR is fined $266.63 when an ambulance arrives one minute late or less, and the company is fined $598.12 for an ambulance that is more than one minute late.

Targets for late arrivals are set for three regions: city of Knoxville, east Knox County and west Knox County. All of AMR's October fines were for late arrivals within the city: 224 late arrivals for life-threatening calls accounted for $127,017.59 in fines and 72 late arrivals for less-serious calls accounted for $41,407.19 in fines.

AMR must hit a 90% mark for on-time arrival to be in compliance. In Knoxville city limits, "late" means it took an ambulance longer than 10 minutes to arrive. In the rest of the county, it means an ambulance took longer than 20 minutes to arrive. In October, ambulances arrived on time 91% of the time in east Knox County and 94% in west Knox County.

In addition to tracking response times, AMR also is scored on how well providers provide care once they arrive. Scoring above 90% on all calls, regardless of region, gets the company a credit toward the fines it owes for arriving late. Providers scored 93% in October, which means AMR's late fines were reduced by 45%. Without the credit, AMR would have owed Knox County $168,424.78 .

Jerry Harnish, the director of operations for AMR in Knox County, told Knox News delayed response time "is nothing surprising" because there were more calls on days when crews were busier. Plus, he said, AMR is required by contract with the University of Tennessee at Knoxville to station eight ambulances at Neyland Stadium during football games. That takes those ambulances off the road for other calls for 8-10 hours on game days, Harnish estimated.

"There was no real change in staffing (from previous months to October)," he said. "It's what happens in a busy system."

What happened Oct. 19?

Tennessee played Alabama at Neyland Stadium on Oct. 19, requiring eight ambulances. Harnish told Knox News that meant 10 ambulances were available to respond to life-threatening calls throughout the county.

Shortly before 9:50 p.m., a 55-year-old man who had been watching the Vols fell down a flight of stairs and hit his head on the concrete floor, according to a Knox County Emergency Communications District report obtained by Knox News.

The call was classified as life-threatening, which meant the Knoxville Fire Department sent a highly trained paramedic to the scene. Paramedics provide life-saving care until an ambulance arrives, which is supposed to be within 10 minutes for that type of call.

KFD arrived eight minutes after the call and told dispatchers the patient was unconscious and bleeding profusely, according to the report. There were no ambulances available, so the paramedic on the scene asked his battalion chief to drive his SUV to the home in case they had to take the patient to the hospital themselves.

Harnish told Knox News the ambulances that night were tied up on other calls or waiting with other patients at hospitals, a requirement that creates delays in responses.

AMR requested an ambulance from a neighboring county as the patient's condition deteriorated.

Twenty-eight minutes after the 911 call was made, the firefighters loaded the patient into the SUV and drove him to the University of Tennessee Medical Center's emergency room. It was a last-ditch effort after the paramedic determined there was no other way to care for him at the scene.

KFD canceled the calls for an ambulance and arrived at the hospital at 10:31 p.m.

The man died at the hospital, though his injuries were severe enough it's impossible to know whether he would have survived if he had arrived earlier.

Harnish called it a busy night, saying at the time of the call for the man's head injury there were 18 emergencies occurring at once. He declined to describe the priority levels of the other calls.

Ambulance delays have been a problem in Knox County and nationwide

Delayed ambulance response times, long emergency room waits and hard-to-access services are a problem nationwide.

AMR promised improvements from its previous performance, which gave it an edge over other competing providers when Knox County's contract was up for renewal early this year.

Response times improved in the first few months of the contract that kicked in Feb. 1, but didn't meet the contract's required 90% on-time arrival requirement. AMR was given a grace period of three months to improve response times before fines came into play, then racked up fines in May and June for late arrivals.

July was the first month when ambulances arrived on time at least 90% of the time across the county. AMR, according to reports to Knox County, was consistently on time until October.

AMR credited its improved response to two initiatives it started this year.

Nurse Navigation gets patients help from primary care, such as clinics, when an ambulance might not be the best option. Nurses can secure rides for patients or access to urgent care clinics.

AMR also piloted a program that uses trucks to drive a skilled paramedic to an injured or sick person while an ambulance with lesser-trained medical technicians arrives separately. There are two types of ambulances used in Knox County: advanced and basic. Advanced are equipped for life-threatening calls, while basic ambulances serve less serious calls classified as priorities 2 and 3.

Under the new program, a basic ambulance arrives at the scene once it becomes available and the paramedic who arrived first in the rescue truck can "upgrade" it to an advanced ambulance. That's dependent on AMR having enough paramedics working. If there aren't enough paramedics on duty, a KFD paramedic is the highest-level provider available. In that case, a KFD paramedic could upgrade the basic ambulance by riding it to the hospital.

That scenario, however, creates problems for the fire department. While a KFD paramedic is helping a patient, the fire crew the paramedic is part of has to remain out of service. If a fire occurs, that crew cannot respond.

headline: TDOT: Ask Congress for another $478 million so Tennessee's road projects aren't delayed
fullText:
UPDATE: This story has been updated with additional information from TDOT.

Tennessee Department of Transportation officials have asked lawmakers to lobby their federal counterparts for hundreds of millions of dollars to repair roads destroyed by Hurricane Helene.

Gov. Bill Lee, lawmakers and transportation officials have assured Tennesseans the state has the money it needs for the repairs and complete scheduled projects, but a Nov. 27 TDOT email obtained by USA TODAY Network-Tennessee paints a different picture.

The amount of work needed to fix roads and bridges in East Tennessee is daunting, U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger told Knox News.

"Several bridges and roads remain closed as TDOT continues to assess structural integrity and make the necessary repairs," said Harshbarger, a Republican from Kingsport who represents the eight counties hit by Helene. "Many counties are facing challenges with debris removal and have suffered significant damage to infrastructure that needs to be replaced."

State Rep. Jeremy Faison, a Republican from Cosby, said that although Tennessee received $32 million from the U.S. Department of Transportation to fix Interstates 26 and 40, that money is a drop in the bucket. TDOT estimates Tennessee will need $478 million more.

"The state just simply doesn't have the money for I-26 and I-40," he said.

The interstates are not just important to his constituents, Faison said. They're an economic "lifeline for Tennessee."

"Just about 40,000 people each day come down I-40," he said. "That's cut down to nothing right now; that impacts every bit of our revenue."

TDOT's plea to lawmakers

The email to state lawmakers from TDOT Director of Legislation Jay Klein says Tennessee needs $478 million from the federal government. He included a suggested message they can forward to senators and representatives in their plea for funds.

"As Congress debates funding relief for recent storms," TDOT's draft to lawmakers says, "we are asking you to please prioritize the remaining $478 million needed to restore Tennessee roads and bridges as a result of Hurricane Helene."

Faison told Knox News it's not possible for the state to pick up the cost of repairs up front, as Tennessee law requires. He thinks Tennessee will eventually get federal money but they're looking for expedited funds so regular road projects don't get delayed.

Tennessee's unique way of paying for road improvements, called "pay-as-you-go," requires the state to pay for any infrastructure projects up front instead of taking out debt like most other states do.

"To ensure any existing projects in the TDOT 10-Year plan are not affected, we are asking for the full reimbursement requested by the Federal Highway Administration," the suggested message says.

TDOT spokesperson Beth Emmons told Knox News the agency has already used money slated for 10-year plan projects to sign repair contracts for the State Route 107 bridge in Greene County, where traffic will return in June, and the State Route 81 bridge in Washington County.

"Without additional emergency funding being made available for reimbursement or additional appropriations, projects in our current 10-Year Plan could be negatively impacted due to the costs of recovery," Emmons said in an email.

TDOT's 10-year plan prioritizes and schedules road projects across Tennessee. It includes updating the Interstate 75 interchange at Emory Road in Knox County.

Faison hinted lawmakers should reprioritize projects in the wake of Helene.

"We're not a rubber stamp for the administration when it comes to the budget," he said. "We have the authority to also weigh in heavily. When we move into session this year, you will see a push from those of us in East Tennessee to direct some of those funds to recovery efforts in East Tennessee."

The other projects can be categorized as planned improvements versus the immediate needs to fix East Tennessee roads and bridges that washed out, Faison said.

"We still have seven bridges that still have to be built."

Allie Feinberg reports on politics for Knox News. Email her: allie.feinberg@knoxnews.com and follow her on X, formerly known as Twitter, @alliefeinberg.

headline: Your income is the key to winning the fight with student loan debt | Dave Ramsey
fullText:
Q. I have $100,000 in student loan debt. Since the amount is so large, is there a special place in your Baby Steps plan for it? 

A. I hope you have a nice, large income with which to fight that big pile of student loan debt. I’ve seen even worse situations, though. I’ve talked to people who went $200,000 into debt for a four-year degree in a field where they’ll make $45,000. Yes, that kind of thinking and behavior is out there, and it’s ridiculous.

The fact that it’s a large amount of student loan debt doesn’t change anything. Baby Step 2 is where you pay off all debt except for your home. So, don’t let this student loan debt hang around for years and years. You’ve got to get focused and intense about getting control of your money. That means living on a strict, basics-only monthly budget. After that, start throwing every nickel and dime you can scrape together, and save toward paying off those student loans as fast as possible.  

Your income is your largest wealth-building tool. You can’t save, and plan for the future, when all your money is flying out the door to pay off debt.

Q. My wife and I are completely debt-free, and we’re saving up for our first house. We currently have about $140,000 in savings, and we’d like to buy a home with cash when the time is right. Where should we put our money, so it will work for us while we save more?

A. If I were in your shoes, and maybe looking at a window of three or four years, I’d just park the cash in a good money market account. You won’t make a lot off it, but your money will be safe. I mean, all you’re looking for is a smart place to stash it for a little while. 

When it comes to long-term investing, I’m a big fan of growth stock mutual funds. The problem with that in your situation would be the volatility of the market. By the time you’ve saved up more money, and spent time deciding on a house, the market may be down. 

You two are in a great place financially right now. With the path you’re on, just imagine how incredible it will be in a few years to have a new home and be debt-free! 

Dave Ramsey is an eight-time national bestselling author, personal finance expert and host of The Ramsey Show. He has appeared on Good Morning America, CBS This Morning, Today, Fox News, CNN, Fox Business and many more. Since 1992, Dave has helped people take control of their money, build wealth and enhance their lives. He also serves as CEO for Ramsey Solutions.

headline: 'We're some dogs': Lady Vols show what they're made of in close win over Florida State
fullText:
Talaysia Cooper saw the open Florida State player and knew where the ball was going. She sprinted to the corner and took flight.

Cooper smacked the ball into the stands as soon as Amaya Bonner released the 3-point shot. The crowd at Food City Center erupted. She followed with a 3-pointer, a jump shot and a steal, fueling a run that allowed Tennessee to build a 20-point lead in the first half.

But the lead was erased by Florida State in the third quarter and the game went down to the wire. And Cooper once again fueled the Lady Vols when it mattered most.

The redshirt sophomore guard scored 12 of her 22 points in the fourth quarter, lifting Tennessee to a 79-77 win over the Seminoles (8-2) in the SEC/ACC Challenge on Wednesday. It was a significant win for Tennessee (6-0), which beat its first power conference opponent of the season.

"It just gives us energy," junior forward Zee Spearman said of Cooper. "You see the whole bench went crazy. I feel as if once she gets going, the whole team goes behind her. And it's like, we all can see that, and we all follow her."

Spearman was the only other Tennessee player to score in the fourth quarter, with 10 of her 13 points. She got active on the boards to score putbacks and drove inside to get to the rim instead of settling for 3-pointers. Spearman also hit the game-winner, draining a fadeaway jumper to give Tennessee the two-point lead with 24 seconds left.

Spearman's jumper wasn't the look the Lady Vols were looking for, but coach Kim Caldwell was glad she took the shot.

"She was poised. She was under control. She believed in it," Caldwell said. "She had some huge offensive rebounds for us down the stretch, too. I think our offensive rebounding in that fourth quarter won us the game."

The Lady Vols scored six second-chance points and had eight of their 23 offensive rebounds in the fourth. They outpaced FSU in second-chance points 19-6 and outrebounded it 50-39.

Sophomore forward Alyssa Latham was a key contributor off the bench, with nine points, seven rebounds and a block in 17 minutes.

"If we get (Spearman) and Alyssa going, it's going to be a hell of a season," Cooper said. "Not many people can guard that, to be honest."

Caldwell expected the matchup with Florida State to be a game of runs as both teams wanted to push the pace. But things almost fell apart completely for Tennessee in the third quarter when it couldn't get a stop and the Seminoles put up 30 points.

Caldwell called a timeout halfway through the third when FSU was on a 17-2 run. Ta'Niya Latson, who scored 38 points, had just stolen the ball from Cooper and hit an open layup without a single Lady Vols player running back to try to stop her.

Caldwell believed the team "quit a little bit" for a moment. After the third quarter, with the score tied 57-57, she reminded her team that this wasn't unexpected. Now it was about who wanted it more in the final 10 minutes.

RECRUITING: Why Lady Vols recruiting revival under Kim Caldwell is significant for the future of program

"We didn't just melt and pout and quit and panic," Caldwell said. "We just continued to be resilient, which is big, and the more we can see that, the better. And (Cooper) was a really good example of that. She was frustrated, she was frustrated, she was frustrated, and then she got over it . . . She was just able to get through it because she wants to win."

The win over Florida State was important for Tennessee. Not just because it was the first power conference opponent and not just because it closed out a tight win. It showed exactly what this team is made of.

"We're some dogs," Latham said. "We not going to stop playing, we're a very resilient team . . . You can see we have a lot of chemistry, we have fun while we're playing. So it's going to be a really great season."

headline: Knox County Schools pulls 48 books from libraries under new Tennessee law: See the list
fullText:
Correction: This story has been updated to remove the reference to all books in the list being fiction. Some books are nonfiction.

Knox County Schools leaders have identified 48 books the district will pull from its libraries and classrooms to follow a new state law.

Schools have until winter break to remove the titles.

The Age-Appropriate Materials Act of 2022 was amended this year to require schools to remove materials containing nudity or descriptions of sexual excitement, sexual conduct, excess violence or sadomasochistic abuse, according to state obscenity laws.

The 2022 law requires each public school library to publish the list of materials in their collections and periodically review them to make sure they are "appropriate for the age and maturity levels of the students who may access the materials."

It also requires each local board of education and public charter school governing body to adopt a policy to establish procedures for the development and review of school library collections.

Which books will be pulled from Knox County Schools?

Here are the books that will be removed:

Books removed from elementary schools

  • "There's Going To Be A Baby" by John Burningham
  • "Draw Me A Star" by Eric Carle
  • "In A Glass Grimmly" by Adam Gidwitz
  • "In The Night Kitchen" by Maurice Sendak
  • "A Light in the Attic" by Shel Silverstein
  • "The Way We Work" by David Macaulay

Books removed from middle schools

  • "The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian" by Sherman Alexie
  • "13 Reasons Why" by Jay Asher
  • "Just Listen" by Sarah Dessen
  • "Attack on Titan Vol. 2" by Hajime Isayama
  • "Mrs. Peregrine's Home For Peculiar Children - Graphic Novel" by Ransom Riggs
  • "You: The Owner's Manual for Teens" by Michael F. Roizen
  • "The 57 Bus" by Dashka Slater
  • "Everything, Everything" by Nicola Yoo

Books removed from high schools

  • "Me, Earl, & The Dying Girl" by Jesse Andrews
  • "Go Ask Alice" by Anonymous
  • "Chopsticks" by Jessica Anthony
  • "Girls on the Verge" by Sharon Biggs Waller
  • "Perks of Being A Wallflower" by Stephen Chbosky
  • "A Stolen Life" by Jaycee Duggar
  • "The Carnival of Bray" by Unknown Author
  • "Lighter Than My Shadow" by Katie Green
  • "Water for Elephants" by Sara Gruen
  • "Locke and Key: Alpha & Omega" by Joe Hill
  • "Locke and Key: Clockworks" by Joe Hill
  • "Locke and Key: Welcome to Lovecraft" by Joe Hill
  • "Identical" by Ellen Hopkins
  • "Tricks" by Ellen Hopkins
  • "The Kite Runner" by Khaled Hosseini
  • "Grown" by Tiffany D. Jackson
  • "DUFF" by Kody Keplinger
  • "The Walking Dead: Book Ten" by Robert Kirkman
  • "Gender Queer" by Maia Kobabe
  • "Monstress, Vol. 2: The Blood" by Marjorie Liu
  • "Last Night at the Telegraph Club" by Malinda Lo
  • "Empire of Storms" by Sarah J. Maas
  • "Tower of Dawn" by Sarah J. Maas
  • "Wicked" by Gregory Maguire
  • "Sold" by Patricia McCormick
  • "The Bluest Eye" by Toni Morrison
  • "Skin" by Ted Dekker
  • "Out of Darkness" by Ashley Hope Pérez
  • "Forgive Me, Leonard Peacock" by Matthew Quick
  • "Beautiful" by Stacy A. McGillen
  • "I Am Not Your Perfect Mexican Daughter" by Erika L. Sánchez
  • "Blankets" by Craig Thompson
  • "Squad" by Maggie Tokuda-Hall
  • "Slaughterhouse Five" by Kurt Vonnegut

Five of these books ‒ "Tricks" by Ellen Hopkins, "The Bluest Eye" by Toni Morrison, "Sold" by Patricia McCormick, "Identical" by Ellen Hopkins, "Empire of Storms" by Sarah J. Maas ‒ were among the 11 most banned books nationwide in the 2022-23 school year.

Book bans spread across the country

Nationwide, since 2021, school boards have discussed and even implemented book bans, often involving books that have sexual references or LGBTQ+ or race-related issues.

A majority of the targeted books were written by or about a person of color, a member of the LGBTQ+ community or a woman, according to reports released from the American Library Association and PEN America, a free speech advocacy group.

What is the process for selecting books in Knox County Schools?

The district follows state guidance on educational materials. When a district needs new books in a specific content area, administrators refer to state-approved lists of textbooks and materials. They have to choose from that list, Assistant Superintendent of Academics Keith Wilson told Knox News.

How did we get here?

Separate from the changes in state law, Knox County Board of Education's leadership has been looking at banning certain books over the past year.

Earlier this year, school board chair Betsy Henderson asked Superintendent Jon Rysewyk for his staff to make a presentation on the process for challenging books and how librarians select books for schools.

headline: Crews contain three wildfires on a windy day near Great Smoky Mountains National Park
fullText:
Firefighters battled multiple brush fires on a windy day in Sevier County.

The county adjacent to the Great Smoky Mountains National Park is under an "elevated fire danger" warning. Fires near Wears Valley, Gatlinburg and Seymour are contained.

Walden’s Creek near Shagbark: Fire has grown to 81 acres. Crews asked Sevier County Electric System to temporarily pause power service to the Shagbark community to keep one fire from spreading. That fire is 100% contained, according to Waldens Creek Fire Department.

Multiple fire departments assisted Sevier County with the fire. The scene was turned over to the State of Tennessee Forestry Division for monitoring.

Flat Branch Road/Spur between Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge: Fire is estimated to be 5 acres and crews are fighting hot spots. Tennessee's fire response page says the Flat Branch Road fire is 100% contained as of 11:30 a.m.

Creswell Road/East Union Valley near Seymour: Crews are extinguishing hotspots. It was 8 and a half acres and is now contained.

"Sevier County emergency officials announced that all three brushfires across the county are now 100% contained," a Sevier County Government news release said.

Drivers are asked to stay away from the areas for safety and to let crews through.

Foothills Parkway West between Walland and Wears Valley is now open, Great Smoky Mountains National Park officials announced around 2:30 p.m. Dec. 5. The road had previously been closed due to a nearby wildfires.

East Tennessee will experience wind chills that will drop into single digits in higher elevations and in the teens in lower elevations through Dec. 10, according to the National Weather Service in Morristown. Cold, dry air is moving into the area and temperatures are expected to drop.

“We are deeply grateful for the bravery and dedication of the emergency personnel who worked tirelessly to contain these fires under extremely challenging conditions," Sevier County Mayor Larry Waters said in a news release. "Their professionalism and commitment to protecting our community are truly commendable.”

There have been no injuries or structural damages that have been reported with these three fires according to a Sevier County Government Facebook post.

Get fire warnings

Sevier County Emergency Management Agency suggests downloading the CodeRED Mobile Alert app for fire warnings:

"Due to windy and dry conditions and low humidity, the fire Danger is HIGH. No Burn permits are being issued for today," Walden Creek Volunteer Fire Department said on Facebook.

headline: Mulling Tennessee playoff game while waiting on David Sanders to sign
fullText:
Tennessee got good news in the College Football Playoff picture and on national signing day this week.

But it’s hoping for much better news on both fronts in the coming days. Penn State losing and David Sanders signing could help with that.

On this week's podcast episode of "The Volunteer State," UT beat writer Adam Sparks and columnist John Adams break down the Vols' final scenarios in the playoff, including who they’ll play and where. And they look back on the win over Vanderbilt that earned UT’s way into the 12-team bracket.

Plus, a review of signing day raises some big questions. Will Sanders, the No. 1 offensive tackle in the 2025 class, sign with the Vols? And what's the future hold for blue-chip quarterback George MacIntyre?

To hear the full discussion, listen to the podcast. But here are a few highlights.

Will David Sanders sign? Will George MacIntyre start after Nico?

If Sanders signs with Tennessee, as expected, he should compete to play immediately. If something goes awry in his signing, it would be a major loss to the Vols, and their only consolation would be a bigger budget to spend NIL money on transfers.

Nevertheless, UT needs to sign Sanders sooner than later.

VOLS SIGNING CLASS Tennessee signs QB George MacIntyre, waits on 5-star David Sanders

As for MacIntyre, Sparks believes he'll follow the path of other highly-rated quarterbacks under Heupel. He'll eventually earn the starting job or transfer elsewhere. Tayven Jackson, Nico Iamaleava and Jake Merklinger have faced that same situation.

Could Penn State fall in CFP and play Tennessee?

Tennessee's last hope of hosting a College Football Playoff game depends on a blowout in the SEC or Big Ten title games.

But even if those blowout losses occurred, the CFP selection committee might not drop the losing teams behind Tennessee in the rankings. There's probably a greater chance that a championship game loser falls in the rankings but only changes Tennessee's opponent.

No. 2 Texas (11-1) plays No. 5 Georgia (10-2) in the SEC championship game on Saturday (4 p.m. ET, ABC). No. 1 Oregon (12-0) plays No. 3 Penn State (11-1) in the Big Ten championship game on Saturday (8 p.m., CBS).

Adams thinks the likely scenario is that Tennessee plays Penn State in the first round. Adams and Sparks discussed the likelihood of other scenarios.

Have Vols turned the corner just in time for playoff run?

Iamaleava played his best SEC game in the Vols' 36-23 win over Vanderbilt.

Does that mean he's turned a corner? Maybe.

Sparks said Iamaleava has gained confidence and comfort in the offense, and he's playing at a higher level. But UT fans should be cautiously optimistic, keeping in mind Vanderbilt's pass rush was almost nonexistent against Iamaleava.

Sparks and Adams believe Tennessee can win at Ohio State or Penn State or certainly against either team at Neyland Stadium, if it got a home game. But the matchup won't be easy. Both Big Ten teams tout a strong defense.

Again, to hear the full discussion, listen to this episode of "The Volunteer State."

headline: University of Tennessee officer, former Knoxville cop, arrested for Peeping Tom, stalking
fullText:
A University of Tennessee police officer was fired and arrested Dec. 4 after fleeing police in Georgia, who were seeking to arrest him on charges of Peeping Tom and stalking.

Anthony Rizo turned himself in to UTPD on Wednesday morning at the department's request. He had been wanted by the Paulding County Sheriff’s Office. The arrest warrant says Rizo knowingly and willfully fled from Georgia.

Rizo drove to Dallas, Georgia, about 35 miles northwest of Atlanta, on Nov. 29 to the home of a man he believed to be in a relationship with Rizo's estranged wife, according to the arrest warrant. Rizo texted the man, telling him to open the door, and then looked through the windows of the man's home as he played a video game. Rizo's intent, said the warrant, was to harass and intimidate the man.

Peeping Tom is a felony charge in Georgia. Rizo will be extradited to Georgia.

Rizo worked at UTPD for seven months and was fired Dec. 4 before he was arrested. He was not on duty when he drove to Georgia, according to spokesperson Ryan Moore. Rizo previously was employed at the Knoxville Police Department from March 2021 to May 2024 and the Metro Nashville Police Department before that.

“We have high expectations for the behavior of our officers both on and off duty,” UTPD Chief Sean Patterson said in a statement to Knox News. “His alleged behavior does not reflect the values of our agency, and he is no longer employed by our agency.”

There are dozens of pending court cases in Knox County tied to arrests Rizo made as an officer. Assistant Knox County District Attorney Sean McDermott did not immediately respond to questions about how the district attorney’s office will handle those cases.

In 2023, Rizo was recognized by Mothers Against Drunk Driving with a silver enforcement award for making 55 DUI arrests in 2022, according to a post on X by KPD in June 2023.Tyler Whetstone is an investigative reporter focused on accountability journalism. headline: Tennessee football transfer portal tracker: Updates on who's in, who's out for Josh Heupel
fullText:
Tennessee football lost more players than it added in the transfer portal following the 2024 season, but it was active in both directions.

Eighteen UT players entered the portal, including 13 on scholarship. And the Vols added four players.

The spring portal is open April 16-25 for new players entering it. Players cannot transfer from one SEC school to another school during the spring portal window, per conference rule.

Here's a look at who left Tennessee from the 2024 team and who was added for the 2025 roster, with the latest announcements at the top of the list.

Players added by Tennessee football in transfer portal

Offensive lineman Sam Pendleton (Notre Dame)

Notre Dame transfer Sam Pendleton started the first seven games of the 2024 season at guard for the Fighting Irish and served as a backup in the College Football Playoff.

Pendleton, a 6-foot-4, 310-pounder, has three seasons of eligibility remaining. In 2023, he played two games as a freshman and took a redshirt. In 2024, he played 13 games, including half the season as a starter at left guard. He also practiced at center at Notre Dame, which makes him a candidate to play multiple positions for the Vols.

Pendleton was a four-star recruit in the 2023 class, according to 247Sports Composite. He is from Lawsonville, North Carolina, located about 260 miles east of Knoxville, and he attended UT’s junior day event as a recruit in January 2022.

Running back Star Thomas (Duke)

Duke transfer Star Thomas is a veteran running back and an all-purpose producer with more than 2,500 yards from scrimmage and 22 TDs in his Division I college career. He led Duke in rushing with 871 yards and seven TDs last season. He also made 20 receptions for 153 yards and one TD.

Thomas has one season of eligibility remaining, which he recently regained when the NCAA Division I Board of Directors granted a blanket waiver for an additional year of eligibility to former junior college transfers.

Thomas played one season at Coffeyville Community College. Then he transferred to New Mexico State, where he accounted for 1,529 yards from scrimmage In 2023, Thomas was named All-Conference USA second team alongside NMSU teammate Diego Pavia, now Vanderbilt’s quarterback. During that 2023 season, Thomas had 653 yards rushing, 200 yards receiving and six total TDs.

Wide receiver Amari Jefferson (Alabama)

Alabama transfer Amari Jefferson took a redshirt in 2024. The 6-foot, 197-pounder was a standout at Baylor School in Chattanooga. He chose Alabama over Georgia and Tennessee out of high school. He also originally committed to play baseball at Tennessee in 2021 before he started getting recruited heavily for football.

Jefferson was a four-star recruit ranked No. 212 in the nation and No. 5 in the state of Tennessee in the 2024 class by 247Sports Composite. He was the TSSAA Division II-AAA Mr. Football in 2023.

Offensive guard Wendell Moe (Arizona)

Arizona transfer Wendell Moe was an All-Pac-12 selection as a redshirt freshman in 2023. And he played 760 snaps as an anchor on the Wildcats' offensive line in 2024. He started three games in 2022 but took a redshirt.

Moe, a 6-2, 339-pounder, started 27 games over three seasons at Arizona, mostly at left guard but also at right guard. He should fill immediate need on UT's offensive line, which must replace as many as four starters.

Tennessee football players leaving via transfer portal

Linebacker Kalib Perry (Louisville)

Kalib Perry announced on Dec. 30 that he was entering the portal, and he committed to Louisville on Jan. 6. The junior had been in the rotation the last two seasons. In his UT career, Perry recorded 61 tackles ,2.5 tackles-for-loss, two blocked punts and one forced fumble in 37 games.

Perry has one season of eligibility remaining. The 6-3, 231-pounder from Georgetown, Kentucky had his most productive season at UT in 2024, recording 26 tackles in 12 games. He started against Florida, Alabama and Ohio State in the College Football Playoff.

Wide receiver Squirrel White (Florida State)

Squirrel White announced on Dec. 27 that he entered the portal, and he committed to Florida State on Jan. 5. He has been one of UT’s most productive receivers of Josh Heupel’s tenure. He had 131 receptions for 1,665 yards and six TDs over three seasons.

The 5-foot-10, 167-pound slot receiver led the Vols with 803 yards receiving in 2023. But his production dropped to 34 catches for 381 yards and two TDs in 2024. White, a native of Birmingham, Alabama, has one season of eligibility remaining.

Tight end Holden Staes (Indiana)

Holden Staes announced on Dec. 26 that he was entering the portal, and he committed to Indiana on Jan. 9. The 6-4, 248-pounder spent two seasons at Notre Dame and then the 2024 season at UT. He had 15 receptions for 131 yards and one TD for the Vols in 2024. Staes has one season of eligibility remaining.

Quarterback Gaston Moore

Walk-on Gaston Moore announced on Dec. 26 that he planned to enter the portal. The 6-2, 212-pounder took a redshirt at UCF in 2020. He transferred to UT as a walk-on in 2021 and spent four seasons as a serviceable backup quarterback for hte Vols. He has one season of eligibility remaining.

Moore was 26-of-44 passing for 273 yards, two TDs and three interceptions in 14 games during his UT career.

Tight end Charlie Browder

Walk-on Charlie Browder announced on Dec. 26 that he planned to enter the portal. He enrolled at ETSU. The 6-7, 255-pound walk-on spent the 2021 season at UCF. Then he played the past three seasons at UT. He had two catches for 10 yards and played six games for the Vols.

Defensive end Jayson Jenkins (Florida State)

Jayson Jenkins announced on Dec. 23 that he entered the portal, and he committed to Florida State on Jan. 5. The 6-foot-6, 281-pounder was part of UT's deep rotation on the defensive line in the 2024 season. He had nine tackles, 3.5 tackles-for-loss, two sacks, one forced fumble and one safety in the most productive season of his career.

Jenkins, a native of Bordentown, New Jersey, was a three-star recruit in the 2022 class. He played 20 games over three seasons with the Vols. He took a redshirt in 2022, so he has two seasons of eligibility remaining.

Defensive back Christian Harrison (Cincinnati)

Christian Harrison announced on Dec. 22 that he was entering the portal, and he committed to Cincinnati on Jan. 9. Harrison is a 6-foot-1, 191-pounder from Atlanta. He played 26 games with four starts over three seasons at UT. He took a redshirt in 2023, so he has two seasons of eligibility remaining.

Harrison made 33 tackles, including three for loss, in his UT career. He started at nickelback early in the 2024 season after projected starter Jourdan Thomas suffered a season-ending injury in preseason practice. But by midway through this season, Boo Carter, an SEC All-Freshman performer, moved ahead of Harrison in the rotation.

His father, Rodney Harrison, was a two-time All-Pro, two-time Super Bowl champion and a member of the New England Patriots Hall of Fame as one of the top safeties of the past 30 years.

Running back Cam Seldon (Virginia Tech)

Cam Seldon announced on Dec. 14 that entered the portal, and he committed to Virginia Tech on Dec. 29. He played 19 games over two seasons at UT. He rushed for 224 yards and one TD on 48 carries, including 55 yards in the Citrus Bowl to finish the 2023 season. And he added 113 yards as a kick returner.

Seldon entered spring practice as RB2 behind Dylan Sampson. But he suffered a shoulder injury, underwent surgery in March and rehabilitated over the summer. He never regained his place in the rotation.

Seldon, a 6-foot-2, 222-pounder, is from Browns Store, Virginia. He was a four-star recruit and ranked the No. 5 athlete in the 2023 class by 247Sports Composite. He has two seasons of eligibility remaining.

Tight end Luke Shouse

Walk-on Luke Shouse entered the portal on Dec. 13. He spent two seasons at Ole Miss and the past two seasons at UT. The 6-6, 250-pounder did not appear in a game in the 2024 season.

Wide receiver Nate Spillman (Charlotte)

Walk-on Nathan Spillman announced on Dec. 12 that he plans to enter the portal, and he enrolled at Charlotte. He is the older brother of UT freshman linebacker Edwin Spillman.

Nate Spillman took a redshirt as a freshman in 2023. He played three games in 2024, playing a combined 14 snaps against Chattanooga, NC State and Kent State. Spillman was a three-star recruit from Nashville in the 2023 class, and he has three seasons of eligibility remaining.

Wide receiver Nathan Leacock (Purdue)

Nathan Leacock announced on Dec. 12 that he was entering the portal, and he committed to Purdue on Jan. 6. Leacock, a 6-3, 220-pounder from Raleigh, North Carolina, was a four-star recruit in the 2023 class. But he has been buried on the depth chart the past two seasons.

Leacock played in six games for the Vols. In 2023, he played in the UConn game. In 2024, he played in five games and made one catch for 13 yards against Chattanooga. He has three seasons of eligibility remaining.

Wide receiver Chas Nimrod (South Florida)

Chas Nimrod entered the portal on Dec. 11, according to his social media post, and he committed to South Florida on Jan. 4. The redshirt sophomore played 27 games with starts over three seasons. He made 29 catches for 315 yards and one TD in his career.

The versatile Nimrod plays slot receiver and outside receiver. In 2023, he made five starts as the Vols dealt with injuries to outside receivers. In 2024, he mostly served as Squirrel White's backup at slot receiver.

Nimrod is a 6-3, 202-pounder from Bentonville, Arkansas. He was a three-star recruit in the 2022 signing class. But he took a redshirt in 2022, so he has two seasons of eligibility remaining.

Quarterback Ryan Damron (Stephen F. Austin)

Walk-on Ryan Damron announced on Dec. 7 that he was entering the portal, and he committed to Stephen F. Austin on Jan. 9. He spent two seasons at Tennessee, and he has three seasons of eligibility remaining. He took a redshirt in 2023 and played in one game against Kent State in 2024.

Damron, a 6-foot, 205-pounder, was a record-breaking passer at Henry County High in Paris, Tennessee. He was a three-star prospect in the 2023 class.

Linebacker Jalen Smith (Mississippi State)

Jalen Smith announced on Dec. 6 that he entered the portal, and he committed to Mississippi State on Dec. 19. The 6-foot-2, 230-pound Smith made 34 tackles in 12 games this season. The redshirt freshman is from Grayson, Georgia, and has three years of eligibility left. He appeared in five games as a freshman.

He was a three-star prospect in the 2023 class.

Cornerback Jordan Matthews (Vanderbilt)

Jordan Matthews announced on Dec. 6 that he'll enter the portal. On Dec. 18, it was reported that Matthews committed to Vanderbilt. The 6-2, 182-pound Matthews was a backup cornerback this season. The redshirt freshman is from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and has three years of eligibility left. He appeared in five games as a freshman.

He was a four-star prospect in the 2023 class.

Wide receiver Kaleb Webb (Maryland)

Kaleb Webb announced on Dec. 5 that he was entering the portal. He committed to Wake Forest on Dec. 11 and then flipped his commitment to Maryland on Dec. 17 after Wake Forest coach Dave Clawson resigned.

Webb, a Powder Springs, Georgia, native, caught 28 passes for 214 yards and one TD in the past two seasons. He took a redshirt in 2022 and has two seasons of eligibility remaining.

The 6-3 Webb had 16 receptions for 166 yards and one TD as a redshirt freshman in 2023 for his best season. He was a four-star prospect in the 2022 class.

Running back Khalifa Keith (Appalachian State)

Khalifa Keith announced on Dec. 4 that he entered the portal, and he committed to Appalachian State on Dec. 28. The Birmingham, Alabama, native played in 16 games in two seasons at UT. That included 12 games in 2023 and four games in 2024, which means he qualifies for a redshirt and has three seasons of eligibility remaining.

Keith, a 6-1, 239-pounder, rushed for 124 yards and one TD on 32 in his UT career. He also caught one pass for 8 yards. Keith was a three-star recruit in the 2023 class, according to 247Sports Composite.

Offensive lineman Vysen Lang (Troy)

Vysen Lang announced on Dec. 3 that he entered the portal, and he committed to Troy on Jan. 13. The Pike Road, Alabama, native played nine games in his UT career, and he has three seasons of eligibility remaining.

Lang, a 6-4, 340-pounder, served as a backup center and guard for the Vols. He was a three-star prospect in the 2023 class, according to 247Sports Composite.

headline: UPDATE: Kidnapped Virginia children found safe in Alabama
fullText:
The Augusta County Sheriff’s Office in Virginia announced the arrest of Shanice Davison on three counts of child abduction at 7:18 p.m. Dec. 5.  

“The Alabama Highway Patrol and US Marshall Service took Davison into custody in the Birmingham area of Alabama after a brief pursuit on I-495,” reads a Facebook post by the department. “Davison was taken into custody without incident. All three children were safe and unharmed.”

The Amber Alert for the three children was lifted after they were found.

EARLIER: 3 children abducted in Virginia might be in East Tennessee, in 'extreme danger,' TBI says

Davison is described as 35 years old, 5'6", 184 pounds, with black hair and black eyes. They are possibly traveling in a black newer model Nissan Sentra with an unknown tag, according to Virginia State Police.

Both of the girls were wearing pink jackets, and Jai’Marcus was wearing a black and dark blue jacket with neon zippers.

headline: David Sanders, No. 1 tackle in class, signs with Tennessee football despite Ohio State push
fullText:
David Sanders, the No. 1 offensive tackle in the 2025 recruiting class, signed with Tennessee football on Thursday, ending a delay that stressed Vol fans.

Sanders had long been the No. 1 target of the Vols in this 2025 recruiting class. But he didn't sign with UT's other 24 signees Wednesday, the first day of the early signing period.

Well, the wait is over. Sanders is a Vol, he announced on "The Paul Finebaum Show."

"I just feel like they separated themselves very easily and just being around the program, it was easy to connect with their coaches, connect with their players, and connect with their recruiting class," Sanders said..

The 6-foot-6, 270-pound Sanders is a five-star recruit and the No. 5 overall prospect in the 2025 class, according to the 247Sports Composite. He plays at Providence Day School in Charlotte, North Carolina, where the Vols have had recruiting success under coach Josh Heupel.

Tennessee's No. 2 rated signee in its top-10 class is also from the Tar Heel state. Four-star defensive lineman Isaiah Campbell is from Durham, North Carolina.

TRACKING TENNESSEE'S NO. 1 RECRUITS Hits and misses, from Nico Iamaleava to Eric Berry

Tennessee withstood threat of Ohio State flipping David Sanders

Sanders had been committed to the Vols since Aug. 17. And he visited Tennessee multiple times this season and was on hand in Charlotte for the Vols' 51-10 win over N.C. State on Sept. 7.

Ohio State made a late push to flip Sanders, which included the tackle visiting the Buckeyes for their 38-15 win over Indiana on Nov. 23.

But Tennessee kept Sanders as the gem of Heupel's 2025 signing class. He signed on Thursday and plans to enroll early in January.

Sanders could have a chance to play immediately. Left tackle Lance Heard is projected to return next season, but he'll likely be the only starter back on the offensive line in 2025.

Sanders could compete for the right tackle spot with Larry Johnson, Jesse Perry, Bennett Warren and others.

headline: Why David Sanders Jr. took a last-minute visit to Ohio State before signing with Tennessee
fullText:
David Sanders Jr. didn't feel any pressure to visit other schools after he committed to Tennessee football in August.

But the five-star offensive tackle said he did feel he needed one more look at Ohio State before locking in his future as a Vol.

"I felt like the decision to go to Ohio State was a big one for me and my family," Sanders said Thursday on the "Paul Finebaum Show." "They were very close when it was time to go to Tennessee, when I picked them in August. Ohio State was right behind them.

"I felt it was only right to give them one more shot just to make sure I had made my decision and this was firm on where I wanted to be."

Sanders visited Ohio State for the Buckeyes' 38-15 win against Indiana on Nov. 23, less than two weeks before early signing day. He signed with Tennessee on Thursday, a day after the start of the early signing period.

The 6-foot-6, 270-pound Sanders is the No. 5 overall prospect in the 2025 class, according to the 247Sports Composite. He plays at Providence Day School in Charlotte, North Carolina. He committed to Tennessee on Aug. 17 at which point she said other schools "were very respectful of my decision."

Tennessee signed 25 players in the 2025 class, including 11 on offense and 14 on defense. There are 13 four-star prospects in the class.

Sanders is the top-ranked prospect in Tennessee's class, which he finished off Thursday when he joined the class instead of flipping to Ohio State.

"I appreciate (the OSU) coaching staff just like I appreciate the Tennessee coaching staff because they did a phenomenal job recruiting me as well," Sanders said.

headline: Eagles vs Panthers predictions: Our picks vs spread. Can Saquon Barkley, Birds escape trap?
fullText:
PHILADELPHIA − The Eagles are coming off an emotional and hard-fought win over the Baltimore Ravens, and they should have an equally emotional and hard-fought game next Sunday against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Technically, the Eagles don't have a bye this week, although they are playing the 3-9 Carolina Panthers, a week before they face the Steelers, the AFC North leaders with a 9-3 record.

So this could be the ultimate trap game. After all, the Eagles are 10-2, on an eight-game winning streak, and they can clinch a playoff spot with a win and losses by two other teams.

BORING NICK? How Nick Sirianni went from 'Fire Nick!' to 'boring', saving Eagles season and his job

RECORD PACE: How Eagles Saquon Barkley can set NFL single-season rushing record − and what can stop him

The Eagles have the NFL's rushing leader in Saquon Barkley, who's on pace to break Eric Dickerson's single-season rushing record of 2,105 yards, set 40 years ago. Barkley, who averages 125 rushing yards per game, is also 109 yards away from breaking the Eagles' single-season rushing mark of 1,607 yards set by LeSean McCoy in 2013.

And oh by the way, the Panthers have the NFL's worst rushing defense, allowing 167 yards per game.

So it would be easy to look past the Panthers and start focusing on the Steelers.

But Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said that's not happening. He said the players eagerly passed up "Victory Monday" in order to get some work in.

"I think that would be malpractice by us as coaches and as players if we were up for some games, but not up for some games," Sirianni said. "If you take anybody lightly in this league, it will humble you fast ... Our job each and every week is to be focused on the job at hand, and lock in every single week."

Besides, look past the Panthers at your own peril. They're 2-3 in their last five games. Their last two games were a 3-point loss to two-time defending Super Bowl champ Kansas City Chiefs and a 3-point overtime loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

With that said, the Eagles are favored by 12.5 points, according to BetMGM. So we decided to pick against the spread this week to make things interesting.

Here is how we see the game going:

Our prognosticators are Martin Frank (Eagles beat writer/columnist, Delawareonline.com), Greg Giesen (sports strategist, Delawareonline.com), Tom McGurk (sports editor, Courierpostonline.com), Tom Moore (sports columnist, Phillyburbs.com), Bob Jordan (sports editor, app.com), Bert Bainbridge (sports betting analyst & columnist, Northjersey.com), Tom Haines (Pennsylvania state planning), Brad Myers (high school sports writer, Delawareonline.com), Kevin Tresolini, (college sports reporter, Delawareonline.com), Michelle Ganassi (audience director & die-hard Steelers fan, Delawareonline.com), Shane Brennan (New Castle County reporter, Delawareonline.com), Tom Rimback (sports writer, Courierpostonline.com), Brandon Holveck (high school sports reporter, Delawareonline.com)

Martin Frank

Panthers quarterback Bryce Young, the No. 1 pick in the 2023 draft, is finally starting to play like a − well, not exactly a top pick − decent QB. In the five games back since he was benched, Young has thrown for 1,082 yards yards, 6 TDs and only 3 INTs for a passer rating of 83.5. But Young hasn't faced a defense like the Eagles' top-ranked unit.

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 37, Panthers 22

Greg Giesen

The Eagles lost to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers by a lot. The Panthers lost to the Bucs by three. The transitive property of equality says that Carolina should beat Philly. The transitive property is wrong in sports.

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 42, Panthers 13

Tom Rimback

Phillies great Mike Schmidt − you young bucks should google him − never said it better when asked about the Philly Media (us): "Philadelphia is the only city where you can experience the thrill of victory, and the agony of reading about it the next day."

Watching the 2024 Eagles has a similar vibe. You see how terrible these Iggles are playing, then you look up and they've somehow dominated the game.

The pick: Panthers

Score: Eagles 31, Panthers 25

Bert Bainbridge

The Panthers have shown more fight since picking up their second win of the season in Week 9 against the Saints. They've taken the reigning Super Bowl champion Chiefs to the wire Week 12 and nearly pulled off the upset over the Bucs this past weekend in an overtime loss.

Make no mistake, this will be Carolina's toughest road test of the entire season against an Eagles team on a eight-game winning streak.

Bryce Young and the Panthers keep this one competitive for longer than people anticipate, but Jalen Hurts and Co. ultimately pull away and get back to their normal groove of scoring 28-plus points.

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 31, Panthers 17

Brad Myers

This is a perfect opportunity for a good team to do what good teams do: hammer bad teams. The Eagles need to keep it rolling by thrilling their fans on the way to a 35-7 halftime lead and cruise from there.

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 42, Panthers 21

Tom McGurk

The Eagles haven't been great at Lincoln Financial Field this season, and the Panthers have picked up the pace with four straight competitive games in November. Look for the Birds to jump out to a big lead and take the foot off the gas. They'll get a worry-free W but the Panthers cover.

The pick: Panthers

Score: Eagles 23, Panthers 12

Tom Moore

The Eagles should win their ninth straight, but they won't quite cover the 12.5-point spread.

The pick: Panthers

Score: Eagles 30, Panthers 20

Bob Jordan

Eagles for the win, but the two-score point spread is too rich for me.

The pick: Panthers

Score: Eagles 30, Panthers 20

Michelle Ganassi

All eyes will be on Saquon Barkley, who will be inching toward the NFL rushing record. And I think he will be putting up big numbers. The Eagles will cover the spread and then some. And they should enjoy it as next week they have a tall order vs the Steelers

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 33, Panthers 13

Tom Haines

Should be an easy one in which the Eagles get to sit some starters in the fourth quarter, delaying Barkley's assault on the rushing record.

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 34, Panthers 17

Kevin Tresolini

A week after Thanksgiving, the Eagles should still be feasting. The Panthers are not nearly good enough to thwart the Eagles and their momentum, ensuring the Birds will gobble up another emphatic win.

The pick: Eagles

Score: Eagles 31, Panthers 13

Brandon Holveck

The Eagles beat the Baltimore Ravens without playing to their full capability on offense. The Panthers pose a greater threat this week than they would have a month ago, but the Eagles are the far superior team. They win and cover.

The pick: Eagles

headline: Saquon Barkley: The old-school way Eagles doubled down to help him set NFL rushing record
fullText:
PHILADELPHIA − The move itself was but a blip on the NFL's transaction wire when the Eagles signed fullback Khari Blasingame to the practice squad on Tuesday.

Blasingame had been out of a job since the Chicago Bears released him Oct. 25.

Make no mistake, that old-school move was made for Saquon Barkley, who is 109 yards away from breaking the Eagles' single-season rushing record of 1,607 yards, set by LeSean McCoy in 2013. He's also 607 yards away from breaking the NFL's single-season rushing record of 2,105 yards, set by Eric Dickerson in 1984.

Granted, the Eagles didn't make the move so Barkley can break rushing records. They did it to win games, even though the Eagles haven't had a player listed as a fullback play in a game for them since Stanley Havili in 2012.

That's because Barkley is a much more effective runner with a fullback, a position that has mostly become obsolete in the NFL.

RECORD RUN: How Eagles Saquon Barkley can set NFL single-season rushing record − and what can stop him

PLAYOFF BOUND? How Eagles can clinch NFL playoff berth on Sunday. When can they win NFC East title?

This season, the Eagles have used linebacker Ben VanSumeren in the fullback role more and more as the season has gone along. That is, until VanSumeren tore his ACL in practice last week and went on injured reserve.

So the Eagles used tight end Grant Calcaterra as a fullback last Sunday against the Baltimore Ravens. That is, until starting tight end Dallas Goedert suffered a knee injury in the fourth quarter.

Goedert is not expected to play this Sunday against the Carolina Panthers, meaning that Calcaterra will be the top tight end. So the Eagles signed Blasingame, who could get a practice-squad elevation for the game Sunday.

"We’re averaging a lot of yards in that (fullback) package," Barkley said. "I’m sad to see Ben go down. Ben went out there and gave us his all every single play − at (a position) he’s never done before. It goes back to buying in and doing what it takes for the team to win games.

"Now, for me as a running back, it helps because even if (an offensive lineman) gets beat at the line of scrimmage, or there’s (a defender) there early, (the fullback) can pick up and cover for me. It just makes my job a lot easier. I’m excited to have (Blasingame) here."

The Eagles started using VanSumeren as a fullback on Oct. 20 against the Giants. VanSumeren helped spring Barkley for a 41-yard run that day. In all, VanSumeren got in for five offensive plays against the Giants, leading to 60 rushing yards for Barkley.

Barkley had 176 yards rushing in the Eagles' 28-3 win over the Giants.

VanSumeren was also cited for helping to spring Barkley during his franchise-record 255-yard rushing game in the Eagles' 37-20 win over the Rams on Nov. 24. Barkley had TD runs of 70 and 72 yards that day.

"I think what it's done is give another layer for the defense to have to pay attention to," Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said. "I'm not going to get into the scheme of it, why it's been helpful for us. But one of the benefits is the layer that it gives the defense to have to defend, and have to spend time on, and have to study.

"It’s been pretty productive for us this year. I haven't been on a team that we've utilized the fullback in quite some time."

Barkley has, during his early years with the Giants when they had Elijhaa Penny, a 6-foot-1, 250-pound battering ram from 2018, Barkley's rookie year, through 2021.

"I’ve had a lot of success with it," Barkley said.

The fullbacks, of course, are not on the field to carry or catch the ball. For the Eagles, they're on the field to block − for Barkley.

Blasingame, for example, has 13 catches for 99 yards and 11 rushes for 32 yards in six seasons with the Tennessee Titans from 2019-21 and Bears from 2022 through this season.

Blasingame knows this. That's why he signed with the Eagles.

“Just the opportunity," he said. "The role was expanded as far as fullback. It was the opportunity to play."

Calcaterra got a sense of that too, getting five snaps at fullback against the Ravens. Calcaterra said his objective was simple:

"At fullback, it’s important to just be decisive because Saquon is going to make a guy miss," Calcaterra said. "You want to make it clear for him where his opening is going to be. So based on how they line up, I know which guy I'm going to block.

"If I go in there and dance in the hole, it kind of slows (Barkley) down a step. So go out there, be decisive, try to hit them hard, and spring him."

It's that simple.

headline: Delaware Day 2024: Logan Paul and other unusual First State connections to pop culture
fullText:
Delaware might seem like a mythical place to some, and for good reason.  

The state’s contributions to pop culture and its broader impact on the world are often so unexpected, they feel stranger than fiction. 

We've highlighted just a few unusual things you might not know about the First State in celebration of the annual Delaware Day, a holiday that returns Saturday, Dec. 7. 

What is Delaware Day?  

This holiday celebrates Delaware becoming the first state to ratify the federal Constitution in 1787. But it wasn't until 1933 that governors of Delaware started proclaiming Dec. 7 as Delaware Day, per Delaware.gov.   

Jake Paul beat former Delaware athlete before Mike Tyson  

It's no secret that YouTuber Jake Paul made headlines on Nov. 15 by defeating boxing legend Mike Tyson in a Netflix fight that became the most streamed sporting event in history, with an estimated 65 million viewers tuning in, according to Netflix. But here's a Delaware twist many may not know: Paul's second professional fight, once his most hyped, was against a former player for the Delaware Blue Coats. 

On Nov. 28, 2020, Paul knocked out Nate Robinson, a moment widely remembered by fans of the fight. However, non-basketball enthusiasts might not realize that Robinson played 17 games for the Blue Coats (formerly the Delaware 87ers) during the 2016-17 season. Before his time in Delaware, Robinson was best known for his 11-year NBA career across multiple teams, and as a three-time Slam Dunk Champion with the New York Knicks. 

Oddly enough, the Robinson and Paul bout was an undercard fight. The headlining match was between Roy Jones Jr. and Mike Tyson. The rest has been (strange) history.

Monopoly was created by a woman in Delaware  

The origins of the famous board game Monopoly are rooted in Delaware, where it was essentially created in the early 1900s by a woman named Elizabeth ''Lizzie'' Magie.  

Magie, who was influenced by Henry George's book "Progress and Poverty," spent time in Arden where she worked on a board game called The Landlord's Game, according to the Henry George Institute. Her game was approved for a patent on Jan. 5, 1904. The Landlord's Game eventually evolved into what the world knows now as Monopoly. This year marks the 120th anniversary of Magie securing her patent. 

Delaware man created Heimlich maneuver 

Once upon a time, a surgeon from Delaware created a famous technique that would save many lives. Henry Heimlich is the icon who invented the Heimlich maneuver, a throat-clearing method he popularized in 1974. The technique involves applying sudden pressure on the upper abdomen of a choking victim in order to force them to spit out whatever is stuck in their throat. The surgeon passed away on Dec. 17, 2016. He was 96.

How Delaware became first state to ban child marriage  

It’s easy to assume child marriage has been outlawed in Delaware for over a century, but that’s not the case. The First State made history on May 9, 2018, when Gov. John Carney signed a law banning child marriage for anyone under 18 — no exceptions, even with parental consent. This made Delaware the first state in the U.S. to completely outlaw the practice. 

Between 2000 and 2011, state health records revealed that 200 minors were married in Delaware, most of them girls, according to the Associated Press. The landmark 2018 law marked a significant step in protecting minors’ rights. 

Delaware Blue Coats wear Power Ranger jerseys 

Basketball players often are compared to superheroes, but it's rare to see them dressed like one during a game. That changed on March 17, 2017, when the Delaware Blue Coats — then known as the Delaware 87ers, the NBA G League affiliate of the Philadelphia 76ers — hosted a Nickelodeon-themed night at the Bob Carpenter Center in Newark, Slam reported. 

Nate Robinson and the squad hit the court in pink jerseys inspired by the "Mighty Morphin Power Rangers." Robinson, who dropped 18 points, and the Blue Coats defeated the Salt Lake City Stars in a score of 113-111. After the game, the autographed, game-worn pink jerseys were reportedly set to be auctioned off, with proceeds benefiting the nonprofit March of Dimes.

Small Wonder gift idea: You can now get your low-digit Delaware black-and-white tag on a customizable coffee mug

Delaware State Fair reveals 2025 stars: Taylor Swift won less Grammys than one star who is coming

Jerry Seinfeld teased Delaware company's Gore-Tex

Comedian Jerry Seinfeld's iconic sitcom "Seinfeld" once took a playful jab at Newark-based company W.L. Gore & Associates, famed for its weatherproof Gore-Tex fabric. In the episode titled "The Dinner Party," which aired on Feb. 3, 1994, George (Jason Alexander) proudly sported a new Gore-Tex coat his father bought from a friend.  

The coat’s extreme puffiness became the butt of jokes for Jerry and Elaine (Julia Louis-Dreyfus). The pair even began slapping George’s chest and arm to test if he could feel it through the bulky material.  

What isn't funny is how much money W.L. Gore & Associates has made. The company started out in the basement of a Newark home owned by Wilbert “Bill” and Genevieve “Vieve” Gore in 1958. According to Gore.com, the global enterprise is among the 200 largest privately held U.S. companies and generates $4.8 billion in annual revenues.
