headline: Edge rushing to Rutgers: Salesianum football star RJ Johnson heads to Big Ten program
fullText:
BEAR – RJ Johnson had so many people at his college football signing ceremony, cars spilled into the Food Lion parking lot across the street.

Dozens of family, friends, teammates and coaches came to the Greater Newark Boys & Girls Club on Wednesday night to celebrate the Salesianum star’s signing with Rutgers.

The 6-foot-5, 250-pound edge rusher has been competing in football and basketball since age 6. He became more serious about football a couple of years ago and ramped up the workouts and intensity, and it landed him in the Big Ten.

“Over the years, I just gained a passion for it,” Johnson said. “I took the opportunity, and now I’m here signing to go to college for three or four years and we’ll see what happens from there.”

The NFL could be down the road, Salesianum football coach Gene Delle Donne believes.

“The way he projects … he could be 6-5, 280 tomorrow once he starts working out in a Big Ten setting,” Delle Donne said.

BLUE HENS See who they are: Delaware move to CUSA in FBS reflected in star-studded recruiting class

Johnson also received interest from Penn State, West Virginia, Notre Dame, Syracuse and Minnesota. But the Scarlet Knights and coach Greg Schiano were most persistent, and that made the difference.

“I liked Rutgers because they were consistent with me,” Johnson said. “The coaches, I built a great relationship with them. I like the staff and all the players.”

Delle Donne said Schiano and Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman visited Salesianum, walked the halls and met students. Penn State coach James Franklin landed near Abessinio Stadium in a helicopter on Oct. 18 to watch the first half as the Sals defeated Appoquinimink 21-7.

Franklin was also there to watch Appo junior receiver Jahsiear Rogers and sophomore offensive lineman Layton von Brandt, both of whom have committed to the Nittany Lions. But Johnson put on the biggest show that night, hemming in Rogers at the 10-yard-line on an early play that turned into a fumble recovered by Jayvian Burrell for the game’s first touchdown.

Later, Johnson had a sack, broke up a pass 15 yards downfield and batted down another throw at the line of scrimmage.

“The exposure he brought to our program, I’ll forever be in debt and forever be grateful for what he did for us,” Delle Donne said of Johnson.

Johnson started basketball practice with the Sals on Monday, three days after a 30-27, overtime loss to Middletown in the DIAA Class 3A football championship game. He plans to enjoy his senior season of hoops at Sallies before enrolling at Rutgers.

Delle Donne said once Johnson flipped the switch to football, the sky was the limit.

“RJ was always a really good athlete,” the coach said. “We all know he’s a very good basketball player. He’s always been a talented edge guy. But the most impressive thing is his mentality the past year and a half. How he has really switched his mindset to now wanting to be a football player, especially a Big Ten football player.”

Johnson’s father, Robbie Johnson Sr., played basketball at the University of Delaware and encouraged his son – and others – to play more than one sport.

“If you’re a dual-sport athlete, keep it going because you don’t know which way it’s going to go,” Johnson Sr. said. “The coaches we talked to, when they found out he plays two sports, they loved it. They absolutely loved it.”

Among those in the crowd celebrating with Johnson was Jayden Taylor, the 6-foot-7 senior forward from Sanford who recently committed to play basketball at Delaware.

“Seeing all of these people, it means a lot to me,” Johnson said. “Just knowing you’ve got a great support system outside of football with family and friends, it means a lot.”

headline: From home tours to tree-lighting: Christmas in Odessa commemorates 60 years
fullText:
For many Delaware families, nothing captures the holiday spirit quite like Christmas in Odessa.

Led by the Women’s Club of Odessa, this annual tradition has sought to not only bring holiday joy but also find ways of bettering and preserving the history of the town and community.

And now, for its 60th anniversary, the club is set to mark this landmark year with something special for the community.

Here’s what to know about Christmas in Odessa and other events visitors can enjoy this holiday season.

Longwood Gardens: 5 things to know about the Christmas season 2024

What is Christmas in Odessa?

While the town has been around for centuries, the holiday tradition officially began in 1964.

Inspired by a similar tour three club members took in New Jersey – and created to help collect money for scholarships for students residing in the Appoquinimink School District – the club and several local homeowners presented the first-ever Christmas in Odessa.

The event allowed families and communities across Delaware to come inside public buildings and homes all dressed up for the holidays – many of which have been in Odessa for over a century – and learn more about the town and its history.

Along with fellow community members, sponsors and homeowners, the club has raised more than $300,000 in higher education scholarships for over 200 students, according to the Christmas in Odessa website.

While the event has changed over the years, for Women’s Club of Odessa president and Christmas in Odessa co-chair Carol K. Sheats, it is an opportunity to celebrate and see all that this “special town” has to offer, from homes along High Street to many of its most noteworthy sites up and down Main Street.

'A very special place'

To commemorate this milestone, the Women’s Club of Odessa will release a "60th Anniversary Christmas in Odessa'' coffee table book next month.  

Along with a written history of the annual fundraiser, the book contains 60 pages of “festive holiday decorations, time-honored family traditions and seasonal activities” readers can recreate with their loved ones during the holidays.

The book also contains several photos of Christmases in Odessa past, with a “sprinkling of all the years” that the event has taken place, from its first year up to 2023, according to the club’s marketing and social media representative Jane Mruk.

More holiday fun: Want to feel festive? These Delaware's historic house museums are decked out for Christmas

A limited number of books will be available for purchase on Saturday, Dec. 7 at the Historic Odessa Foundation Visitors Center.

For Sheats, what remains special about Christmas in Odessa is how it has been a family-centered event “right from the beginning.”

As for Mruk, who has “20 years’ experience” of attendance under her belt, this tradition holds “a very special place” in her and her family’s hearts.

She also hopes that this tradition continues to live on and become a “more family-oriented event,” in which family members, both old and young, can make holiday memories that will last a lifetime.

“That’s what’s cool about it,” Mruk said. “There’s something for every age group here.”

When is Christmas in Odessa this year?

Christmas in Odessa will take place Saturday, Dec. 7 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Seventeen public buildings and ten private homes will be open that day. Tickets are required for entry and can be purchased ahead of time online or same day.

In addition to the tours, featured events throughout the day will include Christmas concerts, tea and cookies and a tree-lighting ceremony on the Old Academy lawn to ring in the holiday season.

'Tis the season: Post office sets deadlines for Christmas packages; what to know

There will also be a fresh-cut greens sale at the Fieldstone Stable from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Where can you buy tickets?

Tickets can be purchased in person at the Historic Odessa Foundation Visitors Center through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

More information can be found at www.christmasinodessa.org/.

Other holiday happenings in Odessa

Several town partners will also have their own separate holiday-themed events on the same day as Christmas in Odessa.

The Historic Odessa Foundation presents its annual holiday exhibition through Sunday, Dec. 29, recreating scenes from J.M. Barrie's 1911 novel, "Peter and Wendy.''

Additional details can be found on the Foundation website.

From 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., the Corbit-Calloway Memorial Library will host a wide range of events on Dec. 7.

Features will include a hot chocolate bar, live music and entertainment and a cookie plate and ornament sale fundraiser.

Holiday lineup: A season of holiday magic and miniatures at Brandywine Museum of Art

The Odessa Fire Company Station 24 will host a vendors and crafts fair that same day from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Food will be provided from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

headline: Flights to Nashville will return to the Wilmington Airport in 2025. Here are the details
fullText:
A once-discontinued route out of the Wilmington Airport will return for the spring.

Avelo Airlines announced on Wednesday, Dec. 4, that flights between the Wilmington Airport and the Nashville International Airport would return for twice-weekly flights beginning May 1.

“We’re excited to announce the return of Avelo’s nonstop service to Nashville from Wilmington Airport,” said Avelo Airlines founder and CEO Andrew Levy. “Our customers have asked for its return and we listened. With 14 nonstop options, we continue to share Avelo’s low fares, travel-friendly convenience and industry-leading reliability with our Philadelphia / Delaware Valley customers.” 

Nashville was one of seven flights that had been seasonally suspended last November, to the dismay of passengers who enjoyed the cost and convenience of booking a weekend getaway from Delaware to the Music City.

With the addition of the route in May, Nashville will join 10 other routes that are available for booking through Labor Day 2025.

Here's what to know.

Avelo Airlines extends most, but not all, routes

Avelo Airlines announced on Nov. 26 that its service to 10 of its 13 current routes out of the Wilmington Airport will extend until Labor Day. Previously bookings could be made only until April 2025. 

Three of its current routes, West Palm Beach, Florida; Sarasota, Florida; and Daytona Beach, Florida, can still be booked only until the end of April. 

Courtney Goff, communications manager with Avelo Airlines, said those three routes are considered seasonal and will be reevaluated at a later date. 

All of the newly announced flight routes will fly out twice weekly and flight fares start at around $41, and can be booked online at AveloAir.com through early September.

What flights are available for booking?

Flights available until April:

West Palm Beach, Sarasota and Daytona, Florida are all available for booking between now and April, 2025, and will all be reevaluated, according to an Avelo Airlines representative.

West Palm Beach, Florida (PBI)

Flights to West Palm Beach will take off on Mondays and Fridays until the end of April. The frequency will slightly shift to Sunday and Friday the week of Feb. 16.

This route can only be booked through April.

Sarasota/Bradenton, Florida (SRQ)

Flights to Sarasota will take off on Wednesdays and Saturdays. There will be no flights available to this destination the week of Dec. 8 or from Jan. 5 to Feb. 11. After that, the Wednesday and Saturday schedule will continue until April 26.

This route can only be booked through April.

Daytona Beach, Florida (DAB)

Flights to Daytona Beach will take off Sundays and Thursdays between now and the end of April. The week leading up to Valentine’s Day, flights will slightly shift and take off Sunday, Wednesday and Friday. The week after this will have flights on Monday and Thursday.

This route can be booked only through April.

Flights available until September:

Ten other routes are available for booking between now and September, 2025, including the newly announced flights to Nashville, Tennessee.

Atlanta, Georgia (ATL)

Flights to Atlanta will be available Mondays and Fridays between now and the beginning of June.

Friday, June 13’s flight will be replaced by a Thursday flight the day before. The remainder of June will have flights on Sundays and Thursdays, which will extend until the end of August.

Charlotte/Concord, North Carolina (USA)

Flights to USA will be available Mondays and Fridays between now and the beginning of September.

Fort Lauderdale / Miami, Florida (FLL)

Flights to Fort Lauderdale will take off from ILG on Sundays and Thursdays until the end of August.

Tuesday flights will be available to Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 26, Dec. 3, Dec. 24, Dec. 31 and Jan. 7.

Fort Myers, Florida (RSW)

Fort Myers flights will take off on Sundays and Thursdays until late February. Beginning the week of Feb. 16, flights will take off Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday until the end of April.

Beginning May 2, flights will take off Fridays and Mondays until the week of June 9. A Thursday flight will begin June 12, and then follow a Sunday and Thursday pattern until the end of August.

Nashville, Tennessee (BNA)

Flights to Nashville will begin Thursday, May 1, 2025 and take off on Sundays and Thursdays until Aug. 31, 2025. 

Orlando / Lakeland, Florida (LAL)

Flights will fly from ILG to LAL on Sundays and Thursdays between now and the end of August.

Orlando, Florida (MCO)

Flights are available to MCO on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays between now and the end of April.

The week of Christmas and New Year’s, respectively, will replace their Wednesday flights with Tuesday flights (Dec. 24 and Dec. 31).

Beginning May 2, flight frequency will lessen and take off on Fridays and Mondays until the week of June 9. After this, flights will follow its original frequency pattern of Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday until Sept. 1. 

San Juan, Puerto Rico (SJU)

Flights to San Juan, Puerto Rico, the only flight available outside of the continental United States, will be available on Wednesdays and Saturdays until Dec. 21.

San Juan flights will briefly be shifted to Tuesday and Saturday between Dec. 24 and Dec. 31, and then continue to the Wednesday and Saturday frequency from January through Aug. 30.

Tampa, Florida (TPA)

Flights to Tampa, Florida will take off Mondays and Fridays between now and Sept. 1.

Other ways to use ILG

These routes aren’t the only way to fly through Delaware’s sole commercial airport.

In October, American Airlines’ shuttle bus service the Landline Co. partnered with ILG by launching a shuttle to Philadelphia International Airport. Customers can park, check their bags and go through security at ILG before taking off on a roughly 50-minute bus ride to Philadelphia Airport’s Terminal F. From there, people can disembark to their proper gates and board their flights. 

To use the service, customers can book a flight through the American Airlines website and select ILG as the origin airport before selecting the proper end destination. 

The booking time for your flight will coincide with the shuttle bus departure time from the Wilmington Airport to Philadelphia. The buses shuttle up and back six times per day on days that Avelo has flights taking off from ILG’s terminal.

Wilmington to Philadelphia schedule

  • Depart at 6:45 a.m., arrive at 7:35 a.m.
  • Depart at 8 a.m., arrive at 8:50 a.m.
  • Depart at 11 a.m., arrive at 11:50 a.m.
  • Depart at 1:30 p.m., arrive at 2:20 p.m.
  • Depart at 4 p.m., arrive at 4:55 p.m.
  • Depart at 6 p.m., arrive at 6:50 p.m.

Philadelphia to Wilmington schedule

  • Depart at 8:30 a.m., arrive at 9:20 a.m.
  • Depart at 10:30 a.m., arrive at 11:20 a.m.
  • Depart at 1:55 p.m., arrive at 2:45 p.m.
  • Depart at 3:35 p.m., arrive at 4:25 p.m.
  • Depart at 6:35 p.m., arrive at 7:30 p.m.
  • Depart at 8:45 p.m., arrive at 9:35 p.m.

Each bus seats 35 people and offers free WiFi and in-seat power for all passengers. American Airlines rewards members can also receive AAdvantage miles using the bus service. 

Howard Armstead, a Middletown resident, had just learned about the service when he booked his flight to Chicago for Monday, Oct. 7, and already made his mind up about the service.

"Very convenient. I will do this again," Armstead said. "I just appreciate that they have this out here - the easy parking, cheaper parking. It's also just not as busy as Philly."

Wilmington: Why Wilmington has – again – tabled plans to regulate the short-term rental industry

Delaware investing in ILG's future

Once Avelo Airlines first took off from the Wilmington Airport, Delaware’s days of being without commercial airlines completely turned a corner, even being ranked as one of the busiest airports during the holiday season. 

Since then, the state has invested millions into boosting the aging airport’s infrastructure and making travelers’ lives easier. Over 500 new parking spaces were added recently, and the airport’s terminal expansion broke ground in October. 

The renovated terminal will expand the building by 6,000 square feet, add concession options a TSA pre-check line and more. 

This is just one of the ongoing projects happening in ILG. The small airport also received a few million dollars from the federal government to expand one of its taxiways and bring it up to current Federal Aviation Administration standards.

headline: Did you know Delaware's state dog is not a specific breed? What it is and other state dogs
fullText:
With Brandywine Valley SPCA’s Mega Adoption event quickly approaching it might be a good time to remind Delawareans of the state canine — the rescue dog.

Yes  the "rescue dog" has been the official Delaware state dog since Gov. John Carney signed Senate Bill 37 into law in May 2023. The bill was introduced early last year by state Sen. Jack Walsh and was approved with a wide majority by the state's House and Senate.

While it's not known if the legislation, which was expected to help save rescue animals, has done just that, a Brandywine Valley SPCA spokesperson said the law has put a focus not only on dogs but all animals in need of rescue.

"That just elevates all animals in shelters," said Sara Smith, a Brandywine Valley SPCA spokesperson.

Hundreds of pets in the four-state area will be looking for homes for the holidays as part of Brandywine Valley SPCA’s (BVSPCA) December Mega Adoption Event, which will take place at all BVSPCA locations and other regional participating shelters throughout Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey and Maryland.

The Mega Adoption Event will take place from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Dec. 14 and 15. Dogs, cats, puppies and kittens at all participating shelters will be available for adoption for a $35 throughout the event.

Before designating rescue dogs as the official state dog of Delaware, it used to be a golden retriever.

More: So long, golden retriever. Delaware has new official state dog

Nearly 20 states have an official state dog. Unlike Delaware, most of those are specific dog breeds.

But the First State is not alone in having a state dog that can be just about any breed. Others states whose state dogs are not breed-specific are Georgia, New Jersey and New York.

State dogs

Not every state has an official dog. In fact, less than half of the United States have assigned a breed.

Here is a list of states that have state dogs.

headline: Video shows state police officer kick man's head during arrest; lawsuit claims assault
fullText:
Body camera video associated with a newly filed federal lawsuit shows a Delaware State Police officer kicking a man in the head while other officers restrain him on the ground.

Matthew Jester filed a lawsuit in Delaware District Court on Monday, claiming officers assaulted him during a December 2022 arrest near Milton.

In a written statement, a spokesperson for Delaware State Police declined to comment on the case, citing the pending litigation. They added that an administrative review, "based on all of the facts available at the time," judged that the officers involved acted within policy.

In the middle of the night, police were dispatched to what was reported as a man with a knife trying to burglarize a home in West Rehoboth, according to police reports.

State police tried to stop Jester as he fled the home's driveway in his truck. He led police on a pursuit that ended near Milton after officers successfully punctured his tires, according to police records.

Body camera footage his attorney linked inside the lawsuit complaint shows officers approaching his truck and demanding he place his hands outside.

He complied and was ordered out of the truck. He was put face-down on the ground as an officer gripped the back of his jacket and others piled on, video footage shows.

Two seconds after he is on the ground, an officer the lawsuit identifies as Brandon Triantos approaches and kicks him in the side of his head, the body camera footage shows.

"They have my guy, he is giving himself up and, at that point, the kick is just unnecessary and egregious," said Ron Poliquin, a Dover attorney representing Jester.

Recent: Dover police broke a woman's leg, will now pay six-figure settlement

The lawsuit claims that Jester was posing no threat while Triantos “jams his knee” on Jester’s neck and head. The lawsuit claims that other officers “assisted in the assault” while “hitting, pushing and holding” Jester down while Triantos “continually struck” him with “kicks and knee strikes.”

The video, recorded on another officer’s body camera, shows an initial kick. After that, it's hard to discern what exactly is happening in the subsequent second that elapses as Jester is cuffed.

Why the Delaware officer said he used this force

In a police report authored by Triantos and shared with Delaware Online/The News Journal by Poliquin, Triantos said he intended to kick Jester in the torso.

He claims he didn’t know Jester had shown his hands to officers as he surrendered and that he believed he was trying to flee toward the rear of the vehicle. He also wrote that he believed Jester was reaching for a weapon and so he “administered one leg strike to the area of his upper torso.”

“The kick missed my intended target and struck (Jester) in the upper left side of his head,” Triantos wrote.

He claims in the police report that Jester was not allowing officers to cuff him, so he “administered several knee strikes” to his “upper torso in the area of his shoulders.” He wrote that Jester continued to “struggle” so “several knee strikes by officers involved struck (Jester) in the top of the head."

"I think that explanation is completely contradicted by the video," said Poliquin, Jester's attorney.

In his report, Triantos, who was the nominee out of his downstate troop for the statewide Trooper of the Year award for that same year, wrote that officers found what police commonly describe as drug paraphernalia, as well as several empty beer cans and a knife in Jester’s truck. In documents and the body camera footage, they also described him as “highly intoxicated.”

Jester was arrested and taken to a local hospital. Body camera footage shows that the left side of his face, near where the kick landed, was red. The other side of his head appears bloodied.

Recent: Former Delaware State Police officer sentenced to prison for assault on teens

“Y’all (expletive) bashed me, (expletive) me up for nothing,” he told officers at the hospital, according to the body camera footage.

The lawsuit also accuses an officer of misrepresenting the source of his injuries. The officer can be heard telling hospital staff: “When he got out of the car, he went face first into the ground and the deck and here we are,” apparently referring to a deck attached to a home he crashed near.

“In actuality, plaintiff did not connect with the deck. (The officer) tellingly omits that Corporal Triantos kicked plaintiff multiple times,” the lawsuit states.

Jester was charged with a raft of crimes but ultimately pleaded to a sixth-offense DUI, failure to stop for police signal, resisting arrest, endangering the welfare of an officer and violation of probation, court documents state.

He was sentenced to two years in prison. The court docket indicates he agreed to a treatment program as part of his sentence. He was also assessed $2,750 in various court fines and restitution.

Poliquin concedes that his client led police on what he described as a "goose chase," but said that doesn't give them license to use "excessive force" by booting his head.

"They are only allowed to use enough force as necessary to secure the guy. Clearly, that wasn’t the case here, no matter what he did before," Poliquin said.

Without that standard, "you turn the police force into a rogue operation where they can set their own rules," he said.

Delaware prosecutors responsible for investigating some uses of force by police said they were not aware of the case, according to a written statement by Mat Marshall, a spokesperson for Attorney General Kathy Jennings.

The lawsuit names five officers involved in the arrest as defendants.

In a written statement, state police spokesperson India Sturgis said that “every use of force incident” goes through an administrative review. In Jester’s case, the department determined the troopers acted “in compliance” with state police policy and remain on duty.

She emphasized that "encounters with individuals suspected of committing serious crimes and fleeing and attempting to elude law enforcement often create dynamic and unpredictable circumstances."

Another noteworthy police kick

Triantos' explanation that he simply misplaced his kick is the same defense used by former Dover police officer Thomas Webster, who was captured on video kicking a 29-year-old man in the head as he appeared to be obeying an officer's orders to get on the ground after a foot chase.

The kick, caught on police dashcam video, knocked Dickerson out cold and fractured his jaw. Dickerson had fled from another officer who was breaking up a fight. He later agreed to a $300,000 settlement to dismiss his lawsuit against the city and officers.

Recent: Woman's arrest by New Castle County officers captured on social media under investigation

Prosecutors charged Webster with felony assault. At trial, he testified that his kick was aimed at the man's body. His attorney argued his kick was reasonable to bring the man into custody. A jury acquitted Webster.

He was paid $230,000 to separate from Dover police. Greensboro Police Department in Maryland's Easter Shore hired him. There, he and three other officers forcibly subdued Anton Black, a black teenager, for multiple minutes before he stopped breathing and later died.

headline: When are Hobby Lobby and Mission BBQ coming? New updates reveal progress
fullText:
Hobby Lobby in Prices Corner has an opening date … kind of.

After Delaware Online/The News Journal reported in April that the arts & crafts giant would take over the space above Target at 3240 Kirkwood Highway, original reports slated the opening for fall of this year.

Meanwhile, the retailer’s location in Middletown’s Northside Shopping Center has been in the works for over a year, with a projected opening in “early 2025.”

Half an hour up the road, Mission BBQ is gearing up to open its fourth Delaware location in the coming months, with some visible progress being made on its construction.

Here’s what to expect from the upcoming locations and a look into Mission BBQ's progress.

When are Hobby Lobby locations coming?

Diane Gudahl, special project manager with Hobby Lobby, confirmed that the Prices Corner location is estimated to open “right after Christmas.''

It’s not an official date for those hoping to shop soon, but it’s something.

Plans for the Prices Corner Hobby Lobby started last year when the Prices Corner Shopping Center signed a lease with the retailer.

The craft store giant will take over the former Sears space located above the Target in the shopping center. The space may look obscure from the outside, but an escalator to the left of the Target entrance will transport customers to the nearly 60,000-square-foot space Hobby Lobby will occupy.

Hobby Lobby also plans to open its fourth Delaware location in Middletown’s Northside Shopping Center at 465 Middletown Warwick Road.

The over-50,000-square-foot building will sit next to the new Target and share a parking lot with the Sprouts Farmer’s Market, which celebrated its grand opening on Friday, Dec. 6.

Delaware Online first reported the new location’s opening in October, estimating the opening date in early 2025. According to Gudahl, there are no further updates about this opening date.

When Hobby Lobby opened its first Delaware locations in Dover and Christiana, customers swarmed the aisles with fervor.

Hobby Lobby is known for its wide-ranging arts and crafts supply, with home décor, trendy and seasonal party decorations, floral arrangements and materials for various DIY crafts like beading, knitting, scrapbooking and more.

Hobby Lobby has over 1,000 stores across the country. There are two Hobby Lobby locations in Delaware, located at 59 University Plaza in Christiana and 101 N. Dupont Highway in Dover.

Typical store hours for Hobby Lobby stores are Monday through Saturday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., and stores are closed on Sundays.

Existing Hobby Lobby stores will operate with shortened hours on Christmas Eve, from 9 a.m. until 5:30 p.m., and will be closed on Christmas Day. On New Year’s Eve and New Year’s Day, the store will also operate from 9 a.m. until 5:30 p.m.

More openings: Delaware will soon have a new Chick-fil-A. Here are the details

When will Mission BBQ open?

Another chain people are excited to see open is the planned Mission BBQ coming to Kirkwood Highway.

First reported by Delaware Online in early 2022, the location was not confirmed by the store until late 2023. A quick drive past its planned location at 4433 Kirkwood Highway shows that the location is making significant progress on its construction, but the chances of its originally planned 2024 grand opening seem slim to none.

A representative at Mission BBQ did not respond to inquiries about its opening date. Correspondence between Delaware Online and a representative from the barbecue chain in April of this year stated that no timeline was available for the chain’s opening.

The Milltown location will be Delaware’s fourth location and the Wilmington area’s second.

Its most recent opening at the Concord Gallery shopping center in Talleyville in August 2023 also caused lines to form around the building to get a taste of the chain’s signature brisket, pulled pork and barbeque entrees.

headline: This new Italian American restaurant is opening soon near Delaware state line
fullText:
A new Italian American restaurant is opening Friday, Dec. 6 in the Shoppes at Brinton Lake in Glen Mills, Pennsylvania, just over the Delaware state line.

Testa Rossa Glen Mills has taken over the site that Ruby’s Diner formerly occupied at 919 Baltimore Pike. It's across from White Dog Cafe Glen Mills in the same shopping center.

The concept is from Fearless Restaurants, which also operates the landmark Moshulu Restaurant on Penn's Landing in Philadelphia; White Dog Cafe in University City, Wayne, Haverford, and Glen Mills, Pennsylvania; Louie Louie in University City; Autograph Brasserie and Rosalie in Wayne; and on Daddy O Restaurant & Hotel and Tuckers Tavern on Long Beach Island, New Jersey.

Testa Rossa means redhead in Italian. The menu focuses on homemade pizza, pasta and Italian favorites such as selections of salumi, Italian meat products, cheeses and salads. There are 180 seats indoors including booths and a large center bar, and an additional 100 seats outside on the patio.

“We romantically embrace Italian culinary technique while unapologetically breaking all the 'rules' we just don’t feel like following,” said Culinary Director Merick Devine, who also leads the kitchen at Fearless Restaurants’ Rosalie Wayne.

He said the menu includes meat, fish, and vegetables prepared simply along with desserts such as soft-serve gelato, "floats" made with Chinotto, a bubbly, bittersweet, orange-flavored Italian beverage, and tableside tiramisu.

The restaurant has been designed by Wayne-based Stokes Architecture +Design and incorporates "a mid-century Italian maximalist allure" with 1960s-inspired bold patterns and geometric prints.

A horseshoe-shaped pink marble bar top has round pedestal stools with green leather seats and triangular black-and-white printed backs. Brass shelving spans the back bar while high-gloss red finished display cases flank the bar.

The restaurant has U-shaped booths in blue flame-stitch fabric with silver pinecone table lamps, custom upholstered banquettes, custom-designed patterned tabletops, and scalloped chairs with vibrant colors of orange, emerald, canary yellow, black, and white. Scalloped lemon-colored umbrellas and rattan banquettes are on the outdoor patio.

Chef Devine, a graduate of the Culinary Institute of America in Hyde Park, New York, formerly served as the Executive Chef at White Dog Cafe in Wayne.

Before that, he was chef de cuisine at Frasca Food and Wine in Colorado for over six years. The restaurant was nominated twice for a prestigious James Beard Award as one of the country's most Outstanding Restaurants.

headline: Meet Wilmington authors of 'Accidentally Wes Anderson' & get a free book this weekend
fullText:
If you've wanted a copy of "Accidentally Wes Anderson: Adventures," the new follow-up to the New York Times bestseller by Delawareans Wally and Amada Koval, this is for you.

New Castle County libraries will host the couple Sunday, Dec. 8 at 2 p.m. at Brandywine Hundred Library (1300 Foulk Rd., Brandywine Hundred) for a discussion about the book ($45, Voracious), which will be given out for free while supplies last.

Register for the event here.

The book's October release came four years after the debut of "Accidentally Wes Anderson," which sold more than 500,000 copies.

Spun off their successful string of "Accidentally Wes Anderson" social media pages (most notably Instagram), it was filled with real world spots that mirror the fanciful, highly stylized movie universes created by Academy Award-winning film director Anderson ("The Grand Budapest Hotel," "Rushmore," "The Royal Tenenbaums," "Asteroid City.") 

The new 354-page book builds off the same foundation, bringing the reader along as they highlight 200 new destinations with an Anderson aesthetic from around the globe, telling more detailed stories behind them this time.

MORE ON THE NEW BOOK Wilmington couple enlists Jeff Goldblum & director Wes Anderson for bestselling follow-up

FLASHBACK WALLY Q&A 'Accidentally Wes Anderson': With millions of followers worldwide, quirky site has Delaware roots

Some of the entries are from the Kovals themselves ― including a feature on the U.S. Post Office in Lewes ― but most come from contributors from around the world.

"The book is multi-layered. You can flip through it and look at the pretty pictures or it could just be something cool on your coffee table," Wally told Delaware Online/The News Journal earlier this year. "And if you really want to get into it, you can dig in and find these really interesting fun facts about places that you've heard of or some that you didn't know even existed."

Wally, a Salesianum School graduate, and Amanda, a St. Elizabeth School graduate, first met in Dewey Beach before getting married. They began their Anderson projects while living in New York, but have since moved back to Wilmington. 

“We are thrilled to welcome Amanda and Wally back to New Castle County,” New Castle County Executive Matt Meyer said in a press release announcing the event. “These two unique individuals have found ways through their social media platforms, and now their books, to connect with our inner-adventurer and bring us closer to the world around us. More importantly, they’ve inspired us to explore, each and every day.”

headline: Man charged with rape, murder after woman found dead in Wilmington, police say
fullText:
A 26-year-old man has been charged with rape, murder and several other charges in connection with a September assault of a woman in Wilmington's West Center City, police said.

Kyle Batson of Bear was arraigned Wednesday and is being held in prison. He had been extradited from Maryland, where he was arrested on Sept. 12 for charges unrelated to the assault − though his arrest came the same day 44-year-old Myeshia Triplett was found.

According to Wilmington police, officers were dispatched to the 700 block of Catawba St. just before 9:45 that morning for a death investigation. There, they found Triplett dead.

Four days later, an autopsy confirmed Triplett had been killed, police said. While the department did not provide a cause of death, Batson is charged with strangulation.

INITIAL STORY: Wilmington police say 44-year-old woman was killed during assault in Center City

Detectives identified Batson as the suspect, and in addition to murder and strangulation, charged him with two counts of rape − first and second degree − and abuse of a corpse. He's being held in prison on nearly $2 million cash bail.

Who was Myeshia 'Muffy' Triplett?

Triplett, who went by "Muffy," was born in Wilmington in June 1980, according to her obituary.

She was known for "her deep passion for art, creativity, and her devotion to God, family, friends, and her community," the obituary said. It added that she had "a unique gift for connecting with others, whether through storytelling or creating art."

This "brought joy to her life and to those around her," the obituary said.

"Her sudden loss has left a void that can never be filled, but her legacy of love, creativity, and laughter will continue to live in our hearts," the obituary said.

Batson had criminal history

Court records show that Batson is no stranger to the criminal justice system, with cases dating back to at least 2018.

Some of his previous arrests were for robbery, burglary and gun offenses.

In September 2023, he was also charged with escape after conviction for walking away from a Department of Correction work crew he'd been assigned to in Sussex County. DOC said he'd been working along Route 13 near Laurel.

He was found "nearby" after a "brief search," DOC said last year.

headline: When is President Joe Biden's last day on the job? What's next for him
fullText:
President Joe Biden has said he is "not going away" after leaving the White House next month.

Last month, President-elect Donald Trump was declared the winner of the 2024 presidential race, defeating current Vice President Kamala Harris and securing a second term in office.

And now, with Trump making preparations to assume the role of commander in chief in a few weeks, soon-to-be outgoing President Biden has been getting ready for a post-presidential transition.

Here’s what to know.

47th President: When does President-elect Donald Trump take office? Here's what we know

When is Inauguration Day?

Inauguration Day is scheduled for Monday, Jan. 20, 2025.

The ceremony will be held at the U.S. Capitol building in Washington.

The day will also include several events, such as the swearing-in of President-elect Donald Trump and Vice President-elect J.D. Vance and Trump's inaugural address.

When does Biden leave office?

President Biden will officially leave office that same day, on Jan. 20, 2025.

Following President-elect Trump’s inaugural address, the then-outgoing president and first lady will make their honorary departure.

What will Biden do after leaving office?

Biden said he intends to continue working with several programs on domestic and foreign policy matters post-presidency.

According to Biden, this will include the University of Delaware’s Biden Institute in Newark and the Penn Biden Center for Diplomacy and Global Engagement in Washington, D.C.

Previous reports found that the Biden administration is working on finalizing plans before Trump assumes office, including work on infrastructure, climate change and Ukraine aid.

headline: They want 'innovative solutions.' 5 Delaware schools vie for $100K in Samsung STEM contest
fullText:
Five Delaware public schools were just named state finalists in a national technology contest.

Student teams from middle and high schools were chosen from thousands of U.S. entries, according to the Samsung Solve for Tomorrow STEM Competition, and lie among 300 fellow state finalists. They'll each land $2,500 technology package. And soon, the contest will sharpen to three national winners – and a $100,000 prize package.

The 15th annual competition asked students to utilize the power of STEM to "create innovative solutions addressing critical issues in their local communities." In a press release, organizers said this year's finalists highlight common concerns among young minds nationwide: the climate crisis, mental health and wellness and school safety.

Delaware's finalists were:

  • Caesar Rodney High School in Camden
  • MOT Charter High School in Middletown
  • Millsboro Middle School in Millsboro
  • Newark Charter School in Newark
  • Charter School of Wilmington, with two teams, in Wilmington

One familiar name didn't hit the list this year.

Brandywine High School had gone back-to-back. Last year, students from Brandywine were named national winners in the 14th annual STEM competition – the same national title another team from the school clinched the year before. Students Olivia Erskine, Katherine McDerby, Isabella Chermak and Malti John, alongside STEM teacher Sean Merklin, led a 2023-24 project that has redesigned classic board games to accommodate players of all abilities.

The team won the $100,000 prize package with Samsung products and classroom resources that year. They also scored the new Rising Entrepreneurship award, receiving an additional $25,000 prize.

The school didn't participate this year, according to a district spokesperson.

Now, five other schools in Delaware will try to follow that act.

Schools that advance will be producing videos explaining their projects, progress and vision for Samsung Solve for Tomorrow. By April, more details and national winners will be shared.

headline: How crusty curmudgeon Vic Fangio made defense elite
fullText:
Vic Fangio is an Eagles treasure. He's Philly to the core after growing up in the area and getting his coaching start with the Philadelphia Stars of the former USFL in the 1980s.

Fangio, 66, is as eager to talk about the plight of his beloved Phillies as much as he is Xs and Os on the football field − except when it comes to his own personal analytics. That's off-limits.

"I don't share my process with anybody," Fangio said during training camp. "Even fellow coaches." That includes head coach Nick Sirianni and the other defensive assistants.

We here at the "Eye On The Eagles" newsletter understand, mainly because it's working.

The Eagles have the No. 1-ranked defense in the NFL, allowing just 283 yards per game heading into their game Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. This after they were 30th last season under Sean Desai and his late-season replacement Matt Patricia.

Fangio has turned Jalen Carter into a force at defensive tackle as Carter plays practically every defensive snap, and pretty much dominates those snaps, despite getting double-teamed for most of them. Last Sunday, Carter was dominant in the Eagles' 24-19 win over the Baltimore Ravens.

Here's a photo gallery from the game.

Carter had a sack, 4 tackles, 3 tackles for losses, and 2 QB hits. He played 71 of 72 snaps. And yet, you can make a case that Carter was held by Ravens' offensive linemen on many of those plays. In fact, Fangio himself tried making that case when asked what he could do to get the officials to call those penalties.

"I don't know. You got any ideas?" he said with a laugh. "There was one play in particular where he was grossly held and pulled to the ground. And there was no call, so ..."

But Carter's play might not even be Fangio's best work. That could very well be turning inside linebacker Zack Baun into the NFL's fourth leading tackler this season with 117. Baun is the third NFL player since 1999 with 100-plus tackles, 4 or more forced fumbles and 2 or more takeaways through 12 games.

Baun had spent his first four seasons as an occasional starter − at edge rusher − with the New Orleans Saints. In fact, when Eagles GM Howie Roseman signed Baun to a bargain-basement 1-year deal worth $1.6 million last spring, Fangio said Roseman told him that Baun would be a depth edge rusher and special teams player.

Fangio thought differently.

"When I evaluate players, there’s no checkbox, things to check off," Fangio said. "You just watch the tape, watch the movement patterns, watch the player play.

"After I watched (video of Baun), I said I think he’s an inside linebacker. Luckily it hit."

It was the same in the secondary with rookie cornerback Quinyon Mitchell, who has played practically every snap this season, and fellow rookie Cooper DeJean, who has done the same since becoming the starter Week 5, when the Eagles' current 8-game winning streak began.

There are many other examples. After all, the Eagles have kept playing well on defense even after losing two of their edge rushers in Brandon Graham and Bryce Huff to injury. That currently leaves the Eagles with a three-man rotation, as of now, in Josh Sweat, Nolan Smith and rookie Jalyx Hunt.

For Hunt, the Ravens game represented his first significant action in a game that wasn't a blowout.

When Fangio was asked about Hunt's play, he made an Allen Iverson "practice" reference in honor of the Sixers legend's famous rant from two decades ago. And as usual, Fangio was blunt.

"Some good. Some not so good," he said about Hunt. "Now he's at the point where he's got to improve and build on that. It's a process. The more you practice, the more you play, you get better − in spite of what Allen Iverson ever said."

Saquon Barkley chases Eagles, NFL records

As you might have noticed, Eagles running back Saquon Barkley is on a record-setting pace. Not only is Barkley 109 yards away from breaking LeSean McCoy's franchise record of 1,607 yards set in 2013, but he's also on pace for Eric Dickerson's NFL single-season rushing record of 2,105 yards set in 1984.

And Barkley is a top candidate for the MVP award.

Here is a Saquon Barkley photo gallery.

But the Eagles can also clinch a playoff spot Sunday with a win and help from at least two other teams. What about clinching the NFC East? Here's when that could happen, along with what it would take to get the No. 1 seed in the NFC.

headline: Holiday cheer: Three awesome Christmas light displays in Naples, Marco Island, Fort Myers
fullText:
As a kid, Maria Sloboda loved visiting North Naples’ Victoria Park neighborhood and letting its popular holiday lights fill her with the Christmas spirit.

"It's a whole different world," she says. "It's really neat."

Now Sloboda and her husband, Marcus Peña, help make that magic happen, themselves. They moved to Victoria Park in 2016 and started decorating their own house, too.

"It's just what makes our community unique," Sloboda says. "It's one of the reasons I wanted to live here."

The Sloboda/Peña house is just one of many decorated homes and businesses featured in the Naples Daily News interactive holiday lights map. To see the map online, go to tinyurl.com/5ayvcbpu.

The map shows holiday displays in Naples, Marco Island, Bonita Springs and the rest of Southwest Florida. You can use it for a self-guided tour of the region's best and brightest displays.

Here’s a closer look at Victoria Park and two other awesome Southwest Florida light displays:

Make Christmas Great Again: Victoria Park shines in North Naples

Sloboda was born and raised in Naples, she says, so she’s been visiting Victoria Park all her life.

"We usually went on Christmas Eve right before midnight Mass,” says Sloboda, 34. “We would drive through, and I looked forward to that. It was like the highlight of Christmas Eve. You can just feel the Christmas spirit."

Cars line up every year to see the dazzling displays. The tradition started about three decades ago in Victoria Park, a neighborhood of more than 300 houses in North Naples.

Everywhere you look, you’ll find holiday cheer: Inflatable nutcrackers, snowmen and Santas; lighted Christmas trees; a "tunnel" of silvery-blue lighted arches; and even cars wrapped top-to-bottom in twinkling lights.

For their part, the Sloboda/Peña family puts a political spin on the holidays. That’s their house on Nottingham Drive with the American flag made of Christmas lights, a Republican-style elephant and a waving, inflatable Trump Santa Claus by the mailbox.

"It may or may not be a little controversial," Sloboda says and laughs. "But we always have a Trump Santa and an American flag. Make Christmas Great Again."

Christmas concerts and more: Old Dominion, Bret Michaels, Kenny G, more December shows in SW FL

Christmas lights map: Take a tour of displays in Naples, Marco Island, Bonita Springs

It’s a festive time of year for the neighborhood, she says. People play Christmas music, cook s’mores in fire pits and play Christmas movies on outdoor projectors.

Each street has a different theme, she says. Candy canes on one street. Snowmen on another. Her own street, Nottingham Drive, has a Santa Claus theme.

"My husband goes all out," Sloboda says. "He's a handyman, and he actually decorates a few of the homes in Victoria Park, as well as the entrance."

The holiday displays start lighting up for Thanksgiving weekend and shine all month long in December. And people come from all over Southwest Florida to see the spectacle.

Hundreds of vehicles pass through every night in cars, trucks, golf carts, buses and more.

"We have people come from all over Florida," Sloboda says. "There's trolleys and shuttles. People hook up trailers to the back of their trucks and do little hayrides through the neighborhood and sit in their truck beds. It's pretty neat."

Planning all year long for Edison & Ford’s Holiday Nights

Victoria Park isn’t the only place in Southwest Florida that’s worth a drive. People from Naples, Bonita Springs and elsewhere gladly drive to Fort Myers for the annual Holidays Nights at The Edison & Ford Winter Estates.

The 49th-annual event — featured in our separate Lee County holiday lights map — is in full-swing at The Edison & Ford Winter Estates. More than 30,000 people are expected to visit the sprawling, nightly light display before it ends Jan. 5.

And after all those lights and Christmas trees go dark? It’s time to start planning for NEXT year already.

It never stops, says Mike Cosden, the Estates’ executive vice president. He works closely with a huge team of volunteers and employees to make the popular event happen every year.

“We’re honoring a tradition that’s been going for almost 50 years now,” Cosden says.

The Edison & Ford Winter Estates — the former winter homes of inventor Thomas Edison and car manufacturer Henry Ford — have a staff of 90 employees, Cosden says. And about half of them are involved in installing the holiday decorations every year. Then hundreds of volunteers help the staff run the event once it starts.

The annual event celebrates the holiday season while nodding to the famous people who once lived there — and who celebrated Christmas there at least once, Cosden says.

“The Edison family were very interested in Christmas,” he says. “It was a big holiday for them. They weren’t always here in Fort Myers to celebrate it, but we can represent their historic interest in the holiday here.”

Thousands of lights glow and twinkle everywhere you look at Edison & Ford. The cheery lights, mostly colored green and gold, wrap around palm trees and light poles, line walkways, twinkle from Christmas trees and shine inside the historic homes of Thomas Edison and Henry Ford.

Then there’s the popular Children’s Christmas Tree Trail, a U-shaped pathway lined with mini trees decorated by Lee County students. Those hand-made ornaments include painted flip-flips, paper butterflies, googly-eyed orange fish made from water bottles and lots more.

Rebekah Cramer of Fort Myers wouldn’t dream of missing the annual event. She and husband Ken have been visiting Holiday Nights since they were in elementary school. Now they’re bringing their own kids — ages 6, 8 and 9 — and continuing that tradition.

“Oh, it’s wonderful!” said Kramer, 40, while her family took in the sights on a recent Monday night at Edison & Ford. “We come every year. It’s like a piece of Fort Myers history.

“They do such an awesome job. It’s beautiful.”

Spreading Christmas cheer on Marco Island, raising money for St. Jude

The spirit of Christmas is alive and well at Ron Spering’s house on Marco Island. So is the spirit of giving.

Every year, Spering’s jaw-dropping holiday display draws thousands of people and raises money for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital. People just drop the money in a donation box.

They’ve raised about $20,000 every year, he says. For their fifth-annual display, they're hoping to reach a total of $100,000 raised since the event started.

"So that's pretty neat," Spering says. "People have been very supportive and very generous."

Spering, 73, has been decorating his Marco Island home at 1264 Whiteheart Ave. for more than four decades. The elaborate display has even been featured on the TV news and in newspapers.

"My neighbors are very supportive and helpful — and mostly tolerant," he says and laughs. "It's only been positive input and support."

It’s a passion for Spering.

"I've always loved Christmas,” he says. “Many people play golf down here, and go boating, and go fishing. Well, to me, it's Christmas year-round. I build so much of this stuff, that it's a year-round thing."

And there's a LOT of stuff packing the Spering home with holiday fun, including about 100,000 lights, a 15-foot-tall white Christmas tree, a 7-foot-tall fiberglass Rudolph, an oversized Christmas ornament and many things Spering built himself from wood. Those hand-made items include a manger scene, a Disney castle with Mickey and Minnie, a "Frozen" castle with sisters Anna and Elsa, a sleigh where people can take photos, and a 12-foot-wide, 10-foot-high gingerbread house with lots of gingerbread people.

He's always buying and building new things for the display. "My wife just rolls her eyes," he says and laughs. "I saw an ad at Home Depot for an 8½-foot tall reindeer. So, of course, I needed that."

Spering builds those wooden castles, mangers and other items in a two-car garage separate from the house. He’s working in there all year long.

“That's where I spend most of my time," he says.

As a kid, Spering used to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade and be wowed by the floats. "I thought to myself, 'I'm gonna build stuff like that when I grow up,'" he says. "I love Christmas, anyway. And the fact that we're helping St. Jude now, that's a big incentive."

Spering enjoys watching people visit his holiday display with their kids and grandkids. "It's such a pleasure for me and my wife…" he says. "We just love doing it, and we'll keep doing it."

He's getting up there in age, he admits. But he has no plans to quit anytime soon.

"Every year, the stuff gets a little heavier, and the roof gets higher," Spering says. "But I can't imagine not doing it."

Christmas light displays in Naples, Marco Island, Collier County

These Collier County holiday displays and more can be found online at tinyurl.com/5ayvcbpu. But here are 10 of the featured light displays:

  • 9127 Strada Place, Naples: Shopping center Mercato promises a “stunning” holiday light display with palm and oak trees adorned with twinkling lights and icicles, a banyan tree illuminated with newly installed lanterns and the new Horizon, an immersive light and sound installation perfect for the holidays. experiencemercato.com
  • Nottingham Drive, North Naples: The Victoria Park neighborhood’s annual lights display draws people from all over Southwest Florida. Most of the houses are decked out with lights and decorations. To find the neighborhood, just Google the words “victoria lane naples florida" for directions. That puts you in the heart of the community.
  • 4820 Bayshore Drive, Naples: The annual Johnsonville Night Lights display at Naples Botanical Garden features about 200,000 lights. naplesgarden.org
  • 3940 City Gate Blvd N., Naples: The Magic of Lights drive-through display at Paradise Coast Sports Complex boasts millions of LED lights, a 200-foot Enchanting Tunnel of Lights and various themes, including Prehistoric Christmas, Winter Wonderland, the 12 Days of Christmas and Toyland. playparadisecoast.com
  • 4200 Gulf Shore Blvd N., Naples: The Village Shops promises “Naples' largest Christmas tree shining with lights,” plus garland-wrapped walkways, trees with twinkling lights and illuminated entrances and palm trees. More than 100,000 lights in all. venetianvillage.com
  • 1331 22nd Ave NE, Naples: 10,000 lights in a display that resembles a gingerbread house on 2½ acres.
  • 5370 Bonita Beach Road, Bonita Springs: The display at Coconut Jack's Waterfont Grille features more than 37,000 lights, large wreaths, garlands, bows and a "giant floating Christmas tree" full of lights and glowing ornaments. coconutjacks.com
  • 1264 Whiteheart Ave., Marco Island: Annual display raising money for St. Jude Children’s Hospital, about 100,000 lights, hand-made wooden cut-out characters and items.
  • 1163 Fourwinds Ave, Marco Island: About 8,000 lights and holiday music. Tune to channel 88.1 to hear the music.
  • 1580 Collingswood Ave, Marco Island: The theme includes dachshunds and Disney. Snow machine and hot cocoa stand on select nights. About 40,000 lights.

If you’re having difficulty viewing the online map, visit flo.uri.sh/visualisation/15579641/embed.

How to be a part of the holiday lights map

Do you have an awesome holiday display of your own? Then you can be in the map, too.

Go online and fill out a short form that includes your address, the number of lights in your display and a short description. It's free.

To add your holiday light display, go to naplesnews.com/holidaylights. The displays can be for businesses, homes or venues.. The displays can be for businesses, homes or venues.

headline: Naples facing Orlando Jones in first football state semifinal since 2018. What to know
fullText:
Naples coach Rick Martin opened Monday's practice with a clear and concise message.

"In 75 years of Naples High School football, what you guys did Friday night has only been done 12 times," said Martin of winning a regional title.

"Only three teams have gone on to win this game."

The Golden Eagles (11-2) will travel to Orlando to take on Jones (13-0) in a Class 4A state semifinal at 7:30 p.m. on Friday to try and match the 2001, '03 and '07 teams that made a state title game. The winner will face American Heritage or St. Augustine for the 4A title on Dec. 13 in Miami at Pitbull Stadium.

More: Naples captures first regional championship since 2018 with 17-10 win over Port Charlotte

"The last couple of weeks, we've been saying to each other to not be satisfied," said Martin, in his fifth season leading Naples. "We've been saying that each round. I have challenged these boys all season to be different. To be different than some of the teams that came before them. It's not a knock on any of those guys before them, but if you want to be different and want to go farther than the teams before you, you've got to do different things."

Safe to say, the Golden Eagles were different in a spot that's plagued them each of the last two seasons in regional final losses to Dunbar ― not being able to close out either game. This year against Port Charlotte, Naples' split-back veer was largely stymied until the waning moments as the Golden Eagles rushed 43 times for 186 yards but put the game away with big first-down runs at the end.

Despite the win, Naples' offense did not manage to score a touchdown in the playoffs for the first time in the MaxPreps era, which dates back to 2004. But that's when the defense flexed its scoring muscle.

More: Naples' perfect season, 10 years later: Drive, tenacity, love led Eagles to football title

Brady Clark picked a great time to log his first two takeaways as a varsity football player. The defensive lineman had a pair of pick-sixes, resulting in Naples' only touchdowns in a 17-10 win over the Pirates to punch their ticket to the state semifinals for the first time since 2018.

"They're incredible," Martin said. "Let's be honest, they practically won the game for us this past week with Brady having two pick-sixes. Albertini (Tenor) has had a tremendous season with his contribution. Khari Bendolph, being in the middle of that whole thing, they're a special group of guys."

The Golden Eagles have surrendered just 10 points over its three playoff games, coming out to a mere 3.33 points per game. Back-to-back shutouts against River Ridge and St. Petersburg, coupled with a four takeaway performance against Port Charlotte allowed the unit to exude confidence at a critical time.

The defensive line of Clark, Tenor, Sean Kabengele, and LaCarlos McGee has been elite, combining for 62 tackles for loss along with 29 sacks, 3 forced fumbles, and 2 fumble recoveries. It's allowed the linebacking unit of Bendolph, Vlad Raphael, and Tariq Arbyummi to thrive, as they've managed 26 tackles for loss, 12 sacks, 6 forced fumbles, and 5 fumble recoveries.

"I don't know another group that has two D-tackles like we have," Martin said. "And to have the defensive ends we have, to have the linebacker corps we have. They're special, they're coachable, they love each other, and it shows on Friday night. They fly around and make things happen for us."

Defending Jones will be a tall task, something Martin isn't afraid to admit.

Similar in offensive structure to American Heritage, a team Naples played midseason, Jones has more than a capable offense, averaging 424.4 yards of offense per game. It's headlined by a mobile quarterback in Miami commit Dereon Coleman (183-246, 3,125 yards, 28 TD, 4 INT), a 1,500-yard rusher in JaQuail Smith, and a host of playmakers out wide, including 5-star Florida signee Vernell Brown III (88 rec, 1,364 yards, 11 TD) and 3-star junior Larry Miles (59 rec, 1,098 yards, 10 TD).

Against American Heritage, Naples picked off Dia Bell three times, which accounts for half of the interceptions he's thrown all season. If they can generate pressure against Coleman and put him in uncharacteristic positions, Naples feels good about their chances.

"We hang our hat on our defense," Martin said. "We've got one of the best defensive staffs in the entire country. One of the things I've preached to these guys on defense is how special they could be all season long. To be honest with you, I don't know if we hit that stride until just a couple of weeks ago.

"We may have shown flashes of it throughout the season, but when we finally did it, I think everybody realized it. They felt it. They understood it. Hopefully, we can keep that momentum going and continue that."

The News-Press/Naples Daily News pick: Jones 27, Naples 20

headline: It's a done deal: Fluoride coming out of drinking water in Naples
fullText:
Naples leaders are stopping the practice of adding fluoride into the city’s drinking water.

The Naples City Council made the decision in a 4-to-3 vote following a public hearing Wednesday with at least a dozen speakers on both sides of the issue.

Council members Ray Christman and Beth Petrunoff had asked for the decision to be delayed. Christman called for the issue to be sent to a workshop, and Petrunoff suggested the city hire an expert because of conflicting opinions.

Council member Linda Penniman did not air her position yet was the third vote against the ordinance amendment to stop fluoridating the water.

Fluoridation of the city’s water will end Jan. 1 or earlier if possible.

The debate was spurred months ago by members of Stand for Health Freedom which helped convince the Collier County Commission in February to stop fluoridating the county’s water.

The group also was instrumental in the county commission’s decision in April 2023 to adopt a “health freedom bill of rights” to protect personal liberties in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and what they said was government overreach with shut-downs, mask mandates and vaccine requirements.

More: Naples may stop adding fluoride to drinking water. What to know

The city’s discussion on fluoridation began before a Nov. 22 guidance from state Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo, who recommends that fluoride not be added to public drinking water.

Ladapo has held public health views that are contrary to the U.S. Centers and Disease Control, namely his position against the COVID-19 vaccine for infants and the elderly.

More: Medicated without consent? Collier leaders halt fluoride being added in drinking water

More recently gaining the spotlight is Robert F. Kennedy Jr., president-elect Donald Trump’s nominee for secretary of the U.S. Health and Human Services, who vows to have fluoride removed from drinking water nationwide if he gets the appointment.

Both Marco Island and Everglades City do not add fluoride to their jurisdiction’s drinking water.

What is the background for the decision?

The city council in October heard from members of Stand for Health Freedom and others who called for the fluoridation practice to stop. They reference various studies that it lowers the IQ of children, causes thyroid problems and other medical issues despite the benefits of preventing tooth decay.

In October, the city council asked the city attorney to prepare an amendment to the city ordinance to stop fluoridation.  A first vote was held Nov. 6 with the same 4-to-3 results as Wednesday to stop the practice.

More: Collier leaders pass 'health freedom' ordinance to protect individual liberties

Many speaking Wednesday had addressed the council previously.

Scott Kiley, with Stand for Health Freedom, spoke about a California court ruling in September that has fueled a growing anti-fluoridation movement. He also spoke about a Florida law requiring informed consent and right to opt out of any medical treatment.

And he referenced Ladapo’s guidance that points to lower IQ’s in children and weakened bones in the elderly, among other issues.

“As I’ve said, you did not create this problem but you can end it here,” Kiley said.

Among those speaking to keep the fluoridation policy intact was Dr. Marilyn Sandor, a pediatric dentist in Naples since 2001, who referenced 70 years of a practice where legitimate testing has proven its safety.

 She spoke about how fluoride is a naturally occurring mineral and cannot be compared to a drug, which was the case at prior public hearing where the speaker argued why statins are not added to drinking water for its heart health benefits.

“And please note that just because you can buy fluoride off the shelf in the drug store with a certain concentration does not mean that it is a drug,” she said.

She spoke about how it helps children against tooth decay and prevents lost school hours for cavity treatment. The elderly in nursing homes may not be getting help to brush their teeth so it helps them to drink fluoridated water.

Dr. Alexis Diaczynsky, past president of the Collier County Dental Association, spoke of a study in Australia that found no change in behavior of children exposed to fluoride and a study out of New Zealand that followed people for a lifetime and found no link between fluoride and IQ.

She addressed the court ruling in September out of California that anti-fluoride advocates are misrepresenting as a finding that it poses a health risk to children and has prompted some jurisdictions to stop fluoridating.

The ruling called for the federal Environmental Protection Agency to respond in some regulatory manner that adding fluoride to drinking water poses an “unreasonable risk” of lowering the IQ of children.

“The court stated that the finding does not conclude with certainty that fluoridated water injures the public health,” she said. “It is not saying that fluoride is posing an immediate, irreversible harm to individuals.”

Dr. Douglas Keck, a Naples dentist on staff of Healthcare Network, a nonprofit medical organization that largely serves disadvantaged residents in Naples and Immokalee, said in an interview that he hoped the city would continue its policy of fluoridating the water.

The judge in the California case was only directing the EPA to investigate the issue, but data used for the ruling was from other countries, he said.

He said individuals against fluoridating drinking water are talking about risks where the dosages of fluoride are more than twice what is added in drinking water, which is no more than 0.7 milligrams per liter.

“If you really go look at peer-reviewed research and reputable journals you will always find that fluoride is a safe and acceptable way to preventable cavities and community water fluoridation at the dose recommended is safe and effective,” Keck said. “It doesn’t make sense why you wouldn’t do something that will benefit the whole community.”

What does Ladapo’s guidance say?

 Ladapo’s guidance released Nov. 22 says that, historically, community water fluoridation was a means to prevent tooth decay but said it is readily available in toothpastes and other products.

It referenced research being conducted to review the impacts of overall fluoride exposure in the population but did not cite specifically the research.

The guidance also said many U.S. cities and several European countries, including Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Norway, and Sweden, have stopped the practice.

Ladapo said Florida residents should be aware of safety concerns, including adverse affects on children by reducing IQ, neurobehavioral problems in children tied to mothers ingesting it during pregnancy, sleep disturbance, bone fractures and more.

“Due to the neuropsychiatric risk associated with fluoride exposure, particularly in pregnant women and children, and the wide availability of alternative sources of fluoride for dental health, the State Surgeon General recommends against community water fluoridation,” the directive said.

The guidance said the state health department supports oral health through the school-based preventive dental services that includes screening and dental clinics run by county health departments.

What did city council members say?

Council members stuck to their previous positions from the November public hearing.

Vice Mayor Terry Hutchison said fluoride is readily available in toothpaste and other products.

 “You don’t have to depend on our water,” he said.

He also said the country appears to be a crossroads on the issue, referring to the surgeon general’s guidance, and added that science has changed through the years.

Council member Bill Kramer pointed to the issue of forcing something on people that they don’t want.

“Just because it has been done doesn’t mean we should continue to do it, even if it is the greatest thing ever,” he said. “Our decision is, do we impose this on those who don’t want it.”

Council member Berne Barton said he was concerned about exposing the city to legal action, and not forcing something on people who don’t want it.

He asked the city’s attorney, Matthew McConnell, if the city would be in a bad position given the surgeon general’s guidance and was told the city was not at risk.

“We are not doing anything illegal by having fluoride in the water,” McConnell said.

Council member Ray Christman said he had issues with the process the city used to get to this point, without going to a workshop first. The matter moved to public hearings within two months which is much faster than some council decisions.

He also criticized how the outside special interest group, the members of Stand for Health Freedom, has held sway while eight homeowners associations in the city, representing 80% of the city’s population, had asked earlier this month for a delay.

“That plea was simply ignored,” he said.

On what he called the substance of the argument against fluoridation, the advocates against it are referring to fluoride levels twice the amount used, Christman said.

Naples Mayor Teresa Heitman pointed out that the city has been fluoridating the water for decades and the issue of stopping it has come to the council at least twice since 2008.

She said the council does not have to workshop everything and said the process used for the fluoridation debate has been fair.

“I’ve had the white coats on one side and another group on the other,” she said. “This is not an easy decision because when I look in the room I see people I respect.”

She went on to say she sees more mounting evidence for why the city should no longer keep the practice.

headline: Great Wolf Lodge water park has ‘Snowland.’ How to celebrate holidays at Florida resort
fullText:
Who doesn't want to pretend they're in a snowy mountain resort for the holidays when it's 85 degrees outside?

With the recent opening of Naples' Great Wolf Lodge resort, Florida families can immerse themselves in a winter wonderland during their annual Snowland event.

Great Wolf Lodge is a family-friendly resort featuring an indoor water park and other activities for all age groups. According to its website, the resort chain is "North America's largest family of indoor water park resorts."

The Southwest Florida location opened its doors last month. Sitting near the Interstate 75 and Collier Boulevard interchange, the 20-acre resort includes 500 suites, and multiple eateries and hosts several family-friendly attractions, including its 100,000-square-foot indoor water park. 

Where is Florida's Great Wolf Lodge resort located?

 Florida Great Wolf Lodge is located at 3900 City Gate Boulevard in Naples.

How does Great Wolf Lodge celebrate the holiday in their resorts?

Great Wolf Lodge rang in the holidays early on Nov. 25 with its annual "Snowland" celebrations, seeing whimsical holiday décor around their grand lobbies and special seasonal events taking place.

Guests this year can also capture their memories at Snowland selfie stations in the lobby with various props to help create a festive family photo. Certain resorts also offer an immersive "snow globe" experience, letting families have a fun time filled with festive décor, dancing lights, and a hot chocolate bar.

Other fun holiday activities included as part of an overnight stay this year include:

  • “Twas the Night Before Snowland” Yoga Tails – Start your day with a flex and stretch in their fun-filled yoga class that celebrates the holiday season.
  • Seasonal games – Make merry with a round of bingo, learn the reasons for the season with holiday trivia, or try to create the ultimate wonderland experience by completing the Great Wolf Lodge Snowland scavenger hunt.
  • Snowland Arts & Crafts - Grab a Snowland arts & crafts kit, build it and enjoy with your pack.
  • Visits with Santa – Don’t forget to bring your list! On select days between, there will be surprise visits from Santa.
  • Seasonal crafts – Enjoy a DIY jingle bell craft kit, color a picture frame and make a one-of-a-kind snowflake.
  • Frosty Fest Family Dance Party – Have a holly jolly time boogying down.

Is Santa Claus at Great Wolf Lodge in Naples?

Yes, Santa will be at the lodge on select days when Snowland starts. Officials online have previously recommended that patrons call the lodge they are visiting to confirm as his visit will vary by lodge.

When does 'Snowland' end at Great Wolf Lodge?

Guests have an entire month to delve into the holiday festivities. Snowland ends on Monday, Jan. 6.

Is there an additional cost for 'Snowland' activities?

No, the special events and activities are all included with guests' stay.

How to book reservations at Naples Great Wolf Lodge

The website has a "Book Your Stay" button on its front page. Guests can either book online or call 866-462-9653.

What is the 'Snowland' package at Great Wolf Lodge in Florida?

Add a little holly jolliness to your stay. Until Jan. 3, the resort will offer its "Snowland" package. Starting at $49.99, the package includes:

  • One limited edition Snowland Glam Ear (Can only be found in this package)
  • One Peppermint Hot Chocolate Candy Pop
  • One Great Wolf Lodge Sweatshirt Blanket
  • One Commemorative Ornament
  • One Mystery Plush
  • One clear Snowland Drawstring Bag

headline: See deployed Air Force dad, daughter reunite in emotional surprise at Naples elementary school
fullText:
A Naples area kindergarten student got a special holiday surprise in her classroom this week that she's sure to remember for the rest of her life.

U.S. Air Force Airman First Class Gary Parrish has been on active duty for 10 months, including six months in Kuwait. All that time, he hadn't seen his daughter, Emily Angulo Hernandez.

Until Wednesday.

That's when he flew into Southwest Florida International Airport and headed straight for Emily's classroom at Pelican Marsh Elementary School. It was an emotional surprise for sure.
