headline: Who would pay for a new airport and who would run it if Naples moves?
fullText:
As residents, elected officials and visitors of Naples and Collier County continue conversations about the existing airport in Naples and the possible construction of a new facility in the county, a big question is who would pay for it and who would operate it?

It is unlikely to be the Naples Airport Authority (NAA), says Executive Director Chris Rozansky.

The NAA was created by the Florida Legislature in 1969 to operate, develop and improve the airport as a separate governmental entity from the Naples City Council. The City of Naples owns the land on which the airport sits and leased it through 2068.

"By the enabling legislation, the NAA can only issue $15 million in debt and was established to operate the Naples Municipal Airport," Rozansky said in an email this week. "The legislation was later amended to include operation of any other airport it contracted to operate in Collier County, but it’s unclear and unlikely that contemplated a new airport to potentially replace the Naples Municipal Airport."

The $15 million the Authority can borrow would not come close to covering the costs of a new airport, estimated to be $1 billion to $2 billion in 2024 money. NAA commissioned an exploratory study that looked at potential land sites and estimated costs.

"Financing would almost certainly have to be provided by a variety of sources," Rozansky said. "A more detailed financial analysis would be part of the next phase of the study if approved when presented to the Board."

Proceeds from sale of current airport likely needed

"It'd be quite expensive. We're talking probably one to two billion dollars, preliminary cost estimate. And by the way, these are '24 dollars and … these don't include all the relevant costs, because there's four sites. Each site varies a little bit in site work, environmental issues and roads, utilities, et cetera," Rozansky said Tuesday at a breakfast event held by Greater Naples Chamber of Commerce.

"In all likelihood, even though the Naples Airport Authority doesn't own the land, you would almost have to use the proceeds from the sale of the land in order to help bite into that, that massive expense," he said. "Now, what that land is redeveloped into is an entirely separate conversation, but you might guess that if that were to take place, it wouldn't be parks or workforce housing."

NAA estimates raw land at the current airport, "not land encumbered by an airport, (to) be worth more than a million dollars an acre. So you think about 700-plus acres out of that airport that would, that would help pay."

Another source of funding likely would be from commercial activities at a new airport, activities Naples Airport doesn't offer, Rozansky said.

"You're going to have to have revenue opportunities in order to issue debt to help defray the cost of a new airport," he said. "And we know there's tremendous demand. I mean, who wouldn't appreciate not having to make the trek up (Interstate) 75 in season to catch a flight at RSW, however, that wouldn't pay for all of it on its own."

With all four identified sites for a possible new airport in Collier County, it's "not certain who the governing body would be," Rozansky said. "Would it be the county? Would it be a new special district that would burden that debt load? But those are some of the sources funding might come from."

Naples Airport Authority can't make move funding decisions

"We, the airport authority, don't have the authority to make those decisions, those would have to be decided by the city or the county," he said.

Naples City Council in November voted 4-3 to ask the authority's Board of Commissioners to continue the exploratory study to the next phase. The Board hasn't decided whether to do that but has asked the study's author Environmental Science Associates (ESA) to give it a scope of work outline and cost estimates.

"I think it's prudent to at least study the feasibility of what a new airport might look like without opining on what would happen to the existing airport," Rozansky said. "That's a whole nother topic for conversation, because the Naples airport authority doesn't own the land. We lease it from the city of Naples under a 99-year lease that expires in 2068, so the question is, well, what then? Which I think remains yet to be answered."

$4 billion in new income arriving in Collier County every year

Rozansky and Wayne Gaither, Southwest Area Office Director, Florida Department of Transportation District One, were the speakers at the chamber's event titled "Wake Up Naples: Dual Perspectives – SWFL Infrastructure Updates from the Sky and Road."

With the increased population and wealth influx in Florida in the past five years, infrastructure support for that growth is top of mind for state and local officials, and residents.

"We have over $4 billion in new income that comes to our county every year," said Sunshine Ace Hardware President Michael Wynn at the event he sponsored. "What about population projections, according to the Florida Chamber, Collier County's population will increase by 79,000 by the year 2030, which is a growth rate of 17%. But even if their projections are too robust, the fact is that there is robust projections for growth in Collier County and that's going to continue."

The Florida Chamber of Commerce wants to make sure of it. In its 2024 annual report, the chamber put forth its Florida 2030 Blueprint , which called for "growing Florida’s economy to the 10th largest in the world by 2030, the latest income migration numbers are showing that Florida continues to grow at a rapid pace."

Florida sees more than $36.05 billion in net income moving into our state each year, making it "the number one destination for income migration in the United States."

In Collier County, transportation growing pains are obvious on the local roads, the interstate and in the air.

What kind of economic impact does the airport have now?

Rozansky, who has been NAA executive director since 2016, gave chamber members an overview of the airport with a brief history and an introduction as to how it operates and what little control the authority has over flights in the air or flights landing in Naples. That's the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) authority.

The airport has a $781 million annual economic impact on the community, according to FDOT.

"The airport drives an enormous economic impact. You can attribute several thousand jobs, directly and indirectly, to the airport," Rozansky said. "We do have more than 100,000 takeoffs and landings a year, of course, like on the roadways, much of that is in season, very seasonal. … 70% of our traffic is in a five-month window. So that comes with a lot of difficulties."

Those airplanes take off and land at an airport located in the middle of the city of Naples, which grew and was built around it. Airplanes fly over the beach, over downtown Naples and its famous Fifth Avenue and Third Street restaurants and shops every day, multiple times a day.

The increase in the take offs and landings, especially since the 2020 COVID pandemic, have prompted increased noise complaints, demands for closure of the airport, demands it be moved, demands that something be done.

"We actually recently learned that through some technology that the airport actually serves more than 300,000 passengers a year," Rozansky said. "Think about that. Primarily residents, second homes. Of course, there's also an element of tourism, and people are doing business here."

Rozansky asked Wynn about the $4 billion coming into the county annually: "Do they happen to say how that wealth is arriving here in town? Probably on Runway 523, would be my guess. They aren't flying into Punta Gorda, like I do sometimes."

With the expected population growth, "I think it's prudent and important to look at your long-term transportation needs," Rozansky said. "Particularly you look at the growth projections. You know, we're a little over 400,000 today. The conservative estimate is that the county will build out at over somewhere about 800,000 to a million residents. Eight hundred thousand to a million residents. Think about that."

Having an airport in the community that doesn't require a trip along I-75 can be a plus, he said.

"There's a lot of positive benefits with an airport in your community. However, we also know there's a significant noise component, and it's challenging because the weather's nicer. People want to be here. They want to be outdoors, enjoying the quality of life. That's what people come here for," he said.

"You do have this the challenge with noise exposure, it's really important to know the Naples Airport Authority, or any other airport, has very little control over aircraft in flight, almost none. We're like a sophisticated highways maintenance department. Our job is to take care of the airfield and the airport facilities. We have almost zero control over who uses that airport."

And the airport can be used 24 hours a day, even with the voluntary curfew in place at Naples Airport between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. The FAA doesn't allow mandatory curfews.

The Naples Airport encourages compliance with the curfew through a leaderboard and a list of violators made public on the airport's website.

"It's a very noise sensitive community, and people want to enjoy peace and quiet, especially at night," Rozansky said.

headline: Canandaigua breweries host keg tree lighting ceremonies: The details
fullText:
CANANDAIGUA — Rochester has its iconic Genesee Brewery keg-tree lighting, a 10-year-old holiday tradition that draws thousands and is expected to once again on Friday night at the Rochester brewery. 

But for the last two years, local breweries in Canandaigua have been encouraging craft beer fans to get in the holiday spirit and “Get Lit Canandaigua.” 

Participating breweries hold their own staggered keg-tree lighting ceremonies in a fun way designed for customers to attend all of them or hang out at their favorite.

This year’s event starts at 5 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 7, at Peacemaker Brewing Co. 

The event has been successful and a big draw in bringing people to Canandaigua the last two years, said David D'Allesandro, co-owner and founder of Frequentem Brewing Co., who helped organize this year's event.

"People seem to enjoy themselves and it brings people to Canandaigua on a relatively cold and potentially slower weekend," D'Allesandro said.

And that's all good news for the local beer community, D'Allesandro added.

"I’ve always been of the opinion that it’s a community between the breweries," he said. "The more we can do to help each other, the more the whole pie grows. When the pie grows, everyone gets a bigger slice."

Canandaigua Get Lit schedule 

In addition to the keg-tree lighting at 5 p.m., the Sand Shapes will be performing from 6 to 9 p.m. Dec. 7 at Peacemaker Brewing Co., 39 Coach St., Canandaigua. 

Next up is Frequentem Brewing, 254 S. Main St., Canandaigua. Its lighting is set for 6:30 p.m. The Cousin’s Maine Lobster food truck will be there, and a holiday edition of Frequentem's More than Just Fruit, a heavily fruited sour with cinnamon and almond, will be released for the occasion.

Other Half Brewing is new to the party, after having purchased the former Young Lion location at 24 Lakeshore Drive, Canandaigua. Its lighting is scheduled for 8 p.m. 

Twisted Rail Brewing Co. is last but not least, with its lighting taking place at 9:30 p.m. Twisted Rail is at 169 Lakeshore Drive, Canandaigua. Live music also is planned.

Parking in the city of Canandaigua

The keg-tree lighting is a fun new tradition and a successful event, said Canandaigua City Manager John Goodwin.

Municipal parking is available throughout downtown near Frequentem and Peacemaker, and several lots by the lake are close enough to the Other Half and Twisted Rail. Free long-term and short-term parking is available.

Goodwin urges folks to plan ahead.

"The most important thing is people find a safe way there and a safe way home if they’re going to be drinking," Goodwin said.

Mike Murphy covers Canandaigua and other communities in Ontario County and writes the Eat, Drink and Be Murphy food and drink column. Follow him on X at @MPN_MikeMurphy.

headline: Don't be a Scrooge: Four shows you can't miss in Rochester this holiday season
fullText:
The weather outside may be frightful, but Rochester's theater scene sure is delightful.

It's the holiday season, which means it's time for our favorite, classical tales about grumpy non-believers and whimsical snow fairies to come back to life. Whether this is a storied family tradition or your first time seeing a local show, here are four holiday performances in the Rochester area you won't want to miss.

Dr. Seuss' How the Grinch Stole Christmas! The Musical

We all know the story of the crabby character whose heart is two sizes too small. Now, the antics of the Grinch and his plot to ruin Christmas for the holiday-loving Whos comes to Broadway at the West Herr Auditorium Theatre. The show promises magnificent sets and costumes inspired by Dr. Seuss' whimsical illustrations and music from the original animated special ― including "You're A Mean One, Mr. Grinch."

The Grinch will be in town until Dec. 8, with showtimes at 7 p.m. Thursday and Friday; 10:30 a.m., 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. Saturday, and 1 p.m. Sunday. Ticket prices vary by show and are available at rbtl.org. The performance runs about 85 minutes.

The Nutcracker by The State Ballet Theatre of Ukraine

The Nutcracker is a timeless tale of wonder and imagination, following a Christmas toy that leads a small girl on an adventure through a magical snow kingdom and the land of sweets. The Kodak Center show will feature Tchaikovsky's iconic score and one of Ukraine's most esteemed classical ballet ensembles.

Escape with The Nutcracker on Dec. 11 at 7:30 p.m. Tickets start at $45 and are available at kodakcenter.com.

(P.S. The Rochester Philharmonic Orchestra and Rochester City Ballet hold their annual performance of The Nutcracker earlier in the holiday season, typically shortly after Thanksgiving. Bookmark this show by local performers for next year!)

Elf in Concert

Nobody spreads Christmas cheer quite like Buddy the Elf. After learning he was secretly raised among Santa's elves in the North Pole, Buddy travels to New York City in search of his real (human) father, where he encounters lackluster Christmas spirit. The Eastman School of Music will perform with a full, live orchestra at the Kodak Hall at Eastman Theatre while the film plays on a 40-foot HD screen.

See Elf like you never have before on Dec. 14 at 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Tickets start at $25 and are available at esm.rochester.edu.

A Christmas Carol

Don't be a Scrooge. This adaptation of Charles Dickens' classic story reminds us that it is never too late to have a change of heart around the holidays. Town grump Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by four ghosts who try to get him to change his "humbug" ways and find a life filled with generosity and kindness. The Geva Theatre production promises a show filled with humor, heart and hope.

There will be more than a dozen showings of A Christmas Carol from now through Dec. 29. Ticket prices vary by show and are available at gevatheatre.org. The show runs about 2 hours with a 15 minute intermission.

— Kayla Canne covers community safety for the Democrat and Chronicle. This year was her first time seeing The Nutcracker. Follow her on Twitter @kaylacanne and @bykaylacanne on Instagram. Get in touch at kcanne@gannett.com.

headline: Roc Holiday Village 2024: Hours, events, parking and more. What to know
fullText:
Can you hear the sleigh bells starting to ring and smell the hot chocolate wafting through the air? That's because the Roc Holiday Village is returning to downtown Rochester for its sixth year this week.

This year's fun-filled event will take place on 17 wintery days through Dec. 29 and is the first time the event will be open after Christmas. The festival, presented by Five Star Bank and held inside Dr. Martin Luther King Memorial Park at 353 Court St., begins at 4 p.m. on Friday, Dec. 6.

The Roc Holiday Village launched in 2018, drawing more than 125,000 people in its second year. After a one-year hiatus in 2020 due to COVID, the monthlong holiday festival made its return in 2021. More than 185,000 visitors attended last year's event, according to festival organizers.

Here's what to know about this year's Roc Holiday Village.

Village hours and dates

  • Santa’s Workshop will be open Wednesday, Thursday, Friday 4-8 p.m., Saturday 11 a.m.-8 p.m., Sunday 11 a.m.-6 p.m.
  • The Lodge bar and Frosty’s Food Court will be open Wednesday and Thursday 4-10 p.m., Friday 4-11 p.m., Saturday 11 a.m.-11 p.m., Sunday 11 a.m.-6 p.m.
  • The ice rink will be open, weather permitting, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday 4-10 p.m., Saturday 10 a.m.-10 p.m., Sunday 10 a.m.-7 p.m.
  • Shopping Village will be open Wednesday and Thursday from 4-9 p.m, Friday from 4-10 p.m, Saturday 11 a.m.-10 p.m. and Sunday from 11 a.m.-6 p.m.

Tickets for those events are on sale now at rocholidayvillage.com.

While the Cozy Winter Igloos and Igloo Inns are fully booked for this year's village, you'll still be able to enjoy free outdoor seating surrounding several fire pits, which will be available daily.

Liberty Pole Lighting and Farewell Santa Parade

At 5 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 7, the annual Liberty Pole lighting will take place at the corner of East Main and Franklin streets downtown. It will be followed by a brief parade – with Santa – to the park and Roc Holiday Village. As usual, the Prime Time Brass band will lead the parade.

And around 5:45 p.m. on Sunday, Dec. 22, a brass band will perform around the village and a Farewell Santa Parade will usher Santa back to the North Pole.

Holiday celebrations

The Roc Holiday Village will host the following seasonal holiday celebrations at the Simcona Gingerbread House:

After Christmas, Santa's Workshop will be taken over by the Rec Room's selection of free-to-play arcade games from Dec. 26-29.

Food and drinks

Frosty's Food Court, located on Court Street between Chestnut Street and Manhattan Square Drive, will be filled with a rotating assortment of food trucks. Tables, seating and outdoor heaters will also be set up in the food court area. The list of vendors has yet to be announced.

The Rohrbach Brewing Company is bringing back its "Village Lager" after it sold out in two weeks last year but this time with a new look. Canned cocktails have also been added to bar menus and the Lodge will feature a "build-your-own-board" charcuterie bar, where you can buy a selection of premium cheeses, fresh fruits and artisan meats.

Ice skating

The ice rink will be open from 4 to 10 p.m. on Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays, from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. on Saturdays, and from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Sundays.

headline: Blizzard warning for PA, near-blizzard conditions forecast for New York. Track the storm
fullText:
Heavy lake-effect snow is forecast for upstate New York through early Friday, with Chautauqua and Cattaraugus counties potentially seeing up to 20 inches, according to the National Weather Service.

Winter storm warnings are in place across New York as snow squalls move through the region. Accumulations will vary by location, with the heaviest snowfall expected near the Great Lakes.

NWS meteorologist Dan Kelly reported that snow squalls began Wednesday evening, with additional rounds Thursday morning and throughout the day.

Blizzard warning issued in Pennsylvania: How much snow will fall?

A blizzard warning is in effect for northwestern Pennsylvania, where whipping winds could combine with up to 18-20 inches of additional snow. The warning remains active until 1 a.m. Saturday.

In Erie County, Pennsylvania, accumulations are expected to range from 10-18 inches north of Interstate 90 to 12-20 inches south of the highway, with locally higher amounts. Winds may gust up to 60 mph north of the Thruway and 50 mph to the south, particularly Thursday morning.

Blizzard conditions are defined as snow or blowing snow combined with winds exceeding 35 mph, reducing visibility to less than a quarter mile for at least three hours. These conditions could lead to dangerous whiteouts and significant blowing and drifting snow.

In New York, near-blizzard conditions are expected Thursday in Chautauqua and Cattaraugus counties, particularly along the Thruway between the state line and Exit 57 (Hamburg).

Travel in Erie County, Pennsylvania, is expected to be "treacherous, impossible, and potentially life-threatening," the NWS warned, urging motorists to avoid travel in affected areas.

headline: Bills have major strength of schedule advantage to catch Chiefs for No. 1 seed in AFC
fullText:
The Buffalo Bills have one of the easiest remaining schedules over the final five weeks of the NFL season. The Kansas City Chiefs play one of the most difficult schedules down the stretch.

If Buffalo can make up one game on Kansas City, it has a path to the No. 1 seed in the AFC playoffs.

The Bills (10-2) are on a seven-game winning streak and own the head-to-head tiebreaker after handing the Chiefs (11-1) their lone loss in Week 11.

Buffalo's remaining five opponents have a .419 winning percentage, eighth cushiest. The Bills play New England twice and the New York Jets over the final three weeks. Kansas City has the 10th toughest remaining schedule, with a .581 winning percentage.

Buffalo only faces one playoff team, the Detroit Lions, if the season ended today. The Chiefs play four: the Los Angeles Chargers, Houston Texans, Pittsburgh Steelers and Denver Broncos.

The Bills could launch into the No. 1 seed and control their own destiny with a road win against the Los Angeles Rams and Chiefs loss to the Chargers on Sunday Night Football.

The top seed comes with a first-round bye and home field throughout the conference postseason.

Buffalo's only two losses are to the Texans and Baltimore Ravens, who each have 8-5 records. The Bills would have to lose a minimum of three of their final five games for Houston and Baltimore to potentially jump the Bills via head-to-head tiebreaker.

There are five available playoff spots in the AFC. The Bills wrapped up their fifth consecutive AFC East title last week and the Chiefs clinched a playoff spot but haven't locked up the AFC West title.

Super Bowl 59 is at 6:30 p.m. on Feb. 9 at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans.

Bills and Chiefs remaining 2024 schedules

Bills: at Los Angeles Rams, at Detroit, vs. New England, vs. New York, at New England

Chiefs: vs. Los Angeles Chargers, at Cleveland, vs. Houston, at Pittsburgh, at Denver

Buffalo Bills rooting interests for Week 14

Here's which teams Bills fans should be rooting for in Week 14.

Green Bay Packers (9-3) at Detroit Lions (11-1), 8:15 p.m. Thursday, Prime Video

Who to root for: Lions.

This one is nitpicking but Buffalo plays Detroit in Week 15. The fourth tiebreaker between two teams not in the same division is strength of victory in all games. The better the Lions record, the better it is if the Bills beat them. Buffalo doesn't play Green Bay this year.

Cleveland Browns (3-9) at Pittsburgh Steelers (9-3), 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS

Who to root for: Browns.

And not because you want Jameis Winston to be delivered from pick-sixes. Pittsburgh is only a game back of Buffalo in the AFC playoff picture.

New York Jets (3-9) at Miami Dolphins (5-7), 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS

Who to root for: Whichever team you'd revel more in being one step closer to official playoff elimination.

Los Angeles Chargers (8-4) at Kansas City Chiefs (11-1), 8:20 p.m. Sunday, NBC

Who to root for: Chargers.

Buffalo can overtake Kansas City for the No. 1 seed with a win and a Chiefs loss.

headline: City settles for $1.75M with man alleging police pepper ball caused blindness
fullText:
The city of Rochester has agreed to pay $1.75 million to a city man who alleged he lost sight in an eye when struck by a police pepper ball during the 2020 protests in downtown Rochester.

City officials said Wednesday that the settlement was reached in August with Noah Pointer-Gamory. Court papers show an agreement then to dismiss the lawsuit but do not note a settlement amount.

In his lawsuit, Pointer-Gamory said that he was one of the protesters in front of the Public Safety Building who was fired upon with pepper balls by police during the protests which flared up after news became public about the death of Daniel Prude.

Pointer-Gamory was struck in the right eye "from a short distance," the lawsuit said. He can no longer see from that eye, the lawsuit alleged.

With the settlement there was no admission of liability or fault by the city. More than 100 lawsuits remain unresolved from the police response to the protesters. Many of them are proceeding as a class-action litigation.

Daniel Prude died in March 2020, about a week after he was restrained by Rochester police, but the public did not learn of the homicide for months. The Monroe County Medical Examiner's Office decided that the police restraint brought on asphyxiation; he also had the powerful hallucinogen phencyclidine, or PCP, in his system.

A grand jury determined that the police were not criminally culpable for the homicide.

The city agreed in 2022 to pay Prude's family $12 million to settle their lawsuit against police and city officials.

headline: Skinner secures regional NY Supreme Court justice after decision that recount not needed
fullText:
A month after the general election, the race for a regional state Supreme Court justice has finally been decided.

Local lawyer Erin Skinner, a Democrat, finished second in the race, according to the Board of Elections, meaning she will assume a judgeship next year. Skinner is a confidential law clerk in the appellate division of state Supreme Court

Family Court Judge Stacey Romeo finished first in the four-candidate race for two open judgeships. Her margin was big enough in the eight-county district to secure her victory last month.

Was state Supreme Court race close to a recount?

Skinner and Republican Ed White, a principal law clerk in state Supreme Court, were separated by thousands of votes, with Skinner ahead by nearly 6,000 votes at last count. That left a question of whether the margin would be tight enough to require a recount under state law.

However, the state Board of Elections determined this week that a recount is not mandated, meaning Skinner finished second.

“I am so honored to have been entrusted with this responsibility by the voters, and I am forever grateful to my team for helping me  to achieve this win," Skinner said Thursday. " I look forward to getting to work for the people of the Seventh Judicial District."

headline: No new bar or restaurant for Sandbar Park in Webster next year
fullText:
A new restaurant and bar to take the place of the dearly departed Bayside Pub is not coming to Webster’s Sandbar Park. At least not in 2025.

The issue is cost.

The business at 279 Lake Road on the northern shoreline of Irondequoit Bay would have been a public-private partnership between the town of Webster and Fantauzzo Family Brands, owner of the Salvatore’s Old Fashioned Pizzeria chain.

Back in July, the company announced that the forthcoming establishment would be a new concept and not a pizzeria.

On Tuesday, its founder, Salvatore “Soccer Sam" Fantauzzo, told the Democrat and Chronicle, “I wanted to keep it very similar to how it used to be. I mean, you can’t go from the Bayside to Mario’s Via Abruzzi. So, it was gonna be the Bayside, just tweaked a little bit.”

The town would have been responsible for providing general contracting, electrical, plumbing and HVAC, and would have retained ownership of the building. The town's costs would have been covered by a special bond and recouped by charging Fantauzzo Family Brands monthly rent, including interest on the bond, over 15 years. The company also would have shouldered the cost of building out the interior of the 2,400-square-foot structure.

Fantauzzo expected contractors’ bids to total around $700,000 to $1 million, max.

“So, we thought 15 years to pay back a bond — $6,000 to $7,000 a month makes sense for a restaurant that size in a city like Rochester,” he said.

In late 2022, at a time when former Bayside owners Robert Buono and Tom Ban were interested in the project, a preliminary estimate for the work was put at $715,000.

However, last month, it was revealed that contractors' low bids came in to the town totaling $2.6 million.

Fantauzzo understands that building near the water requires particular things, like extra supports in the foundation.

But, “Do you know what kind of house you could have on the bay for $2.6 million? You’d get a mansion,” he said. “This is basically a square box with two bathrooms, one wall separating the kitchen from dining and a small bar.”

Fantauzzo said Webster Supervisor Tom Flaherty and Chris Bilow, the town’s commissioner of Parks and Recreation, “worked really hard to make this happen. We were all on the same page. We wanted this to be like it used to be.”

But he continues to be puzzled over the projected costs.

Right now, he’s building a Salvatore’s pizzeria in Bushnell’s Basin. “It’s a work of art,” he said. “It’s probably the most gorgeous Salvatore’s we’ll have in our chain.”

The cost is around $600,000.

“People think I’m just a pizza guy, but I’ve built my places from the floor up. I know what things cost. I know what they cost before COVID and after COVID,” he said.

Asked what accounts for the Sandbar Park restaurant's estimated $2.6 million price tag, Bilow wrote in an email: “It only takes one bidder to submit a low bid that would have been more in line with the experience of the restaurateur, (but) that did not happen during this process. The municipal bidding process we are required to follow unfortunately did not produce costs that are the same as a private build that Sam was hoping for.”

Said Fantauzzo, “It’s not like I lost a lot of money on this,” putting his investment to date at around $50,000. “But I was excited about it, and plus it would make people in Rochester happy that we’re bringing back this landmark.” (The town’s investment now stands at $132,000.)

He also said he’s not walking away. “I hope this project isn’t dead in the water.” The last time he talked with Webster officials, “They said they’re going to try other options and get back to me.”

In his email, Bilow wrote: “At this time we do not plan to pursue a brick and mortar facility at the site due to the costs associated.”

It is most likely that based on feedback from the Town Board, for 2025, the town will look into other options for serving food at the site, including with food-truck events.

Bilow said town officials plan to talk with Fantauzzo “as we discuss other options for 2025 and beyond.”

Whatever happens, Fantauzzo — whose vision included offering rides on the bay in flamingo-shaped watercraft and KC and the Sunshine Band playing opening weekend — hopes the town doesn’t put up a park pavilion at the site.

“There are empty pavilions all over Webster,” he said.

The Bayside, a longtime, seasonal destination, closed in January 2022 and subsequently was torn down, the result of an $11.1 million town-led project to revamp Sandbar Park and mitigate flooding.

Owners Buono and Ban had been renting their humble tavern space from the town for $3,500 a month. Initially, they expressed interest in reopening in the town-built structure. They later bowed out, citing unrealistic costs and too many unknowns.

headline: This upstate NY city named best in the U.S. for aging in place. Here’s why
fullText:
An upstate New York city has been named the best city in the country for aging in place, according to a report released by This Old House last month.

Rochester took the top spot for aging in place, which is when a person decides to stay in their home instead of moving into a care facility as they age. This Old House looked at 142 of the largest U.S. cities across 12 metrics to find the best cities for aging in place.

Overall, the report, which included a survey of 1,000 Americans aged 65 or older, found that 89% of seniors plan to age in place, 45% would refuse to move into a nursing home and 47% say their homes aren't accessible for aging, 36% of which can't afford to make the necessary upgrades.

Here's what to know.

Why Rochester is the best city for aging in place

Monthly homeowner costs in Rochester average $1,205, according to This Old House, and the Flower City's average life expectancy is 78.6.

Rochester also received a home health aide care quality score of 3-out-of-5 by This Old House, has an average of 86.2 senior relevant care providers per 1,000 seniors and a regional price parity of 95.2.

See the list: These five New York cities ranked among the best places to live in the U.S.

This Old House's top 10 cities for aging in place

Buffalo also made the list with average monthly homeowner costs of $1,326 and an average life expectancy of 77.5. Here's the top 10 U.S. cities for aging in place, according to This Old House.

  1. Rochester, New York
  2. Grand Rapids, Michigan
  3. Cleveland, Ohio
  4. Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
  5. Winston-Salem, North Carolina
  6. Fort Wayne, Indiana
  7. Birmingham, Alabama
  8. Augusta, Georgia
  9. Buffalo, New York
  10. Lexington, Kentucky

Rental costs: This upstate NY city has the most affordable rent in the U.S.

How This Old House measured a city's aging in place quality

This Old House looked at 142 of the largest U.S. cities across these 12 metrics to find the best cities for aging in place:

  • Housing costs: Based on the city's median monthly housing costs for homeowners with a mortgage and includes mortgage payments, home insurance and property tax
  • Regional price parity: Measures the cost of goods and services in the metro area
  • Senior-relevant care providers per capita: Measures the availability of healthcare services in the city
  • Home health aide care quality: The average care quality score of home health agencies located in the city
  • Life expectancy at county level
  • Crime rates: The sum of violent and property crimes in the city per 1,000 residents
  • Climate risk: The risk of severe natural disasters
  • Air quality
  • Older adults with internet access: Measures the percentage of the city's population 65 and older with access to a computer and internet at home
  • Medicare enrollment: The percentage of the city's population 65 and older enrolled in Medicare
  • Dependency ratio: The availability of a working-age population to provide for the needs of non-workers
  • Tax friendliness: Measures if the state taxes income, social security, pensions, 401(k)s and IRAs

Data used in the report came from sources including the U.S. Census Bureau's 2023 American Community Survey, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and the University of Wisconsin's Population Health Institute.

headline: Nonprofit group needs donations for gift bags for nursing home residents
fullText:
Common Ground Health is seeking donations of items to fill gift bags that will be distributed to Rochester-area nursing home residents this holiday season in hopes of combating social isolation and loneliness.

For two years, volunteers for Common Ground’s Senior Adult Community Engagement Project, or SACE, have assembled and delivered “Not Forgotten” bags to nursing home residents in the community’s most challenged areas.

The bags include new items that seniors living on Medicaid allowances need and often do not have the money to buy.

“Throughout our community, people in nursing homes are experiencing isolation and loneliness,” said Phyllis Jackson, R.N., community wellness project manager at Common Ground, a nonprofit health research and planning organization founded in 1974. “Many do not have family members or friends who visit. Many may lack socialization, joy, love or hope. These donations brighten older adults’ days, which may help improve their health.”

Common Ground also partners with schools and community groups to create holiday cards and pictures. The cards are given to residents on every major holiday throughout the year to let them know that others are thinking about them.

The group is accepting the following new items through Dec. 16:

  • Packages of crew or knee-high cotton socks
  • Packages of footie socks                                
  • Packages of white or gray V-neck T-shirts in sizes medium or large
  • Zippered hoodie sweatshirts or fleece jackets in sizes medium or large
  • Fragrance-free regular-size deodorant
  • Fragrance-free regular-size lotion

  • Packs of soft toothbrushes with covers

headline: How to watch 'Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer' on TV, streaming and more
fullText:
You know Dasher and Dancer and Prancer and Vixen... And chances are, you're familiar with a certain crimson-snouted caribou who does Santa Claus an absolute solid one foggy Christmas night. “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer,” the stop-motion animated holiday classic, returns this week to network television, but you won't find it on CBS.

For its 60th anniversary, a special 75-minute edition of Rudolph will air Friday on NBC, the network announced. After running on CBS for 50 years, the holiday special is getting a homecoming on NBC, where Rudolph first premiered to viewers Dec. 6, 1964.

If you miss Friday's special showing, don't worry. An encore presentation is scheduled later in December. Here's how to watch the "most famous reindeer of all" before Christmas.

When is 'Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer' on?

Rudolph will air Friday, Dec. 6, 2024, on NBC. Check your local station guide for the exact channel.

Louisville, Kentucky viewers can find Rudolph on NBC-affiliate station WAVE. Did you miss Friday's showing? A repeat showing of Rudolph will air Thursday, Dec. 12, according to WAVE's programming schedule.

Rudolph's history: Who created Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer? About the holiday classic 1964 film

What time is Rudolph on?

For Kentuckians, "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" airs 8-9:15 p.m. EST, Friday, Dec. 6, and Thursday, Dec. 12.

Story continues after photo gallery.

Rudolph on Freeform's '25 Days of Christmas' 2024

You can watch Rudolph's adventures also on Freeform's "25 Days of Christmas." Here's a schedule of when "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" airs on Freeform.com in 2024:

  • Dec. 7 at  9:10 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 8 at 6:10 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 16 at 9:20 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 17 at 7:55 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 21 at 6:15 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 22 at 3 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 24 at 8 p.m. ET/PT
  • Dec. 25 at 11 a.m. ET/PT

Does Netflix have Rudolph? Does Hulu?

No, the stop-motion version of Rudolph isn't streaming on Netflix or Hulu, but it is available on other platforms.

Where can you stream 'Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer'?

"Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" is available to stream on Apple TV+, Google Play and Sling TV. As of Friday, for $7.99, you can buy "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" on Amazon Prime Video.

Who created Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer?

“Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” started out as a children's story first released by Montgomery Ward in 1939. The department store asked one of its copywriters, 34-year-old Robert L. May, to create a Christmas story the store could give away to shoppers as a promotional gimmick, according to the Smithsonian.

After buying and giving away coloring books for Christmas every year, Montgomery Ward wanted its own book as a cost-saving measure. Rudolph proved popular, writes Smithsonian. In its first year of publication, 2.4 million copies of Rudolph’s story were distributed to children.

Rudolph would later go on to become a cartoon movie and then famously a 1957 Christmas song performed by Gene Autry.

What is Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer about?

Rudolph is ostracized by other reindeer because he was born with a shiny, glowing red nose. But, on a foggy Christmas night, Santa asks Rudolph to guide his sleigh through a terrible storm, an act that saves the holiday and turns Rudolph into a hero.

Rudolph's stop-motion animated film takes the the original 88-word poem and expands it into a 55-minute movie. In it, Rudolph runs away from home and meets a colorful cast of characters. They include: Hermey, an elf that wants to become a dentist, Yukon Cornelius the prospector, a snow monster and an island of "misfit toys," which Rudolph helps rescue before returning home to save Christmas.

Who narrates 'Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer'?

American singer and actor Burl Ives gives a memorable performance as "Sam the Snowman," serving as the film's narrator and singing the theme song to "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer."

The voice cast also includes:

  • Peg Dixon as Mrs. Donner, Mrs. Claus and others.
  • Billie Mae Richards as Rudolph.
  • Paul Soles as Hermey.
  • Larry D. Mann as Yukon Cornelius and Abominable Snow Monster.
  • Stan Francis as Santa Claus and King Moonracer.
  • Janis Orenstein as Clarice.
  • Alfie Scopp as Charlie-In-The-Box, Fireball and other reindeer.
  • Paul Kligman as Donner, Clarice's father, and Comet the coach.
  • Carl Banas as Head Elf, Spotted Elephant and other toys.
  • Corinne Conley as Doll and others.

headline: Stuck in an airport this holiday season? 7 things to do at some of America's biggest terminals
fullText:
With holiday travel predicted to soar over pre-pandemic numbers this season, it's smart to hope for the best but prepare for the worst.

According to AAA, air travel set a new record during Thanksgiving, with 5.84 million people flying domestically. That number is an increase of 2% compared to last year and a nearly 11% increase over 2019. The same type of increase is expected for travel between the Christmas and New Year holidays.

With this in mind, we've rounded up some interesting ways to spend your extra time in airports across the country, including at Louisville's Muhammad Ali International Airport.

Air travelers in Louisville for instance, can spend time in the airport's elevated bourbon tasting room. For those traveling through Oregon, therapy llamas roam the concourse at the Portland International Airport. Yoga studios are another calming amenity popular in airports across the country such as Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, San Francisco International Airport, Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, and more.

Mesmerizing light and music tunnels, like the 700-foot corridor at Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport, offer a colorful walking journey between concourses, while gourmet restaurants and bars also help travelers pass the time in airports across the country.

To help you fill your time while you wait for take-off, here are seven airports, in alphabetical order, with amenities you might not expect.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport

Chicago, Illinois, flychicago.com

There is plenty of buzz at Hudson Newsstands located throughout Chicago's O'Hare Airport. In 2011, O’Hare became the first airport in the US to offer some of its extra space up to 200 bee hives which are managed by BeeLove. The business's hive-to-jar products, which include jars of local honey and honey-based skincare products, are made from bees living on the premises. BeeLove trains and employs people returning from incarceration.

Bees aren't the only unique aspect of this Chicagoland airport. O'Hare is home to numerous art installations, children's play spaces, a 75-foot-long fiberglass replica of a Brachiosaurus skeleton on display in Terminal 1, a yoga studio, and a full-service spa where you can spend your layover having your finger and toe nails painted or enjoy a relaxing massage.

Denver International Airport

Denver, Colorado, flydenver.com

Looking for something out of this world? Concourse C at Denver International Airport is home to the Meow Wolf gift shop. Meow Wolf, an arts production company that creates immersive, multimedia experiences that transport audiences of all ages into fantastic realms, has locations in Los Angeles, Santa Fe, Las Vegas, Denver, and Grapevine and Houston, Texas.

Fans of Meow Wolf can spend time in this exclusive airport shopping playground where you can snag a piece of the Meow Wolf multiverse. Featuring fantastical artifacts and remnants of the otherworldly portals, travelers can score Cosmic Plushies, Creature Feature Water Bottles, and even Cozy Noodle blankets, plus exclusive Meow Wolf apparel including t-shirts and hoodies.

For those with more time to kill in Denver, enjoy some fresh air at one of the airport's three outdoor decks. Complete with firepits and modern seating, these outdoor decks are open year-round, subject to weather.

Harry Reid International Airport

Las Vegas, Nevada, harryreidairport.com

Jackpot! If you are jonesing to try your luck one last time before leaving Las Vegas, get to the airport early.

This November, one lucky airline passenger won a $1.57 million jackpot at a "Wheel of Fortune" slot machine while waiting for his flight at the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. The machine, located at T1 baggage claim, hit Triple Red Hot Sevens on a gold spin.

Are you feeling lucky? There are dozens of slot machines where travelers can press their luck when departing or arriving on a flight into the famed gaming town.

Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport

St. Paul/Minneapolis, Minnesota, mspairport.com

Located in Terminal 1 of the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport, you'll find a Prince-themed store, named just “Prince” after the renowned American singer and multi-instrumentalist. Shop here for Prince-themed apparel, CDs, vinyl, and more. Prince, who died in 2016, was a Minneapolis local and is known as one of the greatest musicians in the world.

For travelers with a longer layover, the airport has teamed up with the American Heart Association’s nationally recognized Start! Walking program to offer a way to stay fit while traveling. Walk the official 1.4-mile walking path at Terminal 1, or kick it up a notch and add a few more concourses.

Want to learn more about the people and culture of Minnesota and the region while traveling through MSP Airport? The See18 film screening room is the perfect place for both.

Located between Gates C18 and C19 at MSP Airport's Terminal 1, the screening room features 21 new films – most just a few minutes long – around the theme of "Someone That Looks Like Me: Exploring Identity and Place Through Minnesota Arts and Culture."

Muhammad Ali International Airport

Louisville, Kentucky, flylouisville.com

Horse racing, baseball, and bourbon take center stage at the Muhammad Ali International Airport in Louisville.

Located before you pass through TSA security, the Churchill Downs Store offers Louisville and Kentucky-centric items including plenty of Louisville Slugger merchandise, which is perfect for a last-minute gift purchase. Or if you find yourself post-security with time on your hands, there are specialty retail shops with more unique Kentucky items including the Distillery District Marketplace and Hip & Humble, which sells a variety of unique gifts, travel essentials, and female-forward offerings.

For a final sip of bourbon before you leave Kentucky, stop by the one-of-a-kind bourbon experience at the Bourbon Academy Tasting Room. This elevated bar and dining experience is located post-security featuring a great menu, over 80 of Kentucky's best bourbons, and a unique view of the tarmac.

Pittsburgh International Airport

Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, flypittsburgh.com

Fraley’s Robot Repair in the Pittsburg International Airport is not what it looks like. Nothing is for sale here and no robots are repaired at this shop. This is the work of installation artist Toby Fraley, who rearranges the charming scene inside his storefront regularly. Located in  Concourse A, this novelty public art installation called PIT Robot Repair is a faux storefront that emulates an antiquated repair shop – for robots.

Each of the airports we've mentioned offers nursing and changing areas for families who are traveling. The Pittsburgh International Airport goes a step further with a special space for air travelers with autism and other neurodevelopmental challenges. The Sensory Room, Presley’s Place, offers a calming space with stuffed chairs, gentle lighting, and an opportunity to participate in a realistic airplane experience.

Portland International Airport

Portland, Oregon, flypdx.com

Our final stop on this airport tour is ideal for movie buffs on flights that take you through the Pacific Northwest. Oregon's Portland International Airport is home to a 22-seat microcinema, which shows 10-minute shorts made by regional filmmakers and is located after security in the airport’s C Concourse.

And don't forget to be on the lookout for the airport's animal therapy program. Besides adorable canines, llamas and alpacas also help to calm anxious passengers. Additionally, this airport features live trees bathed in natural light and lofty ceilings built with locally sourced Douglas Fir.

Happy travels!

Reach features reporter Kirby Adams at kadams@courier-journal.com.

headline: How a basketball star overcame her difficult childhood with help from Jacqueline Coleman
fullText:
An earlier version of the story incorrectly stated which county Coleman-O'Bryan's mom lived in. The correct county is Garrard.

When Emma Coleman-O'Bryan was 15 years old, she walked into the office of Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman — then the basketball coach at East Jessamine High School — and demanded the team's schedule.

That decision would help reshape the rest of her life, leading her on a path toward becoming the first in her biological family to graduate high school and playing basketball professionally overseas.

Now a nurse at a trauma unit in Destin, Florida, Coleman-O'Bryan said she attributes part of her success to the teachers who never gave up on her — starting with the coach who eventually adopted her.

When she was in her freshman year — going by the name Emma Young, her GPA hovered just above failing at 1.2. Her youth had been full of constant change, as she moved around from relative to relative, trying to avoid drugs in her childhood home.

She was on the verge of another change shortly after joining Coleman's team, when an aunt she was living with said she couldn't take care of the teen anymore, and she'd have to move back with her mom in Garrard County.

After Coleman-O'Bryan explained her situation and how her mom was not in a position to take care of her, Coleman and her husband, Chris O'Bryan, decided to take her in.

"As soon as her and Chris came, it was maybe a five or 10 minute encounter, and I had my little duffel bag, and I was in the car," Coleman-O'Bryan said.

She lived with her coach through the remainder of high school, breaking records as a basketball player and pulling her GPA up to a 3.6.

Coleman, speaking at an event in Louisville last month, praised Coleman-O'Bryan's teachers for helping her grow.

"Her teachers showed up early, they worked with her before school, and they stayed late and worked with her after school. ... We were very fortunate that she had such amazing teachers that cared for her and showed up for her the way that they did," Coleman said.

Coleman and her husband formally adopted Coleman-O'Bryan in 2020, and the two women continue to have a strong bond.

"She understood me without any words, (and) she knows exactly what I'm thinking with looking at me," Coleman-O'Bryan said. "She went from someone that was just a coach and kind of a mentor to being one of the most important people in my life."

After high school, Coleman-O'Bryan played basketball at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, then went on to play with the PBC Flamurtari Vlore in the Albanian A-1 Basketball League for seven months.

"I'm really proud of, my basketball career in general, just because it gave me a lot of opportunity, and I got to grow from it," she said.

Coleman-O'Bryan knew she wanted to "make an impact bigger than herself," however, and decided to finish nursing school in Destin.

"I've always wanted to be a nurse," Coleman-O'Bryan said. "I want to help people ... and nursing was a good way to do that. I think nursing was a great path for me, because I'm a 'people person.'"

Coleman O’Bryan said if she could talk to her 15-year-old self now, she would tell herself “good for you” for where she got to today.

“You stepped out of your comfort zone, and you did it. Look at you now,” Coleman-O’Bryan said.

headline: A task force studying JCPS won't release legislative recommendations ahead of next session
fullText:
Members of the task force tapped with studying whether Kentucky's largest school system is too big have decided to continue meeting through 2025, rather than provide a list of recommendations to lawmakers ahead of the next legislative session.

The Efficient and Effective School District Governance Task Force, which was established through a house resolution during the 2024 session, is comprised of 13 members who were supposed to deliver recommendations on how to improve Jefferson County Public Schools — potentially including how to split it — by this month.

Instead, co-chairs of the task force informed Senate President Robert Stivers and others on Monday that they hope to continue meeting next year before making any recommendations.

"More detailed information is needed to develop a set of recommendations to improve district efficiency and effectiveness," they wrote. "Furthermore, due to the pending selection of a new district superintendent and potential changes at the federal level, additional time would ensure the recommendations would have an impact."

In response, JCPS spokeswoman Carolyn Callahan said the district is happy with what members have learned thus far.

"The task force has seen and heard about the tremendous work and learning that’s happening every day in every JCPS school," she said. "We will continue to share information with task force members and look forward to furthering their understanding of our students, staff and District."

In addition to establishing the task force, lawmakers also provided funding to state Auditor Allison Ball's office last session in order to conduct an extensive audit into JCPS.

During the task force's last meeting in November, members heard from Ball, who said it was too early in that process to answer many of the questions they had. Ball's office was allotted $1.5 million over the course of two years to conduct the audit, which will focus on far more than the district's finances.

The findings of that audit are expected in July 2026.

Krista Johnson covers education and children. Have story ideas or questions? Contact her at kjohnson3@gannett.com.

headline: Here are 6 charming Christmas towns to visit in Kentucky this year
fullText:
Thinking about doing something special this holiday season? Kentucky is home to numerous picturesque small towns, with festive traditions and cozy celebrations, that create the perfect backdrop for a holiday getaway.

From Maysville's twinkling Downtown Twilight Christmas Parade to Covington's German-inspired Mainstrasse Christkindlmarkt, each destination offers a unique way to embrace the season.

Whether shopping for one-of-a-kind gifts in Georgetown, exploring Berea's artsy winter wonderland, or sipping a warm bourbon cocktail in Bardstown, the Bluegrass State promises a holiday experience filled with cheer, tradition, and unforgettable memories.

Here are six charming towns to visit during the holiday season in Kentucky:

Bardstown, Kentucky

visitbardtsown.com

Known as the "Bourbon Capital of the World," Bardstown transforms into a winter wonderland that blends Southern hospitality with timeless holiday traditions. A highlight of the season is the "Merry & Bright" event at My Old Kentucky Home. This beloved annual celebration invites visitors to experience the magic of Christmas in one of Kentucky’s most famous historic landmarks. Now through Jan. 6, 2025, guided tours led by costumed interpreters bring the mansion's rich history to life, sharing stories of Christmases past, from colonial times through the Roaring Twenties.

In addition to the "Merry & Bright" event, Bardstown’s holiday season includes festive parades, unique shopping opportunities at local boutiques, and special holiday-themed tours that showcase the town's historic landmarks.

Berea, Kentucky

visitberea.com

Whether exploring Berea's renowned arts scene or simply soaking in the cozy ambiance, a Christmas visit to Berea promises to be filled with festive cheer and timeless memories. Known for its rich Appalachian heritage and vibrant arts community, Berea transforms into a winter wonderland during the holiday season, with festive lights adorning historic buildings and handmade ornaments decorating every corner.

Take a stroll through the Old Town Artisan Village, where local craftspeople showcase their unique creations, perfect for finding one-of-a-kind gifts. Enjoy the warmth of a traditional Appalachian Christmas with events like holiday markets, caroling, and special performances at the historic Boone Tavern Hotel.

Covington, Kentucky

meetnky.com

Known for its eclectic blend of German-inspired shops, cuisine, and entertainment, Mainstrasse Village in Covington becomes a festive haven during the holidays filled with twinkling lights and Christmas cheer.

Each December, this charming village undergoes a magical transformation into the enchanting Mainstrasse Christkindlmarkt, a German-inspired holiday market that captures the spirit of the season.

Wander through the market stalls, where skilled artisans showcase handcrafted gifts, ornaments, and decorations that make for perfect holiday presents. Savor a delectable array of traditional German treats, from bratwurst and pretzels to sweet pastries and mulled wine, all while enjoying the sounds of live, mesmerizing music that fills the air.

Georgetown, Kentucky

georgetownky.com

Georgetown pulls out all the stops to celebrate the holidays. In one visit to this picturesque and walkable Victorianesque downtown, visitors are whisked away into a quaint Christmas town.

Shoppers can check off every item on their holiday lists at the one-of-a-kind locally-owned shops and boutiques lining Main Street: Georgetown Antique Mall, Heirlooms & Gretchen’s stained-glass studio, Birdsong Quilting, Hockensmith Fine Art Editions Gallery and Press, featuring the works of world-famous equine photographer John Stephen Hockensmith, and more.

Grand Rivers, Kentucky

grandrivers.org

Nestled between Kentucky Lake and Lake Barkley, the quaint town of Grand Rivers becomes a magical holiday destination each winter.

At the heart of the celebrations is Patti’s Festival of Lights, a beloved annual event that illuminates the town with over 1.5 million sparkling lights. Visitors can visit the beautifully decorated 1880s settlement, where each corner is adorned with twinkling displays, festive wreaths, and holiday scenes that create a warm and welcoming atmosphere.

The Festival of Lights is a must-see attraction, offering a picturesque setting for families and friends to gather, enjoy holiday treats, and create cherished memories.

Maysville, Kentucky

visitmaysvilleky.com

Experience a holiday season straight out of a Hallmark movie when you take a trip to Maysville.

Begin your festive celebration at the Christmas Market, where the Downtown Twilight Christmas Parade sets the stage for an enchanting evening. As the parade winds through town with a dazzling array of floats, the market comes alive with live music, handmade arts and crafts, baked goods, and a variety of food vendors.

Extend the magic with a visit to the Old Washington Historic District, where the charm of a 1700s village provides the perfect backdrop for nostalgic holiday cheer.

Happy holidays!

headline: Should you take a magnesium supplement? Here are 3 things to know
fullText:
I recently wrote a column about supplements, and in response I received an email inquiring about the benefits of magnesium. As I explained in that previous column, taking supplements is a controversial issue, and it inspires several questions. For example, is it better to get what you need from your daily diet? If so, how difficult is this, and is it likely that your diet can cover your needs? On the other hand, if you don’t get enough and are deficient, how important is this to your health?

Conversely, can you take too much and it becomes harmful?

My view on supplements is that first and foremost, try to cover your needs with a healthy diet. Next, if a supplement is not too expensive and a case can be made that it “should” enhance health in some way, it can serve as insurance that you are covering all bases, just in case. But don’t overdo it.

Let’s consider the case in favor of supplementing magnesium, a mineral that is believed to contribute to health by promoting a host of important bodily functions. If so, it logically follows that deficiencies can cause problems, and supplementing may help prevent certain health conditions. In general, magnesium supports immune function and helps keep the level of inflammation in the body in check. Both are very important, especially when it comes to inflammation because it promotes such serious illnesses as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes.

The impact, of course, is dependent on the degree of effect arising from the supplement which is difficult to determine and contributes to controversy.

More: Should you take dietary supplements? Maybe, but it's complicated. Here's what to know

What are the benefits of taking magnesium?

Magnesium is believed to be beneficial in at least five ways.

First, is the effect to help control blood pressure by serving as a counterbalance to calcium in the bloodstream. Calcium triggers vasoconstriction, narrowing the artery, raising pressure. In contrast, when magnesium replaces calcium by binding to the smooth muscle in vessel walls, it prevents narrowing. In addition, damaged arterial walls become stiffer, offering greater resistance to blood flow which raises pressure. Magnesium binds (captures) harmful substances in the blood before they can cause damage.

Second is the effect to keep bones strong by promoting the use of calcium to harden bones. Magnesium also helps the body make key enzymes that stimulate production of osteoblasts (new bone cells). These effects contribute to the prevention of osteoporosis.

Third, magnesium helps keep heart rhythm steady by regulating the electrical stimulus that passes through the heart muscle. It does this by again counterbalancing effects of calcium, helping the heart relax between beats. When magnesium concentration is too low the heart beats faster, plus it increases the risk of an irregular heartbeat.

Fourth, magnesium helps regulate blood glucose by making cells more sensitive to the effects of insulin. Increasing insulin sensitivity can help reduce the risk of prediabetes and Type 2 diabetes caused by insulin resistance. The key is moving glucose out of the bloodstream, preventing accumulation in the blood and damage that occurs when the concentration of glucose gets too high.

Fifth, magnesium stimulates protein synthesis, helping to keep muscle mass intact and strong. It does this by stimulating mTOR, a protein that promotes cell growth and proliferation, plus it controls cell metabolism.

What is a magnesium deficiency?

When you don't get enough magnesium over time, whether from your diet and/or supplements, you can end up with a deficiency. You may not feel it right away because your body tries to hold on to what little magnesium it has, which attests to the importance of magnesium.

 Signs of magnesium deficiency may include loss of appetite, being tired and feeling weak. If your magnesium status is “extremely low,” more pronounced symptoms may appear, including numbness and tingling, muscle cramps, disruption of heart rhythm, etc.

Who is more likely to have a magnesium deficiency? Older folks, plus those suffering from some illnesses, including kidney disease and gastrointestinal problems such as Crohn’s or celiac disease because they can interfere with how your body handles magnesium. There also may be interference from some medications. If any of this applies to you, and especially if you are on meds for heart disease, cancer, or other serious health problems, be sure to check with your doctor before supplementing.

What about too much magnesium? It can cause nausea, diarrhea, muscle weakness, low blood pressure and fatigue. And if you take very high doses, it can cause more serious problems. As stated above, don’t overdo it.

How much magnesium do I need?

Experts estimate that at least half of adults don’t get enough magnesium in their daily diet, which, of course, supports taking a supplement. Overall, diet plus a supplement, how much do you need? Dose varies with age, but for most adult females, the minimal recommended daily allowance for magnesium is approximately 310 mg, and for males 400 mg.  

Since taking too little or too much magnesium can cause problems, the best policy is moderation. I try to cover my daily magnesium needs mostly with my diet, and I supplement with a modest dose as insurance that I’m getting enough.

Regarding diet, emphasize leafy green vegetables, beans, and raw nuts. In my case, I make a daily blend that I have written about many times. My main ingredient is leafy greens, with a large portion of raw spinach, kale, collard greens, etc. My wife buys large bags of a mixture of leafy greens at Costco, and I go through them pretty quickly. I also add a handful or two of raw almonds or walnuts to the mix. Other ingredients include chocolate flavored plant protein powder, an apple and an orange, a mix of frozen fruits, finishing off by filling the blender with either soy milk or water.

Reach Bryant Stamford, a professor of kinesiology and integrative physiology at Hanover College, at stamford@hanover.edu.

headline: Gerth: Kentucky caves to cancel culture. Churches reject Krampus but keep Santa. | Opinion
fullText:
Forget what the conservatives and Fox News tell you.

Walk through any store beginning around Halloween, check out the lights that have gone up in your neighborhood, look at my daughter’s computer-printed Christmas list — complete with sizes and links to make ordering easier — that’s about as thick as a 1975 Sear’s catalog.

There is no war on Christmas. It’s alive and well.

There, is however, a war on Krampus.

Just ask the people in Pikeville.

If you’ve never heard of Krampus, you’re not alone.

What is Krampus?

Krampus is a mythical goat-man, rooted in our pagan past, who has been part for the German Christmas tradition for centuries. Only in the past couple of decades has he made his way to America.

According to German tradition, Krampus is kind of like Santa’s alter-ego.

On the feast of St. Nicholas, which is Dec. 6, he travels with the jolly old elf. But while St. Nick fills good children’s shoes and stockings with gifts, Krampus whips the bad ones with switches, and the worst ones he drags off to hell.

For some in America, Krampus and Santa have actually morphed into one being. My grandmother, two generations removed from Frankfurt, Germany, for instance warned of Santa bringing you switches if you were bad, and was known to scare her misbehaving kids by peering into windows while wearing a Santal Claus mask.

(Santa was also known to have lived in the cellar of her home on Lampton Street, and would bang on pipes, air ducts and floor boards when kids acted up.)

People all over Germany would be waking up to find their children beaten or dragged off to hell — if only Krampus were a real thing.

Sure, I know. The Germans can be a dark people.

Don’t believe me? Go back and read Hansel and Gretel, the old German fairy tale that involves abandoning children, starvation, cannibalism and murder.

Krampus ain’t got nuthin’ on the brothers Grimm.

Krampus celebrations in Kentucky

Anyway, Krampus celebrations began to spring up in the United States around 2004 about the same time an artist published a book of vintage Krampus greeting cards, according to the History Channel’s website.

There’s a Krampus Night celebration on Saturday at the Art Sanctuary on Shelby Street in Louisville and on Friday, there’s a Krampus Cruise on the Mary M. Miller riverboat.

Lexington has Krampus celebrations, too.

I’ve never attended a Krampus event, but from what I can tell, they appear to be campy sorts of things. For instance, the one at the Art Sanctuary has a burlesque show, music and a costume contest.

As far as I can tell, no children are harmed in these events.

This year, the good folks in Pikeville wanted to get in on the fun.

The city government there planned a winter festival event for the city park on Dec. 10 that was to include photos with “Krampus and Lady Krampus,” free “Fright Bites,” which organizers said is a “horrible Christmas treat,” ice skating and heavy metal Christmas music, according to Mountain Top Media.

Cancel culture churches and Krampus controversy

And then the complaints started from the cancel culture folks in Pikeville — the churches.

I tried to reach a pastor that a social media friend tells me was the most outspoken against Krampus. He didn’t get back with me. His Facebook page, where my friend said he has been most active, has been wiped clean.

Gerth: How I miss the days when Rand Paul was the crazy one in Washington | Opinion

This isn’t the only place where Krampus has courted controversy. The Catholic archbishop of San Antonio, Texas, has objected to a parade there this week featuring Krampus as “nightmare-inducing.”  The parade will go on.

I suppose the opposition is the same as the opposition that we sometimes see from some churches surrounding Halloween and occasionally affects other areas of our lives. Years ago, I can recall a group in Oldham County that tried to get the book “The Witches,” by the great children’s author Roald Dahl, banned from schools there.

The argument goes something like this.

“Oooh. Witches. Monsters. It’s satanic.”

Ultra-conservative churches keep Satan alive

Actually, there’s no group more responsible for keeping Satan alive than the ultra-conservative churches. They feed on having an evil being (dang near as powerful as God) for which they can blame all things they don’t like — from gay marriage to gambling. But I digress.

Anyway, good folks at Pikeville gave in and just before Thanksgiving, announced they were canceling the event.

"After careful consideration, we have decided not to move forward with the planned Krampus event,” the city said in a press release, the Appalachian News-Express reported.

“While we recognize that the origins and history of this mythical character vary across cultures and traditions, we believe it is in the best interest of our community to forego the event at this time. The City of Pikeville is committed to offering a diverse and engaging array of events throughout the year, celebrating different traditions, cultures, and perspectives. We will continue to explore opportunities to provide enriching and inclusive experiences for everyone,” the city said.

Gerth: Lawmaker who said her white father was a slave tops Leftover Turkeys list | Opinion

The city has a Christmas event planned. Just not with Krampus.

I’ve tried to reach Pikeville Mayor Jimmy Carter, but no one answered the phone at city hall, and Carter didn’t call back in response to an email. But the event is canceled nonetheless.

Obviously, the city is OK with a mythological fat guy who practices magic and breaks into people's houses, but it’s not OK with a mythological goat-man who comes and disciplines their children — albeit in an overly harsh fashion.

Just wait until city officials there hear what people do on Halloween.

headline: 'A larger living space:' Fifth Wheel RV is ultimate luxury glamping experience on wheels
fullText:
Families with children often look for certain features when shopping for a new home, such as a mudroom, a large backyard, or a flex room. DINK couples — that’s those with a dual income and no kids — can do with a little less space. In fact, they might be looking for something a bit more mobile, like the Jayco 2025 North Point Fifth Wheel.

Larry Cunningham, president and general manager of Cunningham Campers in Clarksville, Indiana, said most potential Jayco 2025 North Point Fifth Wheel owners are people who will live in it for a few months out of the year, but there are those who might make it their full-time residence. After all, it boasts all the amenities of a typical house. It just so happens to be on wheels.

Large living space

A wide-body camper is one that features a wider frame than most, allowing for additional living, storage, and towing space. According to Cunningham, these are typically 96 inches wide. The new Jayco 2025 North Point Fifth Wheel, however, boasts a 102-inch width.

“It’s a larger living space,” he said, “and that allows (for) wider slide-outs, bigger sized furniture, bigger beds.”

Cunningham added that campers with those highlights are usually 45 or 48 feet in length. But because of the 2025 North Point’s width, Jayco was able to fit those features into a 43-foot long space.

Naturally, moving this fifth wheel is no easy feat; it requires a heavy-duty, three-quarter to one ton truck to get it on the road. But as Cunningham pointed out, a comparable amount of space in a motorhome could cost up to $300,000, whereas the 2025 North Point starting price is significantly less than that — and Cunningham Campers will be offering it at a $43,000 discount during next month’s ​​Discover Boating Louisville Boat, RV, & Sportshow.

Bath and a half

“This is what we call a bath and a half unit,” Cunningham explained. “It’s got — like a house — a (primary) bathroom there in the bedroom, then a half bath out there in the kitchen.”

The primary bath is spacious and boasts an adjustable, handheld spray head as well as a solid seamless countertop. Its adjoining bedroom features a front wardrobe design with drawers and a hamper — a new feature to the Jayco North Point — as well as a king-sized bed. Additional sleeping areas are available in the living room, on the trifold sofa beds.

“So, you’ve got two more beds up there if you wanted them,” Cunningham said. “You can sleep a lot of people if you really wanted to, but it’s more of an entertaining environment.”

The space also features a set of recliners that face a TV on a televator, which sits just above an electric fireplace.

All the comforts of home

Speaking of entertaining, the fifth wheel is also equipped with everything one might need to whip up a full meal. The residential appliances are all GE, including the refrigerator, convection microwave, and sink.

There’s also an oversized stove and oven, as well as fun features such as a pullout cutting board over the trash can and a built-in spice rack inside a cabinet door. The cabinets themselves all come with soft-close doors with magnets, so owners don’t have to worry about them slamming or accidentally opening while hitting bumps on the road.

Of course, there are options for al fresco cooking and dining, too. Outside, the fifth wheel boasts a grill, a second refrigerator, and ample storage.

“Some people call it glamping — glamour camping,” Cunningham said, “(but it’s more of) a movable residence. … It’s designed to be more comfortable for a longer term because it is functioning as a home.”
